en: The *Wenju* (Words and Phrases) and *Wenju Ji* (Record of Words and Phrases) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Combined Edition, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang;
the *Wenju* spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, recorded by his disciple Guǎngdìng.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming.
The Śramaṇa Mingde of Shuangjing compiled the collated text and recorded the annotations within the sutra text. [Commentary:
In the past, my former teacher resided at Baoyun Monastery and frequently lectured on this scripture; his disciples gathered in great numbers, competing with one another to record [his teachings].
Having heard this, I have privately transcribed it into scrolls; yet, as the brush was entrusted to another's hand, it has become entangled with the profound and far-reaching intent.
Furthermore, regarding the citations from the sūtras and śāstras, many of the words are erroneous and misleading. Each time I encounter such texts, I cannot help but feel regret.
Recently, during the course of my lectures, I recalled the essential meanings he had grasped and composed this record, while also drawing upon Guishan’s *Suyin* (Exploring the Obscurities).
This work from the secular classics of the Middle Kingdom is thus provided as a practical aid;

it is my hope that readers will not regard its subject matter merely as a matter of emotional interest, but will instead contemplate its benefits for the cultivation of insight. Recorded on the third day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era.

[Commentary] To explain the textual passages of this sūtra, the major outline is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the entry into the text. Regarding the explanation of the title, there are two sub-sections.
First, the formal titling of the work.
[Textual Passages] *The Words and Phrases of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
[Commentary] The four characters "Gold" (*jīn*) and so forth are that which is explained; the two characters "Text and Phrases" (*wénjù*) are that which explains.

The title of the sūtra to be explained is fully contained within the *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning); as for the "Text and Phrases" that explain it, "text" refers to the sūtra’s wording, while "phrases" refers to the chapters and sentences—also known as *jiūdòu*.
By means of these chapters and sentences, one demarcates the sūtra’s wording so that its expressed meanings each have their own distinct divisions.

The former Master of Jingxi of Qi said: "Because the general meaning of the commentary on the title has been explained in full detail, the text of the sūtra itself is merely divided roughly into chapters and sections;
thus, the title 'Wenju' (Textual Phrases) is for this very reason. However, the establishment of these two characters is likely a mark of humility.
If one examines the great meaning of the commentary on the sūtra, it is not slight; furthermore, the fact that the interpretation of all sūtras is called "Wenju" is precisely because of this.
Because they share a common title, the title of the scripture is used here to distinguish it. Second is the designation of the teacher who expounds it. [Wenju:
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, recorded by his disciple Guanding. [Ji:

The naming according to the place of residence is as explained in the usual commentaries. Part Two: Entering the Text, which has two sections: first, establishing the three divisions; second, [the detailed analysis].
The "initial" refers to the transmitted version.
[Wenju]: These four fascicles contain a total of eighteen chapters.
[Ji]: This differs from the seven fascicles and twenty-two chapters translated by Paramārtha; therefore, it specifies "four fascicles and eighteen [chapters]."

Regarding the division into nineteen chapters, some claim that there is a chapter on "Entrustment" (*parindanā*) as the nineteenth; this is erroneous, as none of the various translated versions contain such a chapter.
Second, the correct determination of the three divisions: first, citing the judgments of various masters;
second, a general presentation of their differing views.
[Text]: "From of old, the divisions have differed in terms of expansion and contraction.

[Commentary]: "Expansion" means advancement; "contraction" means retreat. This refers to the fact that the various masters' divisions of the three parts differ in their respective advances and retreats.
2. The second part correctly clarifies the judgments made; 3. First, the masters of the north of the River.
[Text]: The masters of the north of the River Yangtze consider the first chapter to be the introduction; from the "Life Span" chapter down to "Sacrificing the Body" as the main praise of the Buddha;

and from the "Four Heavenly Kings" chapter downward as the great vow to protect the sutra, and from "Removing Illness" downward as the great compassion that receives and guides sentient beings. These constitute the main text for the dissemination of the teaching.
[Commentary] Because the Four Heavenly Kings each made vows before the Buddha to protect those who preach and listen to this sutra, it is said that they "protect the sutra through great vows.

Examples such as the Elder Flowing Water curing illness and saving the fish, and the Prince Sattva sacrificing his body to feed the tigress, represent the "great compassion" with which he receives and assists sentient beings.
This is the intention of this master; although it differs from the views of Paramārtha’s earlier and later translations discussed below.
The general meaning is the same. Second, the Masters of Jiangnan.

[Wenqu]: The various masters of Jiangnan take the first chapter as the introduction (*nidāna*), from the "Life Span" chapter downward as the main body (*śarīra*), and from the "Four Heavenly Kings" chapter downward through thirteen chapters as the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*).
[Commentary] This is similar to the current division into three sections, though it is somewhat obscure; the half-chapter on the lifespan belongs to the introduction.
Furthermore, the Master Paramārtha’s two initial judgments are as follows.
[Text] The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha divided the new text into twenty-two chapters: the first chapter serves as the introduction;
from the "Life Span" chapter down to the "Relinquishing the Body" chapter, nineteen chapters constitute the main body; and the final two chapters constitute the dissemination.
[Commentary] During the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha retranslated this sūtra, titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-rāja-sūtra*, by adding four chapters— namely,

the "Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies," the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions," the "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī for Purifying the Ground," and the "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows by Relying on Emptiness"—
to the eighteen chapters of the version translated by Baoyun, resulting in a total of twenty-two chapters; he then composed a commentary (*śāstra*) upon it.
To explain this, it says "the new text," and so forth. Second, the clarification of the meaning. [Wenju: The commentary by Paramārtha states:
"The 'Life Span' chapter clarifies the fruit of the Teacher; the two chapters on 'Repentance' and 'Praise' clarify the cause of the disciples;

the 'Bestowal of Prophecy' is the fruit of the disciples; and 'Curing Illnesses' is the cause of the Teacher. From the passage on the Four Heavenly Kings downward, the power and function are correctly discussed, with the former referring to the Teacher."

If the cause of the elder brother and the fruit of the younger brother are already established as the primary [teaching], how could the subsequent relationship of teacher and disciple, cause and fruit, be considered the "circulation" (the secondary teaching)?
[Commentary] This further refutes the view of those in Jiangnan who claim that the bestowal of predictions and the removal of illness are entirely contained within the circulation;

thus it says, "the subsequent relationship of teacher and disciple, cause and fruit," etc. It should properly read "the cause of the teacher and the fruit of the disciple," for the current text appears to be inverted. Second, showing the present teacher.
Section Two: Refuting Various Masters Based on Principle. Part One: A General Rebuke of Human Sentiment.
[Text] The Master now states that the division of the text is based on human sentiment;

all such sentiments hold that the Preface does not distinguish the Way, and that since the transmission has ceased in the later period, one cannot discuss the causal relationship between teacher and disciple. This interpretation is incorrect.

[Commentary] This directly refutes the meaning of the True Truth (*satyārtha*), while incidentally [addressing] the masters of the north; by means of these two masters, he judges that both the teacher and disciple, as well as cause and effect, are situated within the "Correct Division" (*samyak-bhāga*).

His intention is that the "Introductory Division" (*nidāna*) does not at all explain the path of cultivation and realization, and by the time one reaches the "Circulatory Division" (*pariṇāmanā*), the flavor of the Path has already ceased, leaving nothing but its most trivial remnants; therefore, he refutes them collectively, saying: "This interpretation is not so. (2) Particular Refutation.

The "Pervasive" (tong) also has three meanings, for the words of the superior, middle, and inferior [sections] are all excellent.
[Commentary: It means to seal off. The three parts together constitute a single scripture; how could their principles and meanings not mutually encompass one another?
For example, if the initial section on the "Preface" (xu-fen) describing the inception were not related to the latter two sections, what would it be called?

The sequence of the "Correct Exposition" (*samyag-deśanā*) is precisely that which is developed and described within the Introduction (*nidāna*), while the "Circulation" (*pravartana*) is that which is proclaimed and disseminated within the Circulation section.

Otherwise, how could these be called the sections of "Correct Exposition" and "Circulation" within a single sūtra? If one were to discard the Introduction and the Correct Exposition for the sake of circulation, what dharma would remain?

Therefore, each of the three parts possesses its own threefold meaning; the expressions "superior," "middling," and "inferior" correspond to the seven excellences (*sapta-sauṣṭhava*). This is the time [for this teaching].
"Excellent" means wondrous. As the *Sūtra* says, it is "excellent in the beginning, middle, and end. If it were to be cut off, how could it be called excellent?
Second, it universally benefits the faculties of the two assemblies.
[Wenju: Furthermore, since the root-natures of sentient beings who attain the Way are not fixed, how could there be an introduction lacking flavor that would cause its circulation to cease?
Since the heterodox views have not ceased, there is no harm in explaining the master-disciple relationship and the principle of cause and effect;

as stated in the Preface, this is likewise free from error. Within the circulation [of this text], the correct intent is further emphasized to urge its propagation, which does not deviate from the meaning of the Sūtra.

[Commentary: The capacity of the sentient beings for whom this sūtra is intended varies in the speed of their benefit; it is not necessarily the case that they all attain realization during the *maulī bhūmi* (the main body of the teaching).

Therefore, it is said that their faculties and natures are indeterminate. How could it be that the flavor of the Dharma is entirely absent from the *nidāna* (introductory) section, while the flavor of the Dharma is exhausted, diminished, or trivial within the *madhyama* (middle/main) section?
Since this is not the case, the causes of Liu-shui (Jāli) and the fruits of Hsin-hsiang (Śraddhālakṣaṇa) are further explained within the *pariṇāmana* (concluding/dispensation) section.

What harm is there in this? It is rather more beneficial. "Dushuai" (督率) means to supervise and lead; "lìquàn" (勵勸) means to encourage and exhort. Second, citing the sutra [the *Lotus Sūtra*]. [Commentary]:

Furthermore, within the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is clarified that the Rishi Asita was a teacher who, according to the "Bestowal of Prophecies" chapter (*Keśisaṃbodhi-parivarta*), received the fruit-prophecy from his disciples.

All teachers have judged this to belong to the "Circulation" (*Prativedha*) section. There are such precedents, and thus there is no contradiction in principle. Granting or withholding [a classification] depends on the person.
There is no need for such painful attachment.

[Commentary] The Master is Śākyamuni himself. In the "Chapter on the Attainment of Wisdom" (Dàduōpǐn), it is explained that in a past kalpa, the Buddha served the Rishi Asita in the form of a king to seek the Mahāyāna Dharma;
therefore, he is called the Master. In the "Chapter on Holding the Dharma" (Chíhǎnpǐn), he received a prediction concerning Prasenajit.
The kalpa and land of attaining Buddhahood are themselves the fruit of the disciple;
thus, the Dharma masters of old judged that from the "Dharma Master" chapter (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) onwards, the *Lotus Sūtra* belongs entirely to the Propagation (*Prasāraṇa*).

This is universally accepted, and its meaning is identical to the judgment of those in Jiangnan who hold that the current section on propagation involves the cause and effect of teacher and disciple. Therefore, it is said that there is no contradiction in principle; however, one must not treat this as definitive.

Regarding the "holding" [of the text], it is said that giving and taking depend on the person. Second, according to the meaning, the present section is divided into two parts. First, the division of the sutra;
second, the initial determination of the three divisions of the text.

[Textual Commentary]: Now, starting from "Thus have I heard" and continuing through the section on the Lifespan, the assembly of devas and nāgas concludes at the chamber of the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
The section on the introduction extends from "At that time, the four Buddhas... downward; the section on the formal exposition extends from the "Chapter on the Four Kings" downward;
and the section on the circulation of the sutra extends to the end of the scripture.

[Commentary] Now, dividing it into three parts is largely similar to the tradition of Jiangnan; however, because the introduction occupies more than half a fascicle, I shall cite the views of the three masters.
Refuting the True Meaning. Second, demonstrating the meaning of the three parts. First, the formal demonstration.
[Text] "Preface" means to introduce that which is about to bring benefit; "Main Body" means correctly responding to the capacity of the audience to discern the Way;

"Circulation" means "flowing" refers to pouring down, and "circulating" refers to being unobstructed; it is intended that the waters of the True Dharma shall flow from now on to pour upon future sages.
The teaching and its expedient means shall not be obstructed in future generations.

[Commentary] "Jiang" (將) means "to be about to. Since the circulation of the true doctrine occurs after the introductory section (*nidāna*), this present introduction shall provide the benefit of both parts;
hence it is said, "it will have benefit. "Zhengdangji" (正當機) means "properly corresponding to the capacity"; "zheng" (正) signifies "directly corresponding."
This explains the path of repentance and praise through the discernment of karmic conditions. The weirs are for fish; the snares are for rabbits.
The weirs and snares are metaphors for verbal teachings; the fish and rabbits are metaphors for the underlying principles.

It is because one desires to cause these verbal teachings to flow on into the future—through the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma—and to enable all living beings to grasp the underlying principles that it is said they shall not be obstructed in future ages.
Second, citing the sutra. [Wenju]:
The sutra says, "Words of superior, middling, and inferior quality are all good," which is precisely this meaning.
[Ji]: Second, explaining the objection. Part one: establishing the objection.
[Text] One who harbors doubt asks: "How can the Introductory Section (Nidāna) enter into the Main Body (Bhūta-deśanā)?

[Commentary] Since it is designated as the Introductory Section, it should properly conclude with the Introductory Chapter (Nidāna-parivarta); how then could it further enter into the remaining half-chapter of the Main Body, the Life Span (Āyuṣ-pramāṇa)?
There are two explanations to resolve this; first, citing an example from another school.
[Text]: This is the pattern of all scriptures. For instance, the *Vimalakīrti* lacks a "Chapter on the Introduction," yet its introduction is contained within the main exposition;

the main exposition of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* is contained within the introductory chapter; and the introductory section of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is included within the main body of the text. Since this is the case for all scriptures, there should be no cause for doubt;
why then do you alone become confused about this?
[Commentary] Since the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes the causes and conditions for purifying a Buddha-field as its primary theme, it lacks a formal "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*).

Consequently, various masters have designated the half-chapter concerning the purification of the Buddha-field as the introductory section. As stated in the "Introductory Chapter" of the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*:
"The Buddha, knowing that the assembly had already gathered, addressed Śāriputra: 'If a bodhisattva wishes to know [all phenomena] by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*)...'"
When it is stated that "one should practice the Prajñāpāramitā and all other dharmas," this already constitutes the main body of the teaching;

yet, as the text is located in the introductory section (*nidāna*), if the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* were to take "longevity" as its primary theme, and since there is no formal introductory chapter, the gathering of the assembly within the "Chapter on Longevity" serves as the introduction—this refers to the Northern Edition. As for the Southern Edition, [the text] concludes...
Master Ci (Zhiyi) took the passage on "attaining the lifespan" from the *Jūshōmon* (Chapter on the Gathering of the Assembly) and titled it the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nyorai-honji-bun*).
Regarding these three sutras, some masters place the introduction within the main body, while others place the main body within the introduction; they analyze and interpret them without any doubt.
How could one alone doubt the present judgment that places the introductory section within the "Lifespan" (*Juryō*) chapter? Second, to clarify the intent of this sutra.

[Commentary on the Text]: This was intended by the compilers of the sutra to resolve doubts through four Buddhas; thus, the text arose in isolation, its phrasing being exceptionally striking, as they drew from the Introductory Section (Nidāna) to place it within the Chapter on the Lifespan (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta).
[Commentary]: This is derived from the intention of the chapter divisions in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.

It is thought that if the title of the "Chapter on Lifespan" were placed after the assembly of devas and nāgas in the Hall of Faithful Signs (*Śraddhāliṅga-śālā*), the passage concerning the four Buddhas severing doubts would appear abruptly and isolated;
hence it is said to be "prominent" (*zhǎnjué*). "Zhǎn" (嶄) is pronounced with the *chán* rhyme; it describes the appearance of a precipitous mountain ridge. If the text were isolated...
When they arise, they are like mountain crags—steep and precipitous, with no mutual connection.
For this reason, the title "Peaceful Lifespan" (*An-śòu-liàng*) is placed within the introductory section. Third, the conclusion according to the present intent.
[Text] Now, following the convenience of the meaning, we cannot divide it into equal sections.
[Commentary] Although the section belongs to the main body of the teaching, it is actually part of the introductory portion; how could one follow the title and thereby cause the meaning to be lost?
[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the formal explanation of the sūtra, there are three sections. First, the introductory section (nidāna), which has two parts.
First, the title of the chapter: *The Sūtra of Golden Light, Chapter One: The Introduction*.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrasing, there are two parts. First, the explanation of the introduction, which begins with the presentation of the three meanings.
[Text] The introduction has three meanings: first, sequence; second, narration; and third, initiation.
[Commentary] The meaning of the introductory section (*nidāna*) of a sutra comprises these three aspects. Among various recensions, some contain only one or two, which is due to omission.
In this present sutra, as well as in other great works such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, all three are fully present. Second, the explanation.
The three meanings.
[Wenqu] As for "sequence" (*cixù*): because it occupies the beginning of this single division and stands at the head of all expositions, it is called "sequence.
As for "narration" (*xùshù*): because it introduces what is about to be told and sets forth what will bring benefit, it is called "narration. As for "initiation" (*fāqǐ*): it initiates its...

The passage of scripture beginning with "Faith arises from the teaching" contains these three meanings; therefore, it is titled the "Introductory Chapter" (Xùpǐn). [Commentary] "Xù" (introduction) refers to the thread of a cocoon.
Generally, when a cocoon draws out silk, one first draws out its *xù*; only when the *xù* is exhausted does one see the actual silk.
Now, because the five matters are placed at the beginning, they are like the *xù* of a thread. The character "guān" (to precede/introduce) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*) as "xù."
"About to describe the benefits for the present age" means that this preface describes how there are benefits for the orthodox lineage and its circulation in the current era;
thus, the following seventeen chapters are a descriptive preface. "To develop" (*fa*) means to awaken the faith of sentient beings' capacities.

"To initiate" (*qi*) means to give rise to the teachings of the Sage's response. This preface uses the manifestation of auspicious omens to startle and move the hearts of sentient beings, causing them to...
With hearts full of faith, we look forward to the profound benefit of this teaching. Second, the explanation of the chapter: first, the Sanskrit name is cited.
[Wenju] As for "chapter" (pin), the Sanskrit term is *varga*, which is translated here as "chapter."
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning according to the name, in two parts: first, the direct explanation.
[Text] "Chapter" (*p'in*) has the sense of "category. In this text, the phrases and sentences follow one another by their affinity; these are divided into *varga*s (sections).

[Commentary] Herein, both the words and phrases exist within the sūtras. All teachings that can express [meaning] employ four factors, namely: sound, name, phrase, and phoneme (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*). These are of two kinds:

those existing during the Buddha’s lifetime, and those following his parinirvāṇa. Regarding the time of the Buddha’s lifetime, there are the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
among these, the characteristic of the Brahma-voice is the one that is substantial. The bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes are merely the various modulations established upon that sound.

The establishment of these three [categories] is as follows: sound is a provisional designation belonging to the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*); names, phrases, and phonemes belong to the third aggregate, the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
According to the *Abhidharmapada*, there are fourteen types; according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, seventeen; and according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, twenty-four.

Thus, there are differences in what is established by the two schools, Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Regarding names, phrases, and phonemes, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Names (*nāman*) express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases (*pada*)..."
The phonemes (*vyañjana*) that express these distinctions are the basis for both [names and phrases].

If one considers the compilation by the noble ones after the [Buddha’s] passing—whether on palm leaves in those lands or yellow scrolls here—the names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) contained therein are all established based on the phenomena of shape, manifestation, and color.
Now, to briefly illustrate these two, they are fully endowed with and conform to the four types of sensory objects.
This is because, just as the four dharmas are grouped together to clarify the meaning of "initiation" (*samutthāna*) and so forth, they are designated as the "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*);

and likewise, because they are grouped together to clarify the meaning of "praising the Buddha," they are designated as the "Praise Chapter. Although we are currently explaining the Preface, the thematic significance of this chapter extends throughout the subsequent sections.
Second, citing examples.
[Wenqu]: For instance, as there are *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* sections in the Vinaya, and *skandhaka* chapters in the Abhidharma.
[Ji]: In both the Vinaya and Abhidharma Piṭakas, the phrasing and categories all possess structural divisions such as *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, and *skandhaka*.
Regarding the categories and groupings of the Sūtras: there are five sections and six classes. First, the *pārājika*; second, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, the *pāyattika* (pāyattika);
fourth, the *pratideśanīya*; and fifth, the *duṣkṛta*. These are called the five sections.

If one adds the *sthūlātyaya* (thullaccaya) below the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, they are termed the six classes. Furthermore, if one further distinguishes the "evil speech" (*durbhāṣita*) within the *duṣkṛta*, [the classification becomes seven].

Furthermore, regarding the *Abhidharma* (in full, *Abhidharma*, which means "Incomparable Dharma")—that is, the *Śāstra-piṭaka* (the Basket of Treatises)—it is divided into seven *skandhas* (or *kaṇḍas*).
*Kaṇḍa* means "Dharma-cluster," referring to a single section consisting of a collection of dharmas grouped together by their common characteristics (*jāti*).
For example, the *Aṣṭaka-kaṇḍa-śāstra* consists of: first, the *Karma-kaṇḍa*, which clarifies the three types of karma; second, the *Anuśaya-kaṇḍa*.
The hundred and eight afflictions can be understood through the three knowledges, four concentrations, five faculties, six elements, seven views, and eight miscellaneous thoughts.
Second, regarding the text of the two sutras, the first section is divided into three parts, beginning with the introduction.

[Text] Regarding the sequence of the subsequent sections, the old tradition speaks of five matters; the masters of the *Dichilun* (Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya) add the Buddha, making six matters.
[Commentary] "Masters of the *Dichilun*" refers to the teachers who propagated the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*. The "six matters" are: first, the essence of the Dharma heard;

second, the person capable of upholding it; third, the harmony between hearing and upholding; fourth, the teacher who expounds it; fifth, the place of reliance; and sixth, the companions who hear and uphold it.

Alternatively, seven [sections] exclude the "I have heard" (evam mayā śrutam), while five [sections] include the setting of the Buddha. These two [versions] simultaneously demonstrate the right and the wrong among the assemblies.
[Commentary]: This sutra was assembled by devas and nāgas in the Hall of Faithful Signs; thus, one may obtain it even without hearing the preceding introduction or the subsequent dream.
[This] is the same as hearing [the teaching], yet it may also be considered erroneous; the assembly that heard it was small and lacked proper order, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Since the primary theme of this sutra—discussing the doctrine of eternal life—was situated within the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa (Xìnxiàng), the devas, nāgas, and bodhisattvas gathered there to listen to the intent of the teaching.
It was logical that the four Buddhas did not appear, and thus the assembly naturally dispersed. The spiritual resonance vanished.
In the preface to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it is stated that because the time and place of the golden drum in the dream were different [from those of the actual teaching], none heard it;

thus, regarding the "constant life-span" (śrotrāṇāṃ nitya-āyuḥ), they are considered "hearing together" (*saha-śravaṇa*) in terms of their capacity to hear. However, because they did not participate in the dream itself, they are not "hearing together" in the primary sense.

Furthermore, since the time and place of the preaching of this sūtra are not fixed, the assembly of those hearing together does not follow the sequential arrangement found in other sūtras. This is according to Yi Jing’s new translation.

In the *Sūtra of the Supreme King*, the assembly of those who heard the teaching is listed without differing from other sūtras; the Great Master, foreseeing that the Sanskrit original was about to arrive, provided these various annotations.

[Commentary] II. The direct explanation of the sūtra text has two parts: first, explaining the five meanings based on the sūtra; second, clarifying the absence of the meaning of "hearing together."
This is according to the *Dilun* masters' division of the text into six topics; however, according to the five topics as they appear in the extant text, there are only four.
Taking the first [topic] as five, the first is the essence of the dharma (*dharmatā*).
Thus it is.

[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first is the ancient interpretation. [Section 1: Introduction to the Interpretations of Various Masters] This has four parts; the first is the ancient interpretation.

[Wenju] The ancient interpretation holds that "as" (*ru*) means "not different. Thus it is called "non-different. Because these *wenju* (words and phrases) transmitted by Ānanda are like pouring water from one vessel into another, they are of the same kind as the Buddha's;
therefore, they are termed "as" (*ru*). The principle underlying the phrase "as the text" (*ru wen*) is sound and appropriate. There is no error.
Because it is erroneous, there is nothing that is not called "is"; speaking briefly, the text is such that its words accord with the principle.
[Commentary] The two masters, Sengzhao and others.
[Wenju] Master Zhao said: "Thus" (rúshì) is a term for faith and compliance. When one has faith, the principles heard are brought into accord.
When one follows [this principle], the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
[Commentary] The Three True Realities.
[Wenju] The Tripitaka Master Zhen Di said: "In this manner" means certainty; it is the certainty of number and the certainty of principle. The Buddha...

If one were to say that this sutra contains more or fewer words and phrases than it actually does, having more would constitute the slander of exaggeration (*samāropa*), while having fewer would constitute the slander of denial (*apavāda*).

Ānanda transmitted it like pouring water from one vessel to another—neither more nor less—therefore the number [of words] is fixed. The Buddha taught the principle of signlessness (*animitta*) as being neither existent nor non-existent;
had there been an addition, one would fall into exaggeration, and had there been a subtraction, one would fall into denial. Ānanda transmitted it without adding anything.
Because there is no decrease, the principle is definitive.
[Commentary] Fourth, Nāgārjuna.
[Wenju] "Nāgārjuna explains thus" is a phrase of faithful compliance; "faith" means to say that this matter is exactly so.
Those who do not believe say that this matter is not so.
[Commentary] The meanings of these four passages are all visible; it is only upon reaching the judgment of the four *siddhāntas* that their depth and shallowness are determined.
Second, judging by means of the four *siddhāntas*.

[Text] These four interpretations each rely on the intent of one *siddhānta*. The old explanations are general and do not clearly reveal what principle the text elucidates, nor how that principle is elucidated by the text.
Since this is not clearly manifest, it pertains only to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).
Master Zhaolun relies on "faithful compliance" as the *pudgala-viniścaya* (determination for persons); the principles and texts of the Tripiṭaka are definitive.
"Concentration is the antidote; Nāgārjuna’s faith and compliance are thus the primary meaning," and so forth.
[Commentary] Here it is clarified that whether the holy Dharma is extensive or concise, general or specific, there is nothing that is not a response to an invocation;
such responses do not exceed the four kinds of *siddhānta*. The previous determination of the sequence of the six types of names and meanings was a summary and was extensive; now...
The judgment that each of the six matters constitutes a distinct and minor response leads to such divergent interpretations among various masters regarding the two characters "ru shi" (如是).
Today, the Tiantai master employs the four *siddhāntas* to harmonize and explain them, so that each arrives at the single meaning of the Tathāgata’s responsive resonance (*pratyupabhoga*).

How could this be the same as worldly disputes over whether one is right and the others wrong? Although the previous commentaries on these two characters are consistent with the textual logic, they do not [fully accord with the ultimate intent].
Distinguishing between the great and the small, these teachings generally encompass all [levels]; furthermore, they lack the characteristics of producing the three benefits of the supramundane.

Since they merely achieve the benefit of ensuring that the transmission of the teaching is not erroneous, they belong to the mundane world (*loka*). Although Master Sengzhao possesses words that accord with principle, he does not distinguish between the ultimate and the conventional;

because his goodness consists in generating faith and compliance through his natural endowment, it belongs to the "for the person" (*pauruṣeya*) category, which pertains to the principles of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Furthermore, because it does not engage in analytical discussion regarding the definitive departure from the faults of increase or decrease, it constitutes an antidote.
Although Nāgārjuna’s faithful adherence is similar to that of Master Sengzhao, when he speaks of "faith," he says, "This matter is thus. This is able to manifest the meaning of the Three Truths:
"this matter" is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), "thus" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and "is" is the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). This, with respect to the one...

The phrasing skillfully indicates that the three truths correspond to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). The note states "and so forth" to indicate that one should understand this as previously explained.
Second, the current explanation has two parts: first, the explanation according to the teachings; second, the contemplation of the mind.

These two explanations—namely, the teaching and the contemplation—are both excellent when discussed together, and it is for this reason that they transcend all other schools. The first section is divided into two parts: first, the general [explanation].

[Text] Now, there are two explanations: the general and the specific. Because the Buddha spoke according to the characteristics of the Dharma and Ānanda transmitted it according to the characteristics of what he heard, it is called "as" (ru).
Because the Buddha understood according to the characteristics of the Dharma and Ānanda received it with a capacity like the great ocean, it is called "this" (shi), and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation by way of teaching and transmission, it is clarified as being like [the explanation] by way of precept and reception.

Since this is a general explanation that permeates the subsequent specific explanations and must encompass all four teachings, we know that the "Dharma-characteristics" (dharmalakṣaṇa) are what is expounded by the four [teachings], the Buddha is the master who proclaims the four teachings, and Ānanda is the person who hears and upholds the four.
Speaking from the perspective of their respective divisions, all four are as vast as the ocean.
Second, the detailed explanation of the three [sections]: first, the mutual clarification of refutation and establishment;

fourth, the fact that each of the four teachings successively refutes what is not as it should be before establishing the meaning of its own fundamental teaching. First, the refutation of the heterodox and the establishment of the orthodox:
this refutes the heterodoxy of external paths and reveals the orthodoxy of the Tripiṭaka. Second, first, the refutation of the heterodox.

[Commentary on the Phrases] Regarding the detailed explanation, the opponent says: "The term *akūta* signifies 'auspicious' (*kalyāṇa*). Since the phrasing contradicts the principle, it is not [correctly] according to reason.
Because the phrasing differs from that [of the *Akūta-sūtra*], it is not the case that it is unseeable. *Akūta* occurs at the beginning, while the middle and end are all auspicious."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "Ajita calls it auspicious": the *Śata-śāstra* clarifies that a non-Buddhist asked an internal disciple, saying, "What Dharma does the Buddha teach?
The answer was, "Briefly stated, there are two kinds: the cessation of evil and the practice of good. The outsider said, "Your scripture contains a fault, for it first speaks of evil;
therefore, it is inauspicious. My teacher’s scriptural Dharma is auspicious at the outset, as in the *Vaiśravaṇa-sūtra* and others."

All say that "auspicious" (*ji*) refers to being auspicious at the beginning; because it is auspicious at the beginning, it is also auspicious in the middle and at the end, and thus it is called *ākr̥ta*, which signifies auspiciousness.
Regarding the phrase "the text is inconsistent" (*wen guai deng*): this means using the correct to refute the heterodox.

It is not the case that the scripture initially designates "auspicious" while what is expounded within its sections is exclusively heterodox views. This is an inconsistency with principle and is therefore "not so. Since heterodox views are themselves inauspicious, how could they be called [auspicious]?
Āryadeva states that this interpretation differs from the text and is incorrect; thus, the *Śataśāstra* refutes it, saying:
"To claim that this is auspicious or inauspicious is the breath of wrong view. Second, establishing the correct [view].
[Text]: "Because the words accord with the principle, it is said that the words are as the principle; because the principle accords with the words, it is said that they are thus. [Commentary]:

In the Tripitaka Teaching, the words and the principles correspond to one another. To describe the principle of impermanence and arising-and-ceasing by means of discourse on impermanence and arising-and-ceasing is called "the words being as the principle";
to describe the principle by means of the words is called "thus. Second, refuting difference and establishing identity.
First, the refutation of difference.

[Wenqu]: Now it is said that because the sūtras of the Tripiṭaka begin with "Thus have I heard," asserting that the two truths are each distinct, and because they are not in accordance with reality and are shallow, they are not [the ultimate teaching].

[Commentary] To manifest the principles of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna), one first refutes the non-reality of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; as a conventional expression, it does not coincide with the ultimate truth and is therefore not "as-it-is" (tathatā).
As for the ultimate truth it expresses, it lacks the Middle Way principle and is shallow; thus, it is not [the true teaching].
Second, the clarification of their identity. [Wenqu]:
Because the two truths are mutually identical in the Mahāyāna, it is said that they are "as such" (*tathatā*); because they are profound according to principle, it is said that they "are.
[Ji]: Speaking generally of illusory existence, its very substance is emptiness; this non-difference is termed "as such. This true reality of emptiness is capable of containing all.

The Middle Way differs [from the other two vehicles] because the emptiness analyzed in the Tripiṭaka is fixed and shallow; thus, its principle is termed the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), as it necessarily encompasses both the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.
Therefore, the text designates it as the Mahāyāna. Third, the refutation of the shallow to clarify the deep, which has two parts: first, the refutation of the shallow.

[Text]: Now it is said that because the three types of people hear the same teaching yet each understands it differently, and because their levels of realization and entry differ, [the claim that they are identical] is not correct.
[Commentary]:

To clarify the specific principle, one first refutes the general [view]. It is not the case that the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) equally hear that all phenomena are empty, for they are dull-witted.

The Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles share the same understanding and sharp faculties regarding the hearing of emptiness; however, they do not merely understand emptiness as empty, but are also able to understand the emptiness of emptiness.

Since their respective understandings differ, they are not like the two types of realization within the [Bodhisattva] stage of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa-mukha*). Their realization of emptiness is particularly inferior compared to that [of the Bodhisattvas], and thus it is not the same.
Second, the clarification of the profound.
[Wenju]: That which is heard only by Bodhisattvas is as that which Bodhisattvas have reached; this is the case. [Ji]:

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not extend to the study and practice of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). Although it extensively encompasses beings as numerous as motes of dust, it is only for Bodhisattvas...
Since all sentient beings hear of the Buddha-nature and enter its cultivation through successive stages, and because there is no divergent understanding, it is called "Thus" (tathatā).

Because there is nothing that is not realized within the Middle Way, it is called "Is. Fourth, the refutation of both the negation and the establishment [of extremes] has two parts; first, the refutation of negation.

[Text]: Now, it is said that if one departs from the passage clarifying the "Middle" by means of abandoning the "extremes," then it is not the case; for if there were a Middle Way existing outside of the Two Truths, it would not be [the true Middle].

[Commentary]: In wishing to clarify the Perfect Principle (*yuanli*), one first refutes the partial [teachings]. Although the partial teachings speak of the "Middle," this Middle is merely the fruit of Buddhahood. Furthermore...

The nine realms of cause and effect are fabricated; their nine non-natures are not intrinsically complete (*xingju*). One must gradually sever them through the Middle Way until they are completely exhausted before attaining the Buddha-realm.

Because the Buddha is distinct from the nine [realms], it is not called "as-it-was-in-the-beginning. First, one contemplates the transcendence of the mundane; next, one contemplates the transcendence of the true;

reaching the third contemplation, one simultaneously transcends both truths, and only then does one realize the Middle Way. Since the Middle is not identical to the extremes, it is not [the same as the initial state].
[The section on] Meaning. Within the second [section], the "Exposition" (*wénjù*) states:
Because the nature of words and letters is detached from [inherent existence] and is thus identical to Suchness (*tathatā*), it is said that "all dharmas are such as they are.
This is what is called the Buddha-dharma.
[Commentary] The nature of the words that express [the truth] is fundamentally forgotten; because it is detached and not different from the principle, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā).
It is "only emptiness," "only existence," "only form," or "only mind"—each and every one of these is the Middle Way, for there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma; therefore, it is called "is.
Thus, the text, the principle, and the meaning are ultimately established. Second, the four teachings are concluded.
[Text]: First, by refuting the heterodox to clarify the orthodox, there are the sūtras of the Tripiṭaka; next, by refuting difference to clarify sameness, there are the sūtras of the Shared Teaching;

next, by refuting the shallow to clarify the profound, there are the sūtras of the Distinct Teaching; next, by refuting separation to clarify the Middle, there are the sūtras of the Perfect Teaching. Thus it is.

[Commentary] Question: In the previous explanation, it was stated that the four teachings are named based on their inclusion within the "True" and "Middle" [realms], which is a profound principle; yet now, in concluding the discussion of the four teachings, the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is said to "break the shallow and clarify the deep.
How can this be, given that both the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) and the True-Middle [teachings] are equally shallow? Answer:

Although the principle of the Shared Teaching is indeed deep, because it is intended to encompass those of the Two Vehicles as well as dull-rooted Bodhisattvas, it also incorporates shallow principles. Now, in concluding the discussion of the Separate Teaching, we speak of it alone as the Bodhisattva [teaching].

Because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* expounds only the profound principle, it uses "only the profound" to refute those that include the shallow; this does not contradict the previous explanation of the meaning.
Third, showing that the section possesses all four [characteristics].
[Wenju: Since this sutra is a Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra) that universally addresses various capacities and natures, there is no fault in its making various kinds of explanations.
[Commentary] Second, contemplating the mind.
[Wenju] Regarding the interpretation of "contemplating the mind": because contemplation merges with the object, it is "like" the object;

because it is precisely this contemplation, the sutra says: "One who contemplates in this way is practicing right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called false contemplation. That is to say:
This is its meaning.

[Commentary] By means of the perfect threefold contemplation (*yuan san guan*), one contemplates the mind of cultivated evil within the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; this very evil is called the "evil dharma-realm" (*akuśala-dharmadhātu*), for there is no phenomenon that is not subsumed within it.

Its essence is the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and it is further termed the "three truths" (*trisatya*). Contemplating in accordance with these truths is what is meant by "contemplating while conforming to the truths."

Because the object (*viṣaya*) is not different [from the subject], it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). The object is precisely the correct contemplation; the object is original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which arises as initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).

Although there is a distinction between new and old [stages of] awakening, the essence of awakening (*bodhi-tattva*) is not different; therefore, it can be termed "the object is precisely the correct contemplation. Only through this meaning is the principle established.
If it were otherwise, how could the four propositions—such as "the object illuminates the object"—be established? As for the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the Sūtra: if...
To contemplate the stubborn objects as partial and small, or to forget the mind while falsely establishing such things as "True Suchness" (tathatā), is all termed "erroneous contemplation.

Although this present "correct contemplation" is not defined by the practitioner's conduct, if one wishes to subsume phenomena into principle and practice accordingly upon hearing [the teaching], one must distinguish the contemplated mind from the ten objects;
specifically, while the aggregate-object (skandha) is always present, the other nine await their karmic conditions within the contemplating subject.

One should know that there are ten vehicles for contemplation: those of superior capacity practice one vehicle; those of middling capacity practice up to seven; and those of inferior capacity practice all ten.
If you have not yet mastered the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) yourself, you must consult with teachers and friends on each point individually.

Only after clearly identifying the "medicine" and the "disease" should you begin practice. Do not think that practicing a single phrase is sufficient; understand that subsequent contemplations and insights should be applied accordingly.
Second, hearing and retaining.
"I have heard.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first, the ancient interpretation, which has three sections. First, the ancient masters.
[Text]: Regarding "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*): the old translations state that Ānanda did not take his own mind as his teacher but personally received the Buddha’s intent;

therefore, it says "I have heard. [Commentary]: Outsiders hold the view of a self and thus frequently follow their own minds, whereas Ānanda took the Buddha as his teacher and thus proclaimed, "I have heard.
These two represent the Two Truths.
【Text】Paramārtha says: "I" has the meaning of being a vessel. First, a distracted mind is called a covered vessel because it lacks the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Second, a forgetful mind is called a leaking vessel because, although one may acquire [knowledge], one loses it due to the lack of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Third, an inverted mind is called a defiled vessel because one takes what is not as what is, due to the lack of the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Ānanda is free from these three faults; he is a truly excellent vessel and is worthy of intimacy.
Because there is that which is received, one says "I have heard.

[Commentary] Since I am able to receive and uphold the Dharma spoken by the Buddha, this carries the meaning of being a "vessel"; it distinguishes the three who are vessels from those who are not, thereby manifesting the accomplishment of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Although the specific distinctions between the wisdoms of the four teachings have not yet been analyzed here, this explanation of "I have heard" far surpasses the traditional interpretations.
Third, the Commentary on the Treatise (*Śāstra-vyākhyā*).

[The *Wenju*] states: The Commentary says that because the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and the mind applies itself to listen attentively—through the convergence of these causes and conditions—it is called "hearing.
Because Ānanda and the assembly of listeners recount the Buddha’s final instructions exactly as they personally received them, there is no error.
"I have heard" means:
he clarifies that auditory consciousness arises from four conditions—first, space; second, the sense organ; third, the object; and fourth, attention (*manasikāra*).
Now, it is said that these are "unimpaired": the sense organ is intact, the place where one can hear is the object, and listening attentively is the attention. Only the condition of space is lacking.

The passage below states that the meaning of "the harmony of causes and conditions" can encompass both [the ear and the consciousness]; that is, it is only through the harmony of the four conditions that auditory consciousness arises.
It does not say "the ear hears," but rather "I hear," because "I" refers to the master of the ear.

The *Xin lun* (New Treatise) states that the nine conditions for the arising of auditory consciousness are fully set forth in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Second, the present explanation has two parts; the first explains according to the teachings. First, "I hear."
Each [section] explains two [points]; first, it clarifies the four types of "self.
[Textual Commentary]: The Master explains that there are four meanings of "self": namely, self-self, non-self, no-self-self, and neither-self-nor-no-self.
These four meanings of the true self correspond to the four root dispositions of people, and so forth.
[Commentary] This "self" and "mine" are established by analogy with the four phrases—arising, arising-arising, etc.—found in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*.

Since the "self" is a provisional designation that exists by grasping the aggregates (*skandhas*), and since the phenomena of the aggregates possess the four states such as arising and arising-arising, how could it be otherwise for the self to follow these real dharmas?
As the explanation of "arising-arising" states: "Great arising gives rise to small arising. This refers to the arising of arising within cessation.
Because one grasps at the phenomena of arising and ceasing to form a self of arising and ceasing, it is analogous to how the arising of arising produces the self;
although this self is empty when contemplated, it is not empty in its essence. Therefore, the Tripiṭaka is rich in the first phrase.

Furthermore, one should know that the conventional and real arising and ceasing of sentient beings is their original nature, yet they do not realize it; now, by receiving this teaching, they accord with that original nature.

Is contemplation limited to this teaching alone? No; the same applies to all three [teachings] below it. In the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), because real dharmas arise yet are non-arising, the self within the aggregates is precisely no-self;
thus it belongs to the second phrase. In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), one knows that the aggregates are non-arising yet arise;

therefore, one contemplates no-self, yet the "self" [persists]. This is because, according to this teaching, one fundamentally recognizes the true self, and thus views and conceit (*māna*) are particularly rampant.
First one contemplates non-self, next one refutes non-self to establish self, and finally one enters true self;

therefore, this teaching corresponds to the third phrase. A person of perfect capacity immediately realizes that the provisional and the real are neither arising nor non-arising, and that by gathering the permanent aggregates one constitutes the true self.
Since this self is itself the Middle Way, both truths converge therein; thus it is said: "Self and non-self."
However, because the meaning of the non-dual true self is intended here, this teaching corresponds to the fourth phrase;

for since the fundamental teachings were directed toward specific capacities, the four meanings of the self are assigned to the four root natures, and the subsequent expounder has distinguished them as explained above—hence the note "and so forth."
Second, the clarification of the four types of hearing.
[Textual Commentary]: Hearing also has four meanings, namely: hearing what is heard, hearing what is not heard, not hearing what is heard, and not hearing what is not heard.
These are assigned respectively to the four methods of teaching, and so forth.
[Commentary]: "I" is the master of hearing; "hearing" is that which I employ. This "master" is a conventional person (*prajñapti-pudgala*), while this "employment" is a real dharma (*dravya-dharma*).

However, if one understands the principle of the master, the meaning of hearing will manifest of itself. Yet, the master is a general discussion of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereas hearing is specifically derived from the act of speaking and listening;
thus, there is not a slight difference between them. Because further instances of hearing arise based on the causes and conditions of hearing, it is called "hearing-hearing. Since [this is so]...
That which arises from conditions ultimately returns to destruction; this refers to hearing arising and ceasing. Hearing is devoid of the four natures (*catur-lakṣaṇa*);

because there is no hearing at its very locus, it is said that "hearing is not heard. This refers to hearing being without birth. Although in truth there is no hearing, within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) there is hearing;
therefore, it is said that "not hearing is hearing. This refers to hearing being immeasurable. Since the two truths are themselves the Middle Way, it is called "not hearing the Middle."
Furthermore, it cannot be obtained; how could one say "I have not heard" when, throughout forty-nine years, not a single word was spoken?
Since there is neither center nor periphery, what is there to hear? This "hearing" is non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). The attention (*manasikāra*) is the same as before.
Second, the joint explanation of "I have heard. Third, the initial hearing. Fourth, the capacity.
[Text]: There are four kinds of Ānanda: namely, Ānanda of Joy, Ānanda the Worthy, Ānanda the Keeper of the Treasury, and Ānanda of the Ocean;
these four names were established based on four distinct conditions.
[Commentary] Within the Tripiṭaka Teaching, Ānanda possesses four virtues in a single person and thus receives four names. One name, "Treasury" (Kośa), appears in the Āgamas;
the remaining three appear in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*. Here, the minor names are now expounded in relation to the meanings of the Four Teachings.
As for the name Ānanda: in Sanskrit it means "Joyful," and in the vernacular it means "Flower. He was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment, and the entire nation rejoiced.
Therefore, names should be established based on conditions; as they accord with the law of arising and ceasing, the name "Dharmatrāta" (Holding the Dharma) is appropriate for upholding the Tripiṭaka.
For the teachings of the Shared Vehicle, where the essence and phenomena are identical to principle and differ from worldly views, the name "Bhadra" (Worthy) is appropriate.

For the Distinct Teaching, which correctly discusses the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as motes of dust and presides over many matters, the name "Pitāmaha" (Treasury) is appropriate. For the Perfect Teaching, which elucidates the beginning and the end...

Since the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is both profound and vast, it is appropriate to use the name "Ocean. Second, he was able to receive [the teachings] from the four Buddhas and the first three of the four Tripiṭaka masters.
[Textual Commentary: Ānanda, who is filled with joy, is my "I"; through hearing, I personally received the teaching from the Buddha of the sixteen-foot body and upheld the Three [Baskets].
Because the Dharma of the *Pitaka* conceals [the ultimate truth], it is said, "I heard from the Buddha.

[Commentary: This teaching analyzes phenomena as empty but does not include the Middle Way; therefore, one perceives the Buddha’s body as being only sixteen feet tall. Second is the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

[Text]: "Worthy Ānanda, 'I' and 'non-I' refer to hearing and not hearing. Because I have personally received from the Buddha—the sixteen-foot body and the sublime, special body—the Dharma that sustains and penetrates all, I speak of 'I' and 'non-I,' and of 'hearing' and 'not hearing.'"

[Commentary] Having contemplated that the essence of phenomena manifests two kinds of emptiness—namely, "emptiness alone" (buta-kū) and "not-emptiness alone" (fubuta-kū)—the bodhisattvas of dull faculties, being identical to those of the Two Vehicles, perceive only "emptiness alone.
This is because they lack the realization of the Middle Way’s true reality; for them, form and mind are not fundamental.

Since the Buddha originally manifested his body and wisdom through illusory power to sustain the residual habits of his vows, these ultimately revert to ash and extinction. Because his physical form has limits, it is said to be "sixteen feet" in height.

If a bodhisattva of sharp faculties receives the direct transition from the Separate Teaching to the Perfect Teaching, they realize that "emptiness of emptiness" is the true substance within original enlightenment.

This is the wondrous form-and-mind attained at the stage of Buddhahood; because its physical bodies and wisdom are equal to this substance and are boundless, it is called the "Distinguished Body" (Zhuntè)—venerable, exalted, and extraordinary—and is also termed the "Retribution Body" (Bāoshēn).
It is merely a single Buddha-body that appears differently according to the sharp or dull capacities of sentient beings.
Because there are two types of physical forms, it is said that one must make this distinction regarding the Buddha-body of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

One should understand that for those of dull faculties, even if they see the Buddha at a height of ten *li* up to a hundred billion *li*, this is because they rely on the mere emptiness (*śūnyatā-mātra*) and thus the Buddha’s majestic presence has a limited extent.
Conversely, when those of sharp faculties see the Buddha at a height of sixteen or eight feet, this is because they rely on the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) and thus there is no such limitation.

Therefore, the commentary on the phrases of the "Praise of the Thirty-two Marks" in the *Jinlong Zunwang Jing* (Sūtra of the Honored King Golden Dragon) states that this is precisely a praise of the *zhunte* (special, exalted body).
Third, the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
[Textual Commentary]: Ānanda, the Keeper of the Storehouse, is without self; yet through the function of his non-hearing, he hears and personally receives the Buddha of the *zhunte* body.
Because it maintains distinct dharmas, it is said that there is no self, and that one neither hears nor does not hear.

[Commentary] This teaching causes the beginner to hear that although the Middle Way is not fully endowed with the nine realms of the environment and its inhabitants, it is not without the wondrous form and wondrous mind of the Buddha-realm;
therefore, the vision of the Buddha is exclusively the boundless and sublime *vairocana* body (*viśiṣṭa-rūpa-kāya*). This teaching...

This is because from beginning to end, it is not shared with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) nor with Bodhisattvas who dwell in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as it is that which is cultivated and realized. Fourth, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

[Text] It says: "Ānanda, 'self' and 'non-self' are non-dual; through their non-dual application, one does not hear the 'not-hearing,' for one has personally received the Dharma-body Buddha and upholds the Perfect Dharma.
Therefore, it is said that "self" and "non-self" are non-dual in their application, and one does not hear the "not-hearing."
[Commentary]: Because the characteristics of the world taught in this teaching are eternal, there is not a single dharma that is not the Middle Way.

Although [the followers of] the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) share the same vision of the Honored One’s Distinctive Features (Zun-te), they supplement this with separate cultivation, whereas here [in the Perfect Teaching], all are inherently complete by nature. Thus, the Dragon Girl says:
"The subtle, pure Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks. To manifest that the entire nature is complete, it is named after its supreme distinctiveness.

Because it is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), this teaching instructs people to contemplate the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of suffering and pleasure, thereby giving rise to the will to bestow [benefit] and to rescue [others].

By taking the poison of afflictions as that which is to be eliminated and subdued, one cultivates and attains the three causes, which are termed the "nature-virtue body" (*svabhāva-guṇa-kāya*) and the "retribution body" (*vipāka-kāya*). These two are collectively named the Dharma-body.
This is because one seeks to dissolve the cultivated through the nature; thus, suffering is itself rescue, and there is no rescue apart from it, while poison is itself [the antidote].
Exhaustion is itself non-exhaustion; practice is itself non-practice; Buddhahood is itself non-attainment. Ānanda transmitted these Four Truths of Non-action, which are themselves non-explanation.
Therefore, he was one who personally received the Dharma-body Buddha. The three divisions [of the teachings] possess four capacities for the faculties [of sentient beings].
[Text]: "This sutra is taught through the three vehicles because when one sound is preached, each understands it according to their own capacity;
therefore, it must be distinguished, and so forth. [Commentary]: Question: Above, the four teachings were explained; why now do you speak only of the three vehicles preaching and listening? Answer:

Within the three vehicles, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas must be discussed in terms of the *Zang* (Treasury) and *Tong* (Common) teachings, whereas if one clarifies the Bodhisattvas, all four teachings must be encompassed. Thus, the three vehicles are collectively [treated].

The treatise distinguishes the four teachings separately regarding the listeners; since it is taught that there are three vehicles, there must be four Buddhas. Although the Buddha speaks with a single voice, each understands differently, and thus a single body is seen as distinct.
The previous explanation of the "combined body" (sambhogakāya) was intended for this point. Second, the explanation according to the contemplation of the mind.

[Text] Regarding those who practice through contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*): if one performs the contemplation of "clinging to the superior and loathing the inferior," this is "self" and "hearing hearing.
If one performs either of the two types of contemplations that analyze the essence—entering emptiness from the conventional (*cong-ja-ru-kong guan*)—this is "non-self" and "not hearing not hearing.

If one performs the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional (*cong-kong-chu-ja guan*), this is "non-self" and "not hearing hearing. If one performs the contemplation of the Middle Way (*zhongdao guan*), this is the "True."
"I have not heard what I have not heard.
[Commentary] The above four sets of four phrases concerning "I have heard" are distinguished according to the practitioner’s mental contemplation.

"Grasping at the superior" and so forth refer to the sixfold contemplation (*ṣaḍvidhābhāvanā*) of impure dhyāna: grasping at the superior as pure, wondrous, and detached; and regarding the inferior as suffering, coarse, and loathsome.

Regarding the hindrances, they are discussed in relation to the nine stages as being mutually superior or inferior. "I" and "my," and "hearing" and "what is heard," pertain to the conventional realm of arising and ceasing within the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
Previously, this was discussed from the perspective of the three vehicles, where one enters the principle by contemplating the arising and ceasing through knowledge and understanding.

Now, we address the case of ordinary people who practice without such knowledge; they merely achieve mundane dhyāna. Since these are conventional realms, whether one knows them or not, phenomena are fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "the arising of arising," our present school explains it as follows: either from the perspective of the capacities of those to be converted (*vineya*), or by means of the analytical contemplation of the essence (*svabhāva*) through the two types of contemplation.

While in the former case, the conventional is distinct from the ultimate, in the latter case, the conventional differs from the ultimate; thus, the analysis of phenomena is applied individually to the first phrase.

Now, because the ultimate is identical [to the conventional], the analysis of the essence is applied collectively to the second phrase. As for the latter two types of contemplation, there is no difference between them.
Previously, in relation to the interlocutor and based on the teachings I have heard, the four phrases could be applied to four types of persons.

Now, however, in discussing the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one must proceed from the perspective of a single person and a single moment of thought (*citta-kṣaṇa*). Therefore, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fmen*) states that within the "single mind and three contemplations," seeing the four sets of the Four Noble Truths within a single moment of mind already encompasses the four realms of rebirth;
how then could it lack the mundane dhyānas? Thus, it is said that [the stages] must be sequential, though they are distinguished here according to the individual practitioner.
Because they are characterized as being without before or after, one cultivates only the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*). Third, the three [factors] harmonize simultaneously.
[Commentary: The text has two parts; first, the ancient interpretation, which begins with Master Zhaolun.
[Text]: Regarding "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), Master Zhaolun says it is the time when the Dharma King initiates his movement and a sublime assembly gathers.

[Commentary]: "Initiates" (*qǐ*) means to open; "movement" (*yùn*) refers to the movement of the times; "sublime" (*jiā*) means good; "assembly" (*huì*) means to conjoin. This is precisely the time when the capacity of the sentient beings (*jī*) and the response of the Buddha (*yìng*) are perfectly conjoined.
Second, regarding the Two Truths: first, the presentation of their established doctrine.
[Text] The Tripitaka Master said: "Whether the voice is too high or too low, it is either excessive or insufficient and thus unfit for hearing the Dharma;
only when it is at the proper pitch is it truly 'at one time'."

[Commentary]: This interpretation is the same as that of Sengzhao, who explains "unity" (*yi*) by focusing solely on the capacity of sentient beings (*ji*), rather than on the non-high-and-low nature of the mind that accords with response (*ying*).
When the minds of all sentient beings are neither high nor low but remain in a state of equilibrium, this is precisely the moment of being one with the Buddha;
therefore, it is said that "the time of equilibrium is itself the One Time. This second chapter concludes with the explanation of Zhang’an.
[Text] "In my private opinion," it means that when one is in a high position, pride does not arise; when in a low position, one does not indulge in the five desires;
and being neither indulgent nor proud is the state of equilibrium.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "in my private opinion" (*si wei*): after the Great Master passed away, when Master Ding recorded these textual passages, he added this himself.
This explanation is termed "private" because its meaning is not self-evident. It is intended for those who might fail to understand the distinction between the true and the false;

thus, it is explained here. "High" refers to arrogance—relying on oneself and looking down upon others, thereby being unable to practice the Buddha’s Dharma—and is thus described as "arrogant pride that does not lead to practice.
"Low" refers to being addicted to and entangled in the five desires, becoming utterly deluded.
If one abandons these two states of mind, how can one receive the Way? These two are the greatest obstacles to the Path.

To ensure that people of today do not become attached or negligent, they should cultivate themselves during ordinary times so as to immediately realize the state of a sage. Second, the present explanation has two parts: first, an explanation based on the teachings; second, an explanation based on causes and conditions.
First, the explanation based on causes and conditions provides a general interpretation.
[Text] The Master explains that this is the moment when sentient beings respond to the Dharma and the Buddha’s compassion responds to their capacity through teaching.

[Commentary] This is the time when the causes and conditions of response and stimulus merge as one. First, a general explanation is given because it does not clarify with whom the response and stimulus are discussed as being one, nor does it distinguish between the shallow and deep levels of the Three Truths;
therefore, it should be explained in general. Second, a specific explanation is given according to the Truths and Wisdom. There are two parts to this.
Regarding the initial explanation of the time [of the first fruit]:
[The *Wenju* states] "This is also the time of awakening to the true vision of the truths; it is also the time when the Dharma-eye becomes clear and illuminates the world;
it is also the time when the Buddha-eye shines forth," and so forth.

[Commentary] Question: Since the wisdom of the Truths (satya-jñāna) resides only in the capacity for resonance (the sentient being) and the response (the Buddha), and since the "single" and "paired" aspects are not identical, how can one discuss them in terms of both the general and the specific?
Answer: Wisdom is precisely the capacity for resonance, and the Truth is precisely the response. When wisdom and the Truth coincide, they are termed "resonance and response as one.
Why? Because the Buddha takes the Three Truths as his essence; he does not respond to sentient beings by means of a [separate] essence apart from these.
Sentient beings have no means of attaining union with the Truth through wisdom alone; as when Subhūti contemplated emptiness in his stone cave, Śākyamuni praised him, saying, "You have seen my body.
This is not only true regarding the principle of the Truths, but applies equally to all wholesome qualities.

As it is said, "If one upholds the five precepts, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni dwells within your home. Thus, we know that the Buddha takes the three Truths and all wholesome qualities as his very essence.
When sentient beings cultivate goodness and perceive the principle of the Truths, this is precisely the moment when resonance and response merge into one.
Now, it is clarified that the three truths encompass the four teachings, as is commonly analyzed. This constitutes the first of two explanations.
[Text]: As for the term "one" (*eka*), if one considers prior thought and subsequent awakening, these two are not one;
it is at the moment of sudden, expansive awakening when the delusions of thought and awakening are severed that one speaks of "one time."

[Commentary] This refers to the characteristic of the unification of the preceding truths and wisdom. First, it excludes the state of non-unification, meaning that prior reflection (*cintā*) followed by subsequent cognition (*jñāna*) constitutes the deluded mind of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
When wisdom arises, both reflection and thought are stilled; one awakens with sudden clarity and only then becomes one with the Truths.
Therefore, it is said that they are simultaneous. In all four teachings, the Truths and wisdom share this same characteristic of unity. (2)
Contemplative Understanding.

[Wenju] Regarding contemplative understanding: entering emptiness from the conventional and attaining the Truth simultaneously; entering the conventional from emptiness and responding to the capacities of beings simultaneously;
and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way and the Dharma-nature simultaneously, and so forth.

[Commentary] The preceding section explained the teachings according to the classification of doctrines (*jiao*), which pertains to the realization attained during the Buddha’s assembly; the present section explains the teachings according to meditative contemplation (*guan*), which pertains to the practice undertaken after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
While the former was divided into four teachings, here they are unified within a single mind; thus, while the phrasing is the same, the meaning differs. Fourth, the masters of the teachings.
Buddha. [Commentary on the Text] The text has two parts: first, the ancient interpretation; second, the True Meaning (Paramārtha) school.

[Commentary on the Text] Regarding "Buddha," the True Meaning school states that there are three meanings: omniscience, which distinguishes him from non-Buddhists; and great compassion, which distinguishes him from... [the Śrāvakas].
The equality of the two vehicles [is shared with] small bodhisattvas; others do not possess this. [Commentary]:
Those who have not yet shattered ignorance are called "small bodhisattvas. Because when they realize the stage of the Dharma-body, the three meanings become manifest, they do not shatter [ignorance].

They differ from the two vehicles because they differ from outsiders (*bāhya*). Because they differ from both outsiders and the two vehicles, they are simply [distinguished by] one meaning: the bodhisattva. Thus, the bodhisattva is doubly distinct from outsiders and the two vehicles.
Having attained two meanings yet not being equal [to others], the Buddha is able to transcend them; therefore, he is fully endowed with the three meanings.
This is the second interpretation of the *Śāstra*.
[Textual Commentary] The *Śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha is the ninth title; the Buddha is named "Awakened" (*buddha*), having awakened to both the mundane and the supramundane.
Because he has attained clear and great awakening regarding the constants, the impermanent, the numbered, the unnumbered, and so forth, he is called a Buddha.

[Commentary] Since the World-Honored One corresponds to the tenth [title], the Buddha is the ninth; this is based on a combined enumeration. If the "Tamer of Men" (*Puruṣadamyasārathi*) is opened as a separate title, then the Buddha becomes the tenth.
When these ten titles are complete, he is named the Honored One of the World (*Lokajyeṣṭha*); this is the capacity.
That which is awakened to as the object of awakening consists of the three pairs of dharmas, beginning with the mundane and so forth. The first pair concerns the ordinary and the sagely:

the mundane refers to the six classes of ordinary beings, while the supramundane refers to the four types of noble ones. The next pair concerns the small and the great: the impermanent refers to the dharmas of the ordinary and the Small Vehicle, while the permanent refers to the Mahāyāna dharma.
The final pair concerns the conceivable and the inconceivable: the conceivable refers to the six classes of ordinary beings and the three teachings [of the Tripitaka].
These numbers are all conceivable dharmas; only that which is perfect and beyond number is an inconceivable dharma.
Because these dharma-gates are clearly and instantaneously realized within a single mind, one is called a Buddha. Second, the present explanation has two parts:
first, according to the teachings.
