[Text] The Master of Tiantai says: "The Buddha exists by virtue of the *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) as the sixteen-foot Buddha; by virtue of the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths), as the sixteen-foot and the *vairocana* (lofty and distinguished) Buddha;
and by virtue of the *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all modes), as the Dharma-body Buddha. These three Buddhas cannot be said to be identical or distinct;
they are neither identical nor distinct, yet they are both identical and distinct."
[Commentary: Since "Buddha" (Buddha) is translated as "Awakened," there are three bodies, which are constituted by three kinds of awakened wisdom (*jñāna*).

If the Sarvākārajñatā (all-encompassing wisdom) constitutes the *śruti-piṭaka* (Tripitaka) and the Buddha of the six-foot stature, and if there are two Buddhas based on the Mārgajñatā (path-encompassing wisdom), this refers to the wisdom within and beyond the realms (*dhātu*) according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Within the realm, the Mārgajñatā constitutes the "Shared Teaching" (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), which consists merely of the emptiness of the six-foot stature.

Because dull-capacity bodhisattvas manifest expedient means for the sake of emptiness, the lineage of those outside the realms (the *bāhyaka-mārga*) achieves the "common" (*sāmānya*) and "distinct" (*viśeṣa*) aspects of the Middle Way;
the Honored One with a Distinctive Body (*vairocana-viśeṣa-kāya*) takes these two types of bodhisattvas as those who emerge from the Middle Way.

Thus, the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is established within the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), as well as the Common and Distinct Teachings, as the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*) in whom all phenomena converge. Although [these Buddhas] respond to four types of capacities, they are in fact none other than the three Buddhas.

Regarding these three Buddhas, they cannot be definitively established as identical, because where there is difference, there is no non-difference; nor can they be definitively established as distinct, because where there is difference, there is no non-difference.

Thus, one must forget both identity and difference, for this is the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*). Therefore, in discussing identity and difference, one must transcend the boundaries of specific categories.
Second, [this is] in terms of contemplation.

[Text]: Regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guan-jie*): through the contemplation of emptiness (*kong-guan*), one realizes that all phenomena (*dharma*) possess a single characteristic; through the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*), one realizes that all phenomena possess various characteristics;

through the contemplation of the middle (*zhong-guan*), one realizes that all phenomena possess neither the characteristic of identity nor difference—and yet they possess both identity and difference, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "all dharmas" are what are awakened to by the three contemplations, this means that each one awakens to the three truths (*trisatya*).

Thus, when the conceptualization of the distinctions between the three truths is forgotten through the awakening to emptiness, it is called "emptiness of ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); hence it is said to be "one characteristic.

When the awakening to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) perceives that all three truths are capable of establishing phenomena, it is called the "Tathāgatagarbha"; hence it is said to be "various characteristics. Within these various characteristics, the awakening to the three truths functions as a negation (*pratiṣedha*).

Because illuminating [the three bodies] simultaneously is called the primary principle (*paramārtha*), it is said that there is neither the characteristic of identity nor difference, yet they are both identical and different.

Previously, this was explained according to the teachings (*śāsana*), whereby the three wisdoms were separately shown to encompass the three bodies within the four *yānas*. Now, as this is explained according to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it must reside solely in the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) teaching.
If the Perfect contemplation is perfected, the three bodies of the four *yānas* are obtained spontaneously without seeking; it is like dust clearing from a mirror.
"Pure images manifest according to their forms to cause this discrimination," thus it says "and so forth. Fifth, the dwelling place:
he dwelt at Vulture Peak Mountain in the great city of Rājagṛha.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first, the dual heading.
[Text]: "As for 'dwelling,' the Buddha is the one who dwells, and Rājagṛha is the place where he dwells.
[Commentary]: The Buddha is the person who dwells; the city and mountain are the place where he dwells.

A person must necessarily have a dharma by which they dwell, just as in the world, an evil person necessarily dwells in their home by means of evil dharmas, while a good person dwells in their home by means of good dharmas.
It is likewise so now; when it is said that the Buddha dwells at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the royal city, how could it not be that the Śūraṅgama-samādhi is the dharma by which he abides?
Therefore, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana.

This Buddha’s dwelling place is called the "Eternally Quiescent Light" (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*). "Muni" refers to the person, and "light" (*prakāśa*) refers to the dharma; this is the union of person and dharma.

One may naturally distinguish between the "dweller" and the "abode"; yet when viewed from the perspective of Mount Cheng, both are dwellers, while Mount Cheng itself, in relation to the City of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), becomes the abode.
In every place, one follows the turning of the Dharma; it is just as the elixir of immortality (*rasāyana*) transforms iron into gold.
Thus, the *araṇya* site of Magadha is named the Field of Quiescent Extinction (*nirvāṇa-kṣetra*). How could this present Mount Cheng not be likewise? Therefore...

If one knows that the mind-factors capable of abiding cannot be distinguished [from the mind], yet speaks only of the physical body abiding upon earth and stone, then discourse regarding the great and small aspects of the subjective mind and its objects becomes useless.
Therefore, is there not a profound purpose in designating both the agent of abiding and the locus of abiding?
Second, the dual explanation of the two [aspects]. First, clarifying the dharmas that give rise [to them]. Second, the ancient interpretation. First, the Satyasiddhi school.
[Text] The Satyasiddhi school clarifies that there are eight abidings of the dharma: first, abiding within the great trichiliocosm; second, abiding in the place of reliance, which is the royal city;
third, abiding in the fivefold dharma-body with its life-span present; fourth, abiding in majestic deportment and benefit.

The five objects abide in the dwellings of dhyāna; the six [objects] abide in the dwellings of the Brahmās; the seven noble [objects] abide in the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth;
the eight great bases abide in the three samādhis; and the ultimate truth abides in the Great Vehicle.

[Commentary] This master explains that "abiding" (*sthiti*) does not merely refer to the physical substance of matter abiding in a city or mountain; rather, he clarifies eight kinds of phenomena capable of abiding:
(1) abiding in the trichiliocosm, which manifests the vastness of the transformations (*nirmāṇa*) that abide; (2) abiding in the basis (*āśraya*), which manifests the present capacity to abide;

(3) abiding in the fivefold division, which manifests the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates (*skandha*) that abide—these five divisions being precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation refer to the precepts associated with the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The remaining liberation is called "illumination," and the wisdom that knows this liberation is called the "eye of knowledge and vision.

This means knowing for oneself the first fruit through to the fourth fruit. Thus, these three preceding elements, when residing within the fruit, are designated as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Regarding its lifespan:

Regarding the present: because one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are extinguished. Thus, when the body is reduced to ashes, morality (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) remain;

liberation (*vimukti*) is the extinction [of defilements], and the knowledge of extinction (*kṣayajñāna*) is the wisdom that realizes and perceives this extinction. Consequently, while life is still present, the five aggregates abide in the four stations (*catasraḥ sthitayaḥ*).
Since all postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—are governed by the Dharma, one is able to benefit sentient beings throughout the five regions.

Regarding "abiding in the dhyāna-abodes": *dhyāna* refers to the four *dhyānas*, which are the heavens of the two realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*). They are called the "Brahma-abodes" (*brahma-vihāra*) because they are the dharmas of the devas of these two realms.
Furthermore, they are called the four Brahma-abodes because one dwells in the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and because one's own mind is always equal toward sentient beings.

By cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in addition to the four *dhyānas*, one is born in the Brahmā-heaven; therefore, they are termed "Brahma-abodes. (The text does not explicitly mention sympathetic joy and equanimity.)

Briefly stated, there are seven "saintly abodes" (*āryavihāra*), which refer to the three samādhis—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Because these three are cultivated by the noble ones (*ārya*), they are called "saintly abodes.
The eight "abodes of the great stage" (*mahāsthānavihāra*) are the Constant, Quiescent, and Radiant Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsvara*);
because all mental deliberation has ceased, it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha*). These eight meanings are all the dharmas in which the Tathāgata is able to abide. (2)
Commentary on the *Śāstra*.

[Text] The four abodes (*catvāraḥ vihārāḥ*) as explained in the commentary encompass the eight abodes: the celestial abode (*deva-vihāra*) and the Brahma-abode (*brahma-vihāra*) encompass the celestial abode;

the meditative abode (*samādhi-vihāra*) and the noble abode (*ārya-vihāra*) encompass the fivefold life-sustaining abode (*pañca-vidha-jīvita-vihāra*); and the Buddha-abode (*buddha-vihāra*) encompasses the great-place abode (*mahāsthāna-vihāra*). Furthermore, there is the trace-abode (*padasthāna-vihāra*), which is the royal abode.
In the city of Rājagṛha, he encompassed its boundaries and relied upon the three abodes of majestic deportment.
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Buddha dwells in Rājagṛha; Nāgārjuna explains the "Dharma capable of dwelling" by means of four meanings:
namely, the celestial, the Brahma-like, the noble, and the Buddha. According to Paramārtha, the eight dharmas do not exceed these four; therefore, the Great Master [Nāgārjuna] employs these four.
In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, the "divine abode" (*deva-vihāra*) and the "abode of truth" (*satya-vihāra*) as taught by Master Paramārtha are identical in both name and meaning;
however, while the former refers to the four immeasurable concentrations (*catur-apramāṇa-samādhi*), this [latter] subsumes two within two.

Furthermore, the "noble abode" (*ārya-vihāra*) and the "noble abode" as taught by Paramārtha are identical in both name and meaning, yet this additionally subsumes the fivefold life-span (*pañca-vidha-āyuḥ*); this, then, subsumes one within one.

This subsumes two [categories]. The Buddha’s dwelling (*buddhavihāra*) and the dwelling in the Great Realm of True Reality (*tattvārtha-mahāsthāna-vihāra*) differ in name but are identical in meaning;
thus, by subsuming one with one, the four dwellings discussed here already encompass the five mentioned there.

Furthermore, the treatise states that among these four dwellings, he dwells in the "Noble Dwelling" (*āryavihāra*) and the "Buddha Dwelling" out of compassion for sentient beings, and dwells in Rājagṛha as his "trace dwelling" (*padavihāra*).

Furthermore, this meaning subsumes the three abodes of the True Truth (*satyadharma*), because the royal city is the place of reliance, because the royal city is within the great trichiliocosm, and because the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) do not depart from the royal city. Question:

Since the Buddha is able to abide in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, why is it necessary to speak of the three [abodes] of the noble Brahmā heavens? Answer: The Tathāgata’s own practice truly resides in the *Śūraṅgama*.

Because Rāma dwells in the remaining three dharmas for the sake of benefiting others, if his mind does not dwell in dharmas such as those of Brahmā, how could his mouth be able to preach the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables?
Therefore, the *Miaole lun* (Treatise on the Sublime Joy) states regarding the "four dwellings":

"From the broad to the narrow, the superior encompasses the inferior; thus, the 'Heaven' [dharma] encompasses a wider range of capacities, while the 'Buddha' [dharma] is the most narrow. Since the two middle ones are discussed alternately, it is so stated."

From the broad to the narrow, since the Buddha’s dwelling is supreme, there is no virtue he does not encompass; thus, the three categories—the noble and so forth—are explained as being the virtues of ordinary and small-vehicle practitioners.
Second, the current explanation has two parts: first, the teaching.

[Text] The Master of Tiantai said: "The Buddha of the six-foot body dwells in the Truth (satya); the Buddha of the combined body of the six-foot and the exalted special body (vairocana) dwells in both the Truth and the Middle Way;
the Buddha of the exalted special body dwells in both the Conventional (saṃvṛti) and the Middle Way; and the Dharma-body Buddha dwells in the Middle Way."

[Commentary] The treatise clarifies the four abodes (*vihāra*), yet their meaning remains general. Therefore, our school elucidates that the Buddha of the Four Teachings abides in the three truths (*satya*), further discussing both the shared and exclusive modes of abiding.

Because the analytical observation of phenomena (*dharmapratyavekṣaṇā*) taught in the Tripitaka is clumsy, the resulting Buddhahood is limited to a body sixteen feet tall, abiding solely in the truth of reality (*tattvasatya*).
The observation of the essence of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) taught in the Shared Teaching is skillful and capable of... [text fragment ends].

Because one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, the Buddha attained manifests as two bodies according to the capacities of sentient beings—whether sharp or dull: a *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) body for those dwelling in the true [nature], and a *zhùzhēn* (lofty and distinguished) body for those dwelling in the middle.
Because the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*) expounds the middle and cultivates sequential contemplation, the Buddha it attains is exclusively the *zhùzhēn* body;

this is because one must separately cultivate the adornments of conditions (*yuán*) and understanding (*liǎo*). Thus, this Buddha dwells in both the conventional and the middle. The Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*)... [is different].

In the ultimate meaning, the Middle Way is endowed with all dharmas; because the myriad practices within the cause are cultivated without cultivation, and the myriad virtues upon the fruit are accomplished without accomplishment, the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are thus named the *dharmakāya*.
Abiding solely in the Middle Way, how could the Buddhas of the three preceding teachings be separate from the *dharmakāya*?
Now, we shall clearly distinguish the four differences therein; therefore, each of the four Buddhas abides [in their respective state].
The Dharma abides in the mountain city. There are two contemplations. [Commentary on the Text]:

The contemplation of the understanding of emptiness (śūnyatā) abides in the true; the contemplation of the provisional abides in the conventional; and the contemplation of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha) abides in the Middle Way.

[Commentary] Within a single state of mind, one perfectly cultivates the three contemplations and abides in the three truths. By means of this dharma of abiding, one dwells in the place where one resides.
If one does not cease for even a single thought-moment, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one practices the Buddha’s conduct.

As the Sūtra says, "In these places, stupas should be erected"; this is precisely that meaning. Second, clarifying the place where one dwells. Part two: first, the city; second, the first [sub-section].
Exegesis on the Causes and Conditions.

[Textual Commentary]: Regarding "Rājagṛha" (the City of the King’s Abode), the *Śāstra* extensively explains the causes and conditions for its initial establishment. It was situated amidst the five mountains;

after being burned seven times and rebuilt seven times, the king came to reside here, hence it is called "The King’s Abode. Furthermore, it is said that when other dwellings were burned, the king’s abode was not burned.
Later, they all cleared away [the grass], saying, "This is the King's Abandonment," and thus escaped being burned. From that time onward, it was called Rājagṛha (The King’s Abandonment).
[Commentary] Although this passage is brief, the meaning can be discerned; if one wishes to know it in full detail, one should consult that treatise.
Second, the explanation of the contemplative practice.

[Text] Regarding the interpretive contemplation (*guan-jie*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a palace: because the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) dwells therein, it is called "King’s Palace" (*Rājagṛha*).
[Commentary] The various contemplative interpretations mentioned above are all "contemplations based on phenomena" (*fu-fa guan*).

Because they do not rely on external objects or meanings to represent the contemplated dharma, this city and mountain constitute a "contemplation based on objects" (*tuo-shi guan*). This is like the current King’s Palace, which relies on the meaning of "covering" (*pi-yi*).
The "Manifestation" (*biao*) refers to the meaning of relying upon sovereignty (*īśvara*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), as it manifests good and evil kings. Thus, the *Miaole* states:
"One should know that good and evil kings are contrasted with the neutral 'abandonment' (*avyākṛta-tyāga*).

It should be understood that the neutral pervades all eight consciousnesses, whereas good and evil kings pertain only to the sixth consciousness, because this sixth consciousness permeates the three natures—namely, the nature of goodness, the nature of evil, and the nature of neutrality."
This indeterminate nature, like the other four aggregates, serves as the object of observation;
taking the natures of good and evil as the subject of observation, one must employ this sixth mind when first cultivating the practice of contemplation.

This is because this mind is able to give rise to the discrimination of delight and aversion, thereby acting as the cause for good and evil. That which is called "good" is so named in contrast to evil.
This is not ultimate goodness because this king-number is fundamentally formed by the habitual perfuming of views and attachments;

even when a person who has perfected the name-and-characteristics stage gives rise to wholesome thoughts, they cannot entirely subdue these tendencies, as they remain inseparable from views and attachments. Therefore, the minds of the ten objects are all termed demonic obstacles;
only through the inconceivable contemplation can they be called "wholesomely pure. If one were to directly use this mind to contemplate the principle of true reality, [it would be ineffective].
It would be like attempting to suspend Mount Sumeru with a lotus fiber—merely increasing conceptual discrimination while rendering the cessation of thought impossible.
If one realizes that this mind is inherently evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*), then inherent evil becomes interfused and harmonious; there is no phenomenon to which it does not accord.

Thus, the seventh, eighth, and ninth consciousnesses are naturally subsumed and become the wondrous contemplation (*miao-guan*). For this reason, it is said that "the object is itself the contemplation. When subject and object have both vanished, thought ceases.
In this discussion, we consider that because the initial stage of practice can be cultivated through the contemplation of perfect subtlety, the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states:

"If one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherent evil' (*shingiaku*), how can one believe in the existence of the conduct of inherent virtue? One must hear of inherent evil because, by knowing inherent evil, one realizes that the cultivation of evil is fundamentally empty;
thus, within the three contemplations and ten vehicles (*sankan jūjō*), there is no delusion to be broken and no principle to be established.
The cultivation of meritorious virtues manifests quiescence as the practice of non-action; therefore, these virtues are invoked by their intrinsic nature to designate this practice.
If this meaning is obscure, then to merely claim that the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the subject of contemplation will ultimately not constitute the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*).

How could it be that the three preceding teachings do not take the sovereign of good and evil as the subject of contemplation? Furthermore, one must understand that it is not only Chengshan who takes the aggregates (*skandha*) as the object.
Since all contemplations of phenomena must involve contemplating the aggregates (*skandhas*), Miaole states: "Furthermore, the objects of all contemplations do not transcend the five aggregates.
Now, these mountains and so forth are presented in terms of the aggregates for the sake of convenience;

thus, when various texts simply speak of "objects and wisdom," one knows from the commentary—that the objects of all contemplations do not transcend the five aggregates—that there is nothing in the "contemplation based on events" (*shishi guan*) or the "contemplation based on dharmas" (*fufa guan*) that is not contemplated.
The implicit statement that "this mountain" and so forth refer to the *skandhas* (aggregates) is because the term "mountain" conveniently expresses the meaning of the *skandhas*.

Therefore, when the word "aggregate" (*skandha*) is explicitly stated, it is not convenient for the various textual passages; thus, although it may be inconvenient, one simply speaks of "object and cognition" (*viṣaya-jñāna*).

While not explicitly stating "the five aggregates," there is no observed object that is not an aggregate. Hence, the preceding sentence says they do not transcend the five aggregates, and one simply speaks of "objects."
The *Zhiji* (Exposition on Wisdom) states that contemplating a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇacitta*) is itself emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.

Although it does not explicitly mention the aggregates (*skandha*), since a single thought-moment is not something other than the aggregates, for anyone to rely on this and insist that the objects of contemplation do not include the aggregates is a grave error that contradicts the texts and subverts the meaning.
Furthermore, to perversely insist that "only within the *Zhi Guan* (Calming and Contemplation) is there the contemplation of practice" is likewise mistaken.

The *Fadeng* (法得) [treatise] distinguishes between the various phenomena of the objective spheres (*āyatana*) and the dharmas, whereas the *Guan* (觀) [treatises] do not distinguish the aggregates (*skandha*).

This is merely a personal preference for establishing one's own rules. Since none of the contemplative methods in the various texts exclude the aggregates, what hindrance is there? Furthermore, in the *Miaole* (妙樂), it states that when contemplating the aggregates, one must clarify the skillful means of correct cultivation;

yet, distinguishing the objective sphere and the mind—how could this be anything other than "discarding the foot-measure to adopt the inch-measure"? (i.e., rejecting the comprehensive for the trivial).

Is "simplifying the mind" not precisely the act of discarding conceptual thought to grasp the inconceivable? How can one so stubbornly oppose this and insist that one should not simplify the aggregates?
Furthermore, this person clings to various texts, asserting that contemplating the mind by relying on events or phenomena (*shōji-fuhō*) cannot be practiced;

they claim that only the contemplation of dharmas according to practice (*gyōkan-hōkan*) as found in the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) may be cultivated. They then cite scriptural precedents to admonish the writings of heterodox teachers.
According to that text, it says: "The twelve divisions [of the canon] are named based on their reliance on phenomena;

although they possess the names of the 'three contemplations,' the ten objects and ten vehicles are not listed under the heading of a single division, but rather a single phrase is applied [to each]. How could this single phrase suffice to expound the gates of contemplation?
Is it not the case that people nowadays claim one can practice by taking phenomena as the object or contemplating the mind, without needing to rely on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? How could this be so?

Is this not entirely the same as the heterodox masters of past generations? Now, evaluating the *Yili* (Examples of Meaning), it is evident that this person’s explanation is utterly ignorant of Jingxi [Zhiyi]’s intent in refuting them.

Why is this? The *Yili* addresses doubts primarily because heterodox masters erroneously claimed that the ten objects and ten vehicles of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* constitute only gradual and circular contemplation;
it was solely for the sake of Master Ding who held that the twelvefold scripture consists of the contemplation of the mind.
The text states that by practicing the "sudden-sudden" contemplation (*dun-dun guan*), one immediately attains it; therefore, Master Jingxi’s aforementioned instruction has this meaning:

it is intended to refute those heterodox masters who claim that the single phrase "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*) in the twelve divisions of Dharma Master Ding’s teachings fully expounds the "sudden-sudden" gate of contemplation.
Since those heterodox masters [already] possess the ten objects (*shi jing*) and ten vehicles (*shi sheng*) of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* themselves...
This gradual perfection is ultimately unwilling to employ the "contemplation of affairs" (*sūtra*) among the twelve divisions of the teachings for cultivation;

how could it be the same as the masters of correct interpretation who, when reaching the sections on the "Contemplation of the City" and "Mountains," provide scholars wishing to practice with the texts on the "expedient means of cessation and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-upāya*), "correct cultivation," and "discerning the objects," thereby establishing their actual practice? If this were so, how could these be considered the "ten objects" (*daśa-viṣaya*)?
Why are the ten modes of practice (*daśayāna*) not listed exclusively [here]? Could it be that you are applying a single phrase alone to expound the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*)?
Furthermore, when have you ever said that contemplating the mind regarding phenomenal dharmas (*shifaguanxin*) can be practiced without relying on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?

Nor have you stated that the "Contemplation of the City and Mountains" and other such practices are sudden-sudden teachings; why then do you denounce them as being identical to the false teachers of past generations? Moreover, in the *Fahua xuanyi*...
The *Yi* (Meaning) section of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "Upon hearing a single phrase, one integrates phenomena into principle;
this is called 'cultivating contemplation' (*xiu guan*) without waiting for the formal observation of an object. This precedent established by our ancestors is clear and can be readily examined.
How can one stubbornly insist that the gate of contemplating phenomena (*shifa guanmen*) cannot be practiced? Such a person further refuses altogether to transmit [the teachings].

The Master of the Dharma records in his private notes that when teaching others to practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one must first have a profound mastery of the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* before practicing according to the various texts on contemplating the mind.
If this is the case, then practitioners of contemplation would have no need at all for a teacher or spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Consequently, among the five conditions, the condition of the spiritual friend would be entirely useless. (Four conditions...)
It is better to lack the conditions for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) than to ever abandon them; as the Great Master said: "If one can personally resolve [the teachings], one may travel alone;
however, if one has not yet mastered the obstacles and difficulties, it is not appropriate to abandon [the teacher]. The Sūtra says:

"By following and learning from a virtuous teacher, one attains the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, one who is fully conversant with the ten stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is a great Dharma Master. This is a... [great Dharma Master].
"Must one necessarily be such a person in order to cultivate the contemplation of phenomena and mind within all texts?

To make such erroneous claims is to obstruct the transmission of the Dharma by failing to proclaim the gates of contemplation; it hinders those of initial resolve from proceeding according to their teachers, causing even greater harm.
Let scholars take note of this. This concludes the second section: the explanation of the causes and conditions of the two mountains and the two beginnings.
[Text] Regarding Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata (Vulture Peak), the *Śāstra* translates it as "Vulture Head. Paramārtha translates it as "Crooked Bird Mountain. It is located to the southeast of Rājagṛha.
Piṇḍava-parvata (Mount Vulture) is to the southwest; Ṛṣigiri-parvata (Sage Mountain) is to the northwest; Kālaparvata (Black Earth Mountain) is to the northeast;
and Śvetaparvata (White Earth Mountain) is in the center. The central area, three *yojanas* in extent, is level and even; this is the royal city.
[This is] a city.

[Commentary: The shape of the mountain peak resembles the head of a vulture; some say it is Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak) because this bird possesses spiritual knowledge of when people die, and because many sages and spirits dwell hidden therein.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that the vulture is black in color and has many offspring.
Second, the explanation by way of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
[Text]: Regarding "the mountain of the contemplating mind," "spirit" (*ling*) refers to divine wisdom, which is *prajñā*; "vulture" (*jiewei*) refers to the myriad virtues, which is *vimukti*;
and "mountain" refers to immovability, which is the *dharmakāya*. That this is constantly contemplated by the mind-king is precisely what is meant by "contemplation."
This dwelling place causes all mental factors to enter therein together. [Commentary:

In the *Wondrous Sutra Commentary*, the three characters were first correlated with the five aggregates (*skandhas*), and subsequently, by contemplating these three characters, they were established as the three virtues;
thus, one realizes that the aggregates are themselves the principle (*li*). In this present text, the explanation is abbreviated, directly using the three characters to represent the three virtues.

Although it is not explicitly stated that the meaning of the *skandhas* (aggregates) should be taken as the substance of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), one must know that the *skandhas* are the retributive phenomena of view-delusion and thought-delusion;
thus, cultivated evil is precisely inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*) that constitutes the three virtues.

If this sovereign of good and evil were not inherently complete within the nature, how could it abide eternally in the secret treasury? If the mental factors and the afflictions were not inherently evil, how [could they be so]?

Because they are able to attain [the same realization], they enter therein together. Second, clarifying the absence of the assembly of co-hearers, in two parts: first, the direct explanation. [Textual Commentary]:
This sutra lacks mention of a co-hearing assembly because there were five occasions. At Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the assembly did not hear what was spoken in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa;
in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, the assembly did not hear what was spoken in the dream; and in the dream, the assembly did not hear [what followed].
After awakening from the dream, he spoke to the assembly; because they were not in a single location, they are not listed among those who heard [the teaching] together.
[Commentary: At that time, there were four occasions at five locations: first, when the Introduction was spoken at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;

second, when the Lifespan was spoken within the chamber; third, when seeing the golden drum in a dream; fourth, when, having awakened from the dream, he went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to speak; and fifth, when the assembly was enumerated.
In the *Praise of the Buddha-land of the Golden Treasure Canopy Mountain King*, when praising Śākyamuni, there are five periods;
however, because the introduction and the account of the dream both take place at Vulture Peak, there are only four locations. Second, the resolution of doubts.
[Text]: If this were so, Ānanda should not have said, "Thus have I heard. However, although he did not hear it himself, the Buddha spoke it again for him;
furthermore, because he attained the Buddha’s Samādhi of Awakening and was able to realize it for himself, he was permitted to say, "Thus have I heard."
[Commentary] The intent of the question is this: while the four Buddhas taught on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and Ānanda was in the Śraddhālakṣaṇa Hall, why is it said "Thus have I heard"?
Although this is answered below, in the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness), the assembly appointed Ānanda as the Buddha’s attendant, and Ānanda requested four vows from the Buddha:
first, not to accept worn-out robes; second, not to accept separate invitations; third... [text continues].
Unlike other bhikṣus who must see for themselves what they have not yet seen, when I requested that the four unheard sūtras be spoken again, the Buddha granted my request.

Furthermore, those who have attained the Buddha-awakening samādhi (buddha-avabodha-samādhi) are empowered by the Buddha’s awakening-force; because they are like the Buddha, it is called "Buddha-awakening.
Those capable of self-realization do not depend on repeated instruction. However, on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment, Ānanda...

I was only twenty-five years old when I first became an attendant; according to the previous scriptures, even those two venerable elders still prefaced their teachings with "Thus have I heard," let alone one who was recently in the chamber of Śraddhādhimukta.
[Commentary] Second, the introduction; it is also called the "Separate Introduction. First, the two names are listed.

[Textual Analysis] From the passage "At that time, the Tathāgata... onwards is the introductory section (*nidāna*). Because it introduces the following seventeen chapters, it is also called the "Separate Introduction" (*pratyeka-nidāna*).
It is termed "separate" because it distinguishes this sutra from other sutras, and because it serves as the basis for the specific title. Thus, it is called "separate."
[Commentary] Although these are alternative names, they also possess varying lengths. To describe the "Preface Chapter" (序品) exhaustively, there are distinct divisions;

because this separate preface differs from those of other sutras, it is established with a specific name, "The Golden Light" (金光明). Thus, we know that this preface is the original source for the alternative names.
Second, the explanation of the two prefaces. First, a general indication of the textual characteristics of the two prefaces. First, the specific [explanation].
Regarding the two aspects of the marks, first is the explanation of the seven distinctions. First, the seven sections of the sutra text:

[Textual Commentary] The seven distinct meanings are as follows: first, from "At that time, the Tathāgata... down to one and a half lines, which is the distinction of entering meditative concentration;
second, from "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*... down to the twenty-seven verse lines, which is the distinction of the narrative description; third, from... [text continues].

1. From the end of the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) is the section distinguishing the doubt; 2. from "In this way, the Great Being... is the section distinguishing the auspicious response (*praṇidhāna*);
3. from "Śraddhālakṣaṇa sees the Buddha... is the section distinguishing the expression of doubt; 4. from "The four Buddhas said... is the section distinguishing the cessation of doubt;
5. from "From the desire and form realms... is the section distinguishing the gathering of the assembly.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the sequence of the seven [stages].

[Text] Regarding "arising": the Buddha is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), yet when sentient beings strike upon him, he wishes to respond; therefore, he manifests the ritual procedures.
Although the Tathāgata is eternally quiescent, he still delights in entering concentration to roam within the *dharmatā*, and emerging from it, he expounds the King of Sutras for the sake of faith.
Having heard that the profound Dharma and the Dharma of doubt are both for ordinary people with short lifespans, they consequently harbor doubts.

Through the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit, this doubt can induce a response; because of this response, the four Buddhas appear. Once the Buddhas appear, the doubts are dispelled; because the doubts are dispelled, the Buddhas immediately cause those doubts to cease.
Since the rain of Dharma is about to fall, the great assembly gathers like clouds. These seven matters differ from other sutras.
The distinctions have been stated; the seven distinctions are now concluded.
[Commentary] As for those who first enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), their great awakening is suddenly perfected, illuminating all while remaining eternally tranquil.

Their present entry into concentration is intended to demonstrate the ritual procedure, causing people to delight in concentration. Next, regarding the sequential narration: having entered the wondrous concentration, they perceive the nobility of the Dharma. Immediately—

In this context, when the King of Sutras is described as being "issued forth" from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the narrator has not actually demonstrated the characteristics of emerging from concentration;

rather, because stillness does not obstruct illumination, it is merely said that he has "emerged. The Buddha’s intent in not emerging from concentration while preaching this sutra is fundamentally to reveal that within stillness there is illumination.
Next, regarding those who harbor doubts: since the constant Dharma has been described as that which the Buddha has realized...
Xinxiang then raised doubts regarding whether the "Life Span" chapter could be called a "Response to the Dharma" (Fashuiying) or similar; this can be clearly understood from the subsequent text.
Second, the three distinct categories are explained.
[Wenju]: Alternatively, one may distinguish three parts: first, from "At that time" onwards, it is named the "Narrative Introduction" (Xushu xu); second, from the "Life Span" [chapter] onwards...

The lower fascicle is titled "Preface on the Manifestation of Auspicious Omens" (Part 3), which begins with "At that time" (Section 4) and continues with the "Preface on the Assembly of the Multitude" starting from "The Tathāgata," and so forth.
[Commentary: At times the Great Master made such distinctions, and Zhǎng'ān recorded them alongside the previous seven; the differences lie merely in their opening and closing arrangements.
Second, the description of the characteristics, which consists of two parts: first, the formal presentation of the narrative description.

[Text] Regarding the phrase "narrating the introduction": it refers to the first five lines of the subsequent seventeen chapters. It narrates the Chapter on the Lifespan (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) as three parts:

first, two lines narrate the merit of the fruit; next, one line narrates the arising of doubt; and finally, two lines narrate the severing of that doubt (the details of which may be sought elsewhere).
The final one and a half lines narrate the intention of the Chapter on Repentance (*Pratikarma-parivarta*) to destroy evil and give rise to goodness.
The following one and a half lines describe the "Chapter on the Difficulty of Producing Good and Destroying Evil," and so forth.

The next six lines describe the "Chapter on Emptiness" regarding the destruction of evil, specifically the destruction of the three obstacles, and so forth. From the section on the Four World-Protecting Kings downward is the description of that chapter, which is easy to understand.
"Great Eloquence" refers to the description of that chapter. "The Mother of the Niliṇa Ghosts" refers to the description of the Goddess of Merit (Śrī).
Since this chapter concerns the same female deity, it refers to the Earth Goddess; since this chapter concerns Mahābrahmā and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it refers to Vaiśravaṇa;
since Vaiśravaṇa is the general and Brahmā and Śakra are the lords, by mentioning the lords one obtains the generals and subordinates;
and since the Kiṃnaras and others are those under his command, by mentioning those under his command one obtains their jurisdiction. All that I have now spoken...

"Buddha’s secrets" refers to the introduction of the two chapters on "Excellence in Collection" (*Sangiti-paryāya*), which state that worldly secrets can be used to govern a nation and supramundane secrets can be used to attain the Way;
thus, it is known that these two chapters are introduced here. "If one hears this sutra" marks the transition to the chapter on "Ghosts and Spirits" (*Bhūta-graha-paryāya*).
Within the chapter on ghosts and spirits, there is a clear exposition of the merit of listening to the Dharma for the sake of the eight classes of beings.
Regarding "The Protected," and so forth: the two lines beginning with "wearing pure garments" describe the Chapter on Prophecy (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*).
Because the three great beings and ten thousand devas possess a pure mind of profound reverence, as pure as space, they protect the prophecy. Regarding "If one should hear," and so forth:
this describes the Chapters on the Removal of Disease and the Flowing Water, etc. That hearing the names and taking the medicine results in all diseases being eliminated is what is called "good."

To have obtained a human body and further be able to cultivate meritorious deeds through giving is to have successfully attained the human path. For a fish to hear the name of the Buddha is to have successfully attained the heavenly body;
this is precisely what is meant by the "heavenly path. Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) is described in the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body":
that the tigress was immediately liberated after consuming flesh and blood—is this not indeed Right Livelihood? If one hears even a single line regarding repentance...

In the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha," it is said that among the Buddhas of the three periods of time, most of these bodhisattvas were formerly Buddhas—that is, past Buddhas—and are also future Buddhas.
To be praised by these bodhisattvas is to be praised by the Buddha himself.
The intent of this narrative can only be vaguely apprehended; it cannot be grasped with complete clarity, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the section on those who harbor doubts: it describes how when one contemplates profound meanings, one inevitably harbors doubts concerning the Dharma realized and the lifespan of the Realizer.
Regarding the section on severing doubts: the Buddha originally intended for doubts to be severed so that faith may arise. Regarding the section on the Chapter of Repentance:
its primary purpose is to destroy evil, while its secondary purpose is to generate goodness. Regarding the section on the Chapter of Praise: its primary purpose is to generate goodness.
The "Chapter on Emptiness" (Śūnyatā-parivarta) is presented here to refute evil; this chapter guides the cultivation of wholesome states and the extinction of unwholesome ones.

Since the current text specifically addresses the elimination of the three obstacles, it cites Mahābrahmā and Śakra as the leaders of the Vaiśravaṇa (Daśadig-vaiśravaṇa) host, and the Kinnaras and others as those led by Vaiśravaṇa.
Thus, the chapter is introduced by naming its presiding deities. This concludes the formal discourse on the perfect accumulation of merit.
This section on the "Correct Discourse on Governing the State" and the "Skillful Gathering for Listening to the Sūtra" are both categorized as the Secret Store because they flow forth from it;

thus, these two chapters are described using the term "secret. Regarding the description of the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): because his mind was purified like space through hearing the sūtra, he obtained the prediction;
now it is said that his body and mind were free from defilement. Regarding the description of the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body": [it refers to] consuming the Prince's body.
Having already attained liberation, it is shown that his life is sustained not by improper food; therefore, the single phrase "right livelihood" is now used to describe this.
Regarding the "Chapter Praising the Buddha": although there are three sections in which bodhisattvas praise the Buddha in verse, these bodhisattvas are for the most part ancient Buddhas;
even if they are practitioners of the path, they are nonetheless Buddhas of the present. Thus, when the current Buddha praises the practitioner, [it is likewise so].
This is because it concerns the Buddha that his chapter is described; "fǎngbò" (彷彿) means an appearance that is not distinct.

The character *wěi* (薳) is pronounced *wěi* and means "distant," as in the expression "one must not exceed one's own clear boundaries. Second, showing both [the subject and the description], there are two parts:
first, the inquiry is raised.
[Text] Question: Who composed this commentary? [Commentary] Part two:
The answer, which first presents the old interpretation and refutes its errors.

[Text] The old masters who compiled the *Ji jing* (Collected Scriptures) say: "If that were so, then this would be a treatise (*śāstra*) and not a scripture (*sūtra*); furthermore, it would contradict the scriptural text, for the text says: 'I...'"

Now it shall be explained. Some say this refers to the "characteristics of faith" (*śraddhā-liṅga*). If that were so, since the characteristics of faith have already been described in profound detail, what matter could possibly give rise to doubt?

[Commentary: Among the former masters there were two schools of thought. One school held that Ānanda refuted [the claim] by stating, "This is a treatise (*śāstra*), not a sūtra," because it was spoken by the Buddha.
Those works produced by disciples of the Three Vehicles after the passing of the named Sūtras are all called Śāstras.

A Sūtra says: "I shall now expound the dharmas of repentance and so forth. How could the dharma of repentance have been spoken by Ānanda? Is this not a violation of the text? The golden drum in the dream is the Buddha’s Dharma-body;
because one strikes it with wisdom, the dharma of repentance is expounded according to the capacities of beings. It must be so.
Because he knows that the golden drum is the Buddha’s true self, it is said, "I speak. Second, Xinxiang (信相) refutes this, saying:
"If it were Xinxiang, who has already narrated the beginning and end in detail, he should not harbor such doubts. "Narrating in detail" (*xuànù*)—*xuàn* is synonymous with *xuán* (suspended/pending).
The second part of the double inquiry clarifies the first [point], which is the clarification of the Master’s intention.
[Text]: Furthermore, how could it be that one who did not compile the sutra suddenly composed a preface, and the Master then claimed it was composed by the Buddha himself?
[Commentary] Two difficulties arise; the response applies to both. First, the difficulty arises. [Wenju] The objector says:
"If that is so, it is then the main scripture itself; how can it be called a 'Preface'?"

[Commentary] If this were spoken by the Buddha, it would be the "True Doctrine" (Zhengzong); how then could it be called the "Introduction" (Xù)? Second, the answer applies to both [the True Doctrine and the Introduction].
First, he uses the cause to illustrate the fruit.
[Wenju]: This poses no hindrance; if even a Bodhisattva can sit in dhyāna, join his palms, and speak ten million verses, how much more so the Tathāgata?
The power of his secret speech (*mukha-guhya*) responds to the capacities of beings; what is there that it cannot accomplish?
[Commentary] It is not only that he was able to respond to this; the Buddha’s composition of the preface also demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration does not obstruct preaching.

Verifying this through the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha’s narration was indeed occurring while in samādhi. How could the thousands of myriads of verses be restricted solely to the "Proper Teaching" (*samyak-śāsana*) section?

The Buddha’s secret speech regarding the fruit adapts to the capacities of beings; how could it be that he does not provide an introduction or a general explanation when teaching the correct doctrine? Therefore, the conclusion states: "What is there that he would not do?
Second, citing texts to prove this conclusion has two parts: first, citing the relevant passage from the current text as proof.
[Commentary on the Text]: The text states, "I shall now expound the dharmas of repentance and so forth. This is a clear proof. [Commentary on the Record]:
Second, citing the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as an analogy. [Text]:
Within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the emanation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) expounds the six *pāramitās*, yet it is likewise entitled with a preface; this is the analogy.
[Commentary] In the introduction to that sutra, it is explained that the Buddha extended his broad and long tongue and emitted immeasurable light;
each ray of light transformed into precious flowers, and upon each flower there was a manifested Buddha preaching the six *pāramitās*.

Since that [passage] is titled an "introduction" (*nidāna*), how could it be the main body of the sutra (*sūtra-pradeśa*)? Second, following the specific introduction (*pratyeka-nidāna*), the text is analyzed in seven parts: first, entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*); second, the specific [manifestation].
The initial outline of the sections.
[Wenju]: The explanation of "entering meditative concentration" is divided into three parts: first, one phrase and one character clarify the subject who enters;
second, two characters and two phrases clarify the dharmas entered into; and finally, the last two phrases provide the conclusion.
[Commentary] In order to clarify both the person who travels and the dharmas through which they travel, the character "traveling" (遊) is placed at the beginning of this section.
One must understand that the explanation of the meaning does not follow the same pattern as the literal reading of the text. Second, the sequential explanation; first, the person who travels.
"At this time the Tathāgata was traveling.
[Commentary] The text has three parts: first, the explanation of "at this time," second, the ancient interpretation.
[Wénjù] Regarding "at this time," Zhéntì says there are five kinds of three times: first, the time before preaching, the time of preaching, and the time after preaching;...
Second, at the time of refuting the non-Buddhists' doctrine of existence in the past and future; third, at the time of establishing that there is hearing when there is speaking;

fourth, at the time of planting seeds, maturation, and liberation; fifth, at the time when the Buddha wishes to speak, the assembly wishes to hear, and it is neither high nor low, but perfectly balanced.
[Commentary] Second, the present explanation.

[Text] Now we shall discuss only the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the capacity [of beings] to attain the Way: whether it is when the wisdom-eye attains the Way and the wisdom merges with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
or when the dharma-eye attains the Way and the wisdom merges with the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); or when the Buddha-eye attains the Way.
When wisdom merges with the Middle Way, the Buddha wishes to traverse the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and observe when sentient beings attain the Path;
therefore, he says, "At this time.

[Commentary] This does not employ the five kinds of three times used by ancient masters, but rather discusses the time when the Buddha, discerning their capacities, perceives that they have attained the Path.
The Way is like a thoroughfare that must be traversed by unifying the three wisdoms with the three truths; only at that time is the Tathāgata’s manifestation of discerning capacities fully realized.

When it is said that the Buddha “desires to equalize,” this refers to the mode of his transformative teaching (*huayi*), and does not mean that he only now perceives and knows through his illumination.
There are two explanations regarding the Tathāgata’s [discernment]; first, a brief indication.
[Text] "Tathāgata" is the first of the ten epithets.
[Commentary] Regarding the two explanations, the first points to others for a detailed exposition.
[Text] The explanations of the Tripiṭaka masters regarding "Tathāgata" are numerous and are not recorded here.
[Commentary] Second, the essential explanation of the three [aspects]. First, the explanation based on compassion and wisdom. First, the explanation based on the meaning.
[Text] Now, it is said that "wisdom" is because its illumination of principle is equal to that of all Buddhas; it is said "like" (tathā) because its compassion is equal to that of all Buddhas;
it is said "come" (āgata) because all Buddhas should abide within the secret treasury (*guhyagarbha*), yet they appear in the world solely for the sake of compassion.
"Therefore, he comes.
[Commentary] In the *Fahua wenju*, it is explained that each of the three bodies possesses the meaning of "suchness" (*tathatā*) and the meaning of "coming.

Here, "suchness" is interpreted through the mutual merging of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, while "coming" is interpreted as the appearance of the Response-body in the world. Provided that the meaning is established, it matters not whether the interpretation is general or specific; this applies to the Buddha.
If one follows wisdom, it should be understood as in the *Guhyagarbha*: he comes to the triple world solely for the sake of conforming to compassion. Second, citing scriptural evidence:
the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states, "He comes by means of the path of suchness to achieve perfect enlightenment."

[Commentary] That which is able to mount [the vehicle] is wisdom; that which is the path according to reality is principle. Their coming together to achieve [enlightenment] is the manifestation of compassionate response.
This first explanation is based on the practice of wisdom. [Text] The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
"It comes from the eleven kinds of emptiness" refers to its arrival in terms of wisdom; "it comes from the six *pāramitās*" refers to its arrival in terms of practice.
Regarding the practice:

[Commentary] Although it simply says "comes," it already fully possesses the meaning as explained above; that is, in terms of merit and wisdom, one comes to adorn the Dharma-body, and that which is adorned is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness).
This is the explanation of the name "Tathāgata" found in the "Brahmacarya" chapter of this Great Sūtra. Third, in terms of exposition.
The proof and explanation are in two parts. First, citing the treatise:

[Wenju] The commentary explains that understanding according to the characteristics of dharmas is termed "suchness" (tathatā), while explaining according to the characteristics of dharmas is termed "coming.
[Ji] Second, the explanation and establishment.

[Text]: Now it is explained that because one understands the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the three truths as they truly are (*tathatā*), and because one speaks of the characteristics of the three truths as they have come (*āgata*), one is called a Tathāgata.
[Commentary]: The primordially existing Dharma takes the wondrous True, the Conventional, and the Middle as its characteristics; when wisdom accords with this understanding, it is itself the Dharma.

Because it responds to the hidden [reality], it is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*). To speak of this Suchness is to describe the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which appears according to the capacities of sentient beings;

therefore, it is called "Coming. Previously, the discussion focused on compassion and wisdom, the meaning of which was still general. Now, by clarifying the explanation of the characteristics of the Three Truths (*trisatya*), the meaning of the Tathāgata is explained without exception.
The characteristics of the Three Truths are precisely the Three Dharma-bodies (*dharmakāya*); the Dharma-body is perfect and complete. To accord with this—

The "understanding" therein refers to the perfection of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body) of the three *prajñās*. Speaking in accordance with this, the "liberation" therein refers to the perfection of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) of the three liberations.
When viewed from the present perspective back toward the former, there is no lack of distinction between them. Third, the explanation of the character "wandering" (*you*).
[Text]: "To 'wander' (you) means to traverse and enter. Now, the Dharma-nature neither enters, abides, nor exits;
as the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: 'The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata. How, then, can one speak of wandering?
It is precisely because he guides sentient beings through compassion, leading them by example to enter [the Way], that he is said to wander."
To cause sentient beings to partake of the flavor of ambrosia, one should also speak of "abiding," and to proclaim it for the sake of sentient beings, one should also speak of "emerging.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Skillfully entering, emerging from, and abiding in hundreds of thousands of samādhis"—this is precisely that meaning.
[Commentary]: This refers to the Tathāgata entering the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) by means of ultimate wisdom (*niṣṭhājñāna*).

Regarding the *dharmatā* that is realized and the resultant wisdom that realizes it, the distinction between "subject" and "object" is established for the sake of meaning; however, their substance does not meet.

This is because when initial awakening reaches its ultimate limit, it is identical to original awakening (*mūlajñāna*), and thus only the wisdom of True Suchness (*tathatā*) remains. If this is so, who is it that can enter? And what [is there to enter]?
The entering, abiding, and emerging are all likewise; this is also intended to lead in accordance with the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Now, the term "wandering" (*yóu*) is used to lead sentient beings to study the Buddha’s entry into principle, thereby demonstrating the aspect of entering. It is to cause sentient beings to abide in accordance with principle that the aspect of abiding is demonstrated.
"Ambrosia" (*amṛta*) is the medicine of immortality, which serves as a metaphor for the eternal principle for the sake of sentient beings.
It should also be said that this taste of nectar both emerges and does not emerge; yet it emerges and emerges, for it is the King of Sutras, the Lotus Sūtra.

Regarding the great bodhisattvas who surge forth from the earth, though they do not enter into the profound nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) or into hundreds of thousands of samādhis, they are said to have "skillfully entered";
their emergence and abiding are likewise so. If even the bodhisattvas are thus, one can know that the fruition, the Buddha, is even more so. Second, the object...
Wandering in the Dharma.
Regarding the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, the sphere of activity of all Buddhas.
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, clarifying the profound and vast *dharmatā*; second, first, a direct explanation based on the text; second, first, explaining "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
The measure is profoundly deep.

[Textual Commentary: Regarding "immeasurably profound," this is intended to clarify the entry [into the realm] by distinguishing and revealing its essence as lofty and vast. Because its essence encompasses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is called "immeasurable";
because it penetrates through to the three truths (*trīṇi satyāni*), it is called "profoundly deep. It is not something belonging to the Two Vehicles or lower stages.
Because it is that which Bodhisattvas have attained, it is said to be immeasurable and profoundly deep.
[Commentary] One who wishes to clearly demonstrate the sphere in which the Buddha dwells must first distinguish and reveal the loftiness and vastness of its essence;
thus, by means of the *dharmadhātu*, its vastness is revealed. This Middle Way dharma is not a realm (*dhātu*), yet it is the realm itself; because this realm has no exterior, it is so called.

Furthermore, the "Immeasurable" is manifested through the three truths. Although both the ultimate and conventional truths reach their consummation, they are accessible to the Two Vehicles and represent only a partial realization for Bodhisattvas.
As for the Middle Truth, none can enter its realization except through perfect, true wisdom.
Herein it is clarified that the essence of the three truths is neither superior nor inferior; rather, they are the secret treasury of the Three Virtues.
The treasury of the secret is the very bottom of the *dharmatā*; therefore, it is said that only by reaching the ultimate does one accord with the sutra’s praise of its profound depth.
"Profound" (*shen*) carries the meaning of "high. One must understand that the *dharmadhātu* and the perfect three truths (*triratna*) are non-dual and without distinction;

here, we take these two names to manifest immeasurable profundity so that it may be easily perceived. Having manifested this, we next distinguish it: if one were to rely on the perspective of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), [it would be otherwise].
"Perfect" (yuan) excludes the partial; if we take the Bodhisattva as the standard, the "deep" excludes the shallow, for from the stage below the Buddha downward, all are considered lower grounds.
Since even the Perfect Sage is already distinguished [from the lower], how much more so the three teachings? Second, to explain the two characters "dharma-nature" (faxing).
[Text]: "Dharmatā" refers to the Dharma in which [the Buddhas] roam. That which serves as the standard for all Buddhas is called "Dharma";
that which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, and which neither transmigrates nor changes, is called "nature" (dharmatā).
[Commentary] Previously, it was clarified that height and breadth are the virtues of the essence; now, it is clarified that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is the essence of these virtues.
This explains the meaning of the two characters [of the title] to reveal the essence of height and breadth. What is called "Dharma" has the sense of a "normative rule" (*pramāṇa*).

Because all Buddhas follow this norm and thereby accomplish the myriad virtues, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is what is called Dharma. Now, regarding this *dharmatā*:

Among the three vehicles and six paths, who does not take this as their standard to establish themselves? Because they are deluded regarding the functional utility of the inherent nature, although they follow this standard, they deviate from it;
thus, the three obstacles are formed. It is like the seven groups of practitioners: who does not take the Buddha as their teacher?

Yet, because there are those who comply and those who oppose, they are divided into those who are bound and those who are liberated. Now, in order to manifest that which is taken as the teacher by means of the ultimate compliance with its function, it says: "That which all Buddhas have..."

The "track" (軌) is termed the "Dharma," and that which is called its "nature" (性) has the meaning of being unchanging; this refers to the substance of the four virtues (*catur-guṇa*), for it does not undergo transition or alteration.
One must know that these four pervade all dharmas, down to the fundamental causal realm (*hetu-dhātu*) of even the hells;
there is not a single thing that is not eternal, blissful, self, and pure. That the worldly characteristics are eternally so—this is what is meant. Second, further...
Regarding the interpretation of the meaning, there are three parts; first is the interpretation based on what is illuminated by true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

[Textual Commentary: It is not the principle illuminated by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) of the Two Vehicles that constitutes the *dharmatā*.
This is because the *dharmatā* of the Two Vehicles is shallow, not profound; it is limited, not immeasurable. What is meant here is the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
The principle illuminated by this wisdom horizontally encompasses the entire Dharma-realm and vertically penetrates the three truths; therefore, it is said to be immeasurable and profoundly deep.

[Commentary] The "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) means that the afflictions have been completely severed. The "knowledge of non-arising" (anutpādajñāna) means that the afflictions will not arise again.
Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains these two knowledges, saying: "In the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), if one correctly knows for oneself: 'I have already known suffering...'"

The abandonment of the origin [of suffering], the realization of cessation, and the cultivation of the path are called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). If one correctly knows for oneself, "I have known suffering;

it will not arise again," the subsequent three cases are explained as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* defines the knowledge of exhaustion as the exhaustion of afflictions and the knowledge of non-arising as the non-arising of future retribution.
However, both of these knowledges equally illuminate the emptiness of phenomena; here, they are briefly distinguished based on two aspects.

From the stage of the Bodhisattva Chengyi (Cittavajra) up to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), the dharma-nature of the Two Vehicles is not the Middle Way; therefore, it is shallow and incomplete.
Because it does not fully encompass both matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), it is limited. As explained in the *Yathābhūta-jñāna-śāstra*, eleven types of wisdom are clarified:

the first ten are shared with the Two Vehicles, whereas only the wisdom of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is not shared with them—namely, the knowledge of the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena.
To realize, as it truly is, that there is no obstruction—this wisdom which illuminates horizontally and penetrates vertically—is the present *dharmatā*.
Second, the explanation by way of the principle being identical with phenomena.
[Text] Furthermore, "immeasurable" does not mean that there is some separate dharma named "immeasurable. Vairocana pervades all places;
all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Because they are all the Buddha-dharma, they are all the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Since the Buddhas traverse them all, it is called "immeasurable. Furthermore, it is not that there is some separate dharma named "profound," namely...
All phenomena are truly non-existent; there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). A single form, a single fragrance—none are not the Middle Way.
Because they are all the Middle Way, they are profoundly deep.

[Commentary] The profound and vast *dharmatā* is the dwelling place where Buddhas roam; it further transcends the pure sphere of practice of Bodhisattvas. Fearing that [others] might not [comprehend this],...

The "Attainer" (the realized one) says: "If [it were claimed that] apart from the present ordinary person's *dharmas* of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*), as well as their physical and mental states and their causes and effects, there were a separate *dharmatā* where the Buddha dwells, then it would indeed be necessary to specifically negate this. However, it is not that there is some other separate dharma called 'immeasurable' or 'profound.

Rather, wherever the term 'all places' (*sarvatra*) is used, it must include the three lands (*tri-bhūmi*), and all dharmas therein correspond to the causes and effects of the nine realms (*navadhātu*). If [this were] negated..."
If this Buddha-dharma is exclusively pure and exclusively good, then the defilements and evils of the three lands and nine realms must be severed;

how, then, can they be called "all being the Buddha-dharma"? Therefore, one should understand that all defilements and evils are none other than the inherently endowed *dharmatā-niṣyanda* (nature, practice, and understanding) Buddha-nature.
It is not merely good and pure; its nature is defiled and its substance is evil, yet these are entirely the *niṣyanda* Buddha-nature. If such dharmas as these are all...
Buddha-nature refers to the three lands and nine realms where the substance of cultivation and defilement is empty, and its nature and virtues comprise the ten realms;
this is the essence of perfect enlightenment, omnipresent and reaching everywhere—this is what is called Vairocana pervading all places.
Since all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, how could there be a single thought-moment, a single speck of dust, or a single person that is not the realm of Dharma-nature in which the Tathāgata dwells?
Regarding "immeasurable," one must further understand that all defiled and evil phenomena are profound in their very essence; thus, they are called "profound.
In reality, there is no separate dharma of profundity. Therefore, it is said that "the phenomenal is itself the true. Within form and fragrance lies the Middle Way;
though deluded sentiments regard form and fragrance as being merely partial aspects of form, when analyzed, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
It is "entirely" so because it consists solely of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.

If there were even a speck of a phenomenon outside of these forms, it would not be called "solely" [those five], nor would it be the Middle Way. This Middle Way is secret, wondrous, and its inconceivability is inexhaustible;
thus it is termed "profound. Third, citing treatises and other sources, there are two parts concerning the analogy of the mind. First, the citation of the analogy.

[Text]: For example, the Commentary explains the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*) as follows: "Taking sentient beings of the eastern direction as the object is called 'vast' (*vipula*);

taking those of the four cardinal directions as the object is called 'great' (*mahat*); and taking those of the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir as the object is called 'immeasurable' (*apramāṇa*)."
[Commentary] Second, based on this, the three [aspects] are explained. First, it clarifies that the Middle Truth is immeasurable.

[Text] According to this, that which takes the dharma-nature of the True Truth as its object is called "broad" (guǎng); that which takes the dharma-nature of the Conventional Truth as its object is called "great" (dà);
and that which takes the dharma-nature of the Middle Way as its object is called "immeasurable" (wúliàng).

[Commentary] The treatise explains the four immeasurables—loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). They are called "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*) in terms of their objects, while they are called "equalities" (*sama*) in terms of the mind.
Regarding these [immeasurables] with sentient beings as their object, three types of names are obtained based on the extent of their objective scope:

namely, vast, immeasurable, and so forth; now, following that same logic, three names are established within the context of the ultimate and conventional truths. The Sūtra indicates that [the Bodhisattva] dwells therein.

The immeasurable nature of phenomena (dharmatā) manifests the principle of the perfect fusion of the Middle Way; it is not merely the reality of emptiness nor the conventional existence of biased falsity.
Second, it clarifies that the Middle Way must necessarily encompass and integrate both.
[Text]: "If one takes the Middle Way as the object of cognition, this is the threefold wisdom taking the three truths as its object within a single moment of mind.
[Commentary]: When the Buddha, responding to the capacities of sentient beings, employs provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), he illuminates only two of the truths;

since this does not encompass the Middle Way, it is not a roaming within the immeasurable *dharmatā*. Now, employing ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) to illuminate the principle of the Middle Truth, there is nothing that is not encompassed therein.
It is said that if one takes the Middle Way as the object-condition, then the three knowledges are identical within a single mind; for this reason, the Middle Truth is termed "immeasurable.
Here, the three fetters, their objects, and the wisdom [that perceives them] correspond to one another.
[Wenju: This object is immeasurable, and only the immeasurable wisdom of a Buddha can take it as its object-condition, just as a box and its lid correspond perfectly.
The two vehicles and those of the lower stages cannot fathom its limits or depths.

[Commentary] As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Only the Buddha exhaustively investigates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. How could there be any limit or exhaustion to the principle of the provisional and the real?
This is truly because the Buddha has attained inexhaustible wisdom and is thus able to exhaustively investigate it; now, this case is likewise twofold.
Because the wisdom of those who rely on lower stages is limited, they cannot fathom the shoreless shore or the bottomless depth [of the Buddhas].
Second, explaining the sphere of activity of all Buddhas, which has two parts; first, the Dharma.
[Text]: "The sphere of activity of all Buddhas" explicitly reveals that the Buddha-wisdom is immeasurable and profoundly deep;

because the Buddha-wisdom is immeasurable and profoundly deep, the sphere of activity is likewise immeasurable and profound; and because the sphere of activity is immeasurable and profound, the Buddha-wisdom is also immeasurable and profound.
[Commentary] Scholars should know that original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) serves as the locus for initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*), which constitutes the Buddha.
Only when the initial [enlightenment] fully accords with the original does it become so; were it otherwise, how could each be called "immeasurable" and "profound"?

Although one was already in profound accord upon first sitting at the site of enlightenment, now, in order to guide sentient beings, the appearance of union is manifested, and it is said that one "wanders through the practices of all Buddhas."
Section Two: Providing an Analogy.
[Wenju] To raise the box is to manifest the lid; to raise the lid is to manifest the box; this is precisely the point here.
[Ji] To raise the place where it is kept (the box) is to manifest the lid that travels within it. Section Three: Conclusion.
"Surpassing the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas.
[Commentary] This passage has two parts: first, a direct explanation based on the literal text; second, a brief explanation according to the underlying meaning.
[Wenju] "Surpassing the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas" is the precise distinction; it means that bodhisattvas have not yet reached this level.
Because the practice of the wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi*) has not yet become profound and vast.
[Commentary] Second, citing texts for an extensive explanation, first from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
[Text] The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states: "When a bodhisattva attains the nine kinds of dhyāna, the first is called 'dhyāna of intrinsic nature' (*svabhāva-dhyāna*). If one enters this dhyāna..."

He immediately enters the realm of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the purity of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), the very name of which the followers of the Two Vehicles do not hear, let alone its practice.

Upon entering the ninth stage of the pure, purified dhyāna (*viśuddha-viśuddha-dhyāna*), all afflictions—both those common to all beings (*sāmānya-kleśa*) and those specific to them (*āsādhāraṇa-kleśa*)—whether manifest (*vartamāna*) or latent (*vāsanā*), are completely exhausted;
therefore, it is called the pure, purified dhyāna. From the lower stages downward, there remain residual habits (*vāsanā-śeṣa*); the Buddha, however, abides in the tenth stage.
If one enters this dhyāna at the summit of the stages (*bhūmi-agra*), one surpasses all bodhisattvas.

[Commentary: The nine kinds of dhyāna are: first, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, all-encompassing (*sarva*); third, difficult (*duṣkara*); fourth, all-gates (*sarvadvāra*); fifth, virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*); sixth, all-practices (*sarvacaryā*);
seventh, removal of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*); eighth, this world and other worlds (*ihaloka-paraloka*); ninth, pure purity (*viśuddhi-viśuddhi*). Text.
The middle section briefly indicates the first and last two dhyānas. As for the ninth dhyāna, it refers to the transition from the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) into wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*);

therefore, it is said that all pervasive and specific afflictions, whether manifest or latent, are completely exhausted. From the tenth stage downward, there still exist both manifest and latent afflictions.
