According to the commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is not separately opened; the tenth stage is itself equal enlightenment.

Regarding the statement that "the afflictions of both the general and specific categories, as well as their active outbursts (*pradhāna-kleśa*) and residual habits (*vāsanā*), are all exhausted": "general" refers to the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), and "specific" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

The active outbursts of the general afflictions are exhausted at the seventh stage of the *Śraddhā-bhūmi* (Faith) within the Perfect Teaching; however, their residual habits are exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood, as these are shared with the specific [afflictions].
This is because our school distinguishes sixteen categories of residual habits for the Small Vehicle by dividing them into four groups of four. As for the specific afflictions, they are forty-two.
Regarding the stage of severing afflictions, as is commonly practiced, the presence of residual habits (*vāsanā*) is explained in detail in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), although all views are completely severed, residual habits still remain.

When one reaches Equal Enlightenment (*samantabhadra-bhūmi*) and enters the Gate of the Double Profundity, after cultivating all mundane matters for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, the realization of principle becomes distinct and the residual habits become as thin as a faint wisp of smoke.
Since that [text], the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, explains the purification of dhyāna by being free from all views, it clarifies only the severing of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of views;

however, if one cites the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, which states that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) sever the habit-energies of craving and that the tenth stage is equivalent to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), does this not then enter into the "Deep Mystery" (*chong-hsüan*)?
Therefore, we know that after the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) are severed, one further enters the Deep Mystery to sever the habit-energies; the textual evidence for this is quite clear.
Clear and distinct. Second, the "Pure Name. [Wenju] states:
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "When the mind is pure, one has already transcended all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*); this is precisely that meaning.
[Ji] explains: Because the Buddha’s own nature-pure mind transcends all meditative concentrations acquired through cultivation, it is so described.

"Having purified the mind, one has already crossed over all dhyānas and concentrations" means that because one has reached the further shore of all dhyānas and concentrations, it is said "already crossed.
This is a second interpretation based on the underlying meaning.
[Wenju] Furthermore, this cites a high level of attainment to distinguish it from the profound nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

[Commentary: The Buddha does not exalt himself; he is exalted because he relies upon the Dharma. Now, the meaning of this "high position" is clarified in order to distinguish and manifest the profound depth of the *dharmatā*.
Second, the detailed exposition has two parts: first, clarifying that the explanation of the meaning differs from what preceded.

[Text] Regarding this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the preceding sections have already explained the meaning of the introductory narrative, the main exposition, and the seventeen chapters on the propagation of the teaching as mentioned above.
Now, we shall further discuss the fivefold profound meaning (*pañcavidha-gambhīrārtha*) of the introductory narrative.
[Commentary] However, in the preceding introduction to the various chapters, how could it have been anything other than these five meanings?

Since the seventeen chapters discuss only the three dharmas—generally clarifying their specific characteristics and providing the teaching for sentient beings—the names and so forth were not explicitly manifested therein.
Therefore, I now clearly demonstrate them; the text of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) fully enumerates these five meanings, so that students may know this one [point].

From beginning to end, this sutra explains nothing other than the name, essence, purpose, function, and the characteristics of the teaching; only then can one know that the commentary on the title has fully exhausted the intent of the sutra.
Second, explaining the meaning according to the text, which is divided into two parts: first, the division of the text.
[Textual Analysis] The first twelve and a half lines describe the name, essence, doctrine, and function;
the subsequent fourteen and a half lines describe the propagation and wide dissemination of this scripture, which constitutes the description of the doctrinal characteristics (*śāstrasaṃkhyā*).

Specifically, the first line describes the name, the next line describes the essence, the following three lines describe the doctrine, and the next nine lines describe the function. From "Guarding the World" (*Lokapāla*) onwards, the teaching is described.
[This is] the characteristic.
[Commentary: Part two explains the meaning; part one provides a narrative of four meanings. Part one, the first of these, explains the title:
"This is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*."
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first explains that, according to other interpretations, this belongs to the essence (*tattva*).

[Textual Analysis] Regarding "essence," some say that even a single phrase of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* still describes the essence—just as gold within ore is the essence of gold, which is neither the luster nor the radiance itself, yet one may nonetheless discuss its internal and external applications.
However, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is not the central thesis (*siddhānta*).
"It is not by power, but arises from the power of the principle (dharmatā) of the doctrine; one should know that this phrase precisely describes the essence. [Commentary] Regarding "ore":
the *Shuowen* states that ore is the raw material of copper or iron. As for "internal and external use": light is the internal use because it reveals its own essence;
clarity is the external use because it reflects other objects. This master also understands light and radiance.
The two characters [“body” and “function”] pertain to the function (*yòng*), while “gold” is the primary substance (*tǐ*).
Because substance and function are inseparable, although three characters are listed, the intent lies in the substance. Second, now I shall definitively set forth the names.
[Text] Now, it is explained that the principle is naturally so; yet, as for the division of the text, this belongs to the section on "Narrating the Names.
[Commentary] To designate the Three and manifest the One does not entirely deviate from reason, hence it is said to be "naturally so.

However, as for the division of the text, the subsequent phrase specifically takes the Middle Way as the King of Sutras; since this is precisely the "body" of the narrative, why must the initial phrase be included?

One should understand that when scholars discuss the essence (*tattva*) by means of its function (*kārya*), the phrase describing the name is based on the preceding textual context to explain the three characters of the title;
it is not established through metaphor, but is a direct naming of the profound and vast *dharmatā*.
Since the Buddha himself dwells within this *dharmatā*, he immediately proclaims: "This is the King of all Sutras, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. It is not [merely] called so [by comparison].

Regarding the single character "Dharmatā" (法性), what does it refer to? Because the wise have deeply perceived the subtle purport of the sutra, they establish both an interpretation based on the accompanying text (*fu-wen*) and an interpretation based on the essence itself (*dang-ti*).
First, regarding the interpretation based on the accompanying text, this passage is cited: "To initially set forth the name is most worthy of trust.
Since this specific meaning was already presented in the preceding text-based interpretation, there is no need to repeat it here when explaining the enumeration of names.
[This section] displays [the meaning]. Second, it describes the essence:
"The King of all Sutras. [Commentary:
The text has two parts; first, it refers back to what preceded and indicates what follows.
[Text] Having already explained the King of Sutras above, it is now described once more.

[Commentary] "Above" refers to the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), where the King of Sutras was expounded by means of the teaching-gathering and position-gathering aspects of the "Gathering and Encompassing" (*jiēshè*) Dharma-gate;

that exposition is now concluded. Here, it is further elucidated from the perspective of the Middle Way. This section has two parts: first, distinguishing the correct through contrast with others; second, the initial explanation.
The first part of his explanation provides an introduction. [Wenju] states:
The Tripiṭaka Master says that the three virtues encompass the three types of *nirvāṇa*; the correct severance of the two vehicles severs views;

*prajñā* correctly dispels the attachments of ordinary beings; and the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra primarily transforms bodhisattvas at the initial stage of practice. This present sutra, however, universally applies to all eight stages.
Therefore, people call him "King.

[Commentary] The intention of the Tripiṭaka Master is that the three characters of the sutra’s title are metaphors for the Three Virtues (triguṇa). These Three Virtues are then correspondingly assigned to the three sutras:

the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that the Buddha possesses an essence (svabhāva), while [the other two] clarify liberation and correct severance, thereby dispelling the view of the Two Vehicles that [nirvana] is a mere extinction like ashes.
If one discusses emptiness, it is specifically for the sake of causing ordinary beings to abandon their attachment to existence;

the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s sudden teaching on the principle of the Dharma-body is intended for those at the stage of the ten faiths and the three levels of worthies. Therefore, it is said that among the three aforementioned sūtras of initial practice, each discusses a single virtue and addresses a specific capacity.
However, because the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* fully manifests the three virtues, it is able to universally address the capacities of all eight stages of practitioners. This is the interpretation.
The *prajñā* [pāramitā] accommodates those of the two vehicles; the "ordinary person" stage encompasses both humans and devas as a single station;
and the *dharmakāya* accommodates the five stages of the bodhisattva: faith, abiding, practice, direction, and the grounds (*bhūmi*).

Since there is no capacity for which it does not accommodate, this is the meaning of the King of Sutras' comprehensive subsumption. Second, the refutation of the two [opposing views], the first of which clarifies how they contradict the intent of the teaching.
[Text] These words are difficult to understand. If the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* expounds the profound and subtle sphere of practice for Bodhisattvas, how could it be intended merely for the two vehicles?
If the *Prajñāpāramitā* speaks of the Dharma-body Buddha preaching the Dharma to Dharma-body Bodhisattvas, the assembly listening to the Dharma is not comprised of those subject to birth and death;
how could it be intended merely to dispel the attachments of ordinary beings? The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speaks of the stages from the first bhūmi up to... [and so forth].
In explaining the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), how could it be intended only for bodhisattvas who have just begun their practice?

[Commentary: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* primarily discusses the profound and wondrous Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) and is intended for those with the capacity for the Perfect Teaching; how could it be limited only to the Two Vehicles?

The *Prajñāpāramitā* fully reveals the three kinds of *prajñā*; how could these differ from the Three Virtues? Furthermore, since it is said that the audience consists of those who are not subject to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), how could this be so?
To limit the *Avataṃsaka*’s three bodies to ordinary beings and its three virtues to the full exposition of the ten stages is not only to restrict the scope of the teaching to beginner bodhisattvas;
such an interpretation not only limits the capacity of those to be converted, but also fails to manifest the perfect nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmatā*).
Second, explaining those who harm practitioners.
[Wenqu]: To make this partial statement—that those without wisdom give rise to contempt for various sutras—is incorrect.
[Ji]: Paramārtha’s interpretation is that those with discernment know this to be improper, while those without wisdom claim it to be so.

The three sutras are inferior to this scripture; those who give rise to slander against them will incur transgressions, so how can they be relied upon? Second, the explanation of the present commentary has three parts:

first, a general demonstration of the right and wrong of various scriptural kings; second, determining right and wrong by means of the three truths; third, demonstrating the three truths. First, [the determination of right and wrong] regarding the three truths. First, demonstrating the three truths.
[Text] Now, regarding what is called the "King of Sūtras": if one takes the words as the sūtra, it constitutes the three kinds of conventional truth;

if one takes the principle as the sūtra, it constitutes the three kinds of ultimate truth; if one takes the union of words and principle as the sūtra, it constitutes the three kinds of the Middle Way.

[Commentary]: Within the category of the teachings of a single lifetime (*ekāyana-śāsana*), there are those who take the expressive words and letters as the *sūtra*, those who take the expressed meaning and principle as the *sūtra*, and those who take the union of word and meaning as the *sūtra*.
Therefore, the *sūtras* of a single lifetime do not go beyond the union or non-union of word and meaning.
If they are not in union, the expressive words are merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and do not constitute the three types [of *sūtra*]. This means:

The three categories of conventional existence are: the conventional reality of "real existence" (satya-samvṛti) in the Tripitaka teaching; the conventional reality of "illusory existence" (māyopama-samvṛti) in the Shared Teaching; and the conventional reality of "illusory existence as identical to emptiness" (māyopama-śūnyatā-samvṛti) in the Distinct Teaching.
As for the principles they expound, if these are considered the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there are likewise only three types:

the ultimate truth of "emptiness through the cessation of real existence" in the Tripitaka; the ultimate truth of "illusory existence as identical to emptiness" in the Shared Teaching; and the ultimate truth of "neither existence nor non-existence" in the Distinct Teaching. These are the six.

The three internal types of ultimate truth do not possess the conventional as their substance; rather, one enters the ultimate by means of the three types of conventionality, yet ultimately the meaning of their merging is not established.
If they were to merge according to principle and text, they would not exceed three types:

the Perfect-Integrated Teaching (Yuan-jie), the Integrated-with-Separate Teaching (Jie-jie), and the Properly Perfect Teaching (Zheng-yuan). Within these three, the substance of the ultimate and the conventional is the Middle Way. Which one is the Perfect Teaching?

Fundamentally, the ultimate and the conventional mutually interpenetrate; if one connects this with the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that is its referent is "all phenomena" (*sarva-dharma*), and since the text concerning the illumination of the conventional also refers to "all phenomena," these three types [of truths] are non-dual in their ultimate and conventional aspects.

This is called the "conformity of principle and text," and the meaning of the Middle Way is thereby established. Because the ultimate is itself the conventional, the ultimate is not the ultimate; because the conventional is itself the ultimate, the conventional is itself [the ultimate].
It is neither mundane nor real; it is not the mundane discourse of thought, for such thoughts have naturally been forgotten. It is merely a provisional name given to that which is "within. Question:

In the Distinct Teaching (*bīe-jiao*), the layered mundane world is illusory existence, and thus it can be the text that expresses meaning. But how can emptiness (*śūnyatā*) also be considered "text"? Answer:

"Text" refers to the characteristics of the text—the meaning that is expressed and revealed. If the meaning belongs to the Shared Teaching (*tong-jiao*), then emptiness takes the forgetting of characteristics as its function.
The principle that is expressed now, within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), takes both extremes as its characteristics in order to manifest that which transcends both;

thus, it manifests the "neither-nor" (the Middle Way). Therefore, both emptiness and existence are treated as textual expressions. Question: Among the seven categories, such as the *pitaka* and so forth, all are termed "truth" (*satya*) and "conventionality" (*saṃvṛti*).

How is it that the latter three are named the "Middle Way"? Answer: Does one hear of "truth" and "conventionality" and yet suppose there is no "middle"? It is just as in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
Furthermore, regarding the connection between the general and the specific: since these three—true, conventional, and middle—are all termed "inconceivable," why would they not be the Middle Way?
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* explains, among the seven pairs of two truths, three are also named after the Middle Way;

why then single out this case for criticism? If one takes its meaning, why would the True Truth (*satya*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*), which is neither empty nor existent, not be so named?
The middle answer concerning the departure from extremes is logically inconsistent with the initial stage, for at that point one cannot yet conceive of it and must suddenly forget it;

if viewed from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching], it is merely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) which elucidates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, the preceding *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) explains the sutra in this way:

when contrasted with the Perfect, it is specifically called "breaking" and "departing" to clarify the Middle. This is because what is elucidated does not coincide with the means of elucidation, and thus it is not named the Middle.

When one realizes that the nature of words and letters is detached from all [dualistic extremes] and that there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma, only then is it called the Middle Way of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
To this question—“Why is the Separate and Connecting Teaching (Bie-tong-jie) alone excluded?”—the answer is: Here, the True and the Conventional are contrasted with the Principle and the Text.

Since the Separate and Connecting Teaching is already included within the six [teachings], what is the reason? If one has not yet received the connection [to the Perfect], one is still within the realm of illusory existence (*māyopama-bhava*), which is used to express the very emptiness (*śūnyatā*) [of that existence].

If one accepts [the interpretation] that [the three truths] subsequently belong only to the Middle [Truth], this would merely illuminate the overlapping conventional [truths]. Since the essence of the dharmas already exists within the first six [truths], what would remain to be omitted?
Furthermore, the current text does not explicitly state that there are "seven kinds of two truths"; it only clarifies the single lifetime [of the Buddha's teaching].
Taking the text, taking the principle, and taking the combination of text and principle, there are three conventional scriptures and three true scriptures.
Within these three [categories], the sūtras are clarified in this manner; when the sūtras are gathered into a single transformation, nothing remains unexhausted.
Some individuals establish nine kinds of sūtras based solely on the name *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, taking the characters themselves as the fundamental basis for their meaning.

They claim that if one clings to the three characters of the expressive text (*vyañjana*), they are called the "three kinds of conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*); if one clings to the three characters of the expressed meaning (*artha*)...

The essence of principle is called the three kinds of true truths (*tattva*). If one takes the textual meaning as consistent with the principle, it means that not being biased toward either extreme constitutes the three kinds of middle way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
If one explains it in this manner, would it not be merely interpreting the meaning according to one's own mind? It would surely be a stubborn violation of the intended meaning of the text.

This is because the first two instances of the character "take" (*qu*) are explained as "clinging" (*zhuó*), while the last instance of the character "take" is explained as "not being biased. Is this so?
Why is this said? Because the Great Master, as the king who interprets all sutras, established nine categories to encompass the scriptures of his entire life;
since this sutra expounds the king of the Middle Way, it attains mastery among these nine categories and is thus named the "King of All Sutras.
For what reason do the nine categories consist of only three characters? It is because the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* itself is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
The King of Sutras has already been missing from various scriptures; it is not at all a comprehensive sovereign, and its contradictions are numerous.
Furthermore, regarding these two [aspects], one must determine which is right and which is wrong.
[Wenju: If one speaks of other truths, they are sutras but not kings; if one speaks of the Middle Way, it is both a sutra and a king.
One attains mastery over the nine kinds of sūtras. [Commentary:

If within various schools there are those who claim that the first three [sūtras] express conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), or those who claim that the first three do not accord with the essence of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as expressed, these are all termed "other truths.
While one may obtain such sūtras, they are not called "Sūtra Kings" (*sūtrarāja*).

Because that which does not clarify ultimate truth while possessing conventional truth is such that conventional truth is not identical to ultimate truth, and because there is no sense of a sovereign unifying both the conventional and the ultimate, it is not the "King.

Within various schools, some assert that the Middle Way consists of the ultimate truth possessing the three types of conventional truth and the conventional truth being entirely ultimate—these two truths being non-dual; yet outside of this Middle Way, there is nothing further.
A brief explanation of this scripture is as follows: it speaks of the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*; it speaks of the inconceivable realm of wisdom;
and it speaks of abiding in the suchness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-tathatā*).

Since all phenomena contain and encompass all phenomena, there is nothing that can be expressed apart from the expression itself; how could there be anything expressed outside of the expression? Thus, the principle and the text are in perfect accord.

In the "True Three" (Shinjitsu San), it is shown that the sutras of a single lifetime contain both partial and perfect teachings.

Now, it is judged that whichever section among the various divisions speaks of the perfect Middle Way is the King of Sutras; it is able to universally demonstrate the nine kinds of mastery within the three [categories of] sutras.
Since these sutras are merely different names for the same essence, they attain such mastery. As for the other six sutras, however...
The skillful means employed within this circle are like those of a king over his ministers; how could they not be sovereign? Second, the supreme majesty is revealed through the Middle Way.
Third, it is first explained that the perfect essence (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of all divisions serves as the king.
[Text]: However, this King of Sutras is one [teaching] that establishes its doctrine according to conditions, such that its names differ: in the *Avataṃsaka*, it is called the Dharma-body;
in the Vaipulya, the True Aspect (*dharmatā*); in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the Mother of Buddhas; in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Topknot Jewel; and in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the Teacher of Buddhas.
These are all different names for the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which universally serves as the essence of all sutras.
[Commentary] The Middle Way, King of Sutras, is a single entity in its essence; however, it is established under various names according to the suitability and preferences of sentient beings.
Therefore, the preceding text asks: "If the Middle Way is said to be this Sutra and this King, which sutra speaks of it?

This refers to the teachings on the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and so forth within the four flavors (*catur-rasa*) of the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, which constitute the essence of the Sutra. Nevertheless, one must distinguish these from within the context of the four flavors.
This king is not a king; for example, within the Avataṃsaka section there are three kinds of sūtras: those that are kings among the Perfect (Zhengyuan) and those that connect the specific (Jiebie).
Among these, this sūtra is a king in the context of the Perfect and Specific Teachings, whereas in the context of the Specific Teaching alone, this sūtra is not a king.

Therefore, regarding the Dharmakāya, one must distinguish it from the Three Piṭakas, which consist merely of emptiness and the two truths of reality. Within the Vaipulya section, this sūtra is indeed a king.

Among the nine types of sūtras, the Perfectly Complete Teaching (Zhengyuanjiao) includes the Middle Perfect that connects with the Separate (Zhongyuan-jietie), the Middle Perfect that connects with the Shared (Zhongyuan-jietong), and the Middle Three (Zhong-san).
Because these three are the Kings of Sūtras, the name "True Aspect" (Shixiang) applies to these three types. As for the remaining six, they are not kings of sūtras.

Within the Prajñā section, there are no Tripiṭaka [sūtras]; as for the two [types] and the seven types of sūtras, they are likewise like the Vaipulya (Fangdeng). Among these, three are kings of sūtras and thus receive that name.
Among the Buddha-mothers, the other four are not the King; only the Lotus Sūtra is the King, because it reveals the provisional to reveal the real and bestows the jewel from the topknot.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* speaks of nine kinds [of nirvana], yet all know that within the Perfect (the Middle Way), there is nothing that is not the King of Sūtras.
All sentient beings shall surely attain Buddhahood; who, then, would not take the True Cause as their teacher? Therefore, among all the great Mahāyāna sūtras, this is the Sūtra of the Middle Way.
That kings possess this expansion and contraction is due solely to the single *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), which establishes these various names as the essence of all sutras.
Second, it is by taking the successive kings of past generations as a metaphor.

[Wenju] states: "For example, just as various clans rise in succession according to their destiny—such as the Dragon Masters and Bird Officials who established hegemony at different times for a hundred generations."
Although they differ, the sovereign who unifies them is one.
[Commentary] "The various surnames" refers to the surnames of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors. Fuxi, the Lord of Great Radiance, was surnamed Feng;
Shennong, the Lord of Divine Husbandry, was surnamed Jiang; and Huangdi of Youxiong was surnamed Gong-sun—these were the Three August Ones.
Shao Hao (Jintian), Zhuanxu (Goyang), and Di Ku (Gaosin) were all of the Ji clan;
Di Yao (Taodang) was of the Yiqi clan, and Di Shun (Youyu) was of the Yao clan—these are the Five Emperors. Thus, it is said that they possessed various clans.
"Responding to the destiny and arising in succession" means responding to the destiny of Heaven through the cycle of the five elements' mutual generation. [The characters] *fu*... [text ends].
Fuxi corresponded to the Wood cycle, Shennong to the Fire cycle, and Huangdi to the Earth cycle; the Five Emperors may be inferred in this order.

As for the "Dragon Masters," when Fuxi first established his reign, there was an auspicious omen of dragons; therefore, he recorded the offices by dragon and gave them dragon names. Thus the *Zuo Zhuan* says:
"The Lord Taihao used the dragon as his record, and thus had dragon masters and dragon names. As for the "Bird Officials," it began with Shaohao.
Because there was the auspicious omen of the phoenix, he recorded his officials by means of birds; thus the *Zuozhuan* states:

"When Shao Hao Zhi was established, the phoenix arrived accordingly, so he made it the master of the birds and named [the officials] after birds. Those who establish hegemony according to the times are said to respond to the destiny of ruling the world.
Although the hundred generations differ—meaning their titles and designations are distinct—their unified sovereignty over the realm is all from Heaven.
This refers to the primary lord. Third, it demonstrates that names are established according to their respective sections and provides a corresponding analogy.
[Wenju] The Dharma-nature is also like this: for those who should hear the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* as the "Mother of Buddhas," other names are set aside;
for those who should hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the "Jewel Place," other names are set aside.
[Commentary]: Although names may arise or perish, their essence neither increases nor decreases.
Therefore, from the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) down to the Teacher of Buddhas, each attains mastery within the nine kinds of scriptures. This corresponds to the previous analogy which states:
"Though a hundred generations differ, the sovereign king remains one. Second, this clarifies the essential nature of this scripture as the King of Sutras.
[Text] The Dharma-nature as the King of the Golden Light is also like this.
[Commentary] Taking the principle that accords with the Middle Way as its essence is a general explanation;

yet, when compared to the distinct essences of various other sūtras, this sūtra specifically takes the King of Dharma-nature as its sūtra-essence. This is because the Buddha dwells within the profound...
When the Dharma-nature is extensively expounded, it is proclaimed to be the king of all *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sūtras;
is this not a definitive indication that the Dharma-nature in which one dwells is the very essence designated by the name "Suvarṇaprabhāsa"? This essence is sovereign and is the king of all sūtras.
[Question: Do all three types of sūtra-kings serve as the essence of Mahāyāna sūtras? What is the essence of this specific sūtra?

To which king does it belong? Answer: Although the principle of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) resides within the Perfect [Teaching], it is permitted that the three vehicles rely upon this for repentance.
Therefore, the Great Master explained its essence from the perspective of the Perfect, yet judged the teaching as belonging to the Shared;

in meaning, it corresponds to the Perfect Teaching entering into the Middle Way of the Shared, thereby serving as the King of Sutras. Question: The *Vimalakīrti-mahāyāna-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "If there are three kinds of conventional truths within the Principle..."

It is not that the three kinds of truths (*satya*) constitute the essence of this sutra; rather, it is the true nature (*dharmatā*) and the ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that can serve as the essence of the sutra.
Now, you say that if one takes the words and principles together, they constitute the sutra, which would mean these are the Middle Way within those three [truths].

Since words and principles are combined, both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) would be the Middle Way; thus, the conventional truth would become the essence of the sutra. Is this not in contradiction with that previous meaning?

[Text] The east is the beginning of the directions; "accumulation" (*saṃudaya*) is the cause of suffering (*duḥkha*). Furthermore, the sequence of the months from Jia to Yi corresponds to spring, and that which arises is precisely the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).
Following the east comes the south, which is like growth following birth; since spring is followed by summer, the south represents the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
After growth comes autumn and the harvest; furthermore, the White Emperor belongs to Metal, and Metal is capable of decisive judgment, hence the west.
The direction of the North corresponds to the Truth of the Path; from the autumn harvest until the winter storage, all activities come to rest.
The North is like the Truth of Cessation, for the causes and effects of suffering and its origin have both ceased and are no longer functional.
[Commentary]: Regarding the characteristics of the Four Truths (*catvāri satyāni*), previously [the order was] result first and cause last;

This is because for a beginner contemplating the objects of meditation, it is easier to investigate matters that are proximate;

[Commentary on the Text]: By contemplating these Four Noble Truths, one gives rise to the eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening; because one maintains the principle without loss and guards against the arising of perversions, it is called "guarding and maintaining."

[Commentary]: Since one contemplates the Four Truths within a single mind and does not cease this contemplation, the eye of wisdom arises spontaneously, protecting and upholding the wondrous principle so that it is never lost and inverted delusions do not arise.
Nevertheless, one must deeply examine the perfect contemplation of the Four Truths, all of which are termed "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*):

The section on "Performing the Encouragement to Practice" concludes with a single line.

I shall now explain how the merit produced by practices such as repentance is unsurpassed and capable of destroying all sufferings.
Exhausting all unwholesome karma, with omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) as its root, it is adorned by immeasurable merits;
it eliminates all suffering and bestows immeasurable happiness.
[Commentary] The text has two parts. First, based on the current passage, there is an exposition. Within this, first, the essence of the three dharmas is shown.

[Text] The first three lines clarify the supreme dharmas capable of destroying [obstacles]: namely, the objective dharma (the *dharmatā* of phenomena), the practice dharma (repentance and praise), and the guiding dharma (all-encompassing wisdom).
Therefore, it is said that "repentance and other dharmas" indicates that they are not of a single kind.
[Commentary]: That which can destroy the supreme Dharma exists within the object, the wisdom, and the practice.

Just as a general who intends to defeat an enemy requires physical strength, followed by profound strategy, and finally sharp weapons—(1) because it relies on the body, it is likened to the object; (2) because the body must possess strategy, it is likened to wisdom;
(3) because strategy requires the assistance of troops, it is likened to practice. If these three are complete, the three obstacles will certainly be eliminated.
Second, the explanation of the three dharma-natures (dharmalakṣaṇa). Part one: the individual exposition. First, the distinct teaching. [Wenju]:
If we discuss them as mutually supporting, practice supports wisdom; wisdom manifests principle, and because principle is manifested, it is able to exhaust all suffering.
Because suffering is exhausted, the Dharma-body is manifested. Because wisdom is perfected, the Reward-body is manifested. Because merit is unsurpassed, the Response-body is manifested.
"Manifestation.

[Commentary: The sequence of practice, wisdom, and principle is "vertical," referring to their successive development during the stage of cultivation; the simultaneous manifestation within the three fruits of Dharma, Reward, and Response is "horizontal," referring to their concurrent realization at the moment of fruition.
This is precisely because, according to this teaching, the primordially existent Dharmakāya is shrouded by afflictions.
One must separately establish the functions of conditions and objects so that they mutually assist and manifest one another;

furthermore, because this teaching holds that the three dharmas are inherently complete yet do not subsume one another, the accomplishment of these functions causes the three bodies to manifest simultaneously. Second, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

[Text]: According to the proponents of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), the three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; thus, when one cultivates the three bodies, they are manifested neither vertically nor horizontally. [Commentary]:

The Perfect Teaching explains that there is no dharma that is not the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Using the wisdom of the Dharma-realm to guide practice within the Dharma-realm... by means of the Dharma...
The realms, practices, and the dharma-realm correspond; the realm of phenomena and the dharma-realm are non-dual and one, for there is nothing outside of this and no third.
Thus, it avoids the error of verticality. Since the dharma-realm is not a single [entity] and the cultivated nature remains distinct, it avoids the error of horizontality.
Just as these three dharmas are cultivated within the causal stage, so too are the three bodies manifested at the time of fruition. Second, the summary.
[Text]: Although there is a distinction between the Perfect (Yuan) and Distinct (Bie) [teachings], both are supreme dharmas capable of shattering [obstructions].

[Commentary]: Although the cultivation is gradual or sudden, both are capable of shattering the obstructions within and without the realms; therefore, they are all termed "supreme dharmas capable of shattering.
This is indicated in the new edition of the *Erqu* (Two Graspings).
[Text] Examining the older version, the wording was abbreviated; the new version fully contains the text concerning the three cycles of preaching.

First, the four Buddhas spoke of the eternal fruit, whereby those of superior faculties benefited. Second, the Brahmin spoke of the Dharma-body having no *śarīra*, whereby those of middle faculties benefited.
Third, the Buddha distinguished the three bodies, whereby those of inferior faculties benefited. Now, in this narrative, it says: "I shall now speak of repentance."
The phrase "these dharmas" (*etad-dharma*) refers to the teachings of the subsequent three cycles (*trikoṭi*), which are capable of destroying evil.
[Commentary] The old text contained only the first cycle for those of superior faculties; since the new translation is extensive, there are two further cycles.
In the second cycle, the Licchavi prince preached the Dharma to the Brahmins regarding the permanence of the *dharmakāya*.

The matter of the *śarīra* (relics) is for those of middling faculties. Its third cycle contains a separate chapter on the differentiation of the three bodies (*trikāya*) for those of inferior faculties.
These three cycles are all supreme teachings that completely destroy the three obstructions (*trisaṃvāra*).

Now, in describing that which is capable of destroying [the obstructions], it is stated as "equal teachings" (*samadharma*); by principle, this should encompass the teachings of the subsequent three cycles. Second, the evil that is destroyed.
Regarding the second section on offenses, the first part consists of a general judgment based on the gravity of the offense.
[Textual Commentary]: Next, from the passage "The various faculties are incomplete" onwards, the text of the "Chapter on Emptiness" is presented in two parts.

The first three and a half lines clarify the evil that is to be destroyed; the subsequent three and a half lines clarify the method by which it is destroyed. This first part is further divided into three sections.

The phrase "deficiency of faculties" below refutes the obstacle of retribution; the single phrase "sorrow and distress" refutes the obstacle of afflictions; and the phrase "evil stars and calamitous anomalies" below refutes the obstacle of karma.

[Commentary] This text specifically demonstrates the evil offenses that are to be refuted; as for its being described as belonging to the "Chapter on Emptiness," it is because the refuted objects are now being cited here.

Since the faults [of the opponent] have been exposed and their refutations overcome by means of the various refutations—wherein the "emptiness of the refutations themselves" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) is essential—they shall now be set forth. Question:

Since the method of refutation was already clarified in the preceding passage, why is there yet another method of refutation? Answer: The previous passage concerned the objects, wisdom, and practice, which are the medicinal remedies.

The present passage clarifies the three karmas—specifically hearing, reflection, and cultivation—which constitute the method of taking the medicine; it is the method for ingesting the wondrous medicine.
If one does not take the medicine or does not follow the prescription, how can the illness be cured? These two aspects form three obstacles that can be destroyed.
Second, the judgment; first, it clarifies that the transformation of retribution differs from other sutras.

[Text] In other sutras, it is said that regarding the obstacle of retribution, it is difficult to transform while the cause is still in process, but once the fruit has manifested, there is nothing that can be done.
In this sutra, however, all three obstacles can be transformed.

[Commentary] Even when an evil retribution has already been established, it is now difficult to transform; yet there are also sutras that say past karma cannot be transformed—how much more so once the fruit has manifested!
Although these are all *siddhāntas* (established tenets) taught according to the differing capacities of beings, here we clarify the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*).

If one practices according to the sūtras, there is no failure to attain quiescence, for the Dharma is supreme. Second, it is clarified that the three obstructions arise from the breaking of the precepts.
[Text] A preliminary explanation of the three obstacles resulting from the violation of the five precepts: the violation of the five precepts is the obstacle of karma;
receiving rebirth in the three miserable realms or as humans or devas is the obstacle of retribution; and afflictions being the fundamental cause is the obstacle of affliction.

[Commentary]: Regarding the causes of the three obstructions, how could one possibly present them exhaustively through the various differing explanations of the scriptural gates? For now, we shall proceed from a single perspective based on the violation of the five precepts.
Since the meaning of the five precepts encompasses the profound and subsumes the vast, what dharma would not be exhausted therein?

Nevertheless, as it does not obstruct other approaches, it is said that this is merely "one-sided" (*yiwǎng*). Question: Is it solely because of afflictions (*kleśa*) that the karma of violating the precepts arises? Or does the violation of the precepts itself give rise to affliction?

The answer regarding the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is as follows: due to the karma of breaking the precepts, there manifest much greed and anger; for example, by slandering the sūtras, one becomes deeply attached to false views and sexual desire becomes rampant.
Since these all arise from karma, which in turn gives rise to afflictions, we know that the three obstacles (*trīṇy āvaraṇāni*) are mutually dependent in both their direct and inverse relations.

Second, the detailed explanation according to the topical outline (*kośasthāna*). Part three: first, refuting the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Sub-part one: first, a direct explanation based on the human realm.
Second, first indicating cause and effect.
[Wenqu]: Now, we directly address the retribution for violating the five precepts within the human realm.
[Ji]: Second, examining the effect to trace the cause; first, the retribution for killing.
The sense faculties are incomplete and the lifespan is diminished.
[Commentary] This passage consists of three parts; first, it cites the sutra to demonstrate the point.
[Wenju] "The sense faculties are externally deficient and the lifespan is internally cut short"—these two phrases constitute the retribution for killing.

[Commentary] Regarding "internal premature death," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "to die young. This is verified by two types of causes and effects: [first,] because one previously damaged the bodies of others, one's current sense faculties are impaired;

[second,] because one previously severed the lives of others, one's current lifespan is diminished. [Text] In the past, one damaged the limbs and bodies of others; now, one's various sense organs are mutilated. In the past, one cut off the lives of others; now, one's lifespan is shortened.
[Commentary] Third, citing scriptural evidence.
[Textual Explanation] The Sūtra says: "By the causal conditions of killing, one obtains two kinds of retributive fruits: much illness and a short lifespan"—this refers precisely to that matter.

[Commentary] This refers to the old version of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. It states fully that the sin of killing causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms, and when they are subsequently reborn in the human realm, they receive two types of retribution:
first, being frequently ill; second, having a short lifespan. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that killing results in three fruits:
first, the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), which refers to the three evil destinies; second, the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), which refers to being born as a human.
The three predominant results of being frequently ill and short-lived are: first, that external objects one encounters all lack luster and do not endure for long;
second, the retribution for stealing, which is poverty and hardship, and being abandoned by the devas.
[Commentary] The text has three parts; first, the sutra passage is cited for illustration.

[Wenju] "If one is poor and suffers from hardship" refers to the lack of external supporting conditions (*niśraya-vipāka*); "the various devas abandon them" refers to the lack of internal merit and virtue.
These two phrases constitute a violation of the precept against stealing.
[Commentary] Second, citing scriptural evidence. [Text]:
The scripture says that there are devas and nāgas born together with and bearing the same name as [the Buddha], who possess the merit of acting as assistants;
there is the Goddess of Merit (Goddess Puṇyavatī) who has made a vow to benefit others, whereas a thief does not possess such things.
[Commentary] Regarding "gods of common birth and common name," the thirty-seventh fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa states:
"Just as when a person is born, there are two kinds of gods who constantly follow and attend them: first, those of common birth; second, those of common name.
These gods are always seen by people, yet people do not see the gods. This is verified by three points.
[Text]: Furthermore, one who was formerly wealthy but later becomes poor must surely have been abandoned by the *nāgas* and forsaken by the devas.
[Commentary]: Because they violated the prohibitions and committed various unwholesome deeds, both the devas and *nāgas* necessarily abandon them;
consequently, their reputation and material gains are dispersed and lost. Third is the retribution for sexual desire.
"Intimate relatives engage in strife and litigation, and the laws of the king are applied to them.
[Commentary] The text has three parts; first, the sutra passage is cited to indicate the subject.
[Wenju] "If intimate relatives fight among themselves, and the laws of the king are applied externally"—these two phrases refer to the violation of the precept against sexual misconduct.

[Commentary] "Those with whom one is intimate" refers to parents, brothers, wives, children, and the six types of close relatives. The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states that through sexual misconduct one obtains three fruits:
first, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), which means falling into the three evil realms;

second, the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), which means being born among humans but having two wives who compete with one another, or having a wife who is unchaste; third, the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), which means being covered in much dust and grime. This is what is meant here.
The dispute accords with the treatise. Second, citing scriptural evidence. [Wenju] The Sūtra says:
"If humans provide protection, humans become resentful; if the Dharma provides protection, the Dharma is destroyed. [Ji] Regarding "human protection":
because a woman’s will is weak, she relies on three types of protection—childhood protection by her parents, and protection by her husband upon marriage.
The husband protects [the wife] when he dies; the children protect the Dharma. "Protection" refers to receiving the five, eight, and other precepts.
Third, an analysis based on principle:

[Commentary] "In the past they encroached upon that person; now their own flesh and bone fight and sue. In the past they destroyed another's Dharma; now the laws of the king are brought against them."
This refers precisely to that matter.

[Commentary] In the past, those who disparaged the Dharma of others caused them to violate the precepts; thus, as retribution for the four kinds of false speech, they each engage in mutual anger and contention.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; the first clarifies that the scripture is incomplete.
[Wenju] "Each [party] quarrels in anger"—there should be two phrases here, which may have been omitted by the translator or simply abbreviated.
[Commentary] As exemplified above, the three retributions together comprise two phrases. Second, regarding the fulfillment of the meaning, there are two parts;
first, the fulfillment of the text is shown. [Text] Internally, each person is angry and contentious; externally, everyone lacks faith. This pair constitutes the offense of lying.
[Commentary]:
It is called a "pair" because an odd number is completed by an even one; "anger" (*fen*) is synonymous with wrath. Second, an analysis according to principle:
[Text] "In the past he deceived others with untruths, and now he is constantly deceived; he was angry that his past words lacked reality, and now people have no faith in him."
[Commentary]:
Fifth, the retribution for drinking alcohol is the depletion of one's wealth and possessions.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; first, the introductory section presents the text of the added passage.
[Wenju] To squander wealth and property externally and to fail in ritual propriety internally—this is the retribution for drinking alcohol.
[Commentary] Second, the investigation and demonstration of cause and effect, which is further divided into two parts; first, the direct demonstration.
[Text]: "In the past, one was arrogant and squandered wealth while wasting days; now there is much loss and depletion. In the past, one deviated from moderation;

now one has fallen into deafness and stupidity. [Commentary]: "Moderation" (*zǔnjié*) also refers to ritual propriety and measure. Because of intoxication, one deviates from it. "Deafness and stupidity" (*lóng'ěi*): *lóng* (deaf) is pronounced with the fifth tone; *ěi* (stupidity) means delusion.
Second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
[Wenju] The Sūtra says: "The fierce winds of resentment and the fire of the sinful mind constantly cause it to blaze. This refers precisely to that matter.
[Ji] The Sūtra is also from the *Avataṃsaka*. Because drinking alcohol causes resentment to increase further, this passage can be cited as evidence.
Second, the extensive explanation of the five vehicles. Part one: questioning the application of the five precepts based on the sūtras.
[Text] Question: In explaining the Mahāyāna sūtras, how can the meaning be correlated with the five precepts?
[Commentary] The reason the name "Five Precepts" is drawn from the Hīnayāna Vinaya is to explain the characteristics of the royal law (*rājadharma*) in this present sutra.

Second, by answering through the observance of precepts according to the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*), all dharmas of practice—both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—are encompassed; they are applied according to the depth or shallowness of a person’s intellectual understanding.
Here, the Five Precepts are explained as the division of the Dharma for the five vehicles. This is divided into two parts: first, the general answer.
[Text] Answer: The opening and closing [of the categories] of the five precepts are of great significance.
[Commentary] By means of the names of the five precepts, all phenomena are subsumed; though there may be differences in their extent, these are merely matters of expansion and contraction.

Second, the specific demonstration of the two [aspects]. First, the explanation based on the meaning. First, the allocation of the five precepts to the substance of the Dharma according to its actual depth. Third...
First, clarifying the two categories of humans and devas; first, citing the scripture.

[Wenju] The *Tiwai jing* states: "The five precepts are the great taboos of heaven and earth: above they correspond to the five stars, below they are matched with the five sacred peaks, and within they constitute the five viscera.
Those who violate them defy heaven, offend earth, and bring destruction upon their own bodies."
[Commentary] "The great taboos of Heaven and Earth" (*tiandi daji*): *ji* (taboo) also means prohibition or admonition. The five stars are: the Wood-essence of the East, Jupiter (*Suixing*);

the Fire-essence of the South, Venus (*Yinghuo*); the Metal-essence of the West, Venus (*Taibai*); the Water-essence of the North, Mercury (*Chenxing*); and the Earth-essence of the Center, Saturn (*Zhensheng*). The Five Peaks (*wuyue*) are:

the Eastern Peak, Mount Tai, belonging to the region of Yanzhou; the Southern Peak, Mount Heng, belonging to the region of Jingzhou; [the Western Peak, Mount Hua, belonging to the region of Xizhou; the Northern Peak, Mount Heng, belonging to the region of Yuzhou; and the Central Peak, Mount Song, belonging to the region of Zhongzhou].
Mount Hua of the Western Peak belongs to Yongzhou; Mount Chang of the Northern Peak belongs to Bingzhou; and Mount Song of the Central Peak belongs to Yuzhou.
The five viscera are the liver, heart, spleen, lungs, and kidneys.

While the stars, peaks, and viscera are all correlated with the five elements, when the five elements are paired with the precepts, the three meanings become self-evident: non-killing corresponds to wood, for wood presides over growth and generation.
Killing leads to non-birth; non-lust corresponds to fire, for fire is the lord of illumination; sexual misconduct concerns the private and hidden;

non-drinking corresponds to earth, for earth is stable and still, whereas intoxication causes instability and swaying. Non-stealing corresponds to metal, for metal is associated with punishment and execution, and the thief suffers such punishment;
non-falsehood corresponds to water, which takes on various shapes according to its vessel to manifest non-falsity, whereas falsehood is the opposite of this correspondence.
The Five Elements have already been correlated with the five stars; the Five Peaks (Mountains) and the Five Viscera preside over the Five Elements.

As for the statement in the Sūtra that there are "Five Peaks," this was merely a gloss added by the translator to conform to the conventions of this region. Regarding the phrase "contravening Heaven" and so forth: to contravene them above is to offend the five stars;
to offend them below is to strike against the five peaks; and to offend them within is to [strike] the five viscera.

Subduing the body. Second, correlating with the Dharma. Part two: the specific correlation. Part one: the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. Part one: correlating with the Five Constant Virtues.

[Text] Furthermore, correlating with the Five Constant Virtues: non-killing corresponds to benevolence (*ren*); non-stealing corresponds to righteousness (*yi*); non-lust corresponds to propriety (*li*); non-drinking... [text continues].
Soberness corresponds to wisdom; abstention from false speech corresponds to faith.

[Commentary] Zhao Rui’s *Changduan jing* states: "Benevolence (*ren*) means love. To establish punishments and eliminate harm, while practicing universal love without partiality, is called benevolence.
Righteousness (*yi*) means appropriateness. To discern right and wrong and establish what may or may not be done is called righteousness. Rites (*li*)..."
To advance or retreat according to measure, and to maintain the distinction between the honorable and the humble, is called *li* (ritual propriety).

That by which the wise determine the nature of right and wrong, gain and loss, is called *zhi* (wisdom). That which people receive and uphold, issuing commands to unify the hearts of the people, is called *xin* (trustworthiness).
Now, to oppose benevolence (*ren*) with non-killing, while killing itself is [the very thing that defines it].
He is non-exclusive love; as for stealing, it is contrary to righteousness—stealing is what ought not to be done. He is non-lustful;
as for lewdness, it is contrary to propriety—it causes the distinction between noble and base to vanish and violates the standards of ritual. He is non-drinking;
as for intoxication, it is contrary to wisdom—for one who is drunk cannot discern right from wrong or gain from loss. He is non-falsehood; as for lying, it is contrary to faithfulness.

Thus, people would not believe in accepting [these correspondences]. As for correlating the Five Constant Virtues with the Five Elements, Zheng Kangcheng’s commentary on the "Zhongyong" chapter of the *Liji* states:
"The spirit of Wood is Benevolence; the spirit of Metal is Righteousness; the spirit of Fire is Propriety;

the spirit of Water is Trustworthiness; and the spirit of Earth is Wisdom. Previously, when correlating the Five Elements with the Five Precepts, I adopted this meaning for the sake of its underlying principle.

"By not drinking [one corresponds] to Earth; by not lying [one corresponds] to Water. These two correspond to the Five Classics. [Wenju: Furthermore, regarding the correspondence with the Five Classics:

not killing corresponds to the Book of Documents (Shangshu); not stealing corresponds to the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu); not committing adultery corresponds to the Book of Rites (Liji); not lying corresponds to the Book of Poetry (Shijing);
and not drinking alcohol corresponds to the Book of Changes (Yijing)."
[Commentary: Regarding the response concerning "not killing," as for the "Shangshu" (Book of Documents), its compilation begins from the era of Tang and Yu downward;
it thus honors the system of abdication and cession while disparaging acts of execution and warfare.

The Master, seeing that the House of Zhou had become weak and its edicts were no longer effective, compiled the *Spring and Autumn Annals* based on the records of the state of Lu to serve as a substitute for rewards and punishments, thereby striking fear into rebellious ministers and treacherous sons. This is why he responded with "not stealing."
Regarding the rites of propriety (*li*), there are five types. The *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), in the duties of the Grand Master of the Altars (*Da Zong Bo*), states:

"By means of auspicious rites (*ji li*), one serves the spirits and deities of the states; 'serving' refers to sacrificing to them, offering to them, and boiling for them. By means of calamitous rites (*xiong li*), one expresses sorrow for the misfortunes of the states;

'expressing sorrow' refers to relieving their distress and disasters. By means of guest rites (*bin li*), one fosters intimacy with the states; 'fostering intimacy' refers to causing them to become closely attached. By means of military rites (*jun li*), one brings uniformity to the states; 'bringing uniformity' refers to intimidating those who are in discord."

As for those who commit transgressions and deviations, one draws near the myriad people through *jia-li* (rites of celebration). "Jia" means "good"; it is by means of what the human heart deems good that these regulations are established.

Sexual misconduct is an improper form of interaction; thus, *jia-li* is employed to serve as a warning against such misconduct. The *Shi* [Classic of Poetry] praises what is good and satirizes what is evil—it is not mere idle talk.
The *Yi* [Classic of Changes] is a book for exhausting principle and exhausting nature, characterized by purity, stillness, refinement, and subtlety.

How could those who teach the consumption of alcohol and the resulting confusion ever exhaust its principles or fully realize its nature? Regarding the second, the Dharma of the Two Wheel-Turning Kings, there are three initial points:
opening five pairs of ten aspects. [Commentary on the Text]:

Furthermore, in relation to the ten wholesome paths of action, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three of the body; false speech subsumes the four of the mouth; and the consumption of intoxicants subsumes [the remaining one].
The mind has three [aspects].
[Commentary] The second indicates that the seven are combined into two aspects of the mind.
[Wenju] The mundane [precepts] cannot protect the mouth; they briefly restrain one [aspect]: not lying. The *Śāstra* says that what is grave is this.
False speech already encompasses [the other two precepts]; drinking alcohol is a form of wrong livelihood that increases hatred and delusion.

Since wisdom is the foremost for transcending the world, while the three poisons are the roots of birth and death, if one can refrain from alcohol, it prevents the three poisons of the mental faculty and nurtures supramundane wisdom.
[Commentary]: Laypeople are unable to guard their speech because the five precepts are established specifically for the householders;
since guarding speech in the secular world is truly difficult, only the drinking of alcohol is prohibited.

As for those who "live by wrong livelihood," they sustain their bodies with wine while failing to observe the right precepts, which is termed "wrong livelihood. These three fetters (saṃyojana) are named after the persons from whom they originated.

[Text]: This is the opening of the five precepts to reveal the ten wholesome actions; these ten wholesome actions were employed by the ancient Wheel-Turning Kings and are also termed natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and natural virtues (*prakṛti-kuśala*).

[Commentary]: Although the five precepts were established by the Tathāgata, since they correspond to the ten wholesome actions, they are here judged from the perspective of the outflowing realm (*sāsrava*).
According to the ancient laws belonging to the wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), there are what are termed natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and natural virtues (*prakṛti-kuśala*).
This is because the ten unwholesome dharmas are inherently transgressions by their very nature, while the ten wholesome dharmas are inherently virtuous by their very nature.
Therefore, the wheel-turning kings, in accordance with worldly conventions, taught these categories of good and evil to transform sentient beings. Second, the conclusion and indication.
[Text] All are the root of all transgressions.
[Commentary] Even worldly virtues cannot avoid saṃsāra; though one may be born among humans or devas, one must still give rise to unwholesome karma.
If this is true even for what is wholesome, how much more so for the unwholesome? Therefore, it is said that they are all the root of all transgressions. Second, the analysis of the Two Vehicles.
The fourth [point] concerns the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the objects of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

[Wenju: Furthermore, the five precepts correspond to the five aggregates: non-killing corresponds to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); non-stealing corresponds to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); non-sexual misconduct corresponds to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);

non-lying corresponds to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and non-drinking of intoxicants corresponds to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Thus, the five aggregates open up into the four [foundations of mindfulness].

The Foundations of Mindfulness. [Commentary]: By not killing, the physical form remains complete; by not stealing, the sensation of suffering does not arise; by not engaging in sexual misconduct, perverse thoughts do not emerge;
by not lying, the flow of mental states becomes pure and substantial; by not drinking intoxicants, discernment becomes clear and distinct. These—

Since the aggregates (*skandha*) serve not only as objects but also provide support for mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one may establish the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) within them: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as the foundation of mindfulness of the body;

the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) as the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; the two aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) as the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*); and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as the foundation of mindfulness of the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
From these foundations of mindfulness, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) are fully realized.

[Text]: The foundations of mindfulness open up the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment open up the three gates of liberation; the three gates of liberation open up nirvana.

[Commentary]: Within the four foundations of mindfulness in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the four types of diligence are called the right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*), and the four types of concentrated mind are called...
The arising of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the five roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is called the "roots" (*indriya*); their further growth is called "powers" (*bala*).

The discernment of the four types of stations is termed the "path" (*mārga*), while the application of the path is termed "enlightenment factors" (*bodhyaṅga*). Walking upon the secure path is termed the "right path" (*samyagmārga*). The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are like a level road;
emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are like the three gates of a city; and nirvāṇa is like [the city itself].
The city: the three vidyās transform the five aggregates into the fivefold dharma-body.
[Wenju] Therefore it is said: "Form can give rise to precepts; sensation receives meditative concentration; perception awakens to wisdom; volition practices the path of realizing emptiness;
consciousness gives rise to liberation and immediate knowledge."

[Commentary]: Because it restrains and guards body and speech, it is called "precept" (*śīla*); because it is the correct meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*);

because one uses conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) to realize the emptiness of the body, it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*); because wisdom realizes the voidness within words, the character "penetration" (*tong*) is superfluous in all cited texts;
and because one proceeds without indolence until reaching the fruit of sainthood, it is called "practice" (*caryā*). This gives rise to understanding.
Having liberated one's own consciousness and realized it, this is called the "knowledge of liberation within the body" (*vimukti-jñāna-kāya*).

This is precisely the transformation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) into the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). The four fetters and the five precepts constitute the teaching for the Two Vehicles.

[Text] The *Dīpavaṃsa-sūtra* states: "The five precepts are the talisman for longevity and the seal of immortality; this is the virtue of permanence (*nitya-guṇa*).
To enter and exit without confusion and to come and go without interruption is the virtue of purity (*śubha-guṇa*). To govern the entire person is the virtue of self (*ātman-guṇa*).
To establish the root of the Way is the virtue of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*). These are the five precepts corresponding to the four virtues.

[Commentary] Because those who realize the Mahāyāna understand that the essence of the five precepts is the nature of the mind, and whether they receive or uphold them, each accords with this nature which is endowed with the four virtues, the five [precepts] are none other than permanence, bliss, self, and purity; this is the general correspondence.

Furthermore, one may also correlate the five [precepts] individually with the four virtues: because the mind and the nature of sentient beings are without arising or ceasing, they accord with the nature.
To uphold the precept against killing is to wear the talisman of longevity and immortality; this is the constant virtue.

Because one’s mind is non-lustful and identical in nature to that of all sentient beings, one accords with their fundamental nature by upholding the precept against sexual misconduct; this is called "entering and exiting without confusion.
Because one’s mind and the minds of all beings are moment-to-moment true and free from falsehood or delusion, one accords with nature by upholding the precept against false speech.

The precept name for "uninterrupted coming and going" corresponds to the virtue of purity; because the mind and the nature of sentient beings are not in a state of delusion or intoxication, one maintains the precept against drinking alcohol in accordance with this original nature.
The precept name for "governing the single body" corresponds to the virtue of the self;

because the mind and the nature of sentient beings are themselves Bodhi and are free from the suffering of greedy seeking, one maintains the precept against stealing in accordance with this original nature.
The establishment of the precepts as the root of the Way is the virtue of bliss. Second, regarding the correspondence between the phenomena and the three karmas:

[Wenju] states that the five precepts are subsumed into the three karmas, which correspond to the three absences of error, the three absences of need for protection, and the inconceivable transformation of the three wheels—the three mysteries.
[Commentary]: Not killing, stealing, or engaging in sexual misconduct is the bodily karma; not speaking falsely is the verbal karma; and not drinking intoxicants is the mental karma.

Because these observances accord with one's nature, they are established as the causes for attaining Buddhahood. The Buddha’s three karmas—body, speech, and mind—proceed in accordance with wisdom and are free from fault;
this is termed the "threefold absence of error. Because there is no error, there is no need for protection, which is termed [the threefold non-protection].
The three types of unguarded bodily action manifesting as names are called the Wheel of Supernatural Powers; verbal action preaching the Dharma is called the Wheel of Right Teaching;

and mental action discerning the faculties [of beings] is called the Wheel of Knowing Minds. Because all three crush and grind away the afflictions and karma of sentient beings, and because those of lower stages cannot fathom them, they are termed the "Three Mysteries" (triguhyas).
These three are correlated with the Three Dharmas according to principle.

[Text]: The three tracks, the three bodies, the three Buddha-natures, the three prajñās, the three nirvāṇas, the three knowledges, the three virtues, and so forth—these are the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the "Three.
[Commentary]: The five precepts are themselves the principle; one cessation and one practice both accord with the perfectly interfused Three Dharmas. If one wishes...
Furthermore, in accordance with this principle, it is established that refraining from killing sentient beings accords with the principle of eternal abiding;

this is the *dharmatā-vidhi* (the track of true nature). Refraining from sexual misconduct results in the purity of mind, and refraining from drinking results in the clarity of wisdom; these constitute the *avalokana-vidhi* (the track of contemplation). Refraining from falsehood gives rise to faith and compliance, and refraining from stealing preserves the resources of others;
these constitute the *sambhāra-pariniṣpatti-vidhi* (the track of completing the provisions). Since these correspond to the three tracks (*trividha-vidhi*), they are identical to the One.

Because the three dharmas are mutually identical in their characteristics, one knows that the five precepts encompass all phenomena without exception. [The text] raises these three extensively to establish their names.
[Commentary]: Transversely and vertically they are boundless, equal to empty space and the dharma-realm;
they are also the dharma-gate of the inexhaustible treasury and the samādhi of immeasurable meaning. To state the essential point: they are, in fact, all the Buddha-dharmas.
