[Commentary] Second, clarifying the phenomena and principle of the five precepts by further distinguishing between the partial and the perfect.

Although the preceding section provided a general indication of the meaning of the five precepts, encompassing both the shallow and the profound, if one does not discuss in detail their phenomena and principle, as well as their partial and perfect aspects, how can one precisely recognize the characteristics of upholding and violating them?

This section is divided into five parts; first, the precept against killing. Part two of this [precept] provides a detailed exposition, which is further divided into two: first, a general indication of the phenomena and principle.
Observance and Violation.

[Wenqu] Furthermore, "harming" is termed the phenomenon (vastu) of killing, while "not harming" is termed the phenomenon of non-killing. Those who understand the gate of dharmas analyze phenomena as principle;

thus, the essence of the dharma is called the principle of killing, and the essence of the dharma is called the principle of non-killing. One should know that the precept of non-killing has various aspects.
Their theories differ, and their karmic retributions likewise differ.

[Commentary] This is intended to lead practitioners to employ principle (*li*) rather than mere phenomena (*shi*) when refraining from killing; only by upholding non-killing through principle can one be said to possess the full precepts of a beginner.

Here, it is clarified that the essential nature of the Dharma must be distinguished: the essential nature within emptiness (*kong*) is itself emptiness, which pertains to partial contemplation (*pianguan*).
The Perfect [Teaching] is the substance of the precept against killing; all dharmas are none other than the Middle Way, and worldly phenomena are all eternal—this is the principle discussed here.
Because the precept against killing intends to manifest this meaning, it is explained from the perspective of humans and devas up to the ultimate Perfection;
thus it is said that cause and effect are variously different. Second, a detailed explanation of the gains and losses of the partial and the perfect. First, the partial. First, humans.
The heavens serve only the two original humans.
[Commentary: If one practices mindfulness and protection like a horse wearing a bridle or a cowherd holding a staff, the retribution is birth in the human realm for one hundred and twenty years;
one obtains only the fleshly eye and does not possess the four eyes.
[Commentary] Since the merit of upholding the precepts is slight, one must add the protection of guarding the mind, just as with oxen or horses;

if there were no reins and bits, they would bolt away, and if there were no staff, they would trample the crops. This is a metaphor for how, if one does not apply mindfulness, one will commit transgressions regarding sensory objects.
A lifespan of one hundred and twenty years refers to the human realm in the upper direction (the heavens). As for the faculties, they are merely clear; this is the retribution of the fleshly eye.
This may be illustrated by the two heavens.

[Commentary on the Text]: If one’s nature is spontaneously perfected like a river flowing into the sea, the retribution consists of dwelling in the six heavens for an extremely long duration of nine hundred twenty-six billion seven hundred million years;
yet one obtains only the divine eye (divyacakṣus), not the three eyes (trividyā).
[Commentary] Having perfected the merit of upholding the precepts, one spontaneously attains their nature; it is like river water naturally flowing into the ocean of pure precepts.

This does not yet discuss the meditative states (dhyāna-sahagata), but refers only to the retribution of the six heavens. Calculated by human years, the lifespan of the sixth heaven corresponds to that many years [of the human realm].

There, one obtains only the fleshly heavens and lacks the wisdom of the Dharma-Buddha; the other faculties may be inferred accordingly. [This applies to] the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
[Regarding] "Furthermore, for the first two [vehicles]":

[Commentary] If one additionally cultivates the wisdom of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth regarding the guest-precepts (*āgantuka-śīla*), the retribution will be in the *pariṇāma* (transformation) body with a lifespan of seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
yet one will only attain the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and not yet attain the other two eyes.

[Commentary] Regarding the summary of the meaning: apart from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* common to both the *Āgamas* and the *Vaipulya*, the former physician serves as a metaphor for the non-Buddhists who appeared first, while the Tathāgata’s subsequent appearance serves as a metaphor for the visiting physician.

The precepts established by the Buddha are called "guest precepts" (*ātithya-śīla*). Beyond these precepts of ritual action (*vastu-śīla*), one further cultivates the precepts that accord with the Path and the unattached precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*).
When the stage of these precepts reaches its ultimate limit, according to this teaching, they are extinguished like ashes; it is not said that there is any karmic retribution.

Now, according to various Mahāyāna texts concerning those born in the land of skillful means who receive the life-span of transformation (*pariṇāmika-āyu*), it is not stated that there is a limit to the lifespan in this land;

rather, it is simply that the fruits [of past karma] are shifted and transformed. If it is now said that they remain for seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this must mean that only after such a number of kalpas have passed do they enter the land of true retribution (*samyak-vipāka*).
If one were to destroy the delusions as numerous as motes of dust while remaining in this land, that too would be possible.

Regarding the Dharma-eye, this treatise now discusses those of the Two Vehicles who have first attained birth; they obtain only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). This is the second [section], which correctly demonstrates the two types of Bodhisattvas at their initial stage.
[Commentary on the Text]: If one further cultivates wisdom regarding the permanent and the impermanent, the karmic fruit will be to receive the Dharma-nature body within the Lotus Treasury Ocean.
[They] attain the five eyes and attain eternal life. [Commentary:

The meaning is that, according to the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), one sequentially cultivates the path of the three truths. "Eternal" refers to the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-satya*), which is the wisdom praised by the Buddhas as well as the sovereign precepts;
"impermanent" refers to the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), which is the wisdom that accords with the path and is unattached.
Prior to the precepts is emptiness, followed by the provisional; now, following the sequence of the discourse, the wisdom of emptiness occupies the next position.

When it says "and so forth," this refers to the wisdom of the Middle Way. These two are acquired in accordance with meditative concentration and the full precepts, and they arise in the first bhūmi within the Reward Land known as the Flower Treasury Ocean.
Therein, the Buddha-eye partially manifests the four eyes, which then merge into one; for this reason, it is so named.
The five eyes are obtained, and the same applies to the faculties (*indriya*); since longevity is the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*), it already pertains to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Because the sutras speak both of the "faculties" and again of "longevity," they must be mentioned together. This concludes the two analogies.

[Text]: "If even compared to the Buddha, [the lifespan] is such that the sense faculties are incomplete and the life span is diminished, how much more so for those prior [beings] whose faculties and lifespans were [even further reduced]?
[Commentary]:

This teaching employs analogy regarding the Buddha with two intended meanings. If it is to be understood as a direct instruction (*śāsana*), it uses the cause to infer the result, distinguishing between the partial and the complete.

The two [vehicles] differ from the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) and the Separate Teaching (biejiao), for while the beginning and end of the latter are exclusively the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, the beginning and end of the Perfect Teaching are entirely the Buddha-Dharma;
therefore, they are said to be "incomplete" and "diminished. Second, regarding the two types of the Perfect [Teaching], the first shows their characteristics.
First, clarifying the mastery of the meaning and its maintenance. First, a brief indication of the literal maintenance (shihchi).
[Text] If a person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) upholds the precept against killing as a matter of fact, [Commentary] this means not harming or killing the life-force of sentient beings;

this is the same as the wheel-turning king’s (cakravartin) precepts of the partial and limited vehicles (pianxiao), yet it is fundamentally different from them because of the reason for not killing, which is what will be clarified in the following passage concerning contemplation of principle (liguan). Second, the detailed explanation.
Regarding the third point on maintaining principle (*li*), this first section clarifies maintenance by way of its essential nature (*ti*).
[Textual Passage]: Furthermore, maintaining the precept against killing according to principle means not destroying the body while conforming to the single characteristic;

it is the non-interruption of ignorance and craving while giving rise to clarity and liberation. It is the state where the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātv-āyatana*) are not damaged or injured, and where neither seeds nor fruits arise.

[Extinguished. [Commentary: This principle is not killing. If one does not understand that the nine realms are inherently complete within the nature, but merely says that "realizing all phenomena as the principle" constitutes the full wave being water, this still conflates the general and the specific; thus, the perfect cultivation has not yet been revealed. Therefore, Jingxi said: "If..."
Since not discussing the "endowment" (ju) belongs to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), one must realize that this body is a provisional conglomeration;

that the three delusions, ignorance, and craving, as well as the real dharmas of the three aggregates, are all inherently complete within the nature, and because the nature is without differentiation, it is called the "single-characteristic nature.

Since it is called "liberation through clarity" rather than "bondage through darkness," and since it is the inherent completeness of the nature, how could it be subject to destruction or injury? Ignorance and craving are the "sons" [of the nature], whether provisional or real.
This fruit is the entire embodiment of nature; how could nature itself arise or cease? Through such a wondrous contemplation, what was an obstacle becomes a virtue;
it does not require transformation or removal to constitute the precept of non-killing in accordance with principle. Second is obtaining retribution in accordance with nature.

[Text] Having accomplished wisdom, they dwell in the eternally quiescent light-land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-kṣetra*), where their lifespan is eternal and profound; they are fully endowed with the five eyes and attain mastery over the faculties:
with the ear they see, and with the eye they hear; they attain mastery over life, freely determining its length.
[Commentary: From the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), all are termed "accomplishing wisdom" and "dwelling in the Constant Quiescent Light.

This refers to the partial and complete fruition of both the primary and secondary retributions (*niśraya* and *sambhoga*). Because there is no further retribution after the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is called "constant life";
it is profound and serene, without decrease or loss. The five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) are fully possessed, and the same applies to all the sense faculties (*indriya*), being free from impairment.
As for the external functions, the six sense organs interpenetrate; briefly stated, this refers to mastery over the eyes and ears.
Manifesting the lifespans of the ten realms—whether long or short—is mastery over life. Third, the conclusion indicates cause and effect.
[Text] This is called ultimate observance of the precepts, the perfection of the sense faculties, and the non-diminution of life.
[Commentary] Second, clarifying the transgressions that accord with one's intent; first, a general indication of the two types of transgression.

[Text] Furthermore, for those of the Perfect Teaching, how could they merely maintain [the precepts]? This is not only the precept of non-killing and pure compassion; they also practice "killing" from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*) and "killing" from the perspective of principle (*li*).

[Commentary] Regarding these transgressions of phenomena and principle, if one does not understand the nature-inclusion (*xingju*), the violation of function, and the dharma-gate of killing, then [one cannot truly uphold them].
Compassion can manifest the appearance of hostility to provide an explanation; how could this not be something that Bodhisattvas of the three previous teachings are incapable of performing?
Therefore, the *Pumen shu* clarifies that the dharma-gate of anger is for the sake of accomplishment;

one must constantly contemplate Avalokiteśvara, knowing that one must attain the intent of "killing by nature" for compassion to be truly non-referential (*anālambana*). Thus it is said: "Only killing, only compassion. This is the name.
The offense of acting with intent. Second, specifically showing the two characteristics. First, citing a person to clarify the matter of killing.
[Commentary]: For example, King Śānta killed five hundred Brahmins and gave them the eye to see the Buddha and a lifespan of ten kalpas.
[Commentary] In the "Chapter on Noble Conduct" (*Ārya-caryā-parivarta*) of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the Buddha spoke of a past life as a king named Śāntamati.
At that time, when he was devoted to the Mahāyāna and no Buddha existed in the world, he served a Brahmin for twelve years as his teacher.
He subsequently exhorted that Brahmin to resolve upon Bodhicitta, but the Brahmin did not believe him and slandered the Dharma. The king then killed the Brahmin.
One does not fall into hell because there is no sin of killing. This leads into the Chapter on the Brahma-Faring (*Brahmacarya-varga*), where the Buddha speaks of the fruit of a compassionate mind:

abiding in the stage of regarding all beings as an only son. Kāśyapa raises an objection, saying: "If a Bodhisattva abides in the stage of regarding all beings as an only son, why did the Buddha in the past, when he was a king, take the life of a Brahmin?
The Buddha replies: "I took his life out of loving concern; it was not done with an evil mind."
When those brāhmaṇas die and are reborn in the Avīci Hell, they immediately experience three thoughts: first, they know for themselves that they have come from the human realm;
second, they know this is hell; third, they know for themselves that they were killed by the king because they had slandered the Dharma.

Having reflected on these matters, they immediately gain faith in the Mahāyāna. At that moment, their lives end and they are reborn in the world-system of King Amṛtadundubhi, where they enjoy a long lifespan.
It is said: "For ten kalpas, I was in that position; how then can this ten-kalpa lifespan be called 'killing'?
One must clarify that regarding the dharma-gate of killing, it causes beings to conceive affection so that they achieve objectless compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*);

only then does it accord with the commentary’s statement that "it is solely killing and solely compassion. Second, clarifying the principle of killing according to the sūtras, part one: the direct explanation.

[Text] Furthermore, the practice of the Dharma-gate of "killing" means to dismantle and wash away all accumulated attachments, thereby purifying all afflictions (*kleśa*). It is like a tree spirit breaking off its branches so that it does not receive the resentment of the birds; it is like the kalpa-ending fire burning wood until both ash and charcoal have vanished. Thus, Aṅgulimāla said: "I vow to sever the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*. I cannot maintain the precept against killing. All worldly dust and toil are the seeds of the Tathāgata. [Translation] Furthermore, the practice of the Dharma-gate of "killing" refers to the analytical dispersal and cleansing of all accumulated attachments, thereby purifying all afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is like a tree deity snapping off its branches so as not to suffer the malice of predatory birds, or like the fire at the end of an eon (*kalpāgni*) consuming wood until both ash and charcoal are utterly extinguished.

Therefore, Aṅgulimāla declared: "I vow to sever the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*. I am unable to uphold the precept against killing. All worldly passions and vexations are the seeds of the Tathāgata."
Only when these seeds are completely severed is one called a Buddha.
[Commentary] Previously, it was discussed from the perspective of non-severance, termed "maintaining non-killing"; now, because severance is clarified, it is said that "one commits killing.

Since the Perfect Teaching itself discusses the two meanings of severance and non-severance as being simultaneous, and since the six stages of identity (*liù jí*) are clearly established, there is severance precisely within identity.

Therefore, "non-interruption" may also be clarified through the single character "identity" (ji). There are two meanings: first, that the substance of obstruction is identical to virtue, such that no obstruction exists to be discussed;
this constitutes the meaning of "interruption. Second, since obstruction is already identical to virtue, when has obstruction ever been interrupted? This constitutes the meaning of "non-interruption.
Thus, the subtlety of both "interruption" and "non-interruption" lies in the fact that afflictions are identical to bodhi and birth-and-death are identical to nirvana.
The various Mahāyāna sūtras state that the contemplation of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun guan*) possesses these two gates.

Here, because it involves severing [delusions], it is termed "killing by principle" (*lisha*). Thus, it is said that one analyzes and eradicates the accumulation of attachments; karma and the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are taken as the tree to be severed.
The tree spirit is a metaphor for the person practicing contemplation, and the kalpa-fire is a metaphor for the wisdom capable of severing. (From *Dazhidu lun*, fascicle 3)
10. It is like this: suppose there is a great tree in a vast marsh where many birds gather to roost. A single pigeon arrives last and perches upon a branch; the branch immediately breaks.
The spirit of the marsh asks for the reason, and the tree spirit replies: "This bird comes from the tree of my enemy;
it has eaten the seeds of that nyagrodha tree, and if it should void its droppings here, those seeds falling to the ground would grow into a wicked tree."
Furthermore, if it were to arise again, the harm would surely be great; therefore, it is better to sacrifice a single branch so that what is preserved is vast.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: he has no such fear toward Māras, external delusions, or karma, yet he fears the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

The two vehicles, in turn, act toward the Bodhisattva just as those birds did—they destroy his Mahāyāna mind and forever extinguish his Buddha-vehicle mind. In this passage, however, [the author] uses only...
"Enmity, birds, pervasive attachment," and so forth; as for "the kalpa-fire" and so on, this is also from the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*. The second fascicle of that treatise states:

"Although the two vehicles have destroyed the three poisons, their residual traces are not yet exhausted, just as when wood or grass is burned by fire, smoke and charcoal remain because the power of the fire is weak.
The Buddha’s three poisons are forever exhausted without remainder; it is like the kalpa-fire that burns [the world]."
When Mount Sumeru and all its lands are utterly consumed until there is neither smoke nor ash, this refers to the Buddha-wisdom, which is precisely the Perfect Wisdom (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).

The severing of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—that is, birth and death—is itself *nirvāṇa*. Regarding this "severance," to speak of it in terms of attaining the meaning is called "violating the principle" (*li-fan*);

to speak of it in terms of breaking through through contemplation is called "not maintaining the precepts. This serves as a sincere proof; the same applies to the meanings of all subsequent violations of principle.
To bring all afflictions (*kleśa*) to fulfillment is the lineage of the Tathāgata. This is both the "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*) and the "adversarial lineage.

Since delusion is not a defilement of the nature, how can it be called the Buddha-lineage? It is so named because one knows that [delusion] is itself the nature; since the fundamental nature of cultivated defilements is empty, this emptiness is termed "extinction," which is the very killing of principle.
Second, the attainment of retribution.
[Text] Having accomplished the adamantine, subtle, and wondrous Dharma-body, which is profoundly still yet responds to all, he manifests only through killing and only through compassion;

he assumes forms within the nine realms of existence according to what is appropriate, displaying long or short lifespans as they are perceived, and employing either deficient or complete faculties to transform and deliver sentient beings.

[Commentary] Since both the transgressions of fact and principle accord with the dharma-gate of killing as a manifestation of inherent virtue, once the dharma of killing is perfected, one attains the Dharma-body.

Manifesting forms throughout the nine realms and displaying the length of one's life, as well as the presence or absence of sensory organs, this sovereign function is partially attained at the stage of the true cause and fully realized at the ultimate fruit. This concludes the section on excellence.
[Text]: The various precepts and practices mentioned previously are shallow, limited, and obstructed; they are not the universal path.
Because the vast and far-reaching perfect precepts differ in their direct route yet converge in their ultimate realization, this is called the "ultimate observance of the precept against killing."

[Commentary] First, we shall exclude the inferior paths of humans and devas, the immediate practices (*upāsaka*), the shallow principles of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Vaipulya* vehicles, and the gradual teachings of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*).
These are all narrow and obstructed; they are not the path for penetrating the non-duality of the cultivated and the inherent nature.

[Textual Commentary]: If one maintains the precepts and performs actions seeking agreeable fruits—those who seek such agreeable fruits find them to be impermanent and quickly decaying;
they are entirely the property of others, foul-smelling like the fruit of excrement, and harmful like poisoned food. A person of wisdom should not seek them.
Even if one were to attain it, the mind would not find it sweet or joyful; why then do you so earnestly drink bitterness and eat poison, thereby bringing about your own ruin?

[Commentary] Human and celestial deluded pleasures are considered "agreeable" (kamanīya). Because one wishes to establish the principle and maintain it, one must reject the conventional precepts (vṛtti-śīla) and proceed accordingly.
To seek the retribution of one's desires while resenting the pleasures of the outflows (*sāsrava*) is like a wise child who would not seek to eat the fruit of an *āmra* tree found amidst dung.
Just as worldly fine food mixed with poison will kill if eaten,
so too a person of contemplative wisdom should not seek that which is merely a "flower-reward" (*puṣpa-vipāka*), for their heart finds no satisfaction therein.

Delighting in this, they give rise to joy. How is it that ordinary persons observe the precepts for the sake of desire? Second, regarding the explanation of the retribution according to the scriptural text:

[The *Wenju* states: "The poverty of the four castes is precisely the suffering of the swirling currents within these three realms; how could it exceed the three obstacles of the stream of existence?"
To obstruct the Buddha’s ultimate heavenly realm and abandon it is what is called theft; it is not non-theft.

[Commentary] Regarding the four castes—the Vaiśya, Śūdra, Brāhmaṇa, and Kṣatriya—although among humans two are considered low and two high, since they lack the wealth of the sages, all four castes throughout the three realms belong to the poverty of the swirling waters. *Fú* (澓) means to flow in eddies.
Even if one possesses deep water-like concentration and maintains the precepts while seeking agreeable fruits, one is truly trapped by the swirling eddies of existence;
because of this wandering through the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), it is called the "outflow of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*).

It is not merely one among the four outflows, for it fully possesses the causes and effects of the outflows and the three obstacles (*tri-āvaraṇa*), which are capable of obstructing the vision of the Buddha, the God among Gods (*devātideva*). It is likewise an obstruction to the Heaven of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-deva*).
Because it creates an obstruction, the meaning is that one abandons [the Dharma]; this constitutes a transgression against the principle even while maintaining the practice.

According to the sutras, the retribution for this is poverty, suffering, and hardship, as well as being abandoned by the devas. Second, regarding the two vehicles: first, the refutation of the maintenance of the principle as a transgression;
first, the refutation based on those with worldly desires.

rather, it is the transformation of delusion into wisdom, wherein there is neither abandonment nor cultivation, and thus birth itself becomes extinction, being without suffering and without exhaustion.

Hence it is said that "one does not seek through dharmas. As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "The Buddhas teach the dharma of emptiness to deliver those who cling to existence; if there were clinging to emptiness..."

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) consists of three: first, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and third, space (*ākāśa*). Taken collectively, these three are what is referred to;

however, that which is realized by the two vehicles is specifically cessation through deliberation. Now, this analogy originally derives from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains it as follows:
the body of the golden-winged bird (*garuḍa*) is three hundred *yojanas* long, and it is able to fly from one Mount Sumeru to another Mount Sumeru; such is the bird.
When he first spread his two wings, before they were fully formed, he intended to fly away, but fell into Jambudvīpa to undergo suffering such as death or that equal to death;
midway through this, he felt regret, thinking, "I wish to return to the heavens, but I cannot lift myself up. This is originally a metaphor for a bodhisattva falling to the stage of the two vehicles;
here, it merely borrows the analogy of the two vehicles. Second, citing a sutra to clarify the retribution for theft.

[Commentary] Regarding the "gate of stealing the Dharma": this refers to the Buddha’s teacher, the intrinsic evil (prakṛti-pāpa), which is therefore termed the "Dharma-wisdom. Because one enters through this, it is called a "gate.

and fourth, sentient beings—so too it is with the Bodhisattva. When eighty years remain before the True Dharma disappears from the world, he teaches the Tathāgatagarbha for the sake of all sentient beings;

[The text] values [the four great vows] more than grasses and trees; that sutra uses the metaphor of the four eaves to represent four matters, while the meaning of the current passage seems to use them as a metaphor for the Four Great Vows (caturmahāpraṇidhāna).

this is merely an increase in the affairs of desire; it is not the absence of desire.
[Commentary]: Regarding "holding the mind not yet pure, like a monkey bound by chains carrying a bowl of oil":

the Great Sūtra provides an analogy. Suppose a great multitude fills an area of twenty-five *li*. A king commands a minister to carry a bowl of oil through the midst of this crowd without spilling a drop;
if he should spill even a single drop, his life shall be taken. Furthermore, the king dispatches another person following behind him with a drawn sword.
"Your servant, having received the King’s decree, shall uphold and practice it with all his heart. Although he may encounter the five desires, his mind shall not be attached to them.

That sutra uses the metaphor of twenty-five *li* to represent the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), and the metaphor of a drawn sword to represent impermanence (*anityatā*). In the present text, the metaphor of the ordinary person upholding the precepts is used;

the drawn sword may be compared to the sins of the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*). To sever and abandon the coarse [sufferings] of the present in order to seek the subtle [rewards] of the future is as follows:"
