[Text]: "If one follows the doubts of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, it should be said that his lifespan is finite; if one follows the explanations of the four Buddhas to resolve the doubt, it should be said that his lifespan is infinite.
[Commentary]: This second point demonstrates the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanlun).
[Text]: Now, it is not said that the lifespan is finite, nor is it said that the lifespan is infinite;

rather, the term "lifespan" (*āyus-pramāṇa*) is used directly because the intention is to provide a comprehensive discussion of the lifespans of the three Buddhas, rather than addressing them individually.

[Commentary] Because it is not a partial title, the two characters "three lifespans" (*sāyuṣka*) are able to express [the meaning]. Second, regarding the Reward Buddha (*saṃbhoga-buddha*), there are three integrated explanations.
First, it clarifies that the essence of the Reward Buddha is perfect.

[Textual Explanation] To explain by taking the essential meaning according to the convenience of the sense: if this were precisely the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya*, why would one take this [lifespan] of the *saṃbhogakāya*—
which is "above, merging with the Dharma-nature, neither measurable nor immeasurable"— and apply it to the "below, responding to sentient beings,
where there is both measurability and immeasurability"?

[Commentary] Above, regarding the title of the chapter, if one does not lean toward either of the two characters "Life Span" (*āyus-pramāṇa*)—neither exclusively existence nor non-existence—then it encompasses both [the Dharma-body and the Response-body], which is convenient for the text.

If one follows the convenience of the meaning, since this sutra takes the merit of the fruition as its primary theme, it is appropriate to explain the chapter title by means of the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (Response-body).
For the *saṃbhoga-kāya* is that which, above, merges with the ultimate and, below, responds to the world; thus, the doctrine of the three bodies is naturally fulfilled.
Because the accomplishment of the destiny is thus, these two characters pertain precisely to the *saṃbhogakāya*. Second, clarifying how one reaches the perfect through doubt:
[Wénjù] states that when limited doubt elicits an immeasurable response, one immediately reaches the perfect.
[Commentary] The meaning of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) is clearly revealed because the four Buddhas respond to the doubt regarding short lifespans by means of their long lives;

thus, Śraddhālakṣaṇa comes to realize that the Wisdom of the Reward Body is fully endowed with the three bodies (trikāya). The "Three Clarities" (traividyā) are derived from the title of this chapter.
[Text] The scribe titles this chapter based on the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*) attained by [the Bodhisattva] Śraddhālakṣaṇa;

by citing one, he subsumes all. [Commentary] The title "Life Span" (*āyuṣ-pramāṇa*) refers specifically to the *saṃbhoga-kāya*. This is because it is what was perceived through the perfect understanding of Śraddhālakṣaṇa; "subsumes" (*pi*) means that it is appropriate.
By citing the single *saṃbhoga-kāya*, it encompasses the three bodies (*trikāya*). Second, the conclusion and demonstration of the establishment of the title.
[Text] For this reason, it is titled the "Chapter on the Lifespan.
[Commentary] Second, the re-explanation; first, showing the alternative interpretation at that time.
[Text] Furthermore, at one time, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" was re-explained.

[Commentary] Since the Great Master did not expound this teaching only once, Chāng-ān recorded it in its entirety upon hearing it on one particular occasion, establishing distinct titles for the sections.
Second, explaining the characteristics of differing interpretations, which is divided into two parts: first, the headings and enumeration of the chapters.

[Text] It is also divided into three parts: first, the Profound Meaning (*xuanyi*); second, the Citation of Scriptural Evidence; and third, the Return to the Source. [Commentary] Regarding "Profound Meaning":
the *Wenxuan* states, "The wise and sagacious have a profound insight," with a note explaining that "profound" (*xuan*) means "penetrating.

This refers to departing from the literal text to reveal its underlying meaning; hence it is called "Profound Meaning. Regarding "Citation of Scriptural Evidence": although the meaning has been wondrously realized, it must accord with the scriptures.
Therefore, citations are introduced as evidence to inspire faith; returning to the source is the title of this chapter, which serves as the heading for the scripture.
Regarding the "source," the three bodies (trikāya) are elucidated through the *Ayuṣpramāṇa* [Longevity] chapter, which does not depart from the *dharmatā*.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* subsumes all things within this source, causing their meaning to reach ultimate fulfillment. Second, the explanation according to the chapters. Part One: The Profound Meaning (*Xuan-yi*). Sub-part One: Direct Demonstration.
The Lifespan of the Three Bodies (I): First, the Sambhogakāya (Response Body). First, its lifespan.
[Wenju]: Regarding "profound meaning," "lifespan" refers to life. That is to say, the life-faculty obtained through retribution, which maintains continuity without interruption, is termed "lifespan."
[Commentary] Two measures.
[Wenqu] Because the extension and contraction of the numerical period is termed a "measure," it is called "life-span measure" (*āyus-pramāṇa*).
[Commentary] Three conclusions.
[Text] This explains the lifespan of the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body) based on causes and conditions.

[Commentary] "Causes and conditions" refers to the mutual interaction between response and stimulus as their cause and condition. This concerns the first of the two types of Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body) lifespans.
[Text]: Furthermore, "āyuṣmat" (long-lived one) means "to receive. It refers to the mutual containment and reception of the union between object and wisdom:
non-conceptual wisdom receives the non-conceptual object, and the non-conceptual object receives non-conceptual wisdom, just as a large box contains a large lid;
thus, "āyuḥ" has the meaning of "receiving."
[Commentary] Outside of cognition there is no object, and outside of objects there is no cognition. Since the intense grasping of names and forms has ceased, the subject and object are eliminated;
thus, there is no conceptual discrimination. Like a box and its lid being mutually independent, the essence itself is called "Great. Second, the measurement of the scope [of this realization].
[Text]: "Pramāṇa" (measure) means correspondence. Because the object and the cognition correspond, it is called "pramāṇa. [Commentary]:
When the object and the cognition both pervade [each other], this is termed "correspondence. This correspondence is in reality without boundaries;
thus, in terms of its meaning, it is called "pramāṇa. (The three fetters.)
[Text] This explains the lifespan of the *vipākabuddha* (retribution Buddha).
[Commentary] Regarding the three bodies, this is first the lifespan of the *dharmakāya*.
[Text] Furthermore, "lifespan" (*āyuṣ*) means "long. It is termed "long" because it is eternal and unchanging.
[Commentary] The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unchanging and devoid of past, future, or present; this is the true meaning of "long-lasting.
Based on this meaning of long duration, the lifespan of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is explained.

Second, regarding "measure" (mātra): [Textual Explanation] "Measure" means to weigh and evaluate. This eternally enduring lifespan is neither a great number nor a small number, nor is it something that can be quantified through correspondence.
If one fully knows it, it is not associated [with conceptualization]; if one does not fully know it, it cannot be said to be either expressible or inexpressible.
There is no way to name it, yet one forcibly employs scales and measures to describe its longevity.
[Commentary] "Scales" (xuán) means to measure. The lifespan of eternal duration is truly beyond measurement; one forcibly employs the "double negation" (neither-nor) to measure it.
Regarding the phrase "the measure is neither many, etc.," this sets forth the characteristics of measurement: first, it is neither a number such as much or little;

second, it is neither known nor unknown; third, it is neither spoken nor unspoken. This reveals that the lifespan of the Dharma is an inconceivable realm. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The inconceivable is that which is not determinate.
If one were to claim that apart from what can be expressed, the lifespan of the Dharma is definitively inexpressible, [that would be a misconception].
To speak of these as "definitive" is not inconceivable; the intent of the two preceding pairs is likewise so.
To evaluate in this manner is to measure by way of permanence and duration.

Furthermore, regarding the methods of evaluating quantity—such as whether a lifespan is long or short, exhausted or inexhaustible, partial or complete, and expressible or inexpressible—one evaluates the dharma-lifespan accordingly.
The essence of the Dharma-life is neither speech nor silence. [Three knots.
[Wenju: This explains the lifespan of the Dharma-body. [Ji:
A second time, three pairs are further employed to reveal this, as opposed to the previous direct treatment of the extension and brevity of object and wisdom, as well as the "neither-nor" [state].

Since the explanation of the three lifespans may still be difficult to understand, each is now evaluated through two meanings so that practitioners may recognize the characteristics of the three Buddhas.
The text is divided into three parts; the first section concerns the two meanings of the *saṃbuddha* (corresponding Buddha).
[Text] The first section is divided into two parts: (1) "measurable and measurable," such as the lifespan of Śākyamuni, which is eighty years;
and (2) "measurable and immeasurable," such as the lifespan of Amitābha, which is actually measurable but cannot be fathomed by humans or devas, and is thus called "measurable and immeasurable.
Both this "measurable and immeasurable" and the preceding category are all the deeds performed by the Buddha.
[Commentary] The second section concerns two meanings regarding the Buddha as the fruit of retribution.
[Wenqu] The second section also has two meanings: the Buddha uses the wisdom of suchness (tathatā-jñāna) to correspond to the object of suchness;

since the object is non-conceptual, the wisdom is also non-conceptual. If the object corresponds to the wisdom, then if the wisdom possesses conceptualization, the object must also possess conceptualization.
Distinguishing between this knowledge and ignorance is precisely what the Buddha clarified.

[Commentary] "The object is without discrimination" does not mean that the insentient object is entirely devoid of awareness; rather, it refers to the essence of the mind which is fundamentally free from thought—this is called "the object is without discrimination.
When this thought-free mind is in its entirety awakened, it is called "discriminating wisdom."

When this object and wisdom are ultimately in perfect correspondence—such that there is no object outside of wisdom, yet the object possesses differentiation, and there is no wisdom outside of the object, nor any differentiation within wisdom—then the object illuminates the object and wisdom is quiescent within wisdom.
These two meanings reveal the characteristics of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The third set consists of two meanings regarding the *dharmakāya*.
[Text] The third instance also has two meanings: first, that it is profoundly quiescent and ineffable; second, that through the skillful means of compassion, it may also be expounded.
This state of being both expoundable and inexpoundable is the dharma of the Dharma-Buddha.
[Commentary] Because its essence is fundamentally without marks, it cannot be described; yet because its virtues are manifested through words, it can be described.
Second, citing scriptural evidence, which has two parts. First, citing the present text. Third, first citing two passages to prove the two meanings of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
[Text] Regarding the second citation of evidence: the fact that [the Buddha’s life] lasted eight hundred years proves that it is finite.

That no devas, humans, or the eight classes of beings are able to conceive of or calculate [his lifespan], and that it cannot be known by counting the grains of sand in mountains or drops in the ocean, proves that his measure is infinite.
[Commentary] These two citations from three texts establish two meanings of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
[Textual Analysis] The "boundaries of space cannot be delimited" proves that the object of realization (*pramāṇa*) is non-conceptual;

furthermore, it is stated that only the Tathāgata’s realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) can be conceptually differentiated. Moreover, the subsequent passage states: "The ocean of wisdom is boundless, fully endowed with the waters of the Dharma."
This is also realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*). [Commentary:

The analogy of space corresponds to what was previously cited; the analogy of the indestructible corresponds to the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), which should now be taken as the signless (*animitta*) realized object of non-thought (*amanasikāra*).
Third, three scriptural passages are cited to prove two meanings of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
[Text]: "The lifespan is incalculable; this proof is unspeakable. Yet, when one intends to proclaim the lifespan attained by Śākyamuni Tathāgata, this proof of compassion can be spoken.
Furthermore, hearing these four Buddhas proclaim that the Tathāgata’s lifespan is immeasurable, this proof of great compassion can be spoken."

[Commentary] Question: Previously it was stated that all four metaphors illustrate how the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) can manifest for immeasurable durations; why is this now cited to prove the *vipākaphala* (retribution body) and the *dharmakāya* (truth body)?
Answer: It is not the case that the *dharmakāya* and *vipākaphala* entirely constitute the *nirmāṇakāya*. If they were, the *nirmāṇakāya* would necessarily be subject to cessation;

how then could it extend or contract its duration without ever ceasing or being abandoned? Now, wishing to demonstrate the subtle fusion of the three bodies, the *nirmāṇakāya* itself is used as the proof.

If one is ignorant of this meaning regarding the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, one will be unable to deeply understand the various bodies of the Mahāyāna that respond to the capacities of sentient beings.
Second, citing the new version [of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] in two parts: first, separately proving the two meanings of the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

[Text]: The new edition clarifies that when the Brahmin requested the Buddha’s relics as large as grains of millet and sought the retribution of the six heavens, he immediately realized they were finite.
When the Prince spoke of the inconceivable and difficult-to-understand *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, he said, "The retribution of merit is boundless;
the retribution of merit is boundless. This is proof that the measure is infinite.
[Commentary]: That Brahmin Kauṇḍinya desired to obtain a portion of the Tathāgata’s relics the size of a mustard seed because he knew that the Buddha would enter parinirvāṇa ninety days hence;
thus he sought them, as it could be proven that [the relics] should amount to eighty measures.
From "the prince" downward refers to the reply of the Prince of the Licchavis to the Brahmin. Although these are indeed the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, yet...
From the perspective of merit and retribution, one realizes the supreme *saṃbhoga-kāya*. Second, the general realization of the four meanings of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
[Text]: "Inconceivable and difficult to understand" refers generally to the fact that the realm of wisdom is ineffable, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) and its object is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).

Regarding the four aspects—possessing knowledge or lacking it, and speaking or not speaking—it is sufficient to briefly cite one to represent the remaining three, as all four transcend conceptual thought. Thus, they may be collectively understood through that which is inconceivable and difficult to comprehend;
this is the intent now being described, hence the note "and so forth. Third, returning to the source. Part one: a general clarification.

[Commentary on the Text]: Regarding the "returning to the source," it is also called "restoring the fundamental tenet. Although this exposition of the lifespan is presented through the three bodies (*trikāya*) and six meanings, do not entertain divergent interpretations;
it is simply the meaning of the title of the sutra, *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.

[Commentary] However, the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body, as well as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, are all names for the very essence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and are fundamentally without superiority or inferiority.
Because this sutra specifically employs "gold" and other such metaphors to manifest the dharma-nature, the Buddha first proclaimed it as the title of the scripture;
thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* constitutes the primary source, while all threefold dharmas become its tributaries. Now...

Regarding the explanation of the life span, it must be understood in terms of the three bodies (*trikāya*); fearing that it might be interpreted separately, the original thesis is restated. Second, the manifestation of the returning aspect;
third, first, one should clarify what is being returned to.
[Text] The first section concerning "measurable and immeasurable" merely clarifies the meaning of "illumination" (*prabhāsvara*); because it is illumination, there is large and small, long and short.
The quantities of extension and contraction all manifest within the clarity; this is precisely the meaning of "clarity.
[Commentary] The two—superiority and inferiority—are entirely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), capable of providing great benefit. The two retributions return as light.
[Text] The second [point]: Because the realm of wisdom and the vessel-and-lid correspond in their essential realization, and because form (*rūpa*) is great, Prajñā is also great;
because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal—this is the meaning of "light."
[Commentary] Because the retribution must accord with the Dharma, the Dharma and its retribution are presented together in each phrase;
this indicates that the wisdom which accords with [the Dharma] is entirely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), tranquil yet eternally illuminating. This is the "Three Dharmas Returning to Gold."

[Text] The third point is that whether the permanence, bliss, self, and purity can be spoken or cannot be spoken, the teaching that fills the dharma-realm brings no benefit whatsoever to the dharma-nature, nor does a single word cause any harm to the dharma-nature; this is precisely the meaning of "gold."
[Commentary] It is said that when [the Buddha] is silent, he is always speaking, and when he speaks, it is always the perfect and wondrous Four Virtues. What loss or gain is there in this?

It is entirely the *dharmatā*, which is worthy of honor and respect. The integration and identity [of these states] should be discussed as an analogy to what preceded; therefore, it is abbreviated here. Third, the analogy of "all."
[Text]: "The principle that if one is understood, a thousand follow; if one is deluded, ten thousand are confused—this is precisely the meaning [of this passage].
[Commentary]: If one understands the essence of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, how could its meaning be limited to the doctrine of the three bodies (*trikāya*)?

All phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*) return to this source, which is why "a thousand follow" and "ten thousand are not confused. This clarifies the underlying intent of the three illuminations (*trividyā*).
[Text]: "Since these were heard on two occasions, they have been recorded together," and so forth.
[Commentary]: Both accounts from the two occasions clarify the wondrous principle. Because later students might gain awakening through either one, this intention is shown by the note "and so forth.
Second, the actual clarification of the doubt. First, the introduction to the "Entering the True" chapter.
As explained above.
[Wenju: This chapter is the main exposition, yet the introductory text has not yet been fully analyzed as above. [Ji:
Second, returning to the meaning of the introduction to explain this passage, there are two parts; first, the initial section of the sutra text.

[Text] From "In the city of Rājagṛha" onwards is the third section, the Introduction of Doubtful Reflection, which is divided into two parts: first, the appearance of the person; second, the clarification of the doubt.
The appearance of the person is further divided into four sections: first, the place of origin; second, the rank or status; third, the name; fourth, the praise of virtues.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation according to the text. This has two parts. First, the identification of the persons. This has four sections. First, the identification of the location:
"At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha.
[Wenju] The location is as stated in the text.
[Commentary] The explanation of the terms is as seen in the "Explanation of the Title" in the General Preface. Second, the clarification of the stages:
"There is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. [Wenju] Regarding "bodhisattva":
*bodhi* means the Way (*mārga*), and *sattva* means the mind (*citta*). One practices this Way oneself and is further able to transform others.
The term *mahāsattva* (摩訶薩) refers to one who, by relying on superior practice, establishes themselves in a superior station.
[Commentary] It is translated as "the mind of the Way" (*mārgacitta*); furthermore, because they are able to transform others, this "mind of the Way" is great.
Although this practice encompasses the three preceding teachings, its present station is within the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*). This is the third instance of naming.

His name was Śraddhālakṣaṇa (Xìnxiàng). [Commentary] The text has two parts; the first explains the name according to the teaching. This has three sections: the first directly explains it based on "semblance" (sādṛśya). This, in turn, has two parts: the first explains it based on the name itself.

[Text]: Regarding the "aspect of faith" (*śraddhā-nimitta*): the aspect of faith in the household is distinguished as being within the stage of the semblance path (*sādṛśya-mārga*) when analyzed specifically, and as the stage of the iron wheel (*ayaścakra*) when analyzed comprehensively.
[Commentary]: Since faith extends to both the real and the semblance, and it is said that the "aspect of faith" is not the real because it is a semblance of faith, it is therefore...

This is because it is the precursor to true realization. In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the three stages of worthiness (sān xián) constitute the stage of semblance-faith (sì xìn); only from the first stage (dì yī) onward does one attain true faith.
In the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào), upon entering the stages (zhù), one immediately attains true faith; thus, the ten stages of faith (shí xìn) are designated as semblance-faith.
Regarding the "iron wheel" (tiě lún), the *Benye yingluo jing* uses six types of wheels as metaphors for the positions of the six causes, with the iron wheel representing the [first] stage.

The ten stages of faith correspond to the copper wheel; the ten abodes to the silver wheel; the ten practices to the gold wheel; the ten transferences to the lapis lazuli wheel; and the ten grounds to the mani-jewel wheel.
At the stage of Equal Enlightenment, one attains the iron wheel by severing the views and afflictions of the two truths. Second, this is verified through their characteristics.

[Text]: The subsequent passage states: "One sees a person resembling a Brahmin who strikes a drum with a mallet; the drum is the Dharma-body, and the striking is the arousal of the responsive capacity.
Seeing that the capacity is aroused at this stage, one knows it is not a true strike."

[Commentary] "Bǔ" (枹) refers to a drumstick; it is sometimes written as "fú" (桴). Second, it clarifies that there are "semblances" (*sadr̥śa*) at each stage above. First, it clarifies that within each stage there are semblances.
[Text] Furthermore, the stages of the true and the semblance follow one another stage by stage; there is no stage that does not possess semblances, just as Samantabhadra cultivates the universal.
"The stage of the fulfillment of virtuous conduct is adjacent to the ultimate honor; this resembles [the ultimate], and thus it is 'high'.

[Commentary] That which has been realized is called "true," while that which has not yet been realized is called "resembling. Since the Perfect Enlightenment of Samantabhadra, when viewed from the perspective of the ultimate, is merely resembling it, the name "Virtuous" (Bhadra) is established for it.
Second, it clarifies that its highness and lowness are difficult to fathom.
[Text] Regarding those whose signs of faith correspond to the Path, I do not yet dare to judge their relative status.
[Commentary] Third, setting forth difficulties to verify the reality; Part Two: First, the difficulty concerning those in high positions who have no doubts. First, the objection.
[Text]: An objector says: "If it is identical to Samantabhadra, why is there doubt regarding what appears similar?
[Commentary]: Regarding the two explanations, the first is explained in terms of the provisional and the real.

[Text] This also does not preclude the Bodhisattva acting as an initiator for those who harbor doubts; furthermore, there is no cause for resentment regarding doubts about the Buddha-ground that have not yet been resolved.
[Commentary] Acting as an initiator for others is a provisional manifestation of doubt, while not yet having resolved the Buddha-ground is actual practice involving doubt. These two are distinct.
Citing two sūtras as proof, the *Wenju* states:
"In the *Lotus Sūtra*, Maitreya, who is in his final birth before Buddhahood, likewise harbors doubts;
in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there is a Bodhisattva named 'Doubting Birth' (Śaṅkā-janman), who has not yet fully realized bodhi and for whom I have given this name."
[Commentary] Both the "Dharma" (the teaching) and the "Lotus" (the source/trace) involve Maitreya raising questions out of doubt.

Because the Bodhi of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* Bodhisattvas has not yet reached its ultimate limit, it is said that they have not fully realized their original nature. With Bodhi perfuming the mind, doubt arises;

because of this doubt, they seek full realization, and thus it is said that "Bodhi shall act as my name. Second, the severing of views and the removal of doubts and difficulties. First, the initial objection.
[Text] An objector says: "If doubt has already been severed by seeing the Truths (satyadarśana), how can there be doubt regarding the ten stages (daśabhūmi)?
[Commentary] There are two answers. [Text] The answer states:

"The doubt severed by seeing the Truths is general; there is also specific doubt regarding the ten stages. [Commentary] There are two answers. [Text] The answer states: "The doubt severed by seeing the Truths is general; there is also specific doubt regarding the ten stages."
[Commentary] General doubt obstructs the Truth, while specific doubt obstructs the Middle Way. Since the Middle Way has not yet reached ultimate stability, how could one avoid doubt?
Second, the contemplation is distinguished according to its locus.

[Wenju] Regarding "contemplative understanding," the mind-king is called the "king" and the five aggregates are called the "palace"; one contemplates these five aggregates as empty and quiescent, and as emptiness.
Quiescence is itself nirvana; because nirvana can ward off wrongs and resist adversaries, it is called a "city.
Since those with both initial and subsequent resolve constantly contemplate nirvana while practicing the Path, it is their dwelling place.
[Commentary] Now, as for citing the person and relying on the location: this is because the contemplation of the Dharma arises entirely from the aggregates (*skandha*).

Since the city of Rājagṛha is convenient for designating the aggregates, the location is specified here. By contemplating the palace of the virtuous and evil kings, one understands that both subject and object are empty;
that both persons and dharmas are empty. That which is revealed by these two emptinesses is Great Nirvāṇa, which guards against the five stages of dwelling in ignorance (*pañca-vihāra*).

To ward off the two enemies of death, how could the city exceed this? The name [of this city] refers to the Nirvana of the initial mind’s contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*), while the Nirvana of the ultimate mind refers to the final fruit of wondrous enlightenment.

The present intent is precisely to distinguish the dwelling place of the initial mind; as for clarifying the final mind, it demonstrates that this wondrous contemplation is identical to the wisdom of the fruition.
IV. Praising the Virtues. Section Two: Initial Analysis. Section One: Direct Analysis of the Sutra.
[Text] The passage on praising virtues is divided into two parts: external offerings to the Buddha and internally planting roots of goodness.
[Commentary] This is a twofold analysis of the stages.
[Text] Since this Bodhisattva has planted goodness so deeply as to have encountered many Buddhas, it is also appropriate to provide an interpretation from a high perspective.
"Without a sense of shame," and so forth.

[Commentary] "To plant" means to sow seeds; "shame" (kūi) refers to a sense of moral dread (*hrī*). "And so forth" indicates that one should follow the "Praise of Virtues" chapter to determine that this is identical to the stage of Samantabhadra.
Second, the sequential explanation has two parts: first, external offerings to the Buddha.
They have already made offerings to immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas in the past.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first explains this in terms of material and Dharma offerings.
[Wenju] There are two meanings to "making offerings": first, material offerings, which are easy to understand; second, Dharma offerings, as the Buddha spoke of a hundred...
To study and practice in accordance with the thousand dharma-gates is called the "Dharma-offering.
[Commentary] The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "Among all offerings, the Dharma-offering is the most supreme.
Material offerings are subject to exhaustion, whereas the Dharma-offering is inexhaustible. Second, this is explained in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
[Text] Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxinjie*): the single thought-moment of awakening and realizing the mind is called the Buddha;
the mind endowed with immeasurable merit takes this awakened mind as its support, causing it to become increasingly bright and pure. This is called making offerings to the Buddha.
It is like oil supporting a fire, like food benefiting the body, or like meditative concentration giving rise to wisdom—all of which constitute the meaning of making offerings.
[Commentary]: Within a single thought-moment of ignorance, the entire body [of reality] is fully awakened and realized; this awakened mind is called the Buddha.

The meaning of "providing for the Buddha" (供佛) is that one relies upon the conditions of awakening as the contributing cause (緣因). This can be understood through three analogies. Second, the internal seeds of wholesome roots.
Planting various roots of goodness.
[Commentary] The text has four parts; the first directly clarifies the meaning of planting goodness.

[Wenju] Regarding "planting roots of goodness": the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is called the "earth," and the wisdom that contemplates the *dharmatā* is called the "seed"; one constantly uses this contemplation.
"Contemplation" (*guan*) is called "planting the seed"; "long-practiced non-retrogression" is called "the long-standing seed"; and the "arising of the five roots of goodness" is called "growth.

[Commentary] The essence of original enlightenment is called the "Dharma-nature ground" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*). Contemplating this nature through initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) is termed the "seed.

"Planting the seed for a long time"—its meaning is readily understood. As for the "five roots of goodness," they arise from the fundamental Dharma-nature as immovable faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

When mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these five—are all immovable, they are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Because these faculties arise in a state of superior similarity, they are termed "increasing" (*vṛddhi*).
Second, the meeting with a Buddha is used to explain this; first, three matters are cited as analogies.
[Text] Growth occurs through the movement of wind, the heat of the sun, and the moisture of rain, whereby it gradually increases and becomes lush and beautiful.
[Commentary] Second, by means of the conjunction of the three wheels.

[Text] Wind is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wheel of body; the sun is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wheel of mind; and rain is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wheel of speech. Encountering these three... [Commentary] Two, by means of the conjunction of the three wheels. [Text] Wind is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wheel of body; the sun is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wheel of mind; and rain is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wheel of speech. Encountering the Buddha’s three...
These matters are able to bring great benefit.
[Commentary: The Body-wheel manifests supernatural powers to startle and move their minds; the Mind-wheel discerns capacities and illuminates with wisdom;
the Mouth-wheel expounds the Dharma, moistening them like water. Thus, the three types of knowledge (*trividyā*) increase through these three causes.
[Text]: When *samādhi* (the *Lengyan*) and *prajñā* increase, the *dharmatā* becomes increasingly manifest; when the *dharmatā* is manifest, *samādhi* and *prajñā* become doubly clear.
[Commentary]: *Samādhi* is the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*); *prajñā* is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*); and *dharmatā* is the "causal essence" (*svabhāva-hetu*).
Through the mutual support of these two cultivations and the one nature—illumination arising from cultivation and cultivation being brought forth by the nature—they mutually assist one another.
These three [stages] involve an increase that appears as entering the truth; regarding the increase of the path within the truth, they are collectively termed "the turning toward increased clarity.
Fourth, the two are joined to establish their merit.
[Textual Commentary]: The two meanings of "planting seeds" and "meeting the Buddha" mutually complete one another; by citing this pair, the virtues of the Bodhisattva are extolled.
[Commentary] Second, the explicit exposition of the sequence of doubt and reflection, consisting of two parts: first, the initial section of the sutra;

[Textual Analysis] From "From this mark of faith" (*śraddhāliṅga*) onwards is the explicit exposition of the sequence of doubt and reflection, which is further divided into two: first, the cause of the doubt;
second, the actual arising of the doubt.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation of the two [sections]. First, the cause for the arising of doubt:
The Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa reflected thus: "By what cause and by what condition is the lifespan of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni so short, being only eighty years?"
[Commentary] The text has three parts; first, the primary presentation of the causes for doubt.
[Textual Analysis] Doubt arises from both distant and proximate causes. The distant cause is the proclamation of his entry into *nirvāṇa* after three months;

the proximate cause is the narration [of the teaching], such that if there are those who hear it, they will be able to contemplate the unsurpassed meaning. Furthermore, it is said that it arises because the original vow strikes and stirs the living beings.
Doubt.

[Commentary] Regarding the distant cause, it is because he announced to Māra ninety days prior that his time to pass away had come; this sutra belongs to the latter portion of the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings.
Regarding the proximate cause, it is because while at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he heard the Buddha proclaim the introduction from within samādhi, which subsequently gave rise to his reflection.
Now, although doubt arises for two reasons, it does not arise here because of the absence of fundamental vows.
Second, the explanation of the causes and conditions for these two: first, the causes and conditions are categorized according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

[Text]: Regarding "by what cause and by what condition," this refers generally to all three [aspects] being termed "cause" (*hetu*). Since this passage is concise, the characteristics of "condition" (*pratyaya*) and "understanding" (*pariniṣpatti*) mutually support one another to collectively manifest the "correct" (*samyak*).
Thus, the "correct" corresponds to the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), while "understanding" corresponds to the "conditioning condition" (*pratyaya-pratyaya*).

[Commentary] Generally speaking, the three types—namely the true object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the two conditions of assistance (*upakāra-pratyaya*)—are called the "three causes" because they all reside within the rational nature (*dharmatā*).

When the cultivated object and assistance conditions are each divided into three, they serve as the conditions. In the present text, it is briefly stated: "What are the causes? What are the conditions?

Why must the three [factors] of the nature be combined and designated only as the "true" (*samyag*)? This is because they correspond to the cause (*hetu*). Within the cultivated [factors], the object and assistance conditions are combined into six, which are then reduced to two to correspond with the cause.

Combining these two as conditions constitutes the "conditions" (pratyaya); based on these causes and conditions, doubt arises. Second, regarding the doubt concerning life-span (āyus) based on causes and conditions: [The *Wenju* states:
"The primary cause is eternal and constant, and the life-span is immeasurable; the conditions are able to manifest that the realm of principle is constant and wisdom is likewise constant."
Therefore, since these conditions are not the causes and conditions for the eighty [marks], what now are the causes and conditions for these eighty?
For this reason, doubt arises.

[Commentary] The primary cause is the eternal and enduring principle that is manifested; since the objective realm of that principle is eternal, the arising of wisdom from that entire realm serves as...
Since that which can manifest [the result] cannot be impermanent, and since both merit and wisdom are involved in its manifestation—with wisdom being primary—it is simply called "wisdom.
Because both this object and this wisdom together induce a constant lifespan, one might wonder what the causes and conditions for the eighty-year [lifespan] are.
Only after three explanations does the third section, at the beginning of the eighty-third [chapter], provide a general indication of the lifespans of the three regions of the world.
[Text]: "Eighty years" refers to the three grades of lifespan in the world: the lower grade is forty years, the middle grade is eighty years, and the upper grade is one hundred and twenty years.
[Commentary]: These two specifically indicate the middle grade to serve as a representation.
[Text]: The lower part represents few deaths; the upper part represents extreme old age; the middle part represents neither few deaths nor extreme old age, signifying permanence (*nitya*).

Furthermore, the eighth member of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The eighty-fold cessation signifies that craving has been exhausted, entering *sa-upadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *anupadhiśeṇa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
The exhaustion of craving and freedom from bondage signify my nirvāṇa and bliss (*sukha*). Furthermore, the middle part signifies the center.
The Way, the Buddha, and the Joyful Middle Path manifest purity within the Middle Path; for this reason, his lifespan was eighty years.
[Commentary] All matters of response and transformation appear based upon principle; therefore, external phenomena all internally represent that principle.
How could the lifespan in the Central Land not represent the four virtues? Although the Buddha’s intention is subtle, the Master Zhiyi now relies on the latter four Buddhas to explain it.
Because it ought to manifest the permanent, one may verify the "manifested" (the signified) through the "manifester" (the signifier) to understand the Buddha’s intention.

Third, because they do not know how the intention is manifested, they harbor doubt. [Commentary on the Text]: Śraddhālakṣaṇa did not form this understanding; therefore, he gave rise to doubt as to what the causes and conditions might be.
[Commentary]: If one’s perception of faith reaches the underlying meaning expressed above, one immediately perceives that the three bodies possess the four virtues in their perfection.

How could one then doubt that the manifested traces are necessarily limited in duration, and instead raise doubts as to "how" and "by what conditions"? This constitutes the second point: the actual arising of doubt.
He further reflected: "As the Buddha has taught, there are two causes and conditions by which one attains a long life. What are these two?

First, refraining from killing; second, giving food. Yet our World-Honored One, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas, has cultivated the precept against killing, fulfilled the ten wholesome paths of action, and bestowed gifts of food and drink beyond limit."
[The text] continues until: "To the extent that one's own body—its marrow, flesh, and blood—is sufficient to satiate hungry sentient beings, how much more so other food and drink.
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, mutual doubts regarding principle and teaching; second, first, adhering to the teaching while doubting the principle.
[Text] From the phrase "Again he further thought" onwards is the actual arising of doubt. "As the Buddha has taught" refers to doubt regarding the principle based on the teaching (*āptāgama*).
[Commentary] Second, the delusion regarding the principle that clings to the teaching.

[Text]: The teachings explain that practicing the two virtues of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) results in a long lifespan. Yet, the Buddha’s past cultivation of causes was vast, while his present fruit—the duration of his life—was extremely short.
This contradiction between principle and teaching cannot help but cause confusion. If this principle does not exist, then the teaching is established in vain;
if it is indeed certain [that practice leads to longevity], then where is his long life? This is to be confused by the teaching while clinging to the principle.

[Commentary] That which is spoken by the Buddha is the teaching that expresses (*abhilāpa-śāsana*); the causes and conditions for long life are the principle expressed (*abhidheya-artha*), which is the underlying reason (*yukti*).
The doubt arises from mutual attachment; the meaning of the text is clear. Second, a detailed exposition based on the scriptural text has two parts:

first, the explanation of the two causes and conditions; second, distinguishing the differences from what preceded. Regarding the first part, there are two [subsections]. First, distinguishing the differences from what preceded.

[Text]: Regarding the "two causes and conditions," this differs from what preceded. Previously, cessation (*śamatha*) and practice (*bhāvanā*) were combined as being identical to the conditions for the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
now, it is explained that cessation and practice themselves constitute the causes and conditions.

[Commentary] The preceding [passage] refers to what the Sūtra calls "what cause and what condition. Since the previous explanation took the True Nature (*bhūtatathatā*) as the cause, it then identified the conditions and wisdom (*pratyaya* and *jñāna*) within cultivation as the conditions.
Now, it is stated that there are two causes and conditions for long life;

since these are the Buddha’s cultivated practices of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), each possessing both conditions and wisdom, they are precisely the "revealing conditions" mentioned in the preceding text. This [current section] follows from that.
Because it takes its own action as the causal condition, it differs from the preceding causal conditions. Second, regarding the present explanation, there are two parts;
first, a brief explanation based on the ten wholesome paths of action. First, the direct presentation of the causal conditions.
Third, discussing cessation and cultivation for each of the ten wholesome paths. First, the formal indication.
[Text] Within each of the ten wholesome paths of action, both cessation and cultivation are fully present.

[Commentary] There are two explanations of their characteristics. First, regarding the explanation by way of killing and stealing, there are two parts: first, the explanation by way of the aspects of practice, showing how they are combined and complete.
[Text] Not killing is the goodness of abstention; releasing living beings is the goodness of practice. Not stealing is the goodness of abstention; giving food is the goodness of practice.
[Commentary] Second, it clarifies that this sutra mentions these virtues interchangeably.
[Text] Now, this sutra cites the "abstaining from killing" as the goodness of cessation and the "not stealing" as the goodness of practice,
citing each from one side to clarify both cessation and practice together.
[Commentary] These two examples are discussed individually in eight ways each.
[Text]: If one were to discuss this exhaustively, each [aspect] possesses both cessation (*śamatha*) and practice (*vipaśyanā*); thus, cessation and practice must be clearly understood. [Commentary]:
There are three distinctions between the two virtues of cessation and practice: namely, those pertaining to oneself, those pertaining to others, and those pertaining to both together.

First, regarding practice for oneself, as the text says: "Not killing" is cessation, while "releasing living beings" is practice; "not stealing" is cessation, while "giving food" is practice. Second, [practice] for the sake of transforming others...

Regarding his practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding), as the text states: "If one does not obstruct or deprive [others], it is called the skillful means of *śamatha*; if one encourages [others] to practice, it is called *pravṛtti* (application).
To discuss the ten types of *śamatha-pravṛtti* in full: not killing and not stealing have already been clarified in the commentary;
the eight types are: celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and no sexual misconduct; truthful speech and honest speech; straightforward speech and sincere speech; and non-divisive speech.
To reconcile disputes and avoid harsh speech, constantly practicing gentle words;

to be without greed by practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), without anger by practicing the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*), and without delusion by practicing the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*)—these are all the personal cultivation of *śamatha* (calming).

To personally refrain from the ten unwholesome actions is called *śamatha*, while encouraging others not to commit the ten unwholesome actions is called *pravṛtti* (conduct). Second, regarding *śamatha* and *pravṛtti*:
The detailed discussion of the causes and conditions has two parts:
first, the heading. [Wenju] Now, each one individually possesses its own causes and conditions.
[Ji] Second, the explanation has two parts; first, regarding non-killing, there are four sections. First, the causes and conditions for the wholesome practice of restraint.
[Text]: Now, life is that which all sentient beings cherish; to seize it and harm them is a state of great suffering, while to pardon and release them is joy.
A compassionate heart is the cause, and not keeping implements for killing is the condition.
This constitutes the causal conditions for the goodness of restraint.
[Commentary] Because these are the roots of goodness and these conditions serve as aids for the accomplishment of a compassionate mind, one removes the implements of killing.
These are the two causes and conditions for practicing goodness.
[Text] Now, food is a dependent retribution; if one obtains it, life is preserved, and if one loses it, life perishes. The mind of giving is...
Because giving is complete, this serves as the causal condition for practicing these wholesome deeds.
[Commentary] This may be understood by analogy with the preceding section. The same applies to all nine wholesome paths of action.
[Wenju] Just as it is with the single precept against killing, so it is likewise for all others up to and including the precept against wrong views.
[Commentary] The three *saṃyojanas* indicate the number of causes and conditions for the practice of cessation (*śamatha*).
[Text] In total, there are twenty causes and conditions for the good practice of cessation.
[Commentary] The two *saṃyojanas* constitute the formation of doubt and discursive thought.
[Text] These causes and conditions together brought about the two virtues of long life—both his dwelling and his conduct—which were as lofty as mountains and as thick as the earth;
how is it that today he has come to an end at eighty?
[Commentary] Second, the extensive explanation based on the five vehicles. First, concluding the preceding and introducing the present.

[Text] This has been discussed according to the single path of cause and effect regarding the two virtues of cessation and practice; however, such an interpretation alone is not yet fully adequate to the meaning.
Now, it shall be explained further.

[Commentary] If one were to speak only of the causes and effects of the ten wholesome actions, this would be a shallow and limited teaching that does not fully accord with the Vaipulya (fangděng) sūtras;

this concludes the preceding section. Now, we shall further discuss the gradual and sudden practices of cessation (*śamatha*) pertaining to both the mundane and supramundane realms, as these are truly the cause of Buddhahood;
this is what is being initiated here. Second, to clarify the present extensive demonstration, there are two parts. First:

Clarifying the Meaning of the Teachings, Part Two: First, on Non-killing. Second, first clarifying the characteristics of the practice. First, indicating the characteristics. First, the direct indication.
First, a general indication of the killing of life across the five vehicles. [Wenju]:
The causes for human and celestial rebirth are designated as "life" by means of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths; as for those who practice the three vehicles...
"Wisdom is life; Māra is called the 'Slayer'.
[Commentary: If it were merely that one does not kill and thus obtains the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as a karmic retribution, such goodness would be extremely shallow.

Here, we are clarifying the meaning of "life" as the cause cultivated by the five vehicles, which encompasses profound significance. In Sanskrit, *māra* means "slayer," so called because he is able to harm the world of humans.

Because it is a mundane good, severing the various lives below [the human realm] constitutes the work of Māra. Second, specifically clarifying the practitioner’s practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) in seven parts, first: humans and devas.
[Commentary on the Text]: If one obstructs or seizes away this matter, it is the severing of the life-span of humans and devas; if one does not obstruct or seize it, it is called *śamatha*.
Exhorting others through skillful means to practice is called "practicing goodness.
[Commentary] This matter refers specifically to the goodness of the precepts (*śīla-kuśala*). Regarding the "Three Piṭakas and the Two Vehicles":
[Wenju] If one destroys the teachings of the Three Piṭakas, it is called "killing the lives of those of the Two Vehicles"; if one does not injure them, it is called...
To encourage the cultivation of wholesome means through the practice of cessation is called "practicing the good.
[Commentary] These three matters deliver the Bodhisattva.
[Text] To disparage the practice of *dāna* (giving) up to disparaging worldly wisdom is called "severing the life-force of the Bodhisattva's six perfections."
If one does not create obstacles, it is called "stopping" (*śamatha*), which is the skillful means for good cultivation; to exhort and practice is called "action" (*pravṛtti*), which is good.
[Commentary] Because they cannot realize that the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) are empty in essence, all practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are termed "phenomenal" (*vastu*).
This fourth point extends to the teachings of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
[Text]: If one cultivates the dharma of the body to sever greed, hatred, and delusion, this is the life-force of the Two Vehicles.

To obstruct it so that it cannot be cultivated is called "severing the life-force of the Two Vehicles. If one does not obstruct it, it is called "stopping" as a skillful means; to exhort its cultivation is called "practicing."
[Commentary] This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Fivefold Shared Teaching (pañcābhijñā-sādhāraṇa-śāsana).

[Wenju] To negate and deny the emptiness of essence (svabhāva-śūnyatā) would be to sever the life-force of the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching. If one does not create obstacles, this constitutes the skillful means of the goodness of cessation (śamatha-kuśala);
to exhort others toward cultivation constitutes the goodness of practice (pravṛtti-kuśala).
[Commentary] The faults of preaching the Dharma are termed "non-abandonment" (fei-fei) when one says, "Do not study this," which is called "denying the essence" (bo-ti-kong).

Below the character "empty" (kong), it should state that the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) distinguish [the Bodhisattva path] from that of the Two Vehicles; these may be omitted or abbreviated. These six refer to the distinct teaching (bie-jiao) Bodhisattvas.
[Text]: If one disparages the gradual [approach], this cuts off the life-force of the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching;
to refrain from creating such obstacles is the skillful means of the goodness of cessation (*śamatha-kuśala*), and to exhort others to practice it is the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kuśala*).
[Commentary] Regarding the sevenfold Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are two initial types of compliant practice.
[Wenju] If one slanders the perfect fusion, one severs the life-force of the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching, which is also to sever the life-force of the Buddha.
If one does not create obstacles, this is the skillful means of the goodness of cessation; if one encourages cultivation, this is the goodness of practice.
[Commentary] "Also taking the life of a Buddha" means that for those at the initial stage of this teaching, the Buddha-realm is immediate. Second, regarding the two inverted practices:
first, the two types of inversion are explained.
[Wenju] For a person of the Perfect Teaching, not only do they not destroy all phenomena, but by following the single characteristic, they simultaneously kill all phenomena while following it.
The single characteristic is like that of King Śibi, who by sacrificing his own short life bestowed ten kalpas of longevity upon five hundred others;
it is like the Buddha, who severed all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies, leaving nothing remaining.

[Commentary] To understand that practicing in accordance with or against [the Dharma] is itself the nature of both opposition and compliance, and because this nature is without differentiation, it is called "one characteristic.
Thus, the case of Śyāma killing [his father] and the Buddha’s principle regarding killing are both causes for longevity, because they are identical to the [ultimate] nature.
The conditions for Śyāma are explained as before in the section on the Five Precepts. Second, explaining compliance with the principle.
[Text]: All of these involve words that are contrary [to expectation] but principles that are harmonious; they are not the conduct of those who practice minor deeds. [Commentary]:
Those of the three preceding teachings are all practitioners of minor deeds, for even the initial practices of the Distinct Teaching are likewise minor.
Thus, none of them can immediately turn what is contrary into what is harmonious. This concludes the broad explanation of the second point.
[Text]: As discussed above, each and every dharma possesses both the two virtues of cessation (*śamatha*) and application (*vipaśyanā*), and each virtue has its own causes and conditions.
If one grasps this meaning, then traversing all dharma-gates will be as vast and boundless as the ocean.

[Commentary] From the realms of humans and devas up to the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), all practices of *śamatha* will not be successfully accomplished in the absence of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Nevertheless, taking the precept against killing as an example, one must pass through the remaining nine [precepts] and discuss the causal conditions for the practice of *śamatha* regarding all phenomena;
hence it is said, "like the ocean. Second, citing scriptural evidence.
[Text] Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "By practicing the *dānapāramitā*, one attains long life;
when a Bodhisattva practices *dāna*, he bestows immeasurable life upon sentient beings. ... up to ... "By practicing the *prajñāpāramitā*, one attains long life;
when a Bodhisattva practices *prajñā*, he bestows immeasurable life upon sentient beings. This is precisely its meaning.
[Commentary]: If one does not accept what was stated above, how could each individual crossing (of the river) bestow immeasurable life upon sentient beings?
This gives rise to a second doubt.
[Text]: "Yet our World-Honored One’s practice is nowhere incomplete and his fruition is nowhere unsatisfied; why is it that only today..."

Ten years. [Commentary] Second, clarifying the giving of food. Part one: clarifying the characteristics of the practice. Part two: first, clarifying the provisional and the real regarding the phenomena and methods of the rite.
Part one: clarifying the substance of the ritual food. Part one: clarifying the gravity of the ritual food.

[Text] Next, the explanation of giving food: the hundred flavors, sweet syrups, and so forth are the food of *paribhoga* (enjoyment/retribution); the flesh of the body, marrow, and bones are the food of *vipāka* (primary retribution).
These all constitute the giving of food in terms of phenomenal activity (*vastu*).
[Commentary] The food of the environment is light, while the food of the primary body is heavy. Second, the provisional and ultimate aspects of the food of Dharma are explained.
[Text] The sutra says: "The food of Dharma; the food of Dharma consists of the flavor of worldly dharmas, the flavor of supramundane dharmas, and the flavor of the supreme-supramundane dharmas."
[Commentary] The Sūtra, specifically the "Flowing Water" chapter of this scripture, states:

"In the future, one shall bestow the food of Dharma upon the worldly humans and devas, as well as those of the three supramundane teachings, in a manner that is most excellent and perfectly interfused. Second, clarifying the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s giving:
first, a general explanation.
[Text] Bodhisattvas can act as great benefactors for all sentient beings, causing those who have not yet resolved their minds to turn from the heterodox toward the orthodox,
and enabling those already established in the orthodox to increase their sprouts of virtue— just as the yin and yang nourish plants, or as parents cherish their children.
They provide an abundance of fine silks and cotton so that when one falls to the ground, there is no pain.

[Commentary]: "Turning from the deviant to enter the correct" means causing one to correctly believe in cause and effect. "Meng" (萌) signifies the initial sprouting; it is the first stage when the seed begins to split open.
"Hui" (卉) is a general term for all plants. "Ju" (鞠) means to nurture and raise. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 22, states:
"It is like a prince who stands in a place of great peril where he cannot be protected; wishing to throw himself to the ground, the king then dispatches men [to rescue him]."
He is placed upon thick silk cushions; even if he falls to the ground, he does not die. Second, specifically showing the four [stages]: first, bestowing the food of humans and devas.
[Textual Commentary] He is granted the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
[Commentary] Second, the bestowing of the Tripiṭaka-food.
[Text] Those who have already observed the five precepts speak of how the fires of the three realms are fierce and cause much burning and harm;
they praise the three vehicles as being unconditioned and liberation.
[Commentary] The three kinds of giving encompass both the general and the specific types of food.
[Text] Those who have already entered the realization of the truth disparage the Small Vehicle as "spoiled seeds" and "scorched grain," while praising the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary] The four kinds of giving are the food of the Perfect Teaching.
[Wenju] Even if the people of a starving country were to partake of the royal meal, one takes afflictions as fuel and wisdom as fire;
by these causes and conditions, the food of Nirvana is produced, causing all disciples to relish it with delight.
[Commentary] Because it lacks the Dharma-food of the Mahāyāna, it is called a "land of hunger. The teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun) is like the cuisine of a sovereign;

it is not the food of the common masses. "Cuisine" (*shan*) means excellence, referring to fine food. When one contemplates afflictions from a lower perspective, delusion is itself wisdom—just as firewood assists fire.
Because wisdom takes delusion as its condition, it is able to produce the food of the four virtues, thereby enabling the four... [to flourish].
The eleven disciples all received their respective portions of the sweet delicacies. [This is] the third illustration.
[Commentary on the Text]: All such dharma-gates as these are collectively termed "Dharma-food."
[Commentary] The second [section] concerns the causes and conditions for the practice of cessation (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
[Text] Each and every dharma is fully endowed with both the virtues of cessation and insight; each virtue is fully endowed with its respective cause and condition.
[Commentary] Second, the arising of doubt.

[Text] These various causes and conditions should have brought about the fruit of long life; yet our World-Honored One’s practices were nowhere incomplete and his fruits nowhere unfulfilled—why is it that today he has reached only eighty years?
[Commentary] Second, showing the contemplative practice.
[Text] Regarding the contemplation of the mind as not killing: ignorance is the father and craving is the mother; if one cuts these off, it constitutes a parricidal offense.
However, by contemplating that ignorance is itself clarity and craving is itself the pure essence, one realizes that both subject and object are identical to suchness.
Just as space is quiescent, so too is the skillful contemplation of all mental factors;
this is called practicing skillfully by being able to contemplate in such a way that one attains the eternally abiding life-span of a vajra.
[Commentary] It clarifies that one’s own mind possesses ignorance and craving, which are able to give rise to all afflictions as their progeny; therefore, they are called "parents.
If one cannot realize that these two are inherently evil by nature (*prakṛti-pāpaka*), then one must sever and destroy them, which would constitute parricide.

However, if one contemplates that they are identical to the nature itself, then without departing from delusion and craving, the whole body is entirely luminous and pure; thus, both the subject that contemplates and the object contemplated are ultimately ungraspable.
Since attainment is like empty space and delusive craving is thus stilled, it is called "excellent stillness" (*śamatha*).

Because this very stillness observes all mental factors (*citta-dharma*) and causes them all to become clear and pure, it is further called "excellent practice" (*vipaśyanā*). This is the observation of the mind that perceives all phenomena as eternal;
how could this not evoke the eternal fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*)? Second, the explanation of one's own body and marrow has two parts; first, clarifying the practice.
Section Two: Distinguishing Phenomena from the Dharma. Part One: The Phenomenon to be Distinguished—the Body.

[Textual Commentary] Regarding "one's own body, marrow, bones, blood, and flesh": when this and that are compared, what is taken as "one's own body" is, when examined through wisdom, not one's own body.
This is like the Prince who fed the tiger, or Śibi who traded for the dove; in both cases, he abandoned his own parents and kin.
The essence is not the relinquishing of one’s own body.
[Commentary: Since who among people does not understand that their own body is [not the ultimate], this is now distinguished by wisdom:
when it is inferred that the nine realms are all not one's own body, how much more so the physical substance of human retribution? Second is the Dharma-body as the object of apprehension.
[Text]: "One's own body" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā-tathatā*) of phenomena. The *Śāstra* states:
"Precepts are the skin, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the blood, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the bone, and the subtle, virtuous mind is the marrow."
[Commentary] Since that which is grasped is already deeply examined, the aforementioned exclusion indicates that it is not merely the retribution-body of a human being.

However, if one can understand the dharma-realm of form and mind and thereby relinquish the physical body, this is what is meant here by "that which is grasped. Now, the exclusion of those who cannot understand the dharma-realm and relinquish names as their own bodies must be understood:
for those who take the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as their own body, this is a general statement. If one follows the explanation:

The treatise discusses the body of the true reality (*dharmatā-kāya*) in terms of precepts (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the sublime, virtuous mind (*kuśala-citta*), which constitute the skin, blood, marrow, and bones.
Although these are distinguished individually, each—precepts and the rest—is entirely the true reality itself. Second, clarifying giving through the Dharma has two parts;
first, the giving of the actual body has five parts, the first of which is the giving of the skin.
[Text]: To preach the precepts for others means that the precepts can obstruct transgressions and cultivate merit;
they are signless, supreme, and constitute the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) which is neither maintaining nor violating—this is the giving of one's own skin.
[Commentary] Precepts that proclaim the true mark (*dharmatā*) to others prevent the faults of the two extremes and cultivate the merit of the Middle Way.

Since these precepts are signless (*animitta*), even their maintenance cannot be apprehended; how much less can there be any transgression? When both [maintenance and transgression] are forgotten, this is called the "shore of the corpse" (*śīla-pāra*).
To speak of precepts in this way is what is meant by the "Dharma-body skin. The examples of blood and so forth are similar. Second, the gift of blood.

[Text]: To speak of the various dhyānas, samādhis, supernatural powers, and transformations—manifesting all modes of deportment without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation—is to give one's own blood.
[Commentary]: "The various dhyānas" refers to the nine grades of dhyāna; it also encompasses all dhyānas, both with and without outflows (sāsrava and anāsrava).

Because they have all realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) and have all accomplished the supernormal power of transformation through the unconditioned (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa*), they manifest bodies of the ten realms within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
these are called the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*). Following the previous example, it should be stated that these are neither fixed nor disordered. Third, the gift of bones.
[Text]: To speak of unattached, wondrous wisdom— which is neither intellect nor ignorance, wherein all is extinguished and purified,
which is spoken of day after day yet is never spoken of, and whose teachings all reach the ground of omniscience— is to give away one's own bones.

[Commentary] The merit of one's own practice refers to the cause and fruit of one's own cultivation; the merit of transforming others refers to the agent and object of that transformation.

This is identical in meaning to the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-prabheda*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Second, the correct manifestation of these two: first, the preceding five [subtleties] manifest one's own practice.
[Text] The vastness of the chamber represents the *prajñā* of one’s own practice; the deep blue lapis lazuli represents the *dharmakāya* of one’s own practice;
the exquisite fragrance represents the liberation of one’s own practice; the high throne, flowers, and robes represent the causes for attaining Buddhahood through one’s own practice;
and sitting upon the throne represents receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood.
[Commentary] If these passages are correlated with the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣmatā*), they correspond to:

the subtlety of the realm of the Dharma-body, the subtlety of the wisdom of *prajñā*, the subtlety of the practice of liberation, the subtlety of the stage of the perfection of causes, and the subtlety of the three dharmas of attaining Buddhahood; these constitute the causes and effects of one’s own practice (*svayam-carita*).

If the realm, wisdom, and practice are contrasted with the principle of nature (*dharmatā*) and so forth, the former three correspond to this [nature]; however, this is merely a provisional distinction made from the perspective of emphasizing the specific aspects of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The treatise states that the true nature of the dharmas is perfect and without deficiency in its stages. Second, the latter five manifest marks transform others. [Commentary on the Text]:
Regarding the latter five marks that manifest the merit of transforming others: emitting light manifests the benefit of sentient beings through the mind-wheel;

raining down flowers manifests the benefit of sentient beings through the speech-wheel; and producing music manifests the benefit of sentient beings through the body-wheel. Furthermore, they manifest the ability to...

That sentient beings transform the affliction-obstruction (kleśāvaraṇa) and receive the bliss of the joy of the Dharma signifies that their faculties are complete and capable of enabling them to transform the retribution-obstruction (vipākāvaraṇa).

[Commentary] The Wheel of Mind discerns the capacities of beings; this is the wondrous response and transformation. The Wheel of Speech preaches the Dharma; this is the wondrous [function]. The Wheel of Body manifests supernatural powers; this is the wondrous [function].

Furthermore, the lower stage is indicated by the fact that while those receiving celestial bliss may have either deficient or complete sensory faculties, since both have already transformed their hindrances, they can universally engage in the two kinds of excellence:
benefiting one's own retinue and benefiting others. This constitutes the "agent" and "object" of transformative ability; the other stages follow this same pattern.
[Text] Since it is so for the first stage, each subsequent stage likewise attains this.
[Commentary] Second, the general manifestation of signs:
To state the essentials, all beneficial and unprecedented events existing throughout the entire world appear in their full array.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, the statement of intent which provides a general presentation.

[Textual Analysis] From the phrase "From all worlds... onwards is the general manifestation of characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). While the text for specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) is extensive but its meaning concise, the text for general characteristics is concise but its meaning extensive.
This represents the fulfillment of the ultimate fruit through the completion of the causes of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

[Commentary] The statement that "the meaning is concise" refers to its being limited to ten points; the statement that "the meaning is extensive" is because the term "all" encompasses everything without exception.
Second, the distinct presentation according to the text.
[Text] "All" refers to the ten dharma-realms; "worlds" encompasses the three worlds. "Unprecedented" means that which was absent during the causal stage;

"fully manifested" means that the principle is revealed when the causes are perfected. Regarding the unprecedented nature of the world of lands, it signifies the fulfillment of the true aspect (*dharmatā*);
regarding the unprecedented nature of the world of sentient beings, it signifies the fulfillment of *prajñā*.
The world of the five aggregates has never existed [in its ultimate sense], and thus liberation is complete. To state the essential point: the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the essential point.
Since the true mark is perfected, what dharma would not be fulfilled?
[Commentary: "Encompassing" means that the ten dharma-realms are possessed by all three—sentient beings, Buddhas, and the Mind. Although they possess them...

The distinction between delusion and awakening is already different; the Buddha has already realized awakening, while the mind arises within delusion. When entirely deluded, it is called the "Ten Realms of the Principle-nature" (*li-xing*);

when one believes and speaks of them, it is called the "Ten Realms of the Name-stage" (*ming-zi*); when one realizes their essence in every thought-moment, it is called the "Ten Realms of the Practice of Contemplation" (*guan-xing*);

when the sixteen faculties shine universally, it is called the "Ten Realms of the Stage of Similarity" (*xiang-si*); when the ten [realms] are manifested and the ten [realms] arise in response, it is called the "Ten Realms of Partial Truth" (*fen-zhen*); now, we represent the ultimate fruit.

This is the ultimate realization that one’s own ten minds merge with the essence and function of the Buddha’s ten realms, and that the ten realms of sentient beings are identical to those of the Buddha.

This is the present manifestation of the meaning of the ten realms as the fruit. To fail to provide this interpretation and instead merely claim that "all" encompasses the ten dharma-realms and the three worlds—referring only to the provisional and real, the primary and secondary retributions—is to grasp at the real to form the provisional; such designations are not the same [as the true meaning].
That which is grasped by the sentient-worldly realm as substantial dharmas—the separation between matter and mind—is the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the direct retribution.
The differentiation of the supporting environment upon which this depends is the world of the land (*bhājana-loka*). These are unprecedented [in their manifestation]:

they partially realize the ten fundamental aspects and nearly manifest the ten traces. Although they attain perfect fusion, when compared to the ultimate fruit, the distinction between clarity and obscurity remains as distinct as that between a flower and its fruit.

The Venerable One explains that the merit obtained by a Bodhisattva who has received empowerment is like a single clod of earth, whereas the merit of Wondrous Enlightenment (Sugata-knowledge) is like the soil of the four continents;

thus, when the cause is perfected and the principle revealed, whether for oneself or others, each of the thirty worlds is ultimately pure, sovereign, and unprecedented. Below, the three worlds are assigned to the three virtues.
Furthermore, this follows the logical convenience of the context. Regarding "the lands and so forth": when one is deluded, both the provisional and the real are based upon the lands;

since the wisdom and abandonment of the fruition-stage are entirely based upon the Dharma-body, the true aspect is clarified within the lands. Regarding "fulfilling sentient beings and so forth," the *Vyākhyā* states:

"The unsurpassed among sentient beings is the Buddha. "Buddha" is translated as "Awakening"; initial awakening is the realization of the emptiness of persons, while ultimate awakening is [the realization of the emptiness of phenomena].

Regarding the statement that because phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, one clarifies the perfection of *prajñā* within the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the *Vyākhyā* (Explanatory Commentary) states:
"As for 'supreme phenomena,' *nirvāṇa* is the cause and cessation is its nature; by attaining the eternal form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.

Since the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) have been exhausted, one possesses mastery over the five aggregates; therefore, one clarifies [the perfection of wisdom] within the world of the five aggregates."

One should understand the intent behind the "fulfillment of liberation" through the three [aspects] corresponding to the three [realms]: it is because by citing one of the three virtues, all three are manifested.

Each of the three worlds is perfectly pervasive, mutually fusing and mutually encompassing; this can be understood by comparing it to the "new *ī*" (the character for *ī* with a dot) and the "Heavenly Eye.
As for the essential point of the true reality (*dharmatā*): true reality is signless, and the ultimate fruit is likewise the ultimate forgetting of signs.
This refers to the perfection of both self and others according to the true nature (*dharmatā*).
