[Commentary] The fifth section, "The Preface of Silent Contemplation and the Presentation of Doubts," is divided into two parts.

[Text] From "Faithful Appearance rejoiced" (*śraddhālakṣaṇa-pramudita*) downwards is the fifth section, the Preface of Silent Contemplation and the Presentation of Doubts, which consists of two parts:
first, seeing the signs and rejoicing; second, silently contemplating and presenting the doubts.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation of the two [sections]. First, seeing the signs and rejoicing:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, having seen these Buddhas and these rare events, leaped for joy with great exultation;
he paid homage with palms joined toward all the World-Honored Ones.
[Text]: As for "rejoicing," since they had previously harbored doubts in their hearts, upon seeing the auspicious omen and beholding the Buddha, they knew for certain that they would hear the Dharma;
therefore, they rejoiced.
[Commentary]: Second, silently reciting and expressing their doubts.
With a sincere mind, he recited the Buddha’s name and reflected thus: "The immeasurable merits of Śākyamuni Tathāgata are inconceivable;
yet, regarding his lifespan alone, doubt arises in my heart: how can the Tathāgata’s life span be only eighty years?"
[Commentary] The text is divided into three parts; the first clarifies the intent of voicing one's doubts.
[Wenju] From "With a sincere mind reciting the Buddha's name" onwards is the silent recitation seeking a resolution.
Since the state of doubt cannot be maintained for long, one therefore voices their doubts.
[Commentary] Accumulated doubts do not surface for fear that they will form a "canopy of doubt" (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*). Second, he explicitly raises what he doubts.

[Wenju] He reflects upon the immeasurable merit, marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), radiance, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*), and the preaching of the Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, yet he conceives no doubt regarding these;
it is only concerning his lifespan that doubt arises in his mind: "How is it that the Buddha’s lifespan is but eighty years?"
Because he was mindful of this obscuration of his mind, he remained silent while seeking a definitive resolution.

[Commentary] All meritorious virtues abide by depending upon life; since that life is now shortened, what can be done with the multitude of virtues? Thus, they all harbor no doubt, yet they only think of the brevity of their lives.
This obscuration does not manifest, and thus nothing can be definitively understood. This is the meaning of the three types of silent contemplation.
【Text】As for not speaking: because the four Buddhas have just appeared, their majestic dignity inspires such reverence that he dares not speak.

Furthermore, since doubt has already clouded his mind, he cannot help but reflect. Moreover, having previously reflected in silence and thereby elicited auspicious omens, he now relies on that prior silent reflection to seek a definitive resolution.

[Commentary] Because he is majestic and venerable, he remains silent; because he seeks a definitive resolution, he maintains mindfulness. This can be understood from what precedes. The sixth section, "The Introduction for Dispelling Doubts," is divided into two parts.
[Text] From "At that time, the four Buddhas, with their perfect and universal knowledge... onwards is the sixth section, the text of the introduction for dispelling doubts.
II. Correctly Ceasing Doubts. II.1. Correctly Ceasing Doubts.
[Commentary] II. Following the Explanation. First, correctly ceasing doubts:
At that time, the four Buddhas, with their perfect and universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*), addressed the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa: "O son of good family, you should not now..."
[The text] deliberates upon the shortness of the Tathāgata’s lifespan.
[Commentary: This section has three parts; first, the intention to resolve doubts.

[Textual Analysis: Because the hindrance of doubt covers the mind, one cannot understand the Dharma when hearing it; therefore, this is resolved first, just as, for example, the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*) must first sever [the afflictions].

Doubt is precisely what one must overcome when cultivating the Way. If one possesses the mark of faith yet remains in actual doubt, it is necessary to suppress and halt it. However, if this [doubt] is used to initiate teaching for the sake of instructing others, that is another matter.

[Commentary]: Regarding "doubt covers the mind": among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), doubt is able to shroud both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Why must it be preemptively suppressed?
Alas! If one has not yet resolved the principle and the mind remains joined with doubt, then upon beholding the majestic and honored One, this is the ground for resolving that doubt.
If one stubbornly clings to doubting thoughts, then contemplative wisdom will not open; therefore, it is necessary to cease them so that the mind may receive the Dharma with clarity.

For example, "doubt" refers to a delusion of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) that can obstruct the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); only by severing such doubtful views on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) can one advance toward true cultivation and faith.
The mutual surging of doubt—whether [the Buddha’s actions] are provisional or real—is stilled by the Buddha so that both self and others may obtain benefit. Second, the correct stilling of doubt;
third, the initial section on why the great function should not be [doubted].
[Textual Commentary]: From "You now should not... onwards is the correct stilling of doubt. Why should it not be so? There are three reasons why it should not be so.
First, the "Great Function" (mahāprayojana) should not be limited to eighty years; because this is the Buddha’s Great Function, it should not be so restricted.
[Commentary] A lifespan of eighty years is the Great Function arising from the entire body of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) to respond to sentient beings;
therefore, one should not harbor doubts based on a fixed short duration. Second, the "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) should not be so restricted.
[Text] Second, the ocean of the nature of reality (*dharmatā-samudra*) is profound and cannot be fathomed by speech or thought.
[Commentary] How could the ocean of the nature of reality realized by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni be measured by the mental deliberations of length or brevity?
Third, it is not appropriate for the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
[Text]: "Third, one enters through faith and crosses over through wisdom. Since you have not yet perfected both faith and wisdom, how could you conceive of this through mere intellectual speculation?
[Commentary]:
One who is fully endowed with both true faith and true wisdom is able to know and realize [the truth]. You, however, are not yet so endowed; therefore, you should not [attempt to] do so.
The measurement of these three should not be understood as being established solely in relation to the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Alternatively, it may be that the first two refer to the object of contemplation (*ālambana*) and the last one refers to the subject of contemplation (*manasikāra*). Third, the conclusion by means of scriptural citations.
[Text] The Commentary states: "Because those who wish to measure the immeasurable Dharma would be submerged and drowned, he stops them with what is inappropriate.
[Record] All the Dharmas possessed by the Buddha are entirely immeasurable; if one were to attempt to measure them with a finite mind, one would certainly...
Because they are submerged in an ocean of doubt, the four Buddhas, for three reasons, do not suppress their doubts.
Second, the two Śākyas suppress the doubts.
Why is this? "O sons of good family, we do not see among the gods, the people of the world, the hosts of Māras, the hosts of Brahmās, or the śramaṇas..."
Brahmins and non-humans who are capable of calculating the lifespan of the Tathāgata and knowing its limit—none can do so except for the Tathāgata himself.

[Commentary] The text has three parts; this is the first, explaining that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inconceivable. The second part clarifies that Bodhisattvas are included within the eight assemblies.

[Text] Why is this? The following passage explains the meaning of the three "inappropriatenesses. By stating that none of the eight assemblies can measure it, it explains the inappropriateness regarding the *dharmatā*.
Since the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas possess the pure land of *dharmatā*, they do not fall within the scope of verbal expression.
As for the birth-body Bodhisattvas: if they are householders, they are subsumed under those such as devas and nāgas; if they have left the home life, they are subsumed under the fourfold assembly.
Regarding the inclusion [of the Buddha-body]: although the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) manifests expedient means (*upāya*), it is likewise included among the eight assemblies.
[Commentary: Although the listing of the eight assemblies in the Sūtra is already clear, it lacks the bodhisattvas;

therefore, by way of the provisional and the real regarding birth and the Dharma, the Dharma-nature land is shown to be the land of skillful means (*upāya*) and the land of true retribution (*vipāka*). Since [the Buddha] does not dwell therein, it is not mentioned here.
Second, it is explained that both [ordinary beings and sages] should not attempt to fathom its nature.
[Wenju]: Whether ordinary or sagely, none can conceive or calculate it.
[Ji]: Even the profound and vast *dharmatā* in which the Tathāgata dwells surpasses what is practiced by Bodhisattvas; how much more so [is it beyond the reach of others]?

Generally, even those who are small [in stature] are capable of calculation and deliberation. Second, the explanation of why the *Prajñāpāramitā* should not be dual. First, the correct explanation that the Buddha’s descent is unfathomable.
[Textual Commentary]: "Except for the Tathāgata" explains why the *Prajñāpāramitā* should not be dual. If one were like the Tathāgata, then one would indeed be able [to fathom it].
Since cognition has not yet attained suchness, how can it suddenly be able to know?

[Commentary] Only Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively fathom the wisdom of causes; how then could others know it? Second, this section simultaneously demonstrates the dharmas known by the Buddha, divided into two parts.
First, according to ancient exegesis, because they are cognizable, they are impermanent.
[Text] The former usage of this phrase [means that] what is known by wisdom is an impermanent and measurable phenomenon.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement "this phrase," it excludes only the Tathāgata’s phrase. Since the lifespan is known by wisdom, it is a thinkable phenomenon;
by inference, it is impermanent. Second, the present explanation clarifies that constant wisdom knows the constant.
[Text] The Master of Tiantai said: "It is not so. The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable, eternal wisdom capable of knowing immeasurable, eternal dharmas;
how could that which is known by this eternal wisdom be judged to be impermanent?"
[Commentary]: Those of immeasurable and eternal wisdom ultimately possess no knowledge [of their own] and only then are they fully endowed with knowledge.

This knowledge accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), because by taking the original universal wisdom (*sarvajñāna*) as its entirety, it becomes the Buddha-wisdom. Since one has already known the fundamental nature, how could that nature be impermanent?
Because the ancient masters did not understand this, they took "having knowledge" to be Buddha-wisdom, and thus held that the objects of knowledge are impermanent phenomena. Thirdly...

[The text] states: "By this, one knows the Great Function. [Wenqu] says: "Since the nature of wisdom is already in profound stillness (*míng*), the Great Function can be understood; this explains why the third [point] is not applicable. [Ji] says:

"Because it is wisdom that is without-knowing, it is in profound stillness with the Dharma-nature. Since the Dharma-nature is fundamentally complete and sufficient, it manifests and appears extensively."

Those who appear short-lived are all called "eternally long-lived" because their nature is complete. The sutra’s explanation of the nature of wisdom omits its great functions because they are easily understood.
VII. Introduction to the Assembly:
At that time, the four Tathāgatas were about to proclaim the lifespan attained by Śākyamuni Buddha to the devas of the desire and form realms.
All the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas,
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, through the Buddha’s spiritual power,
all came together and gathered in the chamber of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the sūtra; second, [the comparison of its sequence] with other sūtras. [Wenju] From "At that time, the four Tathāgatas...
onwards is the seventh section, the Introduction on Assembling the Multitude. In other sūtras, the assembly is gathered first and then the auspicious omens appear;
in this sūtra, the auspicious omens appear first and then the assembly is gathered. Thus, the sequence of before and after appears differently in various texts.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of this sutra in three parts: first, the formal elucidation of the assembly in this room. First, a brief explanation of the assembly at that time.
[Text] "Time" refers to the moment when [the Buddha] was about to proclaim and expound [the teaching]. "Assembly" refers to the various devas of the realms of desire and form.
[Commentary] Second, the purpose for gathering the assembly.

[Text] It is because those who benefit from the faith of a single individual such as Śraddhālakṣaṇa are few; since the number of those to be benefited would be great if the assembly were gathered, he therefore convenes the multitude.
[Commentary]: The mention of an eighty-year lifespan reveals the permanence of the three bodies; how could it be intended to benefit only a single person such as Śraddhādhimukta?
Therefore, by means of his supernatural powers, he gathers all those with karmic affinity so that they may hear the Perfect and Eternal [Dharma] and obtain the benefits of the four *siddhārtha*.

When it says "the scope of benefit is vast," does this mean only a single room? No; after this assembly hears it, it shall be proclaimed everywhere. Second, this also clarifies the nature of the entire sutra.
The assembly correctly clarifies that this chamber possesses four types of assemblies, which are also concurrently present in all other chapters; each contains the phrase "fourfold assembly.
First, it clarifies that this sutra possesses the fourfold assembly.

[Wenqu]: There are four types of assemblies: first, the initiating assembly, such as the tree spirit of the *śraddhā-lakṣaṇa* and others; second, the assembly of those who are the primary recipients (*yathābhavyatā*).
The first is the assembly that hears [the teaching] and immediately attains the Way; the second is the assembly of echoes and reflections who come from afar from the ten directions;

the third is the assembly for planting seeds of affinity, who, though they do not attain the Way in their current seat, create the causes and conditions for future lives—such as the case of the flowing water preaching the Dharma to the fish, which served as the cause and condition for their awakening today; this is precisely what is meant.

[Commentary] Regarding the "assembly of shadows and echoes": this refers to the various Dharma-body Bodhisattvas of the Buddhas of the past who conceal their ultimate perfection to assist the Buddha in propagating his transformational teachings.
They act as companions and serve their Lord like a shadow following a substance or an echo responding to a sound.
The names and meanings of these four assemblies are fully explained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra). Second, it clarifies that the assembly is identical to those in other sutras.
[Text] This sutra assembles a multitude of devas and nāgas, which is identical in intent to the *Avataṃsaka*; it likewise assembles a multitude of humans, though the text is abbreviated.
In the new version, there is a multitude of hundreds of thousands of brahmins;
at the beginning of the "Chapter on Repentance," Xinxiang and his retinue go to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain—this is precisely the multitude of humans.
[Commentary]: Regarding the assembly of devas and nāgas herein, how does it differ from that in the *Avataṃsaka*?

Since this new edition states there is an "immeasurable multitude of brahmins," and in the "Chapter on Repentance" it says that Xinxiang (Śraddhālakṣaṇa) went out of the city together with immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—how could these all be spirits?
It is verified that the gathering of the assembly is the same as in other sutras.
Third, [I shall] cease the common understanding that is partial and narrow.
[Wenqu]: It has been handed down that this sutra is related to the hidden realm; it is precisely because it primarily gathers devas and nāgas that humans are not mentioned in brief.
[Commentary]: How can one claim that this chapter merely assembles the host of devas and nāgas simply because the old translation is brief?
The *Samyukta-āgama* (Sāṃyuktika-nikāya) and the *Dharmika* school [assert] that the first two [sections] differ from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and belong to the Vaipulya class.
[Text]: Within the general section on auspicious omens, it says that all unprecedented events in the world appear in their entirety;

yet, while there is no mention of bestowing predictions upon those of the Two Vehicles, it clarifies the permanence and the nature of discernment (*pravicaya*), which accords with the intent of the *Prajñā* and Vaipulya [sūtras].
Therefore, it is judged to be subsumed under the Vaipulya teaching.
[Commentary: All the unprecedented events encompassing the ten realms throughout the entire world appear together; thus, within these ten realms, the three virtues (triguṇa) are fully manifested.
Furthermore, since it is evident that the two vehicles have not yet been granted the prediction of Buddhahood, one knows that this cannot be equated with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* section.

Rather, it clarifies the permanence of the three bodies (trikāya) for those of sharp faculties within the Shared Teaching (pāryāyika-yāna), thereby elucidating the nature of the perfect reality (pariniṣpanna-dharmatā).

Since its discussion of the two kinds of *sarpis* (clarified butter) is no different from that of the *Vimalakīrti*, and since its title does not designate it as belonging to the *Prajñāpāramitā* section while it is designated by the name "Vaipulya" (*fangděng*) in two places, we now judge this teaching to belong to the Vaipulya category.
Within this section, those who obtain the benefit of the Perfect [Teaching] realize the wondrous realization of the "New Yi" within the ten realms; this too may be called an unprecedented event.
The manifestation is complete. Second, one must rely on both the vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) to manifest benefit for the multitude.
[Wenju]: Herein, one should discuss the relative urgency of the vehicle and the precepts;

the fourfold classification determines matters such as rebirth among devas or nāgas, attaining the Way or not attaining it, and the provisional versus the real, as explained extensively in the separate record.
[Commentary] Regarding the four propositions concerning the vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*): first, both vehicle and precepts are urgent; second, both vehicle and precepts are lax;

third, the vehicle is urgent while the precepts are lax; fourth, the vehicle is lax while the precepts are urgent. One must first understand the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the vehicle and the precepts. Furthermore, regarding the ten types of precepts discussed here, we take only these four:

being unimpaired (*anupahata*), unbroken (*abhagna*), unpierced (*achidra*), and unmixed (*asaṃkīrṇa*). Although these are divided into the categorized (*nibaddha*) and the non-categorized (*anibaddha*), they are all included here.

All these are the causes for humans and devas; this is the present precept. It does not take up the unattached wisdom that accords with the Path, nor the mastery and fulfillment that accord with meditative concentration.
Although these six kinds are called the "essence of the precepts" (*śīla-ātman*), they belong to the respective vehicles (*yāna*) of the three contemplations.

Regarding the discussion of the five vehicles, the human and celestial realms are not taken up as [ultimate] vehicles, because although those two are called "vehicles," they do not move toward liberation.
That which does not depart from its essence consists of wholesome matters associated with outflows (*āsrava*) that are subsumed under the precepts; these pertain exclusively to the Three Vehicles.

Since these Three Vehicles encompass the Four Teachings, they constitute the entry into principle and wisdom. Although they are distinguished by depth and shallowness, all involve the movement of afflictions and the emergence from birth and death;
therefore, they are named "Vehicles" (*yāna*). Now, by correlating the four types of precepts with the Three Vehicles and discussing their relative urgency, the four [categories] are established.
Those for whom both the vehicle and the precepts are urgent are the humans and devas present here who have come to hear the Dharma.

Those for whom both are lax are those bound by the sufferings of the evil realms, who are not permitted to join this assembly. Those for whom the vehicle is urgent but the precepts are lax are the various dragons and ghosts gathered here;

those for whom the vehicle is lax but the precepts are urgent—such as the devas attached to pleasure and humans addicted to desire—are not permitted to join this assembly. All of these [belong to the latter categories].

Regarding this class of people, one must further understand that although those gathered here today claim their vehicle is swift and possess both provisional and ultimate teachings, having practiced the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) vehicles with urgency in past lives, they are now within these chambers beholding the four Buddhas.

Yet, though the Buddha-bodies appear different, they see only the manifested and transformational forms; even if they hear of longevity, they must eventually return to extinction. Once extinguished, they do not arise again. If, however—

Regarding those who have cultivated the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] with urgency in past lives, they now behold the four Buddhas as bodies of supreme distinction (*viśiṣṭa-kāya*), each being a single body and a single wisdom.

As for the equality of the provisional and the real among these four—whether urgent or slow—among sentient beings there are those who practice according to the reality, and there are those who manifest through provisional means.

[Commentary] In the new translation of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, at the conclusion of the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), where the four Buddhas have finished explaining how their lifespans benefit sentient beings, there is the Brahmin Kauṇḍinya who, desiring to be reborn in heaven, seeks a portion of the Buddha’s relics as small as a mustard seed.

To fully understand both the origin and the trace is what constitutes the three stages for clarifying the primary tenet and manifesting the essence.

[Commentary] Since those of duller faculties cannot suddenly comprehend the meaning of the mutual fusion of the fundamental and the manifested through a partial discussion of them alone, Śākyamuni fully expounded the three bodies:
namely, the Dharma-body, the Response-body, and the Transformation-body.

Just as lightning exists dependent upon the sky and light exists dependent upon the lightning, the Dharma-body is principle, and the Response-body is wisdom; since wisdom responds to principle, it gives rise to transformation.

The three bodies are identical with the body, yet each is indeterminate; the three bodies are perfectly manifest as one and three. Therefore, the title of this chapter is "Discrimination of the Three Bodies.

The Dharma-body is the essence, while the Response-body and Transformation-body are its traces. When these are taught simultaneously, wondrous understanding arises and conceptual thought is transcended.

In the Mahāyāna, because phenomena (*dharma*) are understood as being non-different from principle (*li*), the interpretation of meaning is restricted solely to phenomena, and the principle itself is not fully revealed.

This concludes the threefold explanation.
[Text]: The essence of emptiness is utterly pure, such that it cannot be defiled by the five obscurations nor purified by the three lights;
it is like the Truth of Cessation, wherein the twenty-five states of existence are extinguished, as well as the extinction of the "city of transformation" (nirvāṇa).
[Commentary]: Regarding the "five obscurations," these are smoke, clouds, dust, mist, and the hand of the Asuras. The "three luminaries" are the sun, moon, and stars.
The principle of eternal cessation is fundamentally unobscured; it is not now purified either. Question:

Suffering is metaphorically compared to mountains, the Buddha-body to the Way (the path), and the ground of wisdom to the earth. Cessation is compared to space and the wondrous void. Since these three already possess the principle, [how can there be further obscuration?]

If one discusses the teaching in terms of the *dharmakāya* realized therein, yet the initial citation of the First Truth (*duḥkhasatya*) for proof and explanation addresses only afflictions (*kleśa*), how can these also be called the *dharmakāya*?
Answer: Each of the four unconditioned truths (*anabhisaṃskṛta-dharmasatya*) is itself the "Middle" (*madhya*).
If it were not the case that all things universally tend toward affliction, then that name would not be the Middle; because it is the Middle, suffering (*duḥkha*) is named the *Dharma*.

The body and the path are the ground of wisdom; because cessation is named "wondrous emptiness," one knows that it is directly through the afflictions that the accumulation [of suffering] is explained and the Dharma-body is revealed—this intention is most wondrous, as practitioners know.
Second, clarifying the Four Truths to resolve doubts, which has two parts: first, revealing the principle to clarify the severance of doubt;
third, revealing the principle to clarify the characteristics. First, revealing the principle to clarify the characteristics.
[Text]: The principle of the Four Truths pervades all places; this is the Dharma-body. The wisdom of the Four Truths that cognizes objects according to their reality is the Reward-body.
Arising from the essence to manifest function, matching the long and the short, is the Response-body.

[Commentary: The preceding explanation of the general auspicious signs—the manifestation of all unprecedented events throughout the world—demonstrated that the provisional and real, as well as the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-vipāka*) of the ten realms, all manifest the three virtues (*tri-dharma*).

Now it is clarified that within each of the provisional and real, primary and secondary retributions of the ten realms, there are the Four Truths (*catuḥ-satya*), and within each truth, the three virtues.
This principle pervading all phenomena is called the *Dharmakāya*; knowing this is called the *Saṃbhogakāya*.

The manifestation of activity is called "response" (*yìng*); this response may be either long or short. Second, showing the characteristics of severing doubt: first, the doubt to be severed. [Textual Commentary]:

Those with the mark of faith see only that the response is short and do not see that the response can be long; if they do not even comprehend the response itself, how could they know the law of retribution?
[Commentary] The two [types of] dharmas capable of severing [afflictions].
[Text] The Buddha cites four analogies to illustrate that which should be increased: a drop of water, a mountain-measure of cinnabar, the dust of the earth, and the realm of space;
yet even these cannot be conceived or calculated to reach their limits, let alone when wisdom merges with the abyss of the Dharma—how profound! How mysterious! Truly.
"It is bottomless, vast, and great; how could it have boundaries? [Commentary]:
The four metaphors were originally intended to clarify the Master Yingchang’s teaching, yet he specifically interpreted them through the lens of the Four Noble Truths.

This was because if Master Yingchang were not entirely the Dharmakāya—wherein the three bodies are one essence—how could he have so wondrously harmonized the two explanations found in the *Śāstra* (the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*)? Therefore...
First, it was shown that his words are skillful and their meaning is profoundly realized. If one were to definitively use [the body] as a single metaphor, how could the words be skillful?
If they were taken as separate meanings, how could the meaning be profound? These three points praise the skillfulness of the intent.

[Text] To cite the manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) in order to explain the retributive Dharma (*vipākadharmatā*) brings about a sudden and clear awakening; such is the skillfulness in severing doubt.

[Commentary] The text uses the metaphor of the long *nirmāṇakāya* to clarify the meaning of the retributive Dharma. When one gains faith and grasps the essential meaning, the darkness of doubt is suddenly dispelled. (2)
[The text] praises and explains the wondrous exhortation to contemplate.
[Wenqu]: The explanation of this verse is as wondrous as this; the practitioner must contemplate it, contemplate it! [Ji]:

The four Buddhas used skillful metaphors to sever the doubts of those with the mark of faith; the wise provided a wondrous explanation to inspire practitioners and bring about understanding. Now that...
Having encountered this, how could one not reflect upon it with scrutiny? Second, regarding the explanation of "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) based on the four foundations of mindfulness:
"mindfulness" refers to the three sublime contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle; "foundations" refer to the four sublime objects—the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.

Since the three bodies (*trikāya*) are not manifested apart from these contemplations and their objects, how can this be called a mere discourse on permanence? This explanation is divided into two parts: first, the application of the verse to the Dharma; third, the abandonment of the particular.
Regarding the general application.

[Wenju: As for the four verses corresponding to the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), since the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness fundamentally resides within the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya), one should have discussed them solely in reference to the verse on Mount Sumeru;
however, they are now applied generally to all [the truths].
[Commentary]: Since body, sensation, mind, and dharmas are merely the five aggregates, one knows that the four foundations of mindfulness originally reside within the Truth of Suffering.
Nevertheless, the cultivation of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is common to all four teachings; here, we refer specifically to the Perfect Teaching.

This means that contemplating the body as pure, impure, neither pure nor impure, and so forth, up to contemplating dharmas as self, non-self, neither self nor non-self—all of these constitute the three truths.
Second, the explanation by way of correspondence.
[Wenju: All waters correspond to the *smṛtyupasthāna* of sensation (*vedanā*), because sensation is able to contain and receive like the ocean’s vast capacity.
Sumeru Mountain corresponds to the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the body (*kāya*), because its physical appearance and its quality of resistance (*sapratigha*) are analogous. The great earth corresponds to...
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness of perception and formations: perception grasps formations because formations are like the earth that bears all things;
regarding the foundation of mindfulness of mind: the mind exists as a mere name, for it is signless like space.

[Commentary]: The foundations of mindfulness of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are simply the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), as these two aggregates are combined here. Now, because we wish to assign them to their respective stages (*bhūmi*), the names of the aggregates are retained.
"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to grasping at marks (*nimitta*); "formations" (*saṃskāra*) refer to the process of conditioning and flux, which is why they are called "formations.

In the phrase "lower formations" (*xià xíng*), the character for "formation" (*xíng*) is pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*). This is the reason for the threefold correspondence with the verses.

[Text]: If one contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), this is the cause for cultivating longevity; if one attains the Way through the foundations of mindfulness, this is the fruit of longevity.
Therefore, the four verses are applied in relation to the foundations of mindfulness.
[Commentary] Since the causes and conditions for eternal life cannot be established without the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this verse is employed as a counter-argument.
Second, resolving doubts by means of the Dharma. Part one: clarifying the causes and effects of the foundations of mindfulness. Part two: first, the characteristics of cultivating the causes.
[Text]: If one contemplates the four "withered" applications of mindfulness, one destroys the four inversions of ordinary beings;

if one contemplates the four "flourishing" applications of mindfulness, one destroys the four inversions of the two vehicles; if one contemplates the application of mindfulness of the Middle Way, it is neither flourishing nor withered, and therein one enters parinirvāṇa.

[Commentary] The four states of withering represent emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the four states of flourishing represent the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the state of neither represents the Middle Way (*madhyamā*).

These are taught as having a sequential cultivation yet no temporal succession; this is precisely the single mind’s threefold contemplation (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*). Therefore, the Buddha’s entry into *parinirvāṇa* between the twin trees—representing the four states of withering and the four states of flourishing—is intended to symbolize this very point.
Second, the characteristics of attaining the fruit. Third, first clarifying the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Fusion is the very characteristic [of phenomena].

[Wenqu] It constitutes the five kinds of liberation, namely liberation from form up to liberation from consciousness. Being liberated from the bonds of the five aggregates is called the five liberations.
Thoroughly penetrating the emptiness and non-existence of the five aggregates is called the five prajñās. This is to be in profound accord with the five aggregates.

Principle is named the fivefold Dharma-body; though it has three aspects, they are neither one nor different, neither vertical nor horizontal—this is called the Secret Treasury and is designated as Great Nirvāṇa.
[Commentary] It is withering and it is flourishing; it is neither withering nor flourishing. In a single kṣaṇa, it cultivates every kṣaṇa, moment by moment, in perfect mindfulness.
Without ceasing, one passes through the five stages; when the semblance of realization arises and one reaches the stage of the ultimate fruit, the three delusions are completely purified.

The mastery and non-obstruction over the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the ten realms is called the five liberations (*pañca-vimokṣa*). The purity of the five aggregates within the ten realms, being like empty space, is called the five prajñās.
The ultimate inconceivability of the five aggregates within the ten realms is called the five dharma-bodies (*pañca-dharmakāya*), wherein wisdom is merged with the five [realms].

Because the principle of the aggregates (*skandha*) is that which is to be realized through profound contemplation (*míng*), it is called "principle" (*lǐ*). Although its essence is one and undivided, it is divided [conceptually];

and because the *prajñā* that contemplates can profoundly realize the *dharmakāya*, and because that which is contemplated is realized through their mutual correspondence, the function of liberation arises.

Although there are three [aspects], the following clarifies the meaning of the secret treasury (*guǎngmiào zàngyì*) as commonly explained. Second, it clarifies the characteristic of the eternal abiding of the five aggregates.
[Text]: "The Benevolent King [Sutra] calls them 'dharmatā-form,' 'dharmatā-feeling,' 'dharmatā-perception,' 'dharmatā-formation,' and 'dharmatā-consciousness.
[Commentary]: 'Nature' (dharmatā) means that which does not change; thus, the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the hundred realms and the eight phases do not undergo transition.

They pervade the ten directions, yet this nature-aggregate is not something separate from the phenomenal realm. It is simply the very substance of the aggregates of good and evil, the defiled aggregates, and so forth, which abide eternally in their own essence."

Know that this is the *dharmatā-skandha* (aggregate of the nature of phenomena); do not seek it elsewhere. These three are the characteristics of the essence, body, and function of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
[Commentary: The *dharmatā* of the aggregates is itself the *dharmakāya*. When wisdom is in profound accord with *dharmatā*, it is the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Both the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya* are neither permanent nor impermanent, yet they are able to give rise to function as both permanent and impermanent; thus their function is eternal.
If used constantly, it is short.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "The Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya are both non-existent, yet their entire substance gives rise to function; they can be eternal, and when their constant function is not constant, it is long," and so forth:
if "long" refers to the four metaphors and "short" refers to eighty years, since all these lifespans are subject to impermanence, why is the "long" now taken up?
Regarding the short and the eternally impermanent: it is by means of the *śaila* (mountain-weight) and other measures that the eternal can be manifested.
If it were not eternal in its essence, how could it be made applicable to humans and devas? Therefore, when Śraddhālakṣaṇa heard of the eighty [kalpas], his doubts were dispelled;

and upon hearing the four parables regarding the impermanence of life, he realized the eternality of the essential body. Thus it is said: "If used as eternal, it is long; if used as impermanent, it is short."
Second, explaining the doubt through the application of the fruit. Part three: First, the doubt to be refuted.
[Text] Xinxiang only perceives impermanence and cannot perceive permanence; he has not yet mastered its function, much less understands its source.
[Commentary] Second, the dharmas that can destroy [the obstacles].
[Text] The Buddha cites four analogies to clarify their function: they are eternal in their traces and infinite, beyond the reach of thought and calculation;
how much more so regarding their essential principle—how could it ever be known by the mind?
[Commentary] These are the three marks of attaining understanding.
[Text] The mark of faith is the removal of delusion, as open and vast as clouds rolling away; such is the skillfulness in severing doubt.
[Commentary] These three [verses] resolve doubts regarding the preceding explanation of the Four Truths; their intent is not different from that, yet they must be investigated deeply.
Regarding the three [aspects], they are explained by way of the four virtues. First, the verses correspond to these virtues.

[Text] Regarding the correspondence of the four verses to the four virtues: the moisture of water that causes growth and flourishing corresponds to the virtue of permanence; the mountain’s ability to rise high corresponds to the virtue of self;
the crushing of the earth into dust corresponds to the virtue of purity; and the emptiness of space being free from suffering corresponds to the virtue of bliss.
[Commentary] Even when the earth is crushed into dust, no mark of purity exists; how then could impurity remain?

Therefore, by means of the quality of purity, it is used as a metaphor for the purity of principle, which is pure even amidst both purity and impurity. Second, regarding the doubt concerning these qualities, there are two parts: first, the manifestation of the function of the qualities.

[Text] The accomplishment of the four virtues is the fruition realized upon the attainment of the result. It accords with principle in being neither eternal nor non-eternal, yet it gives rise to the function of eternity and non-eternity;
it accords with principle in being neither self nor non-self, yet it gives rise to the function of self and non-self;

it accords with principle in being neither pure nor impure, yet it gives rise to the function of purity and impurity; it accords with principle in being neither blissful nor non-blissful... [and so forth].
"Pleasure arises from pleasure, yet there is no function of pleasure.

[Commentary: Regarding the four virtues such as permanence, students must distinguish that while the names are identical, their substantial bodies (*tattva*) differ. First, the substance of permanence, bliss, self, and purity (*nitya-sukha-ātman-śubha*) to which ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are attached consists of the two [delusions of] views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kāma*).
Second, the substance of permanence, bliss, self, and purity established by the two Bodhisattvas consists of the absence of... [text fragment ends].
The essence realized by the three Buddhas—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—is the Middle Way. Now, these four [attributes] are all the Middle;
therefore, they are all manifested through "double negation" (*ubhayānta-varjana*). In principle, one must negate the twelve inversions.

Here, these qualities such as permanence and so forth differ in name but are identical in essence to "neither permanent nor impermanent" and so on. The double negation of the four virtues is itself the Dharma-body.
Fourth, the ability to realize the profound wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).

Since the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are thus unified, one is able to respond to sentient beings by manifesting the application of mastery—whether as eternal or impermanent, pure or impure. Second, the removal of doubts; third, the initial doubt to be dispelled.

[Text]: Śraddhālakṣaṇa perceives only impermanence and suffering, and does not perceive permanence and bliss; since he is still deluded regarding the *saṃvṛti-satya* (the conventional), how could he recognize the *mūla* (the fundamental)?
[Commentary]: This refers to the second category: the dharmas that can destroy [delusion].

[Text] The four Buddhas raise up the function of the four virtues, which cannot be known through thought or calculation; their essence is fundamentally the Dharma of retribution, profound and beyond the reach of deliberation.
[Commentary] This is the third: the characteristics of attaining understanding.

[Text]: Because Śraddhālakṣaṇa, upon hearing this teaching, not only had his doubts removed and his delusions severed, but also gave rise to increased faith and understanding, he was filled with joy and exultation, taking it to heart, and so forth.
[Commentary: If one understands the intent of severing doubt through the Four Noble Truths, these three [points] can be seen. Two verses combine the metaphors:
incalculable kalpas, hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions of Buddhas’ lifespans—thus they are immeasurable and boundless.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the ancient interpretation and its errors;

second, the [explanation of the] phrases. Regarding the passage beginning with "hundreds of thousands of millions," this corresponds to the verse of the analogy. The ancient interpretation contains two errors: first, a distorted reading of the text; second, a biased adherence to the meaning.

[Commentary] Second, clarifying the present intention to refute the ancient [interpretation], which has two parts: first, refuting the biased grasping of the text; second, first, presenting the ancient interpretation.

[Textual Passage]: The old [masters] said: "The four similes all involve things with fixed boundaries that can be exhausted. 'Hundreds and thousands' are numerical categories, and since numerical categories must have a limit, based on this, they [conclude] it is impermanent."
[Commentary] The ancient texts of Qi do not understand the meaning behind the four Buddhas' skillful demonstrations. [The second part] demonstrates the present intent in two sections;
the first demonstrates the profound meaning of the sutra.
[Wenju] The current explanation is not so: that the four Buddhas cite four analogies is precisely using the measurable to illustrate the immeasurable.
Even measurable objects cannot be known through thought or calculation; how much less can the immeasurable Dharma be fathomed?
"Hundred million, ten billion, hundred trillion"—these are cited as numerical methods to clarify the concept of the "innumerable.
[Commentary] The four metaphors for the measurable—hundreds, thousands, and so forth—are numbers that no one fails to know; Sudatta cites these measures and these numbers.
How much more so regarding the immeasurable and the incalculable? Second, [this section] refutes ancient misinterpretations of the sutra.
[Commentary on the *Wenju*]: "Since you are unable to count them repeatedly, how can you know the incalculable?

Even if one were to know the count, know the incalculable, know the measurable, or know the immeasurable, these are merely manifestations of its functioning (*huà-yòng*) and have nothing to do with its essential substance (*tǐ*). This is the error of taking a biased and superficial view."
Not only does this destroy oneself, but it also misrepresents the sūtras.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "there is both concession and refutation": "concession" refers to knowing that [the Buddha] is an emanation (nirmāṇakāya), while "refutation" refers to delusion regarding the Dharma of retribution.

Since the Dharma of retribution is in fact the very essence of the emanation body, yet one interprets the profound text superficially, one destroys oneself and others; having already incurred fault for oneself, one causes others to slander the teaching.
Second, refuting the meaning of biased attachment.
[Text] Regarding the meaning of biased attachment, the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" states: "The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is also eternal, for it preaches the Dharma everywhere;

therefore, it is eternal. One should know that the transformation body possesses both the meanings of eternity and non-eternity. Why do those of the old school suddenly claim it is exclusively non-eternal?
[The text] constantly says "and so forth.

[Commentary: The meaning is that which is explained. The Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya), the Response Body (saṃbhogakāya), and the Dharma Body (dharmakāya)—these three bodies all possess four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
namely, permanence, impermanence, both, and neither. This reveals that while the Three Bodies are one, they cannot be conceived of or described as being either identical or distinct from one another.

Ancient sages were deluded regarding this transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), either by fixating on its impermanence, or by hearing that the transformation-body is identical to the Dharma-body and thus permanent, yet still claiming that while the Dharma-body is permanent, the transformation-body is impermanent.
This is entirely due to their failure to understand the meaning of the word "identical" (ji). Therefore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga-śāstra* (*Qixin lun*) states:

"In accordance with what is appropriate, it is always able to maintain, sustain, and remain indestructible and non-perishing. This demonstrates that the transformation-body possesses all three meanings.
Sufficient. Three or two verses resolve doubts.
For these reasons, it is said that by giving food through the two conditions of not harming living beings, the merit is immeasurable;
therefore, the lifespan of the Great Being is incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, and without limit.

[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, citing the cause to explain the meaning; second, [the explanation itself]. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, interpreting the text by means of actual practice; second, explaining it in terms of causes and conditions.

[Textual Analysis] The two lines beginning with "By these causes and conditions" are verses that resolve doubts. If one treats them as "causes and conditions," the "cause" refers to the immediate [condition].
Taking abstention from killing as the direct cause (*hetu*) and giving as the indirect condition (*pratyaya*), one obtains a long life through these causes and conditions.

[Commentary] "The cause is proximate and the condition is remote" means that because one preserves life by not killing, this serves as the proximate cause for longevity; giving, on the other hand, is the [remote] condition.

Eating sustains life and serves as a condition for longevity; this refers to the meaning of "distant conditions. Second, the explanation is given by way of two conditions. [Text] If one establishes two conditions:
abstaining from killing is the "cessation-virtue" (śīla) of the non-killing precept, and bestowing food is the "practice-virtue" (caryā) of the non-stealing precept.
These are cited alternately; both cessation and practice are the dharmatā and bodhicitta of these two conditions.

Taking these as causes, the cessation of unwholesome conduct and the practice of merit and wisdom are all conditions that can manifest the nature [of the mind], which is neither permanent nor impermanent, yet capable of being both permanent and impermanent. [Commentary:

There are two aspects to non-killing: non-killing itself is the goodness of cessation (*śīla*), while releasing living beings is the goodness of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). There are likewise two aspects to non-stealing.

Abstaining from stealing is the cessation of unwholesome conduct, while practicing the giving of food is the cultivation of wholesome conduct; therefore, each of the ten wholesome paths has both a dimension of cessation and a dimension of cultivation, and all are termed "the two conditions" (*dvaya-pratyaya*) in the sutras.
Regarding these two types of goodness, one may mention either cessation or cultivation interchangeably, as each individually constitutes a condition for long life.

Only when the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is generated do they truly become the cause. As for what is called "dharmatā," it refers to the four vows of non-action, which are the very essence of dharmatā.
Arising is the cause of long life; when these two kinds of conditions can assist the true mind of the Way, one then realizes that the Dharma-body and Reward-body are neither eternal nor impermanent.
They can give rise to the Response-body and Transformation-body, which are both eternal and impermanent; these three bodies as a single essence constitute the wondrous eternity.
Second, the explanation of the Dharma-gate refers to what was mentioned above.
[Text] The dharma-food, non-killing, and so forth are all as explained above.

[Commentary] If one explains the giving of food and non-killing from the perspective of the Dharma-gates, it is fully detailed in the *Sushu* (Explanatory Notes) on the *Yinianxu* (Preface to the Doubtful Thoughts).
Second, resolving doubts based on the fruit.
[Text] Since the cultivation of causes is long, the attainment of the fruit is long; the manifestation of the essence is long, and the arousal of function is long.
This refutes short-lived doubts.

[Commentary] By explaining the "long" to resolve the doubt regarding the "short"—namely, impermanence—the doubt is severed, and the lifespan of eternal abiding is clarified. Therefore, the Great Being (Mahāsattva) is...
The term "Tathāgata" refers to the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*). Therefore, Yi Jing’s new translation renders this line as:
"For this reason, the Great Awakened Honored One. This concludes the fourth verse.
Consequently, you should not now harbor doubts regarding the Buddha’s immeasurable lifespan.
[Text] Therefore, you have now completed one verse.
[Commentary] Second, the joyful faith of Xiang.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Xiang, having heard these four Buddhas proclaim the immeasurable lifespan of the Tathāgata...
He fathomed his deep mind of faith and understanding, and leaped for joy.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; the first explains the characteristics of faith based on what was heard.
[Wenju] "At that time, Xingxiang... and so forth, describes how hearing the verses resolved his doubts and gave rise to faith. He heard that the lifespan was immeasurable.
Those who understand the traces [of the teachings] can make their lifespan immeasurable;
those who harbor doubts can shorten their lifespan to eighty years; and those with deep faith and understanding realize that their fundamental consciousness is neither measurable nor immeasurable.

[Commentary] To explain "original and trace" (*honjaku*): the essence is original and the function is the trace. Hearing that his lifespan is immeasurable, one understands that the trace-function is capable of being eternal—not a longevity that merely exceeds a long duration.
Thus, one realizes that the trace-function is capable of being short—not a shortness that merely falls below it—and the doubt regarding the fixed eighty-year limit departs from this point onward.
As for "deep mind" (*shinjin*): it is the awakening to the high and profound essence of the *vipāka-dharma* (retributive dharma).
The essence of this is wondrously transcendent of both the measurable and the immeasurable. Second, regarding the entry into the stages, it explains "joy.

[Textual Commentary] "Leaping" refers to ascending the stages; "joy" refers to the arising of faith. This is the explanation according to the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha/Śrāvaka), wherein it refers to the aspect of faith.
In the interpretation according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
one leaves behind doubt during the stage resembling the Iron Wheel (*ayaścakra*) and gives rise to faith upon entering the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
If interpreted according to the stage resembling that of Samantabhadra, one leaves behind doubt within the lower stages and attains firm, deep faith at the summit of the tenth stage (*daśama-bhūmi*).
It is like the diamond [vajra] that touches the ultimate reality (*tattva*) and gives rise to joy.
[Commentary: True faith and understanding arise and enter the stage of joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); it is distinct in the first ground (*bhūmi*) and perfected in the first dwelling (*vihāra*).

In both cases, one breaks through ignorance (*avidyā*), which is termed "doubt. Departing from this, these are all explained as the stage of internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the semblance stage (*sambhāra-mārga*). As for the "summit" (*mūrdhan*) of the ten grounds: if...

Not establishing equal enlightenment—that is, not immediately transcending the tenth stage to ascend to the subsequent mind by destroying the delusions of the highest grade of ignorance—this position is called the "Summit of Universal Subjugation" (*sarvārthasiddha-śikhara*).
Because it is moved by the final ignorance, there arises joy and exultation. Third, the attainment of the Way by those suited to the teaching.
When this "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata" was being preached, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

[Commentary] From the passage beginning with "When this Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata... onwards, this is the third section: the initial awakening of those of superior faculties among those present.
[Commentary]: The "initial awakening of those with superior faculties" refers to the meaning of the three cycles of teaching in the *New Sūtra* (the *Lotus Sūtra*).

Cunda’s request for relics is intended for those of middling faculties, and the "differentiation of the three bodies" is for those of inferior faculties. *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated as "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment";
it is the original enlightened nature of all sentient beings, not merely the fruit of reaching the ultimate stage.
Only then is it called "unsurpassed" and "rightly equal. This awakening of the mind penetrates all five [stages], which is precisely this stage of partial realization (*vibhūti-satyābhisambodha*).
When the four Buddhas return to their original state, the four Tathāgatas suddenly disappear.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; first is the explanation based on the causal conditions.
[Wenju] From the passage "The four Tathāgatas at that time" onwards is the fourth section, the cessation of transformation. The Buddha originally appeared for the sake of conditions;
once the conditions have been benefited, he withdraws his transformative influence and returns to his original state, which is why it is said that he suddenly disappears.

[Commentary] This refers to a class of practitioners with the potential for Pratyekabuddhahood who, having converged through similar conditions such as faith and so forth, cause four Buddhas to appear where they were previously unmanifest;
thus, they "return" after having already set their minds [on awakening]. Second, the explanation by way of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

[Text] Regarding the practitioner who understands through contemplation (*guan-jie*): when the wisdom of realization arises regarding the realm of the truths, it is associated with profound contemplation.
This wisdom itself cannot be apprehended as wisdom, nor can the object be seen; since both object and wisdom are quiescent, this is precisely the meaning of "non-manifestation," and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the "objects of the truths" (*satya-viṣaya*): the three truths share a single object, which is original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). Regarding "awakening-wisdom" (*bodhi-prajñā*): the three wisdoms are a single mind, which is initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*).
When the original awakening fully gives rise to the initial [awakening], it is called "arising. When the initial [awakening] merges with the original, it is called "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*).
One who is well-corresponded must forget both. Not forgetting them is like a blockage arising within a conduit; this is expressed as the simultaneous stillness of both.
Therefore, it does not appear.
[Commentary] Part Two: The Chapter on Repentance for the Extinction of Evil. First, the title of the chapter:
*The Sutra of the Golden Light*, Chapter Three: "Repentance."

[Commentary] The section on the text is divided into two parts. First, the clarification of the meaning of *chanhui* (repentance). Second, the first part: the explicit elucidation of its great significance. Fourth, the first part: explaining the name "repentance" (*chanhui*).
Third, the first part: contrasting it with other scriptures.
[Text]: Many Mahāyāna sūtras explain repentance (*pāpadeśanā*) in various scattered sections, whereas this sūtra dedicates this specific chapter exclusively to repentance.

[Commentary]: The *Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra* elucidates the method of repentance for the fourfold assembly; the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* elucidates the method of repentance for the six sense faculties;

the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates King Ajātaśatru’s repentance for his parricide; and the *Avalokiteśvara-āśā-prārthanā Sūtra* elucidates the subduing of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*). Such are the various sūtras [that treat this subject].
Since all gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) are capable of extinguishing transgressions, what dharma would not be a form of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*)?

However, because the conduct of a Bodhisattva transforms prior karma into conditions for benefiting others, it discusses the three types of repentance, such as that of non-arising (*anutpāda*). In contrast, the Śrāvakas seek their own liberation;

even when they clarify repentance, it mostly concerns ritual procedures (*vidhi*) aimed at avoiding the three miserable realms. Therefore, here we shall only clarify the "scattered" [repentances] in accordance with the various Mahāyāna sūtras.
Section Two: Correct Explanation of the Names. Now, the two characters *chàn-huǐ* (懺悔) present both Indic and Chinese phonetic transcriptions.

The Indic term *kṣama* is translated into Chinese as *huìguò* (悔過, repentance of transgressions). Since "repenting of transgressions" encompasses the meanings of the five categories beginning with "submitting the head" (*shǒufú*), the Great Master has here listed both the Indic and Chinese terms side by side;
thus, he explains *chàn* (懺) by "submitting the head" (*shǒu*) and *huǐ* (悔) by "submitting" (*fú*).

This continues until the point where one confesses before the Śāstṛ with a sense of shame and dread (*hrī-apatrāpya*), desiring that those who receive the teaching immediately cultivate the practice of initial submissiveness (*śiro-namana*) and shame and dread upon these two words;
this is the mark of skillful preaching of the Dharma, and thus it cannot be criticized on the basis of Chinese or Sanskrit etymological glosses.
This is divided into five parts, the first of which explains it by way of "initial submissiveness."
[Text] Now, first, I shall explain the names. "Chan" (懺) means "to begin" (*śiras*), and "hui" (悔) means "to submit.

It is like a person in the world who, having offended a king, submits and obeys, not daring to act in rebellion; such non-rebellion is "submission," and such obedience is "beginning. The practitioner is also like this:
by submitting at the feet of the Triple Gem and correctly following the Way, they do not dare to commit wrongs; therefore, it is called "chanhui" (repentance).

[Commentary] The character *shǒu* (首) means that the animal itself confesses its transgressions; it signifies sincerity. Second, there is an explanation based on the distinction between black and white.

[Text] Furthermore, "repentance" (*chàn*) is named the white dharma, while "regret" (*huǐ*) is named the black dharma. Black dharmas must be regretted and not committed again, whereas white dharmas must be aspired to and honored.
Because this discussion combines both the rejection [of the former] and the adoption [of the latter], it is called "repentance" (*chànhuǐ*).
[Commentary] "Qi" (企) means to look up toward; it also implies to revere and honor. The third [section] explains this in terms of abandoning [the past] and seeking [the future].
[Text] Furthermore, *chān* (懺) is named "cultivating the future," and *huì* (悔) is named "reforming the past.

Because one regards the evil and unwholesome dharmas committed in previous days as base and loathsome, it is called "repentance" (*huì*). As for all the wholesome dharmas abandoned in the past, from this day forward—
Because one diligently cultivates through the power of vows, it is called *sāṃkṣepa* (懺); because one seeks to abandon the past and pursue the future, it is called *pratikramaṇa* (悔).
[Commentary] "Bǐ" (鄙) means shame; "chí" (耻) is pronounced as *wùlù* (烏路) and means to loathe. This fourth point explains [the term] by way of disclosure (*āviṣkaraṇa*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
[Text]: Furthermore, "confession" (*chàn*) means to lay bare all faults and expose one's transgressions without daring to conceal them;

"repentance" (*huǐ*) means the mind that severs the continuity [of evil], feeling weary of and regretting it, and abandoning both the agent and the action to cast them away together. Therefore, they are called "confession and repentance."

[Commentary] To disclose past transgressions, sever those of the present, and prevent the continuation of those in the future—this fivefold method explains the two [faculties] based on shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*). First, the general explanation.
[Text]: Furthermore, "repentance" (*sānti*) is called shame (*hrī*), and "regret" (*kaukṛtya*) is called dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*).

[Commentary] To explain *chánghuì* (repentance) solely by means of *cánkuì* (shame and remorse) without yet distinguishing the five types of persons or the categories of humans and devas is therefore termed a "general explanation.
Second, the "specific explanation" distinguishes between humans and devas, as well as the distinctions of phenomena and principle (*shìlǐ*) across the four teachings.
First, the explanation regarding humans and devas:

[Text]: *Cān* (shame) refers to feeling shame before the heavens; *kùi* (remorse) refers to feeling remorse before other people. People see its manifest aspects, while the heavens see its hidden aspects.
Whether subtle or manifest, whether fine or coarse, all are evil; therefore, one speaks of "repentance" (*chàn-huǐ*).

[Commentary]: Humans possess only the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) and thus see only what is manifest; the various devas, however, possess the *cakṣur-abhinirvṛtta* (retributive) divine eye and therefore see even that which is hidden and obscure.
When such a person feels shame, modesty, and abashment, this is called "repentance" (*pratikramaṇa*).

Second, the explanation according to the four teachings (*catuḥ-śāsana*) is based on the fact that this sutra encompasses the repentance of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and since the three vehicles subsume the four teachings, the meaning of shame and remorse is established.

Is it not likewise the case that at the beginning of each of the four teachings, there are the four stages of subduing [the afflictions] and so forth? The expositor, according to the meaning, should elaborate upon this in detail.

Furthermore, regarding the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa) in the four teachings, all require the application of effort; as for the noble ones (ārya), they are spontaneous, which may be analogized to the karmic retribution of humans and devas in the triple world, where volitional action becomes natural.
Moreover, within the worthies and noble ones of the four teachings, there are those who practice and those who realize. Regarding the four teachings—

The principle is fundamentally not a product of artificial construction; therefore, it is further designated as "human and celestial" (deva-manuṣya), "the first three of the four," "the first two of the Tripitaka," and "the first two of the noble ones" (ārya).
[Textual Commentary] Furthermore, humans are "worthy ones" (bhadra) and celestials are "sages" (ārya); those who do not reach the rank of these worthy and sage-like classes perform repentance.
[Commentary] "Worthy" refers to the seven worthies; "sages" refers to the four sages. These are what is attained. There are two aspects: phenomena and principle.
[Wenju] Furthermore, both the worthy and the sages are human-heavenly beings, yet they are the ultimate heavenly beings (*paramārtha-deva*). The ultimate heavenly being is principle.
The noble sages (āryas) fail in these matters; I repent for both the failure in practice and the failure in principle.
[Commentary] Regarding the second, the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-yāna), there are two parts: first, the noble sages.
[Wenju] Furthermore, one feels shame before the sages of the Three Vehicles and embarrassment before the worthies (ariyas) of the Three Vehicles, as one fails to equal these devas and humans.
Therefore, it is called "shame and remorse" (*hrī-apatrāpya*); shame and remorse are called "repentance" (*pratikramana*).

[Commentary] This teaching shows that Bodhisattvas are identical to those of the Two Vehicles in severing delusions; thus, all three vehicles are noble (*ārya*). There are two aspects: principle and phenomenon.

[Text]: Furthermore, the worthy and holy ones of the three vehicles are all humans; because the ultimate principle constitutes heaven, and based on this distinction between humans and devas regarding shame and remorse, it is called "repentance" (*chànhuì*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the three distinct teachings, first are the worthy and holy ones.

[Text]: Furthermore, since even the worthies and sages of the Three Vehicles are not yet equal to the worthies of a Bodhisattva, let alone the sages of a Bodhisattva, one now feels shame before the worthies of the thirty minds and the sages of the ten stages; therefore, it is called "Repentance through Shame."

[Commentary]: The noble stages of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) correctly sever the afflictions of views and thought; the three levels of the Sages (Sanxian) of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) can sever the "dust-like" afflictions and further suppress ignorance.
Therefore, it is said that [the latter] "is not yet" [capable of the former]. Second, regarding phenomena and principle.
[Text] In sum, these worthies and sages are all humans; from the perspective of the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*), they are called "devas.
Discussing this in terms of humans and devas, because of the presence of shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*), it is termed "repentance" (*pratikramaṇa*).

[Commentary] This takes the "Middle Way of Mere Emptiness" (*butong zhong*) as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding the fourfold Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the first two stages consist of sages (*xian-sheng*) and worthies (*xian-ren*).

[Wenju] Furthermore, from the thirty minds (*sanshi xin*) upward, one is judged to be a sage; the ten faiths (*shixin*) are worthies. It is based on this distinction between worthies and sages that shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and repentance (*kaukṛtya*) are discussed.
[Commentary]: From the thirty minds onward, all have realized the Dharma-body and manifest the eight phases [of a Buddha]; therefore, they are judged as "sages.

Because those in the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) remain long separated from the ocean of the wheel of suffering, they are given the name "worthy ones" (ārya). Second, the two aspects of principle and phenomenon.

[Text] In total, these worthies and sages are collectively called "humans" (*puruṣa*); the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*) is called "heaven" (*deva*). Based on this discourse concerning humans and gods, one discusses shame (*hrī*), remorse (*apatrāpya*), and repentance (*deśanā*).
[Commentary] Because they possess virtue, they are designated as the "ultimate meaning. Three times ten makes the number thirty.
[Text] The ten sections combined explain the names.

What serves as this grindstone? It is the single *dharmatā* (real mark), wherein there is no separate real mark; that is, the very mark of transgression itself. For one who attains this locus, there is no transgression that is not extinguished, and no virtue that is not manifested.

[Wénqù] Next, regarding the locus of repentance, the verse of King Ajātaśatru in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Whether harsh words or gentle speech, all return to the ultimate truth;

[Commentary] Regarding "harsh words, gentle speech," and so forth: in the teachings of the seven provisional vehicles (*saptayāna-upāya*), the three obstructions must be extinguished and all practices must be cultivated;
because the subject and object are not yet merged, this is called "harsh words. In the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), all cultivated evils are immediately identical to inherent evil;

The coarse and the subtle are quiescent in their respective places; because the path of conceptual thought is severed, it is said that all return to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding the Four Noble Truths:
the suffering of the two deaths and the accumulation of the five abodes are, by virtue of being identical to the nature (*dharmatā*), such that not a single thing is to be abandoned.

The path of the myriad practices and the cessation of the three virtues are, by virtue of being identical to the nature, such that there is neither cultivation nor realization, yet they are spoken of as "severance."

Regarding birth and death, it is the severance of the very state of non-severance; this severance is such that there is nothing that is not exhausted, and it is also called the severance of the suffering inherent in the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
These four points transcend thought and are all of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*); to know them thus is called "attaining the locus.
