[Commentary] Second, explaining the offerings to all Buddhas. Part one: establishing the intent and dividing the text.
[Text] From "I now make offerings" below, thirty-five lines clarify the purpose of making offerings to the Buddhas. As for why they make these offerings:
it is because I was originally ignorant and blind, yet was shown the way to repentance; since this kindness is profound and heavy, I have raised these offerings.
The text is divided into two parts: first, one line clarifies material offerings (*āmiṣa-pūjā*); second, thirty-four lines clarify Dharma offerings (*dharma-pūjā*).
[Commentary] Part Two: Explaining the Meaning Based on the Text. Section One: Clarifying Material Offerings.
"I now make offerings to all Buddhas throughout immeasurable and boundless trichiliocosms."
[Commentary] "I now," and so forth, means that one clarifies the offering of wealth by means of the Dharma itself. Why?
Because within a single great trichiliocosm there are already hundreds of billions of Buddhas, let alone the immeasurable and boundless Buddhas of all great trichiliocosms.

If wealth were limited, how could it possibly provide universal offerings? This is because one has realized and penetrated that the essence of the offered gift is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). It emerges from there.
Because they arise inexhaustibly and pervade each and every direction, there are matters of wondrous offerings of the six sense-objects before all Buddhas in all lands;
not only are they vast and pervasive, but they also exist eternally throughout the future, performing Buddha-work.
To clarify the dharma-gate of practice for the subsequent section, this is specifically named "Material Offerings. One must understand this.
The two [types of] offerings are divided into two because their essential natures and characteristics constitute different gateways. Regarding the second, the offering of Dharma, there are two parts;
first, the division of the text and the establishment of the intent.
[Textual Commentary: The offering of Dharma is divided into two. First, eight lines and a half clarify the offering of Dharma that transforms others, which accords with the Tathāgata.
To come forth with the Dharma-gate of compassion to rescue and benefit all sentient beings is the cultivation of the Dharma-offering for the sake of transforming others.
The subsequent twenty-five lines and a half clarify the cultivation of the Dharma-offering for one’s own practice:

by cultivating the merits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in accordance with the Tathāgata’s wisdom-dharma gate, this constitutes the cultivation of the Dharma-offering for one’s own practice. Among all forms of offering, the Dharma-offering is supreme.
This is the foremost among all material offerings and Dharma offerings; it is complete in both principle and practice, and for both self and others.

[Commentary] Using compassion for the sake of transforming others is the unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), which is not separate from the three types of wisdom. As for one's own practice following wisdom, since this is already the Buddha-wisdom, how could it be separate from the three types of compassion?
These are spoken of in contrast to one another merely to facilitate understanding; the offering of the Dharma is supreme.
This is because it enables the Buddha’s lifespan to abide eternally and his wondrous transformations to be inexhaustible.

Furthermore, where there is the Dharma-method, both types of offering are perfected; where there is no Dharma-method, even material offerings are rendered futile. Therefore, the offering of the Dharma is rightly called the supreme.
Second, the explanation of the meaning based on the text, in two parts: first, clarifying the dharma-offering for the benefit of others; second, first, causing others to practice, in two parts:
first, the analysis of the text to explain the meaning; second, the analysis of the text. First, the analysis of the text.
[Text] The passage on the Dharma-offering of transforming others consists of two parts: first, four lines on transforming others to cause them to practice;
second, four and a half lines on transforming others to cause them to practice repentance. Regarding the initial practice:

I myself have practiced the Ten Stages as a Dharma-offering, and now I further transform others to cause them to perform the Dharma-offering. It is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps.

Those who were deluded all attained clarity, yet he did not ultimately exhaust his intent; it consists of four parts: first, clarifying the beginning of transformation by uprooting suffering through great compassion;
second, exhorting [them] toward the true cause, the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); third, exhorting [them] toward the true fruit, the great awakening of *bodhi*;
and fourth, exhorting [them] to be diligent and urging them to achieve success swiftly.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning has four parts. First, it clarifies the beginning of the transformation by uprooting suffering through great compassion:
"I shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings throughout the ten directions from all their various sufferings."
[Commentary] Second, the exhortation regarding the true cause: the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
"I shall establish and settle inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* multitudes so that they may abide in the ten stages.
[Commentary] Third, the exhortation regarding the true fruit: the great awakening of *bodhi*.
May those who have already attained stable abiding on the ten stages all become fully endowed with the perfect enlightenment of a Tathāgata.
[Commentary: This fourth exhortation to diligence urges them to accomplish their practice;
for the sake of even a single sentient being, they cultivate practice for billions of eons so as to enable immeasurable multitudes to cross over the sea of suffering.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation according to the teaching and contemplation, divided into two parts. First, the meaning of the teaching.
[Text] Now, because sentient beings are equal, their dispositions and natures are also equal; skillful means for delivering one or many is likewise so.
Without calculating toil, through the accumulation of practices and the amassing of merit, one achieves the Great Enlightenment; thus, the wisdom-virtue is perfected and all suffering is exhausted.
The virtue of severance is thus fulfilled; the text is self-evident and requires no further extensive explanation.
[Commentary] Second, the practice of contemplation.
[Wenju] Regarding the contemplation of the mind: one regulates the single thought-moment so that true illumination may arise, spontaneously realizing the true fruit. One regulates the single...
"All mental factors are likewise so; that the multitude of afflictions among the disciples is transformed according to the will—this is precisely the meaning.

[Commentary] "A single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) refers to taking up any one thought-moment. To harmonize delusion with the True by means of the wondrous Threefold Contemplation is what is called [the transformation].
When true illumination arises—whether reaching the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the six faculties, or the five grades—it is all termed "attaining the true fruit.

Thus, the *Zhi guan yi li* uses the metaphor of a tree: contemplating the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth to achieve the inconceivable is called "producing the sprout," while from the first grade upward, it is all called "producing the fruit.
That cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* gives rise to [this].

The analogy of the sprout arising from the fruit and the present contemplation of the mind as the true fruit of clarity correspond to one another. Regarding the phrase "harmonizing all things equally," it means that when the single-mind contemplation is perfected, it passes through each and every state of mind such that there is no state that does not become contemplation; this is identical in meaning to the principle of the pure mind pervading everywhere and spontaneously merging [with all phenomena].
First, establishing the intent and dividing the text.

[Commentary on the Text: Next, for four and a half lines, regarding "transforming others to cause them to practice repentance": "I have received the Buddha’s teaching on repentance, and I in turn teach repentance to others;
repeatedly lighting the lamp of repentance, the transformation continues without end. The text has three points, the first of which is the desire...
To explain the sequence of the confession, it is precisely for this purpose that the confession is explained;
having thus explained the confession three times: [Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning according to the text. Part one:
being about to explain the confession: "I shall now expound for these sentient beings the subtle, wondrous, and profound method of repentance, namely, the Golden Light."
"Eliminating all evils.
[Commentary] This second part is the actual teaching.
If one can sincerely repent even once for the extremely heavy evil karma accumulated over a thousand kalpas, then such multitudes of offenses—
All are completely extinguished.
[Commentary on the Text] "A thousand kalpas" is a metaphorical expression used to demonstrate that the power of repentance is great.

For example, if a wicked person has committed sins piled up like mountains, yet they can rescue the king from danger and offer even half the kingdom as compensation, how could one still take account of their prior offenses? Even if there were a thousand...
Although one may have committed grave offenses against the Dharma that are heavy and profound, if one can extract the King of Dharmatā and manifest the Dharmakāya from within the Tathāgatagarbha,
then the Great Enlightenment will be brilliantly clear and one will ascend in sovereign freedom; how then could one ever again be bound by the karma of the five ānantarya crimes?

[Commentary]: Since much time has passed and the committed offenses are grave, if one realizes that the offense of parricide is precisely the principle fully contained within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, taking this as the subject of contemplation, the Dharma-nature—gold and so forth—is manifested thereby.

This is called "extracting the obstacles of royal calamity" and transforming them into virtue; for what sin could then bind one? Thus, all five *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses are characterized by liberation. This is then termed...
I shall now explain the method of repentance. Having recited the repentance three times,
I have now expounded this Dharma of repentance from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, which is pure, subtle, and wondrous,
and is able to swiftly eliminate all karmic obstructions.
[Commentary] Second, clarifying the practice of self-cultivation as Dharma-offering. This section is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text and the establishment of its intent;

second, the actual text. From the passage "I shall now abide in" (*māham... pratisthāpayeyam*) downward, there are twenty-five lines and a half of text concerning the practice of self-cultivation as Dharma-offering. This is further divided into two:

the first five lines concern the cultivation of one's own practice, while the subsequent twenty lines and a half concern the cultivation of one's own repentance. The preceding section on self-repentance is hereby concluded.

Why then do we speak again? It is like a goldsmith who, from his first apprenticeship until his white-haired old age, repeatedly heats and hammers [the metal] until the vessel is finished before he rests;

so too, the cultivation of wisdom is like heating, and the practice of repentance is like hammering. When wisdom and repentance reach their ultimate limit, one then stops. There is no fault in speaking of this repeatedly.
The previous section was the gate of personal practice (*svayam-caryā-mukha*); the present section is the gate of Dharma-offering (*dharma-pūjā-mukha*), which constitutes the difference.
The self-cultivation is further divided into three parts: first, the initial phrase designates the chapter, which is "I shall abide in peace";
second, the cultivation of the cause, which refers to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and third, the attainment of the fruit, which is *bodhi*.
[Commentary] From this point downward, the text poses questions and provides answers through analogies, answering by combining the metaphors with the Dharma they represent.

The goldsmith represents the Golden Drum; Śākyamuni is the Master of Transformation. "Initial practice" represents the first generation of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). "White-haired" represents the present fruition.

The subsequent demonstration shows that from the beginning until now, there has never been a moment’s neglect of either teaching and practice or teaching and repentance, which mutually refine one another.

The analogy of "confession" (*chān*) and "explanation" (*shuō*) corresponds to "practice" (*xíng*), while the analogy of "striking" (*dǎ*) corresponds to "practice" and "confession. Wisdom (*zhì*) and abandonment (*duàn*) are likewise so.

The analogy of the vessel being completed refers to a single instance of a sentient capacity (*jī*) attaining the fruit through its own cause; therefore, as long as the fruit has not been attained, one must repeatedly fire and strike it—what is there to be disliked about repeated explanation?
Now, this section below distinguishes the differences: although there are repeated firings and strikings, each has its own specific gateway. Second, the explanation according to the text.
Regarding the second part on the meaning, there are three sections. First, the heading:
"I shall settle [the mind].
[Commentary] Second, the cultivation of the cause.
Abiding in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they take the ten kinds of precious jewels as their feet.
[Commentary] "Precious jewels" refers to the causes of the ten stages; these stages themselves are the precious jewels.
"Feet" means that the ten stages are the foundation of the fruition, and thus they are called feet. Furthermore, the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) are the [feet] of the ten stages.

The "feet" [of the stages] do not refer to other virtues as being unpracticed; rather, they are practiced according to one's power and capacity, with *dāna* (generosity) specifically serving as the foot for the first stage.
If the foot of *dāna* is fulfilled, one enters the first stage; continuing in this manner until the foot of *prajñāpāramitā* (wisdom) is fulfilled, one enters the tenth stage.
Therefore, the ten perfections constitute the feet of the ten stages.

[Commentary] Regarding the "feet," the *Śāstra* preserves two interpretations: first, that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constitute the feet of the fruit; second, that the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) constitute the feet of the ten stages.
As for the "ten perfections," besides the six, they further include skillful means (*upāya*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and knowledge (*jñāna*).

Below, the text explains the intent behind designating the ten perfections as the feet of the stages, as extensively clarified in the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Its characteristics are: the attainment of the fruit of the three supernormal knowledges;
becoming a Buddha through the light of unsurpassed merit and virtue; causing all sentient beings to cross the ocean of the three realms of existence;
and the vow to fully possess all the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the profound Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas and the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
"O World-Honored One, I shall accomplish hundreds of thousands of dhyānas, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, inconceivable dhāraṇīs, and the ten powers.
[Commentary on the Text:

Within the section on the fruit, there is a general clarification of the fulfillment of the fruit, followed by a specific clarification of the fulfillment of the fruit; these may be understood from the text. This is the light of merit.
"Clarity" refers to the two kinds of adornment on the level of fruition; "causing sentient beings to cross the ocean" refers to the turning of the wheel of Dharma on the level of fruition.

[Commentary] The first phrase of the sutra is designated as the general [merit], while the remaining three lines and three phrases constitute the specific merits; these are the adornment of merit (*puṇya-vyūha*).
Radiance is the adornment of wisdom; it does not discuss the light of wisdom apart from the light of form, for the ultimate non-duality of form and mind is realized therein.
Among the three practices, those not explained in the commentary are now briefly listed here, hoping to spare one the need to search through the Dharma-treasury.
One must discuss the eighty-four thousand [teachings], all of which are secret; therefore, they are called "profound merits."
That which is accomplished through the six perfections and the myriad practices is, briefly stated, the ten thousand virtues; extensively, it is immeasurable.

All-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) is precisely the wisdom of the Middle Way, which necessarily illuminates both poles simultaneously, causing the three [wisdoms] to reach perfect consummation.

"Dhyāna" (meditative concentration) refers to penetrating dhyāna and penetrating the fundamental [nature], as all are the Dharma-realm. "Samādhi" (concentration) refers to the *Śūraṅgama* and the vigorous aspect of the original nature; these two belong to the Mahāyāna.
Since both the phenomena (*dharma*) and their underlying principles (*tattva*) are equally clear and tranquil within all things, the hundred faculties (*indriya*) are mentioned in general;

these consist of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*). That is to say, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—these five are able to give rise to all wholesome dharmas and are thus termed "faculties" (*indriya*);
they exclude the five hindrances by warding off doubt, laziness, wrong views, distraction, and delusion, which obstruct these five.

These are termed "powers" (*bala*); their names are identical to those of the five faculties mentioned above, yet their functions differ. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*): first, the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga*);
second, diligence (*vīrya*); third, joy (*prīti*); fourth, tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); fifth, equanimity (*upekṣā*); sixth, concentration (*samādhi*); and seventh, mindfulness (*smṛti*).

These seven are able to bring concentration and wisdom into equilibrium; they are collectively termed "factors of enlightenment" because they constitute the portion of awakening that leads to the attainment of the ultimate fruit.

The Path refers to the Eightfold Noble Path: (1) Right View, (2) Right Resolve, (3) Right Speech, (4) Right Action, (5) Right Livelihood, (6) Right Effort, (7) Right Mindfulness, and (8) Right Concentration.
Because it is free from deviation and error and leads universally to Nirvana, it is called the "Noble Path.
Although the cultivation of the path factors, such as the faculties and so forth, occurs during the causal stage, their realization constitutes the fruit-virtues of the Tathāgata.
"Ni" (尼) is translated as "obstructing and upholding" (遮持): it obstructs all evil and upholds all good.

Its number is either five hundred or eight hundred and four thousand, representing the destruction of afflictions; yet, to speak of its actual number, it is that which can obstruct and uphold all dharmas.
