The first part of the text on the practice of repentance [consists of twenty and a half lines].

[Commentary on the Text]: From the words "To all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones" onwards, the twenty and a half lines clarify the text for one's own practice of repentance, which is divided into two sections;
the first line is a request to the Buddhas.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts. First, the request to the Buddhas:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess great compassion; may they bear witness to my humble sincerity and graciously accept my repentance.
[Commentary] Second, the clarification of the repentance, which has two parts. First, the division of the text.

[Text] The subsequent nineteen and a half lines clarify the text of the repentance (sānti), which is divided into five sections: first, four and a half lines for repenting the obstacle of retribution;

second, one and a half lines for repenting the obstacle of afflictions (kleśa-āvaraṇa); third, six lines for repenting the obstacle of karma (karma-āvaraṇa); fourth, two lines clarifying the dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā);

and fifth, five and a half lines for repenting the two difficulties of good and evil. Within the section on the obstacle of retribution, there are further two parts; the first consists of two and a half lines.
The next two lines request the elimination of the characteristics of retributive obstacles.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the explanation of the meaning, there are five parts; first, the confession of retributive obstacles. First, the presentation of the characteristics of retributive obstacles:
"If, throughout a hundred kalpas, I have committed various evils, by reason of these causes and conditions, I shall give rise to great sorrow and suffering, poverty, and destitution."
Sorrowful, feverish, startled, terrified, and fearful of evil karma, his mind is constantly timid and inferior;

in every place he dwells, there is not even a moment of joy. [Commentary] "A hundred kalpas" refers to the time when the retribution is received. During that time, one receives a body, and this body is itself the retribution.

Since retribution involves action, such action constitutes an obstruction. Poverty, destitution, and suffering are the secondary retributions (niśraya-vipāka); their lack of perfection is likewise an obstruction of retribution.

Furthermore, those who suffer from anxiety, feverish distress, and fear do so because they are externally oppressed by poverty; thus, their internal burning with fear constitutes a karmic obstruction.

Their various committed evils are the suffering of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) and *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate); their poverty and affliction are the suffering of the *rūpa-skandha* (form aggregate);

and their constant mental timidity and inferiority due to anxiety, feverish distress, and fear are the suffering of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). At times, there is none [of these].
That which is called "joy" is precisely the suffering of the *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); all of these are intended as the *skandha* of retribution (*vipāka-skandha*).
[Commentary] To undergo a body for a hundred kalpas and commit various evils with that body—wherein evil serves as the causal condition—is to give rise to sorrow and suffering.

Both the producer and the produced are all obstacles of retribution, precisely because one has obtained the five evil *skandhas* through retribution. Therefore, this commentary is set in contrast with the sutra.

Since one has already realized that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all merely aggregates and not karmic retribution, why is it necessary to understand that the five aggregates constitute various evils before they are called "obstructions of retribution"?
If one performs various good deeds, could these be called obstructions? Second, [the request] for the elimination of evil.
The World-Honored Ones of Great Compassion currently residing in the ten directions are able to remove all fears of sentient beings;
I pray that you will accept my sincere repentance and cause all my terrors to be entirely eliminated.

[Commentary] The prayer "May the Buddha accept my repentance" means that [the sins] will be eliminated; if he did not assist by providing the correct support and guidance for the completion of the repentance, how could the Buddha, despite possessing power, be able to remove the obstacles?
Since this meaning is evident, the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) does not explain it further. Second, the repentance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Part one: dividing the text.
[Text] Next, the passage on the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is divided into two parts: first, two lines that set forth its characteristics; second, one line requesting purification.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning has two parts: first, setting forth the characteristics.
All the defilements of my afflictions and karma—[Note:
"Karma-defilement" (業垢) refers to karma as action; because the mind of affliction moves, it becomes defiled.
Alternatively, since afflictions arise from past karma, they are called "karma-defilement"]—I request purification twice.
I only pray that the present Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will wash away [my impurities] and purify them with the water of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

[Commentary: As for "the water of great compassion," it is only when compassion is of the same essence (*samatā*) that it is termed "great. This compassion serves as the water; there is nothing it does not purify.
Although this compassion is of the same essence, it does not arise without an object. The three types of repentance serve as the conditions; thus, though not previously washed, they are now washed.
The third section is the Repentance of Karmic Obstructions, which is divided into two parts.
[Textual Commentary]: The passage on karmic obstructions consists of three sections. The first two lines discuss vertically the karma created throughout the three periods of time;
the next two lines explain horizontally the manifestation of the ten non-virtuous actions in the present; and the final two lines seek repentance for past karma.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation has three parts. First, the vertical discussion of the creation of karma throughout the three periods of time:
all past evils are now fully repented; present transgressions are sincerely confessed; those not yet committed are henceforth not dared to be done;
and previously committed deeds are not dared to be concealed.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; the first presents them in contrast to the retribution.

[Wenqu]: Those currently undergoing [the fruit] are termed "obstructions of retribution" (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*); those not yet undergone are bound to the practitioner, and if one cultivates the path of goodness, they can act as obstacles.
[Commentary] That which is called "right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*) refers to the present form and mind. For one who has not yet brought retribution to fruition, there exists a binding capacity;

if one cultivates wholesome dhyānas or various untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*), then [the karma] will come to demand its retribution, manifesting the signs of various karmas, or secretly acting as an obstacle.

Unless one relies on the three types of repentance methods according to the Mahāyāna, these obstacles will not be extinguished. Second, the posing of questions and their explanation. First, the posing [of the question].

[The text says: "There has not yet been [an instance of] asking. [Wenqu]: Regarding the past and present, it is necessary to perform repentance; as for the future which has not yet occurred, how can one speak of repentance?
[Ji]: Second, explaining the prevention of arising, this answers the third point by first citing sutras and treatises as proof.
[Text]: Answer: The Sāṃkhyas call this the "theory of future existence," while the masters call it the "theory of future becoming.
A Great Sūtra states: "Because one obstructs the future, it is called 'killing. [Objection: Since the present perishes moment by moment, what is there to kill? [Response:
It is simply the obstruction and severance of the future that is termed "killing. Since both the sūtras and śāstras regard the future as existing, one must perform repentance for it.
[Commentary] The masters of the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* maintain that the future is negated; for if one does not negate it, the continuity of the mind will necessarily arise.
Thus, in the "Chapter on Purifying Karmic Obstacles" of the *New Sūtra*, within the text for repenting transgressions, it is stated that Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time all say:
"May the transgressions already committed be eliminated, and those yet to come [in the future] be extinguished."
Such evils will not be committed again, thereby preventing them from arising in the future. Second, citing examples from the present. [Wenju]:
To further provide examples from the present, consider those laypeople who, while planning their lives, give rise to immeasurable evil thoughts.
Although these deeds have not yet been committed, they will inevitably and suddenly resolve to leave the household life and cultivate the Way in the future.
The matters one contemplates are simultaneously at variance with their conditions.
[Commentary] When householders generally commit transgressions, they abandon the home;
when they generally practice repentance, they must sever what has not yet been obstructed and necessarily change what is currently present. Third, the conclusion of the answer based on the meaning.
[Text] Future karma should also be understood in this way; although it does not yet exist in the present, when its time arrives, it will inevitably manifest.
If one now repents, it will become utterly pure.
[Commentary] "Utterly" (suo ran) means to be completely dissolved. This second section clarifies the ten non-virtuous actions as they arise in the present.
I now repent of all actions of the three types of body, the four types of speech, and the three types of mind;
I repent of all ten kinds of evil karma committed through body, speech, and thought.
[Text]: It can be understood that the three karmas of the present life are expanded horizontally to constitute the ten unwholesome actions.
[Commentary]: One seeks repentance for past karma;

by distancing oneself from the ten unwholesome actions and cultivating the ten wholesome paths, one dwells securely in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and attains the status of a Honored One of Ten Powers (*daśabala*). Regarding the evil karma committed...
Those who ought to receive evil retribution now sincerely repent before the Buddha.
[Commentary] "To distance oneself" means the severance of evil; "to practice" means the arising of good. The "Ten Abodes" refers to the causal stage of the initial mind;
"attaining the Ten Powers" refers to the fulfillment of the final fruition.

[Commentary]: If the ten unwholesome and ten wholesome actions were explained solely in terms of the three miserable realms, humans, and devas, how could they encompass the Ten Abodes up to the Ten Powers?
Once one grasps the meaning of observing and violating the first five precepts, the present meaning becomes intelligible.

The meaning of observing and violating [the precepts] can be clarified through both the Separate and Complete Teachings regarding the Ten Abodes and Ten Powers; since the meaning of the present context is easily understood, it must be explained as follows.
From the stage of the cause up to the final fruition, one discusses the ten unwholesome and ten wholesome actions at each successive stage.

Fourth is the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*): "May all wholesome dharmas existing in this land and in other worlds be entirely dedicated toward my own cultivation of goodness in body, speech, and mind, so that I may realize the unsurpassed path in a future life."
[Text] Next, the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is explained: because sentient beings are stubborn and attached to existence, they are unable to transcend it;

now, in order to repent of these offenses, it is said that one "dedicates [merit] to others. While the passage regarding rejoicing (*anumodanā*) concerns this land and other worlds, the present intention is not so;
rather, whatever wholesome deeds are performed in this land or in other directions are all bestowed upon sentient beings.

Together they head toward the fruit of Buddhahood; just as when the note *sheng* enters the *jiao* register, it can be heard from afar, so too the power of their skillful means is vast, equaling empty space.
Furthermore, the concluding text states that this dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) cannot be interpreted as sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), for the discussion of sympathetic joy appears later in the text.
[Commentary: This is the repentance for the sin of attachment to the causes and effects [of merit].

Because others regard this land and other worlds as places where those of the five vehicles cultivate wholesome dharmas, it is said that one "rejoices" by way of defining the person according to their location.
Now, it is clarified that the wholesome merits cultivated here in this land and in other realms are all gathered up and dedicated so that sentient beings may realize the Unsurpassed Way.
The sound is a metaphor for all virtues, and the horn is a metaphor for dedication; the near and far can be understood through this. As for the greatness of the power of skillful means:

if one skillfully dedicates [merit], it becomes a great skillful means, its merit equal to the vast void; yet if one does not understand what is virtuous, then even the Dharma-realm is not called dedication.
Fifth, the repentance of both good and evil has two parts; first, the selection and demonstration of the textual divisions.

[Text] Explanation of the Eight Difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*): This refers to the eight difficulties discussed within the context of good and evil, rather than the eight difficulties concerning being before or after a Buddha.
The text is divided into two parts: first, four lines point to evil as a difficulty;
next, one and a half lines point to evil obstructing goodness as a difficulty, or alternatively, point to goodness obstructing the Path as a difficulty.

[Commentary] Next, one and a half lines of the sub-commentary explain the primary meaning of "rightly taking up" (*samyak-parigraha*) and "properly obstructing the path. Second, the word-by-word explanation of the meaning has two parts:
first, pointing to evil as a difficulty.

If, within the various realms of existence and the perilous difficulties of the six destinies, one is foolish and lacks wisdom, thereby committing manifold evils, [one must now do so] before the Buddha.
I now repent of all the various difficulties of birth and death in the world, the hardships of diverse sensual desires, and the afflictions of ignorance;

I repent of these many hardships: the difficulty of a fickle and restless mind, the difficulty of associating with evil friends, the dangers of the three realms of existence, and the difficulties of the three poisons.
[Commentary] The text has six parts; the first explains the various perils and difficulties of existence (*bhava*).

[Wenqu] The first four lines concern the difficulty of the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Regarding "the various existences" (*sarvabhava*): this refers to the bodies obtained through retribution within the twenty-five states of existence.
To commit manifold evils with such a body—is this not indeed the obstacle of retribution?

[Commentary] Regarding the "twenty-five states of existence" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*): these consist of the four miserable destinies, the four continents, the six heavens of the desire realm, Mahābrahmā, the four dhyānas, the fruit of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), the *anāgāmin*, and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).

They are collectively termed "existence" (*bhava*) because the karma that produces outflows has not yet been severed. The explanation of the meaning of the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is fully contained in the previous commentary.
Second, the explanation of the perils and difficulties of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
[Text]: Regarding the phrase "the perils of birth and death," there are two interpretations: if one takes the cause, it refers to the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*);
if one takes the fruit, it refers to the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). [Commentary]:

Karma constitutes the peril from [the desire realm] up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); retribution constitutes the peril from [the form realm] up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). It is oppressive.

Cūḍapanthaka is an example of this; the perilous nature of karmic retribution for those below [the noble stages] can thus be known. Second, the explanation of the difficulty of sexual desire. [Commentary]:
Various forms of sexual desire are precisely the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
[Commentary] Regarding the four explanations of the difficulty of frivolity and agitation (1): First, the direct demonstration of the characteristics of frivolity and agitation.

[Text] "A mind that is frivolous and agitated" refers further to the obstacle of retribution; frivolity and agitation are *vitarka* and *vicāra*, and *vitarka* and *vicāra* belong to the category of dharmas of retribution.
[Commentary] This means that the initial mind directed toward an object is called *vitarka* (initial application), while the subtle mental discrimination is called *vicāra* (sustained application);

these are also the states of *citta* and *manas*. Because this belongs to the category of the aggregates (*skandha*), it is classified as a resultant phenomenon (*vipākadharma*). Second, the examples of the noble ones and ordinary beings; first, the noble ones.

[Text]: Just as an Arhat, having exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*) and emerged from meditative absorption, still possesses applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) with a distracted mind, one should know that this restlessness is an obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), not an affliction.

[Commentary] "Emerging from contemplation" means emerging from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is explained that because they are free from delusion and karma, this is verified as being a result of retribution (*vipāka-dharma*).
Second, the ordinary person.
[Text] Furthermore, it cites worldly people who, despite their learning, change their course and fail to establish karmic obstacles; all of this arises from their fickleness and impulsiveness.
Is this fault not indeed an obstacle?

[Commentary] "To turn back and change one's course" refers to those who, for example, have not yet mastered the study of the Sūtras and then wish to study the Vinaya; having not yet mastered the Vinaya, they then wish to study the Śāstras.
Such fickle people will ultimately fail to accomplish their task. This is what is meant by the obstacle of failing to accomplish one's work.
"Obstructing what ought to be done" is a scribal error for "obstructing [the performance of] wholesome deeds. Fifth is the explanation of the difficulty of associating with evil friends.
[Textual Commentary: Regarding the difficulty of associating with evil friends: evil friends can defile a person’s three karmas; this belongs to the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*).

It is like moving a stable to the side of a slaughterhouse. The story of Mengzi’s mother moving her residence because she was next to a place where people wailed, and her subsequent move to a place where there were red and black dyers, illustrates this meaning.

[Commentary]: "Like one who moves a stable"—the character for *jiù* (stable) is pronounced *jiù*; it is a horse-shed, a place where horses are gathered. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-saṃgraha* (*Fǔfǎzàng-zhuàn*) states:
"To associate with the virtuous and hear the True Dharma. For example, in the past, in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, there was a white elephant possessed of great strength and courage;
whenever a criminal was brought before it, the elephant would trample him to death. Later, the elephant stable was struck by fire.
When the elephant was moved closer to the monastery, a bhikṣu was reciting a verse from the *Dharmapada*: "By doing good one is born in heaven; by doing evil one enters the abyss.
Upon hearing this, the white elephant’s mind became gentle and compliant. Later, when it was handed over to the executioners, it did not harm them, but merely sniffed and licked them.
The king summoned his wise ministers to deliberate on this matter. One minister said to the king, "This elephant is tethered near the monastery..."
"It was only because he had heard the sublime Dharma that he acted thus. Now you may tether him near a slaughterhouse; when he beholds the killing, his evil intent will surely swell.
The King ordered the elephant to be tied up at the place of execution. Upon seeing the slaughter, the elephant’s evil intent grew fierce and violent, and its cruelty became even more extreme.
Regarding the phrase "neighboring the wailing" (*kūhuò*): it means learning to wail by being near a grave, and learning to trade by being near a market. (Cai Shi).

The *Huopinqing* states: "Huo" means transformation; it refers to the changing and altering of things. Thus, the character contains the radical for "transformation" (*hua*) and also signifies "wealth.
The *Shiji* records: "Mencius’s mother lived alone and widowed near a cemetery. Mencius would frequently play there.
His mother said, 'This is not a place for a dwelling,' and moved to live beside a marketplace. Mencius again played at being a merchant. His mother said once more, 'No.'"

He was able to reside there, living beside the Academy; his conduct in bowing and retreating was so full of propriety that his mother said, "This is truly where one may dwell after the era of Mencius.
Consequently, he became a great Confucian scholar, authoring seven chapters of books in which he resolved the six difficulties regarding the three poisons.
[Text]: "The three poisons are the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

[Commentary]: In the *Shu* (Sub-commentary), the topical outline states: "Regarding the eight difficulties of good and evil, the *Shanlun* (Treatise on the Good) discusses four difficulties; this can be understood through the *Jingshu* (Commentary on the Sutra).

As for the present 'difficulties of evil,' the Sutra appears to list seven; based on what [criteria] does it speak of four? It is because, according to the principle of the three hindrances (*trīṇy āvaraṇāni*), there are both combined and individual cases."

Combining three [difficulties] makes four; what are these four difficulties? They are: the difficulty of the six realms of existence, the difficulty of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), and the difficulty of restlessness.
Although these constitute three difficulties, the difficulty of karmic retribution—namely, lust, ignorance, and the three poisons—belongs exclusively to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The difficulty of associating with evil friends belongs exclusively to the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). As for the difficulty of the perils of birth and death, it is broadly twofold.
Because it involves both the dissolution of the physical body and karmic retribution, the meaning of the three obstacles as evil corresponds to the four difficulties;
however, one must understand that evil is inherently evil, and thus this evil is itself the contemplation of non-arising. To repent in this manner, all difficulties are instantly eliminated.
It is difficult to be free from obstacles;
it is difficult to encounter such freedom; it is difficult to find a favorable time; it is difficult to cultivate merit; and it is likewise difficult to meet a Buddha.
All such difficulties as these, I now repent.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first clarifies that both good and evil can constitute obstacles. The first part [of this section] clarifies these two meanings together.
[Wenju]: "Encountering no-obstacle obstacles" contains two meanings: first, if one does not cultivate goodness, obstructing obstacles will not arise;

second, if one wishes to cultivate goodness, evil obstructions immediately arise. Goodness itself is not the obstacle; rather, evil comes to block the good, which is what is called "goodness as an obstacle."
This meaning is easy to understand, as ordinary people all interpret it in this way.
Second, since all wholesome states are difficult to practice and can obstruct the Path, are they not indeed "difficult"? This point shall now be explained.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section on the basis for explaining the text, there are four parts. First is the explanation of the "difficulty of encountering no obstacles.

[Text] As for "the difficulty of encountering no obstacles," this refers to those who claim they have no evil and are unwilling to cultivate goodness—such as the followers of the Two Vehicles who enter into emptiness and give rise to the notion of extinction and nirvana, or the notion of peace and security, thereby ceasing further pursuit of Bodhi; this is precisely its meaning.

[Commentary] The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) leave the house and reach the place of fearlessness; because the sign of being free from difficulty is manifest there, they are cited as examples.

Those who temporarily enjoy the human and celestial realms consider themselves to be free from difficulty, yet all shall encounter this very difficulty. Second, the explanation of the difficulty of cultivating meritorious virtues.

[Text] Regarding the difficulty of cultivating merit: many people perform conditioned acts seeking agreeable fruits. For example, there was once a bhikṣu who practiced exclusively for merit but did not cultivate the prohibitions and precepts;
he fell among white elephants with his body adorned with the seven treasures and a golden bowl to receive their excrement.
Furthermore, in the *Sutra of the Original Acts of King Subhavyūha* and other texts, it is said that is this not a case of the difficulty of cultivating merit?

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "such as one person," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 8, states: During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two brothers who left the household life to seek the Way.
One observed the precepts, recited the sūtras, and practiced seated meditation; the other extensively sought out donors to cultivate various meritorious deeds.
When Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world, one was born into a wealthy family, while the other became a [slave].
The son of a merchant, who possessed the strength of a great white elephant, left the household life to study the Way and attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) as an arhat.
However, due to his meager merit, it was difficult for him to obtain almsfood through begging. One day, carrying his bowl, he entered the city to beg for food;

having failed to find anything despite searching everywhere, he went to the stable of the white elephant and saw that the King had provided the elephant with all manner of abundant provisions. He spoke to the elephant, saying: "I..."
"Both you and I share this transgression. The elephant was immediately overcome with grief and did not eat for three days.
The keeper of the elephant became terrified and sought out the practitioner. Upon seeing him, he asked, "What spell have you cast that has made the King’s white elephant ill and unable to eat?
He replied, "This elephant was my younger brother in a previous life; together we went forth from home to study under Kāśyapa Buddha."

He said, "I merely maintained the precepts, recited the sūtras, and practiced dhyāna, but did not practice giving. My younger brother, however, extensively sought out donors and performed various acts of giving;
therefore, his food and drink are fully prepared and of every variety in abundance. I merely practiced the Way and did not cultivate giving;

thus, although I have now attained the Way, when begging for alms, I do not receive such exquisite and magnificent offerings."—From the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) by King Miaozhuangyan.

It is said that in the past, during the final age of the Buddha’s teaching, there were four bhikṣus who conceived a profound and earnest reverence for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as if it were nectar they had not yet tasted.
Thereupon, they made a pact to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way. After dwelling in the mountains for a long time, their clothing and provisions were completely exhausted.
One of them said, "You three simply devote your lives to the Way and do not worry about food; I shall give up my own body and strength [to provide for you]."

They had sworn that the three would provide for one another's needs so that their task might be completed; however, while one of them was traveling through the human realm, he happened upon a king’s procession and became enamored of its splendor.
Having cultivated merit through his practice, he was reborn among humans and gods by the power of retribution, always becoming a king.

The other three deliberated, saying: "I have escaped the cage of bondage; this success is due to the king. Yet the king remained addicted to the fruits of retribution, increasing his involvement in conditioned existence.
It is appropriate to convert those in the pit of fire as early as possible. One person said: "This king is attached to desire and possesses perverse views;
unless there is the hook of affection, he cannot be pulled out. One became a handsome wife, and two became clever sons.

Because of the words of the wife and sons, [the king] would surely follow and comply. Thus, when the conversion was appropriately established, he indeed succeeded in reforming his heterodoxy. The wife was none other than Gadgadasvara (Miaoyin).
The two sons of the Bodhisattva were Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata; the King was Puṇyaprabha.
Third is the difficulty of encountering a favorable time.

[Commentary on the Text]: Regarding the difficulty of encountering a favorable time: it is like the period at the beginning of a kalpa, when one dwells in Uttarakuru and experiences nothing but constant bliss.
Not practicing the Way at all—how could this not be called encountering a difficult time despite having favorable conditions?
[Commentary] For example, at the beginning of the kalpa, the people of Jambudvīpa lived for eighty thousand years, and those of Uttarakuru had a fixed lifespan of one thousand years;
both enjoyed long lives and happiness, and thus did not delight in practicing the Way. Uttarakuru is translated here as "Excellence" (*śubha*), as it excels the other three continents.
Because it is a continent. Fourth, the explanation of the difficulty of encountering a Buddha:
"Encountering a Buddha is also difficult" means that those such as the Brahmin woman Cāṇḍā, Sunakṣatra, and Devadatta all encountered the Buddha and yet fell into difficulty;
by analogy with this, one should say that hearing the Dharma and giving rise to slander, or encountering the Saṅgha and causing schism, are likewise [difficult].
It is difficult.
[Commentary] The *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* (or *Xingqi xing jing*) states: "A talkative young girl, dancing with a basin and thrusting out her belly, came before me and said:
'Śramaṇa, why do you not speak of your own household affairs, but instead speak of the affairs of others? You now enjoy yourself for yourself, yet you do not know my suffering.'"
"O Ye! Previously you consorted with me and I became pregnant; now the month is near and I require ghee and oil to nourish the child, which you must provide to me.
Then, the Deva-Indra transformed himself into a mouse, entered her garment, and gnawed through the bowl, causing it to suddenly fall to the ground.
At that moment, the earth split open, and Ciñcā manifested herself, falling into the Avīci Hell. [End of] *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

In the *Pattravarga*, it is said that Shanxing (Sunakṣatra), who was a son when the Buddha was a Bodhisattva, left the household life and thereafter received, upheld, and expounded the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Having destroyed the fetters of the desire realm and attained the four dhyānas, he associated with evil friends and fell away from his previous four dhyānas.
He gave rise to evil and heterodox views, saying: "There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no nirvāṇa. Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, he felt a sense of dread.
With an evil and perverse mind, Devadatta entered the Avīci Hell. Although he was the Buddha’s own cousin, he committed three of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*):
shedding the blood of the Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṃgha that obstructs the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and killing an Arhat.

Furthermore, having incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father, he completed the preparatory act for killing his mother. Moreover, with an evil intent, he concealed poison beneath his ten fingernails, intending to [harm the Buddha].
Sparting the Buddha’s feet, piercing them, harming the Buddha, and intending to go to Mount Vaideha—upon leaving the city, the earth split open and he fell alive into hell.

These [acts] encountered the Buddha and thus became great calamities. However, the substance of the first three phrases consists of tainted wholesome states that obstruct the cultivation of the untainted;

therefore, they are called "calamities. This phrase, however, involves the commission of a heinous crime (*ānantarya*) and seems dissimilar to the above, because encountering the Triple Gem is considered the most [significant].
Because it opposes what is wholesome, it constitutes an obstacle; this may also be analogized to the aforementioned "obstacles to the wholesome" (*kuśala-mārga-vibandha*).
Second, explaining that the text should be read with both the level (*ping*) and departing (*qu*) tones: first, explaining that the reading of characters applies to both tones.
[Text]: If it is read as the "difficulty" of "hard and easy," this carries the meaning of evil coming to obstruct the good, thereby making the good difficult to accomplish.
If it is read as the "obstacle" of "hindrance," this means that the good itself is inherently difficult, and [evil] can obstruct the Path.
[Commentary] The second [point] relies on the sūtra and belongs to the section on "Going.

[Wenju] Furthermore, according to the sūtra text which says, "I now repent of all such difficulties," one should know that the sūtra uses the term "difficulties" (nàn) in the sense of "obstructing difficulties" (zhàng nán).
[Commentary] Regarding the "Praise by the Three Knowledges," there are two parts: first, establishing the intent; second, analyzing the text.
[Text/Phrase] From the verse beginning "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, upon whom I rely" and continuing for twenty-one lines, this is the third praise.
According to the sequence of the treatise, the preceding offerings of wealth and Dharma involve the body and mind; yet, as the body and mind have not yet been fully manifested...
I now further express my oral praise regarding those who practice this Dharma-gate. What preceded was the Dharma-gate of making offerings;

what follows is the Dharma-gate of the *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) samādhi. The text is divided into three parts: first, one line that sets forth the heading and offers praise; second, nineteen lines that provide the formal praise;
and third, one line that concludes the praise.
[Commentary] The two types of offering can be correlated with body and mind; since speech has not yet been initiated, they have not yet been discharged through the three karmas.
Thus, they are incomplete. Now, by adding the karma of speech, they become manifest and complete, thereby establishing the sequence.
Although one previously practiced cultivation and repentance for oneself and others, the ability to support and benefit the Buddha’s lifespan is termed the "Gate of Offering."

Although the three bodies of the Buddha are now praised and extolled as the method for practitioners to accomplish the contemplation of dharmas—known as the "gate of mindfulness of the Buddha"—and although these dharmas mutually contain one another, two distinct dharma-gates are established based on their predominant characteristics. Second, the explanation of the meaning according to the text;
third, the initial heading and praise.
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are that upon which I rely; therefore, I now pay homage to the ocean of Buddhas.

[Commentary on the Text] "The Buddhas" indicates them horizontally across the ten directions and vertically through the three periods of time; these refer to the *pao-ji* (retributive), *ying-ji* (responsive), and *li-ji* (principle) aspects, which are the *dharmakāya*.
This is an instance where the phrasing is concise yet the meaning is vast—a skillful artistry in establishing the chapter title. "That upon which I rely" refers to relying upon...

The nature of cessation (*śamatha*) is the single essence of the three Buddhas. As for the "ocean of Buddhas": the four eyes enter the Buddha-eye, and the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) enter the knowledge of suchness (*tathatājñāna*);
all lose their original names and are simply called the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom.

It is like an object cast into rock candy, or like flowing waters merging into the sea—there is nothing that is not sweet or salty. Because the nature of cessation and the three Buddhas encompass all phenomena, it is so named.
The Buddha is the ocean.
[Commentary] The two cultivations of retribution and response are the phenomena that fully embody principle; the single nature of the Dharma-body is the principle that fully embodies phenomena.
When the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are thus characterized by their three bodies, what is there that is not subsumed? This is that upon which I rely.
Since it is stated that the dharma-nature is a single essence of the three Buddhas, we know for certain that the other Buddhas are the Buddha of the mind-nature (*cittaprakṛti-buddha*).

This arises from original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) as initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*); it is also the three truths giving rise to the three wisdoms. Without this as a basis, the wondrous repentance cannot be accomplished;
therefore, the initial stage of the Perfect [Teaching] is called "cultivating the practice of a Buddha. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye."

Regarding the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and the knowledge of reality (*yathābhūtajñāna*), there are eleven knowledges in total. The ten knowledges are shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), while the knowledge of reality belongs exclusively to the Buddha.

The ten knowledges are: (1) dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), (2) subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), (3) knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), (4) conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), (5) knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), (6) knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), (7) knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), (8) knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), (9) knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and (10) knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "like casting objects [into water]," just as rock honey is exceedingly sweet and seawater is exceedingly salty, when objects are cast into water, they all lose their original flavors;
likewise, the essence of phenomena (dharmatā) is such that there is nothing within its nature that is not wondrous. How could one not take refuge in and revere this ocean of the Buddha?
Second, the formal praise, which is divided into two parts.

[Textual Analysis: Regarding the formal praise, there are two sections: first, sixteen lines of praise expressed through words (*kyo-gen*), followed by three lines of praise beyond words (*zetsu-gen*).
The praise through words is further divided into two: first, one line of concise praise and concise illustration; second, fifteen lines of extensive praise and extensive illustration.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the detailed explanation, there are two parts. First, praising by means of words. Within this, first is the brief praise and brief comparison:
His golden radiance shines brilliantly like Mount Sumeru; therefore, I now pay homage to the Most Victorious One.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; the first explains the brief praise of the golden hue. This section on the golden hue has two parts: first, comparing its color to other gold.
[Textual Analysis] Regarding the "brief praise," among all the marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana), this briefly praises the golden hue. The *Śāstra* compares it to iron at that very moment.
That gold is immediately compared to sea-gold; sea-gold is compared to dragon-gold; dragon-gold is compared to the gold of Jambudvīpa;
the gold of Jambudvīpa is compared to the gold of the Four Heavenly Kings; and so on in succession until it is compared to the gold of the Sixth Heaven.
Compared to the golden hue of the Buddha’s body, the gold of the Sixth Heaven is like iron.
[Commentary] "Jambūnada gold" refers to a river in the Western Regions named after the Jambū tree; this gold is produced from within that river.
The river derives its name from the tree, and the gold is named after the river. Second, it illuminates objects by manifesting its radiance.
[Text] Furthermore, when the Buddha’s golden light thoroughly illuminated the walls and screens so that no shadows remained, as he entered the city, he emitted light that shone upon the ground.
A certain woman bowed her head in prostration, and her gold hairpin fell to the earth; she saw only a shimmering radiance and did not know what was the ground and what was the hairpin.
Only after the Buddha had passed by and the light subsided did she see the gold hairpin.
[Commentary]: Regarding the two praises of the golden color, the first clarifies that it is the basis upon which all the marks (lakṣaṇas) depend.

[Text]: "However, because the golden-colored body is the locus upon which all the marks depend, and one perceives only the golden color, we know this is a general praise of all the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇānuvyañjanas)."
[Commentary] Second, an explanation of the analogies for the four virtues.
[Wenju] Gold has four meanings: its hardness and indestructibility are analogous to *nitya* (eternity); the wealth obtained by those who possess it is analogous to *sukha* (bliss);

its substance being free from blemish is analogous to *śubha* (purity); and its color being wondrously radiant is analogous to *ātman* (self). Among all the virtues, these four virtues constitute the totality.
[Commentary] This provides two explanations of the brief illustration.
[Wenju] "Just as Mount Sumeru" means that Mount Sumeru is composed of four treasures;
since the Buddha’s body is likewise endowed with the four virtues, we know this is a general illustration.
[Commentary] Second, the extensive praise and extensive illustration. First, the extensive praise. First, the division of the text.

[Textual Analysis] The text for the extensive praise and extensive illustration is divided into two parts: first, twelve and a half lines of extensive praise; second, two and a half lines of extensive illustration.
Furthermore, the extensive praise consists of four sections.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the "Exegesis," it is said that praise corresponds to the *nirmāṇakāya* (manifestation body), while the characteristics of *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* (dharma and enjoyment bodies) are revealed by the mind.

Although there is a distinction between the external and internal—where the manifestation of wisdom is the internal and the realization of wisdom is the external—how could they be separate entities? Therefore, in the New Translation, the four virtues are specifically assigned to the three bodies:
the *dharmakāya* possesses permanence and self; the *saṃbhogakāya* possesses purity; and the *nirmāṇakāya* possesses bliss, thus distinguishing them through their respective perfections.

Because Jiaxiang [Jingying Huiyuan] distinguishes the Separate [Teaching] from the Perfect [Teaching], the three bodies of the Perfect Teaching each possess the four virtues. For one who has grasped this principle, it is understood that the four [bodies] of the present correspond to the Dharma and Reward bodies, while the four [bodies] of the future are likewise so.

One should seek the meaning of this through the texts of the sutras and commentaries. Regarding the first section, the praise of my own virtues: [The text continues: "The four [bodies] of the present are the Dharma and Reward bodies; the four of the future should be understood according to this intent. Thus, one should investigate the meaning within the scriptural commentaries. First is the praise of my own virtues.
His color is unsurpassed like natural, refined gold; his eyes are pure like deep blue lapis lazuli; his merit, majestic power, and fame are renowned;
he is the Buddha-sun, whose great compassion extinguishes all darkness.
[Text]: From the phrase "Regarding its color," there are two lines above and below that extensively praise the unsurpassed golden hue; "unsurpassed, unsurpassed" refers to my own virtue.
[Commentary]: These two lines praise the virtue of purity.
Pure, stainless, and free from all dust and obscurations, the unsurpassed Buddha-sun shines its great light everywhere.

When the fire of afflictions blazes fiercely, scorching the mind with heat, only the Buddha can extinguish it; like the moon, he is cool and refreshing, his body adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, such that one never tires of beholding him.
[Text] From "Excellent, pure, and stainless" onwards, the three lines extensively praise the Buddha’s form as being stainless; "stainless" refers to the quality of purity.
[Commentary] These three lines praise the quality of permanence.
His merit is lofty and sublime; his net of light shines brilliantly as he dwells peacefully within the triple world, like the sun illuminating the world.
Like lapis lazuli, it is pure and free from blemish; its wondrous colors are vast and diverse, each distinct.
Its hue is crimson-red like the rising sun, adorned with nets of light fashioned from crystal and white silver. In such various ways, the Sun-like Buddha is magnificently adorned.

[Text] From "The merit is towering and lofty" (*guǒdé wēiwēi*) downwards, three lines and a half extensively praise the Buddha’s physical form. "Abiding securely" (*ānzhù ānzhù*) refers to the constant nature (*chángdé*).
[Commentary] In the sutra, "towering and lofty" (*wēiwēi*) describes a state of great height. *Phala* (頗棃) is translated here as "water-jade" (*shuǐyù*). This is the fourth praise.
Delighting in virtue:
within the three realms of existence, the surging waves of the great ocean of birth and death toss and disturb my mind; its flavor is bitter and poisonous, most coarse and harsh.
The Tathāgata’s Net-Luminosity can cause it to dry up and vanish; his wondrous body is upright and majestic, with marks and signs of excellence that are extraordinary.
The golden light shines universally upon all, and the great ocean of wisdom fills the three realms;
therefore, I now bow my head in reverent salutation.

[Commentary] From within the three realms of existence, the following four lines extensively praise the Buddha’s physical form, which is able to eliminate the poisons of suffering and is itself bliss.

This is virtue. [Commentary] The pronunciation of *lǎo* (潦) is "lǎo"; it refers to water flowing along a path. Regarding *jiěshǒu* (稽首), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "lowering the head. *Shǒu* (首) means "head.
Kǒng Ānguó says that *jiěshǒu* refers to the head touching the ground. These two [sections] extensively illustrate the two [aspects], and the first part analyzes the text.
[Text] From "Like a great ocean" (v. 2) onwards, two and a half lines provide an extensive analogy, which is divided into two parts:
the first two lines provide an extensive analogy, and the remaining half-line combines the metaphors.
[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the sequential explanation, there are two sections; first, the extensive analogy.
Just as the volume of the waters of the great ocean is difficult to know, the atoms of the great earth are beyond calculation,
Mount Sumeru is difficult to measure, and the limits of space cannot be found.

[Text]: "The ocean of the Buddha’s merits cannot be known by thought and cannot be exhausted by speech; it is where the sphere of mental activity ceases and the path of language is cut off—this is precisely the meaning.

Just as the waters of the ocean are difficult to know, how much more so his merit of permanence (*nitya*)! Just as the dust of the earth is difficult to know, how much more so his merit of purity (*śubha*)!

Just as the weight of Mount Meru is difficult to know, how much more so his merit of selfhood (*ātman*)! Just as the limits of space are difficult to know, how much more so his merit of bliss (*sukha*)!"

"Virtue. [Commentary] These four phrases are metaphors for the preceding four Buddhas; they are explained by citing the Great Master (Nāgārjuna), or they may metaphorically represent the finite and infinite aspects of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), or they may metaphorically represent the Four Truths and the Four Virtues of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
In the "Preface to the Profound Text," the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is revealed.

The Buddha cannot be illustrated by [ordinary] analogies precisely because the three bodies (trikāya) possess mastery over the identity and difference of the three-in-one; therefore, while four analogies may be applied individually to each, they collectively manifest the three.
This text is identical to the previous [explanation]: because the ocean of the four virtues neither increases nor decreases, it is *nitya* (eternal);
because the essence of the ground is pure, it is like a mountain rising high, thus it is *ātman* (self); because it is unimpeded like space, it is *sukha* (bliss). These two are combined.
Analogy:
The Buddhas are likewise; their merits are immeasurable.
[Wenju]: "The Buddhas are likewise" and below constitute the application of the analogy.
[Commentary] The second section consists of two parts: the words of ineffability and the praise.
[Textual Analysis] From the line "All sentient beings with minds" downward, there are three lines of words of ineffability. This text is divided into two parts:
first, one and a half lines which directly express the words of ineffability; second, one and a half lines which cite the analogy and apply it to the subject at hand.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation has two parts. First, the formal negation of speech and praise:
No one possessing a mind can know [this]; even if one were to contemplate it with the utmost mental effort throughout immeasurable eons, one could not know the limits of the Buddha’s merit.
[Text]: "All who possess a mind cannot know it; this is the severance of thought. Since thought is already severed, what can the mouth proclaim?
This is the severance of speech. [Commentary]:
The second part restates the analogy and applies it to the subject matter.
The great earth and its mountains may still be measured; the drops of the ocean waters may also be counted;
yet no one can know the merit of the Buddhas.
[Commentary: The repetition of the analogies and their application to the subject matter can be seen directly in the text.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the explanations in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra Commentary) concerning "words based on conventional expression" (*jīyán*) and "words beyond expression" (*juéyán*), are these both identical in being free from conceptual thought, or are they different?

Answer: The four virtues (*catur-guṇa*) are by nature secret and fundamentally transcend the objects of the mind. The present eulogies are intended to cause sentient beings to enter the secret treasury;

therefore, both "words based on conventional expression" and "words beyond expression" manifest the state of being free from discursive thought. As for "words based on conventional expression," four metaphors are employed to illustrate the four virtues.

Since these qualities cannot be enumerated, and since forgetting conditions transcends words—such that four things serve as metaphors for this—it also reveals the four virtues that forget objective consideration (*ālambana-vicāra*).
Because the Great Master profoundly understood the subtle purport of the scriptural text, he explained that both passages describe states beyond thought. Third, the summary.
[The text states: "May all beings attain such merits as the adornment of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), renown, and praise.

[Commentary on the *Wenju*]: From the phrase "adornment of the marks and signs" onwards, one line serves as a summary. "Marks" (*xiang*) summarizes all the primary marks; "signs" (*hao*) summarizes all the secondary signs.
"Adornment" (*zhuangyan*) means that within each individual mark and each individual sign, all manifold virtues are fully present.
This is for the purpose of adornment.
[Commentary] Regarding the four clarifications on making vows, the first part establishes the intent and divides the text.
[Wenju] From the passage "By means of my various causes and conditions of wholesome karma" onwards, there are fifty-one and a half verses.
The fourth is the practice of making vows (*praṇidhāna*). If there are no vows, it is like an ox without a driver that cannot reach its destination;
it is like a painting without glue, like unbaked clay, or like the moon reflected in water. Therefore, one sustains practice by means of vows;
this is also the repentance for the transgression of retreating. The text is divided into two parts: first, forty-seven and a half lines clarify the making of vows; next...

Regarding the four types of practice, the first concerns rejoicing in accordance with vows; this vow is further divided into two parts: first, nine lines of self-generated vows, and second, thirty-eight and a half lines of vows generated for the sake of others.
Within the self-generated vows, there are again two parts: first, four lines on the fulfillment of the fruit, and second, five lines on the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit.
Regarding the vow for the fulfillment of the fruit, there are four sections: first, one line on attaining the Buddha-way, which constitutes the wheel of intention (*āśaya-cakra*).
The fulfillment of one row for the teaching of the Dharma is the fulfillment of the wheel of speech; the fulfillment of one row for the subduing of Māra is the fulfillment of the wheel of body;
the fulfillment of one row for abiding long in life to benefit others is the fulfillment of compassion.

[Commentary]: It is like a cow without a driver, which refers to a mere cowherd boy. Now, whether one's established vows are many or few, they must not lose the intent of the Four Great Vows (Caturmahāpraṇidhāna).
Furthermore, these Four Great Vows must rely upon the Four Noble Truths (Catuḥsatya); a vow that does not rely on the Truths is called a "wild vow.

Here, we discuss them from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (Pūrṇa), relying on the Truth of Non-action (Anabhisaṃskāra-satya), even though there are two kinds of causes: mundane and supramundane.

When the fruits are all fully realized, they are identical to the nature; thus there is no suffering to be delivered from, no origin to be severed, no path to be cultivated, and no cessation to be realized.
If one can thus universally deliver, exhaustively sever, perfectly cultivate, and wondrously realize, then these vows are not merely "wild" as was the case with the three previous teachings.
If one loses this meaning while reciting the vows, one is not a practitioner of the Perfect Teaching. Second, following the text.
Explanation of the Meaning, Part Two: First, the Proper Clarification of Making Vows; Second, First, Making Vows by Oneself; First, Vowing for the Fulfillment of the Result;
Fourth, First, the Fulfillment of the Wheel of Intention:
"By means of the causal conditions of my wholesome karma, I shall before long accomplish the path of Buddhahood in a future life."
[Commentary: Because the Great Enlightenment is perfectly luminous, it belongs to the karma of the mind (*manas-karma*). Second, the wheel of speech is fulfilled:
by preaching and proclaiming the sublime Dharma, he benefits sentient beings and delivers them from all immeasurable sufferings.
[Commentary] The third vow fulfills the wheel of the body:
it subdues all Māras and their retinues, and turns the unsurpassed, pure wheel of Dharma.

[Commentary] Regarding the *skandha-mara* (the mara of the aggregates) and the *mṛtyu-devaputra* (the mara of death), these generally pertain to the afflictions of the body and belong to the mind; here, we follow the majority view. Fourth.
May his compassionate love be fulfilled.
May he abide for immeasurable and inconceivable kalpas, saturating sentient beings with the ambrosial flavor of the Dharma. [Commentary:
It is not that his compassionate love is without an object; his abiding for such a duration is likewise so. These two vows constitute the first part of the text concerning the perfection of causes.
[Text] Regarding the fulfillment of causes and vows, there are again four [sections]: first, one line on the fulfillment of the six perfections, which is the fulfillment of conditioned merits;

next, one line on the fulfillment of unconditioned merits; next, two lines on the fulfillment of recollecting the Buddha through past lives; and finally, one line on the fulfillment of encountering the Buddhas.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning has four parts. First, the fulfillment of conditioned merits:
"I shall fully accomplish the six *pāramitās*, just as they were achieved by the Buddhas of the past."

[Commentary: The perfection of the six *pāramitās* refers here to the true cause; because it overcomes the six obscurations and is the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) resulting from the correct discourse on abandonment, it is termed "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merit of vows is fulfilled.
Severing all afflictions and eliminating all suffering, one completely extinguishes greed, hatred, delusion, and the like.
[Commentary] This refers to the stage of true realization (*bhūmi*), wherein one manifests forms within the nine realms of existence to subdue sentient beings;

because one spontaneously and effortlessly remains unassociated with afflictions and suffering, this is the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, Master Haidong said that initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) effects this severance.

The "actual severance" (*shitsudan*) of hindrances is the severance by original enlightenment (*honkaku*); this is not a severance that involves cutting off, and its meaning is identical to the two virtues of wisdom and severance in our own school.
Third, the fulfillment of the vows, past lives, and *nenbutsu*.
I shall recollect my past lives— hundreds of births, thousands of births, hundreds of thousands of billions of births— and with constant sincerity and right mindfulness,
I shall always keep all Buddhas in mind as they preach the subtle, wondrous, and unsurpassed Dharma.
[Commentary] Because he recollects his past lives, he sees the Buddhas of the past and also remembers the True Dharma taught by those Buddhas.
Thus, the fourth vow—to meet the Buddhas—is fulfilled.
"By virtue of my wholesome karma, may I always encounter the Buddhas, remain far removed from all evils, and cultivate all wholesome deeds."
[Commentary] By means of past causes, one sees the future Buddhas, distances oneself from evil, cultivates goodness, and accomplishes the causes for wisdom and abandonment.
Second, making vows for others; this constitutes the first division of the text.

[Text] The vow-text for others consists of two parts. The first eight lines and a half are the vow to become the King of Medicine Trees (*bhaiṣajyavṛkṣarāja*), using great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to uproot suffering.
The subsequent thirty lines are the vow to become the King of Jewel Pearls (*maṇirājamaṇi*), using great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) to bestow happiness and uproot suffering.
Furthermore, this is divided into four sections: first, one line generally uproots all sufferings; next, one line uproots the suffering of impaired faculties; next...
The first two lines extract [beings] from the suffering of illness; the subsequent four and a half lines extract [them] from the suffering of royal calamities.
[Commentary: There are two explanations of the meaning. First, the vow to become a Medicine King to extract suffering; second, the vow to become a Jewel King to bestow happiness.

This ability to extract and this ability to bestow are the unconditioned (anālambana) compassion [of the Bodhisattva]. Regarding that which is extracted and that which is bestowed, one must discuss ten successive stages.

This refers to the retribution, the cultivation of causes, the Śrāvakas, the Pratyekabuddhas, the four teachings for Bodhisattvas, the provisional means (*upāya*), and the true retribution—these are the ten kinds of suffering of practitioners which this King of Medicine Trees now uproots.
As a King of Jewels, he should bestow happiness upon these ten kinds of people;
with this intention, one should interpret the text regarding "eradicating" and "bestowing. First, it is divided into four parts: first, the general eradication of all sufferings.
I shall completely extinguish all the immeasurable sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings in all worlds.
[Commentary] Second, uprooting the suffering of impaired faculties:
if there are sentient beings whose sense organs are ruined or incomplete, I shall cause them all to be complete.
[Commentary] Third, it eradicates the suffering of illness.

All those in the worlds of the ten directions who suffer from illness, weakness, exhaustion, or fatigue, and who have no one to protect them, are all caused to be liberated from such various sufferings;
they regain their strength and are restored to their former state.
[Commentary] Fourth, it removes the suffering of royal peril.
For those who have violated the king’s law and are about to face execution, filled with immeasurable fear, anxiety, and distress—such persons are all caused to be liberated.
Even if they are subjected to various forms of physical torment that oppress the body, such as flogging, binding, shackles, and fetters.
May all beings whose minds are disturbed by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sorrows, anxieties, alarms, fears, and various terrors—
by these and other such boundless sufferings and afflictions— attain complete liberation.
[Commentary] The second vow consists of two parts: first, becoming a king of jewels to bestow happiness; second, the analysis of the text.
[Textual Analysis] Bestowing happiness is further divided into three sections: first, sixteen and a half lines on bestowing the happiness of worldly fruits;
next, nine and a half lines on bestowing the happiness of supramundane causes; and finally, four lines that conclude the section.
[Commentary] Second, the detailed explanation of the three [aspects]. First, bestowing the fruit of worldly happiness:
if there are sentient beings afflicted by hunger and thirst, they are caused to obtain various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink;
the blind gain sight, the deaf gain hearing, the mute gain speech, the naked gain clothing, and those who are impoverished immediately obtain a treasure trove.
Their storehouses overflowed with nothing lacking; all experienced peace, security, and happiness, such that not even a single person suffered.
Living beings looked upon one another with harmonious and joyful countenances, their appearances dignified and handsome, pleasing to behold.
Their minds were constantly intent on the good deeds of others; they were satiated with food and drink, endowed with merit, and acted in accordance with the needs of all sentient beings.
Whatever they think of, may they all obtain various kinds of musical instruments—lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, lutes, and cymbals—as well as such subtle and exquisite sounds;
may rivers, ponds, pools, springs, and flowing waters be covered everywhere with golden lotuses and blue utpala flowers;
and according to the thoughts of sentient beings, may they immediately obtain various kinds of clothing and food and drink.
May all sentient beings not hear evil sounds, nor even encounter anything loathsome to behold.
May all sentient beings possess exquisite features and forms, and may they each regard one another with mutual love and affection.
May all the requisites for life in the world appear to them according to their thoughts.
May all sentient beings have their every wish fulfilled; whatever they seek, may they obtain exactly as required, just by thinking of it.
May trees of incense and flowers constantly rain down fine powdered incense and unguents for the body during the three periods of the day, so that those who receive them experience joy and happiness.
[Commentary on the Text]: In the preceding passage, Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) uproots suffering and causes those who lack the sense faculties to possess them;

now, Great Loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī) bestows happiness, such that their sight and hearing become clear and sharp, and they experience joy, pleasure, and the full functioning of all faculties. The phrasing regarding "bestowing" is identical to that of "uprooting," with only a slight difference in nuance.
[Commentary] The *Jīngǔchuī Gǔjīnzhù* states that it is a short *xiāo* (flute). "Saffron" (*utpala*) here refers to the indigo color, namely the blue lotus.
"Constantly at the three times" refers to the three periods of the day. This constitutes the first part of the text concerning the two causes for supramundane bliss.

[Text] From "May all sentient beings always obtain offerings" downward, nine lines and a half constitute two sections regarding the text on the bliss of the causes for transcending the world (*lokottara-hetu-sukha*).
The first three lines and a half cause [beings] to cultivate the completion of external conditions; the subsequent six lines cause them to cultivate the completion of internal causes.

Furthermore, within the external conditions, there are two parts: the first two lines concern encountering the Three Jewels, and the next one line and a half concern being free from the eight [difficulties].
Difficult.

[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the sequential explanation, there are two sections. First, regarding the fulfillment of external conditions for the cultivation of practice, the first is meeting the Triple Gem.
May all sentient beings always obtain offerings to the inconceivable, supreme, and wondrous Dharma of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The pure and stainless assembly, including the bodhisattvas and the great multitude of śrāvakas.
[Commentary: Second, being free from the eight difficulties.
May all sentient beings always remain far removed from the three evil realms and the eight difficulties, encounter places free from such hardships, and behold the Buddhas.
The Unsurpassed King. [Commentary:
The conditions of people differ; some encounter difficulties that are not removed, while others have their difficulties removed but do not encounter a Buddha.
Now, I pray that they may both have their difficulties removed and encounter a Buddha.
[Commentary] Second, regarding the causes for cultivation, there are two internal causes; this constitutes the first part of the text.

[Textual Analysis] Furthermore, these internal causes are twofold: first, five lines concerning being born into a noble family; second, five and a half lines concerning possessing abundant wealth and treasures.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation has two parts. First, being born into noble status:
"May all sentient beings always be born into noble status.
Second, possessing abundant wealth and treasures.
Abounding in wealth and treasures, secure, prosperous, and joyful, their bodies adorned with supreme and exquisite forms, they have accomplished meritorious virtues and possess great renown.
May all women become men, be endowed with wisdom, and practice with diligence and without slackening;
may they all walk the path of the Bodhisattva, diligently cultivate the six *pāramitās*, and constantly behold the ten directions.
Immeasurable Buddhas sit beneath jeweled trees upon lapis lazuli thrones, abiding in meditative concentration with sovereign bliss, expounding the True Dharma which all delight in hearing.

[Commentary on the Text] The causes for human beings differ: some possess great wealth yet are lowly and base, while others are noble and honorable yet are poor. This is due to their differing causes.
May she who is now fully endowed with these qualities be both noble and wealthy; may women, who possess five hindrances, be free from the suffering of those five hindrances.
[Commentary] Regarding the "five hindrances": first, not becoming a Brahma King; second, not becoming Śakra; third, not becoming a Wheel-Turning King; fourth, not becoming a Māra King;
fifth, not being able to become a Buddha. This concludes the three sections of the first part of the text.
[Text]: From "If I, in the present... downwards, four lines conclude the vows for both self and others;
the first two lines conclude those for oneself, and the latter two lines conclude those for others.
[Commentary] Regarding the two explanations of the sutra, first is the summary of one's own [vows]:
"Whatever evil karma I have committed in the present and past lives, and whatever perilous difficulties that ought to result in undesirable and evil fruits—
may they all be completely extinguished, leaving nothing remaining."
[Commentary] Second, binding others:
May all sentient beings, who are bound by the three realms of existence within the dense and firm net of birth and death, have their bonds severed and torn asunder by the sword of wisdom;
may they eliminate all suffering and affliction and quickly attain Bodhi.
[Commentary] Second, regarding rejoicing in accordance with vows, there are two parts;

first, the division of the text. [Text and Commentary] From "If in this Jambudvīpa... down to the fourth line, this section concerns rejoicing in accordance with vows. Rejoicing means to celebrate the cultivation of goodness by others;
it is also the repentance for the sin of envy. The text is divided into two parts: the first two lines concern rejoicing.
Regarding the latter two lines [of the verse], one rejoices in others and oneself.
[Commentary] There are two expositions of the sūtra; first, rejoicing in others:
if all the various deeds performed by sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa and in immeasurable other worlds...
I now rejoice with a profound heart in these excellent and sublime merits.
[Commentary] Second, rejoicing for oneself:
"By means of these merits of rejoicing, as well as the wholesome karma performed by my body, speech, and mind, I vow that in future lives..."
One accomplishes the unsurpassed path and attains the auspicious fruit of purity free from defilement.
[Commentary] The five summaries form two parts; this is the first part.
[Textual Analysis] From the verse beginning "If there is one who pays homage" below, there are nine lines of verse; this constitutes the fifth summary, which is divided into three sections.
The first two lines conclude by establishing the severance of evil, hence it is said that one transcends the sins of sixty kalpas;
the next four and a half lines conclude by establishing the production of goodness, hence it is said that one is revered by kings and great ministers;
the final two and a half lines conclude by establishing the meeting with Buddhas—though good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are not mentioned separately, the Buddhas themselves encompass them.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the sutra in three parts; first, the conclusion regarding the severance of evil.

If one reverently bows to and praises the One of Ten Powers with pure faith free from the net of doubt, and is able to perform such repentance as described here, one shall immediately transcend the offenses of sixty kalpas.
[Commentary] Second, establishing the birth of wholesome qualities:
If there are good sons and good daughters, or kings, Kṣatriyas, Brahmins, and others,
who with reverence join their palms toward the Buddha, extol the Tathāgata, and praise these verses, they will constantly remember their past lives in every place where they are born.
With all sense faculties complete, pure, and dignified, having fully accomplished all manner of meritorious qualities,
they are at all times and in every place revered by kings, ministers, and high officials.
[Commentary] Those with three fetters who encounter a Buddha are many;
it is not the case that one encounters only one, five, or ten Buddhas to plant various roots of merit and hear this repentance.

Rather, it is only after planting various roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of Tathāgatas that one is finally able to hear this repentance.
[Commentary] Part Three: The Chapter on Praise, which gives rise to goodness. First, the title of the chapter:
*The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Four: The Chapter on Praise*.

[Commentary] The phrasing and text are divided into two parts. First, a general explanation according to the meaning. Second, first, showing the intent of the four *siddhāntas*. First, the enumeration.
[Text] There are four meanings for praise: first, from the person who praises; second, from the production of goodness; third, from the eradication of evil;

Thus, based on the realization of principle and the arising of function, these two aspects of cultivation correspond to the single nature; the essence itself is named the Honored One Golden Dragon (Jinlongzun).

These four are the virtues of the three bodies; because the three bodies are fused, these four virtues universally adorn them. Therefore, the three bodies are none other than the four virtues.

Because the supreme distinction is revealed through the principle of identity-in-difference, the objective realm alone universally encompasses all; those who attain the subsequent stages necessarily attain the preceding ones, while those who attain the preceding ones do not attain the subsequent ones, for they do not know what lies beyond.

Because they do not know that it is manifested by the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses), they see it as coming from the outside; they grasp at its physical dimensions and cannot know it exhaustively."

The second is based on the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*). This refers to that which is perceived by all Bodhisattvas from their initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*) up to the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva;

this is called the *reward body* (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). This body possesses immeasurable colors, each color possesses immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and each mark possesses immeasurable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).
Furthermore, the resultant environment upon which it rests is likewise immeasurable, adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
That which manifests according to what is shown is without limit and inexhaustible, free from the characteristics of spatial boundaries;
as appropriate to each case, it is able to constantly maintain itself without being destroyed or lost.

This is accomplished through the perfuming of the untainted practices of the various *pāramitās* and the inconceivable perfuming. This characteristic of experiencing bliss is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body). (End of text) This.

Thus, the Tathāgata, through the functioning of the *dharmadhātu*, manifests the two bodies—the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*—in accordance with the activities of sentient beings' two consciousnesses.
The *nirmāṇakāya* is the body born in this life; the *saṃbhogakāya* is the present "exalted special" (*viśiṣṭa*) body and the *dharmatākāya*.

For those who rely on the *vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of phenomena), they see only the *nirmāṇakāya* and cannot perceive the *saṃbhogakāya*, because their consciousness is coarse and shallow, failing to fathom the profound, and because it relies upon karma.

Since those who possess discernment have already beheld the *saṃbhogakāya*, they are likewise able to see the *nirmāṇakāya*; one should know that this is because True Suchness (*tathatā*) gives rise to two functions.
A practitioner should understand that the manifestation of the Buddha’s bodily marks and signs through the function of True Suchness comprises three grades:

first, as discussed in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the number of marks and signs is equal to the atoms within ten lotus-receptacle worlds; second, as in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (The Visualization of Infinite Life); [and third, as in the *Amitābha-dhyāna-sūtra*].
The Buddha’s sūtras clarify that there are eighty-four thousand marks and signs (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) of radiance;
yet, as explained in this sūtra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, and others, there are thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs.

Since these three sets of marks are the functional manifestation of the entire substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*), whether they are many or few, they are all boundless. Therefore, they are all called "oceans," and none are not venerable.

There is a distinct differentiation between the universal and the particular for the purpose of containing the eighty thousand [dharmas]. The particular refers to the perception of the *karma-vijñāna*, while the universal refers to the perception of the *vastu-vijñāna*.

The marks consist of the thirty-two [major characteristics]. Using the Venerable Golden Dragon to praise the Buddha’s four virtues as subtle, wondrous, and tranquil extinction serves as a general eulogy;

Each individual mark transcends all boundaries, being as boundless as space, eternally abiding and indestructible. Based on this commentary, it is explained that the three bodies (trikāya) are fused and identical.

If one does not know how to specifically praise the *zhuntè* (distinctive marks), one should offer a general praise to the Dragon Honored One (*Nāgarāja*). This is based on the vision of the *karmic consciousness*;
