In the *Commentary on the Buddha Abiding in the Middle Way*, there are six sections that clarify how the manifested and transformational bodies (*nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*) and the sublime physical marks (*vairocanakāya*) are all distinguished based on the resonance and response between the True and the Middle.
As the scriptural text of the *Sūtra Praising the Buddha* from the *Lotus Sūtra* explicitly states:

"Because the Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, it adorns the Dharma-body. Thus, these are the sublime marks of the Honored One. For this reason, Jingxi [Zhiyi] classifies them as being identical to those in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The names of the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics are without discrepancy; furthermore, in the "Chapter on Repentance," there is praise for the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.

thus, the adornments of these marks are also divided into three types. There are differences in the relative superiority and inferiority of the power and function of these three bodies.

[Commentary] Lumbinī is translated here as "Place of Liberation.

Regarding "raising her hand to grasp the tree," this refers to Lady Māyā grasping an *aśoka* tree, from whose right side the Prince was born. Ārya, also known as Asita, is translated as "Incomparable Sage";

"Observing the marks of the Prince, they are so brilliantly clear that it is certain he will become a Buddha and not a Wheel-Turning King.

Although there was no sound, tears emerged of their own accord—this is what is meant by "weeping. Here, "unable to weep for grief" refers to this very act of weeping. This is the birth-body (*janma-kāya*).

Although the commentary (*śāstra*) introduces this by stating that the body born of one's parents must be understood in its true meaning, how could the latter two bodies be entirely devoid of parents?
The reason for specifying this particular case is to demonstrate that the Buddhas of the *zàng* (Āgama) and *tōng* (Vaipulya) vehicles abide in partial truth (*pradeśasatya*).

Because the principle of partial truth does not encompass the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it causes the Buddha-body to be constructed from both fundamental afflictions and residual habits (*vāsanā*) in response to the conditions of sentient beings. If these conditions were exhausted, [the body] would be reduced to ashes and perish.

Because emptiness is eternally without manifestation, it is revealed through the parents to show that there is the mechanism of birth; because all things ultimately return to emptiness, it is revealed to show that there is cessation.
Although they are universally illusory existences, one must also maintain eternal non-existence; thus, according to the teachings, one should distinguish their characteristics.
Second, the distinctive marks of Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Text and Commentary: As stated in the *Śāstra*, the body of the Buddha with distinctive marks (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is majestic and imposing, like Mount Sumeru towering over the great ocean;
all his major and minor marks are likewise majestic and imposing, differing from his ordinary body and ordinary radiance.
This "constant appearance" is precisely the mark of the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* (extraordinary) body of the Buddha.

[Commentary] "Majestic" means lofty; "dignified" means luminous. To speak of it as "venerable, sublime, and extraordinary" refers to the body perceived by those with the capacities of the Separate and Perfect Teachings (*bhedavāda* and *pariniṣpanna-yāna*).
As for the "constant body and constant light," these refer to the bodies perceived by ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). However...
The High and Wise One should understand that regarding the two aspects of the body’s manifestation, there are cases where it must manifest and cases where it need not manifest;

these are all due to the Tathāgata’s power of discerning the capacities of beings and advancing them along the Middle Way. As for those instances where manifestation is required, he manifests accordingly, as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:

"Just as when sitting upon the lotus pedestal," and as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the marks of the dust-motes within the Flower Treasury World, and in the *Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra* regarding the body.
Just as Mount Sumeru is reflected in the great ocean, so too are the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of Amitāyus; his body is eighty thousand *yojanas* in measure and boundless.
All such qualities are the manifestation of the sublime, extraordinary marks (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). There are, however, those that need not be manifested;
rather, by the application of power, they cause even inferior bodies to appear without limit, making them majestic and dignified, understood through the inconceivable.

Yet, when observing this as it is now praised in this sutra—the thirty-two marks as the sovereign, extraordinary *dharmatā-kāya*—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the *dharmakāya* is adorned with the thirty-two marks, each of which is equal in measure to empty space.
Such karmic conditions are all seen through the *karma-vijñāna*; when observed with middling wisdom, the inferior [perception] is that these are boundless forms.
Because it is the nature of wisdom (*jñānatva*), there is no need for it to manifest [as a physical form] for it to be called the *zhunti* (Sanskrit: *vairocana*, "Universal Radiance");

otherwise, how would one reconcile the passage from the *Longzun suozan sanshierxiang shu* (Commentary on the Thirty-two Marks Praised by the Dragon King) which says, "The three [aspects] are fused to praise the *zhunti*"?
Students should understand this well. Third, the explanation of the characteristics of the *dharmatā*.
[Text] As for the Buddha of the Dharma-nature Body (dharmatā-kāya), he cannot be seen by ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, or those on the lower stages;
he is seen only by those who are to be delivered. This is the body that is no-body, the mark that is no-mark.
All-knowledge is his head; the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is his topknot; the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates are his hair; and great compassion is his eye.
The white path is his flawless nose; the eighteen emptinesses are his tongue; the forty unique qualities are his teeth; the four great vows are his shoulders;
the three samādhis are his waist; the Tathāgatagarbha is his abdomen; the provisional and ultimate wisdoms are his hands; and meditative concentration and wisdom are his feet.
It is the Buddha of the Dharma-nature body who is adorned with such characteristics as these.

[Commentary]: This is the body of the wisdom-mark of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of all Buddhas; even ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not know its name, so how could they behold it?
As for its ultimate realization, even the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) cannot fathom it.
Furthermore, because those on the first ground do not know the second ground, the tree deity wept and, shedding tears, entreated the Buddha to manifest his body—this very body is that one.
"All are named as not being the vision of the lower stages; they should only be delivered, etc. This refers to the Mahāyāna *paramārtha-siddhānta*.

When sentient beings with such capacities encounter the Buddha, he responds to them with this very body, causing them to see it. This corresponds to the meaning of "simultaneity" explained previously in the commentary:
the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) and the Middle Truth are simultaneous. "Without a body," etc., does not mean... [text ends].
The obstructive body is the subtle and wondrous body; non-differentiation is the mark of the purity of wisdom.

Because all-knowledge is the head of the myriad practices, it is taken as the head. Because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the foremost among the ten supreme qualities of all dharmas, it is taken as the topknot.
The eighty thousand afflictions transformed into Dharma-gates constitute the numerous and abundant hair. Great compassion is the eye, which perceives suffering immediately.
The white hair between the brows (*ūrṇā-kośa*) is impartial and unstained, being untainted (*anāsrava*); this constitutes the merit of the nose smelling fragrances.
The tongue universally tastes the flavor of principle through the eighteen emptinesses (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*); being unshared, these constitute the forty teeth.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the eighteen unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), great compassion (*karuṇā*), and the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) constitute these forty.
Because these are not shared with the lower stages, the Four Great Vows serve as the shoulders that bear the burden without ceasing.
The three samādhis restrain distraction like a waist-belt binding a garment. These three samādhis are simply the Three Contemplations: emptiness is the contemplation of emptiness;

signlessness is the contemplation of the provisional, for one does not grasp at the marks of emptiness; and wishlessness is the contemplation of the Middle, for one makes no vows regarding the two extremes.
Because it seeks [the ultimate], the Tathāgatagarbha contains the three thousand worlds within its belly; with the hands of provisional and ultimate wisdom, it universally uproots sentient beings;
with the feet of samādhi and prajñā, it thoroughly treads upon the ground of reality. Now, this third body differs slightly from the enumerations found elsewhere;

as the *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states: "The meaning of the body of form-characteristics corresponds to the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the enjoyment-body for others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*)."

Using the same [principle], the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the next; the various Dharma-gate bodies listed here correspond in meaning to the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is the body for self-enjoyment.
Third is the Reality-mark Body (*dharmatākāya*), which takes the principle adorned by these Dharma-gates as the third body.
Now, the two bodies of Principle and Wisdom are combined into the Dharma-nature Body (*dharmadhātukāya*), while that Response Body is opened up [into its distinct forms].
As for the physical body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the sublime special body (*vairocanakāya*), they mutually involve opening and closing; yet the three bodies (*trikāya*) remain undiminished.
Furthermore, one should know that the present Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*) and its associated dharma-gates are precisely the characteristics praised by the Dragon Honored One.
Because mind is form, it is called the former two bodies; because form is mind, it is called a dharma-gate. However, this is now analyzed according to the successive teachings.

Because the gates [of perception] accord with what is seen according to one's capacity, one does not see what lies beyond; thus, subsequent names are established based on superiority, causing the three bodies to appear as having a hierarchy of excellence.
Furthermore, both the *vairocana* (exalted) body and the *dharmatā* body are visions of *karmic-consciousness*.
Because the *vairocana* body incorporates distinct cultivated practices, it is manifested now through the vast and lofty physical characteristics of the *dharmatā* Buddha.

Because cultivation is identical to nature (*dharmatā*), the characteristics of form are concealed; thus, this is explained from the perspective of the Dharma-gate. Both teacher and student should be diligent and discerning in this regard.

Third, the explanation of the three types of activity (*karma*) of the three marks: these are distinguished as three kinds because, when the Tathāgata purifies his Buddha-field, he manifests various levels of cultivation according to the specific capacities and conditions of sentient beings.
First is the activity of the consciousness-born body (*vijñāna-ja-deha-karma*).

[Text]: Regarding the karma of the marks and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana-karman*), as explained in the *Śāstra*: one hundred merits (*puṇya*) produce one mark, and three thousand two hundred merits produce the thirty-two marks;
this is the meaning of the "marks and characteristics" of the birth-body Buddha (*janma-deha-buddha*).

[Commentary] Although this applies to the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao), it is currently treated here according to the Tripiṭaka (San-tsang), because the Shared Teaching is a gateway to the Mahāyāna and those of sharp faculties can perceive the latter two Buddhas.
Thus, we now take the practice of the *pāramitās* within the Tripiṭaka as the cause for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

Regarding the statement that "one hundred merits produce one mark," various interpretations exist in the treatises; here, we clarify one type: [the merit derived from] the sentient beings of a great trichiliocosm.
Whenever one encounters conditions for death, if one rescues each and every being so that they all obtain long life, this constitutes the first merit.

This merit must reach a hundredfold before it completes a single mark. This refers to the subduing of afflictions through the practice of the *pāramitās*, causing those sentient beings to emulate this by practicing it themselves;
thus, the physical body is now visible. Second is the distinctive karma of the World-Honored One.

[Text]: "If one guides all activities of form with the wisdom of emptiness, so that each and every activity is entirely in accord with emptiness—among all such accords, accord with emptiness is supreme.
This is the meaning of the marks of the Buddha’s *viśvabimba* (distinctive) body."
[Commentary] Regarding the "wisdom of emptiness," it refers to the wisdom that realizes the very substance of phenomena is empty; this is cultivated by all three teachings.
Those of dull faculties are only able to empty existence, whereas those of superior capacity know that emptiness is not merely the emptying of existence, but can also empty emptiness itself.

Here, in the context of the *fenbie men* (Gate of Distinction), although the *zunte* (Distinctive/Universal) practice is able to empty both, it remains within the wisdom of the "middle" of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
It guides all marks and activities; since all activities do not transcend the aforementioned six perfections, they are known through the middle way. This is not mere adornment;
rather, it is the adornment that can adorn the essence of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), causing those sentient beings to emulate this by cultivating the seeds [of merit].
Now, one beholds the Honored One’s sublime and boundless body. Third, the explanation of the activity of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
[Text]: If one accomplishes all karmas by guiding them with the wisdom of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), then every single karma is none other than the dharma-realm of the true mark;
this is the meaning of the characteristics of the seed of the Dharma-nature body Buddha (dharmatā-kāya-buddha).
[Commentary] "True Reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the Middle Way. Taking the entirety of the Middle and True Principle as the wisdom that contemplates it is called "wisdom of true reality";
thus, true reality is itself wisdom. It is not that there is a separate wisdom which, by virtue of what it illuminates, receives the name "true reality.

Regarding "leading to the accomplishment of all karmas": how could these karmas be apart from the aforementioned six perfections? Because they are practiced in their totality, each one is [the perfection].
Because it is the nature [of all things], there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*); because it subsumes all within one, there is nothing that is not the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, Saṃjñeya said: "Abiding in the suchness of the nature of all phenomena, one embraces all phenomena within all phenomena.
To cultivate in this manner, severing the attachments of the three teachings, is called "inconceivable activity" (*acintyakarman*). It causes those sentient beings to emulate this cultivation.

Now, the Dharma-body Buddha seen here is identical to the characteristic of empty space. Second, based on the principle of perfect interfusion, there are three [points], the first of which is the primary interfusion.

[Commentary on the Text]: The three bodies, the three types of characteristics, and the three types of karmic activities cannot be categorized as either vertical/horizontal, simultaneous/distinct, or identical/different.

If they were any of these, they would not be pure; they would not be subtle, wondrous, and quiescent. Because they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct, they are absolute.
"Every word praises that which is beyond reach.
[Commentary] The Perfect Buddha’s sudden realization of the three bodies (*trikāya*) and three marks (*trilakṣaṇa*) can also suddenly manifest the three kinds of cultivated marks.
If this perfect capacity functions within a single thought-moment to cultivate the karma of the three marks, one is able to perceive the three bodies and three marks within a single body.

Because one realizes that the three bodies are the secret treasury, the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) necessarily possesses the *dharmatā-saṃbhogakāya*, and the *dharmatā-saṃbhogakāya* necessarily possesses the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).
Since this is the case for the visible bodies, it is likewise for the cultivated practices (*karmayoga*).
In this way, one may finally eliminate the conceptual attachments to "vertical" and "horizontal," or "identity" and "difference. [The qualities of] permanence, bliss, self, and purity are subtle.
The meaning of "wondrous quiescence" is thus established. In the past, the Honored King of the Golden Dragon was a person of the Perfect Teaching (*enjin*), who practiced and realized all at once;
therefore, he praised the three bodies within a single body. This was intended to manifest that the three aspects constitute the secret treasury.
By first praising through words and then transcending words, he sought to cause sentient beings to realize and practice the Perfect Teaching. Second, the clarification of skillfulness.
Praise.

[Commentary on the Text]: This sutra primarily praises the marks and signs of the *vairocana-kāya* (body of universal radiance), while incidentally including the *dharmatā-kāya* (dharma-nature body) above and encompassing the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body) below;
it elucidates these from a central perspective. Such is the skillfulness of the true praiser, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the eulogistic phrases of the Sūtra, these thirty-two marks demonstrate the transcendence of words; they reveal that which is able to adorn—that which is "not-adornment.
Is it not so that this adorns the primary essence, the marks of the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of sublime characteristics)?

It may also be said that it is neither born nor a phenomenon (*dharma*), yet it is born and is a phenomenon. Above, it encompasses the *dharmatā*; below, it subsumes the *nirmāṇakāya* (the body of birth). The intended meaning lies herein.
This is the intent behind the Dragon Honored One’s skillful praise.
Regarding the wondrous function of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividya*): [Textual Commentary] Each and every mark clarifies its function;
for instance, the mark of the level soles of the feet means that no demonic or heterodox forces can cause it to waver, no existence or non-existence can move it, and no extremes can shake it.

Regarding the Dharma of the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head: it neither bows to ordinary people, nor does it bow to sages, nor does it bow to those who have attained partial realization, and so forth.

[Commentary] The three marks and three karmas, when viewed according to their perfect aspect (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*), are manifested as differentiated for sentient beings; yet when analyzed according to the various teachings (*śāsana*), they are integrated and non-dual.

Furthermore, regarding the initial "peaceful and stable" marks that constitute the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), these signify being unmoved by Māra and by the heterodox. "Māra" refers to the delusion of craving (*tṛṣṇā-moha*), while "the heterodox" refers to the delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-moha*).

Since [the practitioner] abides in the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), these two cannot move him. If it concerns the *vairocana* (Universal) Buddha who dwells doubly within the conventional, this refers to the immeasurable Four Truths;
thus, ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles lack these two [truths], and so they cannot move him. If it concerns the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)...
The Buddha dwells solely in the Middle Way; within the three teachings of heterodox outsiders, all dualistic extremes are, in their very place, the Middle. How could any extreme move him?
Finally, because his fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) and the invisible crown of his head cannot be seen, he is represented by the fact that [the Dharma] does not pay homage to him.

To say that "the Dharma does not pay homage" means it is the nature of things (*dharmatā*); for the physical body has emerged beyond both craving and views, and thus, as the nature of things, it does not [pay homage].

Regarding the ritual of paying homage: for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), it is naturally the case that they do not pay homage to the two types of *dharmas*—the "dust-like" phenomena within and beyond the realm of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*)—even though these are honored as preeminent.

For the sages of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* vehicles, whose bodies are the *dharmatā-kāya*, and for the Buddhas of the ultimate, perfect, and central [teaching], it is naturally the case that they do not pay homage [to each other].

Since this is so for the initial and final stages, the application of the thirty characteristics of the middle stage can be understood accordingly; yet, even so, one does not pay homage to ordinary persons.

The Sage speaks by way of both cause and effect, rather than focusing exclusively on the fruit. The references to "separate sources" and the subsequent notes "and so forth" point to the various extensive texts that explain the excellent characteristics.
[Record] Second, the explanation of the meaning based on the sutra, in six parts: first, the praise; second, the seven great oceans of marks.
Among all forms, his form is the most supreme, radiant with the glow of gold; among all sounds, the Buddha’s voice is the most excellent, like the deep and distant thunder of Great Brahmā.
His hair is dark blue-black, curling to the right with a fiery luster; even the color of bees, emeralds, or peacock feathers cannot serve as a metaphor for it.
His teeth are brilliant white, like white jade or snow, clearly manifesting his golden countenance with distinct definition; his eyes are long and wide.
Pure and stainless like a blue lotus blooming in the water, his tongue is broad and long, its color crimson and radiant,
shining with light like a flower newly born; between his eyebrows is a tuft of hair, white as a conch or the moon,
curling to the right and lustrous as pure lapis lazuli.
[Commentary] The thirty-two major marks constitute the "great," and the eighty minor marks constitute the "small.

Since each individual mark and excellence is the Dharma-realm, boundless and bottomless, they are called "oceans. Specifically, the first phrase praises the fourteenth [mark], the subtle and wondrous golden light;
hence it says, "superior color. The next phrase praises the fifteenth [mark], the bodily radiance. The following three lines offer praise.
28. Brahma-voice, deep and far-reaching. (4) One line of praise. 79th among the secondary marks:
Hair color like blue beads. (5) One line of praise. 22nd: Possession of forty teeth.
(6) One line of praise. 29th: Eyes. (7) One line of praise. 27th: Tongue large and thin, covering the face up to the hairline.
In these eight sections, one praises the thirty-one minor marks, beginning with the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows;
among these, one is a minor mark and seven are major marks. Second, there is the praise of two minor marks as oceans.
His eyebrows are fine, long, and arched, shaped like the crescent moon; their color is a lustrous black, surpassing that of a king of bees.
His nose is high, round, and straight, like a cast gold ingot; it is exquisitely delicate and soft, positioned at the center of his face.
[Commentary] The first line praises the third [mark]: the eyebrows are like the crescent moon. The second line praises the second [mark]:
the nose is high and beautiful, with no visible nostrils; "xiūyáng" (修揚) means long and raised—that is, the eyebrows are both high and long.
"Miànmen" (面門) refers to the mouth. Thus, three times he praises the ocean of the great marks.
The Tathāgata’s supreme marks are sequential and most excellent.
[Commentary: Since it says they are "sequential and most excellent," this refers to a comprehensive praise of all thirty-two marks. Furthermore, he praises the ocean of the four great marks.
Attaining a flavor that is truly authentic and peerless; from each and every pore, a single hair grows in a clockwise curl, soft, fine, and deep blue like the neck of a peacock.

At the very moment of birth, his body emits a great light that universally illumines immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions, extinguishing all sufferings within the three realms and causing all sentient beings—including those in the hells and the animal realm—to experience complete happiness.
Furthermore, hungry ghosts, humans, devas, and others were all at peace and free from affliction; all immeasurable evil realms were extinguished.
His physical form was subtle and exquisite like a mass of molten gold, his countenance pure and clear like the full moon, and his body radiant like the rising sun.
His deportment and majestic bearing were like those of a lion; his long arms hung down, reaching past his knees when standing.
Just as the wind moves the branches of the *sāla* tree, his halo extends one fathom and can illuminate the immeasurable;
like the gathering of hundreds of thousands of suns and moons, the Buddha’s body is pure and wondrous, free from all defilement. Its radiance shines universally upon all buddha-fields;
the Buddha’s light is majestic, its brilliant flames so intense that they completely eclipse the light of immeasurable suns and moons, acting as a lamp for the sun of the Buddhas.

Illuminating immeasurable realms, causing all sentient beings to follow the light and see the Buddha’s body, which is adorned by the accumulated merit of hundreds of thousands of karmic practices cultivated in the past.

[Commentary] The first two phrases praise the twenty-sixth [quality]: that the saliva in the throat obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors. (24) The second and fourth [phrases]... [text fragment].
The thirteen hairs on the head are upward-pointing, blue-black in color, soft, and curl to the right; this is praised in four verses. The three arms extend downward, reaching the knees;

this is praised in four verses. The ninth [mark] is the standing hand reaching the knee; this is praised in four verses. The four [marks] include the halo extending one *vyāma*; this is praised in four verses.
The fifteenth [mark] is the bodily radiance, each side of the face being one *zhang* (丈) wide; this statement of "one *vyāma*" is made in reference to the Buddha. Since the hand already reaches...
The knees are each one *zhang* from face to face. Since this is verified as the constant radiance (*nitya-prabhā*), it is known that all the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise constant marks.
Thus, when praising the "Exalted Form" (*vairocana-rūpa*), one should know that it does not require a large body or numerous marks;

rather, when the consciousness of karma (*karma-vijñāna*) perceives the Middle Principle (*madhyama-tattva*), this is precisely what is called the "Exalted Form. Students should understand that if one were to measure this body of one *zhang* and six *chi*:
Thus, one does not perceive a boundary, nor is there any transition; what is seen remains as it was before, like the pure room of Vimalakīrti.

Although that room is but ten feet square, it can accommodate hundreds of thousands of gods and humans, and can also hold thirty-two thousand lion thrones, each eighty-four thousand yojanas high. Yet, from the very beginning, its measurement has undergone no change whatsoever.
It is by means of the inconceivable power of the three liberations that this is made so; thus, when one now praises the marks of the exalted body as being eternal, is it not indeed so?
That they are subtle, wondrous, and quiescent—this statement is validated.

Apart from these four great marks, the sutra text may further praise the causes of his deeds, such as emitting light to uproot suffering and bestow joy, as well as the fruits of his merit; all are as described.
The sutra text requires that all [the marks] be explained through tenfold benefits;

as for two minor marks, because they are evident in the text, the commentary does not specifically point them out—namely, "the face is like the moon," which refers to the fortieth mark, the purity of the face being like the full moon, and "the body is free from impurities," which refers to the eleventh mark, the cleanliness of the body.
Fifth, it further praises one minor mark: the ocean-like [mark].
The arms are slender, round, and straight like the trunk of an elephant king.

[Commentary] This refers to the fourteenth mark, that the fingers are long, slender, and round. "Yōng" (傭) is pronounced as chǒu xiōng (丑凶) in the sense of being even or straight; it is also pronounced yóng (容).
This concludes the second set of six further praises regarding the ocean of the two great marks.
The hands and feet are supple and sensitive, inspiring love and respect without weariness.
[Commentary] This refers to the fourth mark: "The hands and feet are soft and supple, surpassing other parts of the body.

The thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics are fully detailed in the *Fajie Cidi* (Successive Order of the Dharma Realm) and the *Longzun Zhiqu* (Wisdom Skill of the Dragon Honored One); although brief here, they are comprehensive. The three repetitions are analogous.
I praise them.
The Buddhas of the past and future are as numerous as motes of dust, and the Buddhas of the present are likewise so.
To all such Tathāgatas, I now prostrate with body, speech, and mind purified. With excellent incense and flowers, I make offerings and present them.
[They] praise, eulogize, sing, and extol with hundreds of thousands of merits.
[Wenju: From the passage "the Buddhas of the past and future" onwards is the third section, which universally classifies and praises the Buddhas' Dharma-body as equal, with one mind and one wisdom;
the same applies to their response and transformation bodies. Specifically, it takes one Buddha and one mark as the starting point for praise, applying it universally.
The passage "the Buddhas are likewise all thus" refers to the meaning expressed in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which states:
"The merit of recollecting the virtues of a single Buddha is equal to that of all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Regarding the phrase "purity of body and speech," there are two interpretations:

first, it means that the three karmas (*trikarma*) of the one being praised are pure, and I now pay homage to them all; second, it means that the one who praises is pure by virtue of [the purity of the object].
Exquisite flowers and incense represent the purity of the body; making these offerings represents the purity of the mind; and singing hymns represents the purity of speech, and so forth. [Commentary:
Although the dust-motes of the three periods of time are infinite, they are spoken of as "one. This is because the past does not perish, the future does not arise, and the present does not abide.
The Dharma-body is equal, and the retributive and responsive bodies are without difference. One is not separate from the many, and the many are precisely one. Thus, birth is non-arising.
Since the Buddha is already the Buddha, how could he be different from the Buddha? Therefore, praising one category [of Buddhas] is to praise all.
This passage further praises the *viśiṣṭa-kāya* (the distinguished or special body). Why is this? As stated previously in the commentary:

"If one sees the four Buddhas as identical to the *viśiṣṭa-kāya*, with a single body and a single wisdom, this is the eternal body; for the assembly of disciples is one. If the four Buddhas were not identical..."
Because these transformed disciples are numerous, we know that the "exalted special marks" (zūntè xiàng) refer solely to the meaning of a single body, a single wisdom, and eternal abiding;
it is not necessary to discuss the manifestation of a vast physical form. As for the title *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā*, the character "wèn" (ask) is an error;

[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the title; second, the demonstration of what is expressed by means of emptiness according to the four teachings.

"Emptiness" (śūnyatā) takes the deconstruction of characteristics as its meaning; therefore, within the teachings of a single lifetime, the four types of emptiness differ. If one does not discern them, one will be deluded by the names and obscure the principle.

This section is divided into two parts: first, listing the four [types of emptiness] according to their respective sections; second, the formal judgment of the four emptinesses. Regarding the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the actual classification of the four emptinesses.
[Text] Now, emptiness should be understood as having four kinds: first, entering emptiness by extinguishing form, whereby form itself is emptiness;

[Commentary] "Entering emptiness by extinguishing form" refers to the Tripiṭaka Teaching (*Tripiṭaka-yāna*). For the time being, speaking in terms of form, it means that all dharmas are extinguished.
To analyze and shatter the aggregates of views and craving so that they do not arise is the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* (the Shared Teaching);

having first explained that there is real extinction, one then enters emptiness. "Form itself is emptiness" refers to the Shared Teaching; because it realizes that cause and effect are not produced by the four modes of being (*catuskoṭi*), and since it explains that they are illusory existences, form itself is emptiness.
"Entering emptiness through the cessation of extremes" refers to the Distinct Teaching; here, the Middle Way constitutes emptiness, and it is not merely...
Both emptiness and existence are themselves empty and void; one does not realize that within this [emptiness] both emptiness and existence are contained.

Therefore, only after sequentially extinguishing these two extremes does one enter the emptiness of the middle. That which is "the extremes are themselves emptiness" is the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

When the qualities of virtue are complete within the Middle Way, what extreme is not itself the Middle? Only provisional and only empty—these three are all beyond dependence. To suddenly shatter all marks is called "immediacy" (ji).

[Commentary] The three kinds of *prajñā*—the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and letters (*vyañjana*)—are one in their threefold nature; thus, being a single dharma, they are established as three within that oneness.

Regarding the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), because those of dull faculties did not previously realize it, this present chapter fully expounds the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) to guide their prior repentance and praise, thereby accomplishing these two functions. [Text] It is also that which guides and accomplishes the function, the essence, and so forth.

it is only through non-attainment (*anupalambha*) that one realizes the three bodies (*trikāya*). If it were not ultimately empty, how could there be non-attainment? Therefore, perfect emptiness (*paripūrṇa-śūnyatā*) guides.
Regarding the realization of the fruit-virtues through myriad practices, that which constitutes the fundamental substance is the profound and vast *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) pervading all phenomena;

because of these two kinds of "self," birth and death are vast and chaotic. Now, by means of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), all phenomena are guided to manifest and establish the essence of the sūtra.
Second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
[Text] Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: "If it were not for this emptiness, nothing whatsoever could be accomplished or established as superior;

This is the meaning of the statement: "All sentient beings are Prajñā. Those of sharp faculties understand this immediately upon hearing the above.

[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation, there are two sections. First, the intention to explain emptiness:
Since emptiness has already been extensively explained in countless other sutras, it is explained here in brief.

Because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and their wisdom is meager, they are unable to fully comprehend the infinite meaning of emptiness; therefore, this honored sutra explains it concisely.
Through various causes and conditions involving diverse and wondrous skillful means, I have given rise to great compassion for those of dull faculties;
I now expound this sublime sūtra according to my own understanding and in accordance with what I know of the inclinations of sentient beings.

[Commentary] The text has two parts; first, the explanation of the eight [aspects]. First, the explanation of what is extensively taught in other sutras. This consists of two parts: first, a general indication of the characteristics to clarify the intent. [Wenju]:

[Text] If it refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, then this sutra would not be included within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) category. If it does not refer to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, then how is it that other sutras do not extensively clarify the meaning of emptiness? This being so, what is the case here?

[Commentary] The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "From fresh butter (*navanīta*) comes matured butter (*ghṛta*)," which serves as an analogy for how the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* emerges from the Vaipulya [sūtras].
Thus, one knows that the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* follows after the Vaipulya. Since this sūtra belongs to the Vaipulya category, how could it point to the *Prajñā[pāramitā]* as having already been taught?
Second, regarding the answer given at the conclusion of the latter section, there are two parts: first, the direct answer; second, the general response. First... [text continues]

[Text] The answer is: in the introductory sections of various sutras, the compilers should establish a sequential order, while their subsequent sections are all subsumed under the preceding examples.
[Commentary] Because this sutra is a later section of the Vaipulya (fangděng), Xinxiang heard that the Buddha had only three months remaining before his parinirvāṇa;
thus, harboring doubts, he pointed to the *Prajñāpāramitā* as having already been taught. Second, citing three sutras:
first, citing the Āgama; second, the actual citation.

[This refers to] the period from the latter part of the Āgamas up until the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

"Hearing the Bestowal of Prophecy.

[Text] One should perform a fourfold analysis (*catuskoṭika-vibhaṅga*): either both name and meaning are extensive, as in the eighteen emptinesses, the twenty emptinesses, or the twenty-four emptinesses;

In its broad sense, it is as follows: terms such as *dharmatā*, *bhūtalakṣaṇa*, *bhūtakoṭi*, *tathatā*, and *dharmadhātu* share a single meaning despite having many names.
[Commentary] Regarding "the eighteen emptinesses" and so forth:
the essence of emptiness is one and the same; it universally sweeps away all objects, and names are established according to those objects. As for...
Fire has different names according to the objects it burns; the meaning of these names cannot but differ.
Therefore, when internal phenomena cease, it is called "internal emptiness" (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*); when external phenomena cease, it is called "external emptiness" (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
When the eighteen objects cease, they are called the "eighteen emptinesses. The twenty emptinesses and the twenty-four emptinesses are likewise thus. Therefore...

When both name and meaning are established extensively, a single term "emptiness" (śūnyatā) is used to signify only the sense of total dissolution and eradication; thus, both name and meaning are concise.

If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were to be established with numerous names, they would merely signify the meaning of the fundamental nature itself. Second, the detailed exposition of the fourth [section] has two parts;
first, the presentation of the heading.

[Commentary: To establish only the two kinds of emptiness is what is meant by "conciseness. This name [emptiness] invokes a meaning that pervades the ten realms;

from ordinary beings up to the Buddhas, all possess sentient beings and the five aggregates. Question: Since the stages up to the Śrāvaka involve the emptiness of both sentient beings and phenomena (*dharma*), why does the *Śāstra* state that even at the stage of the Buddha there are still sentient beings and phenomena?
Is it not the case that they are not merely non-existent, yet are also called "non-existent"?

What is the meaning of this? The answer is: The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) speaks of emptiness, yet its ultimate conclusion is the severance of existence like ashes; thus, upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, the phenomena of birth are forever cut off.

The Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) speaks of emptiness, yet its essence is eternally abiding. Furthermore, it is not only the awakened nature (*buddhatva*) that is eternally abiding; one must know that all phenomena of birth are entirely eternal.
Therefore, as long as the phenomena of birth have not been emptied, they appear as the base, vulgar, and inferior states of ordinary beings.
If the Dharma is empty, it is sublime, vast, and great; thus, the ultimate fruit gives rise to the unsurpassed Dharma, which is the very culmination of emptiness.

Therefore, Jingxi said: "When the three thousand [realms] are perfected in the fruit, they are all termed 'Eternal Bliss. If the three thousand were lacking, how could there be the Dharma-realm or the environment for support?

This refers to extensive knowledge.

When the sutras state that "the faculties of sentient beings are dull," this means that their present capacities cannot awaken to the principle of immeasurable emptiness and they are deficient in wisdom.
This is an exposition based on the wisdom of hearing and retaining [the teachings]. It is similar to what is taught in the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Since the extensive treatises are generally considered cumbersome, I have composed this treatise for those who delight in concise texts that encompass many meanings.

Furthermore, regarding the profound and vast meanings of all Buddhas, I have here explained them in accordance with the *dhāraṇī*. This chapter provides a brief exposition of the immeasurable meaning of emptiness.
This is identical to the explanation in that *dhāraṇī* regarding the profound and vast meaning. Fourth, the explanation of the meaning of immeasurable emptiness has two parts;

[Ji: Since it discusses the dharma-nature, and "nature" (*prakṛti*) does not undergo change, this is the constant virtue (*nitya-guṇa*); the true mark is the reality within the midst [of phenomena].
The commentary on this chapter states: "Seeking the Tathāgata’s true *dharmakāya*. The new edition reads: "The *dharmakāya* is eternal and real;
being real, it is my virtue, its sovereignty is inexhaustible. Since it possesses eternity and self, how could it lack bliss and purity?

[Text] "Diverse and wondrous skillful means" refers to the skillful application of *siddhānta* (established tenets) as explained above:

[Text] Regarding the passage on "arising the mind of great compassion": because sentient beings are attached to existence and their afflictions are grave, the great compassion is likewise grave.

[Commentary] The eight explanations concern knowing the intentions of the assembly.

[Commentary] 2. The actual explanation of emptiness, divided into two parts: first, dividing the text and establishing the intent; second, the division of the text itself. 1. Dividing the text.
[Textual Analysis] From the passage "This body is false and deceptive" downward, forty and a half verses constitute the second section, which correctly elucidates emptiness.

This is further divided into two parts: first, from "The body is false and deceptive" downward for nineteen and a half verses, which clarifies the objects of the two types of emptiness—emptiness of persons and emptiness of phenomena;
second, from "Good daughter, you should contemplate" downward for twenty-one verses, which clarifies the contemplation of the two types of emptiness—emptiness of persons and emptiness of phenomena.
[Commentary] Regarding the second point, establishing the intent, there are two parts;
first, a direct demonstration. [Text] Without an object, contemplation is not correct; without the object of contemplation, it is not manifested.

[Commentary] As for "without an object" and so forth: since the objects of both arising phenomena (*jishō*) and the Dharma (*hōshō*) are all the wondrous Three Truths, they are called the "objects of the two emptinesses. They arise.

Since the contemplation of dharmas is entirely wondrous through the three contemplations, it is called the "wondrous state of the two emptinesses. When the contemplation is triggered by this wondrous state, that contemplation becomes upright and wondrous;
when the contemplation illuminates the state, that state becomes manifest. Thus, both state and contemplation are made upright and manifest.
Second, the citation of proof.
【Text】One should cite the tenfold examination of object and wisdom within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Insight) to clarify their inconceivability.
As the subsequent text states: "The inconceivable wisdom and its inconceivable object; the inconceivable wisdom and its inconceivable illumination. The new edition reads:
"Suchness and the wisdom of suchness"—this is precisely the meaning.
[Commentary] Regarding the tenfold examination of objects by wisdom: "objects" refers to the ten objects, and "wisdom" refers to the ten vehicles.

As for the ten objects: first, the object of the aggregates; second, the object of afflictions; third, the object of illness; fourth, the object of karmic signs; fifth, the object of demonic deeds; sixth, the object of meditative concentration;
seventh, the object of various views; eighth, the object of overweening pride; ninth, the object of the two vehicles; tenth, [the object of bodhisattvas].
When the spheres of the Bodhisattva’s realms manifest before him, nine [practices] await their arousal;

whether they manifest or are aroused, each and every sphere requires the cultivation of the tenfold wisdom of contemplation (*daśa-yāna-avalokana-jñāna*). Regarding these ten vehicles: first, contemplating the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*);

second, arousing the bodhicitta based on that realm; third, skillfully establishing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; fourth, the universal shattering of dharmas; fifth, discerning the open and the obstructed.
Sixth, the Section on Cultivating the Path; seventh, the Section on Counteracting Aids to Opening; eighth, the Section on Knowing the Successive Stages; ninth, the Section on Patient Acceptance;

tenth, the Section on the Absence of Craving for Dharmas. These ten collectively constitute the ten kinds of objects that transcend all thought. Therefore, regarding the attainment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), it is said to transcend the five stages [of the Ten Faiths];

regarding the attainment of semblance [realization], it is said to transcend the ten faiths; regarding the attainment of partial realization, it is said to transcend the forty-one stages; and regarding the attainment of wondrous enlightenment, it is said to transcend them all.
This is able to exhaustively discuss the ultimate severance. The following passage is when Samantabhadra (Dense-Armour) himself explains the meaning of "mystery" (*guhya*);
thus it is called the state where both object and wisdom are inconceivable. The new edition says "dharma," which refers to the object. "As" (*ru*) means "not different.
The fact that all terms are repeated is likely because object and wisdom are fundamentally non-different; it is only due to the differences in [deluded] sentiment that they are now [reiterated].
Because they are not different, the Great Being of Dongyang said: "First is the suchness of original nature; second is the suchness of the extinction of fetters.

Because wisdom is not different from its object, it is called "suchness-wisdom" (*tathatā-jñāna*); because the dharma-object is not different from wisdom, it is called "suchness-suchness" (*tathatā-tathatā*).
All of this clarifies the meaning of the inconceivable. Second, the exegesis of the text according to its phrasing, in two parts: first, clarifying the arising of dharmas; second...
Regarding the two initial sections of the "Object of Emptiness," first is the analysis of the text. [Commentary on the Text]:

The clarification of the object of emptiness is further divided into two parts: first, from "This body is false and deceptive" downward for seventeen and a half lines, clarifying the object of real dharmas;
second, from "The elements of water, fire, and wind" downward for two lines, clarifying the object of conceptual construction.
[Commentary] Regarding the second section on establishing the intent, there are five parts; first, the direct demonstration of the two aspects.
[Text] "Real dharmas" refers to the contemplation that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are non-existent, and the contemplation of the sixteen-fold emptiness of persons;

because these reach the ultimate principle, they are called "real dharmas. Although the body has not yet died, it is provisional and foul-smelling, and is therefore called a "contemplation of the provisional."

[Commentary] Regarding the term "real dharmas" (*dharmatā*): in contrast to the inferior conceptualization of the pure as impure—which is a contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*)—here, one directly contemplates the principle (*tattva*) within both the five aggregates and the provisional person; therefore, it is called "real dharmas.
Although the inferior [contemplation] also involves the meaning of producing conceptualizations, this section demonstrates two alternative names.

[Text] It is also called the "practice of wisdom" (*prajñā-caryā*) and the "practice of conduct" (*caryā-caryā*). Direct entry into emptiness is named the practice of wisdom; practicing while incorporating objective phenomena is named the practice of conduct.
It is also called the "right path" (*samyak-mārga*) and the "auxiliary path" (*upāya-mārga*). Contemplation of emptiness that accords with principle is named the right path;
the contemplation of impurity that destroys greed is named the auxiliary path.

[Commentary] Regarding "practice" (*caryā*): because one further cultivates formal practice (*vastu-caryā*) upon the basis of the wisdom-practice (*prajñā-caryā*), it is called the "practice of practice.

As for the "aids to the path" (*pakṣa-mārga*): by means of the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*), one destroys attachment to phenomena; by means of right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), one destroys the delusions regarding the principles that constitute obstacles. Thus, they are called "aids to the path.
This clarifies both the Great and Small Vehicles, both of which cultivate these two [types of practice]. First, the Small Vehicle is clarified.

[Text]: Those of the Hīnayāna who cultivate the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to sever the fetters are called "those liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*); those who cultivate the factors conducive to the Path (*pakṣya-dharma*) to sever the fetters are called "those liberated both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the three types of liberation, "liberation through freedom from doubt" (*aniścitavimukti*) is not mentioned because those liberated both ways have mastered both internal and external scriptures.

Since there is no room for doubt regarding the names [of these practices], and since this treatise now discusses the "Principal" (zheng) and "Aid" (zhu) paths, I shall first clarify these two. Second, I shall clarify the "Great" [Vehicle]. [Commentary on the Text:

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that when a bodhisattva generates the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), it is in correspondence with *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge); this constitutes the cultivation of the Principal Path.

To sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and purify Buddha-lands constitutes the cultivation of the Aiding Dharmas. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, these are termed the "Great Vehicle" (mahāyāna).

The concept of "escorting" (*bingcong*) refers precisely to this meaning. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies that right wisdom involves distancing oneself from and further distancing oneself from the ten signs to abide in Great Nirvāṇa;
furthermore, it involves the contemplation of white bones and the shattering of the twenty-five existences to achieve the Samādhi of the Universal Monarch (*Cakravartin*).
[Commentary]: *Sarvajña-mahā-śāstra* (The Great Treatise on All-Knowledge) translates [the title] as "The Playful Supernatural Powers of Universal Wisdom.

It is called "playful" because one attains mastery over the triple world; it is so named because the supernatural powers attained through cultivation arise predominantly from the nine notions, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth, thus taking these conceptualizations as aids to the Path.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the great carriage is equipped with the white ox of the perfections (*pāramitā*), which is termed the "Right Path."

The attendants serve as aids for the right wisdom of *nirvāṇa*, which is far removed from the ten signs—namely, the signs of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, arising, abiding, and perishing, as well as the signs of male and female.

Because it is able to detach from these deeply, that which is detached from is not trivial. Furthermore, within the stage of the Truths (*satya*), there is the clarity of the aids to the Path (*mārga*).

Practices such as the contemplation of white bones and other such matters are used in the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) to break through the objects of the concentration of phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*).
The three delusions that obscure the manifestation of the Buddha-nature are eliminated through the combined cultivation of the primary and auxiliary practices of the Sovereign Samādhi;

this is called "penetrating meditation" (dà chán) and "seeing the dharma-realm" (jiàn chán). Regarding the four clarifications (*sì míng*), the sutras and śāstras contain both extensive and abbreviated versions.
[Text] Various sutras discuss these two meanings together, yet they differ in their respective breadth and brevity.
[Commentary] This present chapter discusses these two meanings within the context of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
[Text] The present sutra briefly clarifies the intent of the primary and auxiliary practices.

[Commentary] This refers to the "abbreviated" [treatment] of both [truths]. Regarding the second part, the sequential explanation, there are two sections: first, clarifying the objective realm of real dharmas; second, the division of the text.

[Textual Analysis] The objective realm of real dharmas further has two parts: first, from "From the falsity of the body" below, ten lines and a half discuss the objective realm in terms of the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha*);

second, from "From various causes and conditions" below, seven lines of verse discuss the objective realm in terms of the cause of origination (*samudaya*). One contemplates this suffering and its origination.
And one gives rise to the path that leads to cessation; if one can perceive the Four Truths, then one attains the severance of birth and death.

Once the existence of birth is exhausted, one will no longer undergo further existences, and so forth, regarding the realm of suffering. Furthermore, from the two lines following "the falsity of the body" (*kāya-mṛṣā*), nine lines of verse clarify the realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Next, from the line "the village of the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana-grāma*), nine lines of verse clarify the realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Next, from the [line concerning] the body...
"Empty, void, and false" (the first line) concludes the two types of empty objects regarding the aforementioned phenomena of arising.

[Record] Regarding the second part, the sequential explanation, there are two sections. First, clarifying the object of the fruit of suffering; within this, first is the object of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

This body is false and deceptive, like an empty village. [Commentary] The text has two parts. First, it explains that this body is false and deceptive. Second, it explains how its substance is falsely conceptualized. Regarding the first: first, one conceptualizes the grasping of the aggregates (skandhas) as a self.
