[Text]: This body is false and deceptive; for those who take it as the object of the emptiness of arising, they grasp at the aggregates (*skandha*) to form a body, thereby giving rise to the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which conceives of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.

[Commentary] Regarding "grasping the aggregates to form a body": the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) combine and are conventionally designated as a "body," just as when one grasps five fingers, they are called a "fist.

Ordinary people (pṛthagjana), failing to understand this, cling to this conventional designation as a self (*ātman*). There are sixteen such [views], beginning with: 1. self, 2. sentient being (*sattva*), 3.
life-sustainer (*jīva*), 4. living being (*poṣa*), 5. one who is born (*jantu*), 6. one who is nourished (*purusa*), 7. a person (*pudgala*).

There are eight types of reckoners, nine types of agents, ten types of those driven by the fetters (*anuśaya*), eleven types of those who arise, twelve types of those driven by the fetters to arise, thirteen types of experiencers,
fourteen types of those driven by the fetters to experience, fifteen types of knowers, and sixteen types of viewers; now, for brevity,

these are summarized as the "five selves," which are the conceptualizations of a self and what belongs to a self— whether as identical to or distinct from— the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, as being real.
When a person falsely conceives of a self, a person, or a sentient being within the aggregates (*skandha*), they are falsely conceiving of a self, a birth, or a life-span within the five aggregates.

When they falsely conceive of a self that receives the retribution of a single lifetime’s lifespan within the dharmas such as the aggregates, they are falsely conceiving of a self whose life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) maintains continuity without interruption; it is because of this grasping [that these misconceptions arise].
The conceit of a self and the notion of a body give rise to what is called the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). Since these two entities are fundamentally empty and unobtainable, [the text says]:
"If one realizes that their arising is false and deceptive, then seeking for a body is impossible, and the view of a self does not arise;
other views and cognitions are likewise stilled. Thus, with respect to the provisional body, it serves as the objective realm of the emptiness of arising (utpattiniḥsvabhāvatā).

[Commentary] Because one falsely clings to the existence of arising while in reality there is no arising, "arising" is termed "falsehood. Since it is fundamentally non-arising, the quiescence of the body is seen as being beyond even comparison or description.
Second, examining the original cause to realize its falsity has two parts: first, the formal examination; second, the initial examination of the causes for conventional designations.
Regarding the first, the examination of the causes for conventional designations:

[Text] Furthermore, upon examining the origin of this body, it begins with the false name [of a person] based on the physical remains of the parents, which arises from a single moment of deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
[Commentary] "A single moment of deluded thought" refers to the time when a male enters the womb; he perceives the mother as the object of grasping (*grāhya*) and sees the father...

This is the object of contention: one conceives lust for the mother and hatred for the father; regarding the father’s emission as one's own, through this deluded thought, one attains entry into the womb.
For a woman, it is the reverse. This is explained in detail in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Regarding "the beginning of provisional names":
the names "male" and "female" originate from these deluded thoughts; thus they constitute the beginning. Second, examining the actual phenomena (*dharmas*) by means of two [methods].

First, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). [Commentary on the Text]: These two drops of red and white constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). The experiencing of pleasure and pain constitutes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). The conceptualizing of this pleasure and pain constitutes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
The possession of the three natures constitutes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Consciousness abiding therein constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

[Commentary] "Red and white" refers to the physical remains (the *śarīra*). The "three natures" (*tri-svabhāva*) refer to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate. The "two great elements" refer to the six great elements.
[Text] Furthermore, semen and blood are the earth element; moisture is the water element; warmth is the fire element; and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind element.

The four great elements surrounding the space—this is the mind-element of emptiness (*ākāśa-dhātu*). It dwells in dependence upon this; this is the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). This is the beginning of these real dharmas.
[Commentary] The five aggregates and six elements are the real dharmas that serve as the basis; if such is their original cause, then [the text] concludes by showing this in two parts.
[Text]: Contemplating this body and its name, one sees they rely upon false and deceptive phenomena; how could they be real? Therefore, they are called "false and deceptive. [Commentary]:

The body is an illusory substance and the name is a provisional designation. Since both are produced through deluded thoughts and from semen and blood, one may verify that the body and name are false and deceptive.
The two explanations are like an empty village.
[Text] "The empty village" refers to the body, which is called an accumulation, like a bubble on water that arises when the surrounding air forms a bubble;
the name [of the bubble] also arises. As soon as it arises, it has cessation; as the name of the bubble ceases, so too does the name of the body cease.

Because the bubble of the aggregates (*skandha*) arises when the power of ignorance and karma relies upon the physical bodies of the parents, and the name of the body arises when the bubble of the aggregates arises, and the name of the body ceases when the bubble of the aggregates ceases, it is therefore called "empty."
[This refers to] the "aggregation.
[Commentary: The power of ignorance as karma—karma being precisely the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)—is what is meant by "ignorance conditions the formative forces.

Whether at the time of first performing an action or at the time of entering the womb, as previously explained, the consciousness of a male or female gives rise to desire and aversion toward the parents.
Because one mistakenly believes that the parents' fluids are one's own, due to this deluded thought, one takes on a fetal body; these two substances are the "remnants," namely the red and the white.
Regarding the second [section], the emptiness of the nature of the two bodies as objects, there are two parts: first, establishing the intent, and second, dividing the text.
First, establishing the intent:
[Text]: From the "village" of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one proceeds to clarify the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*). How is this known?

Because this passage merely scrutinizes the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) without discussing the self (*pudgala*) or persons; therefore, we know it is the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts.
[Wenqu] The text consists of three sections: first, one line explains the six sense faculties (ṣaḍāyatana); second, three lines explain the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana);
and third, five lines explain the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu).
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation has three parts; first, the clarification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
The village of the six entrances (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) is where the bandits of the fetters dwell; all abide in themselves, each unaware of the others. [Commentary] The text has four parts;
first, the explanation of the six entrances has three parts; first, the explanation of the two names.
[Text]: Regarding the "six entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*): they are the six sense faculties (*indriya*). Because they are able to produce consciousness, they are called "faculties.
Because they are the destinations toward which objects proceed, they are called "entrances. Furthermore, because they are that into which consciousness enters, they are named the "six entrances."
[Commentary] Second, an examination of three matters.

[Text] Examining its original source, there are but three matters: namely, life-force (*jīvitendriya*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Like congealed cream or thin curd, these undergo a transformation every seven days;
blown by the skillful wind, they expand the five *kalala* (embryonic stages), and by grasping the pure matter of the four great elements, the eye is formed.
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding life-force (*jīva*), warmth (*ūṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*): the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that at the stage of the *kalala*, there are already these three things.
"Vital breath" (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) is called the life-force; being neither putrid nor decomposed is called warmth, which is the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) sustained by karma.
Therefore, the physical elements such as earth and water do not become putrid or decayed. Within this [process], that which is called "mind" (*manas*) is designated as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*);
it is the momentary awareness and cognition. The harmonious conjunction of these three factors proceeds from birth until growth, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Regarding the transformation every seven days while in the womb: the first week is called the "impure state," appearing like solidified butter; the second week...
The first seven days are called the *arbuda* stage, resembling a blister; the second seven days are called the *peśī* stage, resembling a mass of congealed blood;

the third seven days are called the *ghana* stage, because it becomes increasingly thick and firm; the fourth seven days are called the *praśākhā* stage, because the four limbs and their distinctions take shape;

the fifth seven days are called the *keśaromanakhasthiti* stage, because hair, body hair, nails, and teeth appear; the sixth seven days are called the *indriyabhāvasthiti* stage, because the five sense organs become fully developed. Here, "five" refers to these five stages.
The "blister" (phuppha) refers to the stage of form (*rūpa*). The three knowledges (*vidyā*) comprise six categories.

[Commentary on the Text: If the sense faculties (*indriya*) are established, they possess the function of producing consciousness; thus, while matter (*rūpa*) is divided into five, the mind (*citta*) is treated as one.

[Commentary] The five faculties together with the preceding consciousness constitute the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*); thus, the six faculties are complete. Regarding the two explanations of "village":
[Text] Because consciousness dwells in dependence upon the faculties, it is called a "village."
[Commentary] The third explanation concerns where the thieves of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) dwell.
[Text] Because the defilements (*rajas*) enter from this [place], it is said to be "where the thieves of the fetters dwell.

[Commentary] Since the defilements give rise to the fetters, which are able to destroy the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*), they are called "thieves of the fetters. The fourth explanation concerns their mutual lack of awareness.

[Text]: The eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the body touches, and the mind conditions; each has its own respective object of observation and they cannot be confused with one another.
Therefore, it is said that they do not know one another.
[Commentary] This means "to wait upon" or "to attend. Second, the explanation of the twelve bases (*āyatana*):
the eye faculty perceives forms; the ear discriminates sounds; the nose smells various fragrances; the tongue relishes flavors;
the body faculty greedily experiences various tangibles; and the mind faculty discriminates all phenomena. Thus, each of the six sense faculties has its own respective object.
The various sensory objects do not function through other conditions.
[Commentary] This passage has four parts; the first concerns the opening and enumeration of the categories.
[Wenju] From "From the eye-faculty receiving form" onwards, it clarifies the twelve *āyatanas*, further dividing "form" into ten and adding one more *āyatana*.
By partially opening up the mind, it becomes two, thus forming the twelve *āyatanas*.
[Commentary] To open up "form" (*rūpa*) into ten refers to the five faculties and the five objects. "Partially" means that within the *dharmāyatana*, two kinds of phenomena are subsumed:
first, mental phenomena (*caitta*), which exclude the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and take only the associated mental factors (*caitasika*); second, non-... [text fragment ends].

Mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) consist of past and future form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is here called "a small portion" refers specifically to the past and future form-phenomena among those that are not mental phenomena.

When the category of mind is divided into two, it refers to the sense-base of mind (*mana-āyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*). Furthermore, even within the sense-base of phenomena, it refers only to a small portion, namely:
Within the two types of the *dharmāyatana*, only mental factors (*cittadharma*) are subsumed; the mention here of "two" merely cites the full number.
Second, the explanation of the general and specific names:
[Text] "The objects enter the faculties, and the faculties also enter the objects; as they mutually interpenetrate, they are generally termed 'entrance' (*āyatana*); they give rise to the faculties."

Because the power of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is predominant, it is specifically termed the "root" (*indriya*); because the meaning of defilement is predominant, they are specifically termed "objects" (*viṣaya*).
[Commentary] Each of the three explanations refers to their respective objects.
[Wenju] Since a single root and object mutually interpenetrate, it is said that each takes its own as an object.
[Commentary] The four explanations clarify that [the sense organs] do not function with respect to external conditions.

[Text] Because the faculties of another do not enter this object-field, and this object-field does not enter the faculties of another, it is said that they "do not function with respect to external conditions."
[Commentary] Regarding the first of the two [sections on] the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*): first, the number is established and the names are explained.
[Text] From "The mind is like an illusion" onwards, it clarifies the eighteen elements. To further expand upon this, the mind is counted as eight and the forms as ten;
because these are distinct and do not overlap, they are termed "elements" (*dhātu*).
[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning according to the text, in three parts: first, it clarifies that consciousness pervades all sense organs.
The mind is like a magical illusion, galloping through the six sense objects while constantly engaging in false conceptualization and discrimination regarding all phenomena;
it is just like a person running toward an empty village and being harmed by the six thieves, yet remaining ignorant and failing to avoid them.
[Text] The passage consists of three parts: first, "the mind is like an illusion"; second, it clarifies that consciousness pervades all sense faculties;

and third, even if the eyes and ears do not encounter their respective objects, the mind still pursues and anticipates them, hence it is said to "gallop about. This is like a person sitting at home who gallops across the world [in his mind].

Because of ignorance (*moha*), one does not know that the sense bases (*āyatana*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are empty and perilous, and thus they inflict harm like bandits. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says:
[The Master] said:
[Record] To pursue past conditions and anticipate future ones is like galloping; it is as if one were running about.

This is an analogy provided by citing the example of a person who, while sitting upright in a single room, directs their thoughts toward the world at large. To be stained by the conditions of sensory objects while so seated is called "galloping while sitting."
Unless one relies on the wondrous emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is no way to still the racing thoughts; thus, those of dull and inferior capacity are harmed by the six thieves.

As stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on King Guṇaratna," it says: "Suppose there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket and ordered a man to look after and nourish them.
He commanded that if even one snake should give rise to anger, he must be executed according to the law in the marketplace."
Terrified, the man abandoned his basket and fled. At that time, the king again dispatched five *caṇḍālas* who followed him with drawn swords;
one of them concealed his sword and feigned friendship. The man did not trust him and sought refuge in a village to hide himself.
Once he had entered the village, seeing no people, he sat down on the ground. Then he heard a voice from the air saying: "Now..."
At night, six great bandits were about to arrive; the man became terrified and fled again.
On the road he encountered a river with swift, surging waters, so he gathered grass and wood to fashion a raft and crossed the current. Having reached the other shore, he was safe and free from harm.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: hearing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he contemplates the body as a chest and the four great elements as snakes.
The five *caṇḍālas* are the five aggregates (*skandha*). The feigned intimacy is craving. The empty village is the six sense bases (*āyatana*).

The six thieves are the six external objects (*viṣaya*). The river is affliction (*kleśa*). The raft is the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Reaching the other shore of eternal bliss is *nirvāṇa*.
Second, it clarifies that consciousness (*vijñāna*) constantly resides within the faculties and their objects.

The mind constantly relies upon the spheres of the six sense organs; each knows its own respective object of observation as it follows along with forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.

[Commentary on the Text] In the passage "the mind constantly relies upon" and below, it clarifies that consciousness is always present within the organs; therefore, it says "the consciousness of the six organs is always present."

Because of the sense objects (*viṣaya*), they are called "objects of perception. If one were to claim that consciousness does not reside in the faculties (*indriya*) and objects, then why is there immediate awareness as soon as they encounter them?
Because there is immediate awareness, it is therefore always present within the faculties and objects. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:
"When the faculties are unimpaired and the mind desires to hear, and there is again a sound, through the conjunction of these various conditions, hearing is attained. This is precisely that meaning.

[Commentary] "To perceive and to cognize immediately" means that one cognizes as soon as one encounters an object. To cite the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) as proof for the meaning of immediate cognition:

it states, "If the mind desires to hear, then consciousness resides in the faculty. Furthermore, according to the *Jingxing* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*), the third [point] clarifies that consciousness constantly goes out and returns.

The mind dwells within the six sense organs like a bird cast into a net; wherever the mind goes, it constantly resides there, following after the various sensory objects without ever momentarily abandoning them.
[Commentary] The passage beginning "the mind dwells within the six sense organs" clarifies that consciousness within the faculties emerges and enters repeatedly, like a bird [caught in a net].
As a net moves in and out, opening and closing, pecking at one thing and abandoning it to circle back again without a moment’s rest, so too is consciousness within the net of the sense organs.
It may reside in the ear or in the eye; its coming and going is not fixed.
Yet, although it is not fixed, it can be said to be ever-present, and so forth.

[Commentary] "Emerging and entering alternately" means emerging when facing an object and entering immediately when not facing one. Regarding "the interval between emerging and entering," Master Ying says it refers to the act of emerging and entering;
it also has the sense of being set up or arranged. The *Zhuangzi* states that "small wisdom is characterized by intervals," meaning there are obstructions and barriers.
"Picking one and abandoning one" means abandoning one mesh of the net and then picking at another mesh.
Because the eye is obstructed and difficult to bring out, the treatise states that one is constantly aware when confronting sensory objects (*dharmas*).
Third, regarding the two objects of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the first part provides the heading.

[Textual Commentary]: From "The body is empty, hollow, and false" onwards, one line constitutes the third section, which establishes the two types of emptiness regarding the objects of the dharmas produced above.
[Commentary] Second, the citation and explanation of the two [points]. First, it concludes by establishing that the objective realm is empty;
the body is empty and illusory, incapable of being nourished or sustained.
[Text]: "The body is empty and cannot be nourished. This refers to the preceding [statement], "the realm of the arising of emptiness is nourished. This is one of the sixteen [aspects of emptiness].
Since that which is nourished is empty, the fifteenth and sixteenth [aspects] constitute the completion of the realm of the arising of emptiness.

[Commentary]: "Nurturing" (*poṣa*) refers to the view of nurturing (*poṣadṛṣṭi*) among the sixteen [views]. It is the false discrimination that "I am able to nurture others," as well as the calculation that "I am the parents who nurture.
These two summarize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as the objective sphere.
There is no dispute, nor is there a presiding master.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first, an anticipatory explanation of the absence of a master, second, a specific examination of the mind.

[Wenju] Regarding "nor is there a presiding master": this concludes the preceding discussion on the objective realm of the emptiness of dharmas. The *Bequeathed Teaching* states: "These five faculties [are governed by] the mind..."
Regarding the claim that the mind is the "master" of the faculties at the very beginning of conception, it is designated as the master because it arises prior to the various faculties;

however, in reality, it cannot control them. Since the faculties are vast and contrary [to its will], the mind suffers affliction when they do so, and when the body falls ill, the mind likewise follows suit. How, then, can it be considered the master?

[Commentary] Since a master must necessarily be able to exercise control and attain sovereignty, these two conditions—being afflicted by another and [the other] being unable to control one—are not established; thus, one knows that the mind is not the master.
Second, they mutually investigate who the master is.
[Text] At times, they further debate with one another regarding the master: for example, earth possesses the four subtle elements and is dull, and is therefore controlled by water. Water...
However, three *paramāṇus* (subtle atoms) are constrained by fire; fire, consisting of two *paramāṇus*, is constrained by wind; wind, possessing one *paramāṇu*, is constrained by the mind (*citta*).

Since the mind possesses no *paramāṇu*, it is able to act as the master. Furthermore, because the principle of being the master is not established when it is itself afflicted by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is said that there is no true master.

[Commentary] The four subtle elements (*paramāṇu*) are color, odor, taste, and tangibility. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that because earth possesses color, odor, taste, and tangibility, and is heavy, it has no activity of its own;
water, having little odor, excels earth in its activity; fire, having less odor and taste than water, excels water in its power;
and wind, having less color, odor, and taste than fire, excels fire in its activity. Regarding the phrase "the mind has no equal": this refers to the mind in comparison to the [four elements].

The "Great" (mahābhūta) is designated as the primary because it does not depend on the subtle for its excellence; however, if one considers them in terms of being subject to affliction, they do not constitute a primary.
Second, a retrospective explanation of "non-contention" (araṇā).
[Text]: There is no contention or dispute. If one reckons that the four great elements exist, there is mutual opposition, like four snakes coexisting.
When the four elements contend with one another, disputes may arise; yet now we observe that the four great elements are empty and cannot attain emptiness itself.
Therefore, it is said that there are no disputes. This is the conclusion of the meaning of the emptiness of dharmas mentioned above.

[Commentary] Although all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they are fundamentally devoid of volition; how then could there be dispute? All such conflict arises from emotional conceptualization.

Thus, the four great elements are like snakes and the six sense objects are like thieves. If one contemplates their fundamental emptiness, then all phenomena are quiescent; who then would engage in dispute?
Therefore, by means of non-dispute, the realm of the emptiness of phenomena is established. Second, the realm of the cause of accumulation is explained.
Section Two: Comparative Analysis of the Text of the First Part.

[Textual Commentary] From the verse beginning "Arising from the conjunction of various causes and conditions" down to the seventh line, seven verses are presented to clarify the object through the cause of origination (*samudaya-hetu*), which is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
This text is divided into three parts: first, two lines clarify the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*); second, three and a half lines clarify origination (*samudaya*).
The first line and a half of the section on "Mutually Devouring" clarify the realms of good and evil.
[Commentary] The second section distinguishes two pairs; the first pair distinguishes them through conceptualization.

[Text] The first three are the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), and the last one is the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*). The first three are the objects of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), and the last one is...
These are the objects of the contemplation that aids the path (*bodhipakṣya-dhyāna*): the former one arises from ignorance, and the latter one ceases through the extinction of ignorance.

[Commentary] The first three are the objects of the correct contemplation of wisdom (*prajñā-carita*), which are established as three categories within this very object of accumulation (*samudaya-viṣaya*), namely: accumulation (*samudaya*), arising (*samudaya-ākāra*), and so forth.

The latter one is the object of the contemplation that aids the path for those whose conduct is practice (*caryā-carita*), which is a conceptual construction (*parikalpita*). These constitute the nine.

Since the text of the *Caryā-sūtra* is continuous and both passages speak of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as if they were difficult to distinguish, the primary and auxiliary aspects are discussed by contrasting the first three with the latter one to differentiate them.

Furthermore, regarding the former "first" [of the three], it refers to the very first of the three objects of accumulation (*saṃgraha-viṣaya*), which is contrasted with the subsequent "imaginary" [nature] to discuss arising and ceasing; this former [nature] is said to arise from the various...
It is said that things exist through the combination of causes and conditions, and that they are established by the gathering together of earth, water, fire, and wind;
subsequently, it is stated that when the elements of water, fire, and wind disperse and perish, this is not it the very characteristic of the arising and ceasing of the four great elements?
Yet, to say that both arising and ceasing proceed from ignorance demonstrates that this arising and ceasing is inseparable from delusion and falsehood. Therefore, regarding the preceding arising...
It is said that from the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) until its subsequent cessation, it is said to disperse and perish; this is the link of death (*maraṇāṅga*).
When combined with sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, these are the fruit of ignorance (*avidyā*) and, furthermore, the cause of ignorance.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "Old age and death have a fruit, which is ignorance; ignorance has a cause, which is pointed out as old age and death. Thus, there is birth (*jāti*).
All cessation arises from ignorance. Second, this is distinguished in contrast to the Lesser Vehicle.

[Commentary on the Text]: If one were to discuss arising and ceasing directly, it would not differ from the Lesser Vehicle; for ignorance fundamentally does not arise, yet it arises, and it does not cease, yet it ceases.
Thus, arising and ceasing are non-dual, yet they appear as dual.

[Commentary]: Regarding the arising and ceasing of ignorance as discussed above, which teaching does not conform to this? If one wishes to understand this fully, one must discuss the Small and Great Vehicles.

In the Small Vehicle, it is taught that the four great elements truly arise from ignorance and truly cease with ignorance. In the Great Vehicle, it is taught that the four great elements are originally empty by nature; therefore, they are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished.

This is because there are three teachings within the Great Vehicle, among which the Shared Teaching holds that the essence of the four great elements is inherently empty, and thus they are fundamentally without birth or extinction.

Due to ignorance, one perceives arising and ceasing as being like the arising of an illusion and the ceasing of an illusion. In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the substance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is itself Buddha-nature;
because of ignorance, the four great elements undergo arising and ceasing, yet their nature is without the marks of arising and ceasing, though they appear to have them.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the substance of the four great elements is likewise Buddha-nature; however, because this nature inherently possesses the four great elements of the nine realms, there are [nine such natures].

Whether the four great elements arise or perish, they are all the Dharma-realm; therefore, their nature and characteristics are both non-arising and non-perishing, which is the inconceivable discourse on arising and perishing.

Thus, when the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that the characteristics of the world are eternal, its meaning being such, it follows that within the three teachings of the Mahāyāna, one may clarify that what is fundamentally non-arising arises, and what is fundamentally non-perishing perishes.

The cessation of non-duality as duality is not here discussed in terms of the general and the specific, but rather in relation to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Second, the explanation of the meaning according to the text, which has three parts:

first, clarifying the characteristic of "accumulation and origination" (*jiquxiang*); second, the general explanation of this in terms of birth and dharmas; third, the specific selection of suffering as arising from accumulation. First, the general explanation of this in terms of birth and dharmas, which has three parts: first, distinguishing suffering from its origin in accumulation.

[Text]: "Arising from various causes and conditions" refers to both suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*). Since one intends to clarify the meaning of the origin, it must be explained as the causes and conditions of the origin. [Commentary]:
Suffering is the fruit of the world, and the origin is the cause of the world. Both of these causes and effects are produced by causes and conditions.
Although what is being analyzed here involves the fruit of suffering, its intent is to clarify the causes and conditions for the arising of accumulation (*samudaya*).
Regarding the meaning of the paired phrases in two parts:

[Commentary] the first three phrases concern the causes and conditions for the arising of conventional designations (*prajñapti*), while the latter five phrases concern the causes and conditions for the arising of substantial dharmas (*dravya-dharma*).
[Commentary] Regarding the three refutations, the first section on the causes and conditions of the Lesser Vehicle consists of two parts;

first, it introduces the Lesser Vehicle. [Text] The Lesser Vehicle refutes the four great elements down to the subtle dust of the *paramāṇu* (neighboring atom). From these subtle dusts, coarse dust arises;
this is used as the cause and condition for the arising of the provisional and the real.
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The infinitesimal (*paramāṇu*), the minute (*aṇu*), gold-dust, wood-dust, rabbit-hair dust, sheep-hair dust, cow-hair dust, and window-dust.

According to the Small Vehicle’s existential gate, it is asserted that the infinitesimal first possesses spatial divisions in the ten directions; therefore, it does not refute the "neighboring atom" (*anu*), taking this as its causal basis.
2. Refuting the Incorrect.

[Wenju: Now it is clarified that when coarse matter can be analyzed to exhaustion and subtle particles are likewise exhausted—when both coarse and subtle are entirely exhausted—what thing could serve as a causal condition?

[Commentary] "Even subtle dust is exhausted" means that even the *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom) is deconstructed. Since these two types of dust are deconstructed, causes and conditions cannot be established.
Second, there is a separate explanation regarding the arising of phenomena, which is twofold: first, the provisional name of causes and conditions.
Arising from the conjunction of various causes and conditions, it possesses no solidity or substance.
[Commentary] The text is divided into three parts; first, the explanation of "arising from various causes and conditions.

[Wenju] Regarding the term "causes and conditions": ignorance (*avidyā*) is the internal affliction that acts as the cause, for one fails to realize the two kinds of emptiness regarding phenomena and persons, and thus becomes defiled.

Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) externally serves as a condition for attachment to the spheres of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), and because ignorance (*avidyā*) moistens craving so that the accumulation of karma can arise, it is said that [karma] arises from the conjunction of various causes and conditions. [Commentary:
Here, it is appropriate to employ the *Awakening of Faith* (Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra), which states that ignorance acts as the cause to produce the three subtle states and objective realms.

Regarding the statement that "the six coarse [delusions] are exhausted through dependent origination," the meaning of the commentary is as follows: The "three subtle [delusions]" refer to the aspect of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*), the aspect of evolution (*pravṛttilakṣaṇa*), and the aspect of manifestation (*nirbhāsalakṣaṇa*).

These are the three types of aspects produced when fundamental non-awakening (*mūlābodhi*) perfumes True Suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is said that internal delusion, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), acts as the cause.

The "six coarse [delusions]" refer to: the aspect of cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇa*), the aspect of continuity (*anubandhalakṣaṇa*), the aspect of grasping (*upādānalakṣaṇa*), the aspect of conceptualizing names (*nāmavikalpalakṣaṇa*), [the aspect of attachment to the self], and the aspect of the arising of suffering (*duḥkhābhinirvṛttilakṣaṇa*).

The characteristic of initiating karma (*karmārambha-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of being bound by karma (*karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*) constitute the secondary branches of non-awakening (*abodhi*).
With respect to external objects, the arising of the characteristics of wisdom and so forth gives rise to the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), which are termed "defiled craving" (*rāga*).

By means of defiled attachment to external spheres of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), the two forms of non-awakening permeate the mind of the two types of grasping, thereby forming the characteristic of initiating karma. Thus it is said that ignorance moistens craving, and the accumulation of karma arises suddenly.

If one cannot distinguish at all that delusion regarding the single dharma-realm constitutes the internal affliction of ignorance and so forth, how could such a person manifest the present wisdom of emptiness of the Middle Way?
Second, the explanation of their existence through conjunction.
[Text]: Because karma arises, there is the single thought of entering the womb, which brings about the fruit of suffering.
[Commentary]: "Because karma arises" refers to the characteristic of the arising of karma. "There is... and so forth refers to the characteristic of being bound by karma to suffering.
What is here called the "fruit of suffering" is the provisional person formed by grasping at the aggregates (skandhas). [The third explanation is that it] possesses no solidity.
[The text says: "True.

[Commentary on the Words: This single thought that entrusts itself to the womb is produced by the mind of ignorance and craving; since this mind is already illusory, the mind thus produced is likewise illusory.
When one investigates its beginning and end, both the subject (the producer) and the object (that which is produced) are entirely empty. Therefore, it is said that it does not exist.
"Solid and firm.
[Commentary] Because the two types of non-awakening—ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—act as causes, they are able to give rise to the mind.

A single thought-moment of entrusting itself to the womb is the fruit of non-awakening, termed the "mind that is produced. To reckon these causes and effects is called "root and branch. Since both are... [text continues].
Since that which is not awakened to is not real, it is said to be entirely empty and devoid of solidity or substance. Second, as for the causal conditions of real dharmas:
because of deluded conceptualization, the mechanism of karmic power arises; this false and deceptive collection of earth, water, fire, and wind forms a hollow assembly.
[Text] Because of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the five phrases clarify the causes and conditions for the arising of real dharmas.

Due to the failure to realize a single thought-moment through deluded conceptualization, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise based upon entering the womb. Regarding the "mechanism of karmic power": wholesome and unwholesome karma are the master of the mechanism;

the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is the apparatus of the mechanism; and the aggregates of sensation, perception, and mental formations (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-skandha*) perform the movements of going, coming, advancing, and retreating within it.

Cessation is for the sake of self-entertainment; because the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) relies on the six [senses] to enter and abide, it is called an "empty village. Because it is produced by the four great elements (mahābhūta), it is said to be "established.

[Commentary: This is also a false conception; its reliance on the womb in a single thought-moment is no different from what preceded it, but whereas previously it established a provisional person (pudgala), here it establishes the aggregates.

Now, it is established that through the integration of the provisional and the real, they form a single *saṃbhogakāya*. Because one cultivates the two types of emptiness, one destroys the two attachments;
thus, the objective spheres are divided into two. The "operator of the mechanical device" is like a wooden puppet moved by a mechanism;

the "one who manipulates the mechanism" is the person who operates the puppet. Therefore, the cause of karma is used as a metaphor for the puppet being manipulated, while the aggregates (*skandhas*) are the mechanism itself.
The analogy of the fruit is that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is like the physical body of a wooden puppet; thus it is said to be "equipped with the mechanical contrivances.

The three aggregates [of sensation, perception, and formations] are like the movements and comings-and-goings of the wooden puppet; the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is like the spectator, and thus it is said to "entertain itself.
Second, the characteristics of accumulation are explained as mutual devouring.
They increase and decrease according to the seasons and mutually harm one another, just like four snakes dwelling together in a single basket.
The four great venomous serpents differ in their natures: two tend upward and two tend downward, and their directions are likewise twofold.

When these snakes and the elements are entirely extinguished without remainder, the two snakes of earth and water, being heavy by nature, sink downward; the two snakes of wind and fire, being light by nature, rise upward.
[Commentary] The text has two parts. The first part explains cause and effect through four sections; the first of these explains increase, decrease, and mutual injury.

[Text] Regarding "increasing and decreasing according to time" and "mutually injuring one another": to discuss increase and decrease vertically, as in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are ten distinct stages:
from the stage of the *kalala* it is called "increase," from the stage of vigor it is called "flourishing," and from the stage of old age it is called "decrease. Horizontally...

Regarding the discussion of increase and decrease: when fire increases, water decreases; when water increases, fire decreases; and the same applies to wind and earth. Furthermore, in every moment there is arising and ceasing:
arising is increase, and ceasing is decrease. Moreover, because new sense faculties arise, they increase; because the phenomena of the sense faculties cease, they decrease.
Furthermore, the text below states: "According to the seasons, they mutually harm one another: the wind in spring, the fire in summer, and..."
"Regarding the increase and decrease of water in the earth during winter, and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the vertical division into ten stages, the *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: (1) the stage of *kalala* is distinct; (2) the stage of *arbuda* is distinct;
(3) the stage of *peśī* is distinct; (4) the stage of *ghana* is distinct; (5) the stage of initial birth is distinct; (6) the stage of infancy is distinct... [and so on].

The time of the seven-year-old child is different; the time of the eight-year-old youth is different; the time of the nine-year-old in full vigor is different; the time of the ten-year-old facing old age and death is different.
Furthermore, although there is arising and ceasing moment by moment within the mind, one must know that the four great elements likewise increase and decrease accordingly.
Moreover, the "new" sense faculties refer to the time of birth, while the "old" sense faculties refer to the time of death. Furthermore, they are sustained and nourished by food and drink.
Blood and flesh constitute the "new," while tears, earwax, and so forth constitute the "old. Regarding the second [section], there are two explanations for the four snakes in a single basket;

first, the explanation of the four snakes based on their retribution clarifies the four characteristics. First, the section concerning the snakes and their retribution clarifies the four characteristics.
[Text]: For example, when four snakes are first in their basket, they are called "born"; when their strength is equal, they are called "mighty";
when they contend with one another over who is stronger or weaker, they are called "sick"; when they fight until exhausted and temporarily cease moving, it is called "peaceful";
once they have rested, they fight again; when the snakes grow weak, it is like "old age"; when they are severed, it is called "death. Such increases and decreases constitute the body of fruition.

[Commentary] A snake possesses strength that can overcome the weak and the like; this retribution may be compared to the body, which has the four characteristics of birth, old age, sickness, death, increase, and decrease.
Second, regarding the snake as a cause, the four parts are clarified: the four parts of affliction all possess poisonous harm, which is precisely the cause of the snake.
By means of this cause, it can induce the four great elements and the four characteristics. First, the four parts are individually shown to induce retribution.
Second, first explaining the arising of the four great elements.
[Text]: Thus, it depends on the four parts of accumulated karma: hatred is like earth, desire is like fire, delusion is like water, and ignorance is like wind;
these four parts are mutually contradictory.
[Commentary] Second, explaining how the four marks are brought about.

[Text] It should properly be stated that greed brings about old age, hatred brings about illness, and delusion brings about death; by analogy, it should be said that the "equal portion" (sāmagrī) brings about birth.

[Commentary] The Sūtra presents the three characteristics; the sub-commentaries and other works provide examples that lead to the characteristic of arising. Second, the collective accumulation of karma leads to suffering.
[Text] The characteristic of the accumulation of karma involves mutual devouring, which causes the four great elements to increase or diminish, and so forth.
[Commentary]: The preceding explanation of the four snakes, although speaking of the retribution of suffering, intends to clarify the causes and conditions of accumulation (*saṃudaya*).

Therefore, it concludes by summarizing that "the karmas of accumulation bite one another, causing great increase or decrease," attributing the efficacy to accumulation; this is the primary intent of this sutra.
Second, explaining the two [snakes] within the same basket: first, the body is taken as the basket.
[Text]: "Sharing the same space within a single box" clarifies that while the box is of one nature, the snakes are distinct and possess venomous stings.

The four great elements (mahābhūta) harbor eighty-four thousand afflictions (kleśa), which share the same meaning as being harmful, as explained in the Mahāyāna sūtras. Taking the provisional body as the box, the body sustains the four great elements just as a box contains snakes.
When the box is destroyed, the snakes depart; when the body perishes, the great elements vanish—like birds [flying away] from a cage.
"Regarding the passage 'the cage,' etc.:
[Commentary] *Shi* (螫) is pronounced *zhi-lie* (知列) or *shi* (釋); *hao* (郝) refers to the administration of poison.

The Sūtra cites four snakes as a metaphor for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), intending to clarify that each of these four parts possesses the quality of toxicity and harm; one part alone is fully endowed with twenty-one thousand [such qualities]."
The four elements together cause the destruction of the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom accumulated over eighty-four thousand immeasurable kalpas;

this is clarified by this Great Sūtra through the meaning of the "body-sustaining four great elements," "non-arising and non-accumulation," and "the snake having no venom. This is like a bird in a cage;
the subsequent passage reiterates this, and the commentary provides a rough explanation, hence it notes "and so forth. Second, [this is] in terms of karma.
[It serves as] a casket. [Wenqu:

Furthermore, by the power of karma it acts as a casket; karma sustains the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). When karma exhausts itself, the elements disperse like a bird dwelling in a cage that seeks an exit everywhere.
The mind is likewise: not for a single thought-moment is it bound within the body-casket, yet it constantly seeks its way out.
To race outward in this manner is to seek death in every thought-moment; it is not the way to bring peace to the body.

[Commentary] Because past karma still persists, the four great elements have not yet dispersed. To clarify this, he again cites the caged bird to illustrate that the "karma-casket" must be understood.

The present commentary cites "karma-sustenance" (業持) to reveal the general meaning of the accumulation of causes; thus it says, "the bird of the mind. The "bird" is a metaphor for the four aggregates.
Racing outward toward the six sense-objects, one constantly seeks birth and death rather than the peace of the *dharmakāya*.

If a person, in every thought-moment, contemplates the breaking of precepts, they will instead seek the hells; thus, the five aggregates of past karma will perish and one shall go forever to *niraya*.
Third, the nature [of these three] differs from each other; first, the explanation is given in terms of a single body.
[Text]: As for their natures being distinct: the two that ascend are Yang, and the two that descend are Yin. Why are they contrary? It is because their natures are distinct.
How can those with distinct natures combine to form a body? There are also two [sets] regarding the directions:

the four great elements correspond to the four cardinal points—Wind in the East, Fire in the South, Earth in the West, and Water in the North. Furthermore, they correspond to the four seasons: Wind in Spring, Fire in [Summer], and so forth.

In summer the land is in the south and in autumn in the west; winter belongs to the east and south, which are associated with Yang and ascend, while the west and north belong to Yin and sink downward.
Thus it is said that two directions ascend and two descend. Regarding the various directions, if they are discussed in pairs:

the east ascends and the west sinks; the south rises and the north descends. If one discusses the four intermediate corners (diagonal directions), the eastern direction encompasses two corners, one of which is Yang.
The upper part is one dimension of darkness; the remaining three directions below are likewise so.

[Commentary] Regarding "the nature of the elements being different" and so forth: although it is said that the body is formed by the harmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), since their elemental natures are distinct, how could they possibly combine to form a whole?

This clarifies that within the process of formation, each constituent part perishes in its own place; yet, due to deluded perception, one fails to realize this disintegration and instead clings to the formation as something stable and enduring.

As for the statement that "the arising of attachment corresponds to the four directions of the four great elements," this reveals that the internal four great elements possess the nature of the four directions.

By examining the ascent and descent of the four directions, one finds the great elements to be mutually contradictory; when corresponding to the cardinal points and the intermediate directions (*vidiś*), the intent is the same throughout.

This is truly because the nature of the internal substance and the external time and direction are fundamentally one. Thus, the principle of the mutual induction of the environment and the body, as well as form and mind, is established. Therefore, now...
The Sūtra specifically uses the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to clarify the accumulation of karma. Second, the explanation is given in terms of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
[Wenju]: Some say that within a single faculty, all four great elements are present—two above and two below, and so forth.

[Commentary]: This is because the six sense organs are all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The four interpretations [of the term] all state that they are extinguished without remainder.
[Text]: "Extinguished without remainder" refers first to the dissolution and dispersal [of the body], meaning that wind and fire move upward, while earth and water move downward.
When one traces downward from the top, one cannot find wind or fire; when one examines below, one does not see earth or water.
Therefore, it is said that they are all extinguished without remainder.

[Commentary] "Bi" (比) is pronounced *bi-li* (反); it means "to reach. Seeing that a person dies and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) disperse, one then claims that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has ceased.
The warmth has already returned to the upper parts, while the flesh, bones, blood, and sweat must return to the lower parts;
yet upon investigation, they have no place of departure, because fundamentally they never came. If there were coming and going, it would not be within the scope of this teaching.
Second, the bond arises from the accumulation of karma.

[Text]: "The profound differences in the rising and sinking of the fruits of suffering arise from the accumulation of good and evil karma; the heavens and hells diverge accordingly," and so forth. [Commentary]:

The Sūtra cites the extreme variation in the rising and sinking of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) precisely to clarify that the objects of accumulation (*upādāna-vastu*) follow diverse paths of good and evil.

This is because the four great elements are not exclusively evil, as they also pertain to tainted goodness (*sāsrava-kuśala*). Thus, the third section clarifies the objects of accumulated good and evil.

The two natures of mind and consciousness are restless and never still; following karma, they receive retribution, falling into the various realms of humans and devas according to their actions as they descend into the various states of existence.
[Commentary] The text has three parts; first, the explanation of mind and consciousness.

[Text]: Regarding the phrase "the two natures of mind and consciousness are restless and do not cease," the *Śāstra* explains: "Mind, intellect (*manas*), and consciousness are one dharma with different names.

In relation to enumeration, it is called 'mind' (*citta*); because it can produce [subsequent states], it is called 'intellect' (*manas*); because it discriminates, it is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*). It further states that there is another distinction:
that which arises first is "mind," that which arises next is "intellect," and that which subsequently discerns is "consciousness. This is analogous to the case of "intellect" and "consciousness."
[They] can be unified as one. [Commentary:
Those who study this school must understand both the object (*viṣaya*) and the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). If one discusses contemplation, one must clarify the three consciousnesses:
namely, the ninth *amala-vijñāna*, which is the immovable consciousness; it corresponds to the true cause of Buddha-nature and may serve as the Middle Contemplation. The eighth [consciousness]...

The ālayavijñāna is the indeterminate ignorance-consciousness; since the nature of this ignorance is the *jñāna-hetu* (revealing cause) Buddha-nature, it may be regarded as the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

The seventh consciousness, the ādānavijñāna, is the consciousness of discrimination; since its nature is that of delusion, it corresponds to the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditional cause) Buddha-nature and may be regarded as the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*).
Since these three consciousnesses are non-dual and inseparable from the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), they are...
What dharma is not subsumed within the secret treasury? Where does it not pervade?

One who cultivates the perfect contemplation will certainly be able to realize that one mind and one speck of dust—the three supreme consciousnesses—are both the wondrous principle that is revealed and the wondrous contemplation that observes.

If we discuss the objective realm (*ālambana*), we value only what is proximate and essential; it is simply the sixth consciousness of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) that serves as [the basis].

Regarding the knowledge of the wondrous three realms (*tri-viṣaya*), since the three consciousnesses have never for a moment been separated from the single seeing and single thinking, this very mind constitutes the wondrous three contemplations (*tri-vipaśyanā*) that manifest the wondrous three truths (*tri-satya*).
Although there is but a single consciousness, it has never failed to employ the three consciousnesses as the contemplation, nor has it ever failed to take the three consciousnesses as the object.
If one were to claim that our school does not clarify the three consciousnesses, but only [at the] first...

Sixth, regarding the manifestation of the principle of the three truths: if one now explains the title [of the text] and follows the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) in presenting the three consciousnesses as the "wondrous" three dharmas, what purpose would this serve?
Within a single conscious mind, by what means could there be the three truths and the three contemplations?

Therefore, it is impossible to universally perceive or discuss the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). Here, because we clarify the realm of accumulation (*sambhāra*), we cite the scriptural passages that provide a comprehensive explanation applicable even to the Lesser Vehicle.

However, in the sixth [chapter], the single dharma of mind, intellect, and consciousness is distinguished by three capacities, establishing three names according to their respective numerical categories.
That which is designated as "mind" (*citta*) is so called because it corresponds to all categories such as the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

That which is named "intellect" (*manas*) in the sense of being "that which gives rise to" is so called because it serves as the basis (*āśraya*), upon which all causes and effects arise; this is because it possesses the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Furthermore, it is distinguished as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it is able to discern and differentiate its objects of perception; thus, it is named consciousness.
Moreover, although there is only a single consciousness below [in the text], three names are established based on the differences of the three time periods.
The previous explanation concerned only a single moment, in the sense that it possesses resistance and can produce discrimination. The former was a horizontal explanation, whereas this is—
In the first explanation, the arising of atoms (*paramāṇu*) is initial, their gradual accumulation is subsequent, and their full manifestation is final; how is this not "vertical" (*ūrdhva*)?
The second explanation concerns the two natures.
[Wenju]: Regarding the "two natures," the mind has both good and evil natures; likewise, the *manas* and the *vijñāna* also possess both good and evil natures.
Because they are distinct, they are said to be "two natures.

[Commentary] Now, there are two meanings of "nature" (*xing*): first, the unchanging ultimate truth is called "nature"; second, that which follows conditions through defiled habituation is called "nature.
This statement regarding the difference in nature refers to the nature of defiled habituation. These two natures pervade the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*).
The one is entirely the two. Third, the explanation of agitation (*caukṣa*). Part one: the formal explanation of agitation. Part one: explaining by way of the primary number (*gaṇanā*).

[Text] "Agitation" means that when the mind arises before [the breath], it is also accompanied by counting; when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises after [the breath], it is also accompanied by counting.
Because both are present, it is called "restlessness.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of restlessness in terms of being dragged by karma. First, clarifying the dragging by karma.

[Text] Furthermore, when the four great elements are disintegrating, wholesome and unwholesome karmas compete to drag one along; because one does not know from which [karma] one will follow, it is called "restless."

Even when movement occurs solely through this karma that has not yet expired, the mind is constantly engaged in vitarka and vicāra; how much more so when pulled by karma—how could one not be restless?
[Commentary] Second, explaining the two types of pulling.
[Text] There is "pulling by maturation" and "pulling by force. Although one performs good deeds in this life, if the evil karma of a previous life has matured, it will manifest when its time comes.
Because one receives an evil retribution upon their union [with the next state], it is said that they are "dragged by ripening" and "dragged by force.

Although a person has committed evil, at the moment of death, if a powerful and intense wholesome mind arises, they will ascend according to that goodness; thus, being "dragged by ripening" and "dragged by force" more clearly manifests as a state of agitation.
[Commentary] Two examples explain "following karma.
[Text] It is also said that one falls into the various realms of existence by following what is produced by karma, and so forth.

[Commentary] This corresponds to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). If one understands these two types of attraction, one will know how retribution is received. Second, the explanation of conceptualization.
When the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind disperse, perish, and dissolve, the various impurities, both great and small, overflow externally;
the body becomes infested with worms, no longer desirable, and is cast away among the burial mounds like a decayed log.
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, the formal explanation of the characteristics; second, the specific explanation of the time of dispersal, extinction, and destruction.

[Text] "At the time of dispersal, extinction, and destruction by the elements of water, fire, and wind... The following two lines clarify that when karma has expired, one abandons the vessel of suffering.

Because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is exhausted, it is said to be "dispersed," as this is due to the departure of the wind element. Because the warmth (*uṣman*) is exhausted, it is said to be "extinguished," as this is due to the departure of the fire element. When the water element is exhausted... [text continues].
Because the body then rots, it is said that "the great and small impurities overflow and spread outside," and because the bones and flesh disintegrate and dissolve,
it is said to be "like a decayed piece of wood.
[Commentary] This provides two explanations for the "great and small impurities."
[Text] Regarding "large and small impurities": the body is the large; the four limbs are the small; the feet are the large; the toes are the small;
the hands are the large; the fingers are the small. Thus, as one proceeds further and further, both the large and the small are entirely foul, stinking, and impure, overflowing [with filth].
This is called "aiding the path" (aṅga).
[Commentary] It is called "aiding the path" (*mārga-sahāya*) because it is able to destroy sensual desire and establish right contemplation. Second, explaining its functional capacity:
first, explaining how it destroys desire and aids the right [path], with the first part being a brief demonstration.

[Text]: "If one correctly contemplates and subdues the afflictions (*kleśa*), yet they are not subdued, one should cultivate the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an auxiliary to destroy the mind of desire.
[Commentary]: Second, the extensive demonstration of the three [stages]. First, citing the *Śāstra* to clarify the auxiliary that supports the primary practice.
[Text] The Commentary states: "The three liberations are the gates to Nirvana; the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are the methods for opening the gates;
the nine perceptions of impurity and so forth are the auxiliary methods for opening the gates. Impurity is the primary gate for destroying desire."

[Commentary]: Regarding the "three gates of liberation," these refer to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). They are called "gates of liberation" because they lead from the three types of realization to the fruit;
liberation and nirvāṇa are one and the same entity. As for the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa-dharma*) which serve as the method for opening these gates:

in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), the sixteen aspects of contemplation constitute the three gates of liberation; in this present chapter, however, it is precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle that constitute the three gates of liberation.
If one wishes for this gate to open, one must cultivate it by means of testing and refining through the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Just as one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) within the reality of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way, so too does one test and refine through the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) up to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
The same principle applies to testing and refining the three gates of liberation and the ten benefits of the Hīnayāna; in all cases, these are accomplished through the factors of enlightenment.

The method for opening the door consists of nine contemplations: first, the contemplation of bloating; second, the contemplation of disintegration; third, the contemplation of being smeared with blood;

fourth, the contemplation of festering pus; fifth, the contemplation of bluish discoloration; sixth, the contemplation of being devoured; seventh, the contemplation of scattering; eighth, the contemplation of bones; and ninth, the contemplation of burning. If categorized according to the Hīnayāna, there are two types of persons:

first, those who destroy the person (pudgala-vināśaka), who seek only the cessation of suffering and reach the contemplation of burning to become persons liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta); second, [those who cultivate both].

When a person who does not destroy the Dharma comes to dwell upon the contemplation of the skeleton, yet does not advance to the contemplation of burning, they may attain merits such as the emission of radiant light and become a person fully endowed with both forms of liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

Herein it is clarified that when a Bodhisattva perceives the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of dhyāna, it is called "penetrating dhyāna" (*prativedha-dhyāna*), which is eternally distinct from that of the Small Vehicle.
Although the Great and Small Vehicles differ, both employ the contemplation of impurity to assist in opening the three gates of liberation; thus, they are alike in their assistance.
Because it opens up the nine perceptions of impurity to break the vanguard of desire, it is called the "Initial Gate. Second, it demonstrates the greatness of the power of progress and cultivation.

[Text] If one progresses in the cultivation of the *prātikūlyavimokṣa* (perception of repulsiveness) and the great perception of impurity—whether regarding one's own body or another's body, a single body or multiple bodies—one...

Even if the country, the many mountains and forests, the cliffs and crags, and all things—both the environment and its inhabitants—are entirely impure, and even if this is not yet the case, if the power of one's mental conception is perfected, a sense of dread will arise;
this can greatly assist the Path and bring forth right wisdom.
[Commentary] Initially, one cultivates the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and enters into the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) and the "great impurity.

Regarding what is called "great," this refers to contemplating both oneself and others; the proper name for this is the "small impurity," which consists of the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*). If one contemplates both the primary [body] and the secondary [possessions], it is called the "great impurity":
namely, regarding a house as a burial mound, money as a dead snake, soup as excrement, and rice as white [pus].
Insects on robes are like stinking hides; mountains are like heaps of flesh; ponds are like rivers of pus; groves and forests are like dry bones; and rivers, seas, and oceans are like pools of filth.
These are called the "Great Impurities" and are also termed the "Great Renunciations. "Renunciation" (pai) means turning one's back on these pure and clean five desires;
"abandonment" (she) means relinquishing the mind of attachment. Third, citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* to reveal the remedy for desire.
[Text]: The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "The contemplation of impurity is both real and false. It is called 'real' because it can destroy afflictions;
it is called 'false' because it speaks of purity as being impure."

[Commentary] This clarifies that when the power of the antidote of insight-attainment is strong, the untainted (anāsrava) state arises swiftly. Second, it clarifies how the two emptinesses assist the correct [path].
Third, first there is a general indication based on the meaning.
[Text] This contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) also possesses both the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).
[Commentary] Second, citing a sutra to provide a specific illustration.
[Text]: The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Observe minutely each joint of the white bones; which among them is 'I'? The eight-colored radiant light also lacks a self;
since the self cannot be found, this is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The person who refines the bones does not possess the eight colors."
Seeing that the four great elements have no substantial reality is precisely the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
[Commentary] "The eight kinds of colored light-flow" refers to the eight types of color: earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white.
The *Dharmadhātu-krama* states: "Seeing the color of earth is like seeing ground that is yellowish-white, pure, and clean; seeing the color of water is like..."
Deep, moist, and clear water appears as the color of fire, like a pure fire without smoke;

it appears as the color of wind, like a wind that is utterly pure and free of dust; it appears as the color blue, like a mountain of refined gold; it appears as the color yellow, like a *campaka* flower;
it appears as the color red, like the dawn clouds of spring; it appears as the color white, like conch shells or snow. (The Three Fetters)

[This] accomplishes the auxiliary [practices] for the sake of the correct [path]. [Wenju: This explains, based on the auxiliary paths, that one ultimately achieves the correct path through the arising of dharmas.

[Ji: In order to remedy desire, one cultivates the dhyāna of phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*), yet through the correct contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), one thoroughly realizes impurity.
Since the object is the dharma-dhātu, one does not perceive a provisional person within the bones or the light, nor does one perceive real dharmas;

it is only by practicing these primary and auxiliary methods in conjunction that this becomes the auxiliary method for opening [the realization] of the Mahāyāna. Second, the explanation of the contemplation of the two emptinesses of persons and dharmas.
Part One: Dividing the Text and Establishing the Meaning. First, dividing the text.

[Text] From "O virtuous daughter, you should contemplate" below, these twenty-one lines constitute the second section, clarifying the contemplation on the two emptinesses of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
This is divided into two parts: first, eight and a half lines clarify the cultivation of the causes for the two emptinesses of phenomena and persons;

second, twelve and a half lines clarify the arising of the function of the perfected fruit. Within the section on the causes, there are further two sub-sections: the first three and a half lines clarify [the emptinesses] in relation to suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

Regarding the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—the subsequent five lines beginning with "From the essence and characteristics of ignorance" clarify this contemplation by means of the twelve links of dependent origination.

This is further divided into two parts concerning suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*). First, the one and a half lines beginning with "O virtuous daughter" clarify the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Second, the two lines beginning with "Thus, these great [elements]" clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
[Commentary] II. Establishing the Thesis. 3. Part One: Clarifying the Fundamental Greatness of the Truths and Dependent Origination. A. Part One: Clarifying the Universal Greatness. 4. Part One:
Questioning from the Perspective of Exclusive Hīnayāna.

[Wenju] Question: Since the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are teachings of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), how can they be the contemplative gateways of a Bodhisattva?
[Commentary] Now, in explaining perfect emptiness (*paripūrṇa-śūnyatā*), how can one instead employ the Four Truths of the Śrāvakas and the Dependent Origination of the Pratyekabuddhas?
Second, the answer is given by way of the commonality with the Mahāyāna.

[Text] Answer: The Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are the objects of contemplation common to all three vehicles (*triyāna*), just as a great highway is used by both the noble and the lowly.
"Traveling together does not mean belonging to the same group; though they practice together, they are distinguished as belonging to the common people.
[Commentary: The Buddha taught that the Truths and Conditions apply universally to both the Great and Small Vehicles.

Since Bodhisattvas penetrate all four teachings, they are like a great public road where various groups travel together, not necessarily restricted to the Small Vehicle. Regarding the threefold question, what is the meaning of "penetration"?
It consists of four characters.
[Wenqu] What is the general meaning?
[Ji] Regarding the broad explanation of these four, the first part clarifies the universality of the Four Noble Truths.
[Text]: The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "In the past, I and you did not see the Four Noble Truths," and so forth; it further states: "Ordinary worldlings have suffering but no truth;
Śrāvakas have both suffering and the truth of suffering; Bodhisattvas understand suffering as being without suffering and possess the true truth;
the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess the true and the real. Why is this so? Because the followers of the Two Vehicles contemplate existence.
The Bodhisattva who measures the Four Truths contemplates the finite and infinite Four Truths.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "In the past," etc., it means that because the Buddha and those of the three vehicles did not perceive the true reality of the fourfold Four Truths when they were formerly ordinary beings, they wandered for a long time through the birth-and-death of the limited realm (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*). Since the verse text had not yet concluded, this is cited in full.

The commentary states: "Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have suffering but no truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). Although they encounter great suffering, they do not regard it as a calamity because they lack the discernment to know it as suffering.
"Śrāvakas have both suffering and the truth of suffering. This is because, according to the Tripiṭaka, they do not fully realize non-arising (*anutpāda*); thus, it is said they have suffering.
Because they can discern and know it [as such], they are said to possess the truth of suffering. As for "Bodhisattvas and others... [the text continues].

Regarding the statement that the three teachings—Common, Distinct, and Perfect—equally penetrate the illusory nature of phenomena and are equally able to liberate one from suffering such that there is no suffering in the very place where it arises, yet True Reality (satya) exists, Zhan’an’s Commentary states:
"True" means "genuinely real. Thus, we know this refers to the two kinds of true reality: the sequential and the non-sequential.
Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas, etc.," the fruit of Buddhahood is the ultimate perfection of the absolute reality; this is what is known.

Although the wisdom of the four teachings varies in depth, all are based upon the Four Noble Truths. Below, [the text] further cites two types of the Four Noble Truths from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* to explain and establish the preceding point.
Regarding those with "limited" capacity, such as those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, they do not know the *tathāgatagarbha*;

therefore, the Four Noble Truths they contemplate ultimately remain limited. As for Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Complete Teachings, because they have realized the nature of the *garbha*, the Four Noble Truths they contemplate... [are unlimited].

The Truths are all limitless yet simultaneously possess limits; because one who knows the profound must necessarily know the shallow, individuals of distinct capacities successively contemplate the limited and the limitless.
Those of perfect capacity contemplate the four truths in their entirety within a single thought-moment. Second, it clarifies that the conditions are universal.

[Text]: The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "There are four kinds of contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination: by contemplating with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;

by contemplating with middling wisdom, one attains that of a pratyekabuddha; by contemplating with superior wisdom, one attains that of a bodhisattva; and by contemplating with the most superior wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a Buddha."
