[When one realizes that] there is the fault of being ensnared by the net and the error of being covered by darkness, and understands that the aggregates are empty and quiescent such that the veil of darkness cannot cover them,
and the net is torn asunder so that the snare cannot obstruct— this is the accomplishment of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

[Commentary] To explain the ten *paryavasthānas* (entanglements) individually: anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), resentment (*upānāha*), and malice (*pradāśa*) are called "anger.
Hiding one's own transgressions is called "concealment. The dulling of the mental consciousness is called "torpor," while the darkening of the five sense-faculties is called "sleep.

Indulgence in play is called "restlessness," and the agitation of the three types of action (*kāya-vāk-manas-karman*) is called "excitement. To commit a fault in private and not feel shame for it is [lack of shame].

It is said: "Lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*) refers to committing what is improper in public without feeling bashful before others; "lack of remorse" (*anapatrāpya*) refers to being unable to bestow wealth or the Dharma through generosity;

"avarice" (*mātsarya*) refers to the heart being tormented by distress at the prosperity of others; "envy" (*īrṣyā*) [is likewise so named]. These are afflictions (*kleśa*), which here specifically refers to the delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*).

Although both the delusions of insight (*darśana-heya*) and the delusions of thought are collectively termed afflictions, they are distinguished here such that the term applies specifically to the delusions of thought. "Ensnarement" (*pāśa*) means to bind. This second section explains [the afflictions] according to the Great and Small Vehicles.

**Section Two: Discussing the Exhaustion and Non-exhaustion of the Two [Types of] Severance; First, Clarifying that the Severance of the Two Vehicles is General while that of the Bodhisattva is Specific.** [Textual Commentary]:

That which is severed by the Two Vehicles is general *dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* (afflictions of views), whereas that severed by the Bodhisattva is specific *dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*. As stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*:

"If the knots and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers will immediately adhere to the body. This means that because the specific views have not been severed, one is adhered to by the flowers.
[Commentary]: All the names and categories of afflictions within the realm (*dhātu*) also apply to that which is outside the realm;

however, by distinguishing them through the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that serves as their obstruction, one understands their commonality and distinction. Regarding the "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti), when the celestial maidens scattered flowers, the Śrāvakas were touched by them while the Bodhisattvas were not.

Thus he was rebuked, saying: "Because the habit-energies of the fetters (*kleśa-vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers adhere to your bodies. This refers to the severing of the common [afflictions].

It has not yet been possible to distinguish them. Second, the clarification that in the Buddha-ground both the general and the specific are entirely forgotten, which consists of two parts; first, the formal demonstration.
[Text] It is said that the Buddha severs the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); whether generally or specifically, their ultimate exhaustion resides solely in the Buddha.
[Commentary]: Although it is said that Bodhisattvas can sever specific views (*pṛthag-dṛṣṭi*), their severance is not yet ultimate; such perfection resides only in the Buddha.
If one reaches the stage of Buddhahood, not only are specific views exhausted, but pervasive views (*sāmānya-dṛṣṭi*) are also brought to their limit. Why is this?

It is because these [views] are accomplished through the various seeds and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the sentient beings within the six realms throughout the ten directions; thus, they were not yet fully severed during the causal stage.
Since only a Buddha reaches the ultimate limit, it is said that whether generally or specifically, the ultimate lies in the Buddha. Second, the citation of proof.
[Wénjù] The Śāstra says: "Among sentient beings, the unsurpassed is the Buddha; among dharmas, the unsurpassed is Nirvāṇa. There is no other.
It is said that [the Bodhisattva] has severed [delusion] because he is no longer confused regarding the provisional and real stages of Buddhahood.

[Commentary: Regarding the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) that give rise to the essence of phenomena, which are fundamentally non-existent, there are both general and specific attachments to defilement; thus, they become inferior.

At the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimalā-bodhi*), these two types of attachment are exhausted, and since both are now supreme, it is called "supreme" (*anuttara*). It is said that he is "not confused" regarding the provisional and real stages of Buddhahood.

Second, explaining that in the Buddha-ground there is both abandonment and non-abandonment. First, clarifying the differing explanations in the sutras and treatises. First, clarifying that there is abandonment.
[Text] The sutras and treatises differ; some say that the Buddha’s supreme wisdom abandons the most inferior delusions, for the power of ignorance is great.

The Buddha’s wisdom can sever the wisdom associated with a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*), such that both the primary afflictions and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are exhausted without remainder.
[Commentary] Wisdom is supreme because its awakening is ultimate; delusion is supreme because its confusion is ultimate.
Now, as delusion is about to be exhausted and only the most subtle remains, it is designated as "lowest of the low. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the awakened mind first arises..."
The mind has no initial characteristic because it is far removed from subtle conceptualization; thus, the mind is eternally abiding.
Because delusion is subtle, it is difficult to discern and difficult to eliminate; therefore, only the highest of high wisdom can sever it completely.

Even though the delusions of the lowest of low grades are subtle, the power of ignorance is so great that they can obstruct wondrous enlightenment. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies the qualities possessed by the consecrated Bodhisattvas.
The merit [of the preceding stages] is like a single clod of earth, while the merit of wondrous enlightenment is like the soil of the four continents.
The obstruction of the final ignorance is such that how could its power not be great? It is not the Buddha-wisdom that gives rise to these delusions;

rather, it is the wisdom corresponding to non-forgetfulness of even a single thought that constitutes ultimate awakening. "The simultaneous exhaustion of both the two kinds of habituation" encompasses both the general and the specific. (2)
[The text] clarifies that there is no severance.
[Wenqu]: Some say that those who possess a superior state are called "those who have severed," while those who possess the unsurpassed state are called "those who have nothing to sever.

[Ji]: "Those who possess a superior state" refers to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi). At this stage, one must cultivate pure meditative concentration (dhyāna) to sever subtle [defilements].

Because he is mindful, he is called the Unsurpassed One who has severed [all defilements]. This refers to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); since cultivation and realization have both been forgotten, what further remains to be severed?
Second, the two applications are harmonized through the *siddhānta*.
[Text]: "This is beneficial according to the country, the time, the person, and the realization," and so forth. [Commentary]:
Regarding these views of "severance" and "non-severance," the teachers who rely on the scriptural texts hold to their respective positions and their disputes do not cease.

Now, by employing the four *siddhāntas* to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings, I shall harmonize them; thus, there is no basis for dispute to arise. "Country" refers to the geographical domain.
When sentient beings, according to their capacities and wherever they dwell, joyfully seek to hear of the Buddha’s wisdom— whether it involves cessation or non-cessation— at that time,
one should provide the appropriate remedy according to the occasion. For those who would destroy evil through the meaning of either cessation or non-cessation,
and for those who would give rise to goodness through either cessation or non-cessation according to what is suitable for each person, awakening constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For those who enter the principle through awakening—whether with or without severing [afflictions]—these four capacities are taught; this has two meanings when investigated:
first, that the Buddha’s wisdom is beyond words and thought; second, to clarify the fulfillment of the two paths: the direct and the auxiliary.
[Text]: "The realization of the Unsurpassed Way" refers to the fulfillment of the correct path of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena (*utpatti-dharma-śūnyatā*).
"Subtle and wondrous merit" refers to the fulfillment of the auxiliary path of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena.
[Commentary] The realization of the dharma of unsurpassed birth arises from the two kinds of emptiness; thus it is called the "unsurpassed path.
Because the auxiliary practices are conjoined with and cultivated alongside the primary [path], they are termed "sublime virtues. Second, the perfection of the virtue of abandonment is explained.
He opens the gate of ambrosia, displays the vessel of ambrosia, enters the city of ambrosia, and dwells in the chamber of ambrosia, causing all sentient beings to partake of the flavor of ambrosia.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first, a brief explanation of ambrosia.

[Text] The line and a half beginning with "Opening the gate of ambrosia" clarifies the perfection of the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*). Ambrosia is the divine medicine of immortality for the various devas;
those who consume it have long lives, their bodies are at ease, their strength is great, and their physical radiance is vast.
This is used as an analogy for the Buddhas' virtue of cessation, which abides in Great Nirvāṇa—true, eternal, blissful, self, and pure—thereby making known that this virtue of cessation is perfected.
[Commentary] The four [qualities], beginning with life, correspond respectively to permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Second, the detailed explanation of the various phrases has four parts;
first, the correspondence with the four stages of the *Avataṃsaka*, which begins with the direct correspondence.
[Text] However, the meaning of this passage further intends to universally correspond to the various stages (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

It says "opening" because it opens the gate of ambrosia at the initial stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), thereby blocking the two extremes and revealing the noble path. It shows "displaying" in correspondence with the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), manifesting them individually.

It refers to "entering" in correspondence with the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), whereby one turns toward phenomena and enters into principle (*tattva*). It refers to "abiding" in correspondence with the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).
The Dharma-nature is the chamber; as for the flavor of the food, the Subtle Enlightenment partakes of this flavor itself and simultaneously bestows it upon others.
[Commentary] Although that [teaching] includes both the distinct and the perfect, here we take the perfect because the thirty distinct stages have not yet attained the ambrosia.
2. Dispelling Doubts.
[Wenqu]: It is not that those on the lower stages do not transform others; however, their own practice is not yet perfected, and their transformation is not yet extensive.

On the Buddha-ground, the fruit is perfected, the merit of cessation is fulfilled, and the power of compassion is great, such that one can open up the Ten Abidings and demonstrate the Ten Practices for the sake of sentient beings.

Entering the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśamī-bhūmi-praṇidhāna*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one partakes of the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta-rasa*), becomes fully endowed with the requisites of merit, and achieves both the virtue of severing [defilements] and the transformation of others;
thus, both purposes are fulfilled.
[Commentary] This is explained because there may be doubts among later generations. "Transforming others" means causing them to attain what one has oneself attained. (2) Pairing.
The Four Wisdoms of Prajñā. [Commentary]:

Furthermore, these correspond respectively to the four wisdoms of prajñā: opening corresponds to the wisdom of the path (mārgajñatā), showing corresponds to the wisdom of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), entering corresponds to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), and the locus corresponds to the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
The flavor of food corresponds to the Buddha’s dwelling in Great Parinirvāṇa. Based on this...

"Compassion causes sentient beings to attain these four wisdoms; even at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), there is no hindrance to the meaning of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*)," and so forth.

[Commentary] Although the treatise provides many explanations, they still pertain generally to the three vehicles (*triyāna*). However, since these four are all spoken of in terms of the "Ambrosia" (*amṛta*), they specifically belong to the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).
By means of the three wisdoms within one mind (*ekacitta-trijñāna*) to dissolve all marks, it is called the Wisdom of the Path (*mārgajñatā*); opening the gate of the three wisdoms within one mind...

The wisdom that establishes the names of all phenomena is called the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths); it is shown as the vessel where the three wisdoms are unified, simultaneously negating and establishing, and is named *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
Entering the city, the three wisdoms are unified, simultaneously illuminating and establishing, and is named *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all modes).
By means of these four wisdoms abiding in Great Nirvana, all sentient beings are enabled to attain these four wisdoms; this is what is meant by "attaining."
This refers to the flavor of the teaching. Regarding the three points corresponding to the great matter of the *Lotus Sūtra* [Wenqu]:
Furthermore, it corresponds to the *Lotus Sūtra*’s opening, showing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is because the Buddha’s virtues are perfected;
he appears in the world for the sake of this great causal matter to open and show the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings.
The meaning of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is also clearly revealed.
[Commentary: That Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the present nectar (*amṛta*).

Regarding the opening and so forth of that [nirvāṇa], when contrasted with the present four phrases, there is only a slight difference in the point of entry and realization; their essential meaning is not distinct. These four correspond to the four virtues of nirvāṇa.
[Text]: Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" are most conducive to the fruit of cessation (*phala-prahāṇa*), as explained previously, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Previously, the four virtues were used to explain the meaning of "ambrosia" (*amṛta*); now, these four virtues are applied in contrast to the text concerning "opening" (*apāvaraṇa*) and so on—this is the difference.

Second, explaining the transformation of others (*parārtha*) is divided into two parts: first, dividing the text and establishing the intent; second, the division of the text itself. First, the division of the text.
[Text] "Blowing the Great Dharma Conch" and the following nine lines clarify the fulfillment of transforming others at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). This section is divided into two parts:

first, two lines on transforming others by turning the wheel of the Dharma; second, seven lines on transforming others through the Four Great Vows. Furthermore, within the teaching of the Dharma, there are two sub-sections:
first, one line on the teaching of the Dharma; second, one line on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
[Commentary] Regarding the two meanings of "intention," the first clarifies how wisdom and meditative concentration mutually establish one another.

[Text] In other sutras, the supernatural powers at the beginning startle beings so as to open the way for the subsequent preaching of the Dharma; in this sutra, the supernatural powers at the end complete the preceding preaching of the Dharma. Thus it is.

[Commentary]: The first manifestation of supernatural power causes those who revere the Dharma to hear it with joy; the subsequent manifestation of supernatural power causes them to practice and realize according to the Dharma.

Therefore, the former is said to "open" the way for the latter, and the latter is said to "accomplish" what was initiated by the former. Second, this clarifies that cause and effect are of the same kind.

[Text]: During the stage of cultivating the causes, one attains the correct wisdom of the two emptinesses—of persons and phenomena; upon attaining the fruit, because the perfection of knowledge and virtue is achieved, one is able to preach the Dharma to transform others.

During the stage of cultivating the causes, one attains the auxiliary path of the two emptinesses—of persons and phenomena; upon attaining the fruit, because the perfection of the abandonment of defilements is achieved, one is able to use supernormal powers to transform others.

[Commentary] The direct path of the two emptinesses constitutes the category of the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), while the auxiliary path of the two emptinesses constitutes the category of the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
That is to say, the two causes—conditions and fulfillment—do not establish the two fruits apart from these two causes. Second, the explanation of the text according to its meaning has two parts:
first, clarifying the turning of the wheel of Dharma to transform others; second, first clarifying the preaching of the Dharma.
He blows the great Dharma conch, beats the great Dharma drum, kindles the great Dharma torch, and rains down the supreme Dharma rain.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first is the general indication.
[Wenju] Regarding the citation of four similes for the preaching of the Dharma: the benefits of hearing the Dharma are truly immeasurable, yet these four similes are cited by way of abbreviation.
There is another intended meaning.

[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the separate explanation, there are two sections: first, the separate clarification of the conch and so forth; second, the explanation according to the stages of the teaching. Within the first section, there are four parts:
first, the explanation of the four propositions; first, the clarification of blowing the conch.

[Text] Blowing the conch is a metaphor for changing one’s designation: it refers to the Buddha preaching the *Hīnayāna* Dharma to change the ordinary nature of suffering-tolerance of a common person into the correct nature of a sage;
preaching the *Mahāyāna* Dharma to change the partial natures of both the ordinary and the sage into the perfect nature of the Middle Way.

In the seventh stage of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāptika-yāna*), the first stage of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), and the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), there is likewise this "changing."
The position of the title [of "Patience"] enters from the partial into the central.
[Commentary] This refers to the "Great Sūtra" which says, "Blowing the conch to know the time. Regarding "the nature of an ordinary person at the stage of Patience with Suffering":

this refers to the stage of the "Superior Patience" among the internal ordinary persons (inner-worldly ordinary persons), wherein, regarding the Truth of Suffering, one retains one aspect and one object; this is the nature of an ordinary person.

Furthermore, the "correct nature" (*samyak-prakṛti*) of the sages refers to the first fruit (*prathamaphala*). Those who expound the Mahāyāna Dharma take only the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) as the Mahāyāna.

The "partial natures" (*pianxing*) of ordinary beings and sages refer to the six stages of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*); the ten stages of dedication (*shixiang*) of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) and the ten stages of faith (*shixin*) of the Perfect Teaching are considered "inner ordinary beings.
Because the Middle Truth has not yet been manifested, they are all termed partial natures. This refers to the seventh stage of the Shared Teaching.
Those who reach this point come to know that those who are "perfect" (en) are all at the stage of changing their names;
these three individuals have both shattered ignorance and perceived the perfect nature of the Middle Way. Second, the striking of the drum is explained.

【Text】 "One who beats the great Dharma-drum" refers to beating the drum to admonish and urge the assembly forward as a vanguard. This is a metaphor for the Buddha preaching the Dharma to supervise and encourage deep practice:
in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), this corresponds to the stage of Cultivating the Path; in the Shared Teaching (Pāṭha-sādhāraṇa), it corresponds to the eighth stage;

in the Distinct Teaching (Pratyeka-bhūmi), it corresponds to the ten practices; and in the Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna), it corresponds to the first dwelling. In all these stages, through the power of hearing the Dharma, one collectively advances toward true cultivation of the Path.
[Commentary] "Exhorting to advance" refers to the laws of military formation. The *Art of War* states: "Upon hearing the drum, advance; upon hearing the gong, halt.
The drum is used to maintain the solemnity of the troops and to lead them forward; it signifies supervision and guidance, where "guidance" means leading the way.

In the context of those cultivating the Path, this refers to commanding those at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) to advance toward the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*). In the context of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*), it refers to those at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

The commentary revises the title [of the stage] as follows: breaking through ignorance at the seventh ground and now entering the eighth ground is, according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), called "increasing the path and diminishing births" (*zēngdào xiānshēng*);
according to the Perfect Teaching (yuánjiào), it should be called "entering the second dwelling" (*èrzhù*) to be termed "entering the path of cultivation" (*xiūdào*).

The current statement that this occurs at the beginning of the ten practices (*shíxíng*) or the first dwelling (*chūzhù*) is likely an error. Alternatively, there may be another intention: those who truly cultivate the path do so by means of penetration (*tōng*).

Regarding the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), there are two types: the distinct stages and the perfect stages. Because they both involve advancing through the stages, the *Jin-di lun* (Treatise on Advancing through the Stages) states that the first stage constitutes the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the second through the seventh stages constitute the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages constitute the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
Although these are distinct positions, the principle for the perfect stages can be understood by analogy. Third, the explanation of the "kindling of the torch."

【Text】 "To greatly kindle the torch of the Great Dharma" means that a torch can illuminate itself and also illuminate others; it is like the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, which brings benefit to both self and others.
Just as a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a room for a thousand years, or as one lamp can ignite hundreds of thousands of lamps, so too is the power of hearing the Dharma:
it benefits both oneself and others. This corresponds to the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*) and the [first] stage of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi*).

In the Tenfold Dedication of the Complete Teaching (*yuanjiao*), this stage is also situated within the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*); it is a position where the path and contemplation flow together, benefiting both self and others.
[Commentary] In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), all subsequent stages are taken as positions for transforming others; here, the eighth ground (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) is not taken as such.
The connection here refers simply to the path of emerging into the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the simultaneous flow of both [wisdom and means] as they appear in this specific teaching;

separately, regarding the ten stages of approach (*daśabhūmi*), the intent is likewise the same, because while one internally cultivates the Middle Way, one externally also emerges into the provisional. As for the Perfect [Teaching] being present from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), it is because one acts as a Buddha through the hundred realms, manifesting universally via the Gate of Universal Doors (*samantamukha*).
Since the Perfect is explained from the perspective of its excellence, it takes the "partial realization" (*bhūta-akṣaya*) of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and names it "True."

This refers to the stage of emerging from the provisional (*jia*). All of these are lower-level conclusions indicating the three stages. "Way" (*dao*) refers to external transformation; "contemplation" (*guan*) refers to internal practice.
This encompasses the differences among the three teachings, whereas the remaining text speaks only in terms of the Shared Teaching (*tong*). Fourth, the explanation of "rain upon rain."
[Text]: "To rain down the supreme Dharma-rain" means that this rain can bring to maturity those who have labored like farmers;
though their efforts may be sparse, when the timely moisture falls once, flowers and fruits flourish.

This is a metaphor for how, although one may diligently cultivate various practices, if the power of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) is weak, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, one increases the Path and diminishes birth, maturing spontaneously and naturally flowing into *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

The ocean is like a great river; a boat within it does not require strenuous physical effort to reach its destination swiftly, as all such things belong to the stage of the "two concurrent streams" (*śrota-āpanna*), the meaning of which has been explained above.
[Commentary] "Fushu" means lush and flourishing. "Shizai" refers to seasonal moisture and rain. The "Great Ganges" is the Gaṅgā River.
Second, applying these principles to the four aforementioned sutras.

[Wenju] If one grasps this underlying principle, then the four stages of the *Avataṃsaka*, the four wisdoms of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the four types of knowledge and vision of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
and the four virtues of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* can all be understood accordingly.
[Commentary] Second, [the text] concludes by means of both the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
[Wenju] This single Dharma is vertically aligned with the positions found in various sutras, while horizontally it encompasses all stages;
thus, upon hearing the sound of the Dharma, each according to their kind attains understanding, and so forth.

[Commentary] "Vertically aligning the stages with various sūtras" means that although the names of the four aforementioned sūtras differ, they are merely the stages of abiding, practice, direction, ground, and fulfillment;

therefore, they are called "vertical. "Discussing all stages horizontally" refers to subsuming all the stages of ordinary and sage beings within the four teachings, as was explained above in the commentary on the text, and so forth.
The section belongs to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class.
Therefore, this transformation of others necessarily encompasses the four benefits, and the horizontal inclusion of all stages is intended to be contained therein.
Second, the general explanation of the great meaning.
[Text] Herein, the four analogies all speak of "great" because they expound the Great Dharma; this general explanation clarifies its greatness.
It is not so for those in the minor stages.
[Commentary] The first three are called "Great" (*mahā*), and the last one is called "Supreme and Great" (*parama-mahā*); therefore, it is said that all are termed "Great.
Generally speaking, if one takes the common name, it applies only to the Great Dharma; in terms of meaning, they all converge in the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*), as opposed to the four scriptures.
This meaning is all the more consistent. Second, the supernormal powers (abhijñā) are clarified:
"I now subdue all fetters of enmity and erect the foremost, most subtle banner of the Dharma.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first clarifies the subduing of enmity, which in turn has two parts. First, it clarifies that afflictions (kleśa) constitute enmity.

[Text]: "I now subdue and overcome... and so forth. This refers to the transformation of others through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The "knots of enmity" (*vaira-grantha*) consist of the four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra*), which are the knots of enmity for the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*);
the fifth stage of abiding is the knot of enmity for Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary] Second, it clarifies that the Heavenly Mara is the master.
[Wenqu] Mara is the master of afflictions; to fell a tree, one must remove its roots. To transform sentient beings, one must subdue the master.

If the Mara is not subdued, the path of transformation will not flourish. The method for subduing Mara requires the use of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); it is like being able to act as a victor only after having conquered the enemy.
When the victorious Dharma-king who is invincible to the unrighteous kings of violence establishes the path of transformation at that time, [it is so].
[Commentary] Second, explaining the erecting of the banner.
[Textual Exegesis] To erect the Dharma-banner means the Samādhi of the Dharma-banner; it rises high above all practices and serves as the object of aspiration for all practices.
It is like soldiers looking toward their banner. Because the three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, they are called "subtle and wondrous.

[Commentary] To rise above all practices is the Samādhi of the Dharma Banner (*dharmadhvaja-samādhi*). All the merits of the myriad practices take this samādhi as their sovereign to which they do not fail to return;

thus, it is the point of reference for all practices. "Like soldiers looking toward their banner" means that just as soldiers look to their banner for direction, so too do these practices look to this samādhi.

The *Shouzhǐ* (Pointing with the Finger) says: "The Minister of State (Shàngshū) holds the yellow battle-axe in his left hand and grasps the white banner in his right, and with it he waves [to command].

Regarding military authority (*bīngquán*), it is said that the General grasps the banner and waves it to exhort the multitude; furthermore, it is said that upon hearing the drum they advance, and upon hearing the gong they halt, following his directions and commands.
The *Wǔhuái* (Five Contemplations) thus brings order, and the *Sāndé* (Three Virtues) emerges below from the essence of the *Sānmèi* (Three Samādhis). One should embody this.
If the essence were neither vertical nor horizontal, how could it transcend the various practices, how could it destroy the five abodes, and how could it subdue the devas of the celestial realm?
Such is the nature and function of the indeterminate supernormal powers. Second, the explanation of the Four Great Vows for transforming others;
first, the removal of textual obscurities to reveal the meaning.

[Text]: The seven lines following "From delivering all sentient beings" constitute the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) for transforming others. Although the fruits have already been realized, the original vows do not cease;
therefore, it is said that the four great vows benefit beings, and they are also called the four truths (*caturāryasatya*) benefiting beings.
The four great vows are the mind of the vow, while the four truths are the objects of focus.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Although... and so forth: since one proceeds according to the Four Noble Truths by means of the Four Great Vows, and the Four Noble Truths are eternal, how could the vows ever cease?
Because the person seeks Buddhahood with the intent to benefit sentient beings, and now that this goal has been attained, how could they forget to grant salvation and deliverance?

The Four Great Vows are shown here as having a basis; these vows are none other than unconditional compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), and their object is the unconditioned Four Noble Truths (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya*).
Without conditions and without effort, how can one vow to deliver sentient beings from birth-and-death into nirvāṇa?
It is because afflictions are themselves bodhi; it is because one vows to study the Dharma-gates so that delusions become wisdom;
it is because one vows to accomplish the Buddha-way so that birth becomes cessation. Otherwise, how could one extensively deliver and eternally deliver them? Second, following...
The Exegesis of the Text, Part Four: First, causing [beings] to transcend the Truth of Suffering.
To cause all sentient beings to cross over the ocean of birth and death, forever severing the immeasurable suffering and affliction of the three evil realms. [Wenju]:

"Causing all sentient beings to cross over" is the first of the great vows; it is also the act of causing those who have not yet crossed over the Truth of Suffering to transcend that Truth of Suffering.
[Commentary] The sūtra states that the three evil paths are "permanently severed. This must be discussed in terms of the ten stages of crossing over and severing.
Second, it causes the cessation of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The afflictions burn fiercely, scorching all sentient beings; there is no rescue or protection, and they have no place of refuge.

[Commentary on the Text] The first line, "The afflictions burn fiercely," is the second great vow; it also signifies that while the Truth of Origination has not yet been severed, one vows to bring about its cessation.
[Commentary] It must be understood that the five stages of dwelling burn away the births within the ten realms. The third [stage] causes one to realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
I satisfy these beings with the sweet flavor of the cool, refreshing nectar (*amṛta*), causing them to be free from the feverish heat of affliction.

[Text] The single line beginning with "From me, the ambrosia... is the third great vow; it is also that which causes those who have not yet realized the Truth of Cessation to realize the Truth of Cessation.
[Commentary] When discussed within their respective sections, there are four kinds of ambrosia; when analyzed across the divisions, there is only one perfect and eternal [ambrosia]. (4)
They cause them to rest in the Noble Truths;
for immeasurable eons, they practice all various deeds, making offerings to and revering the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
and steadfastly cultivating the path to Bodhi, seeking the Tathāgata’s true Dharma-body by relinquishing all that is cherished, including their limbs, joints, hands, and feet.

[The text includes] his head, eyes, marrow, and brain; his beloved wife and children; his wealth, money, and precious treasures; pearls, necklaces, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and various other diverse objects.
[Commentary: The text consists of four parts; the first explains the truths by means of *dāna* (generosity).

[Text] From "Throughout immeasurable kalpas" onwards, these four lines constitute the fourth great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). This also refers to those who have not yet established themselves in the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) and brings them to rest therein.
Here, giving (*dāna*) is identified with the Four Noble Truths: giving stands in opposition to stinginess (*mātsarya*). Stinginess and greed are that which obscures oneself;

they are the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), for through the karma of origination, the fruit of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is summoned. Giving can destroy stinginess, which is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*); the extinction of stinginess is [the Truth of Cessation].

The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). [Commentary: It is not only in the practice of *dāna* that this is so; it applies equally to all four truths and five perfections (*pāramitā*). If these five do not rely upon the truths, they will neither be unmoving nor emerge; how, then, could there be any perfection?
Furthermore, one must know that here we rely on the truth of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-satya*). This concludes the brief explanation of the two.
The Scripture Text:
[Commentary on the Words] "Immeasurable kalpas" refers to the height of accumulated merit; "practicing all various deeds" refers to the breadth of the encompassed dharmas.
[Record] The three *dānas* (giving) encompass the six *pāramitās* (perfections).
[Text] The treatise states: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses the six [perfections]," and so forth.

[Commentary] In the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Dānapāramitā* is explained as follows: "If a bodhisattva practices the perfection of generosity and is able to give rise to the six perfections, at that time it is called the fulfillment of the perfection of generosity.
How does giving give rise to the perfection of generosity? There are inferior, middling, and superior [levels]. If, by means of...
Giving coarse food and drink with a gentle heart is called the lower [level of] *dāna*; being able to give clothing and precious objects is called the middle *dāna*;
and being able to give one's head, eyes, blood, flesh, kingdom, wealth, wife, and children is called the upper [level]. How does giving give rise to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*)?
The Bodhisattva reflects that sentient beings do not know of the poverty of future lives, and therefore practices [generosity].
If one practices giving with an evil mind, yet in future lives possesses merit and lacks nothing, then one is able to maintain the precepts.

How does one give rise to patience? When a Bodhisattva practices giving, if the recipient insults him, or asks for too much, or asks at an improper time, or asks for what should not be asked, at that moment the Bodhisattva reflects:
"I am now practicing giving because I desire to seek Buddhahood."
The Path likewise has no person who causes me to practice giving; it is for my own sake that I do so. How could anger arise?

Having reflected thus, one practices patience. How could laziness arise? When a Bodhisattva practices giving, they constantly exercise diligence, desiring to practice both types of giving—generosity with material things and generosity with the Dharma—and diligently seek wealth and the Dharma to achieve fulfillment. How could distraction arise? When practicing the perfection of meditation...

When a bodhisattva practices giving, they are able to eliminate stinginess and greed, cultivate a single-minded mind, and remove the five hindrances through a sense of shame; this is called the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā).

Furthermore, with the mind relying on giving, they enter the first dhyāna and proceed up to the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); how is it that this gives rise to the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā)?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they know there is a karmic fruit and harbor no doubt, thereby being able to destroy wrong views and ignorance. Moreover—

The differentiation between pure and impure giving results in different rewards; this is called the arising of wisdom. Therefore, it is said that the meaning of *dāna* (generosity) subsumes the six perfections.

Although the other five perfections also mutually subsume one another, they are not the intent of the present text; thus, we shall discuss only *dāna*. As the foremost of the six, it subsumes [the others] with ease.
Fourth, the section concludes with "the other shore" (*pāramitā*).
[Text]: To relinquish body, life, and wealth so that they are equal to the future limit (paścimakoṭi), attaining the indestructible and eternally abiding—this is called a *pāramitā*.
Because it is high vertically and broad horizontally, it is said that one "practices all deeds" (*sarvacaryā*).

[Commentary]: Birth and death constitute the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), and nirvāṇa constitutes the posterior limit (*aparākoṭi*). The body, life, and wealth—these three belong to the category of objective phenomena (*vastu*).

By contemplating these three, as well as the mind that gives and the object to which one gives—the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*)—one realizes that they are, in their very place, empty, provisional, and the Middle Way.
Therefore, through these three virtues of equality, one attains nirvāṇa. This is not achieved by means of a permanent cause producing a permanent fruit.
How could one fail to destroy the permanent and enduring? Practicing *dāna* (generosity) in this manner is called a *pāramitā*.

Because its three virtues are profoundly deep, *dāna* rises high; because its three virtues are immeasurable, *dāna* extends wide. Since these sentient beings delight in brevity, the Tathāgata skillfully taught this single *dāna*;
yet, while following and cultivating all practices, one must still understand that once the fruit has been discussed, the subsequent practice of *dāna* brings benefit.
When one encounters such things, how could one not hear them and immediately practice accordingly?
*Jinguangming jing wenshu wenshu ji* (Commentary on the Words and Phrases of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*), Combined Edition, Volume Five,
Phonetic Glossary.

[Sūtra] *Xiǎn* (pronounced xiān; meaning "few" or "scarce"). *Chěng* (pronounced chèn; meaning "to gallop" or "to race"). *Qiè* (pronounced qiè; meaning "a small box" or "a chest"). *Zhī* (pronounced zhī; meaning "limbs," specifically the four limbs of the body: hands and feet).

【Text】 *Śat* (pronounced "yè," meaning iron sheet). *Huò* (cut with *hú guō*). *Jìn* (pronounced "xìn," meaning the residue of embers or flames). *Guàn* (pronounced "juàn," meaning to entangle, hang, or bind/capture).
*Jīn* (pronounced "jīn," meaning the strength of muscle). *Huī* (pronounced "huī," meaning to signal with a banner or flag). *Máo* (pronounced "máo").

[Commentary]: *Pao* (pronounced *bào*) refers to blisters, where the skin of the face swells with qi. *Ning* (pronounced *níng*) refers to the cessation of [disease]. *Zhàng* (pronounced *zhàng*) means distension or swelling. *Yù* (pronounced *yù*) refers to accumulated blood or clots.

*Shī* (pronounced *shǐ*) means excrement. *Ruǎn* (pronounced *ruǎn*) refers to wriggling insects. *Áo* (pronounced *áo*) refers to the legs of a crab. *Qí* (pronounced *qí*) refers to the mane on the neck of a horse.
*Téng* (pronounced *téng*) refers to a pen where pigs lie down. *Zhé-xiè* (*zhé* pronounced *zhé*; *xiè* pronounced *dié*): *xiè* refers to layered clothing.
The Combined Edition of the *Wenju* and *Wenju Ji* of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang;
the *Wenju* expounded by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai and recorded by his disciple Guǎngdìng.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Siming;
the Śramaṇa Mingde of Shuangjing compiled the combined text and recorded it alongside the sūtra.
[Commentary] Regarding the three major chapters of the *Fenliuxing* (Circulation) section, the first part consists of four sections. First is the title of the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings."
The Sixth Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" [Commentary].
The text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the causal conditions; second, the explanation of the persons by way of their locations. First, the clarification of the locations.
[Text]: "The Four Heavenly Kings are the foremost of those who ascend and the first among the celestial abodes of the lower realm; they occupy half of Mount Sumeru. [Commentary]:
Among the twenty-eight heavens, all belong to the realm of ascent, and these [Four Kings] constitute its head. When the three realms are divided, this [lower realm] is at the beginning;
furthermore, regarding their location, they occupy half of Mount Sumeru, which is the basis for the six heavens of the desire realm.

Regarding the heavens: the two [lower] heavens rely on Mount Sumeru, while the Trāyastriṃśa dwell upon its summit; the Four Great Kings reside halfway up. In the Sanskrit language, it is called Sumeru;
here [in Chinese], it is translated as "Wondrously Exalted. It rises eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the water and is composed of four precious substances. Second, the emergence of humans.
[Text] The king of the eastern golden terrace is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; this translates as "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó). He governs the gandharvas and pūtanas.
The king of the southern lapis lazuli terrace is named Virūḍhaka; this translates as "Increasing" (Zēngzhǎng). He governs the kumbhāṇḍas and piśācas.
The king of the western silver terrace is named Virūpākṣa; this translates as "Diverse Speech" (Záyǔ).
He leads the *piśāca* and venomous *nāgas*; the king of the northern crystal terrace is named Vaiśravaṇa, which translates as "Much-Hearing" (*Bahuśruta*).
He leads the *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas*.
[Commentary] "Dhṛtarāṣṭra" means he protects and sustains the land. *Gandharva* is translated as "Fragrance-Seeker. He is a Heavenly Lord (*Devarāja*).
*Sulaka* means a deity; *Pūtana* means a "stench-demon" (*chou e-kuai*), the most eminent among hungry ghosts, or as some say, a ghost that presides over fever diseases.
*Cūḍanikā* means "one who causes increase," so called because they cause the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of oneself and others to flourish.
*Kumbhāṇḍa* means "jar-shaped"; they resemble a winter melon and are ghosts who practice sorcery and bewitchment (*yanchen-mei*). *Pretas* means "ancestral ghosts."
The most inferior among the *preta* (hungry ghosts) are the *pralāpaka* (those who speak incoherently), so called because they can utter various kinds of speech.
The *piśāca*—translated here as "ghosts that devour vital essence"—consume the vital essence of humans and the five grains; they are also called "mad ghosts.
*Vaiśravaṇa* is translated as "Much-Hearing," for his fame and merit are renowned in the four directions. *Yakṣa* is translated as...
Because they are light, agile, and swift as they fly through the air, the *rākṣasas*—which means "the terrifying" in Chinese—are also called "the violent and evil.
Second, the purpose of this section.
[Wenju]: Upon hearing this sutra, these Four Kings were filled with joy; each led five hundred attendants and made a vow to protect the sutra. From...
Because this serves as the heading [for the section], it is titled "The Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings.
[Commentary: Regarding the second part, the explanation of the three types of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), this section relies upon concrete phenomena (*vastu*).

This is because both the objects and the wisdom [of these practices] are each established by borrowing from the meanings of specific phenomena. One must understand that reliance upon phenomena often involves the inclusion of doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), such as the case of the city of Rājagṛha.
Furthermore, observing the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) represents Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as the manifestation of the three virtues; how do these five and three differ from the four truths?

This is precisely the method of clarifying the objective realm and contemplation by relying on the events of resonance and response. It is divided into two parts: first, showing the characteristics of contemplation.

[Text] Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: the principles of the Four Noble Truths—Suffering in the East, Origin in the South, Cessation in the West, and the Path in the North—are the four heavens.

The wisdom that realizes the Four Noble Truths constitutes the Four Heavenly Kings. Protecting the realm of the Four Noble Truths is called "Protecting the Country. Protecting the mental factors is "Protecting Sentient Beings. "The World" refers to others; teaching the mental factors to others is called "Protecting Other Sentient Beings. The "Eight Divisions" (aṣṭavidha) are... [Translation] Interpretation by way of contemplating the mind: The principle of the Four Noble Truths—Suffering in the East, Origin in the South, Cessation in the West, and the Path in the North—constitutes the four heavens. The wisdom that realizes the Four Noble Truths is the Four Heavenly Kings. Protecting the realm of the Four Noble Truths is termed "Protecting the Country.

Protecting the mental factors is "Protecting Sentient Beings. "The World" refers to others; explaining the mental factors to others is termed "Protecting Other Sentient Beings. The "Eight Divisions" are...
Beneath the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) there are sharp and dull faculties of both view-delusion (dṛṣṭi) and thought-delusion (saṃjñā); the Lotus Sūtra refers to these as ghosts and spirits.
Furthermore, beneath the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) there are likewise view-delusions and thought-delusions; these constitute the eight classes of beings.

[Commentary: Regarding the Four Truths and the four types of wisdom, down to the individual discussion of *darśana-heya* (afflictions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation) for each truth—why does no teaching [other than this] speak of them?
Now, since the meaning of the teaching explained here is exclusively based on the Perfect [Teaching], the contemplation or non-contemplation elucidated therein pertains to the three teachings.

The four heavens must represent the principle of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) truth; the four kings, in turn, represent the wondrous wisdom of non-conditioning that illumines phenomena as being identical to principle, which is called "protecting the realm of the truths."

To understand bondage as liberation is called "protecting the mental factors"; to explain this to others is called "protecting the world. Regarding the general and specific [distinctions], the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (passions) share the same substance;
when they act as obstacles, they are termed "ghosts and spirits" (*bhūta*). In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are not a few differences in how these are indicated:

therein, ghosts and spirits are used merely as metaphors for the five sharp [afflictions], while insects and birds are used as metaphors for the five dull [afflictions]; here, however, it is the sharp [afflictions].
The "dull" and "similar" ghosts and spirits merely take what is of the same category. Second, the clarification of benefits.
[Text]: If one does not illuminate the principle of the Four Noble Truths, the two delusions of view and thought will invade the Sovereign of the Mind and destroy its realm.

When the Sovereign of the Mind perishes, the kingdom of the objects is ruined; when the mental factors—the subjects—are scattered, both the objects and the wisdom become possessed by ghosts and spirits.
When vexation can contemplate suffering and its accumulation, and one restrains views and thoughts, then the kingdom is secure and the people are at peace;

being able to explain the Four Truths to others is to protect other lands and to ward off their views and thoughts so that they may attain peace and happiness— this is what it means for the contemplation of the mind to serve as the Four Heavenly Kings who protect the world.
[Commentary] Furthermore, it is first clarified that if one does not contemplate [the truth], the wondrous wisdom of the sovereign mind (cittarāja) will not arise;

if the realm of reality (dharmatā) is damaged, the principles of the truths will not be manifested. When the sovereign mind reaches the point of scattering, it demonstrates how the three virtues (triguṇa) are deluded and become the three obstacles (triskandha).
Although it is discussed that the delusion regarding the three obstacles arises from afflictions (kleśa), it is said that they are all tormented by ghosts and spirits.
The observation below correctly demonstrates that this contemplation is beneficial: ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself clarity, serving as the wisdom that contemplates;

this contemplation observes that suffering and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) are themselves *nirvāṇa*, and it observes that the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*) is itself *bodhi*. Regarding "restraining and controlling" and so forth:

while remaining unmoved by various views, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); without severing delusion and craving, one gives rise to all forms of clarity and liberation.
In governing these [beings], how could they alone not be free from harm? Rather, one can manifest the principles and perfect the virtues.
Because the principles are manifested, the realm of the Truth (諦境) is secure; because the virtues are perfected, the mental states of the people are at peace.

Since one has personally realized and mastered this by transforming the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) into the eighty thousand concentrations and wisdoms (*samādhi-prajñā*), how could it be otherwise when causing others to cultivate and realize them?
The manner in which one obtains benefit by practicing contemplation based on the task of entrusting oneself to the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings is, in brief, as follows.
Regarding the twenty-three chapters of the sutra text, there are two parts: first, establishing the intent and dividing the sections; second, establishing the intent.
[Text] From here below, these thirteen chapters constitute the section on the Propagation (liutong).

Out of the Buddha’s compassion for the final age, he ensures that evil does not obscure the True and Correct King of Sutras, so that it shall not be obstructed in future generations; thus those with the karmic affinity may obtain the correct teaching and hear the correct Dharma.
Therefore, it is called "Propagation."
[Commentary] "Ji" (the end) also means "the final period" or "obstruction. This section on the dissemination [of the teaching] consists of seven chapters.
[Textual Analysis] There are generally seven points: from the Four Heavenly Kings to Vaiśravaṇa Devaputra, they make vows to exhort and encourage human kings to widely proclaim this sutra;
the correct discussion on the skillful assembly [of conditions]; and the clear exposition that the heavenly kings protect and assist those who propagate the sutra.

This demonstrates the methods for propagating the sutra in former times; the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" clarifies that the merits of listening to the sutra cause devas, spirits, terrestrial deities, rivers, seas, and bodhisattvas to all provide protection;
the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies" verifies that the merits of listening to the sutra are not in vain;
and the "Chapter on the Flowing Water that Cures Illness" cites the merits of listening to the sutra in the past to verify its protective power in the present.
Holding [this teaching] without error, the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body" cites the *Sūtra on Past Deeds* to exhort disciples not to begrudge their own lives for the sake of the precepts;
the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" clarifies how all Bodhisattvas extol the Buddha-dharma,
explaining that what they proclaim brings profound and heavy benefit, and so forth.
[Commentary] "Method" (*fanggui*) refers to the method and paradigm. The two [sections on] the emergence of the celestial deities comprise five segments.
[Text/Phrase] The Heavenly King’s taking of the vow also consists of four parts; the Five Kings protect the petitioner with divine power.
The "Great Eloquence" chapter enriches the speaker through eloquence; the "Goddess of Merit" chapter pledges to provide material wealth to benefit the petitioner. This is what is explained.
In the "Chapter on the Earth Deity," he pledges the rich essence of the earth’s flavor to request the place for preaching;
in the "Chapter on Samantabhadra," he pledges martial prowess to crush external enemies, repel internal calamities, and establish peace for those who request, preach, and listen.
Furthermore, the Heavenly King protects his kingdom, Mahāprajñā protects his teacher, Guṇakara protects his assembly, and the Earth Deity protects his land. Samantabhadra... [protects] the Dharma.
"By offering fat [as an oblation], one wards off calamities so that the sutras and Dharma may spread widely," and so forth.
[Commentary] "Gao-yu" (fat/riche) refers to fertile soil; it means land that is excellent and rich.

As the *Shiji* says, "To the east, he cut off the gao-yu lands. This is an example. The character "yu" (肥) is often written as "wei" (味) below it. "Rang" (攘) means to eliminate or remove. Furthermore...
The Heavenly Kings descend and follow from the *Abhyudgata-parivarta*; each of these discussions possesses five capacities.
This chapter is presented in six sections.
[Wenju] Regarding the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," there are six rounds of question and answer, constituting six segments. First, he addresses the Buddha.
First, the exposition of the capacity to protect the state; second, the petition to the Buddha describing the matters of protecting the state;

third, the petition to the Buddha demonstrating the ritual models; fourth, the petition to the Buddha requesting the benefits of the Dharma; fifth, the petition to the Buddha describing both prosperity and decline;
sixth, the petition to the Buddha speaking verses in praise of his virtues.

[Commentary] Second, the correct explanation of the sūtra text in seven parts. First, the first five chapters explain the section on the Heavenly Kings making vows to encourage and exhort human kings to widely proclaim this sūtra;
this is divided into five parts. First, the "Four Kings Chapter," which explains how the power of the heavens protects those who request [the teaching];
this is divided into six parts. First, describing the capacity to protect the state; second, the initial division of the text.
[Text] The first section is divided into two parts: 1. Addressing the Buddha; 2. The Buddha’s confirmation of the address. The first part [addressing the Buddha] is further divided into two:
1. The narrative by the sūtra compiler; 2. The actual address to the Buddha.
[Commentary] Regarding the second [section], the explanation of the meaning, there are two parts: first, the four kings address the Buddha; second, the initial narrative by the sūtra compiler.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka,
and the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa all rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground,
joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
[Text] The expression of reverence is as in the original passage.

[Commentary] First, regarding the designation of the Northern Heavenly King: in the Western lands (India), the north is considered the position of honor. As for "baring one shoulder": this is the etiquette of the West;
when a disciple approaches a teacher, he must bare one shoulder to signify that he is ready to perform service. Second, the main part.
The first part of the text on the white petition to the Buddha establishes the doctrinal meaning.

[Commentary on the Text]: The main text of the petition to the Buddha is divided into two sections: first, praising the sutra; second, describing how the various devas who protect it have the power to believe in the Dharma, and for this reason praise the sutra.
Desiring that the sutra be widely propagated, one describes the power of those who protect it. The praise of the sutra consists of three parts, beginning from here.
The passage beginning with "The Golden Light" praises the essence of the sutra; the passage beginning with "From the Bodhisattva Adorned" praises the core tenet of the sutra;

and the passage beginning with "Because this sutra can illuminate" praises the function of the sutra. The formal exposition contains many such praises; these three [sections] thus briefly encompass the extensive details.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the explanation of the meaning of its function, there are two parts. First, praising the sutra. Within this, first is the praise for the essence of the sutra:
"World-Honored One, this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra is a subtle and wondrous scripture, the king among all sutras, protected and remembered by all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones."
[Text]: "The principle of the dharma-nature is what the Buddha protects and keeps in mind. Since words explain this principle, it is called the "King of Sutras.
Since it is called the "King of Sutras," we know this is a praise of its essence. [Commentary]:
The principle protected and kept in mind by the Buddha is immeasurable and profoundly deep; horizontally it encompasses all phenomena, and vertically it exhausts the entirety of the Dharma. If...
If it were not so, how could it be called the "King of Sutras"? To explain this principle, the *Wenquan* states that the King of Sutras refers to the principle (*li*).

Thus, while the sutra text is merely the expressive medium (*nengquan*), the "King" resides solely in the principle. When explaining the title, why then is it said that the text is named the "King of Sutras," which encompasses all scriptures?
This refers to both the text and the principle, as these two aspects differ; how are they to be reconciled? The answer is: if one considers the texts of the first three teachings...
In principle, this would constitute an obstacle; however, since we now follow the Perfect Teaching (*vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), both text and meaning are non-dual.
There is no meaning outside the text, and no text outside the meaning. When explaining the title, if the text were treated in isolation, how could it be called the "King"?

Now, when this commentary points to the meaning as not encompassing the text, that actually belongs to the previous teachings. One must believe that text and meaning are integrated; thus, this scripture is the King, and its significance is such.

The secret and wondrous [teachings] cannot be sought through the emotions; now, the King of Sūtras does not distinguish between the praise of its essence and the introductory chapter. Second, the praise of the sūtra’s core:
it adorns the profound and wondrous merits of bodhisattvas, is constantly revered by all devas, and is able to cause the heavenly kings—
The arising of joy in the mind is also praised by the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*). [Commentary on the Text:
Regarding the substance and the cultivation of practice, this enables the Bodhisattva to be endowed with the two adornments (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*) and to achieve the ultimate fruit.

Since it speaks of "adornment," one knows this is a praise of the fundamental doctrine (*mūla-artha*): the Celestial World, the Pure World, and the World of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-artha*) all revere and look up to this ultimate stage, bestowing the three [kinds of] gifts.
Offering through action is the body; joy is the mind; and praise is the mouth. [Commentary:

Regarding cultivation based on the essence, the essence is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). When this gives rise to and achieves initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), it is then termed "cultivation based on the essence.
The essence possesses both the cause and fruit of the Buddha-realm’s two adornments; the entire essence constitutes the two adornments of cultivation, which are non-active (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

That which is not adornment is itself adornment; now, taking the two adornments of the ultimate fruit as the central theme, the *Sutra of the World* states that "the various heavens encompass these three.
However, there ought to be four [categories], so it is likely that the text is missing or erroneous.

Alternatively, since the Heavenly Kings are originally among the born-deities (*upapāduka*), the commentary does not list the names and meanings of these four heavens; they appear in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, Chapter on King Guṇa.
The *Śāstra* states: First, worldly devas, such as various kings; second, devas by birth, ranging from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana;
third, pure devas, namely those of the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] and the pratyekabuddhas;

fourth, devas of meaning, namely bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because they perceive that all phenomena have the meaning of emptiness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies three kinds of devas.
First, the nominal heavens, which are the worldly heavens; second, the birth heavens; third, the pure heavens, which encompass all three vehicles.
Third, praising the utility of the sutra:
this sutra can illuminate the palaces of all the heavens; this sutra can bestow happiness upon sentient beings; this sutra can cause...
The rivers of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals will become parched and dry up;
this sutra can eliminate all fears; this sutra can repel enemies and bandits from other regions; this sutra can remove the calamity of famine and high grain prices; this sutra can cure all epidemics;
this sutra can extinguish the portents of malevolent stars and celestial anomalies; this sutra can dispel all sorrow and affliction.
To state the essentials: this sutra can extinguish the immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings.
[Commentary] Furthermore, from the hells below up to the bodhisattvas above, as long as ignorance is not yet exhausted, there is universally present the heat of affliction;
this sutra can eliminate it, like the moon’s refreshing coolness. To know this is to praise its function, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "upward to Bodhisattvas," since the sutra does not explicitly mention the word "Bodhisattva," and it states that [this teaching] can extinguish the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings, it refers generally to the nine realms as "all. The textual passage has four initial sections:
first, those in the celestial realm who can bestow happiness upon sentient beings; second, this sutra [addresses] the three evil realms below.

The phrase "the various rivers sink into the three realms of existence" is like a great river that has been scorched, dried up, and exhausted; this refers to the extinguishing of the sufferings of the three evil destinies.
It is erroneous for some sūtras to add the two characters "able to cause" (*neng ling*) above the word "exhausted.

Third, it can eliminate fear; this refers to the beginning of the human realm. First, the statement "all fears" is general; subsequently, it specifically clarifies the destruction of the three obstacles.
The three calamities of evil—namely, the sword, famine, and pestilence—are the "enemies" that constitute obstacles to retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

Together with these, they are called the "three calamities. Evil stars represent the obstacles of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); because karma comes to demand its retribution, evil stars appear. Sorrow and affliction represent the obstacles of mental afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
(4) "Lifting up the essentials" refers collectively to sentient beings within the nine realms. Second, the description of those who provide protection.
The first section of the text. [Commentary on the Words]:
From "World-Honored One" down to "this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*," this is the second part, which describes the text on protecting the nation.

It is divided into two: first, protecting the nation internally through the Dharma; second, protecting the nation externally through strategic counsel. Protecting the nation through the Dharma is further divided into four parts, the first of which is protection... [text truncated].

The means by which a state is protected are fourfold: first, protecting the state through the Dharma; second, protecting the state through the retinue of devas; third, protecting the state through the deva-eye; and fourth, protecting the state through the celestial eye.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of these meanings, there are two parts. First, the internal protection of the state through the Dharma, which has four sub-sections. First, the basis for protecting the state.
World-Honored One, when this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra is widely proclaimed among the great assembly,
we four kings and our retinues, having heard this unsurpassed flavor of the nectar-like Dharma, shall increase our physical strength, mental vigor, and courageous resolve,
and be endowed with all majestic virtues.

[Text]: Regarding the reason for protecting the state: by hearing this sutra, one obtains four benefits—an increase in the body, an increase in the power of radiance, an increase in courageous mind, and an increase in virtuous qualities and dignity.
Furthermore, one obtains two further benefits, namely that the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom both attain growth.
Since the state causes the propagation of this sutra and thereby brings about such dharma-moistening, how could it not be protected?
[Commentary]: Second, protecting the nation through the Dharma.
"World-Honored One, we four kings are able to expound the True Dharma and practice the True Dharma; acting as Dharma-kings for the world, we govern the world according to the Dharma."

[Text] To explain the reason for this: this meaning precisely corresponds to the contemplation of the mind. To protect the objects of the Four Truths by means of the wisdom of the Four Truths is the cultivation of the True Dharma.

To guide all mental factors by means of the wisdom of the Four Truths so that those mental factors do not function is called practicing the Prajñāpāramitā; this is the ability to expound the True Dharma from within.
Thus, the reason this "Protection of the State" is called the "World-Protecting King" is that it correctly governs the realm.
[Commentary] This explains the reason for protecting the state: if there were no Dharma, how could one protect and sustain the realm?
Therein are both internal and external aspects; the external refers to worldly dharmas, while the internal refers to mental dharmas. If one merely practices and speaks of the world...

The principle of the "intermediate" [teachings] renders this sutra not a Vaipulya (fangdeng) teaching; one must understand that the Heavenly King is entirely an ordinary being in both mind and speech.
Yet, one should know that every phrase contains both mundane and supramundane meanings.

It is simply because these phrases conveniently manifest the internal meaning that it is said they "correspond precisely with the contemplation of the mind," as seen in various passages within the "Chapter on the Spirit General Vaiśravaṇa."
Furthermore, when following worldly conventions to explain and analyze, and even arriving at the account of how one obtains a name, the understanding of the actual facts is entirely abandoned;
thus it says, "The inconceivable wisdom-realm presently perceived, the inconceivable wisdom-light," and so on, up to:
"I am able to abide in the suchness-nature of all phenomena, and within all phenomena, I encompass the realm and wisdom of all phenomena. If...
Therefore, it is called "esoteric power" (*guhyaka-śakti*); for while externally manifesting as a great general of spirits and ghosts, is this not because there is a principle that is esoteric?

Thus, there is the "esoteric of phenomena" (*vastu-guhya*). Although the current text of the sutra does not explicitly reveal the Great Master’s realization of the intent, he nonetheless taught through practice the Dharma of the Truths and Wisdom to protect the world and bring peace to the people.
As for the phrase "the mental factors do not function," it refers to the mind and mind... [text fragment].
If the entire substance of the numerical dharmas were the provisional means (upāya) and the mind-king (citta-rāja) of prajñā, then the practice of numbers would be directed toward erroneous objects;
now that the King is correct and guides them, they do not proceed [into error]. By practicing "non-proceeding" yet proceeding, one practices profound prajñā and reaches the other shore.
"The Three Heavens protect the state.
World-Honored One, we, the Four Kings, along with all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, shall govern the world according to the Dharma and ward off all evil spirits who consume vital energy."
[Text]: "The leader of the faction who protects the nation" refers to this as well being in accord with the contemplation of the mind.

The mind-king leads the faction of mental factors to subdue the various afflictions (*kleśa*)—both sharp and dull—of views and thoughts. It is like the celestial kings together with their retinues warding off all evil spirits;
it is like the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) with his seven treasures and a thousand sons, such that wherever he goes, the four quarters submit to his virtue. The Four Kings [act likewise].
When he presides over five hundred locations together, what evil is there that he does not eliminate?

[Commentary] The meaning is the same as explained above. "Party" (dǎng) refers to a faction or retinue, namely the Eight Divisions (aṣṭakula). "Party" (dǎng) means a cohort. "To lead the party" (shuài dǎng):
the character *shuài* is pronounced *lǜ*, meaning to guide and lead. This matter is explained below by way of the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) subduing the four [continents].
The directions are likened to the celestial kings who ward off evil spirits; the seven treasures refer to the wheel, elephant, horse, woman, pearl, minister, and army.
The four heavenly kings protect the nation with their divine eyes.
World-Honored One, we four kings, along with the various spirits and ghosts of the twenty-eight divisions and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other spirits, [are here].
The gods, with their pure divine eyes which surpass those of humans, constantly observe and protect this Jambudvīpa, World-Honored One;
for this reason, we are called the Kings who Protect the World.

[Commentary] Regarding the protection of the nation by means of the divine eye: it is because they possess a divine eye obtained as a karmic reward, which sees through all things so that nothing, however obscure, remains unilluminated, thereby providing defense.
"If one nurtures [the good] at its earliest stage, what evil would not be eliminated?

[Commentary]: Those who possess the eye of heavenly retribution do not acquire it through cultivation; upon receiving a celestial body, their eyes necessarily penetrate obstructions and illuminate the dark and hidden.
"Ment" (萌) refers to the initial splitting of a seed; "du" (杜) means to block or obstruct. This refers to using the heavenly eye.
To illuminate thoroughly is to prevent the roots of calamity before they sprout and to block the sources of evil as they gradually arise. Second, protecting the state through external strategies;
first, the outline of the section, which has two parts. First, the outline of the section.

[Textual Analysis] Second, from "If this land has various declines and losses" onwards, this constitutes the third section: the wisdom-strategy for protecting the state so that internal and external conditions may be brought into harmony.

[Commentary] Part Two: Stating the Intent. Part Three: First, the Causes and Conditions for Exhorting Others to Listen. This has two sections. First, exhorting the Dharma Master to serve as the external condition:
"If in this land there are various depletions, such as enemies and bandits invading the borders, famine, pestilence, and all manner of hardships..."
If there be any bhikṣu who receives and upholds this sutra, we, the four kings, shall together entreat him that, by our power,
he may quickly go to those kingdoms, cities, districts, and counties to widely proclaim and disseminate this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sutra,
so that all such various hundreds of thousands of calamities and depletions shall be entirely extinguished.
[End. [Commentary:
First, if the king’s realm is beset by many calamities and various hardships—namely, war, famine, and disease—I shall, through my strategic wisdom, exhort the Dharma Master to go;
or I shall exhort him to go through my majestic spiritual power; or I shall exhort him to go by manifesting my form; or I shall exhort him by appearing in his dreams.
"If a Dharma Master goes forth to widely proclaim this sutra, it will be like the sun rising in the morning; the mists and fogs will naturally dissipate.
This is an exhortation regarding external conditions.

[Commentary] Regarding "the sun rising in the morning," the *Erya* states: "That which is east of the mountain is called the morning sun (chāoyáng); that which is west of the mountain is called the evening sun (xīyáng)."

"Fen" (pronounced with the *fu* and *wen* finals) refers to inauspicious vapors. The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "If the ordinances of summer are practiced in winter, the vapors will become dark and murky.
The *Chunqiu Yuanming Bao* states: "Fog is the vapor of yin and yang; when yin and yang are enraged, they become wind; when they are disordered, they become fog.
Now, the rising sun is used as a metaphor for the propagation of the Great Sūtra, and the clearing of the fog and mist serves as a metaphor for the cessation of the three calamities.
This is the cessation. Second, he exhorts kings to cultivate internal causes:

"World-Honored One, if the territory of any king should be reached by one who upholds this sutra, that king ought to go to that person’s place to hear and receive such a subtle and wonderful sutra; having heard it, he should rejoice and furthermore..."
“World-Honored One, we four kings shall protect, remember, revere, and honor such persons;
furthermore, with diligent minds, we shall protect that king, his kingdom, and its people, eliminating their misfortunes and afflictions so that they may attain peace and security.”
[Text] Next, if the king’s mind lacks wisdom and fails to illuminate calamities, he will succumb to darkness; yet if he possesses clear insight, strange portents will not arise.
