Since the Master has now come to attend upon the king upholding the Dharma, the king must listen with single-minded devotion. If the king listens diligently, the heavens will likewise protect him with diligence.
Thus, what is worthy of protection shall be protected, and one person’s fortune and reliance shall extend to all quarters of the world.
That the king’s person and the state are secure and free from calamity is due to internal causes;
however, if there is a Dharma-protecting King abroad but his inner mind is not reverent, then harmony will not prevail and disasters cannot be averted.

[Commentary] "To uphold the law" means to maintain it. "The one person" refers to the King. "Celebration and goodness" means that when the King possesses virtue, the people of the myriad regions rely upon him;
this is as stated in the *Shangshu*: "When the one person has cause for celebration, the myriad people rely on him.
Therefore, the King receives these statutes and brings peace to the state. Regarding "passing through famine," the *Erya* states that there are five grains.
When grain does not ripen, it is called "famine" (jī); when vegetables do not ripen, it is called "scarcity" (jìn). Regarding states, cities, districts, and counties, the *Wangzhi* says:
"Within the four seas, there are nine provinces (*zhōu*), each spanning one thousand li.
In each province, there are three states of one hundred li, six states of seventy li, and one hundred and twenty states of fifty li, totaling two hundred and ten."
The realm consists of nine provinces and one thousand seven hundred seventy-three states. The *Zuozhuan* of the *Chunqiu* states:

"Any settlement that houses the ancestral temple and the spirit-tablets of former lords is called a 'du'; otherwise, it is called a 'yi'. It further states: "Senior high officials receive a 'xian' as their fief; junior high officials receive a 'jun'.
These two [provisions] encourage the provision of offerings for the fourfold assembly through various causes and conditions.
World-Honored One, if there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who receive and uphold this sutra,
or if there are any kings who are able to provide for them and bestow upon them all that brings peace and comfort, we, the Four Kings, shall likewise cause these kings, their nations,
and all their people to be entirely secure, peaceful, and free from all affliction.

[Text] Second, if a king does not practice generous giving, his fortune and merit will diminish—just as if one does not diligently cultivate the fields, the granaries and kitchens will have little grain.
[Therefore,] one should exhort the king to expend his wealth to provide for the fourfold assembly. When the fourfold assembly attains peace, they provide the king with the resources of merit;

thus, the entire nation and its kin will be free from all suffering. Through the harmony of these internal and external causes and conditions, one can bring about a bountiful year of overflowing abundance.
...and so forth.
[Commentary] "Upāsaka" is translated here as "male lay follower" (jìnshì nán), and "upāsikā" as "female lay follower" (jìnshì nǚ).
This is because those who have accomplished the precepts are capable of drawing near to and serving the two groups of the renunciant community. As for "flowing and spreading":
This is the exegesis. Third, [the section on] the causes and conditions for being able to praise that which is praised through the threefold exhortation:

"World-Honored One, if there are members of the fourfold assembly who receive, uphold, read, and recite this wondrous sutra, or if there are kings among men who are able to offer offerings, respect, honor, and praise to us, the Four Kings, we shall likewise cause such kings among men [to achieve their aims]."
Among all kings, he constantly receives the foremost offerings, reverence, respect, and praise;
furthermore, he causes other kings to admire, envy, and extol his virtues.
[Commentary] Third, the king’s person lacks the virtuous conduct of former kings, so his ministers and subjects do not follow him, nor does his speech possess the excellence of former kings.

The Dharma teachings are not being chanted in neighboring kingdoms today; I now urge Your Majesty to practice the three types of service through offerings and reverence. To revere this body is the action of the body (*kāyakarman*);
to respect it is the action of the mind (*manaskarman*); and to praise it is the action of speech (*vākkarman*).

Indeed, to honor the lowly by means of the high, and to take the laconic as one's teacher of eloquence, is a merit of great magnitude. By means of such celestial power, you shall cause neighboring kingdoms to pay homage from afar.

The feathered writs proclaim his praises, and songs of admiration and envy resound; the three karmas are most reverent. As the superior transforms the subordinates like the wind bending the grass, so it is with neighboring states.
Since this is the case, there is nothing among the people, their oxen, horses, or the wild grasses that does not turn lowly toward him.
This is the harmonious convergence of causes and conditions between the one who praises and the one being praised, such that the sound of hymns overflows into neighboring lands, and so forth.
[Commentary: "The virtuous conduct of the former kings" refers to the practice of the former kings' Way and virtue;
if such conduct were manifested in one's own person, it could serve as a model for customs. "Legal sayings" refers to the words of the sages and the precepts of the classics;
if these were proclaimed from the mouth, they could be used to instruct the people. Since the ruler lacks these qualities, the people of the state [are likewise lost].

If you do not follow their instructions, neighboring states will not sing of your virtue; therefore, I now exhort your subordinates and urge Your Majesty to revere the Way and honor the Teacher, cultivating merit and remedying faults.
To maintain gravity and respect in body and mind, and to cultivate oneself with humility, is the practice of the Way and its Virtue (*moralò*).
To offer praise with one’s mouth is the method of the canonical admonitions. Indeed, by distinguishing between high and low, one clarifies the principle of humility.
The mind is sovereign and lofty while the people are humble; for one who governs a state, the people constitute the fundamental basis, and thus one must be diligent and modest to gather them.

To take the laconic as the teacher of eloquence means that because the laconic person possesses inner clarity and purity, they externally renounce all affectation and ornamentation—thus their great eloquence is like silence.
Therefore, they can serve as teachers of minor eloquence within the mundane world, constantly cultivating themselves.

If governing a state should be conducted in this manner, how much more so now when we request the Dharma for transcending the world and pray for the blessings of the people—how could it be appropriate to be arrogant and disrespectful?

To treat the Three Elders as one would a father and the Five Reformers as one would elder brothers according to Confucian rites, and to humble the King’s own dignity to serve them as teachers—this is where Confucianism and Buddhism reach a single principle.
Regarding "feathered writs" (*yuxi*), the *Wenxin Diaolong* states that a writ (*xi*)...

"Jiǎo" (曒) means to manifest and reveal outwardly; it signifies being bright and clear. It is sometimes called a "lùbù" (露布), likely because it was written on an unsealed wooden board and distributed for public viewing.
Yán Sīgǔ’s commentary on the *Hànshū* regarding the "Gāojì" (高紀) states:
"A 'xí' (檄) is a document written on wooden slips, one chi and two cùn long, used for summoning. When there is an urgent matter, bird feathers are added and inserted [into the top]."

This demonstrates his swiftness. What is now called "feathered writs" (*yùxí*) refers to proclaiming [the message] through refined rhetoric, describing in full detail the excellence and brilliance [of the ruler].
The *Erya* states: "The dignified and lofty air is the virtue of the ruler; it does not cause [the people] to lie prostrate.
The *Lunyu* says: "The virtue of the gentleman is like the wind; the virtue of the common people is like the grass. Where the wind blows over the grass, the grass must bend."
"Lai" (萊) refers to the *lai-li* grass; it is sometimes written as "ye" (葉) or "cai" (菜), which are errors in the character.
The second point concerns the intent behind the elimination of the text.
[Commentary: If one searches the scriptural text clearly, this can be seen.
[Commentary] It is said that "it can be seen" because the preceding intent is used to explain the sutra. Second, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment;
this is divided into two parts.

[Wenju] Next, the Buddha’s text of confirmation and fulfillment is divided into two: first, the combined description and praise of the sutra; second, the description of its ability to protect the state.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts. First, a combined description praising the Sūtra:
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Four Heavenly Kings who Protect the World, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
You Four Kings have in the past already made offerings to, paid respect to, revered, and praised immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas."
[Text] Regarding the four kings’ initial praise, since the scripture’s exposition accords with reason, the Buddha describes it to bring it to completion.
He completes its primary substance by praising it three times; thus it is said that the Buddha, in agreement, describes it as "Excellent! Excellent!

His general praise at the beginning concerns this single teaching, while his subsequent description brings to completion its universal eulogy of the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Since all Buddhas are born from this Dharma, he cites many.
This praises the perfection of the One.

[Commentary] Since the essence, substance, and function of the *Catuḥmahārājakāyika-sūtra* accord with the Buddha’s realization of the wondrous principle of the three virtues, the Buddha confirms that all Buddhas are born from this Dharma.
As for the essence, substance, and function—since these are the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), how could there be...?
First, that a single Buddha does not arise from this; second, an exposition on the ability to protect the nation, which is divided into two initial sections.

[Textual Commentary]: From "From the presence of all Buddhas" below, it establishes his ability to protect the nation, which is further divided into two: first, an exposition on protecting the nation through the Dharma;
second, an exposition on protecting the nation through the eye of wisdom.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, the description of protecting the nation through the Dharma, in four sections. First, the description of the reasons for protecting the nation:
having planted various roots of goodness in the presence of all Buddhas.

[Text] Regarding the protection of the nation by the four Buddhas, all of whom corroborate and complete the preceding explanation of the reasons for protecting the nation: it is because one hears this sutra and attains benefit that the Buddhas now describe this present benefit. This is truly due to the fact that the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the ultimate [attainment] are not two different things.

Since these two states of mind are thus inseparable, yet the former mind is more difficult to achieve, I therefore pay homage to the initial arousal of the mind. This citation of the former establishes the latter. [Commentary] This passage explains that the four Buddhas—Dharmapāla, Rājapāla, Guṇapāla, and Dharmarakṣita—corroborate the preceding discourse on the reasons for protecting the nation.

It clarifies that the present attainment of benefits described by the Buddhas arises from hearing this scripture. This is because the initial resolve to attain enlightenment and its final perfection are non-dual; although they are identical in essence, the initial generation of the bodhicitta is far more difficult to accomplish. Therefore, the author pays homage to that first arising of the mind, using the former as a basis to validate the latter.
The latter serves to clarify the former.

[Commentary: "The ultimateity of the arousal of the mind" refers to the planting of roots of goodness in the past as the arousal of the mind, and gaining benefit upon hearing the sutra today as the ultimateity.
Comparing these two states of mind, because the planting of seeds in the past was truly difficult, the Buddha confirms and praises that prior planting.
However, these words regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta and so forth are from the verses of praise spoken by Kāśyapa to the Buddha in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra;
thus, the Buddha’s initial resolve simply employs those words to establish his present intention. Second, he describes how he protects the world through the Dharma.
[The Buddha] teaches the True Dharma, practices the True Dharma, and governs the world by means of the Dharma, becoming a king of men or a king of gods.

[Commentary on the Text: From the phrase "teaches the True Dharma" onwards, it describes how he protects the world through the Dharma. The preceding section stated that he is able to teach and able to practice;
therefore, he is called a "World-Protector" (Lokapāla). This passage further establishes that because he is both able to teach and able to practice, he earns the title of World-Protector.
"Yun" (Cloud).
[Commentary: Regarding "as stated below concerning the World-Protectors," the meaning of their correspondence with the contemplation of the mind is as previously described.
Third, this is an extraordinary account of the celestial eye protecting the state.
Today, you have long benefited all sentient beings by practicing great compassion,
bestowing upon them all instruments of happiness, obstructing all evils, and diligently encouraging all virtues. For this reason,
if there is a king who can offer worship and respect to this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, you should truly protect him in such a manner.
[He] contemplates the cessation of their suffering and bestows upon them peace and happiness.

[Commentary on the Text]: From the passage "From this day forth, you all... onwards, it transcends and summarizes the matter of his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) protecting the kingdom; though the sequence is slightly disordered, there is no loss of meaning.
The preceding section states, "With a pure divine eye that surpasses the human eye," wherein the Buddha describes how he has benefited [beings] throughout the long night.
As for the celestial eye, it illuminates at night without depending on the light of the sun; therefore, it is called the "long night.
[Commentary] Fourth, recounting how the celestial faction protects the state:
"If you, the Four Kings, along with your retinues and immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities, can protect and mindfully regard..."
A sutra such as this is precisely that which protects and upholds the true Dharma of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

[Commentary on the Text]: From the passage "You, the Four Heavenly Kings, and your retinues... down to the section recounting how the celestial hosts protect the nation, the text directly states that they protect the nation;
the Buddha now further praises this as protecting the true Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
[Commentary] Second, it describes protecting the nation with the eye of wisdom.
When you, the Four Kings, and the other hosts of devas, along with hundreds of thousands of spirits and asuras, engage in battle, you devas shall always achieve victory.
If you can protect and keep this sutra in mind, you will be able to completely subdue and overcome [all adversaries].
Regarding all sufferings— namely, enemies, thieves, famine, and pestilence— if there are members of the fourfold assembly who are able to receive,
uphold, read, and recite this sutra, you should also diligently protect them with a devoted mind, removing their decline and afflictions and bestowing upon them peace and happiness.
[Text] From you, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the other hosts of devas below, down to the description of the harmonious protection of the nation through the Eye of Wisdom above;
it says that by requesting the Dharma Master to enter the realm and repelling evil, this merit is attributed to oneself, whereby one can repel the armies of the asuras.

You have exhorted the King to listen to the sutra and provide for the fourfold assembly. The Buddha describes that such internal wisdom and external merit truly constitute the elimination [of obstacles].
"Subduing all sufferings and being able to bring about peace and happiness," as stated in the text, and so forth.

[Commentary] Previously it was called "exertion" (*utsāha*), and now it is called "the eye of wisdom" (*jñānacakṣus*); these two expressions are seen in their respective contexts. "Exertion" refers to wise strategy, while "wisdom" is named the "eye" because its function is to discern and illuminate.
As for "concordance" (*sāmagrī*), this refers to what was previously called the internal causes and external conditions—the harmony of causes and conditions.
Regarding the passage beginning with "After they have assembled, they shall expel evil," etc.: previously, when reporting to the Buddha, these were explained in three distinct sections;

now, however, they are recounted in a single comprehensive summary that encompasses those previous distinctions. The second part, reporting to the Buddha regarding the protection of the state, is divided into two initial sections.
[Text] The second section, the white [announcement] to the Buddha recounting the matters concerning the protection of the state, consists of two parts: first, the white [announcement] to the Buddha;
second, the Buddha’s confirmation of the white [announcement]. This latter part also has two sub-sections.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts: first, the white [announcement] to the Buddha; second, first, the king’s adherence to human law and the heavens’ removal of enmity and calamity.
At that time, the Four Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*,
in future ages wherever it may circulate— whether in kingdoms, cities, towns, districts, or villages— at whatever place it arrives,
if the various kings govern the world according to celestial laws and are further able to reverently and with a sincere heart listen to and receive this wondrous sūtra..."

Furthermore, by honoring, making offerings to, and supporting the fourfold assembly that upholds this sutra, we shall, through these causes and conditions, hear such subtle and wondrous sutras from time to time.

Having heard them, we shall immediately gain increase in physical strength, mental progress, and courageous vigor, and be endowed with all majestic virtues. Therefore, we and immeasurable spirits shall always remain hidden.
I shall personally provide protection wherever these sublime scriptures are circulated, ensuring they encounter no obstacles;
I shall likewise guard and mindfully protect the kings and their subjects who listen to this sutra, removing all their afflictions and hardships so that they may all dwell in peace and security,
and causing enemies and bandits from other regions to retreat and disperse.
[Text] First, wherever this sutra is circulated, if the king personally receives it upon his head and provides for the fourfold assembly,
I and my retinue vow to remain invisible and yet manifest their benefits for him.

[Commentary] Those who govern the world according to the celestial laws follow the ancients in ruling the people, modeling their conduct on Heaven and administering transformation through punishment that must correspond to the offense and rewards that must correspond to merit;
this is the "Celestial Law" (*tianlü*). Second, when neighboring states raise armies, Heaven’s mandate causes them to retreat in haste.
If there is a king who listens to this sutra, and a hostile enemy of a neighboring state conceives the thought,
"I shall assemble the fourfold army to destroy that kingdom," then by the majestic spiritual power of this sutra,
at that time another enemy will arise against that neighbor to create obstacles, causing various forms of decline, affliction, calamities, and pestilence within its borders. At that time—
When our enemies have committed such evil deeds as these and mobilize the fourfold army to set out for this kingdom with the intent to invade and subdue us,
at that time we, together with our retinues of immeasurable and boundless hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities,
shall conceal our forms and provide protection and assistance, causing those enemies to naturally retreat and disperse, and giving rise to various terrors and anxieties.
Even the military forces of that country cannot reach [this land], let alone be able to cause any destruction.

[Commentary] Second, if a wicked neighbor raises an army to invade and displace a virtuous country, I shall conceal my form and stir up various terrors and manifold difficulties, causing their soldiers to retreat in plain sight;
since they will not even disturb the borders, how much less could they destroy [the land]?

The middle section says "and so forth. [Commentary] "Chìzhú" (斥逐) means to expel or drive away. The "four armies" (*sìbīng*) refer to elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. "Guīwǎng dǎofá zhě" (規往討伐者) means to plan and seek to go on an expedition of punitive conquest;

"guī" (規) means to plan or seek. The variant reading "qīn" (親) is an error in the character. "Dǎo" (討) means to punish or execute. A precedent in the *Zhuàn* (傳) states: "When bells and drums are used, it is called [a formal campaign]."
Regarding "to strike" (*fa*), some write it as "to punish" (*fà*); this does not mean to punish by inflicting humiliation, but rather to redeem one's offense by paying gold.

As for "armies," twelve thousand five hundred men constitute an army; the Son of Heaven has six armies, while the feudal lords have three. This second section on the Buddhas describes their accomplishments;
first, the headings are set forth.
[Text] Next, the Buddha’s exposition and confirmation also consists of two parts.
[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the sequential explanation, there are two sections; first, the exposition and confirmation of the initial meaning.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Four Heavenly Kings and others, saying: "Excellent, excellent! You Four Kings are indeed able to provide protection."
That which I have cultivated over hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas— namely, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi— and those kings among men who uphold this sutra,
reverently making offerings to it, shall thereby purify their misfortunes and afflictions,
bringing them peace and happiness; furthermore, they shall be able to provide protection for their palaces, residences, cities, towns, villages, kingdoms, and frontiers, and so forth.
He causes all enemies and bandits to retreat and disperse, extinguishing their misfortunes and afflictions so that they may attain peace and security;
he also ensures that all kings within Jambudvīpa are free from calamities, decline, strife, and litigation.
[Text] From "At that time, the Buddha praised... down to "...there shall be no strife or litigation," this describes the fulfillment of the first intention.
Regarding the aforementioned "manifesting invisibility to protect the state" (*gūḍharūpa-rāṣṭrarakṣa*), the Buddha explains that this invisibility is for the protection of the Triple Gem:
"I" refers to the Buddha-Gem; "cultivating bodhi" refers to the Dharma-Gem; and "the kings having no strife or litigation" refers to the Saṃgha-Gem. This describes them.
By protecting one, one can accomplish three.
[Commentary] That which is called "the Saṃgha" is characterized by the absence of strife and litigation; this absence of strife is precisely harmony. Second, this explains the subsequent meaning.
O Four Kings, you should know that in this Jambudvīpa there are eighty-four thousand cities, towns, and villages, and eighty-four thousand human kings.
Each, within his own kingdom, enjoys pleasure and happiness; each attains sovereignty over his own realm.
Regarding their respective wealth, treasures, and precious jewels, each is self-sufficient and does not encroach upon or seize from others, according to their past karma.
Having cultivated and accumulated their karma, they receive retribution according to that karma;

they do not give rise to evil thoughts or greed for other lands, but each gives rise to a mind of self-benefit, a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of peace and happiness, a mind free from contention, a mind free from destruction, a mind free from bondage, and a mind free from flogging.
In their respective lands, they naturally give rise to love and joy, with superiors and subordinates living in harmony and concord.
Just as water and milk blend together, their hearts cherish one another, increasing all roots of goodness;
by these causes and conditions, this Jambudvīpa is peaceful, secure, and prosperous, with a flourishing population and fertile lands.

Yin and yang are harmonized, the seasons do not overstep their order, the sun, moon, and stars do not deviate from their constant courses, and wind and rain arrive at their proper times. Free from all calamities and misfortunes, the people enjoy abundance.
Truly content with their own wealth, their minds free from greed and stinginess, and likewise devoid of envy, such persons practice the ten wholesome deeds;
when their lives end, they are mostly reborn in the heavens, filling the celestial palaces and increasing the number of heavenly beings.
If, in future ages, there are kings who hear this sutra, as well as the fourfold assembly who honor, revere, uphold, and recite this sutra, those kings [shall likewise attain these merits].
This shall bring peace, happiness, and benefit to you, the Four Great Kings, as well as to your retinues and the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities.
Why is this? Because if you, the Four Great Kings, hear this sutra from time to time, you will have already obtained the water of the True Dharma;
you will partake of the flavor of nectar, increase your physical strength, and possess mental vigor, courage, and majesty.
Virtuous ones, if any king of men can listen to and receive this sutra with a sincere heart, he will have already been able to make offerings to me;
if he makes offerings to me, he is making offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
and if he can make offerings to all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, he shall obtain immeasurable and inconceivable merit.
By these causes and conditions, all these kings of men should receive protection; likewise, their queens, concubines, ladies of the inner court, retinues, and princes should also receive protection.
Their decline and afflictions shall be extinguished, and their happiness shall flourish.

Their palaces and halls shall be peaceful, secure, and pure, free from all calamities. The deities who protect the dwellings shall also increase in majesty and virtue, and they too shall receive [protection].
There is immeasurable joy and happiness; all the inhabitants of those lands experience every kind of pleasure from the five desires, and all evil matters are entirely extinguished.

[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts. The first part, "From the Four Heavenly Kings... one should know that this Jambudvīpa... and below, correctly describes his intimidation and retreat through impartial compassion.
[Wenju] From "From the Four Heavenly Kings" down to "one should know that this Jambudvīpa," this describes the fulfillment of the subsequent intent.

Above, he intimidated him with celestial majesty and forced him to retreat with celestial power; it was as if he were loathing [the world] and loving the good. The Buddha exhorted him toward a mind of impartial compassion.
Those who previously committed evil will be self-reproachful, while those who practice good will be self-composed;
this is not because evil is slighted or goodness is favored, but to fulfill the intent of encouraging them to withdraw from wrongdoing.
[Commentary] "Yù" (豫) means peace and composure. These two points together exhort all states to each maintain their fundamental occupations.
[Text] Furthermore, he exhorted the various kingdoms: "Each should maintain its own occupation, abide within its borders in self-contentment, and not give rise to greedy aspirations.
When kings are harmonious, the people will not suffer untimely deaths; when the Dharma flourishes, it permeates the heavens. The Buddha told Śakra:

"The causes and conditions for strife result in the diminution of humans and devas. To be able to practice compassionate harmony throughout the world is not merely making offerings to me; it is [to honor the Buddhas]."
Making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time does not merely settle them in one king, but settles them in all kings;
it does not merely settle them in one kingdom, but settles them in all [kingdoms]. Therefore, through compassion and harmony, the second intention is thus fulfilled. So it is said. . . .
[Commentary] "To covet" means to long for. "The Buddha addressed Śakra" refers to the text of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Regarding "the sūtra’s mention of the rod of thorn":

"thorn" (*chu*) is another name for the *jing* plant, which can be used as a staff; "to strike" (*ta*) means to beat. According to the *Guangya*, "moist" (*wo shi*) means beautiful, supple, and fertile soil.
"The seasons do not overstep their order" means that the four seasons are harmonious. "The mind is free from greed and stinginess."
Because he is free from greed, he does not seek much; because he is without stinginess, he is able to practice giving.

As for the empresses, concubines, and palace women: the Son of Heaven has one Empress, three Consorts (Furen), nine Ladies-in-Waiting (Pinfei), twenty-seven Generations-Wives (Shifu), and eighty-one Attendant-Women (Yunü).
The *Fengsu Tong* states that "concubines" (*cainu*) refers to women selected for their physical beauty. Third section.
He addressed the Buddha to show him the scale [of his undertaking]. Part Two: The Initial Division of the Text. [Commentary on the Words]:
This section, "The Threefold Address to the Buddha to Show the Scale for a Human King," is divided into two parts:

first, the articulation of his aspirations; second, the demonstration of the rules and models. There are six aspirations: first, the desire to bring peace to one's own person; second, the desire to bring peace to one's wife and children; third... [and so forth].
1. To establish palaces; 2. To lead as a supreme king over the four desires; 3. To encompass all merits through the five desires; 4.
To have no sorrow or suffering in the kingdom of desire.

[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning. Part two: first, addressing the Buddha; second, first, expressing the vows. There are six textual passages for the desires, listed as in the commentary. First.
Desiring to bring peace to one's own person,
at that time the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in future ages, if there are kings who wish to protect their persons..."
[Commentary] 2. Desiring to provide security for his wife, children, as well as the consorts, palace ladies, and various princes;
[Commentary] 3. Desiring to provide security for the palace.
The palaces and residences obtain the foremost protection.
[Commentary: Among the four types of dominion over desires, the dominion over the body is the most preeminent; it possesses the inconceivable virtues of a sovereign.
[Commentary] The five desires encompass all meritorious virtues.
If one wishes to gather an immeasurable mass of merit, [one should practice them].
[Commentary] In the six desire-realm heavens, there is no sorrow or suffering.
The land is free from enemies from other regions, and devoid of all anxieties, afflictions, and painful matters.
[Textual Commentary] The six vows are as written in the text.
[Recorded Notes] Second, showing the model; of the six, the first shows that one must not be negligent.
"World-Honored One, such a king of men should not be negligent or allow his mind to be distracted; he should give rise to a heart of reverence and humility.
[Commentary: Second, showing the adornment of the Dharma Hall.
One should adorn the foremost, most subtle, and supreme palace with various fragrant liquids used for sprinkling the ground,
scatter various flowers, and arrange a great Dharma throne— a lion throne— further embellished with immeasurable rare and extraordinary treasures,
and provided with various countless, subtle, and exquisite banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies.
[Commentary] Third, he instructs him to wash and bathe.
One should cleanse oneself by bathing, anoint the body with fragrance, and adorn oneself with fine, clean robes and necklaces. Sitting upon a small, low seat, one should not exalt oneself;
one should relinquish self-importance, remain free from negligence, humble oneself, and eliminate pride and arrogance.
[Commentary] Fourth, it shows exclusive listening to the sutra:
listening to and receiving such a sublime scripture with right mindfulness, conceiving of the Dharma-preacher as the World-Honored One.
[Commentary] Fifth, it shows speaking with a serene countenance.
Furthermore, within the palace, he gave rise to a heart of compassion for the queens, princes, handmaidens, and retinue;
with a serene countenance, he spoke to them and exhorted them to provide various articles of offering to honor the Dharma Master.
[Commentary] Sixth, he shows that [the king] should rejoice within himself.
At that time, having already exhorted and transformed [others], the king immediately gave rise to a heart of immeasurable joy and happiness;
harboring a sense of gladness, he redoubled his self-exertion without becoming weary, performing many acts of benefit and generating even greater reverence for the Dharma-preacher.

[Text]: From "The World-Honored One is such a king of men" onwards is the second [section], which demonstrates its scale. Although the sequence does not follow the six numbers, it is sufficient for the purpose above:
to establish peace for the body. Now it is shown that one must not be negligent; by restraining the mind, the body becomes peaceful. Above, there was a desire to settle the palace;
now it is shown that the Dharma Hall is adorned, with banners and canopies reflecting above and incense and flowers shining with splendor.
By making offerings to the Triple Gem below, the Palace of Bailing shall be free from calamity; above, the King shall lead with excellence.

Now, by demonstrating bathing and the anointing with incense, he encourages reverence and removes arrogance, so that the body may be respectful here and peace prevail throughout the eight directions there. Above, the King seeks to gather a mass of merit;
now, he demonstrates right mindfulness in listening to the sutras. Through right mindfulness in listening to the sutras, one can achieve immeasurable merit.
The Devas of Virtue exhaust their power to protect; the Earth Devas exhaust their power to support; the Ghosts and Spirits exhaust their power to guard the subjects;

and those who love their superiors and desire to bring peace to their wives and children now show gentle countenances and speak with them, exhorting them to cultivate merit and practicing goodness both internally and externally, so that many may be moved and benefited. Now that the sovereign desires the state to be free from sorrow and suffering, they manifest themselves.
One should rejoice within oneself and exhort oneself to forget weariness, thereby redoubling one's beneficial deeds.
This refers to the saying: "When one person is delighted, the four seas become tranquil.
[Commentary] Each point corresponds in number to the six vows mentioned above. "Bailang" was the name of a hall during the Han dynasty; when it was struck by a fire from heaven, it was said:
When calamities befell the land of Han, the tails of sea-birds (*chīyú*) were placed upon the ridges of palace roofs to avert them;

thus the disasters ceased. The world was ignorant of the reason for this and called them *chīwěn*. "Eight Horizons" (*bāhóng*) refers to the eight directions; "restful beauty" (*xiūměi*) means excellence. "Self-exertion" (*zìlì*) means to encourage and strive.
Regarding the "Four Seas" (*sìhǎi*), the *Bówùzhì* states that the four quarters of heaven and earth are all interconnected by seawater.
The land occupies but a tiny portion within it. The seven Rong, six Man, nine Yi, and eight Di differ in form and kind;
taken as a whole, they are called the "Four Seas," which signifies their proximity to the ocean. Second, the exposition of the accomplishment [of the treatise].
First, the division of the text and the establishment of the intent.
[Text] Next, the Buddha’s exposition and confirmation consists of two parts: first, the confirmation of the six methods; second, the confirmation of the six vows.
Regarding the four kings, their discourse concerns six matters and is limited to the present world;
whereas the Buddha’s discourse concerns a single matter yet benefits immeasurable worlds across countless eons—thus he confirms it with double the emphasis.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the interpretation of the text through its underlying intent, there are two parts. First, the specific exposition; within that, first, the exposition of the six methods for accomplishment.
First, the exposition of the method for settling the body:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings: "At that time, the human king should don white, pure, and fresh garments."

Adorned with various necklaces arranged in perfect symmetry, holding a fine white silk canopy of exquisite quality, his attire and deportment never deviating from the proper standard, he personally went out to welcome the Dharma-preacher. Why was this?
Because for that king, with every step he took, he was making offerings and encountering hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas.
Buddha, the World-Honored One.

[Commentary on the Text: From the passage where the Buddha addresses the Four Heavenly Kings downward, the extensive propagation and listening to the sutra constitute the description and fulfillment of the methods for stabilizing the person;
above, this directly demonstrated that the mind must not be negligent, while now it further demonstrates the ceremonial procession—leaving the palace and receiving [the Buddha] at every step.
Encountering nayuta Buddhas, his methods double and his person becomes even more at ease. [Commentary] Regarding "feathered insignia" (*yuyi*):
the *Han Shu*, "Basic Annals of Gaozu," states, "Ji Xin mounted the King’s carriage with the yellow canopy and the left-side *daò*. The note says: "The *daò* is a banner made of feathers;
it is a canopy made of yellow silk that covers the *daò*. It is positioned on the left side of the crossbar of the imperial carriage."
Regarding the "upper pouring" sacrifice, Yuṅ said: it is made from the tail-hair of a *máin* ox, shaped like a dipper; it is placed either on the head of the outer horse or on the crossbar (*héng*).
Because the *dào* consists of feathered banners used as the ceremonial insignia of the Son of Heaven, they are called "feathered insignia" (*yùyí*).
"The Emperor personally went forth" means he went in person. Second, this describes the ritual methods of An-guo.
Furthermore, one attains transcendence over the hardships of birth and death throughout such kalpas.
[Commentary on the Text]: The phrase "furthermore attaining transcendence over the hardships of so many kalpas" describes the method for establishing peace in the nation;
whereas previously one merely ceased the suffering and grief of a single lifetime, now one transcends the hardships of birth and death for so many kalpas.
[Commentary] "The hardships of so many births and deaths" refers to a number of kalpas equal to the number of Buddhas encountered.
Third, the method for establishing security for one's wife and children is described.
Furthermore, throughout those same kalpas in future lives, one will constantly obtain and inherit the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) at every step.

[Text]: "Furthermore, regarding the succession of becoming a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) in future lives, this describes the method for ensuring the peace and security of one's wife and children:

a Wheel-Turning King possesses a thousand daughters of jade (yumnü) and sons, all of whom are without resentment or opposition; thus, throughout that many eons, his wife and children remain constantly at peace."
[Commentary] The fourth section describes the method by which King An (An-wang) attained sovereign power;
he likewise obtained such inconceivable and sovereign power for benefits in the present life.
[Wenju] The phrase "likewise obtained such sovereign power in the present life" describes and confirms the aforementioned "peace established for the king."
This describes the method for presiding over [the palace].
[Commentary] The fifth section describes the method for accomplishing the palace:
one will constantly obtain the most supreme and exquisite palaces of the seven treasures belonging to humans and devas.
[Text] "Obtaining the most excellent palaces of the seven treasures from the permanent" describes the method for establishing [the practitioner] securely within the palace mentioned above.
[Commentary] This sixth section describes the method for encompassing merit mentioned above.
In every place of rebirth, they increase their lifespan; their speech is eloquent and clear, and they are trusted by others.

They are free from fear or apprehension and possess great renown, always being revered by humans and devas. In the heavens and among humans, they experience supreme and wondrous bliss, attain great power, and are endowed with majestic virtue.
Their physical form is subtle and exquisite, being the most beautiful and dignified of all, and they constantly encounter the Buddhas.
[One] encounters spiritual friends and achieves the fulfillment of an immeasurable mass of merit.
[Commentary on the Text]: From "in whatever place of birth" up to "fulfilling an immeasurable mass of merit," this describes and establishes the method for gathering merit as contained therein.

[Commentary] Second, the exposition and fulfillment of the six vows. Regarding the six sections, as stated at the beginning of the *Śāstra*, this first section expounds and fulfills the vow for establishing one's own person.

"You, the Four Kings, are such kings of men; seeing these various and immeasurable merits and benefits, this king ought to personally go forth to welcome the Dharma Master, whether from a distance of one *yojana* up to a hundred thousand *yojanas*."
For ten days, one should conceive the thought of a Buddha toward the Dharma-preacher and reflect thus:
"Today, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, with his perfect wisdom, has entered my palace to receive my offerings and preach the Dharma for me;
having heard this Dharma, I shall immediately become non-retrogressive from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

[Text] From "You Four Kings" below, it describes the fulfillment of the six kinds of vows and desires; from the Four Kings down to the stage of non-retrogression, it describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow for the peaceful abiding of the body.
[Commentary] Second, this explains and establishes the aforementioned "bringing peace to the nation.
It means that one has already encountered hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, has already made offerings to all Buddhas of the past,
future, and present, and has attained ultimate liberation from the sufferings of the three evil realms.
[Text] From "Having already attained [this]" up to "the suffering of the three evil realms shall finally end," this describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow for the peace of the state.
[Commentary] The third section describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow for the peace of wife and children.
I have now already planted the causes for hundreds of thousands of immeasurable universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Śakras, and Brahmās.

[Commentary on the Text] From "I have now already planted the causes for the universal monarchs, Śakras, and Brahmās" onwards, this describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow regarding the settling of his wife and children.
[Commentary] Fourth, this explains and confirms the aforementioned inclusion of the accumulation of merit:
having already planted the seeds of boundless roots of goodness, and having caused immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings to cross over birth and death,
one has gathered an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit.
[Text] From "having already planted boundless roots of goodness" onwards, the following describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned desire to gather a mass of merit.
[Commentary] The fifth section describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow to establish the palace.
The members of the harem and their retinue have already obtained protection; all misfortunes concerning the palace and its dwellings have been entirely extinguished.
[Textual Analysis] From the harem and the palace, there shall be no calamities or decline; this describes the fulfillment of the aforementioned vow to bring peace to the palaces and halls.
[Commentary] The sixth section describes and establishes that the king’s dominion is foremost.
It means that within his realm there are no enemies, bandits, or thorns, and he cannot be invaded or oppressed by hostile powers from other regions.
[Textual Analysis] From the phrase "the realm has no enemies or thorns from other regions," the description establishes that the king’s dominion is foremost.
[Commentary] "Ji" (棘) refers to a weapon with thorns; it is identical to the character for *ji* (戟), meaning to pierce and kill. This is a general summary:

"You Four Kings, as such human kings, you should perform such offerings to the True Dharma, and you should purely listen to and receive this wondrous sutra, as well as reverently making offerings to, honoring, and praising the fourfold assembly who uphold this sutra."
The assembly shall also dedicate this most excellent portion of merit obtained here to you and your retinues, as well as to the various devas and spirits gathered here.
Through the manifestation of such virtuous merits, may you always obtain in this present life immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable benefits of sovereignty, majesty, and power;
may you be fully accomplished and endowed with the ability to [apply] the Right [Dharma].
The Dharma subdues all evils.
[Commentary on the Text] From "You Four Kings" onwards, this further summarizes and establishes six dharmas and six vows, causing them all to be fully perfected.

If one can humble oneself to welcome [the teacher] and listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart, this constitutes the six vows and six dharmas; furthermore, these are to be turned back [upon oneself].
The "Heaven of Beneficial Bestowal" (*Lishi Tian*) is also that which can cause the fulfillment and perfection of the six vows and six dharmas.
[Commentary] The fourth section, the petition to the Buddha for the essential benefits of the Dharma, is divided into two parts.
[Text] Fourth, the request to the Buddha that the human king bestow this goodness. This arises from the concluding passage of the third section, which is divided into two parts:
first, the request to the Buddha; second, the Buddha’s confirmation. The request to the Buddha is further divided into two: first, the mental resolve of the human king;
second, the manifestation of the celestial palace.

[Commentary] "By the end of the third section" means that at the conclusion of the previous passage, the World-Honored One stated that one should also dedicate a portion of the most excellent merit obtained from this to the Dharma and others, as well as to the retinue of the Four Heavenly Kings;
because of this, they subsequently sought the benefits of the Dharma. [Second, explaining the meaning, in two parts: First, petitioning the Buddha; second, first, the human king directing his mind.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, if in future ages there are various kings who thus revere the True Dharma, wholeheartedly listen to and receive this sublime sutra, and who honor, make offerings to, respect, and praise the fourfold assembly that upholds this sutra;
and who adorn their dwellings and sprinkle the ground with fragrant liquid, focusing their minds [upon it]..."
When the Dharma is being preached with right mindfulness, we four kings shall also be present among them to listen to this teaching together.
We pray that all these human kings, for their own benefit, will grant us a small portion of the merit they have acquired, O World-Honored One.
Furthermore, these human kings shall burn various kinds of incense at the place where the preachers of the Dharma sit, for our sake.
Making offerings to this sutra.
[Commentary] The signs of two celestial palaces appeared.
This wondrous fragrance reached our various celestial palaces in a single thought-moment; that fragrance immediately—
It transformed into a canopy of incense, its fragrance subtle and exquisite, its golden radiance shining brilliantly, illuminating our palaces,
the palaces of Śakra, the palaces of Brahmā, the goddess Mahāprajñā, the goddess Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhā, the earth goddess Dharaṇīndrā, the spirit Vaiśravaṇa,
the great general of the spirits, the twenty-eight divisions of spirit generals, Maheśvara, Vajrapāṇi, and Maṇibhadra.
The great general of spirits, Kumbhāṇḍī, surrounded by her five hundred sons, as well as the Dragon King Anavatapta,
the Dragon King Sāgara, and suchlike multitudes, each within their own palaces,
perceived this wondrous fragrance and beheld the fragrant canopies whose radiance shone everywhere; that radiance of the fragrant canopies likewise illuminated all things.
The Celestial Palace.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first is the literal explanation.
[Wenju] Because the human king’s mind dwells upon the ultimate scriptures, the fragrance manifests as golden light; by returning this gift, one will certainly attain it. Thus it is said.

The signs of the celestial palaces appear, and the incense reaches the palaces of the devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of the spirits and ghosts; thus it pervades the three dharma-realms.
[Commentary:
From "the human king" to "Golden Light," the mind abiding therein is precisely the three wisdoms of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. Reaching the "Canon" means...
The Three Truths are the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. When wisdom and truth unite, they give rise to the functional activity of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Because form and mind are non-dual, fragrance follows wisdom and pervades everywhere; this expresses the intention of bestowing [merit] upon the heavenly kings below.

It means that if one dedicates the benefit of the Dharma to oneself and others, both self and others shall attain it; thus, illuminating the celestial palaces with light serves as a manifestation that [the power] still belongs to [the practitioner].
Animals, together with devas and ghosts, constitute the three dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). As for what is called the "dharma-realm," it is the incense burned from liberation;
how could that which is not the dharma-realm pervade the substance of the three destinies?
How could that which is not the dharma-realm possibly receive [the offerings] when rubbed by Maheśvara—here translated as Mahādeva—and Vajrapāṇi? This is precisely...
The *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a king whose queen gave birth to a thousand sons.
Desiring to test the order in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future, Kṛkin drew the first tally, Śākyamuni drew the fourth tally, and so on until Ruci drew the thousandth tally.
The second wife gave birth to two sons; one vowed to become a Brahmā King and requested that [the other] invite the thousand [Buddhas]."
Following your elder brother’s turning of the Wheel of Dharma, you vowed to become the Secret-Trace Vajra Deity (Guhyapāda-vajrapāṇi) to protect your brother’s teachings for a thousand years.
It is not that you are an emanation of Ruci; rather, you are Prince Dharmamati. According to the scriptures, there is but one such person;
yet, as for why two images are now depicted at the gate of this monastery, it is because while the manifestations of an enlightened being are boundless, there is no fault in having many.
*Maṇibhadra* is translated here as "Majestic Subduing Conduct" (*weifuxing*); *Anavatapta* is translated as "Without Heat or Affliction" (*wurenao*);
*Sāgara* is translated as "Salt Sea" (*xianhai*). **Exegesis of the Two Contemplations.** [Textual Commentary]:

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: one uses the fire of wisdom to burn the incense of the true mark (*dharmatā*), giving rise to the smoke of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. The reality is that...
"Because the marks are the true Dharma, it is said that the golden light of precepts and wisdom merges with principle; thus, they penetrate and illuminate without obstruction," and so forth.

[Commentary] Although what was explained above discusses the wisdom of the truths, it still pertains to the provisional teaching and demonstrates the power and function of the sutra, yet does not yet discuss [the ultimate].
Regarding the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) discussed here, it aims to investigate the mind so that contemplation reaches the ultimate principle. Thus, Jingxi [Zhiyi] said:

"Although the fundamental [nature] has existed for a long time, and although the Perfect and Sudden (teaching) is truly the foremost, and although the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the principle, when viewed in relation to contemplation, it belongs to the realm of phenomena (*dharma*).

This refers to relying on phenomena to contemplate the mind and borrowing meanings to establish practice; the subtle understanding of the three wisdoms is like fire that can ignite the three truths, thereby harmonizing the mind.

Just as fragrance arises from the removal of stench, one gives rise to the practice of the three trainings; like smoke swirling upward, true original enlightenment shines forth. Therefore, it is called the "Practice of Golden Light.
Because it is darkly merged with the truth, it illuminates without obstruction. One merely awaits the realization of contemplative practice in accord with the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*;

its efficacy will naturally pervade the dharma realms. One should strive only for the manifestation of these signs through internal contemplation, rather than cultivating mental objects that take the five sensory dusts as their focus, which are the realm of demons.
One must certainly attain this; be cautious, be cautious! [The commentary] states that the two Buddhas’ narration is divided into two parts, the first of which establishes the outline.
[Wenju] Next, the Buddha’s narration and completion of the text is divided into two.
[Ji] Second, the sequential explanation is divided into two; the first part narrates and completes the description of how the fragrant light is universally pervasive.
The Buddha told the Four Heavenly Kings: "This radiance from the incense canopy does not merely reach the palaces of you, the Four Heavenly Kings.
Why is this? When these kings of men hold aloft incense burners to make offerings while reciting the sutra, its fragrance spreads everywhere;
in a single thought-moment, it pervades a trichiliocosm, reaching ten billion suns and moons, ten billion great oceans, and ten billion Mount Sumerus."
There are ten billion Great Iron Ring Mountains, ten billion Small Iron Ring Mountains, and various kings of mountains;
ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion Four Heavenly Kings, ten billion Trāyastriṃśa Heavens, and so on, up to ten billion Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana Heavens;
within this trichiliocosm, there are ten billion Trāyastriṃśa Heavens, as well as all nāgas, ghosts, and gandharvas.
The palaces of the gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, as well as the entire void, were filled with various clouds of incense smoke;
these canopies of light-golden hue also illuminated the palaces.
Thus, all the various clouds of incense smoke and canopies throughout this trichiliocosm are due to the majestic spiritual power of this sūtra.
When these kings of men hold incense burners in their hands to make offerings to this sutra, the various fragrances not only pervade this trichiliocosm,

but in a single thought-moment, they also pervade the immeasurable, boundless worlds of the Buddhas— equal in number to the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers throughout the ten directions—
and even within the space above those Buddhas, they form clouds of incense.
In this way, the universal illumination of golden light is also like this.

[Commentary on the Text]: The preceding description of the fragrant light not only reaches the celestial palaces and so forth, but pervades the three dharma-realms and extends to the billions of palaces;
furthermore, it reaches above the buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In summary, it pervades the ten dharma-realms.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "ten billion heavens of the Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception," ten billion refers to a great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

However, these share the same fourth *dhyāna* and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). As for the third *dhyāna*, it governs a medium trichiliocosm; when expressed in terms of a great trichiliocosm, there are one thousand instances of the third *dhyāna*.
As for the second *dhyāna*, it governs a small trichiliocosm; thus, there are one million instances of the second *dhyāna*. Only...
From the four continents up to the First Dhyāna, there are ten billion [worlds];

that the Non-ideation [Heaven] is also said to have ten billion is merely stated from the perspective of looking down from above, or perhaps it is a corruption in the translation. According to Yi Jing’s re-translation, there is no mention of "ten billion" regarding the Non-ideation [Heaven].
Second, the description establishing the excellence of giving and protection has two parts: first, praising the cause.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, having smelled this fragrance, seen this canopy of incense, and beheld this golden light, performed such miraculous transformations throughout Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions. Then, with one voice and in unison, they praised the speaker of the Dharma, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Being! You are able to widely proclaim and disseminate [the Dharma] such as this."
This profound and subtle sūtra is the accomplishment of an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable mass of merit.
If one hears this profound sūtra, the merit obtained is already not small;
how much more so for one who upholds, reads, recites, and explains its meaning in detail for other sentient beings! Why is this? O virtuous son...
Sons, if immeasurable, boundless billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas should hear this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*,
they will immediately become non-retrogressive from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

[Text]: From the passage "having heard this fragrance from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones" onwards, it describes how he became a king of men who practiced virtuous offerings to the devas and was praised by all Buddhas.
First, the cause is praised as being accomplished; next, the fruition is praised as being perfected.
[Commentary] Second, praising the fruit.
At that time, the Buddhas currently residing in the infinite and boundless Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, spoke with one voice, saying:
"Good son, in a future age, you shall certainly attain the seat [of enlightenment]."
At the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he is the most honored and supreme within the triple world,
transcending all sentient beings; through the power of diligent cultivation, he undergoes various ascetic practices, skillfully adorning the site of enlightenment,
destroying the heterodox arguments of external paths throughout the trichiliocosm, and subduing the various demonic adversaries and enemies who manifest strange forms.
O son of good family, you have already realized the path of supreme enlightenment— utterly tranquil, pure, stainless, profound, and unsurpassed—
and are able to sit upon the Vajra Seat to turn the twelvefold wheel of Dharma, which is unsurpassed and praised by all Buddhas;
you are able to beat the unsurpassed, greatest drum of Dharma and blow the unsurpassed, most sublime conch.
The Dharma conch is able to raise the unsurpassed, most supreme banner of the Dharma; it is able to light the unsurpassed, most brilliant torch of the Dharma;
it is able to rain down the unsurpassed nectar-rain of the Dharma; it is able to sever the immeasurable enmities and fetters of affliction;

and it is able to cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of beings to cross the shoreless and fearsome great ocean, attaining liberation from the boundless cycle of birth and death.
[He] encountered immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas during his transmigration.
[Wenju]: As in the text. [Ji]:
The passage from "diligently practiced" (*jing qinxiu*) below clarifies that he was able to excel in practicing asceticism, destroy the heterodox, and subdue the demonic enemies.

Adorning the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), awakening and subsequently attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), and, O son of good family, turning the wheel of Dharma—these are all matters pertaining to the stage of fruition, as explained in detail in the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra* (or *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*). Fifth, the white-robed [layperson] addresses the Buddha to exhort him regarding prosperity and decline;
this section is divided into two parts.

[Text] The fifth section, the petition to the Buddha, which presents both prosperity and decline, is divided into two parts: first, the petition to the Buddha; second, the Buddha’s confirmation of the petition.

The petition to the Buddha is further divided into three parts. The first, from the petition to the Buddha up to "causing all evils and calamities to be completely extinguished," is the first presentation of prosperity, exhorting [the king] to follow it.
From "if there is a human king who conceives a mind of renunciation" up to "the benevolent deities depart," [is the second part].
The arising of such immeasurable evil matters is the second point for raising up those in decline.
To encourage those who follow the World-Honored One—the King of Men—to protect themselves as well as their kingdom and territory is the third correct encouragement.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, the white-robed [deities] address the Buddha, in three sections. First, raising an exhortation; fourth, first, describing the propagation of the sutra;
fourth, the four heavenly kings listen and receive.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is able to..."
One shall obtain various and immeasurable merits of the future and the present;
therefore, if a king of men hears this subtle and wondrous sutra, he shall have already planted roots of goodness before hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable Buddhas.
Out of my reverent mindfulness for such a king of men, and furthermore because I see the immeasurable benefits of his merit, we—the four kings and...
When my other retinues— immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of spirits and ghosts— behold these various auspicious signs of fragrant smoke,
clouds, and canopies within their own palaces, I shall conceal and hide my body; for the sake of hearing the Dharma,
I shall go to the palace where this king resides and to the place where the Dharma is being preached.
[Commentary on the Text] 1. To exhort and encourage: When a king promotes the propagation of the sutra, the Four Heavenly Kings conceal their forms to listen and receive it. 2.
Not only do the Four Heavenly Kings listen and receive it, but Śakra, Brahmā, and the eight classes of deities all assemble to listen and receive it.
3. Thus, this human king becomes a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of wholesome dharmas. 4. Having obtained the benefit of the Dharma, he becomes even more diligent in protecting the state.
[Commentary] Second, it clarifies that the eight classes of deities,
including Brahmā and Śakra, have all assembled: Mahābrahmā-rāja, Śakra-devendra, Mahāprajñā-devī, Guṇakara-devī,
Drḍhā-pṛthivī-devī, Vaiśravaṇa the Great General, the twenty-eight generals of the ghost-spirits, and Maheśvara.
The Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, the mahāyakṣasenāpati Maṇibhadra, Hārītī with her five hundred yakṣa children, and their surrounding retinue;
the Nāga King Anavatapta, the Nāga King Sāgara, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of spirits,
devas, and suchlike multitudes— all these, for the sake of hearing the Dharma, completely concealed themselves.
He manifests his body at the palace where this human king resides, the place where he preaches the Dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding "Śakra Devānām Indra" in the sutra: it is fully called Śakradevānindara, which translates as "The Lord of Gods Capable [of Victory].
The King of Men, who possesses the Three Knowledges (traividya), acts as a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).
"Blessed One, we four kings and our retinues of immeasurable spirits shall all be of one mind toward this king,
regarding him as a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra). We shall act in concert with him in a single course of conduct that accords with virtue, for he is a supreme donor of the Great Dharma."
[Commentary] Having attained the benefit of the Dharma, the Four Ming [Kings] protect the state with even greater diligence.
Satiated by the flavor of the nectar of immortality, they think: "We and those like us should protect this king, eliminating his decline and afflictions so that he may attain peace and security;
furthermore, we shall cause all evil calamities regarding his palace, kingdom, and cities to be entirely extinguished."
"Extinction.
[Wenju] All is as in the text.
[Ji] Second, citing decline to provide exhortation; first, dividing the text.
[Text] Next, the exhortation by citing signs of decline also consists of four points: first, when the King does not propagate the Sūtra, heaven loses its ambrosia, and his majestic power diminishes;
second, Śakra, Brahmā, and the ancient deities all abandon him from afar; third, evil spirits roam in disorder, and calamitous poisons arise in competition;
fourth, these conditions successively combine to form disasters. Why do these disasters arise? Why do evil spirits roam in disorder? Why do the spirits roam?
Why does the celestial deity abandon the heavens? Why does he abandon them and not hear the food of the Dharma? Why is there no food of the Dharma?
Because the King does not propagate the sutras.
[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the sequential explanation of the four points: first, it clarifies that the celestial deities lose the food of the Dharma.
“World-Honored One, if there is a king who, regarding this sutra, gives rise to thoughts of abandonment and does not delight in hearing it,
nor desires to revere, make offerings to, respect, or praise it— and if among the fourfold assembly there are those who receive,
uphold, read, recite, or explain it, yet he likewise cannot revere, make offerings to, respect, or praise us, the Four Great Kings, and...”
The other retinues of immeasurable spirits and ghosts will then be unable to hear this True Dharma;
they will turn their backs on the flavor of the nectar, lose the great benefit of the Dharma, lack power and majesty, cause the celestial hosts to diminish, and increase the realms of evil rebirths.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of how the celestial deities abandon [the land].
"World-Honored One, we four kings and immeasurable spirits shall abandon that kingdom;
not only we, but all the immeasurable ancient virtuous deities who protect the kingdom shall likewise depart."

[Commentary] When the evil man of the three knowledges (*trividyā*) brings about calamity, and we—the various kings and spirits—have already abandoned [the realm], that country shall experience all manner of portents and anomalies.
All the people will lose their wholesome minds; there will be nothing but bondage, anger, strife, and mutual destruction.
There will be many epidemics; comets will appear as portents, and meteors will fall. The five planets and the various lunar mansions will deviate from their regular courses.
Two suns will appear simultaneously, and the sun and moon will undergo eclipses. White and black, ominous rainbows will appear repeatedly. The earth will shake violently, emitting great sounds.
Fierce winds and torrential rains will occur almost daily. Grains and rice will become exceedingly expensive, leading to famine and the suffering of cold and hunger.
There are many hostile enemies from other regions who invade and plunder the country, causing the people to suffer greatly;
there is no place in that land that is pleasant or desirable.

[Commentary] Regarding the term "star" (*xing*) in the sutra commentary, the *Xingshuo* states: "To depart by erasing one's tracks is called 'fleeing like starlight' (*bengxingguang*); the traces of the light follow one another in succession."
Regarding "meteors and eclipses" (*bolishi*): according to the *Tianwen Zhi* (Treatise on Astronomy) of the *Hanshu*, this refers to the "conjunction-eclipses" (*boshi*) of the sun and moon.
Meng Kang’s commentary states: "When the sun and moon lose their light, it is called 'conjunction' (*bo*). Wei Zhao states: "When atmospheric vapors press against them, it is 'conjunction';

when they are diminished or deficient, it is 'eclipse' (*shi*). The *Jingfang Yizhuan* says: "When the sun and moon appear red or yellow, it is conjunction. The *Shiming* says: "The waning of the sun and moon is called..."
"Eclipse" (*śi*) refers to the gradual encroachment and waning [of light], like insects eating the leaves of plants and trees. Regarding the "rainbow" (*hóng*):
the *Erya* states, "The *dìdǒng* is the *hóng*. The *Erya Yinyi* explains: "When two appear and are bright and vibrant, the male is called *hóng*;
when they are dim and obscure, the female is called *ní*. The *ní* is also called *jī*; in Jiangdong it is called *yú*, and in common parlance it is called the 'Beauty' (*měirén*)."
The *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "The rainbow (*hóng*) is 'assault' (*gōng'), meaning that pure yang assails yin.

When these four [rainbows] revolve and bring about calamities, World-Honored One, when we, the Four Kings, along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of spirits and ghosts, as well as the long-standing benevolent deities who protect the lands, depart and distance ourselves, such immeasurable evil events as these arise.
[Text] As in the text.
[Commentary] The third section, "The Proper Exhortation," is divided into six parts:
first, because one desires immediate benefit, one must certainly listen; second, the devas rejoice in the Dharma.
First, because it is for the sake of food, one must certainly listen; second, because it transcends the three [types of] discourses, one must certainly listen;

third, because it brings benefit from beginning to end and accomplishes enlightenment, one must certainly listen; fourth, because the Teacher is superior to Śakra and Brahmā, one must certainly listen;
fifth, because it is the root of all dharmas, one must certainly listen.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation of the six [verses]. First, regarding the desire to obtain immediate benefits:
"World-Honored One, if there is a king who wishes to protect himself and his kingdom so that they may enjoy abundant peace and happiness;
who wishes to cause all sentient beings within the kingdom to fully achieve and possess joy; and who wishes to subdue all [opponents]..."
World-Honored One, if there are kings who wish to protect all their lands, who wish to govern their lands with the True Dharma,
and who wish to eliminate the fears of sentient beings,
they should certainly listen to this sutra and respectfully make offerings to those who read, recite, accept, and uphold it.
[Commentary]: The two classes of devas delight in the food of the Dharma.
We, the Four Great Kings and immeasurable spirits and deities, by means of these roots of goodness from the food of the Dharma, obtain the taste of the unsurpassed nectar of the Dharma;
our physical strength increases, our minds become diligent and courageous, and we augment the power of all the devas. Why is this?
Because this king of men listens to and receives this sutra with a sincere heart.
[Commentary: This refers to surpassing three types of discourses:

such as the discourse on the transcendence of desire spoken by the Brahmā devas, the various excellent discourses spoken by Śakra Devendra, and the discourses of those possessing the five supernormal powers.

Regarding the discourses of the immortals and seers— though there may be hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of immeasurable and superior discourses by the World-Honored One, Brahmā, Śakra Devendra, spirits,
and those with supernormal powers— the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the most supreme among them all.
[Text]: The proponents of the Three Treatises [state that] the *Veda* treatises expound upon the matters of Brahmā; the *Vyākaraṇa* treatises expound upon the matters of the ten wholesome actions;
and the *Sāṃkhya*, *Vaiśeṣika*, and *Lokāyata* treatises expound upon the matters of learning and penetration, and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the four Vedas: these are the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The *Maudgalyāyana-sūtra* states: "In the beginning, a person named Brahmā created one Veda.
Subsequently, there was a seer named Śukra who transformed that one into four: first, the *Ṛg-veda* (Recitation); second, the *Yajur-veda* (Sacrifice);
third, the *Sāma-veda* (Chanting); and fourth, the *Atharva-veda* (Averting Calamities). Next, there was one named Puṣya, who had twenty [disciples].
The five disciples each mastered one Veda and were able to analyze and expand upon them extensively, resulting in twenty-five Vedas.
Next came those named Śuka and Sudharmā; their disciples likewise gradually expanded and propagated these teachings.

Thus, through successive transmission, there came to be one thousand two hundred and six Vedas. What is currently referred to as "four" is named according to their fundamental sources, all of which clarify [the truth].

The *Brahma-karma* is so called because it emerges from the departure from the defilement of desire; thus, it is said that the Brahma-heaven expounds the discourse on the transcendence of desire (*vairāgya-śāstra*).
The *Vyākaraṇa* is here named the *Abhidhāna*; it was composed by Pāṇini to elucidate various scriptures as well as diverse colloquial languages.
Furthermore, it is the fundamental treatise on the names and characters of the West—namely, the foundational texts of worldly writing and the science of phonology (*śabda-śāstra*). It proclaims...
Mastery of the four types of eloquence, he censures worldly dharmas and praises the dharma of renunciation; his phrasing is pure and elegant, while his meaning is profound.
Although this is a non-Buddhist treatise, it contains no heterodox teachings; it must surely have been composed by a Great Being of skillful means.

Sāṃkhya—translated here as "Enumeration" (Shùlùn)—is so called because all phenomena arise from enumeration. It was created at the beginning of the kalpa by the Sage Yellow-Head (Kapila). It is protected by...
The *Lokāyata* (World-Master) is here called *Vaiśeṣika* (Excellence Treatise), because it is the most excellent among all treatises and was composed by an eminent person.
At the end of the kalpa, the non-Buddhist *Ulūka* (Owl) school composed the *Lakṣaṇa* (Characteristics) treatise; this is translated as "Austere Practice" (*duḥkha-caryā*).

Since its author's time of appearance in the world is unknown, the treatise is named after the person who composed it. Because these three sages possessed the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), they are limited to five [elements].
Pervasive. Fourth, obtaining benefit from beginning to end.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has preached this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* for the sake of sentient beings, so that all kings among men within Jambudvīpa may govern by means of the True Dharma, and to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.
Desiring to love and protect all sentient beings, wishing to cause them to be free from all suffering and affliction,

and to turn their backs on and avoid all evils such as enemies, bandits, and thorns from other regions; wishing to ensure that the kingdom is free from sorrow and distress by teaching through the True Dharma so that there is no contention or litigation—
for this reason, O Kings of Men, each should kindle the torch of Dharma within your respective kingdoms.
The blazing True Dharma increases the hosts of devas;

we, the Four Great Kings, along with immeasurable spirits and the various celestial benevolent deities within Jambudvīpa, by this cause and condition, shall partake of the nectar-like flavor of the Dharma, becoming fully satisfied and attaining great majesty and power, as well as complete vigor.
Within Jambudvīpa, there shall be peace, abundance, and joy; the population shall flourish and dwell in happiness.
Furthermore, in future lives, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of inconceivable nayutas of kalpas, they shall constantly experience the most subtle and supreme happiness;
they shall also encounter immeasurable Buddhas and plant various roots of goodness, and thereafter realize Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. All such immeasurable merits as these are entirely [attained].
"The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has spoken.
[Commentary] In the sūtra, "the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha" refers to two of the ten epithets. This is because these two represent the excellence of the Master.
Because the Tathāgata surpasses hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Brahmās by virtue of his power of great compassion,
