and because he surpasses immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Śakras by virtue of his power of ascetic practice,
the Tathāgata therefore expounds this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* for the sake of all sentient beings.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "by the power of great compassion," etc.: because it universally covers the *dharmadhātu* through objectless (*nirālambana*) great compassion, it surpasses the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*) of Brahmā;

and because it benefits sentient beings through inconceivable ascetic practices accumulated over kalpas, it surpasses the cause of the ten wholesome paths (*daśakuśala-karma-patha*) of Śakra. Sixth, because it is the root of all phenomena.
If all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, as well as the kings of men, perform worldly or supramundane state affairs and compose worldly treatises, it is all because of this sutra;

for the sake of causing sentient beings to attain peace and happiness, Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested this sutra and widely proclaimed and disseminated it throughout the world. World-Honored One, by these causes and conditions, these kings of men...
One should certainly listen to, accept, make offerings to, revere, respect, and praise this sutra.
[Text] All is as written.
[Commentary] Regarding "all sentient beings" and so forth: the world refers to the five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, and the twelve gates of dhyāna.
The four dharma-gates for those who transcend the world refer to the cultivation and realization of the Three Vehicles.

State affairs refer to matters such as ritual, music, military expeditions, governing the world, and nurturing the people. The "Treatises on the World" refers to the three aforementioned treatises as well as the *Nyāyapraveśa* and others;
all of these are based upon this sutra, which consists of the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle. Therefore...

The New Edition states: "Whether one desires to be born among humans or devas, desires to attain the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or desires to attain Buddhahood, all must rely on this sutra to repent and eliminate hindrances before they can achieve success.

If one probes the underlying intent of the transformation, it is simply that within the single Buddha-vehicle, three vehicles are taught through differentiation. However, because the section of this sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra) teachings, it still pertains to the universal principle."
Since human beings differ in their inclinations and cannot be exempt from these distinctions, [the Buddha] intends to enable them all to attain peace and happiness according to the five vehicles.
Second, the Buddha’s exposition of the two initial sections of the text.

[Wenju]: Next, the Buddha’s exposition and confirmation consists of two parts. The first part confirms the initial proposal and exhorts [the assembly], stating that if [the teaching] is not propagated, it will decline.

Regarding the phrase "there is nothing further to be established," another interpretation states: in the previous section, two points were established—namely, that [the Buddha] brings about peace and happiness, which is one establishment;

and that he promotes the flourishing [of virtue] while urging the cessation of decline and affliction, which is the second establishment. Thus, promoting the flourishing is the establishment, and urging the cessation of decline is the establishment.
[Commentary] Second, the detailed explanation in two parts. First, the exhortation regarding prosperity and decline.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:

"You, the Four Kings, along with your retinues of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of spirits and deities—if these kings of men can listen to this sutra with a sincere heart and offer worship and respect..."
"You Four Kings, who are revered, honored, and praised, should rightly protect them, eliminate their misfortunes and afflictions, and grant them peace and happiness.
[Commentary] This is the second section: the formal exhortation.
If there be anyone who can widely proclaim and disseminate such a sublime scripture among humans and devas,
performing great Buddha-work and bringing great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings— O Four Kings, you must certainly protect such a person;
do not allow them to be disturbed by external conditions, but let their mind be tranquil and happy, so that they may continue to attain [realization].
"Extensively proclaim this sutra.
[Commentary on the Words]: From "If there be anyone who can perform great Buddha-work among humans and devas," it describes the accomplishment of the exhortation to practice, and so forth.
[Commentary] The sixth section explains the virtues through verses; it is divided into two parts.
[Text] The sixth part, the prose addressed to the Buddha, consists of three sections: first, the praise in verse; second, the Buddha’s response in verse;
third, the joyful expression of vows. The eight lines and a half of the verse-praise are further divided into three: the first line praises the three bodies (*trikāya*); next...
Five lines and a half praise the physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the body, followed by two lines that conclude the praise.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning; third, the initial presentation of the verses of praise. First, the praise of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, placed their right knees on the ground, knelt for a long time, and joined their palms.
Holding his palms before the World-Honored One, he praised him with a verse:
"The Buddha-moon is pure, full, and majestic; the Buddha-sun shines radiantly, emitting a thousand rays of light.
[Commentary] The text has three parts; first, based on the extant text, the three bodies are individually correlated.

[Text]: Now, the three bodies have both general and specific [meanings]. According to the text, these are the specific meanings: emptiness is the Dharma-body, the sun is the Reward-body, and the moon is the Response-body.
[Commentary]: Regarding "emptiness is the Dharma-body," although the word "emptiness" does not appear in the sutra, the sun and moon must necessarily rely upon emptiness; furthermore—
The subsequent text states: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space. Therefore, the Commentary correlates the three—space, the sun, and the moon—with the three bodies: 1.
Space, being devoid of light and darkness, serves as a general metaphor for the Dharmakāya, which is fundamentally all-pervasive; 2.

The sun, which can dispel darkness, serves as a specific metaphor for the Sambhogakāya, which exhausts the three delusions; 3. The moon, which waxes and wanes, serves as a specific metaphor for the Nirmāṇakāya.

The *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) adapts to the superior or inferior capacities of sentient beings; this specific distinction serves as a preliminary foundation for the subsequent discussion on the perfect fusion [of the three bodies]. Second, regarding the meaning of the metaphors, they universally encompass all three bodies. First, taking metaphors to reveal perfection: [The text continues: "Just as the moon’s reflection appears in various waters, though the moon itself remains one and undivided, so too does the Buddha-body manifest according to the differences in the faculties of sentient beings, while the essence of the Dharma-body remains eternally unchanging. This illustrates that although the manifestations differ according to the conditions of those to be converted, the substance of the Dharma-realm is fundamentally non-dual. Furthermore, it shows that while the moon is one, its reflections appear in many; likewise, while the Dharmakāya is one, its manifestations appear in many. Thus, the metaphor of the moon and its reflections reveals the principle of the perfect fusion of the three bodies. Second, taking metaphors to illustrate the distinctness [of the three bodies]: [The text continues: "Just as the moon is one yet its reflections appear in many waters, so too is the Tathāgata’s nature one, yet he manifests in accordance with the differences in the faculties of sentient beings. This clarifies that while the essence of the Dharmakāya is eternally quiescent and free from differentiation, its manifestations adapt to the varying capacities of those to be converted. Therefore, the metaphor of the moon and its reflections illustrates the principle of the distinctness of the three bodies. Third, taking metaphors to illustrate both distinctness and fusion: [The text continues: "Just as the moon is one yet its reflections appear in many waters, and though the reflections are many, their source is the single moon; so too is the Tathāgata’s nature one, yet he manifests in accordance with the differences in the faculties of sentient beings, and though his manifestations are many, their source is the single Dharmakāya. This clarifies that while the essence of the Dharmakāya is eternally quiescent and free from differentiation, its manifestations adapt to the varying capacities of those to be converted. Thus, the metaphor of the moon and its reflections simultaneously reveals the principles of both the distinctness and the perfect fusion of the three bodies. This concludes the section on taking metaphors to reveal the meaning. Third, taking metaphors to illustrate the identity of substance and function: [The text continues: "Just as the moon is one yet its reflections appear in many waters, and though the reflections are many, their source is the single moon; so too is the Tathāgata’s nature one, yet he manifests in accordance with the differences in the faculties of sentient beings, and though his manifestations are many, their source is the single Dharmakāya. This clarifies that while the essence of the Dharmakāya is eternally quiescent and free from differentiation, its manifestations adapt to the varying capacities of those to be converted. Therefore, the metaphor of the moon and its reflections illustrates the principle of the identity of substance and function within the three bodies. [Text] To explain the underlying meaning: emptiness is the Dharma-body; the sun is the Reward-body; the moon reflected in water is the Response-body.
Emptiness is the Dharma-body; the sun is the Reward-body; the moon in water is the Response-body. Emptiness is the Dharma-body; the space within the sun is the Reward-body;
the space within the moon in water is the Response-body. It is the same for the moon.
[Commentary: If one were to pair these three metaphors individually with the three bodies, there might be the misconception that the three bodies are distinct in essence.
Therefore, we now take the objects of the metaphors in detail; their meanings are not restricted, as each metaphor individually possesses all three meanings.
For example, in the single metaphor of the sun: its being above must rely on space, and its appearing below must manifest in water. These three meanings clarify the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The three bodies (trikāya) are fully present; this is the discussion of the three bodies according to the Three Prajñās. The metaphor of the moon is likewise:
it can manifest the application [of wisdom] as the three bodies are fully present; this is the discussion of the three bodies according to the Three Liberations.
The great void is that upon which the sun relies; the sky-sun and the water-sun each inherently contain the void. These three types of emptiness manifest the Dharma.
"The essence perfectly possesses the three bodies; the moon is also like this. Regarding the moon, that which it relies upon is space, the celestial moon, and the moon in water;
within these, space is also contained and manifests. This reveals that the essence of the Dharma perfectly possesses the three bodies. Space pervades both the sun and the moon;

thus, the two explanations of the three bodies are presented from the perspective of the Middle Way’s dual illumination. This, then, is the discussion of the three bodies in terms of the three tracks (trikāya-trimārga).
Second, the text is shown by way of the concluding summary. [Wenju]:

According to the concluding eulogy, emptiness is the Dharmakāya; the moon is the Saṃbhogakāya; and the moon reflected in water is the Nirmāṇakāya. Emptiness is the Dharmakāya; the sun is the Saṃbhogakāya;
and the flame is the Nirmāṇakāya. The manifested Dharma is the Dharmakāya; and the master of manifestation is the [Saṃbhogakāya].
The manifestation of activities by the *saṃbhogakāya* is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
[Commentary] This concluding eulogy presents three metaphors: the moon, a flame, and a transformation. The meaning of each of these three matters must fully possess all three aspects.

For instance, regarding the single metaphor of the moon, it must necessarily depend upon the sky above and must necessarily manifest in the water below; this constitutes the perfection of the *nirmāṇakāya*.

The text concerning the possession of the three bodies (trikāya) states: "Just as flames must depend on fire, and fire must depend on space, so too is the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) fully endowed with the three bodies.
The text concerning the possession of the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) states:

"Just as transformations must have a technique, which is called the 'technique of transformation,' and this technique must reside in a person, who is the 'master of transformation,' so the objects transformed are called 'transformed phenomena. Thus, the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) is fully endowed [with the three bodies]."
The Three Bodies. Furthermore, taking up the phrasing of the "knot" (the summary) once more, one integrates the general with the specific.
[Wenju] Although they are explained separately, their meaning is in fact integrated; therefore, the text says "there is no obstruction," which is precisely the sense of this integration.
[Commentary] Since the Sūtra clearly states that there are no obstructions, if one does not take the Dharma as the definitive basis for the metaphors, how could each [aspect] be mutually interfused?

How then could this be called the teaching of non-obstruction? One should use this principle to harmonize the texts concerning the marks of the body (*kāyalakṣaṇa*), so that each individual mark adorns the three bodies (*trikāya*) and becomes a mark of the secret treasury (*guhyakośalakṣaṇa*). Second, praising the marks of the body; first, the division.
Sectioning the Commentary on the Sūtra, Part One: Initial Sectioning.
[Textual Analysis] The passage praising the physical marks is divided into five parts: first, one line praises the two superior marks, namely the eyes and the teeth;
next, one and a half lines praise the two virtues of wisdom and cessation, namely wisdom and samādhi; finally, two lines praise the two inferior marks.
This means that the first two lines of the couplet "smoothness" and "net-like" are an exclamatory praise stating they are inconceivable; the subsequent two lines are a concluding praise.
[Commentary] Of the two explanations of the sūtra, this is the first: praising the aforementioned two marks.
The Tathāgata’s face and eyes are supremely bright and pure; his teeth are white and stainless like the roots of a lotus.
[Commentary] This second section praises his wisdom and abandonment.
His merits are immeasurable like the great ocean; his abyss of wisdom is boundless, fully endowed with the dharma-water of hundreds of thousands of samādhis.
There is no deficiency or diminution.
[Commentary] The first two phrases provide a general indication that there are both metaphors and the phenomena they illustrate; the next four phrases are specific praises;

two phrases refer to wisdom (*jñāna*), and two phrases refer to abandonment (*prahāṇa*). It is an ocean-deep abyss. The *Guǎnzǐ* says: "Water that emerges from the earth but does not flow is called..."
Yuan: He sighed three times and described the two lower marks:
the soles of his feet were level and full, manifesting the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel; the webbing between his toes was like that of a king of geese;
his radiance was brilliant and dazzling like the King of Jewel Mountains; and he was subtle, wondrous, pure, and refined like purified gold.
[Commentary] 4. Praise beyond words:
"The merit therein is inconceivable.
[Commentary] 5. Concluding praise.
I now pay homage to the mountain of the Buddha’s merits.
[Commentary] Second, a general demonstration of the physical marks and signs. Part one: Universally adorning the three bodies.

[Text] Now, the primary and secondary marks do not reside solely in the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); they also universally adorn the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) and the *upapattidehakāya* (body born of parents).

The "marks and signs" (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) adorn the body of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya); the "marks and signs" as retribution (vipākaphala-lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) adorn the Body of Sovereign Distinction (sambhogakāya);
and the "marks and signs" of the Dharma-gate (dharmamukha-lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) adorn the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
[Commentary] The marks and signs do not belong exclusively to the Response-body; they also extend to the Retribution and Dharma-bodies, as indicated by the items listed here.
The analogy of the gear-network is that the twenty-eight [nodes] above and below interconnect, capable of adorning the three kinds of bodies.
Since the body-phase is one, it appears as three according to how it is perceived, thereby adorning the birth-body produced by parents.

This is because those of the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Vaipulya) schools speak only of partial emptiness; the Buddha-phenomena they perceive are said to be constructed and formed through the conjunction of correct and residual habits, and thus their appearance is not [the true reality].
It is extraordinary that [this body] is merely slightly superior to that of a wheel-turning king;

because it does not know that forms manifest from the mind and instead perceives them as coming from the outside with fixed boundaries, it is called the "birth-body" (*janma-kāya*). This is the body manifested by the Tathāgata in accordance with the capacities of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles;

therefore, it is called the "Adorned Body. As for the "Body of Distinguished Features," it is so named because those of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) are able to believe in the Middle Way.
Exquisite form and exquisite mind transform and create in accordance with conditions; the perceived marks of the Buddha are known to manifest from the mind, having no fixed boundaries.
Sometimes they manifest a great body as numerous as the atoms within ten Lotus Treasury Worlds; sometimes they manifest eighty-four thousand marks and signs;
and at other times, they may appear merely as the six-foot body with the thirty-two marks, causing the capacities and conditions of sentient beings to likewise have no fixed boundaries.
Because it is seen as distinct from the bodies categorized under the *xiang* (characteristic) and *tong* (common/penetrating) teachings, it is called "venerable and special.
Since this is obtained through the Tathāgata’s cultivation of the path, it is called the "Dharma-gate of Retribution Adornment. Regarding the Dharma-gate of Adornment:

those of the Perfect Teaching realize that both large and small bodies, as well as many and few marks, are all inherently possessed by nature; thus, the virtues of cultivation are without effort. Although these marks are form, form itself is [emptiness].
Regarding the mind, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The nature of form is itself wisdom; this is called the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*). The nature of wisdom is itself form;

this is called the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). Now, because it is designated as a "Dharma-gate" (dharma-dvāra) from the perspective of being identical to wisdom, the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇīs are taken as its hair, up to and including meditative concentration and wisdom as its feet.
Because it is identical to form, it is thus named the "characteristics of the Dharma Body."

This is because these marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) evolve according to their respective interpretations, thereby causing the adornments of the three bodies (trikāya) to differ from one another.
Second, a specific indication of the dharma-gates.
[Textual Commentary]: What is now called the praise of wisdom and abandonment (jñānaprahāṇa) refers precisely to the marks and signs of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).

[Commentary] This refers to the fact that the ocean of wisdom is boundless as the merit of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*), while the hundred thousand samādhis constitute the merit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
These two merits are able to encompass all dharma-gates of adornment.
If a student interprets this meaning by dividing form and mind, they will never recognize the marks and signs of the Dharmakāya. (3)
The text demonstrates perfect interfusion.
[Wenju] The text states that "there is no obstruction" does not merely praise the marks of a single body.

[Ji] The preceding analysis of the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies was intended to facilitate easy understanding; therefore, it was necessary to proceed according to the varying capacities of sentient beings.

One must understand the relative superiority and inferiority: the former does not know the latter, yet the latter must necessarily perceive the former, because the former is coarse while the latter is subtle.
Now, these Four Heavenly Kings are Great Bodhisattvas;

when praised from the perspective of the Perfect [Teaching], one sees that their three bodies and the three sublime virtues (triguṇa) are non-dual and indistinguishable. This should be liberation—how could it be separated into two?
The retribution of virtue may be understood by analogy with the Dharma; to manifest this meaning, it is specifically stated that "there are no obstacles.
Only when one understands this intent can one be said to have profoundly penetrated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Dharma-gate. Third, the concluding praise.
The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things like the moon reflected in water, without any obstruction, like a flame, like a transformation.
Therefore, I now bow my head in homage to the Buddha-moon.
[Commentary] The text has two parts: first, the direct explanation of the sutra text;

second, the initial explanation of the text [itself]. [Wenju] At the beginning of the verse, the Buddha-moon is designated; now, the previously mentioned Buddha-moon is concluded as the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Next, because the three bodies are interpenetrating and harmonious, it is said that "there are no obstructions. Next, because it concludes the Buddha-sun, it is said to be "like a flame. Finally, it concludes the Buddha’s transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
Because the body itself possesses the meaning of the four bodies, it is said to be "like a transformation. That all possess the three bodies and four bodies is precisely non-obstruction.
Having concluded [the discourse], one pays homage; this homage to the Buddha-moon is also homage to the Buddha-sun and the Buddha-transformation.

[Commentary] Regarding the classification of the Buddha-moon into the three bodies (*trikāya*): the extant text mentions only the moon in the sky and the moon in the water, which can serve as metaphors for the three bodies.
As for the statement that the Buddha manifests as four bodies: the Dharma-body possesses wondrous form and acts as the transformative agent;

the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (Sambhogakāya) illuminate principle and discern capacities to act as the masters of transformation; and by skillfully conforming to the conditions of sentient beings, they manifest the nine [forms].

The realm-body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) performs transformative activities (*nirmāṇa-karman*); now, because these transformative activities manifest the possession of the three aforementioned [bodies], the treatise states that all four bodies possess both three and four.
This means that if one takes up even a single body, it is simultaneously three and four; this applies to each and every one of them, and only then can they be called "unimpeded" (*asaṅga*).
Second, the conclusion regarding the wondrous [nature] has two parts: first, clarifying that the beginning and end are both three.

[Textual Commentary]: At the beginning of this chapter, the Sūtra is praised; in the praise of its essence and its primary principle, at the end of the chapter, the words used to extol the Buddha differ while their meaning remains the same.

The True Dharma-body of the Buddha is the essence (*tattva*); the purity of the Buddha-moon is the primary principle (*śāstra*); and the manifestation as the moon in water is the function (*prayoga*).

[Commentary] These three chapters concern the Dharma, while the three bodies concern the person; since the person takes up the Dharma and the person is not separate from the Dharma, it is said that although the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same.
"The Buddha-moon is pure" refers to the first phrase of the verse, which establishes the present three bodies.
Second, praising the celestial eloquence as being exceptionally sublime.
[Wenju] states: "The celestial eloquence of the Heavenly King is as wondrous as this. [Ji] explains:
The first praise in the three chapters spoke of how the subtle and wonderful *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra is revealed without vertical or horizontal limitations; now, this concludes it.

Regarding the statement that the three bodies (trikāya) are without obstruction and neither vertical nor horizontal: this is revealed through the initial and final [bodies] manifesting the middle one;

in every phrase, there is nothing that does not discuss the secret treasury (guhyagarbha). The Great Master’s praise of its wondrousness lies precisely in this. Second, the examination of the capacity of the recipient and the response of the teacher:
having clarified above that the three bodies are without obstruction, the meaning remains profound and subtle; thus, fearing that students might [still harbor doubts], [the author proceeds].

While characteristics do not vanish, emotional attachments remain divided; now, it is clarified that the three bodies (*trikāya*) and those for whom they are intended are none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Since there is nothing outside the Dharma-realm, how could there be "self" and "other"? The first question and answer clarify that there is nothing remaining apart from the Dharma.

[Text] Question: Space is used as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya* and the moon as a metaphor for the *saṃbhogakāya*. Does space create the moon, or does it not? If space creates the moon, then the moon is not created by space;
if space does not create the moon, then how can the moon rely upon space? Answer: Space does not create the moon, nor does it create that which is not the moon.

Since that which is not the moon must necessarily rely upon space, so too the *dharmakāya* does not create the *saṃbhogakāya*, nor does it create that which is not the *saṃbhogakāya*. Since that which is not the *saṃbhogakāya* must necessarily rely upon the *dharmakāya*.
"Neither retribution nor non-retribution necessarily depends upon the Dharma.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the Dharma neither acts as retribution nor as non-retribution: since non-retribution is what should be questioned—namely, "The Three Bodies are but a single Dharma-realm;
how can there be an agent and an object of action?"—the phrase "depending upon the Dharma" refers to dependence within the same essence (*tongti*).

Relying on the essence, it is immediately the total function of the essence; the function, in turn, returns to rely on the essence. Through these two questions and answers, it is revealed that they are identical with the Dharma-realm.

[Commentary] Furthermore, one might ask: if the Dharma does not act as a retribution, and non-retribution is not retribution, yet non-retribution must necessarily rely upon the Dharma, then [the same logic should apply here].
The moon does not create its reflection, nor does it create that which is not a reflection; yet the reflection and the non-reflection must both depend upon the moon.
Is the moon, then, also the Dharma-body? Answer: Wisdom is in profound accord with the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Dharma-realm; wisdom is likewise like the Dharma-realm, and so forth.

[Commentary] The reflection is the *saṃbhogakāya* (response body), while that which is not the reflection is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), because it manifests the nine realms and is not merely a Buddha-image.

Regarding the phrase "the Dharma-realm [extends] downward," etc., it further clarifies that the response body is the Dharma-realm; since the three are identical in the secret treasury, how could there be a single body that is not the Dharma-realm?
The question-and-answer regarding the "three and one" clarifies that outside of the capacity (*adhikāra*) of sentient beings, there is no response of the three bodies.

Some people may believe [that the reflection is real], yet because their faculties are mostly directed toward external objects, they regard it as something else. Therefore, this is now revealed to dissolve such doubts.
First, the simultaneous manifestation is established. [Textual Commentary:
Furthermore, the shadow and the image do not constitute movement or non-movement; yet movement and non-movement must depend upon water, and the water likewise...

Is this Dharma-realm false? Answer: It is like the analogy of movement and non-movement regarding the capacity [of sentient beings]. Within all phenomena, there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss;
this is like the Dharma-realm, and it is likewise without hindrance.

[Commentary] "Movement" is an analogy for when the capacity [of sentient beings] has not yet matured and they cannot perceive the Response; "non-movement" is an analogy for when the capacity has matured and they can perceive the Response. It is like water.

For example, the nature of true cause and peace and bliss is precisely Great Nirvana; since it possesses the nature of the three virtues, it is necessarily wondrously fused. How could it not be the Dharma-realm?

Therefore, in the gate of the non-duality of self and other, it is said that although the objects and capacities [of sentient beings] are immeasurable, they do not transcend the three thousand realms;

and although the responsive manifestations may be many, they do not transcend the ten realms. When the objects and capacities respond in harmony, there is no partiality regarding body or land; all are equally eternal and quiescent.
There is no light that is not the Dharma-realm; if you obscure this meaning, do not venture to discuss our present school.

Second, citing scriptural evidence: [Wenju] Furthermore, the *Jingdu sanmei jing* states: "Sentient beings are also delivered. If there were no responsive capacity (*mīgǎn*) in sentient beings, the Buddha would not appear in the world, nor could he attain the realization of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The appearance in the world and the attainment of *bodhi* both arise from the responsive capacity of sentient beings."
The meaning of the *dharmadhātu* is thus established. [Commentary:

It is universally known that through the stimulus of causes one attains supramundane birth and becomes a Buddha; this is true for all four teachings. Now, following the exposition of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), we exhaust the intent of the scriptures.
This is because the natures of self and other are fundamentally non-dual, and only then can there be that which stimulates and that which is stimulated.

When there is a causal capacity that elicits a response from the supramundane, it is because the ten realms of sentient beings (the responsive capacity) elicit responses from the ten realms of the Buddhas (the responding).

This is because the nature of one born in hell and the nature of the Buddha’s hell are non-dual; only through this can one elicit and perceive a response from the hell realm, and the same applies up to the eliciting of a response from the Buddha realm.
Thus, what is discussed in our school regarding response and elicitation all encompasses the ten dharma-realms.

This is to reveal the meaning of non-duality; for if it were otherwise, not only would sentient beings be unable to evoke the Buddha, but even the ten locations would fail to constitute the *dharmadhātu*.
One should investigate this deeply, one should investigate this deeply. That which gives rise to Buddhahood means that sentient beings can act as the supreme conditions for attaining Buddhahood;
whether they comply or oppose, they all assist the Buddha’s practice, and even those who are evil and rebellious [contribute].

The merit of this is most powerful; how could the Buddha Anupamardha have attained the Way otherwise? If evil dharmas were fundamentally not the Buddha-nature, how could they assist the Bodhisattva in attaining Buddhahood?

If the Bodhisattva did not contemplate birth as the Dharma-realm, if there were no compassion of identical essence, and if there were no practice of non-action, how could the fruit of Great Bodhi be accomplished? If it were outside of the Buddha...
There is a sentient being who does not conceive the understanding that outside the Buddha-dharmadhātu there is no Buddha-dharmadhātu, nor that it is unestablished or uncreated;
such a person has not even transcended the Tripiṭaka, let alone the Shared or Distinct [Teachings]. Regarding the two Buddhas’ response in verse, there are two parts:
first, establishing the intent and dividing the text; second, establishing the intent. First, the establishment of the intent. First, the actual establishment.
[Text]: The Buddha’s response consists of twenty-four and a half verses. The reason the Heavenly King praises the Buddha is that the Buddha is able to preach the Dharma;
the reason the Dharma King praises the Dharma is that the Dharma is able to bring about Buddhahood.
[Commentary] That the Dharma can bring about Buddhahood means that the track of all Buddhas is established through the Dharma alone as cause and effect;
because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas attain eternity. The same applies to bliss, self, and purity. Second, citing scriptural evidence.
[Text]: The *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "When I first attained the Way, I contemplated who could be honored and praised;
none surpassed the Dharma, for the Dharma is able to establish all ordinary beings and sages. Thus, the Buddha praised the Dharma in response to the Heavenly King.
[Commentary]: The Dharma is able to establish all ordinary beings and sages because the Dharma fundamentally possesses the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Accordingly, through the conditions of defilement or purity, they arise as ordinary beings or sages. Although ordinary beings are deluded, within their delusion, the provisional and real aspects of the environment and its inhabitants have never been separate from their inherent nature (*prakṛti*).
One must know that when defiled conditions permeate the nature, it becomes defiled phenomena; when pure conditions permeate... [it becomes pure phenomena].
The *Jingren* (lay attendants) all know that nature is defiled and nature is pure; their essence is fundamentally fused, yet they arise as the whole [of phenomena].

Following conditions of defilement, both the defiled and the pure are defiled; following conditions of purity, both the defiled and the pure are pure. Therefore, the *Fenbieermen* (Gate of Distinguishing Non-duality) says:

"The three thousand realms existing in principle are collectively termed ignorance; the three thousand realms when fruition is realized are all called eternal and blissful. This is the defilement of nature."

The purity of the sublime essence of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-rāja*, which the Tathāgata now expounds as the condition for purification, is praised and extolled in order to answer the Heavenly King. This section consists of two parts.
[Commentary on the Text] The text is divided into three parts: first, one line of praise for the essence of the sutra, which answers [the question regarding] its Dharma-body;

second, one line of praise for the core tenet of the sutra, which answers [the question regarding] its Reward-body; third, twenty-two and a half lines of praise for the function of the sutra, which answers [the question regarding] its Response-body.
All are as explained in the text.
[Commentary] Second, the interpretation of the text with focused intent, in three parts: first, praising the essence of the sūtra.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the king of all sūtras, is profoundly deep, most supreme, and unsurpassed."
[Commentary] Second, praising the core teaching of the sutra:
that which was proclaimed by the World-Honored One of the Ten Powers, you Four Kings should diligently protect it.

[Commentary] Third, praising the utility of the sutra, which is privately divided into four parts; first, generally regarding sentient beings, it clarifies the production of goodness and the extinction of evil.
For these reasons, this sublime sūtra can bestow immeasurable happiness upon sentient beings; for the sake of the peace,
comfort, and benefit of all beings, it shall circulate long in Jambudvīpa and be able to extinguish all the immeasurable sufferings of the evil realms within the trichiliocosm.
[Commentary] Second, specifically regarding kings, it clarifies the generation of goodness and the extinction of evil. First, it clarifies their aspiration and desire:

"If the various human kings within Jambudvīpa give rise to a heart of compassion and govern the world with the True Dharma, and if they can cause this wondrous sūtra to circulate, then their lands will be peaceful, stable, and abundant, and all sentient beings therein shall experience happiness."
If there is a king who desires to love his own person and his kingdom, wishing to make them prosperous and flourishing, [Commentary:
Second, explaining the establishment of practice:
he should, with a sincere heart, bathe himself clean and go to the place of the Dharma assembly to listen to and receive this sutra; for this sutra is able to...
All virtuous deeds within these kings of sutras subdue all internal and external enemies and can further eliminate immeasurable fears;
they bestow peace and happiness upon all immeasurable sentient beings.
[Commentary] One attains benefit through the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
For example, just as a jewel tree within a person's home is able to produce all manner of precious treasures,
so too is this wondrous sutra able to produce all the merits of kings, just as clear, cool water can eliminate thirst and exhaustion.
This sublime sūtra is likewise able to remove the thirst for merit in kings;
just as a casket containing rare treasures and extraordinary objects is held in one's hand to be used at will, so too is this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*,
which can bestow upon kings the jewels of the Dharma according to their wishes.
[Commentary]: Third, regarding the protection and mindfulness of the supreme sages, it clarifies the arising of goodness and the extinction of evil.

This subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra is constantly honored and made offerings to by all devas, and is likewise sustained by the majestic power and authority of the four world-protecting Great Kings;
the Buddhas endowed with the ten powers constantly keep this sūtra in mind.
[Commentary]: Fourth, regarding the discourse between teacher and disciple, it is explained that hearing [the teaching] brings about the arising of goodness and the cessation of evil.

If there is one who expounds and praises [it], saying "Excellent!", there will likewise be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ghosts and spirits coming from the ten directions to protect such a person.
If there are those who hear this wondrous sutra, their hearts will give rise to joy and immeasurable exultation.
The immeasurable multitudes within Jambudvīpa all gathered with great joy to hear this sutra;
because they heard this sutra, they were endowed with all majestic virtues, and the vital energy and physical strength of the celestial hosts increased.
[Commentary] The Four Heavenly Kings joyfully made this vow.

At that time, having heard these verses, the Four Kings addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, since ancient times we have never before heard such a subtle and wondrous Dharma of quiescent extinction.
Having heard it, our hearts were filled with both sorrow and joy, and tears flowed down our cheeks."
A thrill passed through their entire bodies, their limbs became relaxed and at ease, and they further attained immeasurable, inconceivable, and perfect sublime bliss.

Having made offerings by scattering celestial *māndārava* flowers and *mahāmāndārava* flowers over the Tathāgata, and having thus performed such worship of the Buddha, they addressed the Buddha again, saying: "World-Honored One, each of us Four Kings..."
Each shall have five hundred spirits who will constantly follow and protect this preacher of the Dharma.
[Commentary] The four kings joyfully made their vows as stated in the text.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "grieving and rejoicing" in the sutra: one grieves over not having heard [the teaching] in the past and rejoices at having heard it now; one grieves that others have not heard it and rejoices at having heard it oneself.
Regarding "tears flowing profusely": *ti* (涕) is pronounced *ti*; *ti* refers to tears, and "profuse" (*heng*) means flowing crosswise.

All ancient editions read "flowing profusely" (*hengliu*), and there is no need to change it to the character "crosswise" (*jiao*). The Great Sutra is likewise; many translations produced by those lacking discernment are in error.

"Tearful" (*yí*) means to flow across. The "Wenxuan" contains Wang Can’s "Fu on Ascending the Tower," which says: "Grieving that my old hometown is cut off and obstructed, tears fall crosswise and cannot be restrained.
As for the commentary: "Tearful" (*yí*) refers to being harmonious and joyful; "unrestrained" (*jiě*)—the character *jiě* is pronounced *hùmǎi*—means to relax and disperse.
[Commentary] Regarding the second [section], the Chapter on Mahāpratisarā: First, the title of the chapter.
*The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Mahāpratisarā*.

[Commentary] The phrasing and text are divided into two parts: first, the explanation of Mahāpratisarā; second, the initial [subdivision], the Dharma-gate of her dwelling, which is further divided into two, the first of which is the full elucidation.

The Fourfold Eloquence. [Commentary on the Text]: There are four kinds of eloquence: minor eloquence, immeasurable eloquence, dual eloquence, and great eloquence. The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are called minor eloquence;

the dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are called immeasurable eloquence; being equipped with both types is called dual eloquence; and that which is neither dual nor illuminating is called [great] eloquence.
Great Eloquence.
[Commentary] It is called "Small Eloquence" because it does not clarify the four teachings and treasuries, but speaks only of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

"Infinite Eloquence" refers to the Provisional Teaching’s emergence into the mundane, which explains the eight gates of the *dharmadhātu* within the realm of dust and sand. "Discriminating Eloquence" refers to the Separate Teaching’s ability to explain the realms...
Because the internal realm and the external two kinds of objects are like sands [in number], they are called the "Dual Discourse.

When the ten realms are perfectly expounded, every phenomenon (*dharma*) is centered within, the dual extremes are extinguished, and phenomena mutually pervade one another; thus, the true and the conventional are distinct yet complete, and the three truths are called the single truth—this is termed the "Great Discourse.
Second, the explanation of the phenomena in which one abides.
[Text] This goddess dwells in the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of Wisdom and abides in great eloquence.

[Commentary] The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the Great Eloquence Goddess (Mahāpratisarā) dwells upon the summit of a high mountain, thatching her dwelling with reeds and weaving grass for her garment;
sitting with one leg raised, she attains within a single mind the wisdom of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, thereby destroying the fundamental afflictions.
When the body and mind of the Dharma-adornment are already integrated and harmonious, speech becomes sovereign; this is precisely abiding in the Great Eloquence itself.
Second, it is able to employ the four *siddhāntas*.
[Wenju] By means of the power of sovereignty, in order to gladden sentient beings, one may speak according to circumstances with one, two, or three modes of eloquence.
It is called "Great Eloquence" because it is appropriate for sentient beings; whether one bestows one eloquence, two, three, or four, it establishes them according to what is appropriate.
It is called "Great Eloquence" because it responds to sentient beings;
whether responding with one eloquence, two, three, or four, it treats them by means of that response. It is called "Great Eloquence" because it awakens sentient beings; if...
To realize the One and to discern it as two, three, or four— realizing all through this single realization— and thus to bring it forth and develop it,
is therefore called "Great Eloquence" (mahā-pratibhāna).

[Commentary] Only when one’s perfect eloquence is profound and subtle, capable of discoursing on the coarse and shallow, teaching according to the capacities of beings without any obstruction, can it truly be so named.

Because great eloquence is thus, this commentary employs it to delight those who are suited to awakening; by discussing the four *siddhāntas*, it enables them to attain the four delights and even the four awakenings.
This means that one *siddhānta* clarifies the four teachings, and likewise each of the four teachings possesses its own four benefits.
Such is the power and function of the Great Eloquence Goddess (*Mahāpratisarā*). Second, the clarification of the meaning of the chapter.
[Text] It is called the "Chapter on Great Eloquence" because one makes a vow before the Buddha to bestow great eloquence (*mahāpratibhāna*) upon the speaker.
[Commentary] Regarding the two sections of the sutra text, first is the division of the text and the explanation of its meaning; first is the division of the text.
[Commentary on the Text] The text is divided into three parts: first, from "He addressed the Buddha" onwards, he bestows the power of great eloquence upon the Dharma-preacher;
second, from "If there are sentient beings who, for hundreds of thousands... onwards, he bestows the power of responsive resonance upon the path of transformation;
third, from "Furthermore, he causes immeasurable... onwards, he bestows the power of practice upon the listeners.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning has three parts. First, the addition of the Dharma Master:

At that time, the Great Goddess of Eloquence addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, regarding this speaker of the Dharma, I shall augment his eloquence for joyful exposition, so that what he speaks may be adorned with sequence and well-attained great wisdom; if there should be any errors within this sutra..."
"Regarding the errors in the words, phrases, and meanings, I can cause this Dharma-preaching bhikṣu to recover them in their proper sequence and grant him dhāraṇī so that he shall not forget them.
[Commentary on the Text] First, the Dharma Master adorns the sequence with the eloquence of joyful speech; this is the great wisdom of verbal eloquence.
This is the *dhāraṇī* of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*), which is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmanirukti*).
[Commentary: By adding the four perfect analytical knowledges, one is naturally able to encompass the three; this refers to the sixteen benefits previously mentioned.
As for the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), within a single syllable one speaks all syllables, and within a single word one speaks all words.

Within a single dharma, one explains all dharmas so as to provide benefit according to those who can be saved. Eloquence of expression (*nirukti-pratibhāna*) refers to the skillful art of speech, adorned in various ways.
Eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*) refers to knowing the destination and ultimate significance of the meanings of all dharmas.
Eloquence of dharma (*dharma-pratibhāna*) refers to the wisdom that penetrates the names and designations of all dharmas. Second is the path of transformative empowerment.
If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher,
for their sake, shall widely proclaim and disseminate this sublime sūtra throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.

[Text]: If there are sentient beings who, through the lower manifestation of the transformative path, cause its dissemination to flow without interruption, it is because the capacity for transformation is added to them.

Since there is no person and nothing to be transformed, and since there is neither the path nor the capacity for transformation, yet through the harmony of causes and conditions, the transformative path flows without interruption.
[Commentary] Previously, the four types of analytical eloquence were added as the means of transformation; now, the persons [to be transformed] are added as the receptive capacity for transformation.
When these two harmonize, the path of transformation becomes inexhaustible. Third, the listeners are added.
Furthermore, they shall cause immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to hear this sutra, so that all these beings may fully attain a mass of fierce and sharp, inconceivable great wisdom;
receive the retribution of incalculable merit and virtue; become well-versed in immeasurable varieties of skillful means;
be able to eloquently expound upon all treatises; and thoroughly understand the various arts and crafts of the world.
They will be able to transcend birth and death, attain non-retrogression, and will certainly and swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

[Commentary on the Text] From the passage beginning "Furthermore, he causes immeasurable... onwards, this is the section on the two benefits bestowed upon the assembly by the Buddha’s empowerment as they hear the sutra, leading them to the stage of non-retrogression.
This is the benefit of the causal addition, which ensures that one will certainly attain Bodhi; this is the benefit of the resultant addition.
[Commentary] "Jing" (經) refers to arts and techniques. The second part concludes by demonstrating the profundity of the benefit.
[Wenju] Although the wording of the scripture is brief, the vow is profoundly deep, and thus the benefit is great indeed.
[Commentary] Third, the Chapter on Goddess Śrī. Part one: the title of the chapter.
*The Sutra of Golden Light*, Chapter Eight: "The Chapter on Goddess Śrī.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; first, the explanation of "merit" (guṇa).
[Text] This goddess abides in the Dharma-gate of the Adornment of Merit, which encompasses all phenomena, and because she takes merit as her primary focus, she is called Guṇakāśī (Goddess of Merit).
Furthermore, because she provides the speaker with everything they require so that nothing is lacking, she is called Guṇakāśī.
Moreover, because she causes the speaker to contemplate the profound meaning of this sūtra day and night, she is called Guṇa (Merit).
The heavens further cause those who hear this to swiftly attain Bodhi; because it possesses these manifold meanings, it is named the "Chapter on Puṇyavatī" (Gongde Tian Pin).
[Commentary] Among the two kinds of adornment (*saṃbhāra*), this corresponds to merit (*puṇya*). Merit can support wisdom to adorn the fundamental principle-wisdom (*prajñā*);

that wisdom is the three types of *prajñā*, and merit is what is manifested by the three liberations (*vimokṣa*). That which is adorned consists of the three tracks (*triyāna*). Whether taken collectively or individually...
One should know that all others are merely different names for the single essence of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
Mahāprajñā (Great Eloquence) and Śrī-devī (Goddess of Merit) have both entered the Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* and are each able to universally encompass all phenomena.

While the former attracts beings through various names and practices according to their inclinations, encompassing all by taking wisdom as primary, the latter encompasses all by taking merit as primary.
Because the primary [wisdom] is able to encompass the subject and object through its distinct modes of cognition, it ensures that the world’s needs are never lacking;
because it can generate right mindfulness, it serves as contemplation for others regarding profound meanings; because it can shatter biased and shallow views, it serves as an antidote;
and because it enables the swift realization of the original nature of bodhi, it pertains to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Second, the meaning of this chapter is clarified.
[Text] This is the third meaning of the *Tianwang hu jing* (Sūtra Protected by the Heavenly Kings): the merit of the intention for requesting the preaching and listening [to the sūtra].
[Commentary] Regarding the two sūtra texts, this is the first division of the text.
[Textual Analysis] The text consists of six sections: 1. From "He addressed the Buddha" downward, it sets forth the four matters of providing for the Dharma Master;
2. From "I have already, in the past... downward, it clarifies the source of merit; 3. From "If there is anyone who can recite...
downward, it exhorts and demonstrates the practice, including both brief indications and detailed expositions; 4. From "At that time, I... downward...
1. "In a single moment" and so forth indicates the descent of the vow to respond like a shadow or echo (5). 2.

"If one can take what one has performed and dedicate it to me" and so forth indicates the request for companionship (6). 3. "One should pay homage" and so forth specifically shows the act of taking refuge and revering [the teacher] (7).
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning in six parts. First, the vow to provide the four requisites, which are the clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine listed in the sutra.
At that time, Guṇakārandavatī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, for this preacher of the Dharma, I shall provide whatever he requires."
He shall provide this person with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and other necessities so that they lack for nothing;
he shall cause their mind to abide in peace and joy day and night, contemplating the phrases and verses of this sutra and discerning its profound meaning.
If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness in the presence of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher shall act for them...
For these reasons, you shall widely proclaim and disseminate this sublime sūtra throughout Jambudvīpa so that it may not be interrupted.
Once these sentient beings have heard this sūtra, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas in future ages,
they will always experience happiness among gods and humans, encounter various Buddhas, and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In Bodhi, the sufferings of the three evil realms are completely exhausted without remainder.
[Commentary] "And other assets" refers to all implements and products of production outside of the four requisites.
Second, this clarifies the source of merit and virtue.
“World-Honored One, I have already planted various roots of goodness in the past under the Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha,
World-Honored One named Ratnakusumaguṇasāgaravaiḍūryakanakaparvata-prabhāsa. Therefore, I now follow whichever direction I am mindful of.”
In whatever direction one looks and wherever one goes, one is able to cause immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to experience all manner of happiness;
they shall lack nothing in terms of clothing, food and drink, or the necessities of life— whether gold, silver, the seven treasures,
pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, jade, or conch shells.

[Commentary] Because he encountered the Buddhas and cultivated and realized the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* dharma-gate in past lives, he is able today to grant all that is sought wherever he propagates this sutra.
"Precious Flowers" (*Ratnapuṣpa*) and the other eight characters are his specific epithets; "Tathāgata" (*Tathāgata*) and the others are his general titles.

He is called "Tathāgata" because he is free from falsehood; he is called "Arhat" (*Saṃyaksambuddha*) because he is a field of merit for the worthy; he is called "Samyaksaṃbuddha" because he knows the *dharmadhātu*.

One who possesses universal knowledge and the three types of supernormal insight is named "Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*); one who does not return again is named "Well-Gone" (*sugata*); one who knows the realms of sentient beings is named "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*);
one who is without equal is named "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara*); one who tames the minds of others is named "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*);

one who serves as the eye for sentient beings is named "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*); and one who knows the three groups [of those to be trained] is named "Buddha. Possessing these ten titles is what constitutes the name.
Those who honor the World-Honored One and plant various roots of goodness take the subtle wisdom of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as the root of all virtues.
A "bi" (璧) is a vessel carved from jade; it refers to what the *Rites of Zhou* states: "With the azure bi, one performs the ritual for Heaven.
A "ke" (珂) belongs to the category of shells, such as conch. Regarding the three exhortations showing the method of practice, there are two parts: first, the brief exhortation and demonstration.
If there is anyone who can recite the subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* three times for me as an offering to the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones; who, having made this offering to the Buddhas, separately offers incense, flowers,
and various delicious foods to me while scattering them in all directions— know that such a person will be able to gather wealth, property, and precious goods.
By these causes and conditions, the essence of the earth increases; the Earth Devas and all the devas are filled with joy.
The grains, sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, and fruits that are sown flourish and thrive; the tree deities rejoice as they produce immeasurable varieties of things.
At that time, out of my compassionate concern for all sentient beings, I provide them with many of the necessities of life.
[Commentary] Second, the extensive exhortation and instruction, which is divided into six parts. First, showing the place where he constantly dwells:
"In this northern direction, the World-Honored One has a city belonging to the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa named Animanda;
in that city there is a garden named Puṇyaprasavābhāsa; within that garden there is a most excellent garden named Suvarṇadhvaja."
"These seven treasures, most exquisite, are my constant dwelling place.
[Note] In the sutra, "Animanda" is translated here as "Possessing Wealth" (Youchai). Second, the demonstration of making offerings by calling out his name.
If there is anyone who wishes to increase their wealth and treasures, that person should, in their own dwelling place,
sweep and sprinkle it clean, bathe their body, put on fresh white garments, and anoint themselves with exquisite incense. With a sincere heart, they should three times recite the name of that Buddha,
the World-Honored One Jewel-Flower Lapis Lazuli, prostrate before him, make offerings, burn incense, and scatter flowers, likewise reciting his name three times.
In the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, one should make a vow with utmost sincerity, separately offering incense, flowers, and various delicious foods to me,
scattering and sprinkling them in all directions.
[Note] Third, recite and maintain divine mantras.
At that time, these words and phrases should be spoken:
(1) *Pāripūrṇa-cārī*, (2) *Samantadharśanirakha*,
(3) *Mahāvihāragati*, (4) *Samantavidhānināgati*, (5) *Mahākāli-pa*.
Tathāgata (5) Parvate sarvadhara (6) Samantabhadraprati- (7) āyana-dharmate (8) Mahāvighuṣṭe (9) Mahāmaitreyasaṃghite (10) Hite śiśabodhi-hite (11) Samantāstā (12) Arthavāha.
[Recorded] (13) *Dhāraṇī*:
These four lines of praise for the incantation encourage its upholding.
This consecrated chapter is definitively auspicious, true, and not false; it is the practice for sentient beings and for those of middling virtue.

The practitioner should receive, uphold, recite, and master [this teaching] for seven days and seven nights; while observing the eight precepts and purifying the mind morning and evening, they should offer incense and flowers to the Buddhas of the ten directions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "Mantra of Empowerment" (*abhiṣeka-pada*): it refers to the conferring of the office of Dharma King by sprinkling the water of *dharmatā* upon the crown of the head of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Now, this Dharma is spoken of in secret, and is therefore called "empowerment. It is certainly the virtue of *prajñā*; it is auspiciousness, the virtue of liberation;
it is reality, the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. One praises the meaning of empowerment through these three virtues, which are equal in their practice.

This refers to the roots of goodness within the practice of various conducts; specifically, for a layperson who observes the one-fold practice of the eight precepts, this lasts for one day and one night.

Based upon the five precepts, one further adds: not wearing flowers or perfumes, not watching or listening to performances by musicians, and not using high or luxurious beds—these eight constitute the *śīla* (precepts).
Not eating past midday constitutes the *upavāsa* (fasting). Five exhortations to turn [the mind] toward [enlightenment].
Directing [merit] toward enlightenment,
one should constantly dedicate it for oneself and all sentient beings so as to fulfill *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
making this vow: "May all that I seek attain auspiciousness."
[Commentary]: This refers to the intent of making offerings, reciting secret mantras (*mantra*), and inviting [the deities].

If one seeks to enjoy the five sensory pleasures for oneself or hopes for wealth and treasures, this is the karma of saṃsāra, which is censured by all the noble ones; how could the Honored Celestials protect such a person?

Rather, it is for the sake of bringing oneself and others to enlightenment that they provide protection. What is thereby attained shall not be a cause for birth and death; one should rely upon this text accordingly.
Now, one should practice the Dharma. Sixth, one should encourage the adornment of the place and wait in attendance.

One should personally clean and sweep the room or dwelling where one resides—whether it be one's own quarters or a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka)—smearing the ground with fragrant mud, burning exquisite incense, and arranging pure, fine seats strewn with various flowers and perfumes.
They cleared the land to await me.
[Commentary] *Āraṇya* is translated here as "Non-contention" (*wu zheng*), because those who dwell there do not contend with the world;
it refers to a place five *li* removed from a village. Furthermore, there is the *Dharma-āraṇya*, which refers to the teaching that all phenomena are originally pure.
The Pure Cause (Jingyin) names this place the Dharma Āraṇya;

it is the "Dharma Āraṇya at the Site of Enlightenment" mentioned at the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. What the present sutra indicates encompasses both of these. The four vows respond to their influence.
At that time, in the space of a single thought-moment, I entered his house and sat upon his seat; from that day and night forth,
I ensured that this household— whether in a village, a monastery, or an open space— lacked for nothing, so that all necessities,
whether money, gold and silver, precious jewels, cattle and sheep, or grain and rice, were all obtained in full abundance.
[He] experiences happiness.
[Commentary: Fifth, he requests to go together.
If you can dedicate the most excellent portion of the roots of goodness you have performed to me, I shall [follow you] for the rest of my life.
Without being distant from those individuals, one should, at their place of residence, protect and mind them with a sincere heart, causing whatever they seek to be accomplished.
[Commentary] This is the sixth section, specifically indicating the taking of refuge and paying homage.
One should, with a sincere heart, pay homage to these and other Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, whose names are as follows: Ratnottama Tathāgata,
Vimala-jvalana-ratna-prabhāsa-rāja-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata, Suvarṇa-arcis-prabhāsa Tathāgata, Suvarṇa-śata-raśmi-avabhāsa-garbha Tathāgata,
Suvarṇa-parvata-ratna-cchatra Tathāgata, Suvarṇa-puṣpa-arcis-prabhāsa-lakṣaṇa Tathāgata, and Maholkā Tathāgata.

One should also pay homage to the Tathāgata Ratnaketu; one should also pay homage to the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva Nityakaruṇā, and the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata.

One should also pay homage to the Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the eastern direction, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu of the southern direction, the Buddha Amitāyus of the western direction, and the Buddha Sūkṣmasvara of the northern direction.
[Text] All is as in the original passage.
[Commentary] Question: In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, it is stated that when the elder sister Guṇavatī and her younger sister Andhā were encountered by a wise master, neither was accepted.
Now, to command that they be offered in worship contradicts that greatly. How are the accounts of these two sūtras to be reconciled?
Answer: The Honored One’s scriptures establish various methods of selection and rejection; the great expedient means manifest forms and display retributions in manifold ways.

In that [previous] case, darkness was confronted to symbolize that birth is inevitably followed by death, and the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) follow one another. In this case, Great Eloquence is confronted to symbolize that merit and wisdom mutually manifest as the two adornments (*dvividha-alaṃkāra*).
Since the four marks are faults, why should they not be driven out together? Since the two adornments are merits, it is logical that they should be cultivated together.
When wisdom advances, the blessings of merit cause birth and death to perish of their own accord; when merit advances, the wisdom of bodhi can be realized.

Now, I shall explain and you shall listen to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. By virtue of your celestial disposition, you must know that the requisites required for this purpose involve the simultaneous extinction of both [merit and wisdom], so that with a mind intent on propagating the sūtra, you may move Guṇakārandavatī to obtain the necessary provisions, all while remaining free from the notions of "I" and "mine."

If the elder sister does not come, how can the younger sister come here? [The former] is for the purpose of propagating the sutra, while [the latter] is for the exclusive cultivation of contemplation;

their respective applications of relinquishing or retaining benefits differ, so how could they be the same? Furthermore, just as a king, a great minister, or a high official may cause one to depart from nirvana through the Lotus Sutra while causing another to draw near to it, we know that the teachings established therein each have different gateways. How, then, can one use those scriptures to challenge what is being taught here?
[Commentary] Fourth, the Chapter on the Earth Deity Sthāvarā. Part 2: First, the title of the chapter. *The Golden Light Sūtra*, Chapter Nine: "The Chapter on the Earth Deity Sthāvarā.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, the correct explanation of the name; second, the establishment of the four *siddhāntas* based on the wisdom that is symbolized.
[Text] The various heavens above may abide in the path of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) as the Dharma-fathers of sentient beings;
this heaven abides in the path of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), serving as the Dharma-mother of sentient beings—this is the first meaning.

For example, just as the yin and yang cover and sustain all plants and trees, the perfection of wisdom nurtures and gives birth to all virtues—this is the second meaning. Each of the remaining perfections has its own specific domain.
That which has not yet perished and has not yet been extinguished is realized through true wisdom as being without marks and without names; this is the third meaning.
That other perfections have equality and superiority, while the perfection of wisdom is without equality and without superiority, is the ultimate perfection; this is the fourth meaning.
[Commentary] The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Upāya is their father.
There is no guide of the multitude who is not born from these. This refers to the celestial deity above, for heaven is yang and thus like a father;
this [deity] is the earth deity, for the earth deity is yin and thus like a mother. This is one sense of the meaning: because father and mother are distinct, they belong to the world (*loka*).
Heaven is Yang and covers above; Earth is Yin and supports below. "Herbs" is the general name for grasses, and "trees" is the collective designation for plants.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the lower section uses these as metaphors: various virtues are combined with the herbs and trees.

Each has its own function—just as the Bodhisattva of Dāna overcomes stinginess, and so on up to the Bodhisattva of Dhyāna who overcomes distraction—the five faculties serve as conditions and causes. Therefore, because they have not yet been extinguished, wisdom destroys the arising of dharmas.
Since it is the foremost among those that destroy evil by means of being nameless and signless, it corresponds to the wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Because both refutation and establishment are forgotten upon returning to the source, it is peerless and unsurpassed; thus, it is called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*). This establishes the four *siddhāntas* within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Second, the names by which it is summoned manifest the four virtues.
[Wenqu] The meaning of the Dharma-gate of the *Prajñāpāramitā* being eternally unchanging is called "firmness" (*dṛḍha*). Being able to sustain joy is called "constancy" (*nitya*).
Being able to give birth to purity is named "earth" (*bhūmi*). Its power and mastery over the self are designated as "divinity" (*deva*). Following from this—
These dharma-gates are therefore called the "Chapter on the Earth Deity Sthāvarā. [Commentary:
"Sthāvarā" (Firm) refers to the quality of permanence; "Earth" refers to bliss and purity, because there is no sensation of suffering; "bearing all" refers to being free from defiled attachment;
and "giving birth to the inexhaustible" refers to the deity's qualities of selfhood (*ātman*), majesty, power, and function, all of which are sovereign.
Second, the explanation of the meaning of this chapter.

[Wenqu]: This chapter represents the fourth intention of the Heavenly Kings who protect the Dharma; it is the "surging forth of the essence of the earth" (*pṛthivīrasa*) which provides nourishment and benefits, and serves as the basis for requesting the teaching and listening to it.
[Commentary] The two sūtra texts are divided into two initial sections.
[Wenju] The text consists of three parts: first, from "He addressed the Buddha" downward, the vow to surge forth from the earth to benefit practitioners;
second, from "At that time the Buddha said" downward, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment; third, from "At that time the Earth Deity" downward, the making of the vow for propagation.

Sūtra. [Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation, which has three parts. First, the initial vow surges forth as the essence of the ground. Within this, first, it clarifies the growth of one's own body.
Within this, first, the arising of the eight matters.
[Textual Analysis] The passage on the initial emergence of the *rasa* (earth-flavor) is divided into three parts.

From the initial address to the Buddha downward, it clarifies the benefits for one’s own person, which generally involve eight matters that increase successively due to hearing the Dharma: because of hearing the Dharma, the flavor of the Dharma increases;
because the flavor of the Dharma increases, physical vigor increases; because physical vigor increases, the *rasa* emerges and increases; and as the *rasa* increases, [the subsequent stages follow].
Therefore, as all things increase, so do the five fruits of sentient beings increase; as the five fruits increase, so does spiritual practice increase;
as spiritual practice increases, so does making offerings increase; and as making offerings increases, so does the propagation of the teaching increase.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation according to the specific subject matter. Regarding the eight [sections], one should first interpret them according to the sequence of their arising. First, "the increase of the flavor of the Dharma.
At that time, the Earth Deity Dṛḍhā addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*..."
In the present world or in future worlds, wherever it may be— whether in cities or villages, in mountains, marshes, or wildernesses,
or in royal palaces and residences— at whatever place this sutra is circulated, O World-Honored One,
I shall prepare a lion throne within that region and have the teacher of the Dharma sit upon it to extensively expound and proclaim this wondrous sutra.
I shall always serve as a guardian in his presence, concealing my body beneath the Dharma seat to venerate his feet;
having heard the Dharma, I shall partake of the nectar-like flavor of the unsurpassed teaching.

[Commentary] "Village" (*grāma*) refers to a settlement; it is called a village because people dwell together there. "Mountains and marshes" (*śaila-jāṅgala*): a place with water below it is called a marsh (*jāṅgala*).
"Guarding while staying overnight" (*rātrau rakṣā*) means to remain and provide protection during the night. These two [factors] cause strength to increase.
It augments one's vital strength.
[Commentary] The flavor of the third stage increases;
this great earth extends sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in depth, from the adamantine foundation up to the surface of the ocean.
All flavors are fully obtained, and the soil becomes increasingly abundant, rich, and fertile, surpassing that of today.
[Commentary] Fourth, the growth of all things:
for this reason, within Jambudvīpa, the medicinal herbs, trees, roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits flourish and thrive.
Its beauty, color, fragrance, and flavor are all fully perfected.
[Commentary] Regarding the "fivefold increase of the five fruits," these refer to what the Sūtra calls longevity, physical form, strength, eloquence, and tranquility;
these five fruits are brought about by food.
Once sentient beings have eaten, their lifespan increases, as do their physical strength, eloquence, and tranquility;

their six sense faculties become complete and sharp, and they achieve such various qualities as majestic virtue and a most exceptionally handsome and dignified countenance. Having accomplished these and other such things, [they proceed].
[Commentary] The six types of cultivation increase;
the undertakings they perform are mostly successfully accomplished, and they possess great power, diligence, and valor.
Therefore, within Jambudvīpa, there is peace, security, abundance, and joy, and the population flourishes; all sentient beings therein experience much happiness.
They should act according to their hearts' desire and follow what they find pleasing.
[Commentary] This is the seventh increase of offerings:
once these sentient beings have attained such majestic power and great influence, they are able to make offerings to this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
And I shall reverently make offerings to the fourfold assembly who uphold this sutra. [Commentary:
This is the eighth point concerning the propagation and increase [of the Dharma].
At that time, for the sake of causing all sentient beings to experience happiness, I shall go to their presence and request the speakers of the Dharma to preach.
He widely proclaims and disseminates such a wondrous scripture.
