[Text] From "For what reason, World-Honored One" onwards, it clarifies that the benefits for the retinue increase through the power of this sutra.
Generally, there are five matters by which they increase successively due to the power of the sutra: because of the power of the sutra, my retinue increases;

because the retinue increases, the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) increases; because the essence of the earth increases, all things increase; and because all things increase... [the rest of the passage follows].
Therefore, the happiness of sentient beings increases; because their happiness increases, their environmental retributions (niśraya-vipāka) are all fully provided.
This "fulfillment" is also termed "increase.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation according to the specific matters of the sutra—these five points are all as in the initial arising of the retinue's increase.

For what reason, World-Honored One? When this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is expounded in detail, the merit obtained by myself and my retinue will be twice that of usual, increasing our physical strength and the vigor of our minds.
World-Honored One, having partaken of the flavor of the unsurpassed nectar of the Dharma, we are now satisfied.
[Commentary] Second, the flavor of the earth increases.
The land of Jambudvīpa, measuring seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, becomes twice as fertile as usual.
[Commentary] Regarding "length and breadth" in the sutra: south to north is called length; east to west is called breadth. Third, all things increase.
World-Honored One, this great earth, the support for all sentient beings, is able to increase all necessary things;
having increased all necessary things, [it brings about] the increase of the four kinds of happiness.
[Commentary: The four types of happiness increase.
It causes all sentient beings to enjoy happiness by using these things as they please.
[Commentary] This refers to the increase of the five types of secondary rewards (*pratyaya-vipāka*):
various foods and drinks, clothing, bedding, palaces and mansions, houses and dwellings, trees, groves and gardens, rivers, ponds, wells, and springs.
Such things as these are all fully provided by depending upon the earth.
[Commentary] Regarding the "increase of gratitude" (*kṛtajña-vardhana*), there are two parts: first, the arising of the six matters.
[Text] From the passage "From the World-Honored One, these multitudes... onwards is called the increase of gratitude; it generally concerns six matters, unfolded in detail.
They increase further because they listen attentively out of recognition of my kindness; because they listen attentively, their merit increases;
because their merit increases, their teaching of others increases; because their teaching of others increases, the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) increases;
because the essence of the earth increases, the enjoyment of pleasure increases; and because the enjoyment of pleasure increases, the giving of faith (*śraddhā-dāna*) increases.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation according to the specific matters: the six [aspects] of the sūtra are also like the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment.
First, one listens; then, through growth, one increases [the practice]. Therefore, the World-Honored One says that all sentient beings, in order to know my kindness, should form this thought:
"I must certainly listen to and receive this sūtra, and I shall offer it worship, respect, honor, and praise. Having formed this thought, they immediately depart from their dwelling place.
Whether in cities, villages, houses, or open spaces, they go to the place of the Dharma assembly to hear and receive this sutra.
[Commentary] Second, the increase of merit:
Having heard and received it, they return to their respective dwellings and should each congratulate one another, saying: "We, today..."
Having heard this profound and unsurpassed sublime Dharma, they shall gather an inconceivable mass of merit;
having encountered immeasurable and boundless Buddhas, they shall attain liberation from the retributions of the three evil realms,
and in future ages, they shall constantly be born among devas and humans, experiencing happiness.
[Commentary] Third, increasing [the merit] by teaching others:
if these sentient beings, while in their respective dwellings, expound this sutra for others—whether explaining a single parable, a single chapter, or a single causal narrative;
or if they further praise a single Buddha, a single Bodhisattva, or even a single four-line verse, or even a single...
The phrase "and the title" refers to the name at the beginning of this sutra.
[Commentary] The flavor of the fourth stage increases.
The World-Honored One, according to the place where these sentient beings dwell, provides ground that is fully endowed with rich, fertile soil, surpassing [all others].
In all other stages, whatever things arise from the ground shall all attain growth, flourishing, and vast expansion.
[Commentary] The five types of sensory pleasure increase,
causing all sentient beings to experience happiness and abound in wealth and treasures.
[Commentary] Sixth, the increase of faith-based giving (*śraddhā-dāna*):
one delights in practicing generosity and maintains a mind that is ever-firm, possessing deep faith in the Triple Gem.
[Textual Exegesis] All is as stated in the text.
[Commentary] Second, the two Buddhas’ confirmation and fulfillment; first, the introductory text.
[Wenju] Second, the two Buddhas’ confirmation and fulfillment.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation; first, the confirmation and fulfillment of the successive increase.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā:

"If there are sentient beings who hear even a single phrase of the meaning of this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, when their lives end in the human realm, they will be reborn at will in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."

[Text] The passage is divided into two parts: first, regarding the gradual increase through hearing the sutra—from the human world to the celestial worlds, and from the celestial worlds to the supramundane—whereby one immediately experiences inconceivable bliss, which is the supramundane bliss.
What the earth deity described was merely the increase within this present world; now the Tathāgata confirms and completes it. Although the text is brief, the meaning is [extensive].
"Extremely long-lasting.
[Commentary] First, regarding the hearing of the sutra and below, in order to establish the meaning of successive development, the subsequent section is extracted and treated as supramundane;
the experience of joy day and night is found in the following passage. Second, it describes the fulfillment of offerings and their increase.
O Earth Deity, if there are sentient beings who, for the sake of making offerings to this sutra, adorn their houses and dwellings—
even hanging up a single banner or a single parasol, or offering even a single garment— and who possess natural palaces made of the seven treasures belonging to the six heavens of the desire realm,
such persons, at the end of their lives, will immediately be reborn there within those palaces of the seven treasures. O Earth Deity, among all those palaces of the seven treasures...
Each naturally has seven celestial maidens with whom they enjoy themselves, constantly experiencing inconceivable and subtle bliss day and night.
[Commentary] Second, describing the fulfillment of offerings and their increase: from the human world to the heavenly worlds; from the heavenly worlds to transcendence.
The meaning of the world’s long duration may be understood by analogy with what preceded, and so forth.

[Commentary] The Sūtra clarifies that making offerings pertains not only to the human realm, but also to descending from the human realm to the heavenly realms, and further down to the supramundane realm.
Although one experiences celestial bliss, because one dwells in the blissful Dharma-realm, there is nothing to be received; therefore—
This is called "inconceivable and subtle bliss. Third, the text of the first part of the threefold vow to protect the sutra.
[Commentary on the Text] The text of the threefold vow to protect the sutra consists of three parts: first, the vow to protect the preacher; second, the vow to protect those who transform others.
The Path is not severed; the three vows protect those who listen to the Dharma.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning. All three are as in the division of the text. First, the vow to protect the preacher of the Dharma:
At that time, the Earth Deity addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, by these causes and conditions, the bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma shall sit upon the Dharma-seat."
At that time, I constantly guarded him day and night without departing, remaining hidden from view beneath the Dharma seat and supporting his feet upon my head.
[Commentary:
These two vows protect the path of transformation so that it remains uninterrupted.
“World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher shall,
for their sake, widely proclaim and disseminate this sublime sūtra throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.”
[Commentary] The three vows protect those who listen to the Dharma.
After these sentient beings have heard this sutra, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas in future ages,
they shall constantly experience happiness among devas and humans, encounter all Buddhas, and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
In Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the sufferings of the three evil realms are all severed without remainder.
[Commentary on the Text] As in the text.

*Hòu* (two pronunciations: *hòu* and *hǒu*). *Bō* (pronounced *bù*; means "to winnow" or "to remove the husks from grain"). *Tuō* (pronounced *tā*).

The Tenth Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Spirits and Ghosts of Saṃjñeya.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the title and the summary; first, the translation of the Sanskrit name; first, the translation of the name itself.
[Text] The original Sanskrit term should be rendered as *Samjñeya-ma*, which translates here as "Secret" (*mi*).
[Commentary] Second, showing the meaning.
[Text] There are four meanings of "secret": namely, the secret of name, the secret of conduct, the secret of wisdom, and the secret of principle; they are like clouds.

[Commentary] "Secret" (*mi*) refers to the secret conduct that accords with the world; "secret practice" (*gyō*) refers to that which can be manifested for others; "secret wisdom" (*chi*) refers to the ability to apply remedies; and "secret principle" (*ri*) refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
All of these are based upon the three dharmas, which are neither vertical nor horizontal, and are not within the knowledge of those who are partial, small-minded, ordinary, or base;
therefore, they are all equally termed "secret. The phrase "notes say... indicates that the essential point lies herein. Second, the clarification of their respective domains.
Section Two: Clarifying those to whom [the deities] belong. Part One: Directly clarifying those to whom they belong.
[Text] "He is indeed the Great General of the Northern Heavenly King.
[Commentary] This second part also clarifies the three generals.
[Text] In each of the other three directions, there is one named Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the south, and Uttarakuru in the west;
each has five hundred retinues.

[Commentary] Second, explaining the divisions under his jurisdiction. Part one: enumerating the number of schools. Part two: clarifying the number according to the cardinal and intermediate directions.
[Text] He governs twenty-eight schools. The *Mayūra-rāja-sūtra* states: "In each of the four directions there are four schools; thus, for the six directions, there are twenty-four schools.
With one school in each of the four intermediate directions, they total twenty-eight schools."

[Commentary] The "six directions" refer to the four cardinal directions, the zenith, and the nadir. The "four intermediate directions" refer to the four corners. The second [section] clarifies the number by means of the five great elements.
[Wenju] Furthermore, it is said that one direction consists of five components, namely earth, water, fire, wind, and space; the same applies to the other four directions.
The twenty *pāda* (sections) and the eight classes led by the Four Great Kings constitute the twenty-eight classes.
[Commentary: Because each of these five has its own presiding deity who maintains them. Second, the demonstration of their functional efficacy.
[Text] Wandering through the world to reward the good and punish the evil is all under the jurisdiction of Vaiśravaṇa.
[Commentary] Second, the purpose for which this chapter was brought forth.
[Text] Hearing the sutra with joy, he makes a vow to protect the speaker; because he receives his name from the one who is able to protect him, it is so called.
"Vaiśravaṇa, and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the note "and so forth": although each of the three Heavenly Kings has their own divine generals, Vaiśravaṇa is the foremost;
therefore, his name alone is singled out to clarify this meaning. Second, the textual analysis of the two sūtra passages. First, the division of the text.
【Textual Analysis】The text is divided into four sections: first, from "He addressed the Buddha" downward, the vow to protect and uphold [the teaching] is made;

second, from "By what causes and conditions" downward, the qualities of those capable of protection are described; third, from "The Great General Vajrapāṇi" downward, the vow to augment the speaker through the power of wisdom is made;
fourth, the homage to the Original Teacher. In the first section, the narrative by the sūtra compiler and the actual making of the vow are both as stated in the text.
[Commentary] Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation of the four sections, the first is the initial vow to protect and uphold [the Dharma]. First, the narrative by the Sūtra-reciter:

At that time, the Great General of Ghosts and Spirits, Vajrapāṇi (Sanzhi), together with the various ghosts and spirits of the twenty-eight divisions, rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
[Commentary] Second, the formal making of the vow:
"O World-Honored One, wherever this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* Sūtra may exist—
in cities or villages, in mountains, marshes, or empty places, or within royal palaces— throughout the present and future worlds, wherever this sūtra resides..."
"Wherever this [sūtra] is circulated, I shall go to that place together with these twenty-eight classes of great spirits and ghosts,
concealing my form to follow and protect those who preach this Dharma, eliminating all evils so that they and the assembly of listeners—
whether men or women, boys or girls— may attain peace and security, even as far as merely hearing this sūtra."
If one upholds, reads, and recites the name of a Tathāgata, the name of a bodhisattva, or the title of this sūtra, I shall attend upon them,
protect them, and guard them, completely extinguishing all evils so that they may attain peace and security;
and it shall be the same for kingdoms, towns, cities, royal palaces, houses, and even empty places.
[Commentary] Second, describing the virtue of being able to protect, which is divided into two parts.
[Text] Describing the virtue further consists of three sections: first, the heading; second, the description; and third, the conclusion.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, in three parts. First, the introduction:
"World-Honored One, for what reason am I named the Great General of the Kumbhāṇḍa spirits, Saṃjñeya? Indeed, World-Honored One, you yourself shall bear witness to this."
[Text] The headings are as in the main text.
[Commentary] In the sutra, "wei" (唯) is pronounced with an upper tone when used for a formal salutation in response; "ye" (野) is used for a response, and "a" (阿) is used for a response.
These two describe the initial section of the first verse, establishing its intended meaning.

[Commentary on the Text]: Furthermore, this is divided into three parts: first, five phrases describing wisdom; second, five phrases describing the object; and third, five phrases describing the correct [realization].
The three successive invocations of "World-Honored One" (Bhagavat) signify that he knows these three aspects.
[Commentary] Second, the general and specific explanations of the meaning. Part one: the general explanation. Sub-part one: indicating the meaning based on the name.
[Text]: Since "spirit" (*shen*) is named as "mysterious," and the description of its name reveals its virtues, one should discuss its mysterious significance.

[Commentary] The deeds performed by the Great Expedient Power (mahopāya) possess both a fundamental essence (*mūla*) and a manifested trace (*śeṣa*). Realizing the Truth through wisdom is termed the "fundamental," while establishing conventional reality in accordance with worldly sentiment is termed the "trace.
Although these are distinguished as fundamental and trace, they are established under a single name. In the past, the fundamental was concealed within the trace;
now, from the trace, the fundamental is revealed. At the moment of manifesting the trace, this is what is called the "concealed name" (*mi-ming*).

It merely explains that the worldly sovereign who leads the divine hosts has a secret counsel; now, as he recounts the merit of the *Rakṣā-sūtra* before the World-Honored One, it is appropriate to reveal its original essence.

This "secret name" should properly signify the integration of principle and wisdom (*prajñā*), rather than being a mere partial or inferior teaching known only to worthy sages, which is why it is termed "secret.
Since the original and manifested traces of Vajrapāṇi (Sajie) have already been revealed here, this serves as verification for the Four Heavenly Kings and all others.
The celestial deities and others are all manifestations of the original source descending to transform beings;

therefore, the present detailed exposition of the esoteric meaning not only reveals the fundamental and manifested aspects of the various deities, but also elucidates the essence, doctrine, and function of the Sūtra.

Second, the interpretation of the meaning based on the names [of the three wisdoms]. Part one: the interpretation according to object and wisdom. Sub-part one: the interpretation of the three wisdoms, which are the three modes of contemplation.

The realm of wisdom is precisely the three truths that are the object of contemplation; this directly reveals that the object and wisdom are neither false nor dual, as the subject and object mutually integrate and the false and the correct are non-dual.
Is it not here that their esoteric names manifest their virtues? The first five phrases of the initial section clarify the esoteric nature of wisdom.
“World-Honored One, I know all dharmas; I understand all conditioned dharmas; I comprehend all dharmas; I know the boundaries of dharmas;
I abide in accordance with the Dharma; I dwell in the suchness of all dharmas; and I contain and receive all dharmas within all dharmas.”
[Commentary] The text has two parts; first, the exclusion of what is not [the secret].
[Wenju]: If wisdom were shallow or deep according to a sequence of stages, it would not be called "secret.

[Commentary]: Regarding "stages of shallow and depth," although there are three distinct wisdoms—first emptiness (*śūnyatā*), next the provisional (*prajñapti*), and finally the middle (*madhyama*)—this could be so described.
What is being discussed regarding the secret? First, concerning the two—exoteric and esoteric—the initial section concerns the mutual fusion of the three wisdoms.
[Wenju] states: "That one wisdom is all wisdom, and all wisdom is one wisdom; that it is neither one nor all, yet is both one and all—this is the secret of wisdom."
[Commentary] It does not go beyond three. The first phrase is that one wisdom is the three wisdoms—the wondrous wisdom of emptiness.

The second phrase is that the three wisdoms are one wisdom—the wondrous wisdom of the provisional. The latter, which is neither one nor three while simultaneously illuminating both one and three, is the wondrous wisdom of the middle.
If one points to all phenomena as "all," it may not necessarily be fully exhaustive, for they are [ultimately] empty.
If one takes the provisional and the middle as being all-encompassing, there is nothing further that remains. Second, showing the fusion according to the text.
[Commentary]: If one grasps this meaning, then among the five phrases, each phrase is a single phrase, and each single phrase contains the five phrases;
they are neither one nor five, yet they are both one and five—this is solely numerical and solely esoteric.
[Commentary] These five phrases correspond to the three types of wisdom as explained below. Second, the five phrases clarify the mystery of the object:

"World-Honored One, I now see the inconceivable light of wisdom, the inconceivable torch of wisdom, the inconceivable practice of wisdom, the inconceivable accumulation of wisdom, and the inconceivable realm of wisdom."
[Commentary] The text has two parts;
the first distinguishes what is not [the secret]. [Wenju]: If an object could be known by wisdom or expressed by speech, then that object would not be secret.
[Commentary]: If it can be known by wisdom, it is subject to thought; if it can be expressed by speech, it is subject to discussion. How, then, could it be secret? Second, showing what is secret.
Second, the initial direct exposition.
[Wenqu] It cannot be known by wisdom, it cannot be cognized by consciousness;
it cannot be named by names, it cannot be expressed in speech—this is called the inconceivable secret realm.
[Commentary]: Since the object is not external to wisdom, how could it be known by the limited and inferior wisdom [of the two vehicles]?

Since consciousness itself is the object, how could it be known by the consciousness of the six classes of ordinary beings? This clarifies its transcendence of thought. Since the object is free from names, how could it be named by the names of various dharmas?
Since the object is free from verbal expression, how could it be expressed by the discourse of the four propositions? This clarifies its transcendence of speech.
This is the deliberation. Second, the attachment to the text. [Wenju]:
Regarding the discussion of the "secret" (mi) based on the number five, the examples may be understood as before. [Ji]:
The previous three wisdoms were said to be "only number" and "only secret"; although there are now five phrases, each phrase says that it is "unfathomable."
"Speculation" (*saṃkalpa*) refers exclusively to the numerical and the esoteric. The three subsequent five phrases clarify the "correct esoteric. [The text states:

"World-Honored One, regarding all phenomena, I have attained correct understanding and correct contemplation; I have attained correct discrimination and correct understanding of conditions; I am correctly able to awaken to and comprehend them."
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first distinguishes what is not [the true meaning].

[Wenju]: If one clarifies the Right Path in contrast to the Deviant Path, or speaks of the Middle by depending on the extremes—claiming that this "right" is not right, or that this "middle" is not middle—all such [positions] are not the esoteric [meaning].
[Commentary] Even the slightest degree of dualistic opposition is not the central truth; it is merely a coarse and manifest phenomenon, and thus the profound meaning cannot be established.
Second, showing the secret [teaching] in two parts: first, directly indicating it from the perspective of principle.

[Text]: That which is the very wrong yet the right, the very extreme yet the middle—where the wrong/right and the extreme/middle are non-dual and without distinction—is what is called "Esoteric" (mim).
[Commentary]: Since the wrong/right and the extreme/middle encompass all phenomena exhaustively by mentioning just one of them, with whom else would one wish to further debate?
When addressing those who wish to achieve understanding, one must forcefully speak of the "Middle and Correct. Second, citing the *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya-sūtra* as proof:
[The Text] states that the meaning is as follows: the *Sāṃkathyaviniścaya* says, "If one discriminates all dharmas with the mind, all dharmas are erroneous;
if one does not discriminate all dharmas with the mind, all dharmas are correct. This is precisely its significance.

[Commentary] The mind penetrates both the true and the false; now, by means of the words "discriminating existence and non-existence," one discriminates between the heterodox and the orthodox, and distinguishes between the Middle and the Extremes.
This causes all dharmas to not abide in the Middle; since such is the fault, the gain [of abiding in the Middle] can be known accordingly.
Second, the conclusion.

[Text] "I practice the Right Path; whether in terms of its object or its wisdom, it is from this that [the name] is derived. Indeed, World-Honored One, you yourself shall bear witness to this," and so forth.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation based on the three types of action (trikarma). This has two parts; first is the explanation.
[Text] Furthermore, these three sections are, in brief, the secrets of body, speech, and mind. The first five phrases speak of "knowing," which refers to the secret of mind (*mantra-guhyaka*).

The next five phrases speak of "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*); since this direct perception pertains to the eye, and the eye pertains to the body, it constitutes the secret of body (*kāya-guhyaka*).

The final five phrases clarify "correct understanding" (*samyag-avabodha*); because of this correct understanding, they speak of "correct discernment" (*samyak-vikalpa*), and this discernment constitutes the secret of speech (*vāc-guhyaka*).
[Commentary] Regarding the term "for the time being" (*yīwǎng*): since this refers to the primary external objects of wisdom, it is stated incidentally to clarify this meaning.
As for the secret name of Saṃjñeya (Dizai), it reveals his fundamental nature; that fundamental secret necessarily consists of the three—body, speech, and mind.

If it were otherwise, how could he manifest the three karmas of a divine general while ensuring the multitude remained unaware? Therefore, prior to the revelation of his fundamental nature, he was not one who provided direct testimony.
None can fathom this, for it is brought about by the Three Mysteries. This concludes the second section.
[Commentary on the Text] The reason it is said that they are not manifest is precisely the meaning of "mystery."

[Commentary]: Although these pertain to the three types of karma, they are not explicitly stated; furthermore, they carry a hidden meaning, much like the term *saindhava*, which no one but a wise minister can understand.
These three fetters (*saṃyojana*) arise first, and the others follow later.
[Text] Having thus described the secret meaning (*guhyārtha*) and fully revealed its appreciation, it shall now be briefly explained once more.

[Commentary] Regarding the two distinct explanations: previously, the five phrases were collectively explained as "Wisdom-Secret" (*jñāna-guhya*) up to the five phrases collectively being "Correct-Secret" (*samyak-guhya*);
however, because the names "Secret" were manifested through "wisdom" and so forth, they were treated as a general explanation. Now, within the first five phrases, they are divided.
Regarding the three contemplations up to the latter five phrases, they correspond to the three bodies (*trikāya*); therefore, they shall be explained separately in two parts.
First, the Great Master uses the three dharmas to provide the explanation. Second, the formal separate explanation. First, explaining the meaning by way of separation.
Second, correlating the combined [phrases] with the title. Third, correlating the five phrases individually with the three contemplations. First, citing the text to demonstrate the meaning.
[Text] "World-Honored One, I know all dharmas. Below this, the meaning is explained through three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*).
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation by means of contemplation: this reveals the original practice cultivated by Vaiśravaṇa (Saṃjñin). Second, the explanation of the phrases based on their meaning.
First, the initial two phrases indicate the objective realm (*ālambana*).
[Text]: The two phrases "knowing all dharmas" and "all conditioned dharmas" share the same objective realm of phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*).
What is it that produces? That which acts as the cause is the first phrase; what is produced? That which acts as the condition is the second phrase.
Because the producer and the produced are unified, all phenomena arise. This is precisely the meaning of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, which states: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions."
[Commentary] That which is capable of producing and that which is produced are both called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).
For example, among the twelve links [of dependent origination], all are capable of producing and all are produced. That which produces is the producer, and that which is produced is the produced;

the produced depends upon the producer, and the producer is named the cause (*hetu*), while that which supports it is named the condition (*pratyaya*). Since causes and conditions are inexhaustible, the production of phenomena is infinite. These are precisely the objects of contemplation.
The first two or three phrases demonstrate the three contemplations; the first phrase of the initial section is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

[Wenju] states: "To 'comprehend all phenomena' means to thoroughly realize their voidness. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty.
This constitutes the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti-praveśa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

[Commentary] To thoroughly comprehend that all things are empty because they lack intrinsic nature due to arising from causes and conditions, and because they are devoid of names and marks due to being ultimately unobtainable—this is what is called "understanding phenomena.
The second phrase clarifies the contemplation of the conventional (parikalpita).

【Text】 "Knowing the demarcation of dharmas" means knowing that emptiness is not [mere] emptiness. By employing the knowledge of the modes of phenomena (*dharmākārajñatā*), one discriminates between the provisional names of the dharmas of ordinary beings and sages, recognizing their distinctions.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "It is also called a provisional name. This constitutes the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñapti-praveśa-vipaśyanā*).

[Commentary]: To thoroughly realize that there is no intrinsic nature or characteristic is called "knowing emptiness" (*śūnyatā-jñāna*). Not being obstructed by the arising of conditions is called "non-emptiness" (*aśūnyatā*).

Because all paths give rise to all aspects, it is called the "knowledge of the aspects of the path" (*mārgajñatā*). This wisdom discriminates the ten realms; like the ocean-seal (*sāgara-mudrā*), the provisional names are arrayed in a forest-like pattern with their distinctions.
However, if one writes the character "wu" (無, non-existence) here, it is certainly an error. The third [section], the final phrase, clarifies this.
Madhyamaka. [Text]:
One who abides in accordance with the Dharma within the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena enters the ultimate truth of the Middle Way by means of the two observations (*dvividha-vipaśyanā*).
As the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* states, it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way; that is, the Middle Way itself.

The contemplation of the single ultimate truth (*ekārtha-paramārtha*) encompasses all phenomena; this is precisely the Middle Way’s correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), which is able to simultaneously illuminate both truths (*satya-dvaya*), and is therefore said to "encompass.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "by means of the two contemplations," etc., this explains the characteristics of abiding securely in practice. If the three contemplations in the *Encompassing Treatise* (*Zhuanlun*) were not identical to these...
If the essence of the contemplation of the mind were vertical, it would not take the two [aspects] as the skillful means and the middle as the true essence;
if the essence of the contemplation were horizontal, it would likewise fail. This treatise discusses the three contemplations as being neither vertical nor horizontal.

If one practices in this manner, one can dwell securely within the dharmas of the ten realms as they are in their original nature. Thus, the cultivation becomes the perfection of nature through the power of the single mind and the three contemplations.
Therefore, Jingxi said: "Because one abides in correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) only then becomes inconceivable.

This refers to the Middle Way as a double negation; because it simultaneously illuminates the two truths, its words encompass both negation and illumination. Negation negates deluded attachment (*kleśa*), while illumination illuminates the nature of reality.
Once deluded attachment has vanished, both truths are the Middle. Since the Middle is not biased, emptiness and the provisional are [both subsumed therein].

Each [text] contains all the sutras; it is said that regarding all phenomena, one embraces all phenomena without resolving them through the dual illumination of the Middle Way—the intent of the sutras is not more clearly revealed than this.
Third, the conclusion of the name of the contemplation is secret. Part two: first, the exclusion of what is incorrect.
[Text] If one contemplates the three as being identical or different, or as being simultaneous or separate, it is not called "mysterious contemplation" (*mi-guan*).
[Commentary] Second, the demonstration of mystery.
[Text] That which is one is three, and that which is three is one; this is called "mystery. If one wishes to know the wisdom, it resides in the teaching; the teaching itself is [the wisdom].

This is the mystery of speech (*mukha-guhya*). [Commentary] Because it is one yet three, it is not "one"; because it is three yet one, it is not "different. Whether viewed vertically or horizontally, they are simultaneously distinct;
this can be understood by analogy. The phrase "if one wishes to know" and so forth employs the mystery of speech to conclude this section. Second, regarding...

The next five phrases correspond individually to the three liberations (*vimokṣa*). This clarifies that while Saṃjñeya has already manifested his own fundamental ground as having realized liberation, he simultaneously encompasses the three truths;
that one attains liberation by means of seeing the truths. First, the text cites the passage to demonstrate its meaning.
[Text] "World-Honored One, I now see... and so forth; the five subsequent phrases are explained according to the meaning of the three truths and the three gates of liberation.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the phrases based on their meaning. First, the initial phrase demonstrates perfect purity.
【Text】 "Manifesting the inconceivable light of wisdom" means that this light is true wisdom, which, like the light of the sun and moon,
is constantly bright and never ceases; this true wisdom illuminates the inconceivable realm of ultimate truth, thereby accomplishing perfectly pure liberation.
[Commentary] Regarding "True Wisdom illuminates the inconceivable True Reality": the essence of True Reality is the *prajñā* of inherent virtue (*xingde*).
When the nature gives rise to cultivation (*xingqi xiu*), it is called True Wisdom. If the Truth were not *prajñā*, how could True Wisdom be produced?
This Truth, being free from bondage, constitutes the fulfillment of perfect and pure liberation. One should know that the principle and the fruit are identical from beginning to end. (2-3)
The phrase "inconceivable torch of wisdom, practice of wisdom, and accumulation of wisdom" indicates the purity of skillful means (*upāya*). [Commentary on the Text:

These are all provisional wisdoms (*prajñā*), like a person holding a torch who illuminates objects by moving in winding ways—sometimes arising and sometimes ceasing—in accordance with the capacities and conditions of beings, directing the cause here or there.
The "assemblage of meanings" refers to the meaning of the fruit; it proceeds from the cause toward the fruit, wherein the cause is discarded once the fruit arises.
All of this is the inconceivable conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) illuminated by provisional wisdom, which constitutes the liberation of skillful means.

[Commentary]: Adapting to capacities and bending accordingly, the arising and ceasing of causes and effects are all the function of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminating the inconceivable conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The essence of this conventional truth is the liberation of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*); when the cultivated arises from the inherent, it is called provisional wisdom.

Being free from bondage constitutes the fulfillment of the skillful means; the principle of pure liberation and the fruit are non-dual, as can be understood by analogy with what preceded. Third, the conclusion.
A single phrase reveals the purity of nature.
[Commentary on the Text: That which is the inconceivable realm of wisdom is the wisdom of the *dharmatā-tathatā* (the suchness of phenomena).
Because this wisdom is in profound union with the *dharmatā-tathatā*, it is called the "inconceivable realm of wisdom. This wisdom illuminates the inconceivable Middle Way.
The single ultimate truth (ekārtha-paramārtha) constitutes the nature of pure liberation.
[Commentary] It was stated previously that the four names—from "light of wisdom" (jñānāloka) to "accumulation of wisdom" (jñānarāśi)—merely designate the wisdom that performs the illumination;

however, while this wisdom is the object of that [illumination], its essence is the truth (satya). Since it is the principle (dharma) that is to be illuminated, the Sub-commentary cites the Sūtra’s teaching on phenomena (dharma).

Regarding suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*), this wisdom and the suchness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*) are in profound accord; thus, the manifestation of object and wisdom reveals that suchness and wisdom are non-dual.

Nevertheless, what is commonly understood by people regarding this teaching ultimately results in a conjunction of two distinct entities, precisely because they do not comprehend the essential nature of object and wisdom.
To know the essence of the object, one must first distinguish it from insentient objects (*jaḍa-viṣaya*) as well as the delusions of the partial and small vehicles (*hīnayāna*).
How could this object, which is the true suchness (tathatā) provisionally established upon the mind, be non-dual with wisdom?

Now, following Aśvaghoṣa, we establish that the essence of the object is so-called original enlightenment (mūla-awakening), while the essence of wisdom is so-called initial awakening (ādi-awakening). Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The meaning of 'awakening' refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought. This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it has no..."
That which does not pervade the dharma-realm as a single characteristic is precisely the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding dharma-body;

based on this dharma-body, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*). This awakening is the nature itself; the arising of the nature through cultivation is termed "initial enlightenment" (*ādi-awakening*).

The *Treatise* states: "Initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment. Since it is said to be free from thought, how could there be any conceptualization? Since it is equal to empty space...

There is nowhere it does not pervade; how could there be a single moment, a single speck of dust, or a single mind that is not the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and the initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*)?

Therefore, it can be said that the sentient and Buddha beings, along with their environments and bodies, throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, constitute the object of contemplation, while the sentient and Buddha beings, along with their environments and bodies, throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, constitute the wisdom that contemplates.
Although the names "object" and "wisdom" differ, their essence is not distinct.
Therefore, although subject and object appear as two, they are non-dual. The object is illumined by the object; the object is illumined by wisdom; wisdom is illumined by wisdom;
and wisdom is illumined by the object. These four lines of discourse are discourse that is itself non-discourse; it is non-discourse that is discourse.

These four lines of illumination are illumination that is itself non-illumination; it is non-illumination that is illumination. This is what is meant by the inconceivable realm of wisdom. Is this not so?

Regarding this realm of wisdom, one must discuss the six identities (*ṣat-tathatā*); here, we are currently distinguishing between the two stages of partial realization (*vibhūti*) and ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā*). The third section concerns the liberation from the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), which is termed "the secret.
First, there is the exclusion of what is not [the truth].

[Textual Commentary]: If the three truths and the three liberations were either identical or different, or if they were arranged vertically or horizontally in a state of mutual separation, they would not be inconceivable (*acintya*).
[Commentary] Second, the demonstration of the esoteric.
[Wenju] Because it is neither identical nor different, and because each is distinct, it is called "inconceivable"; because it is inconceivable, [it is so named].
This is called "Secret.

[Commentary] Both cases follow the previous pattern. Third, regarding the latter five phrases, they are individually correlated with the three bodies (*trikāya*). First, the text is cited to demonstrate the meaning.
[Text] "World-Honored One, regarding the five phrases beginning with 'I [attain] all dharmas,' I shall explain them as the three bodies.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the phrases according to their meaning: the first two phrases indicate the *saṃbhogakāya*.

[Text]: "Correct understanding and correct contemplation. Correct understanding is able to manifest the essence; when the essence is manifested, it is called "correct contemplation. Correct contemplation is the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). [Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "correct understanding is able to manifest the essence," this refers to how semblance-understanding is able to manifest the true essence. As for the true essence...
Once this *prajñā* of inherent nature has been manifested, one is able to contemplate and penetrate fundamental ignorance; therefore, it is called "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*).
As for what is termed the "retribution body" (*saṃbhoga-kāya*), it is called "contemplation" (*darśana*) in reference to the mind, and "retribution" in reference to the body;
all forty-two stages may be discussed in this regard. The second two lines demonstrate the "response" (*nirmāṇa*).

[Text]: "Attaining correct discernment and correct understanding regarding conditions" means that one discerns the capacities and circumstances of beings without waiting for the right time and without missing the opportune moment, responding universally to all;
this is precisely the Response Body (Nirmāṇakāya).

[Commentary]: "Discriminating" refers to knowing the medicine and the illness by means of the Dharma; "understanding conditions" refers to knowing the maturity or immaturity [of the capacity] by means of the faculties.
If one does not understand these distinctions, there can be no response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, when the response-body appears before the capacity has matured, it is called "waiting for the time.

When it appears after the capacity has already been aroused, it is called "missing the time. The simultaneous occurrence of the chick pecking and the hen pecking is the characteristic of responding to the capacity. (3-1)
The phrase "indicating the Dharma" [refers to the following]:
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "That which is truly capable of awakening and understanding is called 'awakening' when it is neither awakening nor non-awakening;
it is called 'understanding' when it is neither understanding nor non-understanding. This ultimate, pure awakening and understanding is the Dharmakāya."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "without awakening" (*wu-jue*) and so forth, this meaning must be distinguished by contrasting it with "retribution" (*bao*).

There is but one Great Awakening (*da-jue*), yet because it possesses three capacities—quiescence and illumination (*ji-zhao*), as well as non-quiescence and non-illumination—it is called the "Three Bodies. "Awakening" (*jue*) is precisely illumination;

because awakening can illuminate the Principle (*li*), it is the Reward Body (*bao-shen*). "Without awakening" (*wu-jue*) is quiescence; because awakening can manifest forms, it is the Response Body (*ying-shen*).

Regarding the statement that the body is now neither conscious nor unconscious: this means it is neither illumination nor stillness. When consciousness can simultaneously transcend both and employ both, it is called ultimate awakening;
this is the Dharma-body. Therefore, the three bodies are termed the three Buddhas.

The realization of these three types is likewise so: with respect to the body, it is called "awakening" (jue); with respect to the mind, it is called "realization" (liao). The three meanings are thus perfectly distinct.
The three bodies are called "mysterious" (mi) in two ways; first, the exclusion of what is not [the mystery].
[Text] If these three bodies were either identical or distinct, whether vertically or horizontally, they would not be called "correct.
[Commentary] Second, the demonstration of the mystery.
[Text]: Because it is neither one nor different, and neither before nor after, it is called "Correct" (Zheng). "Correct" is precisely "Esoteric" (Mi). [Commentary]: This is self-evident.
Second, correlating the two [aspects] with the title. Part one: correlating the three virtues with the title.
[Text]: To clarify the Dharma-body through its primary meaning, it is the sense of "gold"; to clarify Prajñā through the perspective of contemplation, it is the sense of "light";
to clarify Vimukti through the perspective of the inconceivable, it is the sense of "luminosity."

[Commentary]: The preceding text explained the three bodies (*trikāya*) in relation to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), and the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*) in relation to the three liberations.

Each of these triads can be correlated with the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Golden Light) to clarify their distinct meanings. Here, however, the three bodies are unified as the single Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which corresponds only to the character "Gold" (*suvarṇa*).
The three contemplations are unified as the single Prajñā, corresponding only to the character "Light" (*prabhā*). And the three liberations are unified [with the character "Sutra"].

Regarding the single liberation, those who explain it through the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and so forth based on various sutras and śāstras concerning the syllable *A* as being of two natures—one for cultivation and one for realization—are the Perfect Ones (*paripūrṇaka*).
This interpretation unifies the three meanings; this intent is most subtle, and students should understand it.
Second, it is clarified that all five chapters are esoteric.
[Text] The Three Virtues are the subtle and secret treasury; the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the subtle and secret teaching. From this secret teaching arises secret understanding;
one abides in secret principle and practices secret conduct, benefiting others through secret means. Therefore, I am named "Secret.
Indeed, World-Honored One, you yourself shall bear witness to this.

[Commentary: These three virtues are the secret treasury realized by the Buddha; because they are suited to the capacities of sentient beings, he preached the subtle and secret teaching of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
As for Dṛḍhanemi’s original cause, he received this secret teaching and gave rise to secret understanding—this is precisely what is meant by "hearing the secret name.
Abiding in principle is the manifestation of the secret essence (*tattva*); practicing the path is the cultivation of the secret doctrine (*siddhānta*). This is beneficial.
This is because he arises from secret function (*guhyakṛtya*); even those who do not rely on verbal teaching are identical to the Buddha. Second, the clarification of mutual interpenetration.
[Textual Commentary:
Furthermore, these fifteen phrases mutually explain and establish one another; if one correctly understands and correctly contemplates these fifteen phrases...
"All are correct understanding and correct contemplation. "If it is the light of inconceivable wisdom," fifteen phrases—all are the light of inconceivable wisdom.
"If I know," fifteen phrases—all are knowing, and so forth.

[Commentary] Although one may analyze this by dividing it into three bodies, three liberations, three contemplations, and three sections, each of the fifteen phrases is itself the essence and magnitude of the ocean of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*;
thus, the names and meanings explain one another in succession.
This is like the hundred phrases on liberation in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, where each individual phrase is the subtle and secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

The Great Master’s commentary explains that each sentence contains a hundred [sub-sentences], totaling ten thousand sentences. Here, we present the primary interpretation, which consists of fourteen sentences; when fully developed, these can comprise fifteen sentences. Taken together, they state:
"By means of correct understanding (*samyag-avabodha*), there is correct contemplation (*samyak-pratyavekṣā*);

by means of correct understanding, one attains correct discernment (*samyak-vicaya*); by means of correct understanding, one correctly understands the object (*ālambana*); and by means of correct understanding, one correctly awakens to and realizes [the truth]."
Because of correct understanding, there is the light of inconceivable wisdom; and so on, up to:

because of correct understanding, one contains all phenomena within all phenomena. Taking the correct understanding of a single phrase as the primary case, the remaining phrases are likewise exemplified in this manner, resulting in one hundred and seventy-five phrases.
Because their essential nature and measure are unified throughout, it is called a "name."
In the *Yixiang chengshu* (Commentary on the Formation of Meaning), for both the three and the five [categories], the opening phrases are cited as examples;

for the four [categories], there are fifteen phrases each, with the note stating that these are used to explain this [text]. Second, regarding the use of the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) to explain what is employed:

all five are called "Buddhas" because they are the fruition-virtue (*phala-guṇa*); they are all termed "nature" (*dhātu*) because it signifies the meaning of being unchanging. If one takes these five...

Regarding the three sections and five propositions of the present [text], they are able to manifest the fundamental realization of Saṃjñeya as perfect and eternal, his trace-activity as all-pervasive, and the wondrous virtue of his protection of the sutras as deeply benefiting people;
this is the intended meaning of the present school’s exegesis. The text has two parts:
first, the Great Master’s exegesis of the initial five propositions; second, first, showing the differences and similarities of the five natures; second, first, clarifying the three types.
They are not different.

[Wenju] Furthermore, when explaining the five kinds of Buddha-nature, the three names—Correct Nature (zhengxing), Conditioned Nature (yuanxing), and Realized Nature (liaoxing)—are not different from one another.

[Ji] "Correct" refers to the central cause; "conditioned" refers to the auxiliary conditions; and "realized" refers to awakening and comprehension. These are the meanings of these three names according to various masters.

Because they are established as identical, it is said that they are not different. Second, clarifying the emergence and disappearance of the two natures. Part one: the first two schools establish difference.
First, clarifying the characteristics of difference. [Wenju:
Furthermore, one school takes the nature of fruition and the nature of the objective realm as five; another school takes the nature of fruition and fruition itself.
The nature of the fruit consists of five [aspects].
[Commentary: "The nature of the fruit" refers to the fruits of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) realized through the conditions (*pratyaya*) and causes (*hetu*).

"The object" refers to the objects transformed by the conditions and causes, namely the ten kinds of objects such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. Regarding "the fruit and the fruit-of-the-fruit," the "fruit" is specifically located in wisdom.
Regarding "the fruit of the fruit of virtue" (*de-guo-er-guo*): it is distinct from the virtue of the knowledge of cessation (*duan-de*) because it further adds the virtue of cessation itself;
thus, the term "fruit" is stated twice. Both of these pairs are termed "conforming to nature" (*cheng-xing*), all of which takes "permanently abiding and unchanging" as their meaning.
That the objective realm is unchanging means that cultivated evil is precisely inherent evil (*xing-e*). Second, the explanation of opening and closing.
[Text]: If one establishes the nature of the fruit-of-fruit, then the nature of the object-field (*viṣaya*) is subsumed within the nature of the causal condition;
if one opens up the nature of the object-field, then the nature of the fruit-of-fruit is subsumed within the nature of the fruit.

[Commentary]: Regarding that which is subsumed under the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*) as the nature of the objects of cessation: the ten objects, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), are the proximate preparatory methods for correct contemplation;

because they directly give rise to the cause of realization (*vidyā-hetu*), they may be categorized under the causal condition. Regarding that which is subsumed under the resultant nature as the nature of the fruit:
although wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) differ, both are termed "fruit" (*phala*); thus, the two sets of five do not conflict in their numerical count.
[Text] "Deficient.
[Wenju] Although there are differences in opening and closing, they ultimately amount to five numbers.
[Ji] Second, regarding the five phrases in relation to the natures: first, these correspond to the five natures of the first school.

[Text] Now, by correlating the five knowledges with the five Buddha-natures: "I know all dharmas" means that one knows that within all dharmas there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss (*ānanda-dhātu*);
this "nature of peace and bliss" is precisely the Buddha-nature of the True Cause (*tathatā-hetu*).

"All conditioned dharmas" refers to immeasurable merits—the wholesome conditions such as bowing the head and raising the hands—which constitute the Buddha-nature of the Contributory Cause (*pratyaya-hetu*). To realize this...
"All dharmas" refers to the Buddha-nature as the cause of realization (*bodhi-hetu*), which is the wisdom of emptiness (*prajñā-śūnyatā*).
"Knowing the distinctions of dharmas" refers to the Buddha-nature as the cause of the objective realm (*viṣaya-hetu*), wherein the causes and effects of the mundane and supramundane do not overlap.

"Abiding in accordance with dharmas and according to their nature" refers to the ultimate abiding of the fruition-nature (*phala-dhātu*) in the center of suchness. This contains and sustains all things.
The Dharma is precisely the nature of the fruit (*phala-dhātu*) which is capable of dual illumination and inclusive reception.
[Commentary: "The nature of peace and bliss (*sukha-śānti*) is the true cause of Buddha-nature" means that peace and bliss is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*;

it is fully endowed with the three dharmas. Now, speaking of them in combination, it is simply called the "true cause. Regarding "the mundane and supramundane, etc.," the six realms of existence are...
The causes and effects of the three vehicles pertain to the mundane world, whereas the cause that is Buddha-nature pertains to the supramundane.

Regarding the nature of the object (*ālambana-svabhāva*), it is limited to the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) of the nine realms; when viewed from the perspective of the Buddha-realm, these are considered the cause.

Conversely, when the ten suchnesses of the Buddha-realm are viewed from the perspective of the nine realms, they are termed the effect. Because both belong to the subject of contemplation (*darśaka*) and are not classified as objects, the *Awakening of Faith* (Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra) speaks only of...
Because the nine marks constitute the objective sphere (*ālambana*), the aspect of karma is called "subtle within the subtle" and is the realm of the Buddha.

Furthermore, it is said that they are called an "objective sphere" based on the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); however, for this realized one, there is no objective sphere to be spoken of.
Therefore, the objective sphere consists of the phenomena of the nine realms. If so, what is called "Buddha-nature"? It is precisely because of the person who has attained the fruit.
Not only does it accomplish the Buddha-realm, but it can also accomplish the ten dharmas of the nine realms;
therefore, although the thousand dharmas exist within sentient beings, their functional utility is not manifested, whereas for the Buddha alone they are ultimately perfect, harmonious, and sovereign.
Thus, the dharma is the cause and human nature is the fruit. Second, this corresponds to the five natures discussed in the preceding section.

[Text]: If one posits the nature of the fruit-of-fruits (*phalaphala-svabhāva*), taking the discernment of the limits of phenomena (*dharma-pramāṇa*) as the nature of the fruit, and the clear illumination of the fruit-wisdom (*phala-jñāna*) as the limit;
and abiding in suchness (*tathatā*) while encompassing [all things] as the nature of the fruit-of-fruits, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Since the objective realm has already been subsumed within the causal condition of conjunction, one takes the phrase regarding the "delimitation of the dharmas known" as the nature of the fruit.
To exhaustively investigate the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); it is the clear illumination that clearly perceives the delimitation of that which is without delimitation.
As it is said: "The great ocean of the Prajñāpāramitā—how could the Buddha not have reached its bottom? Is this not taking that which is bottomless as the bottom? Indeed, it is.
Because they abide securely in the suchness of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are able to contain and sustain all fruits that share the same name;
this is the spontaneous, eternal dual-negation and dual-illumination subsequent to the fruit. Second, the chapter on "An" provides two sets of five phrases as examples:
first, the example above which correlates and corresponds [to the preceding].
[Text] "If this is so, the two subsequent sets of five phrases should also correspond to the five Buddha-natures.
[Commentary] These two cases must be explained according to the underlying principle.
[Text] Although the Master does not explain them, by analogy the principle should be such; one must explain their meaning accordingly, interpreting the text so that it accords with this.
[Commentary]: The five natures (*pañca-gotra*) are simply an expansion of the three dharmas.

Since each of the three successive sets of five phrases corresponds to the three dharmas, they should likewise correspond to the five natures in each successive set. However, the Master did not explain the meaning of the latter two sets.
Regarding the phrase "it can be seen," Zhiyan feared that later students might not understand, so he briefly pointed out that the *Yili* (Principles of Meaning) should be thus;
he further instructed the lecturer to expand upon its intent, hence the statement, "one must explain it accordingly," and so forth.

In the second section, "the light of wisdom" refers to the nature of the revealing cause (*vyutthāna-hetu*), while "the torch of wisdom" refers to the nature of the objective realm (*ālambana*). This shows that the knowing subject does not confound the object, just as a torch illuminates its surroundings.

The wisdom regarding phenomena is the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*); the accumulation of wisdom is the nature of the fruit; and the objective realm of wisdom is the nature of the direct cause (*hetu*).

According to the Master’s sequence, the nature of the objective realm is the "extinguishing cause" (*jñāna-prabhā*); this is the nature of the fruit, wherein the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*) is not confused with the capacity of the recipient.

This third section provides the correct interpretation, revealing that the essence [of the teaching] is the nature of the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), as it manifests the essence of correct contemplation.
Since it corresponds to the *saṃbhogakāya*, it is the nature of the fruit (*phala-dharmatā*); that which is precisely capable of discernment is the nature of the object (*viṣaya-dharmatā*);

correctly understanding the perfect [nature] is the nature of the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*); and that which is precisely capable of awakening and realizing is the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*).

If one follows the sequential master’s view, the nature of the object is excluded; thus, that which is precisely capable of discernment becomes the nature of the fruit, and after the fruit, it spontaneously differentiates according to the needs of sentient beings.
This is clear. Regarding the "three fetters":
it is for this reason, O World-Honored One, that he is named the Great General Vajrapāṇi.
[Commentary on the Text] The passage beginning with "it is for this reason, O World-Honored One" serves as a summary of the preceding text.
[Commentary] The three vows serve to augment the first two parts; the text first indicates the excellence [of the teaching].
[Textual Analysis] From "The World-Honored One, General Vajrapāṇi" downwards is the third vow, which augments the speaker through wisdom and eloquence.

This section is divided into two: first, augmenting the transformer (the preacher); second, augmenting those to be transformed (the listeners). The augmentation of the transformer is further divided into three adornments.
By means of refined speech, he benefits their vocal karma; by means of various exquisite flavors and vital energies, he benefits their physical karma;
and by means of mental progress and courageous sharpness, he benefits their mental karma. From this cause, he further benefits those whom he transforms—this also constitutes three aspects.
For this reason, he extensively expounds this sutra; this is to cause those who have not yet planted [the seeds of merit] to plant them. If...

There are sentient beings who, having already planted [the seeds], are now being brought to maturity; there are immeasurable sentient beings who, having already matured, are now being liberated—all as stated in the text.
This interpretation of the passage is excellent.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the text based on this [section]. Part one: benefiting the transformer. Sub-part one: benefiting the vocal karma.
"World-Honored One, I, the Great General Vajrapāṇi, shall cause the speech of the Dharma-preacher to be adorned and his eloquence to be uninterrupted."
[Commentary] Second, it benefits the physical karma (*kāyakarman*):
the refined essence of various delicacies enters through the pores, filling and augmenting the strength of the body.
[Commentary] Third, it benefits the mental karma (*manaskarman*).
With a mind that is courageous and sharp, they achieve inconceivable wisdom and enter into right mindfulness;
may they be fully endowed with such qualities as these, their minds free from weariness, their bodies experiencing various pleasures, and their hearts attaining joy.
[Commentary] Second, benefiting those to be converted: first, causing those who have not yet planted [the seeds] to plant them;
for this reason, he is able to extensively expound this sūtra for the sake of sentient beings.
[Commentary] Second, causing those who have already planted [the seeds] to ripen.
If there are sentient beings who have planted various roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, this Dharma-preacher shall,
for the sake of those beings, widely proclaim and disseminate this sublime sūtra within Jambudvīpa so that it shall not be interrupted.
[Commentary] Third, those who are already matured are caused to be liberated.
Having heard this sutra, immeasurable sentient beings shall attain an inconceivable accumulation of wisdom and gather an inconceivable accumulation of merit;
in future worlds, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas among humans and devas, they shall always...
In future lives, they shall experience happiness, encounter all Buddhas, and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
all sufferings and the realms of the three evil destinies shall be forever extinguished without remainder.

[Commentary] Question: Since one has already attained the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-skandha*) and also encompasses the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-skandha*), these constitute both the semblance and the true two kinds of adornments.

They should coexist in the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*) and the land of actual retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*). Why, then, does the Sūtra speak only of "immeasurable thousands of kalpas of humans and devas enjoying happiness"?
Answer: One must understand that all ten benefits are inseparable from these twenty-five [stages]. Among these, the present refers to the stage of humans and devas.

Because it is for the sake of the provisional [rewards] of humans and devas and the actual retribution [of the Pure Lands], the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Beyond the three realms, there is still a realm of sentient beings.
This refers to what is taught in the non-Buddhist *Mahābhūta Sūtra*.

One must know that whether the four lands are considered horizontally or vertically, they are discussed as being situated within the single location of the three realms; students should examine this carefully. Fourth, taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
