Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, whose body is adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, who fiercely upholds such a sublime torch of the Dharma.
Homage to the One Who Has Accomplished Supreme Majestic Virtue.
Homage to the Great Goddess of Merit, the Great Eloquence Deity who has accomplished immeasurable wisdom and merit.
[Commentary on the Text] From "Homage to the Jewel Flower" (*namo ratnapuṣpa*) onwards is the fourth section of the text of homage and respect.

It is said that at the beginning of all the Buddha's sūtras, there is always an expression of homage, though translators have often omitted it; likewise, at the beginning of all treatises (*śāstra*), one must first offer homage. This text is such an instance.
This concludes the discussion; that taking refuge in the Triple Gem can be found in the text itself.

[Commentary] It is said that at the beginning of all sutras there is a verse of homage and respect; this means that those who compiled the sutras invariably placed such verses of homage before the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*).
In this land, translators have preferred brevity and thus omitted them, though some still remain, as in the case of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* (or *Sātyaka-sūtra*).
The *Nigaṇṭhaputtovāda-sūtra* begins with the words: "I take refuge in the Buddha Vairocana, the Ocean of Great Wisdom.

The commentary notes that at the beginning of all sūtras in foreign editions, these words are present; they represent the homage paid by the author of the treatise at the start of his work, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Aśvabhāva-śāstra*.
Regarding the Three Jewels, the Buddha and the Dharma are well known for their great merit.
"Discernment" (*pratibhāna*) refers to the Bodhisattva’s principle of harmonizing the Saṃgha. *Namo* (南無) is translated here as "taking refuge.

[Commentary] Second, the main discourse on the excellent collection of the clear exposition for the King of Men from days past, which involves mastery of the sūtras. Part one: The Main Discourse Section. Sub-part one:
The Title of the Chapter.
The Eleventh Chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*:

"The Chapter on the Correct Discourse" [Commentary]. The text is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the title; second, the direct explanation of the two characters [of the title].
[Text] Regarding "Correct Discourse" (*samyag-vāda*): it is correctly named "Noble" (*ārya*). There are two kinds of noble ones: first, worldly noble ones; second, supramundane noble ones.
"Discourse" (*vāda*) means to investigate and ascertain reality: first, investigating the reality of facts; second, investigating the reality of principles.
[Commentary]: "Sages of the world" refers to universal monarchs (*cakravartin*). The *Book of Changes* says:

"To provide for all things and bring them to practical use, to establish merit and complete instruments, thereby creating benefit for the world—nothing is greater than the sage. The *Guanzi* says: "The sage is like Heaven;
he covers all without partiality. He is like the Earth; he supports all without partiality. These passages all refer to worldly sages and supramundane sages.

This means that those who have attained the fruits of the Three Vehicles and have severed delusions to realize the principle are called "sages" (*ārya*). Regarding the term *he* (核), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it refers to examining the reality of an event.

If one examines the reality of events, the correct discourse of the world can be used to govern the state; if one examines the reality of principles, the correct discourse of the supramundane can be used to reach the Way.
The second section extensively clarifies the four *siddhārtha* (four purposes), namely, the correct discourse of the world.

There are four benefits, all of which cite the *Xiaojing* (Classic of Filial Piety) to establish their meaning. The text is divided into four sections, beginning with the first: the World. [Commentary on the Text]:
This chapter contains the ancient laws of former kings, transmitted from generation to generation. The former kings transmitted the power of the honored signs;
the honored signs were transmitted to those who believe; those who believe further transmitted them to their sons, and their sons transmitted them to future generations.

"Righteousness and sageliness in every generation, and goodness and reality in every generation" is precisely the dharma-speech of the former kings; it is also a name established according to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly consensus).
This is titled "The Chapter on Righteous Discourse.

[Commentary] The "ancient laws of the former kings" refers to the actualities of worldly phenomena; that these differ from generation to generation is the meaning of the "worldly" (*loka*) perspective.
Second, for the sake of humanity.

[Wenqu] The King practices this Dharma; the laws and regulations correspond with one another, the Yin and Yang are thereby harmonized, the sun and moon are thereby made regular, the hundred grains are thereby abundant, the myriad people are thereby joyful, the altars of soil and grain are thereby secure, and governance and transformation are thereby perfected.
"Beauty" refers to the people living in harmony so that there is no resentment between those above and below; it is also established as a name for the *puruṣasiddhānta* (the goal for persons).
It is titled "The Chapter on Right Discourse.
[Commentary] Regarding the "hundred grains," Yang Quan’s *Wuli Lun* states: "Liang is the general name for *shu* and *ji*; *dao* is..."
“Geng” and “nuo” are general names for rice; “shu” is the general name for various beans. Each of these three grains has twenty varieties, totaling sixty.

Fruits and vegetables that assist the grains also have twenty varieties each, making a total of one hundred grains. Regarding the Altars of the Soil (She) and the Grain (Ji), the *Xiaojing Wei* states:
“The She is the presiding lord of the land. Since the land is vast and it is impossible to pay reverence to it all, earth is piled up [to represent it].”
The *shè* (sacrificial altar) is established to repay merit. Ji is the foremost of the five grains;

because the grains are so numerous that they cannot all be sacrificed to individually, the deity Ji is established to sacrifice to them on their behalf. The *Liji* states: "The son of Lishanshi—(Lishi is sometimes written as Lieshi)—Zhu, and Zhou Qi served as the Ji (Minister of Agriculture).

When Lishanshi ruled the world, his son Zhu was able to plant the hundred grains. During the decline of the Xia dynasty, Zhou Qi succeeded him; therefore, he is worshipped as the deity Ji. Gonggong was the ruler of the people.

"This son, Hou-tu, became the presiding deity of the She-altar" (When Gonggong was the hegemon of the Nine Provinces, his son was Hou-tu; he was able to level the Nine Provinces, and thus he is sacrificed to as the deity of the She-altar).

"The people lived in harmony and concord": the populace received and followed his teachings, harmonizing with one another; those high and low, superior and subordinate, harbored no resentment toward each other.
This is the third pair of governance.

[Text] By employing this method, the king ensures that external enemies dare not plot against him, internal traitors dare not cause alarm, malevolent stars dare not appear, evil rainbows dare not manifest, violent winds dare not stir, and torrential rains dare not fall. Thus, calamities and rebellions do not arise, and disasters do not occur.
This is also a name established according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic counteraction), and the chapter is titled "The Chapter on Right Discourse."
[Commentary]: "Internal treason" refers to rebellious ministers and treacherous sons. Kong Anguo said: "Those within the state are called *jian* (treasonous);

those outside the state are called *jiu* (bandits). Regarding "calamity and disorder": "calamity" means that good people encounter misfortune; "disorder" means that ministers and subordinates act in rebellion and defiance. Regarding "disaster":
it means Heaven reverses its seasons, such as when wind and rain are not regulated. Regarding "harm": it means the earth reverses its seasons, such as floods and droughts.
It harms the crops. This is the first of the four primary meanings.
[Wenju] This worldly goodness is fundamentally derived from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*; this correct treatise emerges from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
By skillfully employing this correct treatise, one causes the celestial palaces and celestial bodies to shine with brilliance, and by means of it, one increases celestial power and celestial majesty.
The Will of Heaven rejoices therein twofold, and the Dharma-flavor of Heaven becomes twice as profound and far-reaching;
this is the supreme virtue and essential path of the former kings, and it is established as the name "First Principle *Siddhānta*," titled the "Chapter on Correct Discourse."
[Commentary] Regarding "the original capital of radiant light," the *Four Kings Chapter* states that all state affairs and worldly treatises are derived from this sutra.
Regarding "the ultimate virtue and essential path": "ultimate" refers to the limit of exhausting principle;
"essential" refers to unifying the many through the one. This correct discourse is the ancient law of the former kings—the pinnacle of virtue and the core of the Way.
The first three also belong entirely to the mundane; they are explained here according to their fundamental nature.

Now, this fourth [section] encompasses both the supramundane and the mundane, and thus clarifies the meaning of both the root and its branches, so that those who hear it may understand and realize two kinds of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Those of dull faculties obtain only the essential path of the mundane—this is from the perspective of the branches—while those of sharp faculties awaken to the supramundane.
The essential path of the world follows from the root; increasing celestial virtue must likewise be divided into two parts.

That which follows from the branch results only in birth in the heavens, whereas that which follows from the root resides in the *Arthasatya* (Heaven of Meaning), encompassing both the pure heavens (*śuddhāvāsa*) and the heavens [of the desire realm], because the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* belongs to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
Second, the purpose for its introduction.
[Text] This passage is the second point within the section on the circulation [of the scripture], clarifying how the King who propagates the sutra moves the response of the hidden sages,
and how the Heavenly Kings provide assistance so that his virtuous governance flourishes.
[Commentary] "Mystic Sages" refers to the various devas, as they are the mystic sages; thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* states, "all mystic dharmas.
These two scriptural passages constitute the first division of the text.
[Textual Analysis] The text is divided into two parts: first, the prose section which explains the fundamental facts; second, the verse section which presents the formal argument.
Within the prose, the Buddha addresses the Earth Deity to recount the characteristics of the former Honored One.
[Commentary] Second, the sequential explanation has two parts; first, the prose section.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā: "In the past, there was a king named Baladharaketu.
This king had a son named Śraddhādhāna, who was soon to receive the position of consecration and rule over the kingdom. At that time, the father-king..."
He addressed his crown prince, Śraddhālakṣaṇa: "There is a True Discourse in the world that skillfully governs a kingdom. In the past, I was once a crown prince;
before long, I shall likewise succeed to my father the king’s throne. At that time, the father king took this True Discourse and taught it to me as well.
By means of this discourse, I have skillfully governed the kingdom for twenty thousand years, never for even a single thought-moment having acted otherwise.
When practicing the Dharma, one should have no attachment to one's own kin. What is called the "Treatise on Worldly Governance"?
At that time, King Baladharavaralakṣaṇa spoke these verses for the sake of Prince Śraddhālakṣaṇa.
[Text] As in the main text.
[Commentary] Regarding those who receive the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fascicle 39, states:

"The mother of the crown prince born to a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) is the principal queen, her physical marks being fully perfected. That Wheel-Turning King causes this crown prince to sit..."
Upon a magnificent golden throne, with a white elephant-jewel as its support, a great net and canopy were spread, and a great Dharma banner was erected.
Incense was burned, flowers were scattered, and various musical instruments were played. The waters of the four great oceans were taken and placed within a golden vase;
the king held this vase and poured it over the crown of the prince’s head. At that moment, he was named the one who has received the royal position and entered the ranks of the consecrated Kṣatriyas.
One who is able to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action may also be called a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*). The two verses consist of two initial sections.
[Textual Commentary]:
There are eighty-two lines of verse, which are divided into four parts; the first two and a half lines assemble the assembly, and the next three lines...

The first half [of the verse] poses the question; the next line concludes the question and opens the response; the subsequent seventy-five lines constitute the Brahmā’s answer, which expounds the *Abhidharma*.
The introductory text is divided into three parts: first, one line in which the Buddha describes his majestic appearance, intending to preach the fundamental Dharma of former kings to the Devaputra;
second, one line in which the Buddha describes his majestic appearance and exhorts him to listen; third, half a line [concluding this section].
This clarifies the location where the treatise was spoken.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the sequential explanation of the four parts, the first is the assembly of the multitude. The third follows the topical outline: first, the Buddha describes his own venerable characteristics and expresses his intent to speak, saying:
"I shall now expound the *Rājanīti-śāstra* (Treatise on Royal Ethics) for the benefit of sentient beings, in order to sever all their doubts."
[Commentary] The two Buddhas describe their majestic appearance and admonish [the assembly] to listen:
"All human kings, gods, and celestial kings should joyfully join their palms and listen attentively.
[Commentary] Third, the location where the treatise is expounded is clarified.
The various kings gathered together at Vajraparvata.
[Commentary] This consists of two parts: the two questions posed and the initial division of the text.
[Wenju] Next, the four kings pose four questions: first, they ask why humans are called "devas" (heavenly beings); second, they ask about those who are not devas.

[The Buddha] explained that although he was born as such and named a Son of Heaven (*devaputra*), there are four questions: first, why is one who dwells in the palace of the royal court called a "Heavenly One" (*deva*);
second, why is one who governs the world according to human laws called a "Heavenly One.
[Commentary: There are two explanations for the meaning; the four [questions] follow the division of the text. The first question addresses why a person is addressed as a "Heavenly One."
The Four World-Protectors arose and questioned the Brahma King: "O Great Teacher, Honored Brahma, Sovereign among the gods, who can eliminate doubt and confusion, please sever our uncertainty:
how is it that such a person is named a 'deva'?"
[Commentary] 1. Question: Why is one named a "Son of Heaven" (devaputra)?
Why is a human king also called a "Son of Heaven"?
[Commentary] 2. Question: Why is it that those dwelling in palaces and halls are called "gods" (deva)?
Born among humans, he dwells in a royal palace. [Commentary:
Regarding the four questions, why is a human king who rules the world called a "deva"?
Because he rules the world through the True Dharma (Saddharma), he is named a deva.
[Commentary] This is a question regarding the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), followed by an opening and response.
After the Four World-Protecting Kings (*Caturmahārājika*) had asked about this matter, the Honored Teacher Brahmā (*Brahmā-satpuruṣa*) then spoke these verses.
[Textual Analysis] The subsequent line establishes what precedes and initiates what follows; it may be seen as such, and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the four Brahmā deities’ answers to the two [questions], there are two parts: first, the statement of the intent; second, the division of the text.
First, the statement of the intent. [Text]: Question: Since there are four questions, there are likewise four answers. First, the answer that the deity protected his entry into the womb;
although he is the son of a human, he is called a "Son of Heaven" (devaputra). Second, the thirty-three heavens each contributed a portion of their merit; although he is among humans, he is called...
Although he dwells in a human palace, he rules the world according to celestial laws; although he is a human sovereign, he is called a "deva" (heavenly being).
Although he rules the world as a human, he causes sentient beings to practice virtue so that they may be reborn frequently in the heavens.
Thus, because the effect is spoken of in terms of the cause, he is called a "deva."
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "Son of Heaven" (Tianzi) as explained in the Buddhist scriptures, this passage is the most explicit.

If one follows the Confucian tradition, it is said that because the King is the son of Heaven and the son of Earth, he is called the Son of Heaven. The *Yuan Shen Qi* states: "Heaven covers and Earth bears; therefore, he is called the Son of Heaven.
This text is divided into two parts.
[Text] From "Although you now... onwards is the Brahmin’s reply, which is divided into two parts: first, a brief reply in ten and a half lines;
second, a detailed reply in sixty-four and a half lines. Within the brief reply, there are four sections: first, one and a half lines granting the answer;

second, one line stating "Because of the accumulation of karma," which briefly cites the causes of the past and the results of the present to answer the King's question regarding its meaning; third, five... [text continues].

The three lines of verse following answer his question regarding the meaning of "heaven" by citing three points; the subsequent three lines of verse again answer his question regarding the meaning of "king" by citing three points.
[Commentary] Part Two: Explaining the Meaning According to the Text. Part One: A Brief Answer. Subsection One: Granting the Answer.
"Although you now question me on this matter, I must proclaim and expound the foremost, supreme discourse for the sake of all sentient beings. [Commentary:
This is the second part, answering the King's meaning.]
Because he was born among humans due to the accumulation of karma and rules over a kingdom as a sovereign, he is called a "King of Men" (*narapati*).

[Commentary] Regarding the title "King of Men," the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) states: "One whose virtue mirrors Heaven and Earth is called an Emperor (*di*); one who is born of benevolence and righteousness is called a King (*wang*.
The *Baihutong* (Comprehensive Discussions on the White Tiger Gate) says: "A 'King' (*wang*) means 'one to whom others go'; he is the one toward whom the whole world turns. (Third Answer)
Questioning the meaning of "Heaven" (deva):
While dwelling within the womb, various devas provide protection; or rather, they protect [the being] first before entering the womb.

Although one is born among humans and becomes a king of men, because of the protection of the devas, one is further called a "Son of Heaven" (devaputra). Each of the thirty-three devas, by virtue of their own merit...
Because he bestows [these benefits] upon such persons, he is called a Son of Heaven (devaputra). By the empowerment of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he attains mastery;

he distances them from unwholesome dharmas and prevents them from arising, while establishing them in wholesome dharmas and causing them to increase and expand. He is able to cause many sentient beings to be reborn in the heavens.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts; the first points out three meanings.
[Wenju] The answer to the Deva’s citation of the three meanings refers to the power of merit added during the stages of not yet entering the womb and while entering the womb.
[Commentary]: "Not yet entered," etc., constitutes a single meaning; "possessing virtue" is a single meaning; and "bestowing empowerment" is a single meaning.
Second, the explanation of the answers to the three questions: first, he answers the second question by means of protecting the fetus.
[Text]: "Because he is protected during gestation, he is called a 'Son of Heaven' (devaputra). This answers the second question. [Commentary]:
Those who have not yet entered the state of protection remain in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), while those who have entered protection reside within the womb.
During these two periods, they are frequently subject to harm by spirits; therefore, they rely on the protection of devas. Second, answering the first question by way of the distribution of merit.
[Text]: Because he shares his merit and possesses celestial virtue, he is called a "deva. This answers the first question.
[Commentary]: Thirdly, by means of the application of power, he answers the third and fourth questions.

[Text]: "Empowered by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they cultivate what is wholesome and restrain what is evil; consequently, they will surely be reborn in the heavens. Because the fruit is spoken of within the cause, they are called 'heavenly' (*deva*).
This answers the third and fourth questions regarding those who govern the world through the True Dharma being called 'heavenly.
Half [of the definition] is thus 'heavenly. The three meanings are concluded."

[Commentary]: Regarding the third question above, as for why the royal palace is called a "heavenly" (deva) abode, and the fourth question, as to why one who governs the world through human laws is called a "heavenly" being—the answer here states that although he dwells in a human palace, because he is empowered by celestial power (*deva-bala*), his sovereignty is like that of a god;
this answers the third question. Furthermore, by restraining evil and encouraging good so as to cause people to be reborn in heaven, it answers the fourth question.
Furthermore, there are four points in response to the King’s inquiry regarding the meaning [of this]:
half are called "human kings," and they are also called "Rākṣasa executioners who wield music.

They are able to restrain all evils and are also called "parents" who instruct one to cultivate goodness and manifest the retribution of karmic results. They are protected by the devas, and their various good and evil deeds pertain to both the present and the future.
Presently receiving the retribution [of their deeds], they are protected by the various devas.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first correctly clarifies the three meanings of a "human king. First, it clarifies that one who possesses pleasure is called a king.
[Textual Analysis] From the passage "From half [a person] onwards is called a human king" below, there are three meanings for which he is called a king; thus, the first meaning is...

The joy of those who hold the music stems from the King; the King holds this music and causes peace and harmony throughout the world. Once every five days there is a breeze, and once every ten days there is rain.
The elderly strike the *rang* clay, and children ride bamboo horses—who among them does not attribute this virtue to him?
Therefore, those who hold the music call the King their Master of Music.
[Commentary]: That the King "embraces this music" means that he maintains ritual and music (*li-yue*) to transform the people. The *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiaojing*) says:
"Guide them with ritual and music, and the people will be harmonious and united. The *Record of Music* (*Yueli*) says: "Great music must be easy; great ritual must be simple.

When music reaches its perfection, there is no resentment; when ritual reaches its perfection, there is no contention. To govern the world through yielding and courtesy is the work of ritual and music."
This refers to the transformation of the Way through the descent of the celestial mandate to bring forth clarity and joy.
The *Jingfang Yihou* states: "In times of Great Peace, it rains once every ten days; in a single year, there are thirty-six such rains. This is the response of the auspicious sign of timely rain.
The *Fengtu Ji* says: "The *jirang* (wooden mallet) is made of wood; it is broad in front and tapered at the back, measuring one chi and three or four cun in length."
Its shape is about an inch long and resembles a sandal; on the winter solstice festival, children play with it as a game.

According to the *Yishi zhuan* (Biographies of Recluse Scholars), during the time of Emperor Yao, there was an old man playing *rang* (a wooden disc) on the road who said: "I work when the sun rises and rest when the sun sets;
I drink from the wells I have dug and eat the crops I have tilled. What power does the Emperor have over me? Was this not the virtue of the Ultimate Sage?

He acts without presiding over others, and his profound merit is praised as it sustains the movement of the world; thus, the common people use its benefits daily without realizing it—it is even the plaything of children on bamboo horses.
When a king holds to music in governing the state, he brings peace to the world, so that both old and young may joyfully fulfill their natures.
Second, the explanation of the "King who Blocks Evil."

[Text]: Second, he restrains evil to eliminate harm for the people; thus, the heavens do not suffer from excessive drought, the earth does not suffer from torrential floods, the grasses are not broken or damaged, and the people are free from pestilence.
Who would not turn to him in reverence? Therefore, one who restrains evil is called a "King."
[Commentary] The sutra states that because rākṣasas, executioners (*kaivarta*), and others can restrain violence and evil, they are also called "rākṣasa executioners.
The phrase "are also called" (*yi ming*) governs the subsequent terms, as they are like the chief officers (*kui zu*) among the rākṣasas;
thus, the various ghosts do not dare to commit transgressions. Third, the names of their parents are Kings.
[Text]: Regarding the three types of parents: they instruct on calamity and fortune, guide one toward good and evil, and establish rites and music so that the people know the prohibitions.
Who would not turn to them with virtue? Therefore, parents are named "Kings" (Rājan).
[Commentary] This means that the King is the parent of the people. Regarding "instructing them on calamity and fortune, etc.":

this refers to inflicting punishments upon those who violate benevolence and righteousness, which constitutes the calamity of evil; and recording those who embody benevolence and righteousness by bestowing upon them rank and emolument, which constitutes the fortune of goodness.
He established ritual to regulate their outward conduct and created music to harmonize their hearts. Thus, the *Yueli* (Record of Music) states: "Music is..."
"To act as one toward those who share the same rites" means that where there is sameness, there is mutual intimacy; where there is difference, there is mutual respect.
"The people know the prohibitions" means the people know that there are prohibitory ordinances. These two points together manifest the three meanings of the Son of Heaven.
[Text] Because he acts as a parent to those below him, the various devas protect him, and thus he is called a "Son of Heaven" (*devānām-priya*).

Because he wards off evil so that it does not arise, he shares in the merit of the devas and is therefore called a "Heavenly One" (*deva*). Furthermore, because he enjoys music, the fruit is spoken of in terms of the cause, and he is again called a "Heavenly One.

It is not merely that half of his name signifies the meaning of a "human king" (*rāja*) being established, while the other half signifies a "Heavenly One"; these three meanings are likewise [present].

[Manifestation]. [Commentary]: To speak of the fruit within the cause means that by transforming the people through ritual and music (*li-yue*), they will necessarily be reborn in the heavens. Second, the broad answer has two parts:

first, the analysis of the text and explanation of the meaning; second, the extensive clarification of the faults of non-Dharma regarding the six meanings. First, the extensive clarification of the faults of non-Dharma regarding the six meanings.

If there are evil deeds that are permitted and not investigated, and their offenses are not punished according to the correct teaching, one abandons and distances oneself from wholesome dharmas and increases the accumulation of evil.
Consequently, many instances of treachery and strife arise within the kingdom;

the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven each give rise to resentment because the king permits evil without punishment, thereby destroying the kingdom's righteous Dharma, causing deceit and fraud to flourish, and inviting hostile enemies from other regions.
Vicious thieves will compete to plunder all the wealth, treasures, and possessions belonging to their own people, seizing them from one another;
yet when the world is governed according to the Dharma, such things do not occur.

If such acts are committed, that kingdom will be utterly destroyed—just as a mad elephant tramples a lotus pond, or as a violent wind suddenly arises accompanied by torrential rain, while malevolent stars appear frequently and the sun and moon lose their radiance.
The five grains and fruits all failed to flourish because the king abandoned the Right Path, causing famine in the land;
the gods within their palaces were all filled with grief and distress because the king was tyrannical and failed to cultivate virtuous deeds. These various heavenly kings said to one another:
"This king practices evil and keeps company with the wicked; because he has committed such evils, he has swiftly incurred the wrath of the gods, and because of that divine wrath—"
Before long, the kingdom will fall into ruin; unrighteousness, weapons, deceit, litigation, pestilence, and malignant diseases will gather within its lands.
The devas will immediately abandon that king, causing his realm to perish and giving rise to great sorrow and suffering.

Brothers, sisters, kinsmen, wives, and children will be scattered and driven into exile, and even his own life will come to an end. Shooting stars will fall in succession, and two suns will appear simultaneously.
Furthermore, malevolent bandits will invade and plunder the land; the people will suffer from famine and many epidemics; the esteemed great ministers will abandon their posts and pass away;
elephants, horses, and chariots will perish in a single moment; the family wealth and all that belongs to the kingdom will be mutually seized and looted;
people will die by the sword; the five planets and various lunar mansions will deviate from their regular courses; and there will be various evils and pestilences.
Throughout the kingdom, those who receive favors and emoluments—the ministers appointed to office and the various officials—exclusively practice what is unlawful.
Thus, those who commit evil are uniquely favored with imperial grace, while those who cultivate the wholesome Dharma decline day by day.
People show reverence to those who act wickedly, and their hearts have no desire to record or honor those who practice virtue; consequently, three anomalies arise throughout the world.

The constellations lose their proper courses, bringing down violent winds and rains that destroy the supreme, unexcelled *saddharma* (True Dharma), as well as sentient beings and the very fertility of the earth.
Because they honor the wicked and revile those who are virtuous, the heavens send down hail, famine, pestilence, and death;
the flavor of grains, fruits, and crops diminishes; and the land becomes filled with sickly sentient beings, while sweet and abundant fruits [become rare].
Day by day, bitter and foul flavors increase while wholesome tastes diminish; the delightful places where they once sported all wither away until nothing remains to bring joy.
The exquisite and superior flavors consumed by sentient beings gradually decrease;
their food no longer nourishes the skin, their countenances become ugly, their physical strength wanes, and they never know satiety in whatever they eat.
Power, diligence, and valor shall all be extinguished, while laziness and indolence pervade the land.
Many will suffer from physical ailments that oppress their bodies; malevolent stars will shift, and rākṣasas will roam in disorder.

If there is a king who acts contrary to the Dharma, increases his evil associates, and harms the realms of humans and devas, he will experience much suffering within the three realms of existence, giving rise to such calamities as these.
Immeasurable evil deeds all stem from human kings who, out of attachment to their retinues, allow them to commit wickedness and neglect to punish them.
If those born [as a result] are protected by the various devas, such human kings will ultimately not exist;

for those who practice good attain birth among the devas, while those who perform unwholesome deeds fall into the three miserable realms. All those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three will experience scorching heat.
If a king indulges evil and neglects to admonish it, thereby acting in opposition to the gods and the commands of his parents, he fails to exercise proper governance;
such a person is not a filial son. One must not tolerate or abandon those who incite various forms of wickedness and destroy the kingdom.
[Text] From "If there are evil deeds" onwards, thirty-nine lines and three phrases extensively clarify that one who acts contrary to the Dharma cannot be called a deva and cannot be called a king;
they lose all six meanings [of a true ruler]. The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens each give rise to resentment, saying, "This is not protected by the devas.
Because he is not protected, he is not a son of the devas (*devaputra*); thus, these various heavenly kings each say to one another, "This is a deva."

Because they do not distinguish merit and lack merit, they cannot be called devas. Abandoning what is distant from wholesome dharmas and increasing unwholesome dharmas, there is no cause for being a deva;
how then could one speak of the effect within the cause by praising a person as a deva? Those who give rise to great sorrow and suffering have no sense of attachment to joy;
that pestilence flows everywhere signifies the unrestrained nature of evil; to let loose evil while disregarding the good means... [the text is incomplete].
"Regarding the meaning of 'parents,' and so forth.
[Commentary] Second, the detailed explanation of correct governance (*samyak-nigraha*) in terms of six meanings.
Because he correctly governs offenses, all the devas protect and sustain this king; for he extinguishes unwholesome dharmas and cultivates wholesome ones.

In this present life, one who attains the increase of royal power should be taught that each must perform both wholesome and unwholesome deeds, for it is by demonstrating the causality of karma that one becomes a king.
Protected by the devas and assisted by neighboring kings, he should practice righteous governance for his own sake and for the sake of others.
Toward those who would destroy the kingdom, he should provide proper instruction; for the sake of his life and the state, he should practice the True Dharma and should not commit evil.
Evil should not be permitted; while other matters cannot destroy a kingdom, it must first be filled with many forms of deceit before it can fall into ruin.
Just as a great elephant destroys a lotus pond, so too does resentment toward the devas cause the devas to give rise to afflictions and various calamities that fill the land.
Therefore, one should rule the world in accordance with the True Dharma.
He transforms the kingdom through virtue; rather than following what is contrary to the Dharma, he would sooner sacrifice his own life than cherish his retinue.

Toward both kin and non-kin, his mind is always impartial; he unites the dear and the estranged into one through right conduct. His fame spreads throughout the three realms as he governs the kingdom with the True Dharma.
Because many people practice goodness, they constantly regard the king with virtuous hearts, such that he is able to cause the hosts of devas to look up toward him.
Because he is fully endowed with and perfect in these qualities, his righteous governance is called that of a "King of Men.

All the devas protect this king just as parents protect their own children; therefore, they cause the sun, moon, five planets, and various lunar mansions to follow their respective orbits without failing in their regular courses.
Wind and rain come in their proper seasons, free from all calamities, so that the kingdom becomes abundant, peaceful, and prosperous.

It increases the multitude of people and the various devas; for this reason, O kings of men, you should rather sacrifice your own bodies and lives than commit evil, nor should you abandon the precious treasure of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Because of the treasure of the True Dharma, worldly beings experience happiness;
therefore, you should always remain close to those who cultivate the True Dharma, gathering merits to adorn your own persons and your retinues.
Always knowing contentment, he should distance himself from evil people, cultivate the True Dharma, and establish sentient beings in all wholesome dharmas;
by instructing and protecting them so they may leave unwholesome states behind, the kingdom will thus become peaceful, secure, abundant, and joyful.
This king shall also attain full majesty and virtue, and should subdue the various evil practices of his subjects, instructing and admonishing them in accordance with the Dharma.
This king shall obtain a fine name and excellent reputation, being well able to protect and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
[Commentary on the Text] From the phrase "He shall rightly govern and punish" downward, twenty-four lines and three phrases further elaborate upon six meanings:

"rightly governing and punishing" corresponds to the meaning of "parents"; "being protected by the various devas" corresponds to the meaning of "Son of Heaven" (Cakravartin); and "extinguishing evil dharmas" [corresponds to the meaning of a Buddha].
[Commentary] Because these six scriptural passages intersect with one another from beginning to end, they are not subdivided together with the preceding section.

The lecturer should dissolve them by contrasting the textual passages according to the gains and losses of the six meanings; then their principles will naturally become clear. Second, showing that contemplation clarifies the source, which has two parts:
first, causing one to contemplate the meaning of contemplation.
[Text]: "In this context, one should clarify the meaning of contemplation; reflect upon it yourself," and so forth. [Commentary]:
Regarding the instruction to "reflect upon it yourself," those who have received this school's teachings ought to know the two methods for practicing contemplation.

Therefore, the sub-commentary (*shu*) does not explicitly show them, intending for the reader to reflect upon them themselves. Now, fearing that later students may be unable to distinguish between them, I cannot help but provide a brief explanation here.
Regarding these three types, there is "contemplation based on phenomena" (*vastu-pratītya-vipaśyanā*):

that is, relying on the Deva of the World to clarify the realm of the Truths (*satya*), and relying on the Deva of the Human King to clarify wondrous contemplation. This very nature of a single thought-moment is the Deva of Meaning;

by relying on this Deva, one can prevent such contemplation from giving rise to inverted views. This is the meaning of "Deva-protection," which is Madhyamaka. Contemplation unites with the Deva of Meaning, becoming identical to that Deva.
When virtue is undivided yet names are divided, it is called "Heaven. When virtue is divided, it is the Contemplation of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Because the divine power of the celestial deity (*deva*) adds to the wondrous contemplation, one is able to pass through all objects while attaining perfect fusion; this is the Contemplation of the Provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, for those who rely upon a human king to cultivate the contemplation of principle:

when the contemplation arises from the entirety of the Truths, the Middle Way illuminates both simultaneously—this is the meaning of the "Father and Mother. When the Contemplation of Emptiness subdues delusions, it is the "Chief."
The meaning of "mincemeat" (huài) is the provisional establishment of dharmas through contemplation; the meaning of "delight" (lè) is this truth and this contemplation.

Both of these are free from either vertical or horizontal [distinctions], for within a single mind these six meanings are fully present. Second, posing questions to clarify the two fundamental aspects: first, the posing of the question.
[Text] Question: The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is the fundamental source for correct treatises; what is the meaning of this?

[Commentary] The preceding "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" states that all state affairs conducted by kings within Jambudvīpa and all worldly discourses composed by them all derive from this sutra.
Is it not, therefore, the correct treatise, having the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its very foundation?
Desiring to provide an answer that reveals the root within the branches, he poses this question. Second, the response and demonstration has two parts:
first, the direct demonstration that among the teachings of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sūtras, there is not a single matter that does not originate from principle.

For example, when Saṃjñeya was translated as "Mimi" (Mī), those who commonly refer to him by that name—how could they know it invokes the three secret and wondrous dharmas? Now, within this very scripture...
The enumeration of the fifteen meanings of the secret names thoroughly elucidates the foundation of worldly nomenclature.
This orthodox treatise was spoken by Brahmā; the foundation of Brahmā is revealed in the various sutras as the Dharma-body Bodhisattva.

Wherever the Dharma-body Bodhisattva dwells, it is the Constantly Quiescent Light. Taking the body as an analogy for the mouth, whatever is spoken is nothing other than [the manifestation of that light].
The *Secret Treasury* is the current orthodox treatise, which takes this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as its foundation. How could a derivative matter ever temporarily deviate from the fundamental principle?

Water, waves, and the golden vessel exist simultaneously in terms of both the derivative and the fundamental; because the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* encompasses worldly phenomena, one may point to the names of these worldly things to reveal the fundamental.
This section is divided into two parts: first, clarifying that the derivative is identical to the fundamental; second, [clarifying that the fundamental is identical to the derivative].
The first section, "Regarding the Son of Heaven," demonstrates the fundamental meaning through three points.
[Commentary on the Text]: "Heaven" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which is gold; because the *dharmatā* serves as the basis of reliance, it is called "Heaven.

"Guarding and bestowing merit" refers to light; the merging of the *saṃbhogakāya* with the *dharmatā* is precisely what constitutes "bestowing merit. This is the empowerment conferred by spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
"This is precisely illumination," and so forth. [Commentary:

One should first understand that this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is the Dharma itself and not a mere metaphor, because the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya are alternative names for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
"Heaven" refers to the heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). "Son" refers to the unsurpassed sentient being.
Originally, a person grasps the wondrous Threefold Reality of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* to constitute this provisional person.

This person relies upon the ultimate heavenly realm (*paramārtha-deva*), which is fundamentally free from the eight perversions; this is the meaning of "heavenly protection. This person’s light of wisdom merges with the Dharma-body;
the golden virtue is identical to the Dharma as a shared virtue—this is the meaning of "shared virtue. Because this person should receive benefit, it is termed "illumination" (*prabhā*).
This is due to the application of the power of the heavens. Second, regarding the human king, the three meanings demonstrate the fundamental basis.
[Commentary on the Text]: Furthermore, "parents" refers to gold; because the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) acts as the parents, the warding off of evil is "light," and the grasping of joy is "clarity."
[Commentary]: Because the substance of this wondrous provisional body is gold, it simultaneously possesses both the provisional and the real, serving as the father and mother for all beings.

Because its substance is light, it illuminates that delusions are fundamentally empty; this is the meaning of "prohibiting evil. Because its substance is clarity, it can give rise to all manner of goodness;
this is the meaning of "embracing joy. Second, it clarifies that the end is established from the root.
[Text]: Because this serves as the foundation, one is able to discourse correctly upon it. [Commentary]:
As shown above, the six meanings of the "foundation" (mūla)—the causes and effects across the six stages—are all identical to this meaning.
This meaning is capable of serving as the foundation for all mundane and supramundane affairs. Now, taking this very foundation as the basis, one discusses the correct discourse (samyag-vāda).

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), when those of the corresponding capacity hear of the affairs of governing a state, they immediately penetrate its fundamental essence and are thus able to suddenly govern the four kinds of states.
This is the second example of the conclusion.

[Wenju]: For instance, half of what is called a "human king" and half of what is called a "celestial king" constitute the orthodox treatise on worldly matters; the other half constitutes the transcendental [treatise].
The fact that the beginning and the end of this *Nyāyapraveśa* are interrelated is precisely this meaning.
[Commentary] The Sūtra establishes two designations—human and celestial—for a single person; the intent is to manifest that this treatise applies to both the mundane and the supramundane.
[Commentary] Section Two: The Title of the First Chapter of the "Chapter on the Collection of Merits" (*Sañcaya-parivarta*).
*The Sutra of Golden Light*, Chapter Twelve: "The Chapter on the Collection of Merits.

[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the title; second, the initial explanation of how it is named "Collection of Merits" (*sañcaya*). First, based upon...
This is called "Extensively Gathering the Six Perfections.
[Commentary on the Text] This Wheel-Turning King gathers all wholesome dharmas like a maritime guide; the boundless ocean of goodness is subsumed within the six pāramitās.
[Commentary] The "Guide across the Sea" refers to the shipmaster of the ocean; although the wholesome dharmas are many, they do not exceed these six.
Second, regarding the separate collection of the texts on *dāna* (generosity) and *prajñā* (wisdom), the first explains the inclusion of the six perfections.
[Text] Furthermore, the six perfections are broadly categorized as two, which briefly subsume them: namely, giving (*dāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
[Commentary] Giving can subsume the six, and wisdom can guide the five; because they accomplish the two types of adornment, these two are mentioned.
Second, showing the scriptural text has two parts: first, the actual presentation of the scripture.

[Text]: To take the wish-fulfilling jewel and give it away, or to abandon the four great continents filled with precious treasures as an act of giving, is to accumulate the practice of *dāna* (generosity).
To stand with palms joined and request the Venerable Ratnākara to proclaim and reveal this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is to accumulate the practice of *jñāna* (wisdom).

[Commentary] The Sūtra cites these two examples because their characteristics are profound and vast: [the first] filling the four continents with jewels and offering them all to the Triple Gem, which illustrates the vastness of the undertaking;
[the second] standing with palms joined to hear the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, which illustrates the profundity of the realization of its principles. These two serve as precedents for other practices.

[Text]: Since the wisdom of giving (*dāna-jñāna*) is thus, it is the same for the other dharmas; because they receive their names from practice, this is called the "Chapter on the Well-accumulated" (*Susaṃbhava-parivarta*).
[Commentary]: This king’s mind has greatly accumulated what is good; that his non-contemptuous wisdom regarding giving is profound and vast is evident from the text.
By verifying this, one knows that all other practices he has cultivated are by no means trivial. Furthermore, the chapter is established based on its dual function of *siddhānta*.
[Textual Explanation]: These six perfections are distinct: practicing the first five perfections is the accumulation of merit for the sake of the world (*loka-siddhānta*);
practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is the accumulation of merit for the sake of individuals (*pudgala-siddhānta*);

and all of them as *pāramitās* constitute the accumulation of merit for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-siddhānta*). Because they derive their name from these four types of accumulation, it is called the "Chapter on the Accumulation of Merit" (*Kuśala-saṃcaya-parivarta*).

[Commentary] To summarize, the different enumerations of the six perfections are as follows: the five perfections of the world, when viewed from the perspective of wisdom, pertain to mundane affairs and thus belong to the "benefiting others" [benefit];
wisdom illuminates these five perfections to destroy the evil of grasping at signs and thus belongs to "remedy";

and the realization of the six dharma-realms that transcends all thought reaches the other shore, which is called the "ultimate meaning. This King [the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*] fully assembles these four *siddhāntas*.
Because it is excellent, the title of this chapter is established according to its name. Second, the purpose for its inclusion is explained:
[The *Wenju* states] "This chapter is for the second type of person, the king who propagates the sutra.
While the preceding section clarified how mundane right view moves heaven and earth, this section clarifies how supramundane right view moves the worthy and the holy," and so forth.
[Commentary]: The discourse on governing the state is mundane right view; hearing the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is supramundane, supreme right view.
Hearing of the Buddha’s merits within a dream at night is to move the Sages; seeing the bhikṣu named Ratnāloka is to move the Worthies.
Even those who have entered the stage of "partial realization" (bhūmi) are called "Worthies" when compared to the Buddha. These are the texts of the two sutras.
The second part consists of two sections: first, the analysis of the text; second, the explanation of the meaning.
Regarding the first section, the analysis of the text: [The *Wénjù* states] the text is divided into two parts: first, the address to the Earth Deity; second, the exposition by means of verses.

There are sixty-four and a half lines of verse, which are further divided into two: the first four lines generally clarify the practice of giving (*dāna*) on the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), while the subsequent sixty and a half lines specifically [elaborate upon it].
The *Mingshan ji* (Collection on Clarifying Goodness) is divided into six sections: 1. Six lines and a half clarify the fundamental matter; 2.
Twenty-one lines and a half clarify the request for the Dharma by the Sage King; 3. Thirty-nine lines and a half clarify the Venerable One’s proclamation and dissemination;

4. Forty lines and a half clarify the Universal Monarch’s practice of giving; 5. Fifty-two lines provide a conclusion that correlates the past and present; 6. Sixty lines and a half [conclude the work].
Citing cause and effect as proof and exhortation.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning in two parts: first, addressing the Earth Deity.
At that time, the Tathāgata again spoke to the Earth Deity regarding past causes and conditions, uttering these verses:
[Commentary] The two Buddhas spoke in verse regarding the first two [stages]. First, they generally clarify the practice of *dāna* (giving) on the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).
"In the past, I was once a Cakravartin King; I relinquished the four great continents as well as the great oceans.
Furthermore, at that time, I offered up the four continents filled with precious treasures to the various Buddhas. All that I bestowed was that which I held most dear."
Those who do not see what is pleasing yet fail to renounce it have, throughout countless kalpas of the past, constantly sacrificed their bodies and lives in pursuit of the True Dharma.
[Commentary] Second, specifically clarifying the two types of well-accumulated giving: this refers to the giving of wealth, such as the treasures of the four continents. Please explain this.
This sutra causes immeasurable multitudes to hear the Dharma-giving of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. This section is divided into six parts;
one should explain them according to the text and its meaning. First, it clarifies the fundamental matter.
Furthermore, in the past, incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Ratnottama. That Buddha, the World-Honored One...
After his parinirvāṇa, there was a noble king named Saṃbhava who attained sovereign power over the four continents and ruled as far as the limits of the great ocean.
In that city of his, named Jaladharagarjitasvara, he resided and governed.
One night, while sleeping in a dream, he heard of the Buddha’s merits and beheld a bhikṣu named Ratnākara.
He is well able to proclaim and expound the Tathāgata’s True Dharma, namely this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which is as bright as the midday sun and can illuminate everywhere.
[Commentary] Regarding the power of governing the state: it means that the scope of his transformative influence reaches to the very limits of the ocean. Second, the Illumination.
The Holy King requested the Dharma.
Having dreamed of these matters, the Wheel-Turning King immediately awoke;

with joy pervading his entire body, he departed from the palace and went to the monastery to offer worship and pay respect to the great assembly of noble ones, inquiring of the Venerable Ones within that multitude.
"Is there perhaps a bhikṣu named Ratnākara who has accomplished all merits?
At that time, Ratnākara was sitting motionless within a cave, contemplating with right mindfulness as he recited this *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
Then a certain bhikṣu led the king to his dwelling; having arrived at the place where Ratnākara was, [he found] this Ratnākara...
Therefore, while within the cave, his appearance was extraordinary and his majestic virtue blazed forth;

he then addressed the king, saying, "The one within this cave is the Bhikṣu Ratnākara whom you asked about—the one who can uphold the profound practices of all Buddhas and who is the king of sūtras named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
At that time, King Susaṃmata immediately paid homage to the Bhikṣu Ratnākara and spoke these words:
With a face like the full moon and a majestic splendor blazing forth, I pray that you will expound and proclaim for me this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*,
the king of all sutras.
[Commentary] This was proclaimed by the Venerable Master Sanming.
At that time, the Honored One Ratnāloka immediately accepted the King’s invitation and consented to proclaim this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
Knowing that he was about to preach the Dharma, the devas of the trichiliocosm were all filled with joy.
In a pure, subtle, and pristine place, they filled the ground with various precious jewels and sprinkled it with exquisite, fragrant water, scattering many beautiful flowers.
Pervading that place, the King at that time personally prepared the Dharma-seat, hanging silk banners and canopies, interlacing them with precious ornaments,
and scattering all kinds of subtle, exquisite, and extraordinary powdered incense upon the great and lofty Dharma-throne.
Then all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, mahoragas, kinnaras, and others rained down celestial māndārava flowers from above.
They scattered [flowers] everywhere until the Dharma seat was filled throughout that place;
inconceivable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of immeasurable devas simultaneously came together to assemble at the site where the Dharma was being preached.
At that time, Ratnākara emerged from his cave, and the devas immediately made offerings of sāla flowers, scattering them over the bhikṣu Ratnākara. At that time, Ratnākara...
Having bathed their bodies and donned pure, exquisite garments, they proceeded to the place of the Dharma seat and joined their palms in reverent salutation to this high throne of the Dharma.
Then all the heavenly kings and the various devas rained down *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers, as well as various wonderful blossoms made of many jewels;
and hundreds of thousands of myriad kinds of musical instruments resounded spontaneously in the void without being struck.
The bhikṣu Ratnāloka, a skilled preacher of the Dharma, immediately ascended the high seat and sat cross-legged.
He then brought to mind the inconceivable and immeasurable thousands of billions of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions, who give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings;
as well as King Susaṃmata, who had obtained sovereignty over the entire realm illuminated by one sun and moon—at that time, the preacher of the Dharma [reflected upon these].
He immediately sought out the king to expound and proclaim this wondrous sutra.
[Note] *Cei* (廁) means "mixed" or "filled"; it is a general term for silk fabrics. *Mandāra* is translated as "pleasing to the mind" (*shìyì*);
*mañjūṣaka* is translated as "soft" (*ruǎnrěn*). The old translations are small-white, small-red, and large-red; *bùgǔ* (不鼓) refers to striking with a mallet.

Furthermore, when the Wheel-Turning King practiced giving, at that time the Great King stood with palms joined before the bhikṣu for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Upon hearing the sublime Dharma, he uttered words of praise, saying, "Excellent!
His heart was filled with such profound compassion that tears flowed down his cheeks; yet immediately thereafter, he leapt for joy, his mind overflowing with serene delight.
Desiring to make offerings to this sutra, he then took up the King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels and made a great vow for the sake of all sentient beings:

"May it rain down today throughout this Jambudvīpa immeasurable varieties of rare, extraordinary, and exquisite seven-jeweled treasures, as well as wondrous necklaces; by these causes and conditions, may all immeasurable sentient beings [attain fulfillment]."

All experienced happiness; at that very moment, there fell rains of the seven treasures, various precious ornaments, celestial crowns, earrings, and all kinds of necklaces, as well as sweet delicacies and jeweled seats, filling and pervading the four continents.
Then, King Susaṃcita took these immeasurable seven treasures that filled the four continents and, within the bequeathed Dharma of the Buddha Ratnavijaya...

Nevertheless, when correlating various phrases with these three characters, these three [characters] represent the profound and vast *dharmatā*. When appropriate, one may apply them to other meanings. For example, the phrase "the Buddha’s body is like empty space" is explained by means of the character "empty" (*k'ung*).
