The essence is named *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which is worthy of honor and reverence; it is named "Gold. *Dharmatā* is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, thus it is named "Light.
*Dharmatā* is capable of manifold benefit, thus it is named "Radiance. These three dharmas are non-dual and indistinguishable from one another.

If one points to the events and principles within this chapter—both the phenomenal and the noumenal, the environment and its inhabitants—it is precisely these three that cause the practitioner to penetrate the ultimate meaning (*lakṣya*) without deviation.

Transcending all lateral thought and transcending all discussion, this scripture alone may be named the King of Sutras. Thus we know that its confrontation with the three profundities has a specific purpose;
herein it establishes itself as threefold, first according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
[Commentary on the Text]: Regarding this chapter, as for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, "suvarṇa" (*jin*) signifies the excellent accumulation of the *pāramitās*;
"prabhāsa" (*guang*) signifies the accumulation of the light of *prajñā*, and the accumulation of the radiance of the [other] five *pāramitās*.

[Commentary] Regarding the translation of *pāramitā*: it is called "Reaching the Other Shore" because it is the destination to which one returns; thus, it is translated as "Gold. Because *prajñā* is translated as "Wisdom," it is called "Light.
Because the other five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*) are its practice, they are called "Clarity. This constitutes three pairs—Wisdom, Practice, and Fruit—corresponding to Gold, Light, and Clarity.
Second, this is discussed in terms of the *Ratnakūṭa*.
[Text]: Regarding the discourse on Ratnāloka, he was in a cave; his face was like the light of the full moon;
and his recitation of such a sutra was luminous.
[Commentary]: The "cave" is the place of reliance; "gold" refers to the full moon; that which can illuminate is called "light"; and the recitation is the practice, which is called "luminosity."
This is based on the correspondence between the environment and its inhabitants (*śāsanādhiṣṭhāna*) and the three dharmas.

Regarding the three [types of light], they are discussed in relation to two persons. [The *Wenju* states: "As for the two persons, the one within the cave is the King who was told by the Buddha that he would possess light;
the other is King [Mahāpra]bhāsa, who held a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) and rained down treasures upon the four continents."

[Commentary: One should understand that the "Jewel Darkness" (Ratnāloka) regarding the primary and secondary [receptacle] worlds, and the King's "Rain of Jewels," correspond to the practitioner of the three dharmas;
they are in fact one single *dharmatā* named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. How could radiance ever be separated from gold? How could golden light ever be separated from radiance?
Now, these three names are divided and applied to the primary and secondary worlds, as well as to self and others, and to things, in order to bring about an understanding of the receptacle world.
It does not depart from the correct [nature], nor does it depart from others, nor does it depart from phenomena.
By means of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, taking one is to have all three, and the whole three are one; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, yet lofty and vast.
Every single phenomenon is the ocean of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and every single mind is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). If it were not so, how could it be called the King of Sūtras?
[Commentary] Third, the Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits (13th), Part One: The Title of the Chapter.
*Sūtra of the Golden Light*, Chapter Thirteen: "On Ghosts and Spirits.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the title; second, the formal interpretation of "ghosts and spirits. First, the interpretation of "ghosts" (*preta*).
[Text]: The character for "ghost" (gui) is glossed as "returning" (gui), and it is also said to mean "fear. It is like the *asura*, who possesses much dread;
furthermore, it is said to mean "majesty," in that one causes others to stand in awe of its majesty.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "returning" (guī): the *Shizi* states, "When a person dies, it is called 'returning' (*guī*)," and so forth.
The *Buddha-dhyāna-samādhi-sūtra* says that when the Asuras were at war with the Lord of Devas, wheels of blades descended from the sky;
as the bodies and limbs of the Asura host fell, they became terrified and hid themselves within lotus fibers. If one follows the secular interpretation, Zheng Xuan says: "The Sage..."
The refined vital energy (*jingqi*) of humans is called "spirit" (*shen*); the refined vital energy of the wise and virtuous is called "ghost" (*gui*).
The *Liji* states: "In the realm of clarity there are ritual and music; in the realm of mystery there are ghosts and spirits. This is the second explanation of "spirit."
[Text]: "The divine" refers to capability. Those of great power can move mountains and fill the seas; those of lesser power can manifest concealment and transformation.
[Commentary]: These two points correspond to the title and the chapter heading above.
[Commentary on the Title] This chapter lists universally all the devas, nāgas, oceans, rivers, suns, moons, and various deities;

since the title "Heavenly Deities" has already been established at the beginning, there is no need to repeat it here. Although it universally lists beings from all realms, the text concerning ghosts and spirits is more extensive, and thus this is used as the title for the chapter.
[Commentary] Second, the purpose for which this chapter appears.
[Text] This chapter is the third, in which all devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits,
and terrestrial deities collectively take an oath to propagate and proclaim [the teaching] extensively and universally, thereby encouraging its circulation.
[Commentary] The two sūtra texts are divided into two parts at the beginning.

[Wenju] The text consists of two parts: first, the prose (gadya), and second, the verse (śloka). Within the prose, there is first the presentation of specific instances, followed by the complete offering.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts: first, the prose section; second, the commentary. First, the listing; second, the explanation. First, citing specific instances.

The Buddha told Puṇyavatī: "If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to provide inconceivable and wondrous offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, and who wish to know the three..."
The profound sphere of practice of all Buddhas in the world.
[Commentary on the Text] As for the distinctions of phenomena: the Buddha who arises from compassion and accepts offerings is the *Nirmāṇakāya* (Response-Buddha).
The Buddha who arises from the *Tathatā* (Suchness) and whose awakened wisdom merges with that Suchness is the *Sambhogakāya* (Retribution-Buddha). All dharmas are entirely...
"The sphere of activity of all Buddhas" refers to the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*). Those who interpret it in this way [view] the three Buddhas as distinct;
if one practices ritual offerings, the offerings likewise differ.

[Commentary: Regarding "the Buddha [arising from] equality," etc.: after the fruit [of enlightenment], the Dharma-body manifests through the permeation of compassion to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings; this is...

The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) Buddha, which accords with the capacities of sentient beings, arises from Original Enlightenment; when the wisdom of Initial Enlightenment merges with the Original Suchness, it is called the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) Buddha—this is Initial Enlightenment.
All dharmas are fundamentally the sphere traversed by all Buddhas, which is the Dharma Body (dharmakāya) Buddha—this is Original Enlightenment.
As for the distinct enumeration of these three bodies: they correspond to the two natures of cultivation and the one nature that can give rise to them.
That which arises can manifest that which is manifested; because these are distinct and separate, the four types of offerings are differentiated. The four types of offerings consist of:

(1) the offering of material requisites, which sustains the *saṃbhogabuddha* (Buddha of Enjoyment) and his myriad practices and merits; (2) the offering of the wisdom that accords with principle, which manifests the *dharmabuddha* (Dharma-Buddha);

and (3) the offering that sustains and manifests both [the former two], which constitutes the meaning of making offerings to all three Buddhas. Since the three Buddhas are distinct, the three types of offerings are also distinct. Second, the Perfect [Teaching].
One should make offerings. Such a person ought, with a resolute and sincere mind, wherever this sutra circulates— whether in cities, towns, villages, houses, or secluded places—
to listen to this subtle and wondrous scripture with right mindfulness, undisturbed and with a focused heart.
[Text] Regarding "perfect offering": encouraging others to listen to the sutras and listening to the sutras oneself is the offering of the Dharma, which is the foremost among all offerings.

As for the foremost offering: it is the offering to all Buddhas. The Buddha taught that the written words are the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Buddha), that which expresses them is the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Buddha), and that which is expressed is the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Buddha). To revere the written words is thus to revere these three [bodies].
The Buddha is also one who reveres the Buddhas of the three periods of time, for all Buddhas are born from this [Dharma].
Thus, to make offerings to the written words is to make offerings to all Buddhas, and so forth.

[Commentary] Previously, there was the principle and wisdom (li-zhi), which were disparaged as being "phenomenal" (shi) because they were treated in a fragmented or distinct manner; now, through the act of listening to the sutras, these are integrated.

Therefore, he was praised as the foremost in making offerings according to the Dharma. This inconceivable offering consists in the realization that the listener and the object of listening are non-dual;
thus, within the mere words, one fully realizes the three bodies (*trikāya*). The ability to expound them is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*);
the means of expression is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*) as the recompense body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and that which is expressed is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). It is not otherwise.
If one explains the new *I-dan-lun* (Īśvarapratyabhijñā-kārikā) in terms of subject and object, how could it manifest the Perfect Buddha and the Perfect Offering?

If the text were not the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*), how could it give rise to the heart of reverence held by all Buddhas? If it were not secret and wondrous, how could it perform the perfect offering to the Buddhas of the three periods of time?
The note "and so forth" (*yunyun*) means that one should explain it as previously interpreted. Second, the narration of the repeated hearing.
The second part first presents the heading, which refers to four vows and one exhortation.
[Wenju] Furthermore, at another time, hearing this again, he recorded it anew; in the prose section, he cites the four vows and desires as a single exhortation.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation: first, it sets forth four kinds of vows and desires.

[Text] If one wishes to know the sphere of the Buddha’s activity—wherein "sphere" refers to the Dharma-Buddha, which is the realm of suchness—and wishes to know this, it is the Retribution-Buddha, which is the wisdom of suchness.
That which can hear this sutra is the Sutra of Letters, which consists of written characters.
The name is itself the responsive Buddha; one who can listen and accord with the Buddha’s teaching performs the offering of Dharma.
The offering of Dharma is the sublime offering.
[Commentary] Question: The sutra shows that the practitioner wishes to use sublime requisites to make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods and to know other Buddhas. How is this so?
Question: Why does the Great Master, in his profound practice, use the character "know" (知) to signify that which the Buddha knows?

Is it because these two [the knower and the known] must manifest forms, such that the three bodies (trikāya) all belong to the practitioner? If the cause thus conflates with the fruit, the meaning of making offerings becomes distorted.

How can this interpretation, which contradicts the sūtras, be taken as authoritative? Answer: The previous selection distinguished the specific matters; now, let us rectify this misconception according to the sūtras.

If you wish to know: is it not the case that the profound sphere of practice of the practitioner is precisely the Dharma-body? Since it is the Dharma-body, how could the mind capable of knowing it not be the Reward Buddha?

As for the manifestation of letters, these too are but the mind. If the sentient being and the Buddha were categorically distinct and the subject and object were eternally different, this would belong to the Hinayana teachings;
how could it have any relation to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*)? Now, let us explain the four vows according to the Perfect Teaching. If...

To be deluded regarding the fact that the three bodies of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are simultaneously present within a single kṣaṇa of the dharma-realm, and to suddenly manifest a subtle understanding of the six sense-objects—this so-called "inconceivable" [view] is precisely in contradiction with the sūtras.
Second, it clarifies that a single matter fulfills the four [aspects].
[Text]: Listening to the sutras can give rise to awakening-wisdom; because awakening-wisdom arises, it is equivalent to the Buddha receiving offerings.
This single matter of listening to the sutras fulfills all vows and desires; it is the fulfillment of all distinct matters through the perfection of this one matter.

[Commentary]: The awakened wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods constitutes their life-force. Because they share the same mind-nature as sentient beings, yet lack the cultivation of habitual practice, they do not accept offerings;
thus, while the lifespan of the Buddhas does not perish, it is said to "perish" by way of concealment.
Now, because one listens to the sutras as an act of making offerings, this constitutes receiving offerings from the Buddhas, whereby their lifespan is such that it is not born.
One should understand that what arises is the manifestation of birth; practitioners should realize that there is no difference between the birth of sentient beings and the Buddha.

When wisdom arises through hearing the sutras, it is the manifestation of all Buddhas, because all Tathāgatas share the same wisdom. Thus, the Buddha of partial truth in the stage of contemplative practice and the ultimate Buddha are non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, one realizes that the arising of wisdom is the arising of the three Buddhas, which is the arising of the One.

Thus, the three [aspects] are neither vertical nor horizontal; this is precisely because one wishes to make offerings to and seek to know the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and by merely listening to the sutra, all four vows are fulfilled.
The second part consists of two verses, which are divided into two sections.

[Text] The verse consists of one hundred two lines and a half, divided into six parts: 1. From "If you wish to make offerings" (*yadi pūjayitukāmaḥ*) below, there are eleven lines of verse which summarize the preceding prose;
this is an exhortation to practice by means of citing the perfect and wondrous [Dharma]. 2.
From "Wherever one goes" (*yatra yatra gacchati*) below, there are three and a half lines which cite that listening to the sutra can ward off calamities; this is an exhortation to practice.
3. From "From the place of preaching the Dharma" down to the sixth line, he cites the miraculous omens resulting from listening to the sutra to encourage practice. 4.
From "The majestic power and physical appearance" down to the fifth and a half lines, he cites the efficacy possessed by merely listening to the sutra to encourage practice.
5. From "Mahābrahmādeva" down to the forty-nine and a half lines, he cites how listening to the sutra can bring forth devas and nāgas.
The spirits and deities encourage the cultivation [of the Dharma] by following the six types of assemblies;
the twenty-seven lines and a half below this illustrate how merely listening to the sutra can bring peace and happiness to the land, thus encouraging cultivation, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the second section, the explanation of the six categories follows the divisions as listed in the text. In the first verse, the prose above merely states that one may listen to the sutra;
this is an exhortation to practice by citing the perfect and subtle [Dharma].
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"If one wishes to make offerings to all Buddhas and desires to know the sphere of practice of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should go to those cities, towns, and villages where this sutra is found.
With a sincere heart, listen to and receive this wondrous and inconceivable scripture."
This ocean of merit is immeasurable and boundless; it enables all sentient beings to attain liberation and cross over the great ocean of suffering and existence.
This sutra is profound and excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, such that no analogy can be found to compare it.
Even if one were to take all the sands of the Ganges, the dust of the great earth, the waters of all oceans, and all the mountains—such things as these—[they could not serve as a comparison].
It cannot be used as a mere analogy; for if one enters this sutra, one enters the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Abiding within that profound *dharmatā*, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni, within this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, having been born among gods and humans throughout inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas and constantly experiencing happiness, precisely because of being able to believe in, understand, and listen to this sutra.
Thus, one has already attained this immeasurable and inconceivable accumulation of merit and virtue.
[Commentary] If one enters this sutra, even a single word within it possesses three aspects: namely, teaching (*śāsana*), practice (*pratipatti*), and principle (*naya*).
To be able to comprehend these three is called the "wondrous Threefold Dharma," which is what is meant by "entering this sutra. Otherwise, how could one enter it?

The sutra states that upon entering the Dharma-nature, one enters a Dharma-nature that is immeasurable and profoundly deep; being endowed with these three meanings, it is named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Abiding therein is called "Thusness" (*tathatā*). One then beholds the wondrous essence of the Three Bodies of Śākyamuni.

It must be discussed that through the practice of contemplation, one reaches a stage resembling True Suchness (*samyaktva-nyāma*) and enters the sutra to see the Buddha. Second, by listening to the sutra, one is immediately able to dispel [obstacles].
One should be encouraged to practice by means of [avoiding] calamities.

Wherever one may go—whether it be across a hundred *yojanas* filled with raging fire, or into a village, a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), or a place of Dharma assembly—one should pass through them with a sincere mind to listen to and receive this sutra;
for by listening to this sutra, evil dreams and malevolent sorcery [shall cease].
All anomalies of the five planets and various lunar mansions, calamities, and all evil matters shall be extinguished without remainder.
[Commentary] As for "those who practice sorcery," the Four Heavenly Kings dispatch a deity named Mili-tou-qian-jia-tuo;
in the Chinese language, this means "Lord of Good Deeds," who is the master over sorcery and poison.
[Commentary]: Even if one must pass through a hundred *yojanas* filled with blazing fire, one should sacrifice one's body for the sake of the Dharma.
Third, it cites three instances where listening to the sutras brought about spiritual miracles to encourage practice.
At the place where the Dharma is preached, upon a lotus throne, this sutra is expounded, transcribed, read, and recited.
When the speaker of the Dharma descends from the Dharma seat, the great assembly still perceives them sitting there;
thus, they may see either the Buddha, the World-Honored One, or the physical forms of a Buddha, a Bodhisattva—such as Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī, or the Great Being Maitreya.
Having seen these various phenomena, including all manner of images, they immediately vanish away, becoming no different than before;
having accomplished such meritorious virtues, they are praised by all the Buddhas.
[Commentary] In the sutra, Mañjuśrī is called Wondrous Virtue (Miaode) and Maitreya is called Benevolent One (Cishi).
Fourth, it is stated that listening to this sutra possesses great power to encourage cultivation.
Its majestic virtue and appearance are immeasurable and boundless; it has a great reputation and can repel enemies and bandits from other regions.
It can cause those who are fierce, courageous, and powerful to retreat and disperse; it can shatter formidable enemies and pacify nightmares that afflict the mind.
Such evil matters as these are all entirely extinguished. If one enters into battle, one will always be victorious over others, and one's fame will spread throughout Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, one will be able to subdue all adversaries, remain far removed from all evils, and cultivate all forms of goodness.
Entering the battle array, one attains victory and the mind is always joyful.

[Commentary] Regarding "courageous and fierce" (*vīrya*), the *Shuowen* states it means having great strength. Fifth, he exhorts practice by stating that listening to this sutra can summon devas, nāgas, spirits, and deities.
The Great Brahmā King, the Thirty-three Gods, the Four World-Protecting Kings, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada,
the various kings of ghosts and spirits, the General Saṃjñeya, the Cānāṅga spirits, the Kiṃnaras, the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Sāgara,
the Asura King, the Garuḍa King, the Great Eloquence Deva, the Goddess Puṇyavatī, and other such leaders.
The various devas and others should always make offerings to those who listen to this Dharma, conceiving of them as stupas of the inconceivable Dharma.
Sentient beings who see them shall revere them with joy. The various heavenly kings and others shall likewise reflect and say to one another:
"May these sentient beings fully accomplish immeasurable majestic virtue; if they can come to this assembly of the Dharma..."

Such a person accomplishes the highest roots of goodness; because they hear this profound sūtra, they adorn themselves and go to the place of the Dharma assembly, giving rise to inconceivable right faith, making offerings, and reverencing the unsurpassed Dharma-stūpa.
Possessing such great compassion, they benefit sentient beings; they are vessels for immeasurable and profound Dharma-treasures, capable of entering the very deep.
Because they have listened to this sutra with a pure mind, such persons have already made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas of the past.
By virtue of these roots of goodness and immeasurable causes and conditions, they should listen to and receive this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Such sentient beings are always protected by immeasurable deva kings.
The Four Great Kings who protect the world through their merit of great eloquence, immeasurable spirits, and all the *rishi*s,
diligently and day and night protect the four directions so that there may be no calamities and one may forever be free from all suffering;
as well as Śakra-devānām-indra, the gods of the sun and moon, King Yama, the various deities of wind and water, the deity Vaiśravaṇa, Viṣṇu, and the deity Mahābhadra.
Furthermore, Maheśvara, Agni, and other deities of great power and valor who constantly protect the world day and night without ceasing;
the great powerful ghost-kings such as Nārāyaṇa; the twenty-eight classes of ghosts and spirits headed by Vaiśravaṇa;
and hundreds of thousands of spirits with supernormal powers and great strength—may they all provide protection for these [beings], ensuring they are free from fear.
The Great Ghost King Vajrapāṇi Guhyaka and his retinue of five hundred followers—
all of whom are great bodhisattvas— likewise provide protection for all who hear this sutra;
as do the Great Ghost King Maṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Kumbhīra, Āḷavaka, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, and the Great Deity Yellow-Head.
Each of these deities has five hundred retinues of spirits and ghosts who also constantly protect those who listen to this sutra:
the Asura King Citrasena, the Gandharva, the Nara, the Rāja, the Kiṇa, the Sāmba,
the Maṇicandra, the Niyantra, the Lord of Rain, the Great Deity of Food and Drink, and Mahākāla.
The deity Suvarṇakeśī, the yakṣa Pañcika, the kumbhāṇḍas Carubhraja and Mahātejas,
the devī Pāñcālī, Dharmabhadra, Makara-bhraja, the sūciloma yakṣa, Śūramgama, Mahāpāñca,
and Skandha-cāmara-śakti, as well as other great deities.
Śarabhadri, Haimavata, Sātāgiri, Dhr̥ti, Vibhūti, Āgata, Cīra, Magha, Aṅgulimāla, and other such deities—
all possessing immeasurable supernormal powers and great strength—
constantly and diligently protect those who listen to and receive this subtle and wondrous sutra; as do the dragon Anavatapta and the Dragon King Sāgara.
King Mucilinda, King Elāpattra, the Nanda Dragon King, the Upananda Dragon King, and hundreds of thousands of other dragon kings such as these,
possessing great supernormal powers, constantly come to protect those who listen to this sutra,
never leaving them by day or night; as do the Asura Kings Pāriyātra, Rāhu, Vemacitra, and Maṇicūḍa, son of Śambara.
Pāhali, Vikarāla, Khaṇḍa, and Gandha— all these are asura kings who possess great supernatural power and constantly come to protect those who hear this sutra,
never leaving them by day or night. Hārītī, the Mother of Ghosts,
and her five hundred spirits also constantly come to protect those who hear this sutra, whether they are asleep or awake.
The great female spirits Candā and Caṇḍālī, Kūṣmāṇḍī, and others who devour the vital essence of humans—
all such deities possess great power and constantly strive to protect those in the worlds of the ten directions who uphold this sutra.

Furthermore, the Great Eloquence Goddess (Mahāpratisarā), immeasurable goddesses, and Guṇakārandavatī, each with their retinues, as well as the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā, [shall likewise provide protection].
The great deity of the planted groves and fruits, and all such deities as these, with hearts full of joy, shall all come to protect those who love, delight in, and draw near to this sutra.
[Commentary] The text has two parts; the first is the translation of the manifest text, beginning from "Maheśvara" onwards.
[Text] Maheśvara is translated in other sūtras as "Lord of Heaven" (Tiān Zìzài); in the *Guǎngdìng jīng*, it is translated as "Majestic and Spiritual Sovereign" (Wéilíng Dì);
Maṇibhadra is translated as "Majestically Subduing Conduct" (Wēifú Xíng); Puṇyabhadra is translated as "Accumulated and Perfected" (Jízhì Chéng);
Kiṃpila is translated as "Majestic Like a King" (Wēirú Wáng); Piṇḍola-bharadvāja is translated as "Established Immovable Cart" (Lì Bùdòng Chē).
*Rāva* is translated as "endurance" (*kṣānti*) which brings liberation; *Dharmavara* is translated as "King of Learning";
*Maghavara* is translated as "removing crookedness of mind"; *Śūramitra* is translated as "meritorious activity";
*Kṣemaśreṣṭha* is translated as "harmonious and peaceful sword"; *Viśamati* is translated as "subduing the various faculties"; *Śrāmiti* is translated as... [text truncated].
Ekāgra-ramaṇa is translated as "Delighting in Solitude"; Haimavata is translated as "Lord of the House"; Śatarkṣi is translated as "Great Power Deva";
Bali-rāhu is translated as "Valiant Progression"; Vemacitra is translated as "High and Remote"; Śyāmali-putra is translated as "Heroic Virtue";
Prahlāda-putra is translated as "Majestic Splendor"; and Khara-karṇaka is translated as [the corresponding Chinese term].
*Hūṃ-rava* (Roars like Thunder) is *Kaurava-danti*, translated as "Unconquerable in Battle.
[Commentary: In the sutras, Yama-rāja or Yama-raśa is translated here as "The Twin Kings" (*yamau* means twins; *raśa* means king).
Both the elder brother and the younger sister serve as lords of hell; the elder brother governs the affairs of men, while the younger sister governs those of women.
The *śakrābhilagna* (Double-King) is so called because it experiences both suffering and pleasure simultaneously;
it is also termed *yugma-nārāyaṇa*, which means "the Twin Nārāyaṇas" or "the Hook-and-Chain Wrestlers. *Nanda* means "Joy," and *Upananda* means "Virtuous Joy";

these two brothers are dragons who bring joy to people by sending wind and rain according to the proper seasons. "Virtuous" (*bhadra*) refers to their nature being noble and excellent. *Vemacitra*... [text fragment]
This is frequently referred to as the *Jìngxīn zhèngfǎ niàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Mind of Purity and Right Dharma Mindfulness), translated as *Xiǎnggāo*.
It is also called *Xuējū*; the correct term is *Vemacitra*, which means "Variegated Painting" (*qǐhuà*) or "Jeweled Ornament" (*bǎoshì*).
He was the father of Śakrādevī, the wife of Śakra; his name was Kharaskandha, meaning "Broad Hips. Second, the second section provides an explanation of the first part.

[Text]: "To escape the cause" means to escape the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). "To escape the fruit" means to escape the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). "To deliver beings from all states of existence" means to escape the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "escaping the cause" and so forth, the first section of the text states that [the Buddha] is able to cause all sentient beings to attain liberation and cross over [to the other shore].

Having measured the great ocean of all existences (*bhava*) as suffering, it is said that for all sentient beings to attain liberation and cross over the ocean of existences, they must be freed from the three obstructions both within and outside the realms;
therefore, by correlating cause and effect with karmic retribution across all existences, [the afflictions] arising from delusion are termed "defilements" (*kleśa*).
Sixth, citing the *Ji-tīng jīng* (Sutra on Hearing Only), it states that this can bring peace to the land.
One should take joy in this to encourage its cultivation.
For all sentient beings, it increases lifespan, physical form, strength, merit, majesty, and the adornment of one's appearance beyond the ordinary;

it can completely extinguish without remainder all calamities and anomalies caused by the transformations of the five planets and various lunar mansions; and it eliminates nightmares during sleep so that upon waking, one is no longer distressed.
All such evil things are completely extinguished. By the power of this profound sutra and the great majestic influence of the Earth Deity, its flavor is transformed;

throughout this great earth down to the adamantine base—a thickness of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas—there is no savory essence that does not pervade it all, causing it to well up and benefit sentient beings through the power of this sutra.
It causes the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) to emerge entirely above the ground to a thickness of one hundred *yojanas*.

It also enables the various devas to obtain abundant vital energy, such that their physical strength is replenished and they experience joy and happiness. All the deities within Jambudvīpa give rise to joy in their hearts and receive immeasurable bliss.
By the power of this sutra, the devas rejoice, and the hundred grains and all fruits flourish and grow luxuriantly.
In the gardens and groves, flowers were in full bloom, their fragrant scents overflowing and pervading everywhere;
the grasses and trees grew upright and straight, their forms supple and free from any crookedness.
Within Jambudvīpa, there were immeasurable and inconceivable numbers of nāga girls, who, filled with joy, leaped for delight in every place.
He adorns the lotus pond with various kinds of flowers—blue utpala, red padma, yellow kumuda, and white puṇḍarīka lotuses.
Within his own palace, he dispels all clouds and mists so that the sky is free from dust and obscuration;
the quarters are clear, pure, and bright, as the sun-king blazes forth with a thousand rays of light.
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, they illuminate all darkness and obscurations. With Jāmbūnada gold as their palace, they dwell therein with immeasurable majesty and virtue.
Because the Sun Deity and the Moon Deity have heard this sutra, their vital essence becomes full and robust;
thus the Sun Deity emerges over Jambudvīpa, giving rise to a heart of joy and emitting immeasurable light and networks of radiance.
Illuminating all directions, at the very moment of emergence, he radiates great nets of light that cause the various lotuses in the ponds to bloom.
Within Jambudvīpa, immeasurable fruits ripen in their proper seasons, satisfying all sentient beings.

At that time, the sun and moon shine forth, and the superior constellations move in their courses without failing their appointed measures; wind and rain arrive according to the seasons, bringing abundant and flourishing harvests.
Abounding in wealth and treasures, with nothing lacking, wherever this subtle and wondrous *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* is circulated,
recited, or expounded, that land and its realm shall immediately obtain the increase of the immeasurable merits as described above.
[Commentary] Regarding the four lines following "the *utpala* lotus": there are four colors of lotuses;
the *utpala* is blue, the *padma* is red, the *kumuda* is yellow, and the *puṇḍarīka* is white.
[Commentary] Section Four: The Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies (授記品). First, the title of the chapter:
*The Scripture of Golden Light, Chapter Fourteen:

Bestowing Prophecies*. [Commentary] The text is divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation, which has five sub-sections. First, it clarifies that the present [teaching] constitutes two types.
[Text]: "There are four kinds of *vyākaraṇa* (prophecies); these are now two kinds," and so forth. [Commentary]:
Regarding the four kinds of prophecy, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states that the Buddha told Jianyi (Dṛḍhamati): "There are four kinds of prophecy:

first, the prophecy for those who have not yet resolved their minds [for enlightenment], or those who, though wandering through the six realms, are born among humans and take delight in the Buddha..."
The Dharma states that after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one shall resolve to attain enlightenment;

after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one shall practice the bodhisattva path, and even making offerings to Buddhas and transforming sentient beings—all of these shall pass through such kalpas before one attains Bodhi.
When these two types of persons first resolve their minds and receive a prediction, it is because they have planted various roots of goodness over long kalpas and have delighted in them.
Because human beings and dharmas possess a heart of compassion, upon generating the resolve [for enlightenment], they immediately abide on the stage of non-retrogression;

therefore, the bestowal of predictions and the three mysteries of the prediction are as follows: there are bodhisattvas who, though not yet having received a prediction, practice the six perfections until their merit is perfected.
Then the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings all think: "At what time shall this bodhisattva attain Bodhi? What will his kalpa, land, and disciples be like?"
Regarding the number of his followers, the Buddha severed this doubt by immediately bestowing a prediction (vyākaraṇa) upon him;
while the entire assembly was aware of it, this bodhisattva alone did not know. The "prediction bestowed publicly in the midst of the great assembly" refers to the two types of predictions:

the prediction bestowed immediately upon the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the prediction regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Second, [this section] concerns the instruction.
Explaining these two characters:
[Wenqu] states that "bestowing" (shou) means to give, and "recording" (ji) means to record the events of attaining enlightenment.
[Ji] explains that it refers to the person recorded by the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā).
[Text]: Herein, because the three Great Beings and ten thousand devas are granted the matter of attaining Buddhahood in the future, it is called "bestowing a prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*).
[Commentary]:
This is the fourth explanation of the different names for the prediction.
[Text]: It is also called "bestowing prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) and "bestowing determination" (*niyāma*). Bestowing the number of eons and the extent of the lands is called "prediction";
being thorough, real, and not false is called "determination.
[Commentary]: The fifth clarifies that it is bestowing, not receiving.
[Text]: "That which is bestowed by the Buddha is called 'bestowal' (授); that which is received from him is called 'reception' (受).
Herein, because it is bestowed by the Buddha, it is termed 'prediction' (授記).
[Commentary]: Second, the purpose [of this section].

[Text] This is the fourth point within the section on circulation (prabhāvanā): by citing the causes of his past practice of the sutra, it establishes the realization of the fruit of ultimate perfection;
thus, it demonstrates that the propagation and protection [of the Dharma] is not in vain, thereby exhorting its circulation.
[Commentary]: In the past, when the *Jingxing* (Recitation of the Sūtra) was being performed, the Honored King Golden Dragon praised the Buddha and made a vow, thereby performing the recitation;

ten thousand parched fish heard the Dharma and practiced through its influence, thereby performing the recitation. This served as the cause for their future destiny—just as "will" (*jiang*) implies what is yet to come—they have now obtained the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) that they shall become Buddhas in the future.
This is the verification seen today: whether one personally propagates the sūtra or acts as its external protector.
"Having long since obtained the prediction of Buddhahood, it is not in vain. This section of the two sutras is divided into two parts.
[Wenju] The text consists of two sections: first, the granting of predictions; second, the resolution of doubts regarding those predictions. The granting of predictions is further divided into two:

first, the granting of predictions to the three great bodhisattvas; second, the granting of predictions to ten thousand devas. The granting of predictions to the three great bodhisattvas is again divided into two: first, the assembly of those with common conditions.
Second, the actual bestowing of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

[Commentary: Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts: first, the bestowing of the prediction; second, the bestowing of the prediction upon the three types of Great Beings (*mahāsattva*). First, the assembly of those with common conditions.
At that time, as the Tathāgata was about to bestow the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon this Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa and his two sons,
Rajalakṣaṇa and Prabhāsa, there were ten thousand devaputras, headed by Tejodhipati,
who together came from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to the place where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew.
He sat to one side.

[Commentary: Regarding the past, some versions do not mention that they shared the same object of focus as this sutra, or perhaps they refer to another sutra. Second, the formal bestowing of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa: "In a future age, after immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis..."
After incalculable hundreds of millions of nayuta kalpas, in the world-realm Suvarṇaprabhāsa,
he shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and receive the name Suvarṇaratnacchatraśikhara-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, and so forth.

After this Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, and when both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have completely vanished, his eldest son, Rajata-rāja (Silver King), shall succeed him as the next Buddha in that world-system.
At that time, the world shall be renamed Śuddhadhvaja (Pure Banner).
He shall be known as Jambūnada-kanaka-dhvaja-prabhāsa-saṃdarśana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara... [the rest of the epithets follow].
The Superior Being, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—
after this Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have completely vanished— the younger son, Silver Light, shall next succeed him to the position of Buddha.
The name of the world shall be no different from before, and the Buddha’s title shall be the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Golden Radiance.

[He is] the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
[Commentary on the Text: Regarding the world being renamed "Pure Banner" (Vimaladhvaja), one should discuss it through four propositions; this is one of them.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the world changes its name to "Pure Banner" (Vimaladhvaja), one should discuss this in terms of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. The land changes its name while the name [of the Buddha] does not;
this refers to the case where it is named "Pure Banner. 2. The land changes its name while the name [of the Buddha] does not change;

for example, although Śākyamuni of the past took up the land and named it "Sahā," the present Śākyamuni is also named "Sahā. 3. Both the land and the name change; as in the case of Avalokiteśvara’s succession [to the position].

In the four lands where Amitābha resides, the names do not change; as it is now, in the world where the Buddha Radiant Silver Light Adorns the Golden Banner resides, the names of the world remain as they were, without difference.
Among these, the first [item] is likely an error and should be combined with the second.
Second, the prediction for twenty thousand devaputras. Part One: Sectioning the Text.
[Text] The "Ten Thousand Predictions" further consists of two parts: first, generating understanding upon hearing the sutra; second, the actual conferring of predictions.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the meaning, there are two points. First, generating understanding upon hearing the sutra: this may be a semblance-understanding (sādharmya-bodha) or a partial-truth-understanding (bhūta-eka-deśa-bodha), as the sutra provides no fixed judgment; therefore, one must proceed with circumspection.
When these ten thousand devaputras heard that the three great beings had received their predictions of enlightenment and further heard this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*,
they rejoiced and gave rise to a heart of profound reverence. Their minds were free from defilement and burden, as pure as lapis lazuli,
and as clear, unobstructed, and vast as space.

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "the mind free from defilement and entanglement" is explained as follows in the *Shiyi shu* (Commentary on Resolving Doubts). Second, the actual bestowing of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).

At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of these ten thousand devaputras had matured, immediately bestowed upon them the prediction for the path to Bodhi, saying:
"O devaputras, in a future age, after incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas..."
In a future eon, he shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this world;
they shall belong to the same family, the same clan, and the same name, being called the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, named Nīlanetra-utpala-gandha-kūṭa.
In this manner, ten thousand Buddhas appeared successively in the world of the Buddha-Bhagavān.
[Text] ... [Commentary] Since it is stated that there is no other name for this world, it is simply called Sahā; this is...

Regarding the phrase "the earth changes its name" and "does not change," the note says "and so forth," which means it should be explained as previously stated. Second, the *Yiji* (Notes on Doubts) has two parts;
first, the division of the text. [Wenju]:
From "At that time, at the site of enlightenment" onwards is the second section on resolving doubts, which is further divided into two: first, the question, and second, the Buddha's response.
Answer.
[Commentary] Regarding the two explanations of the meaning, first is the question:
At that time, the Bodhi-tree goddess of the site of enlightenment named Samantavardhanī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, these ten thousand..."
"World-Honored One, these sons of heaven have gathered here in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for the sake of hearing the Dharma;

why has the Tathāgata now bestowed predictions upon them? World-Honored One, I have never heard that these sons of heaven have fully cultivated the six pāramitās, nor have I ever heard that they have relinquished their hands, feet, heads, eyes, marrow, brains, nor their beloved wives, children, wealth, treasures, grain, and silks."
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearls, coral, conch shells, jade, sweet delicacies, food and drink, clothing, bedding,
medicine for the sick and infirm, elephants, horses, carriages, palaces, houses, gardens, groves, springs, ponds, slaves, and servants—
just as other immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas provide various necessities of life as offerings.
Having rendered respectful offerings to the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones of the past, such bodhisattvas shall likewise, in future ages, relinquish immeasurable things held dear—
heads, eyes, marrow, and brains, as well as beloved wives and children, wealth, treasures, grain, silk, and even servants— and shall successively practice and achieve full perfection.
Having fulfilled the six *pāramitās* and completed the cultivation of ascetic practices throughout immeasurable and boundless kalpas, one only then receives the prediction of *bodhi*.

World-Honored One, for what cause and by what condition have these sons of heaven cultivated such supreme and wondrous roots of goodness that, having come from that celestial realm, they were able to hear the Dharma briefly and immediately receive their prediction? I pray that you will explain this.
"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me and sever the net of my doubts.
[Commentary] The text has three parts; first, the shallow practice is used to record the profound.
[Wenju] As for "doubt": shifting mountains and filling the sea is not the work of a single day; the ultimate fruit of Bodhi is accumulated through long-term practice.

Just as one who has recently ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and descended for but a brief moment does not experience the fatigue of long-term listening, and yet hears of inconceivable deeds from the past—
wherein the practice was shallow yet the record profound— one consequently harbors doubt.
[Commentary] The second point concerns doubt regarding the provisional in relation to the real.
[Text]: As for "other bodhisattvas," this refers to those who practice the six perfections. Drawing a cone to point at the earth, there is no place where they do not sacrifice their bodies and lives.

Through the precepts, patience, meditation, and wisdom, they fulfill the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. If one follows the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), entering emptiness from the conventional, their cultivation does not end in a single lifetime;

entering the conventional from emptiness, their movement exceeds as many eons as there are motes of dust. If one follows the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), they proceed directly...

If one practices a single course of action for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, how much more so when practicing all courses of action in their entirety—their measure being incalculable—and yet fail to receive a prediction [of enlightenment];
whereas by hearing this sutra for but a short time, one obtains such a resolution.
[Commentary] "Drawing a cone to point at the ground" means there is not even ground enough to accommodate a cone; it refers to a place where one does not abandon body and life.

"Entering emptiness from the conventional is not limited to a single lifetime" means that according to the *Bodhisattva Shengdi Jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Bodhisattva), one cultivates the six perfections over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
"Direct practice," etc., refers to the characteristics of the gradual and sequential progression through each stage. Third.

The arising of the light of the *dharmatā* is the cause of the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is the stainless mind; its arising from the gold of the *dharmatā* is the cause of the *dharmakāya*, which is the empty mind.
This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is non-dual and indistinguishable from these three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Taking these three virtues as the foundation, it is adorned with immeasurable merits—whether appearing as semblances or as the real—and thus manifests these three virtues. Therefore:

Such is the nature of the benefit of hearing the sutra as the Tathāgata bestows the prediction of fruition (*vyākaraṇa*). Regarding the causes and conditions of the four fingers, both past and present:
[Commentary] "Cultivating according to characteristics" means that one cultivates the currently active practices in accordance with the true reality (*dharmatā*); therein lies wondrous goodness.
"Roots" (mūla) refers to distant conditions (*dūra-pratyaya*). One plants roots of goodness by means of the true reality of distant conditions.
[Commentary] Since all sūtras concern causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), how could one obtain a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) upon hearing [the teaching] once without causes and conditions?

This is a general indication that there are wondrous roots of goodness; it specifically indicates distant causes and conditions in accordance with the characteristics [of practice], and specifically indicates present causes and conditions. Thus, it speaks of "causes."
"Condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to resonance and response. It may arise from internal mind or external teachings acting as causes and conditions.
Why is this so? The following explains the causes and conditions for its manifestation: "Practice in accordance with the true reality" means taking the ten modes of contemplation as one's practice.

The "inconceivable realm" is termed "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Taking this very realm as the contemplation, and this contemplation conforming to the realm, is called "following the characteristics."
Cultivation is not the intended meaning of our present school; this phrase cannot be dismissed. However, regarding these ten contemplations, there are three levels of capacity:

those of superior capacity employ one contemplation; those of middling capacity employ from the second to the seventh; and those of inferior capacity employ all ten. Now, when the ten thousand deva-sons hear the sutra while seated together, they do not merely employ one, but perhaps two or three.
This is the faculty of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*), which cultivates according to the words and enters the stage of semblance (*pratirūpaka*).
The "wondrous and good roots" existing in the stage of reality are explained below as being due to remote causes and conditions.

Since these roots are described as "wondrous," they refer to the seeds planted by hearing the Perfect [Teaching] in the past; thus, it is said that one plants good roots by taking the true aspect (*dharmatā*) as the object-condition. Second, citing the remote conditions.

*The Sutra of Golden Light*, Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on Removing Illness.

[Text] A detailed response concerning remote conditions.

[Commentary] This King of Vaipulya Sūtras is titled "The Removal of the Eye of Illness" not merely because it removes the suffering of illness resulting from karmic retribution;

rather, its meaning encompasses the ten types of illnesses consisting of evil karma and afflictions. Therefore, the text below states: "To treat all the illnesses and sufferings of sentient beings, causing them all to be healed.
The intent of this passage includes the ten types of practitioners; thus, the preceding section constitutes the formal discussion.

"Those of superior faculties produce the fruit directly from the seeds within the object; thus the text says that upon merely hearing these words, their illness is immediately cured.

Because it combines various medicines, one knows that it does not merely eliminate the disease of karmic retribution. Regarding the two scriptural passages, the first provides a general overview while the latter divides the text into sections. [Wenju]:

Fourth, the conditions for establishing a karmic connection; fifth, the conditions for the five assemblies.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning according to two categories. First, the primary condition:
The Buddha addressed the goddess of the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, the Good Woman Devī: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and retain this well in your memory."
I shall now expound for you the causes and conditions of your past vows. In the past, immeasurable, inconceivable,
and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnaśrī Tathāgata,
