[Commentary] Part Two: The Chapter on the Flowing Water (Pravāhaṇa-parivarta).
First, the title of the chapter: *The Golden Light Sūtra, Chapter Sixteen: The Chapter on the Elder’s Son Flowing Water*.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, explaining the name while also removing illness; second, first, explaining "Flowing Water. First, the citation...
The text cites two names. [Wenju] The text says:
"First, it can flow water; second, it can provide water.
[Ji] Regarding the two sections that connect the sutra and explain the two meanings: first, the explanation of the two meanings; first, the individual explanation of the two meanings.

The first explanation concerns giving water, and the second explanation concerns flowing water. Regarding the first, there is great compassion that bestows happiness, followed by great compassion that uproots suffering.
The first of these also has two parts; first, the listing of the two waters. [Wenju:
"Giving water" means giving the water of peace and bliss: first, the peace and bliss of this world; second, the peace and bliss of the supramundane.
[Commentary] There are two interpretations regarding the "two waters.
[Text] "Worldly peace and happiness" refers to, for example, an elephant carrying water to rescue those parched fish.
"Supramundane peace and happiness" refers to, for example, making a vow that in future lives one shall bestow the food of the Dharma and grant the prediction of Bodhi.
[Commentary] Now, this one class [of beings] finds worldly happiness merely in the benefit of karmic retribution, whereas those who transcend the world clarify only the benefit of the single reality.
If we discuss this time, the conditions for forming the Pure Land are met throughout the realms of humans and devas, as well as across the four teachings.
Second, the explanation of the River of Flowing Water (Śrotasvāhinī). Part one: Listing the two waters.

[Textual Commentary] "Flowing water" refers to the water that flows to remove suffering and affliction. First, the suffering and affliction of karmic retribution; second, the suffering and affliction of karmic causes.
[Commentary] "Flowing away" (*liuchu*) means that the water flows out, which is the sense of "removal. There are two interpretations and two types of water.
[Text] Flowing away the suffering and affliction of karmic retribution (*vipāka*) is like treating various patients or rescuing thirsty fish.

Flowing away the suffering and affliction of karmic causes (*hetu*) consists of bestowing the Three Refuges, expounding the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and praising the Ten Epithets of the Buddha.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "karmic causes": apart from the retribution of the fruit, [the Buddha] is able to eliminate all nine types of benefit.
Now, the ten titles and so forth manifest what is eliminated by means of what eliminates them. The *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* calls this "profoundly verified."

The Three Refuges and the Ten Epithets are all complete expositions; although the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (the *Chen* text) lacks the passage on the Three Refuges, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the *Zuisheng jing*) contains it as translated by Paramārtha, and thus it must certainly have been present there.
The ritual for conferring the Dharma cannot be deficient in this regard.
[Furthermore,] these two pairs establish two meanings.

[Text] He requested his father to seek a remedy in order to fulfill the meaning of "Flowing Water" (Śrotas), and he borrowed an elephant from the king in order to fulfill the meaning of "Bestowing Water" (Vāri).
[Commentary] The second section, which simply indicates the title, has two parts; first, the inquiry.
[Text]: Since there are these two capacities, why is the chapter titled solely "Flowing Water"?
[Commentary]: This is answered in two parts.
[Text]: Since the meaning of "water" is clearly manifested within the text, it is unnecessary to trouble oneself by requiring the title of the chapter to be "Flowing Water."
In this way, the sūtra compiler’s skillful artistry is fully revealed through both the text and its title; indeed, there is no greater artistry than this.
[Commentary] Regarding the two explanations of the "Elder's Son": the mutual application of the two names—text and title—is nothing short of exquisite.
[Text]: "Elder" (*śreṣṭhin*) refers to the ten meanings of an elder as explained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
"Son" (*putra*) refers to the son who carries water;
therefore, he is called a "son. [Record]: In the *Fahua shu*, one possessing ten kinds of virtues is named an elder: first, noble lineage; second, high status... [and so forth].
1. Great wealth; 2. Fourfold majesty; 3. Five wisdoms; 4. Profundity; 5. Six years of age; 6. Elderly; 7. Pure conduct; 8.
Perfect etiquette; 9. Praised by those above; 10. Honored by those below—his sons. "Those below" refers to princes and nobles; thus the sutra says:
"In the household of the great elder Jālinīprabha, a son was later born named Śrotapāṇi. Second, taking up the prediction of enlightenment.
[Commentary on the Text]: This passage is the third proximate cause for establishing a karmic connection (*karmapratibandha*) within the section on severing doubts.
[Recorded Notes]: Regarding the two scriptural passages, first, it clarifies the third proximate cause for establishing a karmic connection; second, it divides the text.
[Textual Exegesis] Regarding the "near causes" (*upaniṣad*), there are again two parts: first, the introduction; second, the main body of the near cause.

Within the introduction, there are again two parts: first, the bestowing of grace and the spreading of virtue; second, the people’s praise, both as in the text. Regarding the "near causes," there are again three parts:
first, clarifying the retinue; second, the occasion of seeing the fish; third, the actual rescue of the fish, as in the text.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, the preliminary introduction; second, the bestowal of grace and the spreading of virtue.

The Buddha told the tree deity: "At that time, the Elder’s Son Flowing Water, having treated all sentient beings within the realm of King Devendra-prabhāsa from their immeasurable sufferings and ailments, caused their bodies to be restored to their original state and enabled them to experience various pleasures."
Because his illness had been cured, he took delight in performing many meritorious deeds and practicing generosity.
[Commentary] The people of the two countries praised him, honoring and respecting this son of a householder, saying: "Excellent! This householder is truly able to cause great increase."
"Meritorious deeds can benefit sentient beings with immeasurable life-spans; you are now truly a great king of physicians, skillfully treating the immeasurable grave illnesses of sentient beings.
You must be a bodhisattva who thoroughly understands medicinal prescriptions."
[Commentary] Regarding the second section on the "Proper Proximity," there are three parts; first, the retinue is explained.
At that time, the son of the elder had a wife named Water-Space Dragon-Treasury (Śūnyatā-jala-nāga-kośa), who gave birth to two sons:
the first was named Water-Space (Jala-śūnya) and the second was named Water-Treasury (Jala-kośa).
[Commentary: The occasion of the two seeing the fish was when the birds and beasts were rushing about.
At that time, the elder’s son took these two children and traveled in succession through cities, towns, and villages until they finally reached a large, desolate marsh.
There they saw various tigers, wolves, foxes, dogs, birds, and wild animals, all of whom were eating flesh and blood, exclusively in one direction.
As they fled in haste, the son of the elder thought to himself:
"For what reason and by what cause are these birds and beasts all running away in one direction? I shall follow after them and observe."
[Commentary] Regarding the three correct means of saving the fish, they are privately divided into two parts: first, clarifying the causes and conditions; second, [the specific account].
First, as for the cause: when the son of the elder followed after [the water], he saw a pond whose waters had run dry. Within that pond...
When there were many fish, the elder’s son saw them and gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
[Commentary] Second, a tree spirit manifests its form to show the number.
At that time, a tree spirit manifested half its body and spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Son of Good Family!"
"These fish are pitiable; you may give them water. For this reason, I shall name you 'Flowing Water' (Srotasvat). Furthermore, there are two reasons for the name 'Flowing Water':
first, because you can cause water to flow, and second, because you can provide water. You should now establish the reality that corresponds to your name.
At that time, the son of the elder asked the tree deity, "How many heads do these fish have? The tree deity replied:
When the number of these ten thousand virtuous goddesses was fully reached, the youth Flowing Water, having heard this number, felt a twofold increase in his great compassion.
[Commentary] Regarding the two instances of giving water and food: first, he gave water; second, he took branches from a tree to shield the sun.
O Good Goddess, at that time this empty pond was scorched by the sun until only a small amount of water remained;
these ten thousand fish were on the verge of death and, tossing about in all four directions, saw the elder and felt a sense of reliance upon him.
They followed the direction in which the elder went, gazing after him with eyes never once leaving him. At that moment, the elder rushed toward the four quarters, searching...
Having searched for water but being unable to find any, he looked around in all directions and saw a large tree;
he then took its branches and leaves and returned to the pond to provide shade and coolness.
[Note] "Shi" (恃) means to rely upon. Second, he knew that the source of the water was cut off.
Having created shade and coolness, he further investigated from where the water in this pond originally came.
He went out in the four directions, searching everywhere, but could not find the source of the water. He then ran swiftly to another distant place and saw a great river named Jalamdhara.
At that time, there were also other wicked people upstream who, for the sake of catching these fish, [had constructed a dam].
At this precipitous place, I must cut off the flow of the water so that it does not pass through;

yet, as this breach is situated on a steep and dangerous cliff and difficult to repair, even if a hundred thousand men were to work for ninety days, they would still be unable to complete the restoration—how much less could I do so alone?

[Commentary] "Jue" (決) means to capture or to break through. Regarding the pronunciation of "jue," it is *xué*. The *Guǎngyá* states it means "to pierce"; the *Shuōwén* states it means "the lower flow.
In the *Zhouyì*, the phrase "the fence breaks but is not weakened" (*fān jué bù luí*) is also pronounced *xué*. [The author] borrowed the elephant from the Great King three times.
At that time, the son of the elder quickly returned to the place where the great king was, prostrated with his head at the king's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Joining his palms toward the king, he explained the circumstances, saying:
"For the sake of treating the various ailments of the people in Your Majesty’s realm, I traveled gradually until I reached a desolate marsh, where I saw a pond whose water had completely dried up."
"There are ten thousand fish being scorched by the sun; today they are in dire distress and will soon die.
I only pray that Your Majesty will lend me twenty large elephants so that I may carry water to save their lives, just as you have preserved the lives of myself and these other sick people.
At that time, the Great King immediately commanded his ministers to provide them quickly. Then the ministers carried out the King's command.
The Imperial Edict stated: "Excellent, Great Being, Elder! You may now go yourself to the elephant stable and select as you wish those that will benefit sentient beings and bring them happiness."
[Commentary]: A *jiù* (stall) is a stable for horses; the *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states that *jiù* means "to gather," as it is where horses are gathered.
At that time, Sīmānanda carried water on his back to save the fish.
Then, Liúshuǐ and his two sons took twenty large elephants and borrowed leather from the city-builders.

The leather bag arrived at the breach in the upper reaches of the river where water was being diverted; filled with water and carried by an elephant, it was driven swiftly back to the empty marsh pond.
[The monk] dismounted from the elephant's back and poured the water from the bag into the pond, whereupon the water immediately filled it completely, restoring it to its former state.
[Commentary] Regarding the two types of giving food: first, as for observing the fish’s hunger and distress.
At that time, the son of the elder walked back and forth along the four sides of the pond;
the fish likewise followed him, circling along the bank. Then the son of the elder thought to himself: "For what reason do these fish follow me?"
"This fish must be tormented by the fire of hunger and wishes to seek food and drink from me; I shall now give it to him. [Commentary] *Pángyáng* (彷徉):
the first character is pronounced *fú fāng* (扶方) and the second is pronounced *yǐ zhāng* (以章). According to the *Guǎngyǎ*, it means to stand idly or to loiter; it also means to pace back and forth.
Second, taking food and bestowing it as a gift.
"Good Woman Devī, at that time the Elder’s son, Flowing Water, said to his sons:

'Take one of the most powerful elephants and go quickly home. Inform the Elder father that you must gather all the edible things in the house—including the portions for your parents' own consumption, as well as those for your wives, children, and servants—and load them all onto it.'"
As the elephant returned with great speed, the two sons, following their father’s instructions, mounted the largest elephant and went to their home.
They informed their grandfather of the aforementioned matters.

Then, the two sons gathered all the edible items from the house, loaded them onto the back of the elephant, and quickly returned to where their father was at the pond in the empty marsh. When the elder son saw him, he...
The son returned with a heart of immeasurable joy and exultation; he took food and drink from his side and scattered it into the pond to feed the fish.
Having done so, he reflected to himself: "I have now been able to provide food for these fish and satisfy them."
[Commentary] Second, explaining the fourth section on forming karmic connections. First, the division of the text.
[Textual Analysis] From "In future worlds, you shall bestow the food of Dharma" onwards is the fourth section, the formal formation of karmic connections.

This is further divided into four parts: first, making a vow; second, contemplating the preaching of the Dharma; third, the actual preaching of the Dharma; and fourth, the fish changing their rebirth.
The text on the Fish Repaying its Kindness through Rebirth in Heaven consists of four sections: first, the fish transforms its rebirth to ascend to heaven;

second, the devas repay their kindness by descending to the earth; third, the king sees the light and inquires about the auspicious omen; fourth, the elder seeks instruction and receives a definitive response.
These are as set forth in the text.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning has four parts. First, the initial vow:
"In future ages, I shall bestow the food of the Dharma.
Second, the contemplation of preaching the Dharma.
He further reflected: "I have heard that in the past, in a secluded place, there was a bhikṣu who recited the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
In those sūtras it is said that if sentient beings, at the time of their death, hear the name of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, they will immediately be reborn in the heavens.
I shall now explain this profound teaching for these ten thousand fish."
When the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and the name of the Buddha Ratnashrī are being proclaimed, there will be two kinds of people in Jambudvīpa:
first, those who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; second, those who disparage them and do not give rise to faith or joy.
At that time, the son of the elder will think to himself: "I shall now enter the waters of the pond to preach the profound and subtle [Dharma] for these fish."
Having thus reflected upon the Dharma, he immediately entered the water.
[Commentary: This is the third correct exposition of the Dharma.
He spoke these words: "Namo to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Ratnaśrī of the past."
The Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans,
Buddha, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī, formerly while practicing the bodhisattva path, made this vow:
"If there are sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions who hear my name at the time of their death, may they, immediately upon passing away, attain..."
Upon being reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, at that time the Flowing Water [King] further explained this most profound and wondrous Dharma to those fish, namely:
ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form;

name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; and becoming conditions birth.
Conditioned by old age and death, there arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
[Commentary] First the Ten Epithets are proclaimed, followed by the explanation of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Although the names differ—the Ten Epithets pertain to awakening and the fruit, while Dependent Origination pertains to delusion and the cause—their essence is not different, for the fruit of the Ten Epithets is...

To exhaustively investigate the three virtues within the twelve links of dependent origination is to realize that these are the primordial three virtues; since the three virtues do not change, how could cause and effect be distinct?
Thus, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* states: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;

the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena. All phenomena are the cultivation of these two [aspects of] true reality, yet true reality is a single nature. These three are perfectly interfused.
Neither vertical nor horizontal, the entire body is the cause and the entire body is the fruit. Although sentient beings are deluded, the Ten Epithets do not diminish;
although the Buddhas have realized the ultimate, the Twelve Epithets are not deficient, because all worldly phenomena are eternally abiding.
Now, first proclaiming the fruit, the principle of the fruit has been revealed to give rise to understanding. The initial title "Ratnaśrī" (Jewel Victorious) is its specific name.
The name "Equal to One Buddha-Tathāgata" and so forth up to ten is a general designation for the Buddhas of the three times and ten directions;
all Buddhas possess these qualities. If one takes the general from the specific, they may be designated as "Ratnaśrī Tathāgata," "Ratnaśrī Buddha," or "Ratnaśrī Bhagavān.
Since these three cases are thus established, by analogy, one should likewise say: "Ratnaśrī Arhat," "Ratnaśrī Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Even unto the title "Jewel-Conqueror, Teacher of Gods and Humans"—these ten are collectively termed the Great Sūtras and Great Śāstras.
Tiantai produced their names, and Cien produced their meanings and characteristics; these have already been revealed.

Now, drawing upon various commentaries, I shall further summarize them by way of three triads and one [conclusion] to dissolve these ten titles, so that one may know that each and every one is none other than the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*). If this meaning...
To clarify: "not being disgraced" refers to the names of the three fruits. Since the Tathāgata is placed first, these correspond to the three aspects within the *dharmakāya*.
The Tathāgata is *tathatā* (suchness), which belongs to the *dharmakāya*; "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings) refers to benefiting sentient beings, which is *vimukti* (liberation);
and "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Enlightened One) possesses the two types of wisdom, which is *prajñā* (wisdom). This is because the *dharmakāya* necessarily possesses these two virtues.
Since the next three [attributes] take the "perfection of knowledge and conduct" (*vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna*) as their primary element, they correspond to the three aspects within liberation.
The practice of the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) is liberation; the Sugata’s ability to reach the ultimate is wisdom (*prajñā*);

and the fact that each of the three worlds is eternally abiding is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), because liberation necessarily possesses these two qualities. Since the final three [attributes] take the "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) as their primary element...
The "Sage who tames men" (士調御丈夫) is the foremost; this corresponds to the third of the three [bodies] within the Prajñāpāramitā.
Because seeing one's nature is called being a "great man" (丈夫), he serves as the Teacher of Gods and Men according to the *Prajñā*; he is the Buddha of Liberation who trains all capacities;

he is the Buddha of Returning to the Source, the Great Awakening; and he is the Dharma-body. This is because the *Prajñā* necessarily possesses these two qualities. These nine are the three, and these three are [the nine].
That is to say, each and every thing lacks even a single characteristic; yet the three nines—the three thousandfold world-systems—are perfectly manifest.

Because the nine periods of time and the single moment are ultimately sovereign in their extension and contraction, it is said that the World-Honored One binds the twelve links of dependent origination into three paths:

the three links of ignorance, craving, and grasping belong to the path of afflictions; the two links of volitional formations and existence belong to the path of karma; and consciousness, name-and-form, contact, feeling, birth, and aging-and-death [belong to the path of suffering].
The six sense bases, contact, sensation, birth, aging, and death—belonging to the path of suffering—are indeed states of delusion, bondage, and cyclic existence;
yet their entire substance is the Buddha-nature of the three causes, all of which are inconceivable.

Because they manifest differently according to how individuals observe them, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that by observing this with inferior, middling, or superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of the three vehicles.
When one observes with the supreme wisdom of *tiryak* (transversal) to attain the Bodhi of the Buddha, one realizes that the wisdoms of the three preceding teachings involve conceptual thought;

thus, by observing the twelve *śamatha*, one attains the three vehicles. Only the Perfect Teaching possesses inconceivable wisdom, wherein the substance of ignorance and other defilements is itself the nature of染 (*rañjana*, defilement).
It is not something created by Buddhas, devas, humans, or asuras; each and every thing is eternally abiding, perfectly complete in its own place.

Jingrong then said: "Within the causes, the nature of the fruit is already present. Furthermore, in the *Mysterious Text*, although the three paths and the three consciousnesses exist in their original state, they are non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues of the subsequent fruit.
Once this meaning is grasped, one may then differentiate the twelve distinct names.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to the failure to realize that the six sensations are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle way. Practice (*pratipatti*) refers to relying on [the realization of] non-... [text ends].

The activity of the mind constitutes the formative action (*saṃskāra*), which impels the consciousness (*vijñāna*) toward the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). When this consciousness takes rebirth in the mother’s womb, it is termed name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Form" refers to the two drops [of semen and blood], while "name" refers to the mind alone. As name-and-form develops, it becomes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
"Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the six faculties encountering their respective objects. "Feeling" (*vedanā*) arises from contact and consists of the three types: suffering, pleasure, and equanimity.

Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) refers to being deluded regarding the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), whereby one becomes stained by and attached to pleasure. Grasping (*upādāna*) refers to the entanglement of craving’s defilement, whereby one seeks and pursues objects in the four directions.

Existence (*bhava*) refers to the performance of karma through grasping, which necessitates a future retribution. Birth (*jāti*) refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) in the future once that karma has matured.

Old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and so forth refer to the necessity of transformation and cessation upon birth, which is entangled by sorrow and affliction. These are the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*).

Whether categorized according to the three periods of time, the two periods of time, or a single thought-moment—though these three differ, they all employ the twelve [links] to correspond with the three paths.
Thus, phenomena are identical with principle; each and every thing is ultimately pure, sovereign, neither vertical nor horizontal, yet lofty and vast.
One who contemplates in this manner attains the Bodhi of the Buddha; this is the meaning of the abbreviated Three Refuges.

It is already complete. For the Three Jewels and the three virtues are fundamentally not different in essence; since one has already invoked the ten titles of the Victorious Jewel (*Ratnottama*) with "Namo," is this not taking refuge in the three virtues of the fruition?
Furthermore, the teaching of the profound twelve links of dependent origination is the reliance of the mind upon the three virtues within the causal state.
At the ultimate limit of delusion and awakening, the three virtues are without distinction; their meaning is fully contained within this single, unified body.
All are fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity; this is truly the ultimate fulfillment of the meaning of taking refuge in the Triple Gem.

One should know that the intention of Master Śikṣānanda is profound and subtle. Regarding the four fish who were reborn in heaven as a reward for their gratitude: first, the initial fish changed its karmic retribution and was reborn in heaven.
"Good Woman Devī, at that time, after the Elder’s son Flowing Water and his two sons had preached this Dharma, they returned home together.
Later, on another occasion, while the Elder’s son was reclining, intoxicated from a gathering of guests, the earth suddenly shook violently.
At that moment, ten thousand fish died on the same day; having died, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Benefiting the Heavens.

[Commentary] Generally, when one is first born in the heavens, by the power of their own karma, they have three kinds of awareness: first, they know for themselves that they died from that previous place;
second, they know for themselves that they are now born in this place; and third, they know for themselves what specific karma they previously performed to attain rebirth in the heavens.
Having understood their past deeds, they descended to repay their debt of gratitude.

The two devas, having repaid their debt and descended to the lower realm, once born there, reflected thus: "By what causes and conditions of wholesome karma have we been born here in this Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
They then said to one another: "Previously, within Jambudvīpa, we had fallen among the animals."

While we were in the bodies of fish, the Elder’s Son, the Master of the Flowing Water, gave us water and food, and further explained to us the profound twelvefold chain of dependent origination while reciting the name of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava.
By these causes and conditions, we have been reborn in this heaven; therefore, we shall now go to the Elder’s Son.

To repay his kindness and make offerings to him, at that time ten thousand devaputras descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa, arriving at the house of the great physician, the elder’s son Śrotodatta.
At that moment, the elder’s son was sleeping on an open terrace above the building;
the ten thousand devaputras placed ten thousand pearls and celestial, exquisite necklaces at the side of his head and then departed.
Ten thousand [flowers] were placed at his feet; another ten thousand were placed at his right side; and another ten thousand were placed at his left side.
Mandārava and Mahāmandārava flowers rained down, piling up to his knees.
Various celestial music was performed, producing wondrous sounds that awakened all those in Jambudvīpa who were asleep. The fragrance spread throughout the world.
The son of the water-merchant also awoke from his sleep.
These ten thousand devas, soaring and traveling through the air above, rained down exquisite lotus flowers everywhere throughout the kingdom of King Divaukasa.
Then these devas returned to their original location at the pond in the empty marsh and again rained down celestial flowers, before vanishing from there and returning to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The palace allows him to enjoy the five celestial desires according to his will.
[Commentary] Regarding "sutra-pavilions" (*jing lou wu*): a multi-storied building is called a *lou*; to write it as "pavilion-platform" (*lou tai*) is an error.
This explanation constitutes the first point.

[Text]: There are two kinds of repaying gratitude: first, the good; second, the affairs. Regarding the principle and phenomena, the "four sides" refer to the causes and conditions for the water, food, and drink that repay [the Buddha];
the "ten titles" and so forth refer to the four kinds of moisture.

[Commentary] Regarding the ten titles [of the Buddha], they are categorized as "matters" (vastu) because they pertain to the verbal teachings that express them—just as water and food are called matters.
Second is "principle" (li).
[Wenju] As for principle, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it says: "Giving food causes others to obtain life; this symbolizes causing others to obtain the eternal."
Because one delights in this, one attains *nirvāṇa*; because one causes others to attain awakening, one achieves self-mastery (*svatantra*);
because one seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma, one obtains pure enjoyment as the forty-thousandfold retribution for the grace of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
[Commentary]: It is precisely by resolving the four matters that one realizes the four virtues; thus, it constitutes the benefit of principle.

Because the fish were lax in their observance of precepts, they received bodies with scales and shells; because they were earnest in their practice of the Vehicle, they now encounter a true spiritual friend of the Mahāyāna.

Consequently, they are able to deeply understand the wondrous principle within these matters: receiving food and obtaining life symbolizes the attainment of the True and Eternal, while receiving water and obtaining joy symbolizes the attainment of Bliss.
Manifesting the bliss of *nirvāṇa* within the forest of twelve thorns; liberating the self from the self through reliance on the Dharma of the ten titles;

attaining the wealth of celestial retribution through a pure livelihood in the world; and liberating the nature of purity and virtue—these four dharmas of benefit were obtained through the power of Jalavāhana.

Consequently, he offered forty thousand pearl necklaces as a gift of gratitude and provided the four requisites of food and so forth. Since these manifest the benefit of principle, they are called "benefits."

These forty thousand pearl necklaces not only serve as material offerings, but also symbolize that within each of the thousands of worlds and tens of thousands of such realms, every single dharma is endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These are the forty thousand necklaces of true flavor; they are an adornment that is not merely ornamental, for they adorn the Dharma-body.
This is an offering of wealth that constitutes an offering of Dharma. Were it otherwise, how could it be called "existent"?
Is it through the condition of obtaining a prediction based on sublime roots of goodness?
At that time, when the three kings beheld the auspicious sign of light, King Heavenly Sovereign Radiance (Devendraprabha) of Jambudvīpa asked his various ministers:
"By what cause did such a pure and wondrous auspicious sign, accompanied by great radiance, manifest last night? The ministers replied: "Great King, you should..."

Knowing that the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were raining down forty thousand pearl necklaces and incalculable *mandārava* flowers at the house of the Elder’s Son Flowing Water, the King immediately commanded his ministers and officials:
"You must go to that elder’s house, entice him with kind words, and summon him here. Having received the decree, the great minister went to the house and proclaimed the King's command.
When he called out, "Elder! the elder immediately went to the king's presence. The king asked the elder, "For what reason have you manifested such an auspicious omen?
[Commentary: The four elders provide their definitive answers based on the teachings.
The son of the elder said, "I know for certain that the lives of these ten thousand fish have already ended.
The Great King said, "Now you must send someone to verify this matter.

Thereupon, Shrotapāla immediately dispatched his son to the site of the pond to observe whether those fish were dead or alive and to ascertain the truth. At that time, having heard these words, the son went toward that pond.
Having arrived at the pond, he saw that within it there were many *mahāmandārava* flowers piled up in heaps, and all the fish therein had died.
Having seen this, he immediately returned and said to his father, "Those fish have all already passed away.
At that time, having understood this matter, the Flowing Water went again to where the king was and spoke these words.
When these ten thousand fish all passed away, the king heard of this and his heart was filled with joy.
[Commentary] The fifth section concludes the connection between the past and the present.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the goddess of the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, the Good Woman Devī, saying: "If you wish to know who that 'Flowing Water' was at that time..."
The son of the elder is now this very person; the eldest son, Water-Space (Vāri-ākāśa), is now Rāhula;
the middle son, Water-Treasury (Vāri-nidhi), is now Ānanda. As for those ten thousand fish, they are now these ten thousand devaputras.
For this reason, I now bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the tree spirit manifested half her body.
"You are that very person now.

[Commentary] The fifth section, which reconciles the past and the present: Formerly, the Buddha was uncertain regarding the number of fish, and the tree deity definitively determined it to be ten thousand.

Now, the deity doubts whether his practice is shallow yet his prediction is profound; the Buddha therefore explains the wondrous causes and conditions. Thus, the past and the present are interconnected. Therefore...
This is a summary of the assembly.
[Commentary] Regarding Rāhula, this is translated as "Obstruction" (Fùzhàng), because he remained in the womb for six years; thus this name was established.

A new translation is Rāhula, which means "Obstructor of the Moon. However, the matters concerning his original nature and manifested traces cannot be known with certainty; one should reflect upon them through the context of the surrounding text.
Regarding these ten thousand [beings], they must have been those to be transformed in the past and present, while all others were capable transformers.

As for this capacity to transform, according to what is taught in various sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka*, it consists entirely of having cultivated actual causes over oceans of kalpas and matured those ten thousand [beings] so that they may attain liberation now.

If one adopts the perspective of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* regarding their long-standing accomplishment, this refers to the way they were received as suitable vessels among the provisional manifestations (*jia*).
May those who lecture on this school now receive this prediction; let them know this within their own hearts.
[Commentary] Chapter Six: Relinquishing the Body. First, the title of the chapter:
*The Golden Light Sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen: "Relinquishing the Body."

[Commentary] The section on phrases and sentences is divided into two parts. First, the question: "If one discards much and retains little, [is it right to say: 'The meanings to be discarded are exceedingly many;

wealth, status, and lifespan—should one bear these with the body alone? Is this correct? [Text and Sentences] "The meanings to be discarded are exceedingly many; wealth, status, and lifespan—should one bear these with the body alone? Is this correct? (Is it right to say so?)
[Commentary] The second [section] provides the title based on its essential meaning.
[Wenju] This receives its name from its primary significance: for the recipient, it is necessary that the body be given, whereas other things are not;
for the donor, the primary act is the relinquishing of the body, while the relinquishing of other things is secondary. Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Relinquishing the Body."
[Commentary]: The recipient must be one whose body is pressed by the hunger of a tiger; they seek only the flesh of the body, not life, wealth, or status.
As for the practice of the gate [of giving], it has immeasurable roots originating from past熏習 (*vāsanā*). There are four kinds of samādhis that follow what each person values.
Regarding the "good practice according to one's own inclination," those who delight in practicing *dāna* (generosity) have no regrets regarding their body, life, or wealth.

It is regrettable that while self-cultivation, instruction, sympathetic joy, and praise all reside within giving, if one practices the dāna-pāramitā by relying on a virtuous teacher and the true teaching,
then the mind capable of giving, the recipient who receives the gift, and the body and so forth that are given— all these are empty, provisional, and middle. Thus,
one should practice the unity of phenomena and principle, and the mutual support of auxiliary and primary cultivation, progressing forward.
Since it is called "practicing according to one's original habituation," one acts with joy; or because an action is undertaken suddenly due to the convergence of past conditions;
or because long-accumulated vows cause the contemplation to be perfected; or because one openly declares one’s aspirations so that others may emulate them;

or because one secretly fulfills one’s own heart’s desire to silence the slanders of others; or because compassion is profound; or because secret kindness is profound; or because the mind is truly authentic.

If all four *siddhāntas* are fulfilled, yet the mind is characterized by deceit, both self-benefit and benefit for others will be lost. However, because the Buddha recounted past events (*pūrvayoga*) to cause people to emulate his conduct, the commentary states:
"By citing the sacrifice of one's body in the past, he admonishes present teachers and disciples not to begrudge their wealth or the Dharma.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is easy to give up the body, but difficult to give up the mind. This is because the treatise intends for the practitioner to relinquish the mind of attachment; therefore, it is described as difficult.
In praising the practice of giving to bring rest to worldly affairs, why not rely on the treatises to eliminate the mind of attachment?

Why do people today delight so much in sacrificing their bodies and lives? The answer is that whether suppressing or elevating, accepting or rejecting, all follow the Buddha’s teachings and accord with the inclinations of people's hearts.

While the Buddha’s discourse on the primary and auxiliary practices differs, and people’s preferences for principle and phenomena are unequal, this chapter specifically demonstrates the relinquishing of the body.
How could you dare to use the ease or difficulty [of practice] as a pretext for criticism? Furthermore, you speak in vain of renunciation while clinging to your own views;
you are so rigidly attached to your own person that you would not pluck out a single hair, yet you condemn the sacrifice of life by others as wrong.

Since this contradicts the spirit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), how can you escape the reproach of envying the virtuous? I pray that you will hear the Buddha’s teaching and practice it according to your capacity. (The Texts of the Two Sutras)
The first part of the second section.
[Wénjù] The text consists of four parts: first, the question; second, the answer; third, the assembly’s attainment of benefit; and fourth, the conclusion.
[Jì] Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has four parts; first, the question.
At that time, the deity of the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I have heard that when the World-Honored One was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, you fully underwent immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices, relinquishing body, life, flesh, blood, marrow, and bone.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly explain the causes and conditions of these former ascetic practices, for the benefit of those who dwell here and so that they may endure all [sufferings]."
[Joyful. [Commentary:

The questioner has previously heard that the Great Being healed the sick and rescued the fish, truly providing vast salvation to both small people and tiny insects, granting them benefit for two lifetimes.
Now the assembly wishes to hear of his deeds in which he sacrificed his body and gave up his life—deeds that evoke profound emotion and reach the ultimate limit of resonance.
"How can it be that suffering yields the fruit of happiness? For this reason, I ask. [Commentary:

"The 'small person' refers to those who are like a national malady; the ten thousand 'small insects' and 'withered fish' are those who, by vowing to consume the food of future dharmas, obtain the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
They are like those whose illness has been cured; they are destined to become the vehicles for liberation in future lives."

Therefore, all have received the benefits of two successive generations. Those whose gratitude is profound and whose realization is ultimate guide others through the non-dual interpretation toward difficult practices;
because their gratitude has reached such depth, they relinquish body, life, and wealth as equal to the future limit, and this realization is indeed supreme.
At this very moment when the multitude hears [this teaching] and attains benefit, the tree deity seizes the opportunity to pose a question. The second part [of the response] has two initial sections.

Sectioning the Text. [Commentary on the Words]: The Buddha’s response is divided into two parts: first, the narration of the causal origin; second, the formal elucidation of the occasion for relinquishing the body, which consists of eleven sections:
(1) the earth-treasuries and stūpas surge forth; (2) the great assembly conceives doubt; (3) the Buddha rises to pay homage; (4) the tree deity asks about the homage; (5) the Buddha...
1. The response to the command to pay homage; 2. The command to Ānanda to take [the relics]; 3. Ānanda’s description of the state of the bones; 4. The command to show them to the great assembly; 5.
The compliance with the command to take and show them; 6. The Buddha’s exhortation for the assembly to pay homage—all as recorded in the text.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, the narration of the causal occasion, in ten sections, all as listed in the outline. Regarding the first stage, the emergence of the stupa:
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested supernormal power; by the power of this supernormal power, he caused this great earth to quake in six ways.
In the midst of the great assembly within the lecture hall, a stupa made of the seven treasures emerged from the earth,
with nets of various jewels covering it from above.
[Commentary] Second, the great assembly conceives doubts.
At that time, when the great assembly saw this event, they were struck with wonder.
[Commentary: The Three Buddhas Rise and Pay Homage.
At that moment, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, paid homage to the stupa, circumambulated it with reverence, and returned to his original seat.
[Commentary] The Four Tree Spirits Ask about the Prostration.
At that time, the tree spirit of the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, has appeared in this world and is constantly revered by all. Among all sentient beings, he is the most supreme and most honored. By what causes and conditions [is this so]?"
Therefore, one should prostrate to this stūpa.
[Commentary] The five Buddhas answered the salutation.
The Buddha said: "O Goddess, when I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, my bodily relics were enshrined within it."
"The stupa was built because this body enabled me to quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[Commentary: Sixth, Ānanda is commanded to take [the relics].
At that time, the Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda: 'You may open the stupa, take the śarīra within, and show them to this great assembly.'"
These relics are permeated by the merit of immeasurable six *pāramitās*.
[Note] Seventh, Ānanda describes the state of the bones.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately went to the site of the stūpa, prostrated, made offerings, and opened its door.
Seeing within the stūpa a casket made of the seven precious gems, he opened the casket with his hand and beheld the śarīra, its color wondrously crimson-white;
he then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the śarīra within this is crimson-white in color."
[Commentary] Eighth, manifesting the life-span to the great assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "You may bring it here; this is the true-body relic (śarīra) of the Great Being.
[Commentary] Ninth, receiving the command and bringing it forth for display.
At that time, Ānanda immediately lifted the precious casket, returned to where the Buddha was, and offered it to the Buddha.
[Commentary] Ten Buddhas exhort the assembly to pay homage:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire great assembly: "You all should now pay homage to these śarīras. These śarīras..."
This is the field of supreme merit, most difficult to encounter, which has been cultivated through the perfuming of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
At that time, having heard these words, the great assembly felt joy in their hearts; they rose from their seats and, with palms joined in reverence, paid homage to the Great Being Śāriputra.
Then, the World-Honored One, wishing to sever the net of doubts for the great assembly, spoke of the past causes and conditions of this śarīra.
[Commentary] Second, the explicit explanation of the relinquishing of the body, which is divided into two parts.
[Textual Analysis] From "In the past there was a king" onwards is the section on the explicit relinquishing of the body, which is divided into two:

first, the prose; second, the verses. The prose is further divided into four sections: first, clarifying his original retinue; second, the skillful means for relinquishing the body; third, the actual relinquishing of the body.
Fourth, abandoning subsequent sorrowful attachment.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning. Part two: first, the long prose section. Four parts: first, clarifying the original retinue. Part one: first, the topical outline.
[Wenju] Regarding the original retinue, there are five sections: first, clarifying the original retinue; second, traveling abroad; third, each describing their characteristics.
Fourth, seeing the tiger give birth; fifth, each relates what they have seen.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning in five sections as listed in the outline: first, clarifying the original retinue.
In a past age, there was a king named Mahāratha who practiced the wholesome Dharma and governed well.
In that land, there were no enemies; at that time, he had three sons who were handsome and exquisite, with extraordinary physical forms and supreme majesty.
The eldest son was named Mahāpuruṣa, the middle son was named Mahādeva, and the youngest son was named Mahāsattva.

[Text]: *Mahāratha* is translated here as "Great Innocence. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that *ratha* is translated as "Middle," while *mahāpāṇara* is alternatively said to be translated as "Great Deliverance," though this remains uncertain.
*Mahādeva* means "Great God. *Mahāsattva* is translated as "Great Being" (or "Great Heart").
[Commentary] Second, the account of the journey.
These three princes, while wandering and sightseeing through various gardens and groves, gradually arrived at a large bamboo forest where they halted their carriage to rest.
[Commentary] Each of the three describes their own state.
The first prince spoke thus: "Today my heart is filled with great terror; I fear that some misfortune may befall me within this forest.
The second prince further spoke thus: "Today I do not cherish my own body."
"It is merely that one who is separated from what they love suffers grief and sorrow. The third prince further spoke these words:
"Today I alone am without fear or dread, nor do I have any sorrow or affliction. This mountain is empty and silent, praised by the immortals;
this place is secluded and tranquil, able to allow the practitioner to receive peace and joy."
[Commentary: Regarding the "tigress that has recently given birth":
after the princes had spoken these words, they proceeded further and saw a tigress who had just given birth seven days prior, surrounded on all sides by her seven cubs.
She was emaciated, exhausted, and haggard from hunger; her body was so frail and weak that her life was about to end.
[Commentary] Each of the five princes stated their observations.
Upon seeing the tigress, the first prince spoke thus: "How strange! This tigress has given birth for seven days, and her seven cubs surround her so that she cannot seek food.
If she is driven by hunger, she will surely devour her own offspring. The third prince... [continued].
When asked what this tiger usually eats, the first prince said, "This tiger eats only fresh, warm meat and blood.
The third prince said, "Among you, who can provide food for this tiger?
The second prince replied, "This tiger is starving, its body emaciated and exhausted; with little life remaining, it cannot wait for another time."
If one provides food for him, the lives of other seekers will surely not be sustained; who could do this without sparing their own body and life?
The first prince said, "Of all things difficult to relinquish, nothing exceeds one's own body.
The second prince said, "Because we are now possessed by greed and attachment, we are unable to let go of this body and life; it is because our wisdom is meager that we [fail to do so]."

When they were struck with such terror at these events, those great beings who desired to benefit others and give rise to great compassion for the sake of sentient beings found it no hardship to sacrifice their own bodies and lives. At that time, the princes were filled with profound sorrow;
they remained gazing at him for a long time, never once averting their eyes. Having made this observation, they then departed.
[Commentary] Regarding the two sections on the skillful means of relinquishing the body, this is the first division of the outline.
[Text] From the passage "At that time he thought, 'The moment for me to relinquish my body has arrived'" onwards is the section on the skillful means of relinquishing the body.
These skillful means are twofold: first, the description of contemplative understanding; second, the arousal of vows. Vow and practice support one another, leading to a harmonious birth.
Regarding the "seven days," it is said that seeing seven spots on the head of a tiger cub, one knows that seven days have passed; this is from the *Shanhai jing*.

It also says that after seven days [the eyes] appear between the brows, and after another seven days of not eating, the tiger will surely die. Since the tiger was already at the point of death, he knew it was the seventh day.
Others say that spirits and deities provide such insights, just as the tree spirit counted the fish.

[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, which has two parts: first, the description of contemplative understanding; second, the arousal of vows. Regarding "vow and practice supporting each other":
practice is precisely contemplative understanding; without this contemplative understanding, one's vow cannot be fulfilled—is it not so?

As for "if there is no vow, practice will regress," the text [citing] "from the seventh day after birth until counting the fish by the tree deity" is a retrospective explanation of the preceding fourth section.
The *Jian chan humen ye shu* (Notes on the Contemplation of the Tiger’s Mark) can be seen in the sutra; from "He then formed this thought" below, it describes the contemplative understanding.
At that time, the third prince formed this thought: "The time for me now to relinquish my body has arrived. Why is this?
Since ancient times, I have discarded this body many times, yet it has never served any purpose; nevertheless, I have always cherished and protected it, housing it within a dwelling."
Furthermore, this dwelling [of the body] is provided with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, elephants, horses, and carriages;
it is nurtured according to the seasons so that nothing is lacking. Yet, instead of recognizing this kindness, it responds with resentment and harm. Moreover, it cannot escape impermanence and decay.
Furthermore, this body is not firm; it offers no benefit, is as loathsome as a thief, and is like a walking latrine. I...
Today, one should cause this body to perform the unsurpassed deed by acting as a great bridge over the ocean of birth and death.
Furthermore, if one relinquishes this body, one relinquishes immeasurable abscesses, ulcers, and hundreds of thousands of fears;
this body contains nothing but excrement and urine; this body is as unsubstantial as a bubble on the water; this body is impure and full of manifold [defilements].
The body is a dwelling place for worms; it is loathsome, bound together by sinews, smeared with blood, and composed of skin, bone, marrow, and brain, all held together in mutual dependence.
Observing it thus, one finds it deeply distressing and wearying.

Therefore, I should now renounce it in order to seek the quiescent, unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*—to be forever free from sorrow and affliction, to bring to rest the impermanence, change, and birth-and-death, and to be rid of all worldly burdens and immeasurable [defilements].
Fully endowed with the merits of meditative concentration and wisdom, he accomplishes the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body, adorned with the hundred blessings and praised by all Buddhas;
having realized such an unsurpassed Dharma-body, he bestows immeasurable Dharma-bliss upon all sentient beings.

[Commentary] There are two kinds of contemplation: first, auxiliary contemplation; second, primary contemplation. From the beginning up to "it is truly loathsome and wearying" is the auxiliary path-contemplation.
This refers to using the provisional mental images of the Tripiṭaka teaching as an antidote to the mind that clings to the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*).

From "Therefore, I now... onwards is the primary contemplation. Up to "there are no longer any worldly burdens and afflictions," etc., is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). It is non-existent.

Measuring the meditative concentrations up to that which is praised by all Buddhas is the provisional view (*parikalpita-dṛṣṭi*). From "attaining realization in this way" up to "the joy of the Dharma" is the middle view (*madhyama-dṛṣṭi*).
These teachings must be cultivated with a single mind throughout the preceding and succeeding stages. Second, the description of the vows.
At that time, the prince, being courageous and capable, made this great vow and cultivated his mind with supreme great compassion.
Fearing that his two elder brothers might harbor dread or anxiety, or perhaps obstruct him by creating hindrances, he spoke to them, saying:
"Brothers, you should now return to your dwellings together with your retinues. Then, Prince Mahāsattva...
Returning to where the tiger was, he took off his upper and lower garments and placed them upon a bamboo branch, making this vow:

"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; for the sake of realizing the most supreme, unsurpassed path; for the sake of great compassion that remains unmoving even when giving up what is difficult to give;
for the sake of seeking the wisdom praised by the Buddhas; and desiring to deliver all sentient beings from the three realms of existence, I shall extinguish the fear of birth and death."
"Because of the heat of manifold afflictions.
[Commentary]: First, one employs skillful means; next, one makes a vow. The following six lines constitute the actual formulation of the vow, which are not excluded from the Four Great Vows.

The first two [lines] rely on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) to give rise to the vow to attain Buddhahood; the latter two [lines] rely on the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) to give rise to the vows for compassion and wisdom.
The fifth [vow] relies on the Truth of Suffering to give rise to the vow to deliver sentient beings; the sixth relies on the Truth of Origination to give rise to the vow to sever delusions.

This [section] takes the Truth of Cessation beyond the realms as its primary focus to verify the arousal of the Perfect Mind. This concludes the first sub-section of the third [part], "Properly Sacrificing the Body."
[Text] Regarding "Correctly sacrificing one's body," there are two parts: first, the sacrifice of the body; second, the moving of heaven and earth.
[Commentary] Regarding the two explanations, the first concerns the sacrifice of the body.
At that time, having made this vow, the prince immediately cast his own body down and lay before the starving tigress. At that time, the prince...
By the power of his great compassion, the tiger was rendered powerless; the prince then thought to himself: "The tiger is now emaciated and lacks physical strength;
it cannot obtain the flesh and blood of my body for food. He immediately rose to seek a knife, searching everywhere but failing to find one.
He then pierced his own neck with a dry bamboo stalk to draw out blood, and threw himself from a high mountain peak onto the tiger.
[Commentary]: Second, moving heaven and earth.
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, and the sun lost its brilliance, as if eclipsed by Rāhu, the Asura King.

As they held up canopies and rained down various flowers and diverse exquisite incenses, other devas in the sky, seeing this event, felt joy in their hearts and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent! Great Being, you are truly one who practices great compassion;
for the sake of sentient beings, you are able to renounce that which is difficult to renounce. Among all students, you are peerless."
"O foremost of the brave, you have already attained that which is praised by all Buddhas—the dwelling place of eternal bliss.
Before long, you shall realize the pure Nirvana, free from affliction and fever.
At that time, seeing blood flow and staining the prince’s body, the tiger immediately licked the blood and devoured his flesh, leaving only the remaining bones."
[Commentary] Regarding the "six kinds of earth tremors" mentioned in the sutra: the three types of *kampa* (trembling), *prakampa* (shaking), and *samprakampa* (quaking) refer to the aspect of form;

the three types of *raṇa* (roaring), *praraṇa* (thundering), and *sampraraṇa* (resounding) refer to the aspect of sound. Here, because two aspects—form and sound—are mentioned in brief, it says "earth tremors.
This constitutes the first section of the fourfold division concerning the sorrowful attachment after casting off the body.

[Text]: After he had relinquished his body, his kinsmen were filled with grief and suffering; first, his two elder brothers were distressed and each spoke a verse as they went together to the place where he had relinquished his body.
Next, his parents were filled with grief and suffering.
[Commentary]: Regarding the two explanations, the first concerns the distress of the two elder brothers.
At that time, the first prince, seeing the earth shake violently, spoke this verse for the second prince:
"The great earth and the vast oceans are trembling; the sun has lost its brilliance as if it were shrouded by a veil;
and from the sky above, rains of flowers and incense fall—this must surely be my younger brother who has sacrificed his beloved body."
The second prince spoke again in verse:
"That tigress has been giving birth for seven days now; her seven cubs surround her, yet she is destitute of food and drink, her strength is exhausted, and her life is not far from its end.
My younger brother, moved by great compassion, perceives her distress and fears she will be unable to endure it and will instead devour her own offspring."

Fearing that he would surely sacrifice his own life to save the other’s, the two princes were filled with great sorrow and terror; weeping and lamenting, their countenances grew haggard as they went together back to where the tiger was.
There they saw all the garments and robes their younger brother had been wearing hanging upon a bamboo branch.
Bones, hair, and fingernails were scattered in utter disorder, and blood flowed everywhere, defiling the ground. Upon seeing this, he fainted and could not sustain himself;
he threw his body onto the bones and only after a long while regained consciousness. He immediately raised his head and, crying out to heaven, wailed:
"My younger brother was youthful and possessed talent beyond others; he was especially cherished by our parents, yet suddenly he has abandoned his life!"
"To feed the starving tigress, I shall now return to the palace. If my parents should question me, how shall I answer?
It would be better for me to perish here together with her than to bear the thought of abandoning these bones, hair, and claws.
With what heart could I leave them to see my parents, wife, children, kinsmen, friends, and acquaintances? At that time, the two princes wailed in grief and distress, and gradually departed.
At that time, the young prince’s attendants dispersed in all directions, saying to one another, "Where is our lord now?
[Commentary: The two parents were filled with grief and suffering.
At that time, while the queen was asleep, she dreamed that her breasts were cut off, her teeth fell out, and she found three young pigeons, one of which was eaten by a hawk.
Then, at the moment the great earth shook, the queen immediately woke up in alarm;
her heart was filled with great sorrow and fear, and she spoke these verses:
For what reason today has the great earth and the vast waters become so agitated that all living beings are ill at ease?
Why does the sun lack its brilliant radiance as if it were shrouded by a veil? My heart is filled with sorrow and distress, and my eyelids twitch;
surely these auspicious signs I now behold portend some calamity, misfortune, or bitter suffering.
When the queen had finished speaking these verses, a maidservant who was outside heard news of the prince;
her heart was struck with alarm and fear, and she immediately entered the inner quarters to inform the queen, saying:
"Just now, while outside, I heard the attendants searching for the prince, but they do not know his whereabouts. Upon hearing this, the queen was overcome with great distress.
With tears filling his eyes, he went to where the Great King was;
having heard from outsiders that his youngest and most beloved son had been lost, the King fainted again, choked with grief and suffering, and wiping away his tears, he said:
"How is it that today I have lost the one who was so dear and precious to my heart?"
[Commentary] As per the text. These two verses summarize the first two sections of the prose.
[Wenju] The ninety-three lines of verse are divided into three parts: the first two lines generally clarify the past practices; next, they specifically summarize the prose;
and finally, they provide a concluding synthesis.
[Commentary] Second, the explanation of the meaning, in three parts. First, a general clarification of past practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I sacrificed my most cherished body in order to seek Bodhi; even when I was a king..."
And when he was a prince, he constantly renounced what is difficult to renounce in order to seek Bodhi.
[Text] The first part is as the text states.
[Commentary] Second, the separate verses [expound upon] the long prose; this is the first division of the text.

[Textual Analysis] "I recollect my past lives" and below are the individual verses and the prose commentary; the four lines of verse above concern the superior retinue, which has already been described and is not repeated here.
All other sections are versified. From "At that time, the Great Being" and below, two lines of verse describe the skillful means of giving up the body;
the initial vow is not versified. From "Immediately ascending the high mountain" and below, the actual act of renunciation is versified.
The body is moved; from this point, the verse above describes how the two elder brothers descended [from their realm] after abandoning their bodies.
From this point, the verse below describes how the prince’s parents fell into grief and suffering.
[Commentary] Second, explaining the meaning of the five [sections]. First, the initial verse concerns the primary family members of the original text.

*The Sutra of Golden Light*, Chapter Eighteen: "Praise of the Buddha.
[Commentary] The text is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the agent and object of the praise; second, the Great Master’s praise from the perspective of the causal stage.
Commentary on the Title:

[Wenju] This chapter is named after that which can be attained; it is called "The Chapter on Praising the Buddha" because it praises these three groups of bodhisattvas as being capable of praise, and it is a single Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is praised.
Since the subject (the bodhisattvas) and the object (the Buddha) are combined in the title, it is termed "The Chapter on Praising the Buddha."
[Commentary: Those capable of praising these three groups of bodhisattvas are: first, the assembly listed at the beginning of the sutra; second, the person who initiated the event, Śraddhālakṣaṇa;

and third, the tree deity, the virtuous daughter. Although this assembly includes both monastics and laypeople, and their forms are intermingled with those of humans and devas, since they have all resolved upon the Great Mind, they are all termed "bodhisattvas. The one being praised is the World-Honored One, the Buddha.

This refers to the single Buddha who is the primary teacher, Śākyamuni. This differs from the previous "Chapter on Praise" (Kanon), wherein the one who praises was the Golden Dragon of a past age, while those being praised were the Buddhas of the ultimate fruition throughout the three periods of time. However, according to the previous explanation of the title and chapter headings, these fully encompass the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).
While the current text provides a brief indication, if one wishes to clarify its specific characteristics, it should be stated that the title indicates [the four purposes].
1. The meaning of praising the Buddha encompasses both the subject and the object, which is the joy of the world.
2. The arising of good through the one who praises must rely upon dependent origination; among all conditions, none is more supreme than praising the Buddha. 3.

That the Bodhisattva is able to praise is precisely the generation of goodness for sentient beings. 4. That the object of praise serves as the basis for the one who praises confirms that the Bodhisattva’s teaching is without error or falsehood.

This is precisely the antidote that destroys evil. Fourth, the praise by the Tathāgatas of the tree-spirit for her swift exposition of the great essence, great wisdom, and great function of the stage of fruition (phala-bhūmi) constitutes the entry into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The title contains four meanings;

as for the text and its principles, this present commentary preserves both the concise and the detailed, for there is indeed no omission. This is because the title’s praise of the Buddha truly encompasses both the subject and the object of that which is praised—the fruition.
The Buddha conversely praised the one who gives rise to goodness in others and destroys their evil; this is not convenient for both [parties].
However, if that which is praised serves as the means to inspire good karma in others and destroy their evil deeds, how could this be improper? Therefore, we know it is merely a brief summary.

[Wenju] Regarding the sequence: because of the preceding seventeen chapters, there is this present chapter. Why? Because the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) describes the general framework;
the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Wandering in the Immeasurable and Profound Dharmatā" exhausts the source and reaches the ultimate limit; and the "Chapter on the Lifespan" is the culmination.
The fruition is darkly and profoundly harmonized, extensively capable of giving rise to great function. The Chapter on Repentance exhorts Bodhisattvas;

if one wishes to practice and study, one should do so according to the Chapter on Repentance for the eradication of evil, the Chapter on Praise for the generation of goodness, and the Chapter on Emptiness which guides toward the accomplishment of the Four Heavenly Kings down to the vows of Samantabhadra for the circulation [of the teaching].
This explains the merit of the requester. The *Zhenglun* (Orthodox Treatise) reaches the *Shanji* (Collection of Goodness), clarifying the merit of the speaker.
The Virtue of Ghosts and Spirits; The Arrival at Flowing Water; Explaining the Merit of the Listeners; Relinquishing the Body to Clarify the Merit of the Practitioner.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "What are... and below, which explains the sequence of the various chapters: the phrase "the Introductory Chapter narrates the general framework," etc., was previously explained in the sub-commentary (*shu*).
The Sūtra outlines five chapters, yet here we outline only the "essence" (*tǐ*); this refers to the ultimate fruit—the sphere of movement and realization—which is sublime and vast.
The *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is that which is realized at the stage of Buddhahood, and it constitutes the great essence of this present Sūtra.

From the subsequent chapter on the Lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*) down to the merits of the various other chapters, none transcend the discourse on Great Wisdom and Great Function. As for the phrase "exhausting the source," etc.:
In the ultimate source of wondrous enlightenment, the principle has already been exhausted to its furthest limit and phenomena have reached their ultimate extremity;

thus, the wisdom of all modes is merged with illumination, the myriad practices are stilled, and there is only this single nature without any other path—this is what is called the great essence of the Sūtra.
Since the two wisdoms of the stage of fruition and the span of life are already perfected, the profound and vast essence gives rise to the function of long and short durations.
The confession and praise of the Guide of Emptiness (Śūnyatā-nāyaka) do not exceed the great function [of the Dharma], for the merits of the various chapters are consistent with the essential nature;

[Text] Such benefits as these appearing in the world are all due to the power of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*—the great essence, great wisdom, and great function of the Tathāgata.

"To make the beginning good and the end good" means that since the three parts, such as the Prologue (Nidāna), have all yielded benefit, the three Bodhisattvas, bearing the Buddha’s profound kindness upon their shoulders, give rise to praise;

[Commentary] The text of the sub-commentary (*shu*) is clear. The *Sūtra* states:
"From here, proceeding to the land of Suvarṇaprabhāsa," which is intended to magnify the assembly, showing that the bodhisattvas therein all praise the Teacher Śākyamuni.

I have observed some who, failing to understand this intent, claim that the *Sūtra* and the sub-commentary praise that other Buddha; is this not utterly ignorant? Or perhaps it is feared that later students will follow such others.
Regarding the erroneous interpretation of the scriptural text, I shall now briefly cite the commentary (*śāstra*) to demonstrate it.

As for the origin of the "Chapter on Praise" (*Pūjāparivarta*), it is because the three groups of bodhisattvas all benefited from hearing the sūtra above; thus they praised the Buddha and his teaching. How could this exclude other Buddhas?
Furthermore, the commentary states that "one Buddha is the one who praises"; if one were to claim that [the chapter] praises those other Buddhas, then the "one" who praises would be... [omitted].
Why does the Buddha specifically indicate that Śākyamuni has arisen from meditative absorption? Since this is already clear in the commentaries on the sutra, I shall not cite them at length here.
Second, the actual exposition of the verses, which is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, the detailed explanation of each section. First, the analysis of the text.
